# Hacking on Olo

Olo is a Wayland desktop environment in Rust that captures the look and
feel of BeOS R5, with deliberate modern polish. **North star: everything is
pixel-perfect and beautiful, in light, dark and night modes, at 1×, 1.5×
and 2× (and any other scale).** Every deviation from BeOS should be an intentional
improvement, never an accident.

**Wayland only, no X11.** app_server is a Wayland compositor and nothing
else: there is no Xwayland, no X11 window manager and no `DISPLAY`, and
X11-only programs aren't supported. Don't add X11 code, features or
dependencies; programs that can do either (Chrome, GTK, Qt) are started
as Wayland clients (e.g. Chrome's `--ozone-platform=wayland`).

## The responsiveness rule (applies to everything)

**Nothing may ever block the UI.** BeOS was famous for staying responsive
under load; Olo must be at least as good. This is a hard requirement for
every app, the kit, app_server and the shell, and it is checked in review
like pixel alignment is.

1. **The UI thread only draws and reacts.** Anything that can take more than
   a frame (~8 ms), or that *might* (disk, network, subprocesses, D-Bus,
   large folders, image decoding, hashing, searching, sysfs on a slow
   device), runs on a worker thread and reports back with a message: a
   view's own (`cx.work(work, then)`; `cx.messenger()` for its progress),
   or, for the app as a whole, through a `Proxy` (`olo_kit::proxy()`,
   taken in `message_handler`). No `std::fs` on folders of unknown size,
   no blocking IPC round-trips and no `wait()` on a looper (a window's,
   or the app's). Nor the clipboard: the
   program that copied writes it when it gets round to it (or never, if
   it's stuck), so Paste reads it with `cx.paste_item()` (or
   `paste_as(types)` for one form) and puts it in when it comes, and a
   Paste item is enabled by `cx.clipboard_has_text()`, not a read; never
   `read_from_clipboard`.
2. **Show progress and keep it live.** Long work shows what it is doing:
   counts, the current item, a `StatusBar` for work with a known size, and
   a "Searching…"/"Copying…" state otherwise. Results stream in as they
   arrive instead of appearing all at once at the end.
3. **Everything long can be cancelled** (Stop button, Escape, closing the
   window), and cancelling takes effect immediately (workers check an
   `AtomicBool`).
4. **The interface reacts in the same frame** as the input that caused it:
   pressed states, selection, menus and text never wait for work to finish.
   When an action changes state, the view that shows it says so
   (`cx.invalidate()`) in the same message.
5. **Batch updates** from workers (every ~100–150 ms) so streaming results
   never flood the event loop, and look at shared progress counters on a
   timer only while work is running.
6. **app_server never waits on a client.** Clients that stall must not stall
   the desktop. Nor on the GPU driver: a client's new buffer is checked
   (its first import, milliseconds on some GPUs, every frame of a resize)
   on a worker (`dmabuf_check`), and a commit showing it waits for that
   rather than importing it on the loop. The worker checks on a GPU device
   of its own (Mesa locks per device, and finishing a frame takes the
   renderer's) and holds each buffer till the renderer has let it go, so
   the kernel's freeing of old buffers (1–4 ms a window-sized one, done in
   the next bind into a GPU address space) happens on the worker, never in
   the renderer's bind under its lock; a few at a time (`FREE_AT_ONCE`),
   so a check coming in waits behind two, not a dozen (45 ms, a drag's
   round held back with it). A bind of the renderer's own big
   buffers' leftovers (a screenshot's) still lands in its next import:
   keep app_server's own big GPU buffers few and long-lived. Measure with
   `tools/dev/perf-fuzz` (`{"type":"timings"}` names what held the loop;
   a dispatch of clients' requests names the request in it that took
   most of it: a commit by its role, a new popup, a popup's grab, as
   `Timings::within` notes them).
7. **Stay current without polling.** What is on screen reflects the system
   as it changes: follow files and folders with `olo_kit::watch` (inotify:
   one thread per app, asleep until the kernel has an event; a burst
   gathered for 25 ms and read whole at its end; a path followed whether
   it is a file or a folder, exists yet or not, is replaced by a rename or
   swapped for another folder; the items that changed in a folder come
   with it, so a caller passes over what isn't its business; what a
   change costs follows the change, not how much is followed: a folder
   that comes or goes has only the paths at and under it looked at
   again, each folder watched is counted by the paths that want it, and
   a watch grows and shrinks by what changed, `Watch::add` and
   `remove`, `set` looking only at what differs: the palette follows
   ~37,000 folders, and a folder made or removed among 30,000 was
   105 ms of CPU, now 0.2; a path that's there is watched itself, a
   file's writes and its link count dropping as it's renamed over, a
   folder's items, never its folder, and a path that isn't from the
   nearest folder above until it comes: a watch of a folder wakes for
   every change in it, and the runtime folder changes several times a
   second, 2026-11-15), Tracker's
   own `watch.rs` (changed items stat'ed off the UI thread, a full relist
   on queue overflow, a folder renamed or swapped away watched again at
   its path, the nearest folder above watched for it to come back if
   nothing is there yet, and the folders above each one watched for
   being moved or deleted, which takes it from its path without a word
   to its own watch), and the mount table with `POLLPRI` on
   `/proc/self/mountinfo`. No timers that re-read the disk to look for
   changes; keep busy files (frames, caches, logs) out of a folder others
   follow, and a file that's usually not there out of a busy one (it's
   watched for from its folder): `olo_xdg::state_runtime_dir`
   (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-state/`) for state that comes and goes (an
   upgrade offered, a recording, notifications waiting, what's shared,
   AirPlay's plays), Agent Screens' logs in `olo-screens/logs`. And save
   what changes with every request in batches: Token Pool's vault took
   two saves a request, more than one a second with agents at work;
   a request's bookkeeping now waits up to `gateway::USAGE_EVERY` (30
   s), an account's change still a moment, all of it flushed before a
   handover. What follows them: Tracker's windows, desktop, Trash, Get Info
   and Find results; the file panels; StyledEdit's and Viewer's open
   files (another program's change is shown at once unless there are
   unsaved changes; told from our own save by its time and length) and
   Viewer's Previous / Next; the palette's file index and applications;
   Deskbar's applications, notification count, agent screens and
   upgrade; Agent Screens' list; Preferences ▸ Notifications; Logs' Live
   journal (journald touches the file for readers after each write).
   Follow app_server with `Client::into_events_of(kinds)`, asking only
   for the kinds used (`EventKind`): `Windows` is every window whenever
   anything about any changes, an agent's spinning title ten times a
   second, so only what shows windows asks for it (Deskbar); `OwnWindows`
   is the program's own, only when where they are changes (olo-kit's
   `workspaces::follow`), and `Focus` the focused one as the focus moves (the
   supervisor). `Painted` says a display drew something new (headless
   screens; only to whoever names it, as it comes with frames): Agent
   Screens' Live takes a picture then rather than on a timer.
   app_server writes each event out once for everyone.
8. **app_server never deadlocks.** A hang there freezes the whole desktop.
   Smithay's per-surface lock isn't re-entrant: inside a closure given to
   `with_pending_state`, `with_states`, `with_committed_state` or
   `with_cached_state`, call nothing that takes it again
   (`WindowElement::decorated`/`inner_size`/`outer_size`/`content_offset`/
   `title`/`app_id`/`geometry`, sending a configure, mapping the element).
   Work such values out before the call, and never nest these calls,
   not even on two surfaces (a subsurface and its root: Smithay's
   lock-order checker aborts in debug builds, inside a Wayland handler
   that can't unwind, as `new_fractional_scale` did for a Firefox
   window in Focus). `tests/surface_locks.rs` checks the source for
   this, method calls and bare calls (`with_states(…)` inside another)
   alike; `tools/dev/wm-sweep` exercises every window
   operation on several screens and fails on the first hang. Nor does
   anything else in Olo: every lock is `olo_sync`'s (crates/sync:
   `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Condvar`, never `std::sync`'s, Smithay's own
   included), which in debug builds checks the order locks are taken
   in: a lock taken again by the thread holding it, or two taken in
   both orders anywhere (the deadlock waiting to happen, though this run
   never interleaved them), panics at once with both stacks (run with
   `RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE=1`), so tests, test sessions, the fuzzers on
   debug builds (`olo-fuzz sweep --debug`) and `wm-sweep` find it
   before anyone hangs; release builds get std's
   locks as they are. (So a `Condvar` is `olo_sync`'s too: std's can't
   wait on the checker's guard, which only a debug build shows. Run a
   crate's tests in debug, not only `--release`: Tracker's thumbnails
   built in release for two days with a std `Condvar` and wouldn't
   build in debug.) (It found Smithay's keyboard taking its keymap's
   lock and its state's in both orders.) `tools/dev/lockcheck` looks
   without running: clippy's lints for guards held through a `match`
   or past their last use, `lockcheck lockbud`, a static analysis
   of double locks and conflicting orders across functions and crates.
   (A view has no lock to take twice: it has one owner, who alone
   reaches into it, `Child::update`; everyone else sends it a message.)
   Hold a lock for as little as you can: take what you need, let go,
   then call out; never hold one across a call back into app_server or
   anything that might take another lock.
9. **Every frame within 8.3 ms: 120 frames a second, always.** Olo's
   displays run at 120 Hz, and a frame that takes longer than one
   skips. That covers a whole frame (the app's code, the kit's layout
   and paint, and the GPU) on release builds, filling a 16" MacBook Pro's
   screen, at 1×, 1.5× and 2×. Nothing per frame touches the disk or
   waits on anyone (an icon is decoded off the thread; a desktop entry
   looked up once, on a worker); what a frame lays out is what shows,
   not all there is (a list's rows, `uniform_rows`; the editor's
   paragraphs; History's cards). Nor does it set the GPU up: a swapchain
   made is new GPU memory, 10 ms and more for a big one on Apple's GPU,
   so a window resized by hand gets one as big as its screen on the
   press and shows only its part (`wp_viewport`), made to fit 1.5 s
   after it ends; windows and menus share the device's pipelines and
   glyph atlas, so one opens without building them; glyphs a window will
   show are drawn ahead on a thread. A frame runs on a
   fast core at a high clock: a window's threads ask the scheduler for
   it as it starts (its `uclamp.min`, `olo_protocol::performance::
   UI_UTIL_MIN`, 768 of 1024; threads it starts afterwards don't
   inherit it), app_server's main thread too (`CORE_UTIL_MIN`, 1024).
   Otherwise a thread that's mostly idle is put on a slow core at a low
   clock, and the frame after a pause, the one that matters, took three
   or four times as long there (Activity's first frame of its
   processes: 13–17 ms, 3.7–4.6 with it; text shaped 6× faster). It
   costs nothing while the thread sleeps. `OLO_UTIL_MIN=N` (0 for none)
   to compare. Pictures are
   decoded and resampled on workers (`ImageView`, `pictures::thumbnail`,
   `icons`), the frame only drawing them. `tools/dev/bench` checks every
   app (see Testing).

   A display with nothing new rests (`render::IDLE_FRAMES`, both
   backends): after 3 looks in a row that found no damage it looks
   again only when woken, or when `render::rest_for` says: while the
   desktop is in use (two minutes after anything drew) when the
   keep-warm pixel is due, once a second, and then only every 10 s, a
   safety net (it was every 100 ms whatever; a bare headless session
   idle 10 wakeups a second, 0.2% of a core, now 2 while warm and 1
   after, 0.0%; with Deskbar 15 → 5). Nothing is kept warm on a screen
   nobody sits at (an agent's, `OLO_SCREEN`; `render::warm_now`): the
   pixel buys the first frame after a pause 10–30 ms sooner, which
   nobody there sees, and cost a look and a frame a second on every
   agent's screen for two minutes after anything on it drew. At once
   when woken
   (`Backend::wake`, paced a quarter of a frame after its last look):
   a commit wakes the displays its window is on (every display for a
   popup, a layer or the pointer; none for a window showing nowhere),
   and so do input (pointer motion and scrolling only the displays under
   the pointer, before and after: the first time, every motion woke
   every display, up to four looks a frame each with a DRM test commit,
   and the desktop stuttered), a request that changes something (not `ping`,
   `list_windows` and the other questions), the windows or workspaces
   changing (`tick`), a capture asking for a frame, and app_server's
   own overlays (the level indicator, keyboard hints, the lock screen,
   a wallpaper arriving; a display doesn't rest while one goes up a
   strip a frame). Each look gathers every element and compares them
   (on a real display, a DRM test commit too): 120 a second for each of
   two displays kept an idle app_server at a fifth of a core. Something
   new of ours that shows without a wake shows at the next look, up to
   10 s late: wake for it (at debug level, `app_server::headless=debug`
   or `app_server::udev=debug`, the log says "a resting display found
   something new at its look", with where, headless). None was found
   in minutes of a headless shell session used every way (2026-11-07).
   The event loop sleeps until something comes (clients, input, the
   displays' timers, other threads' channels), or `loop_timeout`: a
   `tick` put off by its 8 ms throttle, auto-tiling's half-second look
   while it's in use, else a second as a safety net (it woke every 16
   ms on real displays, every 100 headless, whatever happened). The keep-warm pixel
   alone doesn't wake a resting display. `OLO_REST=off` looks every
   frame, as before, and `{"type":"set_resting","on":false}` at run
   time. Woken looks come no sooner than a frame after the last, aimed at
   the display's next vblank. Nothing rests while something of
   app_server's own moves (`keeps_awake`: a scroll being paced or its
   glide, a window dragged, the overview, Twitcher, hints, the spotlight,
   the level indicator, a glow fading): a frame of it may change nothing
   to see, and a glide paced by looks went on at ten frames a second.
   A menu open isn't one (a popup's pointer grab, unlike a drag's):
   what its program draws wakes the displays, and counting it kept them
   drawing 60 frames a second while a menu sat open (62 wakeups a
   second, 2.5% of a core; 6 now). What each look asks before drawing
   is kept, not looked up again: the wallpaper is found again only when
   its setting, the screen's size, dark mode or HDR changes
   (`wallpaper::Slot::asked`; finding a pack's picture took two `stat`s
   a frame). `{"type":"timings","quiet":true}` answers with `phases`: what the
   loop spent its time on (each look's parts, `tick`'s, commits, input).

   A frame's budget is the frame less what the GPU then takes to draw
   it: app_server shows a commit once its GPU work is done (the dmabuf
   blocker), so a window drawing in 6 ms whose GPU took 2 more missed
   every other frame. app_server tells clients to draw as it starts
   drawing the screen, not once it has (`send_frames` in `pre_repaint`),
   so they have the whole frame.

   What looks the same frame after frame isn't made again: a view that
   didn't change isn't asked what it shows, an element that didn't
   change isn't laid out, and a drawing whose key is the same is kept
   as it was drawn (its display list: the Olo Book, "Drawing"); a row
   of text keeps its glyphs placed
   (`GlyphRun`: Terminal's rows, the editor's), and work a frame can't do
   in its budget is spread over frames (the editor measures paragraphs
   ahead a millisecond a frame; formatted documents lay out what shows
   first, the rest 3 ms a frame after).

## Fast and light (applies to everything)

**Olo is fast and lightweight: a core tenet, held as strictly as
pixel-perfection.** Every CPU cycle spent has to buy something someone
sees or uses; work that changes nothing is a bug. It is checked in
review, and a change isn't done until it has been measured.

What it means in numbers, on release builds:

* **Idle** (nothing on screen changing): app_server and every app at
  about 0% of a core, asleep. app_server's displays rest (about ten
  looks a second each, see rule 9); an app wakes only for input, an
  event it asked for or work it was given. No polling: no timers that
  look for changes (rule 7), no frames when nothing changed (the bench
  checks an idle second draws nothing), no events subscribed to that
  aren't used (`into_events_of`).
* **A little changing** (an agent's spinner, a blinking cursor, a
  clock): the cost follows what changed, not what's on screen: a
  spinner's row, not the terminal. The whole desktop stays in single
  digits of one core with an agent working in a full-screen Terminal
  (Terminal: 1.2 ms a frame whole, 0.1 ms of it for the grid). A widget
  whose look follows the pointer (lit when hovered, pushed when
  pressed) is a `control_canvas`, handed whether it's hovered, pressed
  or focused and drawn again, alone, when that changes (or an element
  styled with `.hover(..)`/`.active(..)`): no handler, no view asked
  what it shows. Never `cx.refresh()` for it, which draws the whole
  window again (that is for what changes all of it: its look, its
  text's rendering): buttons, sidebars, cards, slim scroll bars and
  tab strips once did, and a pointer swept over Notifications'
  history (a screen of 200 cards) took frames of 9 to 46 ms.
* **A lot changing** (scrolling, a live resize, video): every frame
  within 8.3 ms (rule 9), drawn by the GPU, and no more CPU than that
  takes.
* **Over time**: memory, threads and file descriptors don't grow
  (`tools/dev/perf-fuzz` checks). And what a thread needed for a
  moment goes back to the system, which the C library doesn't see to
  by itself: glibc's allocator raises its own thresholds once a block
  of up to 32 MiB has been mapped and freed (blocks up to that size
  are from then on cut from the asking thread's arena, whose free end
  is given back only at twice that size: never, for an arena of 64
  MiB), and `malloc_trim` returns a thread arena's holes but not its
  end. The compositor's wallpaper thread decodes a picture of 35 MiB
  to show 5, and kept 37 MiB so on every screen, an agent's too.
  app_server holds the allocator to the thresholds it starts with
  (`olo_crash::give_memory_back`, in its `main`): 54.1 MiB of its own
  to 22.6 on a test desktop at rest, and its time on the processors
  over a run of the bench no more (3.6 s as the allocator comes; 3.2
  and 3.4 held: three fifths more page faults, which cost less than
  they save). The kit's apps don't, yet: so held, StyledEdit scrolling
  and typing took a fifth more of a processor and Viewer resizing a
  sixth (what a frame frees went back and was faulted in again with
  every frame), and at rest they held what they hold anyway
  (docs/TODO.md, the performance item, d3). To see what a program
  holds and where: `/proc/PID/smaps` (a build tree's programs hold no
  capability, so it reads), where a thread's arena is an anonymous
  mapping that starts on a 64 MiB boundary;
  `GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.mmap_threshold=N:glibc.malloc.trim_threshold=N`
  in front of `tsession start` tries a setting on every program of a
  test desktop without a rebuild, and `OLO_MALLOC_AS_IT_COMES=1`
  leaves the compositor's as it comes. A first run after the GPU's
  shader cache was emptied holds 8 to 16 MiB more in Deskbar and in
  Tracker than a later one (compiled by Mesa, in use: no threshold
  gives it back); `MESA_SHADER_CACHE_DIR=` an empty folder makes every
  run a first, so that like is compared with like.

How to measure (before and after, the same case, numbers in the commit
message):

* `tools/dev/pw-sandbox DIR start|env|stop`: a sound server of its
  own (PipeWire, its PulseAudio server, WirePlumber) in DIR under
  /var/tmp, with no hardware, nothing from the network, no D-Bus and its
  own state: made-up speakers ("speakers") and microphone ("mic", which
  hears what's played into "talk"). `eval "$(tools/dev/pw-sandbox DIR
  env)"` and run anything that plays, records or changes the defaults
  there, never in the person's (the voice service makes itself the
  default input). A tsession app reaches it with
  `PULSE_SERVER=unix:DIR/run/pulse/native`.
* `tools/dev/cost PID [SECONDS]`: a running process's CPU per thread
  (user and kernel), wakeups and preemptions a second, and for a kit
  app each window's frames and their cost by phase (ui, tessellating,
  submitting). Read-only, so it works on a test session's processes
  and, when the person asks, on theirs.
* app_server: `tsession ipc NAME '{"type":"timings"}'` twice, seconds
  apart: each display's looks, their total and slowest. Asking starts a
  4 ms heartbeat for a minute, so measure its CPU before asking or a
  minute after.
* The pointer standing still: app_server says, always, any key,
  click, scroll or pointer motion it handles 100 ms or more after the
  kernel stamped it (libinput's monotonic stamp; a stall's queued events
  said once), with the longest single thing its loop did since the
  event before (`Timings::input`: a request, clients' requests, a
  frame's part, drawing a display, kept when 20 ms or more): "input
  (pointer motion) came 1840 ms late: the loop was held by drawing
  eDP-1 (1832 ms)", or that nothing in the loop was that long (app_server
  wasn't given a processor, or the event came late to it). A touchpad's
  clicks aren't judged: libinput sends a tap's click as the finger
  lifts, stamped when it touched, so every tap longer than 100 ms read
  as late (Ben's log, 2026-11-13: 18 of them, nothing else late). It
  costs no more than the clock reading it already made.
* **What the person feels** (app_server's `felt`): a key or a click is
  followed from the device to the display, one at a time, in three
  parts: *to reach it* (the device's stamp to app_server handing the
  event to the program: the kernel, the input thread, the loop), *until
  it drew* (the program's next commit: its own work, and whatever kept
  it from a processor), *to the display* (app_server's frame with that
  drawing in it, and the wait for the display to show it). One that
  took 100 ms or more in all is said in the log, at most every five
  seconds, with its parts and what the computer was short of: "a key in
  olo.styled-edit took 451 ms to show: 0 ms to reach it, 450 ms until
  it drew, 0 ms to the display; waited for over the last 10 s: memory
  4% (everything 3%), processors 33%" (a program held still for 300 ms
  in a test desktop). So "typing lags" has a figure and names who was
  late, the program or the compositor or neither, the moment it
  happens. The last 128 are in `Request::Timings` (`felt`), whoever
  asks. The middle part is a guess where a program draws for another
  reason first: a drawing more than a second after the press isn't
  taken for its answer, and a modifier pressed alone isn't followed. A
  made-up press (an agent's, `tsession type`) is followed as a
  person's is. It costs a commit 0.4 ns while nothing is followed, and
  a followed press 51 ns (release). To see what a thread is
  doing while it's held, sample `/proc/PID/task/TID/wchan` and `syscall`
  (readable by the same user): 2026-11-12, under a build, app_server's
  main thread waited up to 142 ms in the GPU driver
  (`drm_exec_lock_contended`: waiting for a buffer's lock, held by
  something else using the GPU; by what, and why, "Windows' buffers
  stay in memory": `sudo tools/dev/gpu-holds` names the holder). And
  what holds a thread while the kernel *makes room for memory* is
  `sudo tools/dev/memory-holds [SECONDS] [--paths] [--all]`'s to say:
  each thread held compacting or reclaiming, by name and by what
  asked (graphics memory: the GPU drivers' pool on the thread's
  behalf; huge pages the program asked for itself; anything else, by
  the kernel's path with `--paths`), how often, how long, the longest
  and how many of 4 ms and over; then how often and how long each
  program had a GPU buffer's pages got. It found that the threads
  that draw (the compositor's loop, a kit app's "display" thread,
  Chrome's GPU process) were held up to 25 ms for 2 MB pieces of
  graphics memory none of them asked for (kernel/TUNING.md, "Graphics
  memory in 2 MB pieces"), which `gpu-holds` can't see (it watches
  locks). Read-only; `--self-test` checks its reading without root.
  With
  libinput on its own thread
  (Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ Scheduler ▸ Pointer) the pointer keeps moving meanwhile ("The pointer
  on a thread of its own").
* `tools/dev/bench` (every app's frames against the budget; `--env
  K=V` gives every app a switch, to compare without a rebuild, as
  `--env OLO_EXACT_PATHS=0`),
  `tools/dev/scroll-check` (smoothness and the first frame's latency;
  `--trace` for each frame), `tools/dev/perf-fuzz` (stalls, slow
  answers, growth). Not beside a build: with cargo on every core the
  same gallery that scrolls 0.95 to 1.04 times as far as the fingers,
  no frame skipped, read 0.00 to 2.20 with five skipped. Look at
  `uptime` first, and wait for a build to end. Nor straight after one:
  with memory full of what the build wrote, buffers are slow to come
  by for every program, and the benchmark's live resizes cost ten
  times the processor (DeskCalc 208 ms for a drag that takes 24), which
  no frame's mark shows. A result that surprises is run again, alone,
  before anything is made of it.
* Where a kit app's frame goes: `OLO_FRAME_PHASES=1` prints each
  frame the display thread draws: beginning it (a buffer to draw in),
  putting it together from the drawings kept, drawing and completing
  it (which waits for the previous frame's GPU work), which part of
  the window it was, how many of the window's drawings, sprites and
  quads it has, how many draws it was ("batches": things of a kind at
  one order are one; ten is usual, a hundred means a drawing whose
  orders pile up; `OLO_FRAME_PHASES=batches` lists them in order,
  `quad14 shadow1 mono133 …`, so what breaks a run shows), and how
  long the looper worked on what it shows;
  and the lines it shaped, glyphs it drew and lines whose glyphs it
  looked up afresh (the rest painted from what each line found last
  time, moved).
  A frame much slower than the same work warm may have run on a slow
  core (rule 9: compare `OLO_UTIL_MIN=0`). Where its time goes inside: sample its window's
  looper with `eu-stack -1 -i -p PID` a few hundred times while the bench's
  pointer sweeps it and count the functions on the stacks (perf isn't
  installed).
  A view whose `body` takes a millisecond or more is named with it
  ("body of olo_styled_edit::DocView: 8.297 ms, and 0.121 putting it
  in the tree"): which view is the slow one, when "bodies" is most of
  a flush.
* **Whose time it is: perf, and `tools/dev/memhist`.** `perf` works
  here for a program it starts itself, in user space, with no call
  graphs: `tsession run NAME perf record -e cycles:u -F 5000 -D 7000
  -o FILE -- /whole/path/to/target/release/olo-app` (`-D`: not the
  launch's seven seconds), drive the app, `kill -INT` that perf, then
  `perf report -i FILE --no-children --sort symbol --stdio`. What's
  refused to an unprivileged user: a process already running (`-p`),
  the kernel's side (`cycles` without `:u`), and every kind of call
  graph (fp, dwarf, lbr). `perf stat --no-scale -I 200 -x, -e
  instructions:u,cycles:u` the same way counts what a stretch of work
  cost: sum the intervals of that stretch, and both kinds of core's
  counts (`cpu_core/`, `cpu_atom/`). Always `--no-scale` here: this
  computer's cores are of two kinds, each counting on its own, a
  thread counted only on the kind it's running on, and perf by
  default scales each count up by the time it wasn't counting, so a
  thread that moved between them was counted up to twice over, at
  random (the same build of Logs measured 5.0 M instructions a frame
  or 9.4 M, run to run: the "noise" was this). Unscaled, a window's
  looper counted alone (`perf stat --no-scale -t TID` over the drag)
  gave 5.140, 5.142 and 5.140 M a frame. Counts barely depend on
  what else the machine is doing, where times do; two builds are
  compared by running each three times, in turn, and taking the
  middle. (Instructions don't see copying: a copy of 3 KB is a few
  instructions and hundreds of cycles. Nor memory: halving an agent's
  spinner frame's instructions in Terminal, the glyphs compared and
  copied one by one, moved its cycles within the noise, what was left
  being a screen's glyphs written and read across cores. On this
  machine, busy with other work, cycles and times vary by a sixth from
  run to run even pinned to two cores: say so beside them.) perf ending a program doesn't
  end what it started: end that too, or the app's next start hands
  over to it and leaves.
  `tools/dev/resize-cost NAME LABEL ROUNDS APP_ID CMD…` is that for a
  live resize: the program started under `perf stat` in a test
  session, its window's corner dragged as the benchmark drags it, and
  the instructions and cycles a step of the drag's own seconds
  printed. Give each step time to be drawn (its `STEP_MS`, 45 by
  itself): at the display's own rate a build that skips frames counts
  as the cheaper one. (Its counts scattered by a sixth and more from
  run to run until it counted unscaled: the two kinds of core, above.
  Three rounds in turn and the medians still.) Read what it says in
  absolute terms: a step's work against a frame's budget (8.3 ms at
  120 Hz), not against another toolkit's.
  When the profile says a fifth of a frame is libc's `memmove` and
  `malloc` and can't say whose, `tools/dev/memhist` can: it runs the
  app with a small probe (`memhist.c`, built into /var/tmp) that
  counts every copy and every allocation against the function that
  asked, exactly, and names the biggest (`memhist run NAME app`,
  `count PID` before and after the work, `report PID --per STEPS`).
  What it found the first time it was used (2026-11-12, lists resized
  live), all in the kits and none of it visible in a frame's phases:
  a shaped line was 3 KB, for the 32 decoration runs it kept room
  for in it, and every label painted copied that twice (now one run
  in the line, the rest on the heap: `DecorationRuns`); every `font()`
  allocated its empty list of features (one shared now); every line
  shaped allocated and copied its text to look in the layout cache
  for a layout that was there (`Lent`: looked up by `&str`); a
  paragraph's lines were each allocated twice on their way to a
  shared string; a paragraph of three rows grew its list of breaks
  twice (`WrapBoundaries`: three kept in the layout); and a view
  drawn again grew its drawing's lists from nothing, four, eight,
  sixteen, each a copy (`Scene::reserve_like`: made the size the last
  drawing's were). Together: a third of the copying and a quarter of
  the allocations of a Logs resize, 15 to 21% of the cycles of
  Notifications'. Apps had the same kind (Logs lowercased every word
  of every row, a new string each, to look it up in a short list).
  And what perf's own listing showed once the copying was gone:
  **a quarter of a Tracker frame was in the GPU's driver**, for 108
  draws of 616 things. A kept drawing gave a thing a new order at
  every change of kind, so a list painted row by row (icon, name,
  arrow; icon, name, arrow) was three draws a row, where three in all
  will do.
  `Scene::next_order` puts a thing in the lowest order of its kind
  above everything it's over (each order's reach is kept; over none
  of it, over none of its things), and with what it's over where
  that's drawn after it anyway (a kind is drawn as painted; sprites
  texture by texture, then as painted). Tracker 108 → 5 draws,
  StyledEdit's Markdown 67 → 12, Disk Usage 54 → 35, Logs 14 → 9;
  the same to the pixel in 60 shots, and a test paints 4,800 things
  at random and checks each is drawn after all it's over. With it:
  a frame takes a drawing that shows whole without cutting each of
  its things by what holds it (`Scene::append`); menus' shortcuts
  are looked up, not searched for (`keys::evdev`, 140 times a
  step); the standard folders are looked for at most every two
  seconds (`places::standard`: a file read and six looks at the disk
  each time a Tracker window said its menus).
* GPU time: a kit app run with `OLO_GPU_TIMINGS=1` prints each frame's
  passes as the GPU timed them, its quads (in screens filled: more than
  one is overdraw) and its sprites. A frame shows on time only if its
  CPU *and* GPU work are done before app_server draws the screen, which
  shares the GPU: headless app_server logs `frame skipped: the GPU is
  still drawing the last one` when it couldn't.
* Measure the case the change is for (idle; a spinner; scrolling a big
  folder; a window full screen on a 16" MacBook Pro's 3456×2234 at 2×)
  on release builds, compare with the build before, and check the
  latency too: a saving that makes the first frame after input later
  isn't one. A guess ("should be cheap") isn't a measurement.

How Olo keeps it (do the same):

* **Nothing changed, nothing done.** app_server's displays rest and are
  woken by what can change them (rule 9); a window's looper sleeps
  until it's told something, a view says what it shows only after it
  was invalidated, and the display thread draws a frame only for a
  commit, a scroller that moved or a drawing that asked to be drawn
  again in time; a window that doesn't show gets no frame callbacks.
  Don't invalidate on a timer to look for changes.
* **A change is news only to who shows it.** One thing that keeps
  changing must not keep the rest of the desktop changing with it. On
  the person's desktop (2026-11-21) two agents' tab titles, a spinner
  turning ten times a second in each, kept three displays drawing 59
  frames a second (a quarter of a processor in app_server), Deskbar
  writing two state files and the notification service a third twenty
  times a second, the Inbox widget's provider writing its widget
  twelve times a second, and Calendar's provider reading every event
  and asking the keyring as often (a third of a processor): each
  passed on what it was handed. Three rules came of it:
  what turns is drawn where it is and passed on to nobody (Terminal's
  titles, "Titles" below: the spinner is left out, the tab's own mark
  turns); a program follows the files that are its own business,
  never a folder others write in (the runtime folder, the settings'
  folder, the widgets' folder: `glance::serve`, `olo_kit::watch` a
  file itself); and a file is written again when what it says
  changed, not when it was made again (a widget's `made` stamp had
  every making written). `tools/dev/rest-check` holds a desktop to it:
  a spinner in a tab's title, then what waits in an app changing ten
  times a second, and the desktop must stay at rest but for who shows
  it (frames, wake-ups, files written; it fails on the build from
  before with 49.5 frames a second and Calendar's provider woken 61
  times a second). To find the next one on a running desktop:
  `tools/dev/cost` on what is busy, and which files change (an
  inotify count of the runtime folder's `olo-state`, of
  `olo-glance/DISPLAY` and of the settings' folder says who writes).
* **Animation at the display's pace.** A step of an animation
  (`cx.on_next_frame`, and a drawing that moves every frame,
  `paint_again_within(0.0)`) runs as a frame starts, when the
  compositor's frame callback comes (`RequestFrameOptions::started`):
  once a frame, whether or not the last step changed what shows. A
  commit between frames that changed nothing asks for the next
  callback (`PlatformWindow::want_frame`: a commit of nothing else)
  instead of starting the next step at once; one drawn between frames
  starts it with the next callback. Started at once, a step that
  changed nothing was taken again as fast as the looper and the stage
  could pass it: a scroll arrow held at a list's end, 114% of a core
  and 176,000 wakeups a second; a screen saver whose picture changes
  less often than the display's frames, its whole drawing made four
  times for each frame shown.
* **Work done once is kept**, keyed by what it was made from:
  Terminal's rows (`RowCache`: each row's cells compared with those it
  was drawn from, only changed rows laid out again), a drawing's
  display list (`paint_key`, `key_by`), a list's rows (`row_key`, and
  `uniform_rows(..).row_key_by(..)` for rows of your own, `sized_rows`
  where they're of different heights: a row whose key is the same isn't
  made again when the view says what it shows),
  window tab looks, the wallpaper's strips. Compare the source (cells, a version counter)
  rather than hashing what you'd draw: finding out what changed must
  cost far less than drawing it.
* **Only what shows, only what changed**: virtualised lists, per-row
  and per-item caches, damage. A kit window's frame draws only the
  rectangles that changed, up to six apart (`MOST_APART`: each a
  scissor every draw is made again under, and what app_server is
  told), not their union: a key typed in StyledEdit draws its line and
  the status line, not the window between them. Where a drawing was
  made again in the same place (a text area painted again for a key),
  the stage compares it with the one it replaces thing by thing
  (`Scene::changed_since`) and damages only what differs, where the
  drawing is a sixteenth of the window or more (a smaller one that
  differs is drawn again whole); a frame then takes from each
  drawing only what falls in a rectangle (`stage::assemble`).
  **The same picture is never a frame**: a drawing of any size made
  again the same as the one it replaces (a view whose body ran and
  painted what it had: a canvas with no `paint_key`, a clock between
  two seconds, a chart whose figures didn't move) is no damage, so
  nothing is drawn or presented for it. Every kind of thing is
  compared for that, paths, ring slices, pictures' triangles, shadows
  and videos' frames whole (any of those not as it was: the stage
  can't say where, and draws the drawing again). Until 2026-11-21 a
  drawing with a path or a shadow in it was never compared, nor any
  small one: the kit's charts example with its body run twenty times
  a second, drawing the same, presented 200 frames in ten seconds and
  used 8.6% of a processor; none and 0.9% now (`CHARTS_SAME=1`,
  counted with `OLO_FRAME_PHASES=1`; the comparison itself is 98
  instructions more for a drawing of 1,500 pieces, `scene_bench`).
  Still give a canvas a `paint_key` where you can: that spares the
  painting too. A line of
  glyphs painted again whole from what it kept (`paint_glyph_run`, as
  every plain line of text, the editor's and Terminal's rows are) says
  how it was made (`scene::RunMade`: which finding of its glyphs, where,
  its clip and opacity), so the comparison goes line by line and reads
  the glyphs of only the lines that differ, and a frame passes over the
  lines away from its rectangles whole (each run's reach): a screen of
  text is a thousand and more glyphs, two copies of them read from
  memory at each line printed (an agent's spinner in Terminal: 85 M of
  the display thread's 180 M instructions, before). Such a line's
  glyphs aren't copied into the drawing either: the drawing shares the
  line's own (`Scene::insert_kept_run`, an `Arc` a line, each glyph
  from the line's whole device pixel), and they are put in place, moved,
  clipped and faded, only where a frame draws them or a comparison
  reads them (the spinner: the looper's 43 M instructions of writing a
  screen's glyphs, 157 KB an update, gone). Nor does a frame copy a
  drawing's glyphs: once a view's drawing is made, its glyphs are
  shared (`Scene::seal`, the list moved behind an `Arc`), the frame
  notes each run of them with where it goes (moved, cut by what holds
  the drawing, at its order: `scene::Put`), and the renderer puts each
  glyph in place as it copies it into the GPU's buffer
  (`scene::Glyphs::pieces`; a drawing that didn't move and shows whole
  is copied as it is, a list's runs one after another as one). A glyph
  cut away whole from a run that partly shows goes to the GPU and
  shows nothing. Check a change to
  any of it with `tools/dev/damage-check` (each app typed in, scrolled
  and selected in, drawn by its damage and drawn whole, the last
  pictures compared at 1×, 1.5× and 2×; look at the pairs it keeps). What a
  thing can touch is its reach, not its bounds (`Shadow::reach`: a
  blur three radii past them), so a shadow falling past what casts it
  is drawn again with what it falls on. `OLO_DAMAGE=0` draws every
  frame whole, the reference to compare shots against.
* **Once a frame, at the last moment** (olo-kit), for a view fed faster
  than frames are shown: a shell printing, a meter on a stream. A
  window's looper lays out and paints what changed as soon as its queue
  runs dry, and its stage draws the latest commit when the compositor
  asks for the next frame; a view invalidated a hundred times between
  two frames was laid out and painted a hundred times for one drawn
  (Terminal in a flood: 15 ms a frame, 0.2 of it seen).
  `Cx::invalidate_at_frame()` in place of `invalidate()` keeps such a
  view for the frame: laid out at once while no frame waits to be shown
  (one change alone is as quick as ever), else when the compositor asks
  for the next (`stage::FramePace`: the stage, with nothing of its own
  to draw, asks the looper, `WindowEvent::FrameDue`, and draws its
  answer at once: 0.45 ms after it was asked, typically, of the 5 to
  10 ms app_server leaves a client). What's kept also goes with
  anything else the looper lays out meanwhile and with each step of an
  animation, and every other frame when the stage has frames of its own
  to draw (a glide), so it is never left behind; a window that isn't
  shown is asked for no frame, and its kept views wait until it is (a
  second at most, if anything else stirs it). `OLO_FRAME_PHASES=1`
  prints `frame due: drawn N ms after the looper was asked`. Everything
  else stays `invalidate()`: what changes at the person's pace gains
  nothing from waiting.
* **A frame waits for the answer to input that's on its way**
  (olo-kit, `stage::INPUT_HOLD`). The compositor sends input and then
  calls for a frame, at once; what a looper makes of the input (a
  wheel's step in a view that scrolls itself, a key, the pointer over
  something that lights) comes back as a commit half a millisecond
  later. With nothing else to draw the call draws nothing and the
  commit is drawn as it comes, in time for the display's next frame.
  With something else to draw (colours or layout a worker brought, a
  caret), the call drew that, and the commit, a moment too late, waited
  for the next call: one frame in which nothing moved, and every step
  after it shown a frame late (the benchmark: "frames moved 0.00×" in
  StyledEdit's code and Markdown). So what a call would draw waits for
  the answer and is drawn with it, once; four milliseconds at most, and
  a looper that makes nothing to show of what it took says so at once
  (`FramePace::holding`, `Stage::input_answered`), only when a frame
  waits. (Drawing the answer at once as well, a second frame in the
  same call, was tried first: no stall, but forty frames more in a drag
  through a document still being laid out.) Three things keep the wait
  what it says. Its four milliseconds run from the first input not yet
  answered: more input to a looper that's taking its time doesn't
  restart them. A timer draws what was kept back when they're over
  (`PlatformWindow::frame_after`), since nothing else may ask for a
  frame by then; it's taken away when the frame is drawn first, as
  nearly all are, so it wakes nothing. And nothing made inside a frame
  call may be input that starts a wait: a wheel's notches are eased in
  by the frame calls themselves (`wheel_step`), one step a display
  frame, and never a step in the frame the looper's answer asks for.
  When each of those took a sliver of the ease too, the sliver kept the
  frame back for its own answer, whose frame took another sliver: every
  notch in the editor and Terminal showed as one jump when the ease ran
  out, 180 ms late, with a core busy throughout (the benchmark: "wheel:
  a frame every 246 ms"; scroll-check's wheel is what finds it, so run
  all three of drag, flick and wheel after touching any of this).
  And the answer is the commit made after the looper took the input,
  not the next commit to arrive: input is numbered as it's sent
  (`WindowEvent::Input`'s number; motion gathered on its way carries
  its last), the looper keeps the last number it took, and each commit
  (`Commit::answered`) and each "nothing came of it" says how far it
  had got. While a document is still being laid out or coloured, a
  worker's commit lands between a scroll step and its answer; taken for
  the answer, it was drawn alone and the step showed a frame late
  (drags through a 20,000-line document just after a change of scale:
  a frame that didn't move in five drags of eight, the steps spread
  0.22 to 0.26 of the fingers' speed about it; numbered, none in 12
  of 12, the spread under 0.005, steps 0.97 to 1.02 of the fingers').
* **What isn't to be seen isn't drawn.** The editor draws on whole
  device pixels, so a scroll step that leaves the text on the same ones
  (the end of a glide, a fraction of a pixel a frame) is kept, not
  drawn: some twenty-five frames at the end of every flick. A wheel
  turned over what neither scrolls nor takes it wakes no looper
  (`Stage::input`: only its end is passed on, for what took the steps
  before the pointer left it). Nor does the pointer moving where no
  move means anything: the display thread sends a window's looper a
  move with no button held only across the edge of something a hover
  changes, a cursor's area, a cut text, an edge a drawing noted
  (`Painter::note_pointer_edge`), or over what follows the pointer
  (`on_mouse_move`, `hears_motion`; with ⌘ held only,
  `moves_matter_with_command`; a drag's alone,
  `moves_matter_while_pressed`; only across the edges its drawing
  notes, `moves_matter_at_edges`); every move while a button is held
  (`on_drag_move`, a drag's), and the first after any other input.
  (The pointer swept over Tracker's desktop, 1,200 moves: 84 → 36 ms
  of CPU, its looper never woken where it was woken for each.)
  Each commit says where (`Commit::motion`, regions in the layers'
  own coordinates as the wheel's are, made with the list of what
  shows); the stage keeps where the pointer went
  (`stage::PointerPlace`), which the looper reads when something moves
  under a still pointer (`hover_again`) and for `mouse_position`. A move
  within 1.5 device pixels of an edge goes too: the stage places a
  scrolled layer by whole pixels, the looper's hit test by the exact
  offset. `on_window_mouse_move` asks for every move (the looper woken
  for each): only Screenshot's region picker does. What changes only
  over parts of itself says where they are as it draws, not by
  hearing every move over it: the ruler gives each marker a cursor's
  area (`Painter::set_cursor_style`), so the pointer over its scale
  wakes nothing; lists drawn in one canvas (search's suggestions, the
  palette's results, the emoji picker's cells, Telegram's chats,
  Notifications' rows, cards and headings with their ×s, Dismiss and
  Mark All Read, its banners' cards, Disk Usage's Collector chips' ×s)
  note each row and hear only the moves across them
  (`moves_matter_at_edges`); what only changes the pointer's shape
  gives it as cursor areas (a banner's links, Telegram's links, names,
  quotes, media and reactions, `bubble::hit_rects`; the Viewer's crop
  frame, `CropFrame::note_cursors`, a drag's shape all over while it's
  dragged), and hears drags alone (`moves_matter_while_pressed`: the
  PDF view, whose shapes were areas already). A drawing whose cursor
  areas changed under a still pointer has the pointer's shape and what
  it's over worked out again once it's drawn (`hover_stale`, set by
  `Tree::record`; what that changes is drawn at the next frame), as no
  move may come to do it. `OLO_EVERY_MOVE=1` sends every move, to
  compare.
* **Ask for less**: events by kind (`EventKind`: `OwnWindows`, not every
  window's title), files by inotify, an event written out once for all.
  Something that wakes every app costs every app: an agent's spinning
  title woke every app's two kit threads ten times a second.
* **Per frame, no waste**: no new strings or vectors for what didn't
  change, nothing quadratic (a check of a whole run per character cost
  Terminal 1 ms a frame), no locks held across calls (Deskbar's status
  deadlocked holding one), no sleeping loops. A body runs whenever its
  view changes, so what it says that didn't change must cost nothing:
  menus' words are shared (`SharedString`: a fixed one never copied,
  `keys::known`'s labels an `Arc`), and items with numbers in them are
  written out, not formatted (StyledEdit made 900 of its 1,510
  allocations a scroll frame saying its menus, its font list included).
  And what changed alone is drawn alone: a view that scrolls itself
  draws its drawing again in the handler (`repaint_node`), not its
  host's whole body (the editor's `scroll_alone`).
* **The GPU draws, the CPU decides.** Upload once and keep textures;
  meshes made once and handed over as they are.
* **Four malloc arenas a kit app** (`olo_kit::run`, `few_arenas`):
  glibc gives each thread that allocates an arena of its own, and what
  a thread frees stays in it; a kit app has a looper for each window,
  the display's thread and its workers (18 to 29 threads), and rested 7
  to 17 MB bigger for it (Terminal with three tabs 153 → 136 MB,
  StyledEdit 103 → 96, Tracker 99 → 91; frames the same). Two saved no
  more and frames ran slower. `MALLOC_ARENA_MAX=N` in the environment
  overrides it, to measure another number without a build; compare
  `RssAnon` in /proc/PID/status (the rest is the program's file).

## Crash reports (crates/crash, applies to every program)

**What a day's logs showed** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "look through the olo
logs for other warnings/errors and fix anything that should be fixed";
`olo-logs --print --since 1d --level warning`, grouped by program and
message). Each was a fault, not a line to hide:
- *Notifications: "keeping …/history.json: No such file"*, 16 times, on
  the minute. An agent screen is the person's account and home, so
  every screen's notification centre kept its history in the person's
  file, each saving over the others'. A program that serves a session
  keeps its files in `olo_xdg::session_state_dir()` (a screen's own
  folder, `state_dir()/screens/NAME`, on a screen), and the kit's saver
  writes through a sibling of the writer's own (`.NAME.saving.PID.N`:
  two programs keeping one file wrote through the same sibling, each
  over the other's bytes; `store::tests::two_writers_of_one_file_never_mix`).
- *A widget's provider left running* (`olo-notifications --glance`,
  three on agent screens whose Deskbar had gone): Deskbar's providers
  end with it (`PR_SET_PDEATHSIG` as they're started, `glances.rs`).
- *A session with no language*: app_server's "failed to get system
  locale" was the whole session having no `LANG` (a display manager
  gives it; Olo's login didn't): Terminal's shells and everything
  started there ran in the "C" locale. olo-session sets what's missing
  from `/etc/locale.conf` and `~/.config/locale.conf`
  (`olo_xdg::locale`, exported to what's started on demand), every Olo
  program takes it as it re-executes (`olo_xdg::upgrade_env`), and
  whatever Olo starts for the person is given it where the starter has
  none itself (`olo_xdg::locale::give`, in `spawn_detached` and
  `open::spawn`; Terminal's shells, `pty.rs`): a running program can't
  be given a language, so it hands it to what it starts. Olo Doctor
  (`language`, "Set the Language") judges what a program started now
  would get: from Deskbar (its own environment, or what it gives; a
  Deskbar from before an upgrade, replaced on disk, gives nothing, and
  that's said with nothing to press), and on demand (systemd's user
  manager's environment, `TempFiles::session_env`). Each fix changes
  one of those, so it's gone once fixed. (It first judged by Deskbar's
  own `/proc/PID/environ`, which is what a program was started with
  and never changes: the fix said "Fixed." and the finding stayed.
  **A check's fix must change what the check looks at.**)
- *A program that didn't reconnect*: a kit app whose event loop ends in
  an error has lost its connection for certain
  (`compositor_lost_check(…, ended)`). Asked of the socket instead, an
  error on the display object (no protocol error for libwayland to
  show) with the compositor's hanging up a moment late read as "not
  lost", and with the loop over nothing asked again: Tracker sat so a
  quarter of an hour. And a connection going is said once, as a
  warning: every upgrade wrote two errors for every program.
- *"the window's new surface is Rgba8Unorm, its pipelines Bgra8Unorm"*:
  a surface made again in another format gets pipelines made for it
  (`remake_surface`), as a change of colour space does.
- *"surface missing from known popups"*, 60 errors a day: harmless (a
  destroyed popup's surface committed once more), and hidden by
  app_server by the line number it was logged at, until the number
  changed. Said at `debug` where it's said, in Olo's Smithay; the
  filter is gone. A message is never hidden by where it is in a file.
- *"Received an event for non-existent source"* (calloop's, 255 a
  day): a resting display's timer for its next look (`SurfaceData::
  retest`) was removed by `wake`, or by a look made sooner, in the very
  round of the loop in which it had come due: calloop gathers a
  round's ready descriptors and due timers together, a callback
  earlier in the round woke the display, and the timer's slot was
  empty when its turn came. Harmless, and Olo's doing: a look not yet
  due is removed as before; one already due is disarmed and its slot
  freed once the round is over (`cancel_look`). Found by the
  `olo-debug-help` helper (the cancelled token matched to the warning's,
  122 µs apart; three mock displays with timers due in a round: one to
  three warnings before, none after).
- Left, and why: "slow frame"
  (the frame timer's own notes); "Failed to destroy old mode property
  blob" and "Unable to become drm master" (headless and mode changes;
  no effect seen); one pointer motion 266 ms late behind
  `set_output_brightness` a day before (not seen since: its writes are
  on a worker).

**A second day's logs** (2026-11-20, the same command a day and a half
after the first pass's fixes; 24,933 lines, 9,791 of them a container
of the person's, not Olo's). What the first pass fixed stayed fixed
(no "non-existent source" from app_server, no notification history
errors, no "surface missing from known popups"). What this one found:
- *Three warnings from every program at every reload* ("the event loop
  ended: …BrokenPipe", "the compositor's connection is gone", "the
  compositor is gone: re-executing to reconnect"): sixty lines an
  upgrade. The first two are the third said earlier: a loop that ends
  on its connection hanging up says so at `debug` (`loop_hung_up`: the
  broken pipe inside the loop's wrapped error; any other error is still
  a warning), and the connection's going is a warning only where nobody
  is told who would say what's done about it. One line a program.
- *"frame called without prior events"* (Smithay's touch, 36 in one
  minute of a finger on the touch screen): a finger that is the pointer
  (on a tab, on Olo's own apps) hands the seat's touch nothing, and
  every report of the screen still ended its frame. The frame is ended
  only when something of the report was the seat's (`touch_frame`,
  `touch_sent`), on the made-up path too.
- *Preferences: "language: locale.conf: No such file or directory"*, 11
  times. Two writers at once through one sibling file
  (`locale.conf.new`), the second finding it moved away: each write
  goes through a sibling of its own. And why two at once: the panel's
  `reset`, which is also how every panel asks at each drawing whether
  Defaults and Revert would change anything, told other programs the
  language as a side effect, the default's and then the opened one's,
  each on a thread: **looking at Language & Region could leave
  locale.conf saying English**. `reset` only resets; the telling is
  where the buttons are pressed (`reset_pressed`), and the latest
  language asked for is the one written. **A function that's used to
  ask "would this change anything" can't do anything.**
- *Deskbar: "a window couldn't be opened: display DP-N isn't known to
  this connection yet"* (an error, at each display plugged in):
  app_server lists a display a moment before Deskbar's own connection
  hears of it, and the bar asked for then is refused, as it should be.
  Deskbar asks only for displays its connection knows; the connection
  saying its displays changed brings it there again.
- *Tracker: "Received an event for non-existence source"* (calloop's,
  once): the first pass's fault again, in the kit's own loop. A
  window's timer for a frame kept back (`frame_after`) was removed
  when a frame was drawn, in the round of the loop in which it had
  already come due. One due is disarmed and its slot freed after the
  round (`cancel_timer`, as app_server's `cancel_look`); a test hears
  calloop's warning with the plain removal and none with this.
- *Phone: "menu keys not in olo_protocol::app_keys"* (a dev build's
  note; a release build says nothing, and the keys were simply not in
  Preferences nor on the shortcuts sheet, and stayed ⌘ whatever the
  profile). Phone's are listed, and so that it's seen without a log:
  the window review reports any menu item with keys the profile
  doesn't list (`app_menu::review`, kind `menus`).
- *Viewer: "ignoring stss atom"* and the like from the MP4 reader behind
  a video's sound, at every video: what it has no use for, said at
  `error` only now (`symphonia_format_isomp4=error`, beside usvg's).
- *"input (pointer motion) came 1692 ms late: the loop was held by look
  (whole)"*, thirteen such in fifty minutes of one afternoon, with
  frames that took 100 to 600 ms "finishing" (the GPU's side), and
  none in the day and a half around it. The log couldn't say what the
  computer was doing: now each such line ends with what was waited for
  over the last ten seconds, as the kernel counts it (`/proc/pressure`:
  memory, disks, processors; `timings::pressure`), so the next one
  says whether it was Olo or the computer. (Looked for and ruled out:
  NVIDIA's GPU waking, a hundred and fifty times that day in the
  kernel's log, none of them at those moments, and none of them Olo's:
  a watcher on its `runtime_status` showed another program of the
  person's opening it. Olo's own stay away from it, as "The discrete
  GPU stays asleep" has it.)
- Left, and why: the surface that "can't be reconfigured" when the
  compositor has gone (a line a window at each reload: true, and
  bounded); Telegram's network library on a dropped connection (it
  reconnects); PipeWire's AirPlay module's notes and a container's
  9,791 errors (not Olo's); PAM's and crashed test programs' lines
  (tests'). A day's log is also every test session's: their programs
  write to the journal as the person's do.

**Open files** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "why is there a 1024 soft limit? the
file limits should be huuuuge … make sure all our apps will raise it as
needed not just app_server"). A program starts with a login's soft
limit on open files, 1,024 (kept low by systemd for programs that
still use `select`), and may raise itself to the hard one (524,288 on
Fedora; "unlimited" isn't given for files). Every Olo program does, as
the first thing it does: `olo_crash::install()` calls
`olo_crash::raise_open_files()` (the same test that holds every
`main` to `install` holds it to this), and what a program starts
inherits it: olo-session first, so its whole session. Why it matters
most to app_server: every client's connection, every window's buffer
(a dmabuf each) and every sync object is a file to it. On three
displays it had 696 open of its 1,024 (295 dmabufs, 166 sync objects,
131 sockets); Deskbar's folding made every tiled window draw anew,
each new swapchain bringing more, and past the limit the kernel drops
the descriptors a program sends: app_server logged "file descriptor
expected … import_timeline" and the program was gone (Terminal and
Tracker, the desktop's icons with it). Reproduced in a test session
(`prlimit --pid APP_SERVER --nofile=N:524288`, N a few over what it
has, then more apps opened). With none left at all, three things
happened and two are mended: a listening socket with a connection it
couldn't take woke the loop for ever (171,619 "accept failed" in a
second and a half; `olo_system::fds::Reserve` now takes the connection
with a descriptor held back and closes it: app_server's three
listeners, its IPC socket and the proxy's), and the GPU driver aborts
when it can't make a descriptor (`DRM_IOCTL_SYNCOBJ_HANDLE_TO_FD ioctl
failed (24)`, SIGABRT), which is the driver's and why the limit is to
be never reached. A session started from a shell held to 1,024 now has
olo-session, the proxy, app_server and what they start at 524,288
(app_server's log: "the most files this may keep open"). Olo Doctor
(`open_files`, finding `open-files`) finds Olo's programs still held
under 65,536 (`olo_crash::OPEN_FILES_ENOUGH`: started by a build from
before, or on a system whose hard limit is low; a Problem when the
window server is half way to its limit), and "Raise the Limit" raises
the running ones in place (`Step::LetOloOpenFiles`, `prlimit` on each
`olo-…` of the account, no password), writing the login's and
systemd's limits first where the hard limit itself is low
(`/etc/security/limits.d/80-olo-open-files.conf`,
`/etc/systemd/{system,user}.conf.d/80-olo-open-files.conf`, with one).

**Following files, the same way.** Every program that follows files as
they change holds one of the account's inotify instances (an Olo
program one for all its watches: `olo_kit::watch` makes it with the
first), and the kernel allows an account 128
(`fs.inotify.max_user_instances`; Fedora leaves it so). Each agent
screen runs its own Deskbar, Tracker, Notifications, Weather and
portal, and each Chrome takes two: with ten screens open 125 were
taken (2026-11-18), and a program starting then got none. Olo Doctor
(`inotify`, finding `inotify-instances`; a Problem from three quarters
taken) keeps 8,192 in `/etc/sysctl.d/90-olo-inotify.conf` and sets it
at once (`Step::WriteSysfs`); an instance costs a little kernel memory,
and only while it's used. And a refusal isn't kept: `watch` tries again
at the next call (it kept the refusal for the program's life, so a
program started then never followed a file), and says in the log what
was refused and that Doctor raises the limit
(`crates/kit-base/tests/watch_refused.rs` makes the kernel refuse by
holding the test's own open files down; it failed before).

**Every Olo program leaves what's needed to look into its crash.**
`olo_crash::install()` is the first thing each program's `main` does
(`olo_kit::run` does it again, harmlessly; `crates/crash/tests/
every_program.rs` fails for a `main` in apps/ or crates/ that doesn't
start with it). It has nothing but libc, so app_server, the session,
brush and the root Wi-Fi healer carry it as lightly as the kit's apps.

- **A report**, one JSON file a crash, in `olo_crash::dir()`
  (`~/.local/state/olo/crashes/PROGRAM-PID-MILLIS.json`; a service
  with no home, as root, /var/lib/olo/crashes), written beside as
  `.NAME` and renamed, so a reader never sees half of one; the newest
  ten of each program kept, four at most from one process. Every
  report has `program`, `pid`, `exe`, `build` (the executable's time),
  `started_ms`, `at_ms`, `kind` and `thread`, and:
  - a panic (any thread's, the program going on or not: a worker's
    panic is reported though the window stays): `message`, `place`
    (file:line:column) and `backtrace` (release builds keep line
    tables, so it names files and lines), from a panic hook that then
    calls std's (its message on stderr as ever). Not one: output whose
    reader stopped reading (`olo-screen --help | head`). Rust ignores
    SIGPIPE, so the write fails and `println!` panics; the hook ends
    such a program as a shell expects of one cut off (141, SIGPIPE's
    128 + 13), with no report (`output_cut_off`; on 2026-11-15 an
    agent's `olo-screen --help | head` read as Agent Screens crashing);
  - a fatal signal (SIGSEGV, SIGBUS, SIGILL, SIGFPE, SIGABRT): `signal`,
    `code`, and the fault's `address` or, for one sent (kill), `sent_by`;
    `core` names `coredumpctl info PID`. The handler is
    async-signal-safe (system calls into buffers on its stack, the
    folders made one by one with mkdir, nothing allocated or locked),
    kept out of line so the handler's own frame is small (a signal can
    come on what's left of a thread's alternate stack: std's
    stack-overflow abort does). Then it hands the signal on: a fault
    to what had it before (std's overflow check, which still prints
    "has overflowed its stack", then the default action, so the core is
    made as it would have been), a sent one to the default action, so
    the program ends as its sender meant (std alone lets a program go
    on after a sent SIGSEGV). An abort after a panic is that panic's
    crash: not reported twice.
- **stderr to the journal when it goes nowhere.** A program whose
  stderr is /dev/null (or closed), as everything started by Tracker,
  Deskbar or another app is (`olo_xdg::open::spawn_app`), connects it
  to the journal's stream socket itself (`/run/systemd/journal/stdout`,
  the stream protocol's header naming it for the program), non-blocking
  so a journal that can't keep up loses a line rather than holding the
  program up. Before, such a program's log and its panic's message went
  nowhere (Viewer's crash in TODO left no trace). A crash's own line
  goes there marked an error (`<3>`), "PROGRAM: SIGSEGV; the report is
  PATH". The kit's log writes colour codes only to a terminal. Not a
  program a test started (cargo's environment, `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`,
  which a test's children have; `OLO_CRASH_JOURNAL` names a socket of
  the test's own): its lines in the person's journal read as the real
  program's (a phone test's service, its stderr discarded, said "can't
  register with BlueZ" and named the stand-in's phone among the real
  service's lines, 2026-11-17). Give what a test starts a log file of
  its own instead (the phone tests' `phoned.log`).
- **Told**: the session's `olo-doctor --watch` follows the folder by
  inotify and tells of each new report once ("Viewer crashed", what and
  in which thread, the program's own icon; more than three at once in
  one note); its click opens Log Viewer on the program's lines from
  just before (`olo-logs --query "program:P since:Nm"`).
  `olo-doctor --crashes [--json]` lists them for a terminal or an
  agent.

Cost: nothing while the program runs (no thread, timer or check);
installing at start measured at 18 µs median (35 µs when it also
connects stderr to the journal; `cargo test -p olo-crash --test crashes
install_cost -- --ignored`), and 33 KB of code in a binary.
`crates/crash/tests/crashes.rs` crashes children for real (a panic, a
worker's panic, a segfault, a sent SIGSEGV, an abort, a stack
overflow; no core, as `PR_SET_DUMPABLE` 0) and checks each report and
how the program ended, and the journal stream against a stand-in
socket.

## The network changing (crates/net, applies to every program that uses it)

A cable pulled, Wi-Fi joined or left, a VPN coming up: anything that
talks over the network goes on, on the new one, without hanging or
failing (Ben, 2026-11-09). A connection lives on the network it was made
on (its address is that network's): when that address goes, nothing tells
whoever is reading or writing it, who waits for TCP to give up, a quarter
of an hour. `olo-net` follows the kernel's own news of links, addresses
and routes (rtnetlink, a thread asleep until there is some: nothing
polls), and on each change, in this order: `generation()` moves on and
`online()` says whether there's a way out to the internet (the kernel
asked which way a packet would go); this process's TCP connections whose
address went are cut (`shutdown`, never `close`: whoever waits on one is
told at once, and makes another); those whose way out changed but whose
address is still there are watched closely (keepalive and
`TCP_USER_TIMEOUT`: the kernel ends one whose peer stops answering for
15 s, and leaves it be while it answers); then waiters are woken and the
`on_change` hooks run. Loopback connections, listeners and other
processes' sockets are never touched. So in a program that talks over the
network:

- keep an HTTP client for the network it was made on, `PerNetwork::new(||
  make it)` and `.get()` for each request: after a change the next
  request makes connections on the new network, not on idle ones left
  from the old (what's under way keeps its own);
- a request that fails because the network changed under it, or there
  was none, is tried again, at once on the new one or once one comes,
  without counting against its tries: `across_changes(patience, ||
  request)`, or by hand with `generation()` taken before it (DiskBackup's
  Drive, the Token Pool's gateway, both before anything of the answer is
  passed on);
- a download goes on where it broke off (`http::Download`: `Range` from
  where it got to, `If-Range` so it's the same file, the whole file again
  passed over to there from a server that takes no ranges), Chrome's,
  the Installer's and Doctor's;
- a wait for a network is `wait_online(until, stop)`, woken by a change
  or `nudge()` (call it after asking a worker to stop); say so while it
  waits (`waiting()`: DiskBackup's "Waiting for the network");
- a long-lived connection that only hears what the other end pushes
  (Telegram's updates) is asked again on a change (`on_change`):
  Telegram's stream is handed its own "too many to send" (`updatesTooLong`)
  and catches up at once, on a new connection.

`pretend_change(online, port)` does what a change does, for tests of what
uses it (DiskBackup's `tests/network.rs`, the Token Pool's
`a_request_goes_on_across_a_network_change`); `tests/netns.rs` makes real
changes in a network of the test's own (a user and network namespace, no
privileges: addresses and routes on its loopback taken away and given
back), and a connection on an address that went is cut 150 ms after (the
burst a change comes in, waited out), a wait for the network ending as
long after a way out comes back.

## Layout

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `crates/app_server` | The compositor (Smithay, forked from Anvil). Draws the BeOS window decorator (yellow tabs), manages windows/workspaces, serves IPC. |
| `crates/session` | `olo-session`: starts and supervises app_server, Deskbar and the desktop; in-place reload and upgrade (see below). |
| `crates/protocol` | JSON-lines IPC between app_server and our apps (`Client`, `Request`, `Reply`, `Event`, `Settings`). |
| `crates/theme` | `Palette` (light/dark), BeOS tint helpers, decorator metrics, font lists. |
| `crates/app` | `olo-app`, the Application Kit: loopers (a thread and its queue, taken one message at a time, asleep when there's none), handlers and messengers with typed messages, timers, `ask` and its `Answer`, `Latest` (what would flood a queue, gathered) and the pool that work longer than a frame runs on. No drawing. |
| `crates/interface` | `olo-interface`, the Interface Kit: a window on a looper of its own; views (`View`: its state, the messages it takes, the `body` that says what it shows) and the elements they're made of, kept and laid out between frames (taffy); what each draws kept as a display list (`Painter`, `canvas`); the display thread (`Stage`), which draws the frames, scrolls and springs without the looper; text, the Wayland client and the GPU renderer, all Olo's own. |
| `crates/interface-macros` | `olo-interface-macros`: the Interface Kit's macros, used by it alone: the `Styled` helpers (`.flex()`, `.p_2()`, `.border_1()`…, generated into `styled.rs`) and `#[derive(Refineable)]` (a style's refinement: the same fields, each optional, laid over a base; the trait is `olo_interface::Refineable`). |
| `crates/kit` | `olo-kit`: the Interface Kit (re-exported whole) with Olo's look, the BeOS widgets, menus and the menu bar, alerts, panels, the editor, icons, the agent tree and socket, the layout review and lint, upgrades. **All apps are built on it** ("The kit" below; the Olo Book, `docs/OLO-BOOK.md`). |
| `crates/kit-base` | `olo-kit-base`: what the kit has that doesn't draw, re-exported by olo-kit under the same names: `instance` (one process per app), `settings`, `notify`, `files`, `places`, `watch`, `tracker`, `metrics` (the spacing system), `Proxy`, `search` (the query language, facets and suggestions), `masonry` (cards in columns), and `store` (an app's own files, written whole), `commands`, the socket agents and the command palette read apps through (its protocol, server and client), with `review`'s findings and `layout_review`'s checks, `list` (a list's selection and type-select), `spell` and `keys` (the keyboard profile's keys). Nothing in it draws. |
| `crates/yuv` | `olo-yuv`: a video's picture as its decoder made it (`YuvFrame`: Y'CbCr 4:2:0 planes, or `YuvMemory`, the decoder's own memory) and the matrix that makes RGB of it. olo-interface draws it (`Painter::paint_yuv`) and re-exports it; what decodes (olo-images, olo-video, olo-vaapi) makes it. |
| `crates/xdg` | `olo-xdg`: freedesktop plumbing shared by app_server and the kit: data dirs, `.desktop` entries, icon lookup/decoding (`load_icon`, in the current theme: `themes`; Olo's icons are drawings rendered for the size and kept, `svg`, a theme's colours over the classic set's, `svg::recolour`: docs/ICONS.md), our own apps (`apps::our_app`), MIME types (`mime::for_path`), opening files and URLs with the right app (`open::open`, `open::handler_cached`: never `xdg-open`; the person's own choice first (`open::set_default`, kept in `~/.config/olo/default-apps.list` in mimeapps.list's form and copied into `olo-mimeapps.list` for other programs; `handler_cached` notices it changed, in any process), then Olo's apps, except that links and web pages go to the browser chosen in mimeapps.list, else `olo-chrome`; Open With's few apps for a kind, `open::handlers_for`: as the person set them (`set_offered`, Preferences ▸ Default Apps ▸ Open With), else the one it opens in, Olo's own for it, then those whose entries claim it or a broader kind, by name, eight at most; worked out off the UI thread by `open::warm` (a folder's kinds, as Tracker lists it) and read by menus from `offer_cached`; `open::kind_of` names a kind by the file's name alone; `open::every_app` is every app whose command takes files (`DesktopEntry::takes_files`), Olo's first, and `Handler::icon` its icon; the person's own kinds of file are `mime::own_kinds` (`set_own_kinds`; `mime::type_for_extensions` keeps the type its extensions all share, else makes one of Olo's own, `application/x-olo-kind-EXT`, which `mime::from_name` gives first); desktop entries are kept until an applications folder changes, `desktop_entry::all_cached`; and the same for other programs: `open::for_others` gives the hidden `olo.viewer`, `olo.styled-edit` and `olo.tracker` desktop entries, each listing every type shared-mime-info knows that Olo opens with it, and an `olo-mimeapps.list` making them the defaults, which GIO, `gio open`/xdg-open and xdg-desktop-portal's OpenURI read before `mimeapps.list` while `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP` names Olo; olo-session writes them into `~/.local/share/applications` at start, makes that folder's `mimeinfo.cache` again when they change (`open::mime_cache`, as update-desktop-database would: GIO only finds an app for a type through it) and removes ones it wrote that are no longer wanted, `X-Olo-Written=true`; and, once Olo's Chrome is installed, `open::offer_browser` writes `~/.local/share/applications/olo-mimeapps.list` naming it for web pages and links, read after every `mimeapps.list` in the config directories so a browser the person chose wins, but ahead of the system's lists), `find_program`, `spawn_detached` (`spawn_detached_app` and `open::spawn_app` for a desktop entry's program, in a scope of its own: `scope`; Olo's own programs keep the launcher's stderr, the session's journal, so what Deskbar, Tracker or the palette starts logs like the rest; others' goes nowhere). Olo's own icons are drawings (`icons/svg/NAME.svg`), rendered for the size asked and kept once rendered (`svg`: the classes a drawing is drawn for its size by, `own`'s cache in `~/.cache/olo/icons`; docs/ICONS.md, "Drawings"); an icon not yet drawn uses its pre-scaled pictures. |
| `crates/release` | `olo-release`: Olo's releases on GitHub (the newest, with its checksum file and commit's time; downloaded, checked, unpacked, put in place): Setup's install, and the program an installed Olo's session asks for upgrades (`olo-release latest`, `install`). |
| `crates/mail` | `olo-mail`: mail accounts read for one-time codes (see "Codes sent by mail"): Gmail and Fastmail over IMAP with an app password kept in the login keyring, natively (rustls with the system's certificates; IMAP: LOGIN, SELECT, SEARCH, FETCH, IDLE; MIME: encoded words, multipart, quoted-printable, base64, charsets, HTML made words); `Watch` an account's mail for a while on a thread of its own (the inbox told at once, IDLE; where else mail lands, a rule's folder or the junk, every five seconds); `standin`, a stand-in IMAP server for tests (an inbox and mailboxes beside it). |
| `crates/calendar` | `olo-calendar`: Calendar's engine (see "Calendar's engine"): iCalendar read and written back whole (`ical`), repeating events worked out (`rrule`), events with their zones, exceptions and occurrences (`event`), CalDAV for every account (`dav`), the accounts and their sign-ins (`account`), calendars kept on disk in step with their servers (`store`), and a stand-in server (`standin`). |
