| `crates/google` | `olo-google`: signing in to Google with a person's own "Desktop app" OAuth client (the consent page in the browser, the answer to a loopback port, PKCE): `SignIn::start(client, endpoints, scopes, app)`, `access_token`, `agent(name)`. DiskBackup's Drive (`olo_diskbackup::oauth` is its scopes over this) and Calendar. |
| `crates/net` | `olo-net`: the network changing under a program that talks over it (see "The network changing"): connections on a network that went cut at once, what's kept for the network (`PerNetwork`: an HTTP client) made again for the new one, requests tried again across a change (`across_changes`), waits for a network (`wait_online`), and with its `ureq` feature a download that goes on where it broke off (`http::Download`).; and one TCP connection as the kernel keeps it (`tcp_info`: `TCP_INFO`'s every figure, the congestion control read and set, BBR's model of the path, which BBR the kernel's own is). `examples/tcp-flow`: flows to measure a congestion control with (tools/dev/bbr3-check). |
| `crates/kmod` | `olo-kmod`: one of Olo's kernel modules built for the running kernel and installed (see "BBRv3 for TCP"): what the services that load them share (apps/gpu-memory, apps/bbr3). |
| `crates/system` | `olo-system`: the system over its own protocols, in process: logind (`power`: reboot, power off, suspend, inhibitor locks), NetworkManager (`network`: status, join including 802.1X, forget), the sound server (`audio`: volume, mute, `watch` change feed), dconf writes, the D-Bus/systemd activation environment. All blocking: call from worker threads. |
| `apps/airpods` | `olo-airpods`: AirPods, natively (see "AirPods"): the session's service and its command line. |
| `apps/phone` | Phone (`olo-phone`): an iPhone's or an Android phone's messages, contacts and one-time codes, spoken to by Olo itself over Bluetooth (see "The phone"): the app (conversations and contacts in a window) and its command line; and `olo-phoned`, the session's service, which gives codes to the browser tab waiting for them. |
| `apps/voice` | `olo-voice`: the voice service (see "The voice service"): every microphone through voice processing, and its command line. |
| `apps/installer` | `olo-installer`: the Installer (first called Olo Setup), a stock Fedora Workstation made Olo in one full-screen program (see "The Installer"). |
| `apps/dconf` | `olo-dconf`: Olo's dconf service (`ca.desrt.dconf`), GSettings programs' settings written into dconf's own database in place of GNOME's dconf-service (see "Other toolkits' programs"). |
| `apps/secrets` | `olo-secrets`: Olo's own Secret Service and Secret portal, programs' secrets kept in place of GNOME Keyring unless Preferences ▸ Security says otherwise, its store opened by the login password (see "Programs' secrets"). |
| `crates/pam-keyring`, `crates/login-key` | `pam_olo_keyring.so`: the login password opens Olo's keyring, the key it gives handed to olo-secrets in the login's kernel keyring; `olo-login-key`: that key's derivation, shared (see "Programs' secrets"). |
| `crates/camera` | `olo-camera`: cameras in process: listed from sysfs (nothing opened till one is asked for), a V4L2 stream (MJPEG decoded by zune-jpeg, or YUYV converted) as BGRA frames; `OLO_CAMERA_FAKE=1` puts a stand-in first ("Test Camera", a moving pattern at 30 frames a second) for tests and headless sessions, which never open a real camera. For a recording's camera bubble (Screenshot's `bubble.rs`), later face sign-in. |
| `crates/face` | `olo-face`: face unlock natively: the infrared camera over V4L2, its emitter through its UVC extension unit, YuNet and SFace run in process (tract), and `olo-faced`, the root service on the system bus. See "Face unlock". |
| `crates/pam-face` | `pam_olo_face.so`: face unlock in sudo's and polkit's PAM stacks (asks `olo-faced`). See "Face unlock". |
| `crates/fido` | `olo-fido`: FIDO2 security keys (a YubiKey) natively: CTAPHID over hidraw, the CTAP2 Olo uses, and the account password sealed by a key's `hmac-secret`, so a touch can stand for typing it. See "Security keys". |
| `crates/eld` | `olo-eld`: an AAC-ELD decoder in Rust (AirPods' microphone stream: mono, 480 samples a frame, no SBR). Huffman tables vendored from Symphonia (MPL-2.0), the standard's band, TNS and window tables transcribed (`tables.rs`); checked against libfdk-aac's decode of a libfdk-made stream (`tests/fdk.rs`: 85 dB) and, with `--ignored`, of a real capture. |
| `crates/voice` | `olo-voice`: what Olo does to every microphone, 10 ms at a time: echo cancellation (its own fullband Kalman filter), noise suppression (DeepFilterNet3, vendored in `vendor/deep_filter`), level normalization (WebRTC's AGC2, vendored in `vendor/sonora`). See "Voice processing". |
| `crates/pool` | `olo-token-pool`: token pooling for Claude Code and Codex (see "Token Pool"): the accounts, their sealed store, the drain order, the loopback gateway and the clients' proxy (its own certificate authority, and which program is connecting, from /proc). |
| `crates/ai` | `olo-ai`: how AI features reach their models (see "AI features"): `ask(&settings.ai, &feature, &Ask)` → the answer's JSON. Blocking; call off the UI thread. |
| `crates/ocr` | `olo-ocr`: the text in a picture, read in process (Robert Knight's Ocrs and RTen, its two models in `data/ocr`, CC BY-SA 4.0): each line's characters and where they are, for the Viewer's and Quick Look's selecting and copying. `read` (for a worker), `let_go` (the models, when nothing has been read for a while), `init` (its four threads, made as the program starts). See "The text in a picture" under Viewer. |
| `crates/preview` | `olo-preview`: native previews of every file kind (text, images, PDF, audio, video, archives, office documents, fonts). Its decoding needs no toolkit (pictures are `Bitmap`s, premultiplied RGBA; token classes are `olo_theme::Syntax`, coloured by `Palette::syntax`)); its views (`PreviewView`, `rich::RichView`, `table::TableView`) are `kit`, on olo-kit, behind its `kit` feature (what the loader finds comes as messages, `kit::Msg`; a document is laid out as its `body` runs, for the width layout says, and draws only what `Painter::visible_bounds` shows; pictures let go leave the GPU's atlas by themselves). Either turns on `gpu`: pictures as planes for a window's GPU (`olo_yuv::YuvFrame`) and video decoded on GPUs. Source code is coloured by syntect's bundled Sublime grammars plus Olo's own in `src/syntaxes` (TOML, with Cargo.lock and other lock files; INI, with systemd units, .desktop entries and git and editor configs; just, `justfile`, `Justfile`, `.justfile` and `*.just`, its recipe bodies bash with `{{ }}` found in them, in the shell's strings too, through `with_prototype`), its scopes mapped onto the theme's token classes (`text::classify`). Spreadsheets and CSV (`table.rs`, sheets shared as `Arc`s): every column, scrolled sideways; the first row as the columns' names when it looks like a header (all text, with numbers or blanks below); number columns lined up on the right; a bar with Search (every word, in all columns or the one chosen beside it; Escape clears, then lets go) and how many rows show ("14 of 120 rows"); a header click sorts (again to reverse): numbers as numbers (a thousands comma, a currency sign or a percent allowed) before text, text naturally and without case ("file2" before "file10"), empty cells last, ties in the file's order. A sheet of more than 40,000 cells is searched and sorted on a worker (cancelled when asked again), the rows shown until then staying put and the bar saying "Searching…". Quick Look's own keys (Space, the arrows, F) stand aside while a field has the keyboard. Formatted documents (Markdown, and Word, OpenDocument and RTF text; PowerPoint presentations are drawn, "Presentations" under Viewer) are blocks (`doc::Block`) set as a page by `rich.rs`: Word, OpenDocument text and RTF are read by `olo-richtext` (`doc::rich`: headings, lists numbered as they count, quotations, neighbouring code lines as one block, tables as tables; empty paragraphs are spacing, left out), an OpenDocument presentation's text by `doc.rs`'s own zip and XML; Markdown is CommonMark with GitHub's tables (their alignment, and styled cells), task lists, strikethrough and alerts (`> [!NOTE]` and the rest, a bar and title in the alert's hue), typographer's quotes and dashes; raw HTML keeps its text (`<br>` breaks, `<img>` is an image, comments go); code blocks are coloured by their fence's language (`text::highlight`, the text preview's grammars); pictures beside the document are shown (local files only, never fetched; a remote one's alt text shows instead), resampled exactly to their device size. The page is at most 680 points wide, centred, body text 13 points on a 20-point line, headings 26 to 13 points with room above them (rules under the first two), lists with hanging indents (bullets drawn, numbers lined up on the right, tasks as `check_box_look`s), inline code on a tint with a small no-break space either side (a line doesn't break between "(" and code), and links in the link hue, underlined under the pointer; they open with `olo_xdg::open` (a relative one beside the document) and a `#heading` scrolls to it (GitHub's anchors). Blocks are laid out once for a width, scale, look and font generation: those in view first (at most 5 ms), the rest 3 ms a frame after, and a spinner shows over a part not laid out yet; only blocks in view are drawn. Agents read each block (`Heading`, `Paragraph`, `ListItem`, `Code`, `Table`, `Image`) and click its links (`Link`). Text and formatted documents' text is selected as anywhere in Olo (a drag; a word with a double-click, a line with a triple; ⇧ extends; an I-beam over it), drawn behind the text in the kit's selection (`style::selection_behind`, the text fields' too): the text preview's places are a line and a byte, hit by each line shaped as drawn (any characters, not only monospaced ASCII), a whole line's selection taking its line break; a document's are a block, one of its texts, a line and a byte (`WrappedLine::closest_index_for_position`, painted row by row from `position_for_index`, just behind each text so a code block's ground stays under it). `PreviewView::copy` gives what's selected (a document's partial selection: paragraphs apart, a list's items a line apart, a table's cells by tabs and its rows by lines; Select All: every block's own text, laid out yet or not), and `open_find` the kit's find bar (`widgets::find_bar`, Viewer's PDFs' too): a text's matches by line, a document's over what's laid out (found again as more is, "…" until it all is), each marked, the one shown selected and centred. With nothing selected or found the views do nothing more a frame (TODO.md in the rich view scrolling at 60 frames a second: 484 to 535 µs a frame before, 499 to 522 after; the text view's listeners cost about 25 µs a frame). Used by Tracker's Quick Look (`PreviewView::new(item, generation, false, cx)`, images capped at 3200 px; a PDF shows its first page as a picture, in the same `ImageView`, the card until it comes, the rest the Viewer's, and its arrows step through the folder as a picture's do: it had shown only its card, and Up and Down did nothing on it) and the Viewer (zoomable: full resolution up to the GPU texture limit, zoom and pan through its `ImageView`). Video (`video.rs`, H.264 in mp4 or Matroska, AV1 and VP9 in Matroska/WebM or mp4, HEVC in mp4 (`hvc1` and `hev1`: `media::mp4_hevc` walks the boxes to its `hvcC` and `colr`, which the mp4 crate skips) or Matroska (`V_MPEGH/ISO/HEVC`, the record in its CodecPrivate, its `Colour`), with `media.playable` set; the mp4 crate doesn't know AV1's `av01` sample entry, so `media::mp4_av1` walks the boxes to it for the track and its `av1C` sequence header, sent before each key frame): a worker demuxes and decodes (OpenH264, rav1d through `olo_images::av1::Decoder`, filmcraft-vp9 through `olo_images::vp9::Decoder`, or rust_h265 through `olo_images::hevc::Decoder`, whose pictures are `av1::Frame`s too: HEVC's from its decoder configuration record's parameter sets, on four threads in display order, its matrix and range the container's, else BT.709 from 720 lines and BT.601 under) up to six frames ahead, giving each picture the earliest outstanding presentation time (VP9's carry their sample's own, and times left behind by samples that showed nothing are dropped) (OpenH264 returns display order; it must be made with `Flush::NoFlush`, as the crate's default flush after every packet breaks B-frame reordering and every B-frame then fails), mp4 times shifted by the track's edit list; `Video::tick` shows frames against a clock that follows the sound's reported position when an `audio::Player` is playing it and runs alone otherwise (no sound server in tests, silent files). Seeks go to the key frame before the target (Matroska: scans back for one, further each time) and drop pictures before it, all but the one still showing at the target (a still screen in a screen recording is one picture, seconds long: seeking into it showed the next change; `seeks_into_a_long_picture`): the last before it is held (made) unless its sample's duration (an MP4's, a Matroska block's own) says it ended first, and queued at the target's time when the next starts after it; past the last picture's end, that one is decoded again (`Lead`). Holding every picture cost a 4K H.264 seek a sixth more (`seek_cost`: 386 ms against 329; with durations, 317); a paused seek still shows its frame. `OLO_SAMPLES=dir cargo test --release -p olo-preview video -- --ignored` checks seeking on test.mp4/mkv (one key frame) and gop.mp4/mkv (one a second), made with ffmpeg's testsrc2, plus av1.webm (svt-av1, Opus sound), vp9.webm (libvpx with `-auto-alt-ref 1 -lag-in-frames 25`, so hidden frames in superframes), av1.mp4 (`av1_in_mp4`: 4 s of testsrc2 through libsvtav1, a key frame a second), vp9.mp4 and vp9-10bit.webm (`vp9_plays`: profile 0 in mp4, profile 2 in WebM; every picture, posters, facts), hevc.mp4, hvc1.mp4, hevc.mkv and hevc-10bit.mp4 (`hevc_plays`: 1080p HEVC with B-frames as `hev1`, `hvc1` and Matroska, remuxed by `ffmpeg -c copy`, and JCT-VC's Main 10 WPP_D in an mp4; every picture, seeks, posters, facts) and bframes.mp4 (any x264-made H.264 High clip with B-frames; `b_frames` checks every picture comes out, in order); `keeps_up` needs av1-1080.mkv (1080p AV1), vp9-1080.webm (1080p VP9), gop.mp4 and av1.mp4 to decode at well over 30 frames a second (72 on the M2 Max, 195 now; VP9 120; av1.mp4 600; `OLO_ONLY=a,b` picks samples; the YUV to RGB fast path is fixed-point with tables, checked against the float path by `yuv_fast_path`). Drawn by the GPU from its planes (Ben, 2026-11-06: "the viewer app can't even play 4k video at 60fps smoothly"): a window's player asks for `Options::yuv`, and each SDR 4:2:0 picture comes as `Picture::Yuv`, an `olo_yuv::YuvFrame` made on the worker (luma packed, Cb and Cr interleaved; 10-bit samples in the high bits of 16; H.264's limited-range BT.601 as OpenH264's, the others' matrix and range as `olo_images::av1::Frame::yuv420` says), which the window paints with `Painter::paint_yuv`: the renderer keeps two pairs of textures a stream (R8/RG8, or R16/RG16 unorm, added to blade), uploads each new picture into the pair the frame before isn't reading, and the surface shader makes RGB with the picture's own matrix (`YuvFrame::rgb_matrix`). A 4K picture is 12 MB rather than 33 of RGBA, and nothing converts it on the CPU; HDR, wide-gamut and 4:2:2/4:4:4 pictures keep the RGBA path. Measured on 4K60 clips (`make_4k60`: 10 s of 3840 × 2160 through NVENC) on a headless 4K screen: H.264 29.6 frames a second before, 60.0 after; HEVC 24.4 to 59.8; AV1 52.2 to 60.0; the window's own work 18 to 25 ms a frame before (making the picture BGRA and a texture of it), 0.5 ms after. Decoded on NVIDIA's GPU where there is one (`olo_video::nvdec`: NVDEC's API through vendor/nvdec-sys's declarations, `libnvcuvid.so.1` and `libcuda.so.1` opened at run time, nothing linked; its parser takes the stream, HEVC as Annex B with its parameter sets before each key frame; each picture NV12 or P016, copied from the GPU into a `YuvFrame`; its colour from the stream's own H.273 numbers): H.264, HEVC (8- and 10-bit), VP9 and AV1, each asked of the GPU first (`cuvidGetDecoderCaps`). What decodes is chosen by `video::Device` (`Options::device`): `Default` follows Viewer ▸ View ▸ Decode With (`settings.video.decoder`: `auto`, `nvidia`, `intel`, `cpu`), `Automatic` is the built-in GPU where it decodes the video, else NVIDIA's (on battery too, unless `settings.video.nvidia_on_battery` is off: Ben, 2026-11-06), else the processor, or one named; a decoder that fails mid-stream hands over to the processor at the last key frame, the video playing on. `Video::decoding` says what is decoding ("NVIDIA's GPU (NVDEC)", "the processor"), `PreviewEvent::Decoding` when it changes, and `PreviewView::set_decode_with` starts the video again on another at the same place, playing or not (the Viewer's View ▸ Decode With). Measured on the 4K60 clips: all at 60 frames a second either way; the process's CPU HEVC 246% of a core on the processor to 41.6% on NVDEC, H.264 100% to 29%, AV1 368% to 26%. Every codec decodes on Intel's (or AMD's) GPU too (`olo_vaapi::decode`: VA-API through vendor/va-sys, libva opened at run time). Fedora's iHD (and Mesa) leave out H.264 and HEVC for their patents, and its Mesa compiles them out of Vulkan Video too (ANV shows AV1 and VP9 decoding only with `ANV_DEBUG=video-decode`); RPM Fusion's `intel-media-driver` (nonfree) has them all, in `/usr/lib64/dri-nonfree`, which libva reads before Fedora's folder, and Olo Doctor installs it (`intel_video`: an Intel GPU on Fedora without it; the fix adds RPM Fusion's free and nonfree repositories by their release packages, as rpmfusion.org says, `Step::InstallRepository`, then the driver through PackageKit). H.264 and HEVC go through cros-codecs' stateless decoders (vendor/cros-codecs: its parsers and what a decoder keeps between pictures, the decoded picture buffer, picture order, reference lists and marking, bumping; its own backends and encoders, which link libva and libgbm, gated off) driving a backend of ours (`decode/stateless.rs`: a picture in one of the session's surfaces, back in the free list when nothing holds its handle; `h264.rs` and `h265.rs` fill VA-API's picture, scaling list and slice parameters as ChromeOS's backend does, HEVC's slices a slice behind so the last says so). AV1 and VP9: cros-codecs' parsers read the OBUs and frames, and each picture's parameters are filled as FFmpeg's and ChromeOS's decoders fill them; references are eight slots of surfaces; AV1's film grain is applied by the driver into a display surface of its own; VP9's superframes and shown-again frames are decoded as libvpx does. A picture comes back by the driver's copy engine (`vaCopy`) into a linear surface in memory of ours (`USER_PTR`, the chroma right after the luma rows, as iHD lays it whatever offset it's given), then into planes: mapping the decoder's own (tiled) surface had the processor untile it, 7.5 ms a 4K picture, and `vaGetImage` 7 ms, so 4K60 dropped to 58; the video processor isn't a copy (it changed pictures). A GPU decoder's pictures are held, not copied out (`Decoder::hold`, `Nvdec::hold`; `OLO_VIDEO_HELD=0` copies, to compare): each decoder keeps up to 16 pieces of page-aligned memory (VA-API's linear surfaces, NVDEC's buffers), copies a picture into one nothing holds, and hands it on as it is (`Picture::held`: its planes' offsets and row pitch), as an `olo_yuv::YuvMemory` on the `YuvFrame`; the renderer imports that memory as a Vulkan buffer (blade's `import_host_buffer`, VK_EXT_external_memory_host) and copies it into the stream's textures on the GPU, letting both go once the GPU is past that frame (a picture it can't import is staged as before, at its pitch). NVDEC's memory is registered with its CUDA context (`cuMemHostRegister`: its copy goes by DMA, not through the processor as into pageable memory), the context shared with that memory and destroyed when the last of it goes (`Cuda`), and made with blocking sync (waiting for a copy, the thread sleeps rather than spins). 4K60 AV1, the Viewer's share of a core, copied → held: Intel's GPU 21.9% → 7.1%, NVIDIA's 30.3% → 21.9%, pinned 13.8%, blocking 7.0% (its video thread 19.9% → 1.1%; 4K60 VP9 7.0%; nothing dropped). `crates/video/tests/reference.rs` decodes reference streams on every device here, each picture against the reference decoder's MD5 (libvpx's VP9 profile 2 and 1080p in tiles, libaom's AV1 10-bit, the HEVC conformance suite's Main 10 in wavefronts; NVDEC takes VP9 only from 128 × 128, said before trying); cros-codecs' per-picture HEVC reference-set warnings are debug notes (ordinary streams do it). `crates/vaapi/tests/decode.rs` checks every picture's MD5 against the reference decoder's (cros-codecs' AV1, VP9, H.264 and HEVC streams: B-frames, H.264 High, HEVC films, VP9's shown-again frames, a reset; a codec no GPU here decodes is said and passed: `LIBVA_DRIVERS_PATH=DIR` points the test alone at RPM Fusion's driver unpacked there). `Automatic` takes the built-in GPU where it decodes the video, else NVIDIA's (on battery too); `Video::decoders` says which GPUs could (the Viewer's menu enables those). 4K60 on the ThinkPad's Intel GPU (Panther Lake, RPM Fusion's iHD 26.3.5), the process's share of a core: H.264 25% (NVDEC 29%, the processor 100%), HEVC 21% (41.6%, 246%), AV1 22% (26%, 368%); a minute of each, with six ahead and the clock waiting for the first picture, played every picture but one (H.264 3600 of 3600, HEVC 3599, AV1 3600, none late; NVDEC's H.264 5 dropped, all at the switch to it), where at two ahead NVDEC had dropped 155, 68 and 176. On the processor, rav1d's and OpenH264's x86 assembly (SSE4 and AVX2, chosen at run time) is built in: nasm assembles it (tools/setup.sh installs it; OpenH264 leaves its assembly out without saying so when there's no nasm, and rav1d's `asm` feature fails the build). `keeps_up` on the 4K60 clips (`OLO_SAMPLES=/var/tmp/olo-4k OLO_ONLY=…`): AV1 32 → 85 pictures a second, H.264 45 → 53–98 (OpenH264 decodes on one thread, as fast as the core the scheduler gives it; its threads crash it), HEVC 108 → 140 (rust_h265, no assembly; the machine was busier for the first); the Viewer playing 4K60 AV1 on the processor 368% → 175% of a core. A frame keeps 8-bit video's samples as bytes (`av1::Planes`, words only deeper; every conversion runs over either through one macro): it had widened them to 16 bits and the queue counted each 4K picture 50 MB, one ahead, so 4K60 AV1 on the processor dropped 1,510 of 3,600 pictures in a minute, now 3 (its video thread 57% of a core → 17.5%). The worker keeps up to six pictures ahead within 80 MB (`QUEUE_BYTES`: six 4K pictures as planes; at 24 MB a 4K picture had two, 33 ms at 60 frames a second, and every hiccup of a decoder's dropped pictures, NVDEC's H.264 150 a minute), and with no sound to follow the clock waits for a late decoder up to 200 ms (`HOLD`: starting, a stall), so a picture shows late rather than the ones after it being passed over; one that can't keep up at all is caught up with by passing pictures over. How smoothly a video played is counted (`Video::playback`: pictures shown, dropped, already late when their turn came, and shown late, more than 25 ms after their time) and logged when the player goes ("video: 3600 pictures shown, 0 dropped, 0 late; decoded on Intel's GPU (VA-API)"); `make_4k60` makes longer clips with `OLO_SECONDS`. Audio decodes with symphonia plus `opus.rs` (opus-decoder, OpusHead parsing and pre-skip trim) for Ogg Opus. `audio::Player` speaks the PulseAudio protocol itself, and its client says who is playing as libpulse does (`application.process.id`, `.binary`, `.user`, `.host`, beside the app's name and icon): Fedora's uresourced follows the programs playing sound by their process, and crashed at every Olo login on the start-up sound's stream (a null process id). Picture editing (`edit.rs`): an `Editor` keeps a list of `Op`s (rotate, flip, crop, resize) with undo/redo and a saved mark, and a worker that loads the full picture once, applies new steps to its last result, sends `EditEvent::Shown` (downscaled for the screen) for `PreviewView::show_edited`, and writes PNG, JPEG (quality 92), WebP, BMP, TIFF or GIF atomically (`write`, through a hidden `.name.saving` file); `edit::editable` says which files it can write back. The Viewer's crop overlay (`crop.rs`: drag a frame, move it or its edges) sits where `ImageView::picture_bounds` says the picture is, `set_still` stopping pan and zoom while it is up. The Viewer's Image menu and File ▸ Save / Save As / Revert use it; Quick Look's footer has Rotate Left / Right (⌘L / ⌘R), which save at once. |
| `crates/fakesound` | `olo-fakesound`: a sound server for tests (enough of the PulseAudio protocol for Olo's players, the sound panel and the AirPods service; it plays nothing and says what it hears: HACKING, "To test sound"). A package of its own with only what it uses (`pulseaudio`, `olo-crash`, `olo-sync`): as a binary of olo-preview it was built again, to the same bytes, for every change to anything olo-preview depends on. |
| `crates/dnf-fake` | `olo-dnf-fake` (`dnf-fake`): a stand-in PackageKit for tests, OS Updates' updates and repositories on a bus of the test's own ("OS Updates", Testing). A package of its own for the same reason as olo-fakesound (it was olo-system's, which it doesn't use); its test drives olo-system's own client of it. |
| `crates/richtext` | `olo-richtext`: formatted text documents in and out, natively (zip and quick-xml): Word (`.docx`: styles, numbering, hyperlinks' relationships), OpenDocument text (`.odt`: automatic and named styles, nested lists, `text:s` for runs of spaces) and RTF (`rtf.rs`: a reader of groups and control words — font and colour tables, the style sheet's names for kinds or else `\outlinelevel`, lists from the list table or Word 95's `\pn`, links from `HYPERLINK` fields, tables from `\intbl` paragraphs, `\cell` and `\row` (`\trhdr` a header), any Windows code page by `\ansicpg` or a font's `\fcharset`, `\u` with its fallbacks skipped, surrogate pairs; pictures, headers, footers, notes, hidden text and unknown `\*` destinations left out — and a writer of plain ASCII with a style sheet, a list table per numbered list and every paragraph's look spelled out, as RTF readers take a paragraph's look from its own words, not its style; the reader takes each kind's look off again). A `Document` of `Paragraph`s (kind: body, title, heading 1–3, quote, code; a list, bulleted or numbered, and its level; an indent; alignment; or a `Table` in the flow: rows of cells of paragraphs, the first row maybe a header, and the columns' widths if they have their own (`widths`, shares of the table after `tidy`: Word's `w:gridCol`s, OpenDocument's column styles, RTF's first row's `\cellx` edges), written ruled across the page in each format) of `Span`s (bold, italic, underline, struck out, size, colour, font, monospace, link), indents beyond the levels in points (`left`, `first`, `right`; read as whole levels and the rest) and tab stops (`Tab`: left, centre, right, decimal), and the document's font. `read`/`write` go by the file's extension; `Document::tidy` runs same-styled spans together and makes a line break a new paragraph (in cells too), and gives every row a cell for each column and every cell a paragraph. Light on purpose (StyledEdit links it; `preview` is far heavier), and round-trip tested; its files open in LibreOffice as they look in StyledEdit (`OLO_RICHTEXT_OUT=dir cargo test -p olo-richtext writes_samples` writes a sample of each; `OLO_RICHTEXT_READ=file cargo test -p olo-richtext reads_named_file -- --nocapture` prints how another program's file reads). |
| `crates/syntax` | `olo-syntax`: source code coloured by syntax, in process: tree-sitter's grammars for 43 languages (Rust, C, C++, Go, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript and TSX, shell and fish, Ruby, Java, Kotlin, Swift, C#, PHP, Lua, SQL, HTML, CSS, JSON, YAML, TOML, XML, Makefiles, Dockerfiles, CMake, Scala, Haskell, Zig, Elixir, Erlang, Nix, R, Julia, OCaml, Dart, Objective-C, Protocol Buffers, PowerShell, INI, diffs), each compiled in, with its highlight query (its crate's, or `queries/`: Kotlin's is Olo's own) whose captures map to the palette's token classes (`class_of`: `function.method.call` a function, `variable` plain inside a string). `LANGUAGES`; `detect(path, first_line)` (a whole name like `Makefile`, the extension, a `#!` line's interpreter, `env -S` and versions too); `by_name` (an id, alias or extension: what a Markdown fence says). A `Highlighter` keeps one text's tree: `edit(&Edit)` per change (`Edit::new` with the lines it's on, or `Edit::in_text` counting them), `job(text)` the parse to run on a worker (one out at a time; a language's query compiles in its first, up to half a second for Swift's), `done(parsed)` takes the tree (edits made meanwhile applied to it; what changed: `Changed`), `classes(text, range)` the query over just those bytes (inner captures and a node's first pattern win). 100,000 lines of Rust: parsed in a second, a keystroke's reparse 16 ms (both on the worker), a screenful coloured in 0.35 ms. The kit's `code` module puts it in the editor. |
| `crates/print` | `olo-print`: printing, natively. `Page`s of `Item`s (text at a baseline with its font, size, colour, width and lines; rectangles; lines; pictures, a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP file's bytes in a box), in points from the top left, made into a PDF by `pdf` (krilla: fonts found by fontdb, Olo's own for text naming none, embedded and subset, text stays text; a character the font lacks drawn from a face that has it, `ttf-parser` telling; bold from a variable font's default instance stroked as well as filled, as browsers print it). `ipp`: CUPS spoken to over IPP on `/run/cups/cups.sock` (else `localhost:631`; `OLO_CUPS_SOCKET` for a test's stand-in, as `talks_to_cups` has): `printers()` (name, description, state, paper), `default_printer()`, `print(printer, pdf, &Job)` (copies, paper, pages, sides). `panel::PrintPanel`: the Print window (printer or PDF File, paper, copies, pages; the printers asked for on a worker); `Paper`, `PAPERS` and `local_paper()` (US Letter where it is used, else A4). |
| `apps/<name>` | One crate per application, binary named `olo-<name>`. Picked up by the workspace glob. |
| `vendor/` | Patched copies of dependencies (`[patch.crates-io]`), libraries owned outright (Blade, codecs' and drivers' bindings), each explained in `vendor/README.md`. |
| `data/icons` | The icon set: drawings (`data/icons/svg/<name>.svg`), rendered for the size they're shown at; see [ICONS.md](ICONS.md). |
| `data/themes` | The other looks of the icons, chosen in Preferences ▸ Themes: each theme's colours for the drawings (`data/themes/<id>/icons/recolour.txt`) and any drawings of its own (`icons/svg/`); see "Themes" in [ICONS.md](ICONS.md). |
| `data/brand` | Olo's wordmark ("Olo" in Sora, light and on dark) and, in `sizes/`, the horizontal logo pre-scaled for the veil and boot splash; made by `tools/mkbrand.py` from the mark (`docs/brand/olo-mark.png`) and the font. See [BRAND.md](BRAND.md). |
| `website/` | olo-desktop.com, a static site: its own small Rust builder (`cargo run --release` there; not in the workspace) puts `pages/` in `templates/layout.html` and writes `website/dist`, its pictures taken from `docs/img`, `data/icons` and `data/wallpapers`. See `website/README.md`. `tools/deploy-website.sh` builds it and deploys it to Cloudflare (the project `olo-desktop`), asking before it installs anything or signs in. |
| `data/session` | `olo.desktop` for the login screen (installed by `tools/install-session.sh`). |
| `tools/` | `install-session.sh` (release build → `~/.local`, session entry → `/usr/share/wayland-sessions`, an atomic system's `/usr/local/share/wayland-sessions`), `dev/tsession` (headless UI testing), `genicon.py`/`genicons.sh`/`mkicons.py`/`iconsheet.py` (icons, see [ICONS.md](ICONS.md)), `mkbrand.py` (the brand's pictures, see [BRAND.md](BRAND.md)), `dev/readme-shots` (the README's and website's 4K screenshots, on an Agent Screen). |

Build: `cargo build -p olo-<app>` (plus `cargo build --bin olo-app-server` once, for headless testing; as root set `CARGO_HOME=/home/ben/.cargo` to share the registry) (repo is owned by `ben`; when running as
root use `sudo -u ben bash -lc 'cd … && cargo build …'` in the main checkout).
How long a release build takes after a change (ThinkPad, 16 threads,
2026-11-05, the whole workspace): the kit (then olo-ui) 92 s, app_server 47
s, a leaf app 2.8 s. A kit change is bound by CPU, not by any one step:
olo-ui 21 s, then some 35 apps compiled and linked at once, about 1,000
CPU-seconds in all (olo-portal alone, with the machine to itself, is 15
s, half of it local ThinLTO). Tried and not kept: `incremental = true`
(103 s, 46 s, 3.4 s) and one codegen unit a crate (159 s, 190 s, 6.1 s);
the linker is already rust-lld (Rust's default on x86_64 Linux since
1.90; 0.4 s for olo-portal), kache already caches. So while working on
one app, build just it (`cargo build --release -p olo-<app>`: a kit
change then costs olo-ui and that app, about 35 s), and the workspace
once at the end, for the session's upgrade.
Builds go through [kache](https://github.com/kunobi-ninja/kache), a
compiler cache (`cargo install kache --locked`, then
`kache init --no-shell --no-service`, which sets `build.rustc-wrapper` in
`~/.cargo/config.toml`): a crate compiled once with the same inputs is
restored instead of rebuilt, in any target directory or worktree. It is
ben's setup, so build as ben (as above); `kache doctor` checks it,
`kache stats --last-build` shows the hits, `KACHE_DISABLED=1` bypasses it.
Olo's Kache app (`olo-kache`, "Kache (apps/kache)" below) shows it all
live (the store, the day's hits and misses, the pool, each build) and
sets and restarts it; `olo-kache --print` says the same as JSON.
Know what it is for: a cache pays off when the same inputs come back
(a branch switched and switched back, a revert, a second checkout or
target directory), not in a straight edit-build loop, where every build's
inputs are new; over a day of such work it served 0.6% of crates for ~2%
overhead (measured 2026-11-01: ~2 min of key hashing and ~12 min of
storing in 12.6 h of compiling). Its daemon is a login service (`kache
daemon install`, done by `tools/setup.sh`), so the cache stays under its
cap without anyone running it by hand. Blaze (indexable-inc/blaze, a
build daemon with its own compiler) was tried the same day and dropped:
it needs more memory than this laptop can spare (OOM at a 10 GB cap
loading the workspace) and could not compile the kit's styles
(`<f64 as Into<f32>>::into` in `ToTaffy`); cargo's loop is 1–3 s for an
edit to an app or the kits in a debug build, and ~90 s for a
release build of every app after an edit to the kits, which is linking
dozens of binaries of 200 MB.
**The toolchain** is a nightly, pinned to a date in `rust-toolchain.toml`
(Ben, 2026-11-15: "just switch to nightly"): for cargo's workspace-wide
feature unification (`.cargo/config.toml`, `[resolver]
feature-unification = "workspace"`, `[unstable]`), which stable doesn't
have. Without it cargo unified features over the packages each command
asked for, so `cargo build -p A` and `-p B` built serde, tracing,
image… with different features and every Olo crate above them again
under a new hash: 59 builds of olo-kit's library and 127 of its
examples lived in `target/release` at once, 310 GB of `target/` used
within two days. Now any selection builds the units `--workspace` does.
Pinned, not `nightly`: each new compiler rebuilds everything and misses
all of kache's store. To move it on: install the new date (`rustup
toolchain install nightly-YYYY-MM-DD --profile minimal -c rustfmt -c
clippy -c rust-src`), change the file, build the workspace and run the
tests; the next sweep removes what the old one built. Measured after the
switch: `cargo build --release -p olo-kache`, then `-p olo-weather -p
olo-doctor`, used the one build of olo-kit's library the workspace's had
(three selections, one unit). The front end runs on eight threads too
(`-Zthreads=8` in `.cargo/config.toml`'s rustflags; Ben: "just use
Zthreads"): a release compile of olo-kit is code generation's, 30 s
with or without it (kache bypassed, `KACHE_DISABLED=1`); what it
shortens is the front end, most of a dev or check build.
Builds are kept lean on memory and disk. Dev builds keep only line tables (file and
line in panics and backtraces), and dependencies keep no debuginfo, so debug binaries
stay small and cheap to link. Full debuginfo made each one 600–850 MB, and twelve
links at once ran a 30 GiB laptop out of memory. Release builds the same
(2026-11-15): Olo's crates keep line tables, dependencies none; of
olo-kache's 290 MB, 258 had been debug info. The line tables stay in the
executable, not split out (`split-debuginfo`): an installed copy's crash
report needs them, and `target/` is swept. On ben's machine,
`~/.cargo/config.toml` sets kache as rustc's wrapper; the workspace's
`.cargo/config.toml` links with mold. kache's store keeps under its own
limit (5% of the disk, at most 100 GiB, unless `local_max_size` in
`~/.config/kache/config.toml` says; Kache ▸ Settings), except for what
target folders still share with it. The target directory is swept by `tools/dev/sweep`: cargo never
deletes an artifact, so every edit to a flag, feature or dependency leaves
the old crate's rlib, binaries and build script behind under a new hash
(olo's `target/` reached 435 GB; one build's live set is ~110 GB, debug
and release together). The sweep removes every unit no build has
considered for two days, with everything in `deps/`, `build/`,
`examples/` and `incremental/` carrying its hash; the first run freed
172 GB in 11 s. A build that considers a unit, compiled or fresh, reads
its fingerprint's files (`lib-NAME`, `dep-lib-NAME`, `output-lib-NAME`),
so their access time (`relatime`: at least once a day) is when it was
last used; `invoked.timestamp` is written only when it's compiled.
(Taken for its last use, every crate from outside the workspace,
compiled once and fresh since, looked unused two days on: 4,284 live
release units went at 00:37 on 2026-11-18. And the sweep holds a
profile's build locks, `.cargo-lock`, `.cargo-build-lock` and
`.cargo-artifact-lock`, while it sweeps it: that night it ran under a
build, which failed to link. A build holding them is waited for, at
most `--wait` seconds, 1800, else the profile is left for the next
sweep. `tools/dev/sweep-check` tries both on a stand-in target folder.) Cargo 1.100 keeps each unit in a folder
of its own (`build/<package>/<hash>/`: its `fingerprint/`, `out/`, a
build script's `run/`), which the sweep didn't see until 2026-11-15
(`target/` had reached 564 GB); it sweeps both layouts. A unit built by
another compiler and last used before the one building here now first
did is swept too, whatever its age: after the switch to nightly that was
430 GB of files (counted uncompressed; `/home` is zstd-compressed and much
of it was kache's blocks, so 44 GB came back at once), and kache's
clean-up then took the 301 GB of its store those files had held.
`tools/dev/sweep --install` (also done by
`tools/setup.sh`) puts it on a daily systemd user timer, `olo-sweep.timer`;
`--dry-run` reports, `--days N` changes the window, and a directory is only
swept when it has cargo's `CACHEDIR.TAG`. Scratch target directories
elsewhere (`/var/tmp/...`) are the person who made them's to remove.

## Writing an app

Apps are written on the kit (`crates/kit`, `olo-kit`: the Interface
Kit, `crates/interface`, with Olo's look and controls). **The Olo Book
([OLO-BOOK.md](OLO-BOOK.md)) is how the kits work and how to work with
them: read it first.** "The kit" below has every widget and what each
does. The shape of an app:

```rust
use olo_kit::{Cx, Element, Menu, MenuBar, ParentElement as _, Styled as _, View, WindowOptions, div, instance, widgets::Button};

struct MyApp { /* state */ }

#[derive(Clone)]
enum Msg { Ok }

impl View for MyApp {
    type Message = Msg;

    fn message(&mut self, message: Msg, cx: &mut Cx<Self>) {
        match message { Msg::Ok => { /* change the state */ } }
        cx.invalidate();
    }

    fn command(&mut self, command: &str, _: &mut Cx<Self>) -> bool {
        match command { "quit" => olo_kit::quit(), _ => return false }
        true
    }

    fn body(&mut self, cx: &mut Cx<Self>) -> Element {
        div().size_full().flex().flex_col()
            .child(MenuBar::fixed(cx, vec![Menu::new("File").item("Quit", "quit").key("q")]))
            .child(Button::new("OK").default(true).on_click(cx.msg(Msg::Ok)))
    }
}

fn main() {
    let args: Vec<String> = std::env::args().skip(1).collect();
    if instance::forward("olo.myapp", &args) { return }     // app id: olo.<name>
    olo_kit::run("olo.myapp", |_| {
        olo_kit::open_window(WindowOptions::new("My App", 480.0, 320.0).min_size(320.0, 200.0), |_| MyApp { /* … */ });
        instance::listen("olo.myapp", olo_kit::proxy());
    });
}
```

(`crates/kit/examples/book.rs` is a whole small one, walked through in
the Book: a worker with progress, a child view, a drawing, a menu.)

* **`olo_kit::run(id, build)`** starts the app (its look, keyboard
  profile and fonts, the agent socket, the crash report) and runs
  `build` on the app's looper; `open_window(WindowOptions, |cx| view)`
  opens a window on a looper of its own around the view `build` makes
  there, and gives a `WindowHandle` any thread can reach it through
  (`WindowOptions`: `min_size`, `max_size`, `fits_content`, `floating`,
  `dialog`, `alert`, `child`, `layer`, `keep_size`…);
  `open_window_here(cx, ..)` opens one on the looper of the window `cx`
  is in (an alert, a panel, a window that belongs to another);
  `proxy()` gives a thread a `Proxy` whose messages
  `message_handler(app, f)` takes on the app's looper;
  `stay_resident()` keeps it running with no windows;
  `on_upgrade(f)` and each window's `View::save_state` keep its state
  across an in-place upgrade
  (`restored_state` gives it back; see "In-place reload"), which is also
  how the app moves to another display (an agent screen's, or back:
  "Moving windows to and from screens"); `on_move_window(f)` says how
  one window of several goes (a `WindowMove`: the arguments and state a
  copy of the app there opens it with, and `gone`, letting it go here,
  or why it can't), and `refuse_moves_while(f)` keeps the app where
  it is while `f` says why. A view
  says what it shows in `body`; what changes it (its `message`) calls
  `cx.invalidate()` (its `body` runs again, and only what differs is
  laid out or drawn); work that can take longer than a frame runs on a
  worker (`cx.work`; see "The responsiveness rule"). There is no
  clipboard manager,
  so an app that quits (or closes its last window) while it holds the
  clipboard stays running, windowless, until something else is copied.
* **`olo_kit::held_clipboard`** (`olo_kit_base::clipboard`): the clipboard for
  a program with no window and no kit loop (a shortcut's screenshot, an
  app that has closed its window). `hold(clip)` puts it on the
  clipboard and serves it until something else is copied, then returns
  (so the program stays running until then); `text(s)` is a `Clip` in the
  forms text pastes as. It goes through
  `ext_data_control_v1`: `wl_data_device` only lets the client with the
  keyboard set the clipboard, and a windowless one never has it. For
  files, as file managers copy them (and Chrome, Electron, GTK and Qt
  paste them): `files(paths, cut)` is a `Clip` of
  `x-special/gnome-copied-files` ("copy" or "cut", then the URIs), KDE's
  cut mark, `text/uri-list` and the paths as text (the kit's clipboard
  offers each form under its own MIME type);
  `copied_files(mime, data)` reads one of `FILES` back (paths, and
  whether they were cut). `offers(types)` says whether the clipboard has
  any of them, as the app last heard (its windows hear while they have
  the keyboard): for enabling Paste. Tracker copies files so, and its
  Paste takes files (moving cut ones, then holding them copied where they
  went), a picture (`Pasted Picture.png`, of its kind) or text (a
  clipping). `hold_then(clip, ready)` calls `ready` once the display has
  it; `read(types)` is what's copied, in the first of `types` offered.
  For another display (a socket's name in `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` or its path;
  None, the environment's): `read_all(display)` is what's copied, every
  form of it; `watch(display, now, copied)` hands each thing copied
  there to `copied`, every form, on a thread of its own (the display
  says when: nothing is asked meanwhile), until the `Watch` is dropped;
  `hold_on(display, clip)` serves `clip` there from a thread until
  something else is copied, taking it off again when the `Held` is
  dropped unless `Held::keep`. Agent Screens joins a screen's clipboard
  to the person's with them.
* **`pbcopy` and `pbpaste`** (`apps/pb`), as macOS's, for people and
  agents in any shell: `pbcopy` puts what it reads on the clipboard as
  text and returns once it's there (a copy of itself, in a session of
  its own, serves it until something else is copied: `hold_then`);
  `pbpaste` prints the clipboard's text (`read`). They're
  `olo-pbcopy` and `olo-pbpaste`, installed with Olo's programs; the
  session (`graphical::command_names`) and the installer link `pbcopy`
  and `pbpaste` to them beside them, never over the person's own.
* **A question never opens a window**: `--help`, `-h`, `--version` or
  `-V` as a window program's first argument is refused with a line on
  stderr and exit 2, before a launch is handed to the copy that runs
  (`instance::forward`) and before a program of its own starts
  (`olo_kit::run`; `instance::no_window_for_a_question`). A program
  with help of its own answers before either (Terminal's `--help`
  prints its options, and it refuses an option it doesn't know:
  `launch_check`). Asked from a shell in the person's session, the
  question used to be a launch: a window on their screen.
* **Single instance** (`olo_kit::instance`): call `instance::forward(app_id,
  &args)` first in `main` (returns true if a running copy took the
  arguments; exit then), and `instance::listen(app_id, olo_kit::proxy())`
  in `run`'s closure; forwarded launches arrive in `message_handler` as an
  `instance::Launch { args, cwd, .. }`. A launch is answered once the
  running copy's looper takes it (olo-kit does that as it hands it to
  the handler; 0.2 ms); a copy ending (its last window closed), or one
  with no handler, drops it unanswered and `forward` returns false, so
  the new process opens it itself rather than it being lost. The
  socket is named for the display (`olo_xdg::display_name()`:
  `wayland-1` also when `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` names the socket by its full
  path; use it for any file kept per display).
  `instance::running(app_id)` says whether a copy is listening. An app
  with several windows should open a new one for `--new-window` (always,
  rather than bringing one forward) and be listed in
  `apps::NEW_WINDOW`: Tracker then offers **New Window** on its program
  (or a link to it) while it runs, and Deskbar in its menu, forwarding `--new-window` to the
  running copy (`apps::app_id_of` maps `olo-x` to `olo.x`). Agents
  do the same with `olo-x --new-window`. Each workspace (of each
  display) has its own
  windows of an app (and so its own group of them): a launch, or opening
  a folder or document the app has a window for, brings forward only a
  window on this workspace, the one the active display shows
  (`workspaces::here(window)`, after `workspaces::follow(cx)`; one on
  another display is elsewhere),
  and otherwise opens a new one here, rather than activate one
  elsewhere, which would go to its workspace or display. (Tracker's folders and StyledEdit's
  bare launch do so, and Terminal's `--tab` goes to a window here; a
  document already open elsewhere is still brought forward there, as two
  windows on one file would disagree.) The kit knows where its windows
  are from app_server's events: `WindowInfo::surface` names each window's
  `wl_surface` as its program knows it.
* **Open in Tracker** (`olo_kit::tracker`): wherever something has a
  folder or file behind it, offer `tracker::LABEL` ("Open in Tracker",
  command `tracker::COMMAND`) in its context menu, and its File menu where
  it has one, and call `tracker::open(path)`: a folder shows in its
  Tracker window, a file selected in its folder's, on the workspace
  showing (`olo-tracker --reveal PATH`, forwarded to the running Tracker
  or starting one). Terminal (a tab's working folder: the tab's context
  menu, the terminal's, Terminal ▸), StyledEdit (File ▸, the saved
  document), the Viewer, DiskUsage, DriveSetup (a mounted volume), the
  backup panel in Preferences and the palette (⌘↩ on a file) use it.
  Other programs reach it through `org.freedesktop.FileManager1`, which
  the desktop's Tracker serves on the session bus (taking the name from
  any file manager that had it; Tracker's `filemanager.rs`): ShowItems,
  ShowFolders and ShowItemProperties are each a `--reveal`, so Chrome's
  Show in folder, Electron's `shell.showItemInFolder` and GTK's and Qt's
  open their file in Tracker. While no Tracker has the name (as Olo
  restarts after an upgrade), D-Bus starts the system's activation file's
  program for it (GNOME's Files on Fedora, which then keeps the name till
  Tracker waits it out): Olo Doctor offers "Always Use Tracker"
  (`checks::file_manager`), the user's own activation file
  (`~/.local/share/dbus-1/services/org.freedesktop.FileManager1.service`,
  which wins over the system's) starting `olo-tracker --file-manager`
  (Tracker serving the name without the desktop or a window of its own,
  staying to answer; passed to a Tracker running already it changes
  nothing), and the session bus told to read it at once
  (`Step::SessionBusReload`). It's the user's, so it applies in another
  desktop's session on this account too (Ben chose it so, 2026-11-05).
  An Olo session names Tracker for it by itself, with nothing to press:
  the same activation file in the runtime folder's services
  (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/dbus-1/services`, read before the user's and the
  system's, gone with the login; olo-session's
  `graphical::name_file_manager`, written once the session's
  environment is exported so a Tracker D-Bus starts finds its display),
  as dconf's is (below); the Doctor counts it as fine. A Tracker D-Bus
  started first is handed the session's `--desktop` and shows the
  desktop (`Tracker::open_desktop`); the session's own `olo-tracker
  --desktop`, which the session looks after, then waits for that one to
  end (`instance::running_pid`, `instance::wait_for_exit`: asleep on a
  pidfd) and ends with it, so the session starts the desktop's Tracker
  again (gone at once, it was started again and again, then left
  stopped).
  A window's yellow tab offers it too, for a window that says what it
  shows (`agent::set_path(cx, path)`: StyledEdit's document, the Viewer's file,
  Terminal's working folder; Tracker's own windows don't need it).
  Tracker's Find results have it as Open Parent (⌘↑, also in their
  context menu, with Open and Quick Look). Don't write another; the
  label and the command are the same everywhere, so agents find it by
  either.
* **Following a setting** (`olo_kit::settings`): `current()` reads
  app_server's `Settings` once (a quick local round trip; fine at
  startup), `watch(f)` calls `f` on a thread now, after every
  `SettingsChanged` and after app_server restarts; send what you need
  through `olo_kit::proxy()` (or a view's `cx.messenger()`). Tracker follows `tracker.default_view` (the view
  new folder windows open in, column view by default) this way.
  `update(edit)` changes them from an app (read, `edit`, `SetSettings`, on
  a thread), and `watch_power(f)` follows `PowerStatus` the same way
  (the screen locking, the displays sleeping).
* **Menus for the command palette** (`olo_kit::commands`, automatic):
  every kit app answers on `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-menus-<pid>.sock`
  with the menu bar of its last active window, flattened
  (`commands::menus(pid)`: path, label, command, keys as shown, enabled,
  checked), and chooses an enabled one as if from the menu
  (`commands::invoke(pid, command)`), logging the command and who asked
  (`asked to choose a menu command`, the sender's name and pid). Both
  block for at most a second; call them off a looper. (`MenuBar`
  keeps them up to date as it draws: `agent::set_menus`.)
* **What a window shows, for agents** (`commands::tree(pid)`, automatic):
  `{"tree":true}` on the same socket answers with a `WindowTree` per
  window (title, content size, active, nodes in tree order: role, name,
  value, bounds in the content's logical pixels, enabled, clickable,
  focused, checked, selected), from what each window's next frame
  records (`agent::record(g, Node {…})`: the kit's widgets do it
  for themselves; nothing is recorded otherwise). A program that isn't a
  kit app can answer for another process with `commands::serve_trees(pid,
  app_id, trees)` (the Olo extension's host does it for Chrome). Layer
  surfaces (Deskbar, the desktop) answer too, marked with their
  namespace (`layer`). `{"hints":[ID…]}` asks only about the surfaces
  named (their `wl_surface` protocol ids, which app_server knows them by)
  and answers as soon as those have drawn, each tree marked with its
  `surface` and cut by `WindowTree::pickable` to what takes clicks and
  what holds it (a window's text, thousands of nodes, goes): keyboard
  hints ask this way, so they never wait on a window nobody can see.
  (`serve_trees` can't tell its surfaces apart and answers it with all
  of them.) `{"path":ID}` (`commands::path(pid, surface)`) answers with
  the file or folder that surface's window shows (`agent::set_path`), or
  null. `{"about":ID}` (`commands::about(pid, surface)`) answers with
  **what the window says of itself for an assistant asked a question
  from it**: a few plain lines of what the person is in the middle of
  there, as things are when asked (`agent::about_from(cx, |cx| ..)`,
  said once for a window: `agent::has_about`), or null. The palette's
  /ask sends it with a question asked with that window in front.
  Terminal says so (`Terminal::about`, `about_text`: that it's a
  terminal, the showing tab's shell, working directory, what's running
  there when it isn't the prompt, and what's selected, up to 4000
  characters; **never what's merely on screen**, which may hold what
  the person wouldn't think to be sending: only what a question asked
  from the window would be expected to carry). An app whose windows
  have something an answer should fit (a document's kind, a folder)
  says it the same way. **Record any text you paint yourself** that an agent should be
  able to read or click (`style::label` does), and give a painted thing
  that takes clicks a role and name (`Node { role: "Button", name,
  clickable: true, … }`), so agents and keyboard hints can pick it.
  `{"focus":ID}` (`commands::focus(pid, id)`) gives the keyboard to the
  widget with that tree id. Blocks for up to two seconds.
* **What looks off, for agents** (`commands::review(pid)`, automatic):
  `{"review":true}` on the same socket runs the layout review (see
  "Layout review" under Testing) over the next frame of every window and
  answers with a `WindowReview` per window (title, content size, scale,
  findings: level, kind, what and where); `olo-screen review` and
  `tsession review` print them (`--all`: Deskbar and the other layer
  surfaces too, found by the processes on the session's display, since
  they have no window to find them by).
* **How a window keeps up** (automatic): `{"frames":true}` on the same
  socket answers, per window, the frames drawn since the last ask and
  the slowest and total time drawing them (`FrameTimes`, microseconds
  from taking input to handing the frame to the GPU), each frame's mark
  (when, how long, where its scroll views were: each scroller's place
  as the display thread drew it, kept by its `Stage`, and what a view
  that scrolls itself said as it drew, `Painter::note_scroll`: the
  editor, Terminal)
  and the GPU drawing them. The UI thread answers it, so how long the
  answer takes is how long the app would keep a person waiting
  (`tools/dev/perf-fuzz`).
* **⌘A in text fields** selects all of the field: a `TextField` with the
  keyboard takes ⌘A, ⌘C, ⌘X and ⌘V itself; otherwise they go to the
  menu's Select All, Copy, Cut and Paste.
* **Full screen**: `WindowOptions::new(..).fullscreen()` opens it full
  screen on the display the person is at, asked before its first frame
  (app_server folds it into the first configure), for something that takes the whole of the person's
  attention and is done from the keyboard (the palm trainer).
* **Fixed-size windows**: `WindowOptions::new(..).min_size(w, h)` with
  `fixed` (preference panels, alerts); `max_size(w, h)` fixes a side
  where it's no larger than the smallest (a Find panel's height), and
  app_server neither tiles nor groups such a window.
* **Dialogs** (`WindowOptions::dialog()`; `alert(..)` for alerts): a
  window that belongs to another and should stay in front of it without
  being its size. The kit marks it with `xdg_dialog_v1` (alerts are also
  `set_modal`); app_server opens it over its parent before its first
  frame (kept on screen), never groups it into the parent's tabs and
  keeps any child above its parent when the parent is clicked, focused
  or raised (`wm.rs` `keep_children_above`). `child()`: a window over
  the app's window with the keyboard (a chat's Info), never a tab beside
  it. A service's dialog for another program (the screen-sharing picker)
  takes `.foreign_parent(handle)`, the `wayland:HANDLE` that program
  exported (xdg-foreign; a portal is given it as the parent window): the
  kit imports it and sets it as the window's parent, and app_server opens
  it over that window as it does over one of the app's own. The other
  way, `cx.export_handle(done)` exports a window of
  ours and gives its handle (None without xdg-foreign), for a program we
  start to open over it: the file panel's look (`olo-viewer --look
  --over=HANDLE`). A window opened over its parent that then sizes
  itself (the look, fitted to its picture once loaded) is centred over
  it again, until it's moved or the person resizes it (app_server
  `keep_centred`, `WindowMeta::centred`).
* **A terminal's keys** (Terminal): a window that consumes the keyboard
  itself takes key events before the menus (its `key_down`), lets the
  menus' own shortcuts through (`menu::shortcut_command`) and shows
  them as pressed (`MenuBar::raw()`). With a command key app_server turns
  into Ctrl (⌘, or BeOS's Alt: the keyboard profile's, followed live by
  `olo_kit_base::keys::command_key`), app_server sends it to a terminal as
  its *right* Ctrl plus Shift and every physical Ctrl as the left one;
  `olo_kit::right_control_held()` says which, so ⌘ and Ctrl are told apart.
  Outside Olo, or with ⌘ off, ⌘ is any Ctrl.
* Background work goes on workers (`cx.work(work, then)`: what comes of
  it is the view's message; `cx.messenger()` for news on the way), or,
  for the app as a whole, a thread that posts with `Proxy::send`, taken
  in `message_handler`.
* Periodic refresh (clocks, graphs): a timer (`cx.every(interval, ..)`,
  `cx.after(delay, msg)`, the kit's `Due`), or, for a drawing that
  moves with time, `Painter::paint_again_within(seconds)` as it draws;
  never to look for changes on disk: watch them (rule 7 above).
* Layer-shell surfaces (Deskbar, desktop): `WindowOptions::layer(namespace,
  layer, anchor)` and `layer_options(|o| …)` (its output, keyboard,
  exclusive zone, margins). One naming an output not known yet waits for
  it. `keyboard` is `None`, `OnDemand` (focus on click: the desktop) or
  `Exclusive` (every key while it is up: pickers such as Screenshot's
  region overlay; app_server gives it the keyboard on the commit it
  first shows with, and the clipboard's offer with it, so it can paste
  or read the clipboard at once). A click on a top or overlay layer that is `None`
  (Deskbar) leaves the keyboard where it was, never going through to
  what is under it; a menu of its closing hands the keyboard back to
  what had it as the menu opened.
* The pointer's shape: an element's `.cursor(style)`, or in a drawing
  `g.set_cursor_style(style, bounds)` over part of it
  (`CursorStyle::None` hides it, as the screen saver does); shapes
  go to app_server by name over cursor-shape-v1, and app_server draws
  its own cursor for them; apps never ship cursor images.
* Staying awake: `cx.set_keep_awake(true)` holds a zwp_idle_inhibit
  inhibitor on the window (no dimming, screen saver, lock or sleep while
  it is visible) until `false` or the window closes; app_server counts
  these in `PowerStatus::app_inhibitors`. The Viewer and Quick Look hold
  one while a video plays.
* Activation: `cx.activation_token(done)` asks for an xdg-activation
  token from the latest input in the window, to hand to another program
  so its window may come forward; app_server honours a request only with
  fresh input from the asking app (or from the token's maker, when it has
  the keyboard: an app opening a link in another hands its click on), a
  click handed on by one of our programs, or a token it issued itself
  (`olo_protocol::launch_activation_token` asks for one,
  `Request::ActivationToken`, for launchers run without a click, unless
  one is in the environment; `issue_activation_token` asks whatever is
  there, as olo-chrome does: the opener's token in its environment may
  be long spent, and a Chrome running already is handed the new one).
* Scrolling: `ScrollWheelEvent::kind` says whether a wheel's
  notches (eased in by the Wayland client, 48 points a notch), fingers
  on a touchpad or their glide (app_server's `continuous` scrolls) moved
  it, and `touch_phase` where in a scroll it is; fingers and the glide
  stretch past an end and spring back (`Elastic`, which the display
  thread keeps for every scroller, and a view that scrolls itself keeps
  its own:
  Terminal's scrollback, the editor). Keep any rounding to lines as a
  running remainder.
* The menu bar opens a menu on press, as on BeOS; pressing the open
  menu's title again closes it, but a menu that slid open as the pointer
  crossed the bar stays open for that press.
* Session lock (the lock screen only): `olo_kit::lock_session` and
  `unlock_session`. See "The lock screen".

### Drag and drop (`olo_kit::dnd`)

**Spring-loaded tabs** (app_server shell/spring.rs): anything dragged
and held 0.6 s (`SPRING`) over a window's yellow tab brings that window
forward, to the front of its group if it's in one, as a click on its
tab would, so what's dragged can be dropped into it; the drag goes on
over it (Ben, 2026-11-09). A drag that leaves the tab sooner brings
nothing forward; nothing waits while nothing is dragged. Tried in a
tsession: a file dragged from Tracker onto the tab of a StyledEdit
window behind it came forward after 0.6 s (not at 0.3) and the drop
opened the file in it; onto a group's tab behind its front one, that
tab came to the front.

Over Wayland's data device, so it works within a window, between
Olo's apps and with any other Wayland program. (app_server tells a drag
where the pointer is as it starts, `dnd_requested`: an app asks once the
pointer has gone its drag distance, and in a quick drag the pointer is
already over where it goes, and still; until it moved again the drag
had no target, and was let go onto nothing.) Escape ends any drag,
nothing dropped: app_server's for a drag-and-drop (its source told it
was cancelled, the window under it that it left: `escape_drag`) and
for a window being moved (back where it was, zoomed again if it was,
an auto-tiled one in its tile), the kit's Frame for a drag inside a
window; the Escape reaches nobody. As in BeOS (the Be
Book's `DragAndDrop.md`), a drag carries the same data in several types
and offers actions; where it is dropped picks the type and the action.

* **Dragging out:** as a press drags (the button still down),
  `dnd::start(cx, drag, done)` with an `OutgoingDrag`:
  `dnd::files(&paths, copy, move)` carries `text/uri-list` (file://
  URIs: file managers, browsers, editors) and the paths as plain text
  (terminals); add types only Olo knows first; `dnd::as_link(drag)` asks
  a folder for links instead of copies (`dnd::LINK_TYPE`);
  `dnd::picture(cx, icon, size, label, hotspot)` makes the
  picture under the pointer (the icon, its name below in the
  selection's colours). `done` gets the action it was dropped as (None:
  nothing took it). On olo-kit the same is `olo_kit::dnd`:
  `dnd::picture(cx, icon, size, label, hotspot)` and
  `dnd::start(cx, drag, done)` from a view, where `done` makes the
  message the view is sent when the drag is over (the pointer left the
  window with the drag and its leaving isn't told: a view that tracks
  hovering puts that right then, as Screenshot's after-recording card
  does). Viewer and Quick Look drag their file out from the
  picture when it fits (a drag that doesn't pan), Quick Look also from
  its footer's icon, Get Info from its icon. Tracker's folders are
  spring-loaded: a drag resting on one for 1 s opens it. Deskbar takes
  files dropped on a running application's row and opens them with it
  (`open::open_with(handler, paths)`: our apps get them all as
  arguments, a desktop entry at once with %F/%U or once each). Dragging
  a row out carries the application's program as a link (ours, or an
  entry whose command is a program alone); Tracker makes a link named
  as the application, and draws links to our programs with their icons
  (`Entry::app_icon`). Hit-test a drag where the button went down: by
  the time it's a drag the pointer has moved on.
* **Taking drops:** a window that takes what's dragged over it part
  by part says so (`View::takes_drops`), and is asked where as it
  comes, as it moves and as a modifier changes (`View::drop_over(offer,
  at)`: the `DropOffer` is its types, what its source allows, whether
  one of this program's windows dragged it out, its files): it answers
  with the part that would take it, as which type and how
  (`DropAccept`; None refuses), and shows it by invalidating itself: an
  item highlights itself, a view or window outlines itself (2 px,
  keyboard-navigation colour). What's dropped comes to
  `View::dropped` (`Dropped`: target, type, data, action, position;
  `paths()`, `text()`), its data read off the looper. A window that
  only takes files, copied, wherever an element takes them, needs none
  of that: `.on_drop(..)` on the element.
  What other programs drag: Chrome (156, on Wayland) drags a picture out
  of a page as `text/x-moz-url`, `text/html`, text and the picture itself
  as `application/octet-stream;name="sun.png"`, with no `text/uri-list`;
  a link as `text/x-moz-url`, `text/html` and text; a link's address and
  text read as UTF-8 from Chrome, UTF-16 from Firefox. Tracker takes, in
  order: files (`text/uri-list`), a file by its contents (saved under
  its name, made safe to save under), a link (a clipping of its address
  named by its text: "Docs link clipping.txt"), text (a clipping).
* **Text:** press on the selection in a text field and drag it out, as
  on BeOS; dropped back in the same field it moves, anywhere else it is
  copied (a folder makes a clipping). Text dragged over a field shows a
  caret where it would go and is put there, selected; files are left to
  the window. StyledEdit makes a move with `Doc::move_text`, so styles
  and undo follow.
* A secondary-button drag asks (as on BeOS): the place it lands shows a
  menu (Tracker: Move Here / Copy Here / Create Link Here).
* Headless screenshots show the drag picture; `tsession down X Y
  [right]`, several `move`s, then `up [right]` drives one.

Tracker selects as file managers do, in every view (`ListState`'s
methods, above): click, ⌘-click, ⇧-click and ⌘⇧-click; a plain click on
one of several selected leaves it alone (a drag from it takes them
all, and a ⌘ or ⇧ drag from one not selected adds it first); the
arrows (in the icon views, across and a row of icons up and down),
Page Up and Down, Home and End, each with ⇧ to extend; typing selects;
⌘A and Invert Selection (Edit menu); a band from empty space in every
view, with ⇧ adding and ⌘ flipping, scrolling on past the edges (the
icon views lay out only the rows it crosses); Enter or a double-click
on one of several opens them all; Open Parent (⌘↑) comes back with the
folder it was in selected. The desktop, whose icons are anywhere and
have no order, takes ⌘ and ⇧ alike as add or take away. A listing
that changes keeps the selection, anchor and cursor by path.
Folders are listed on workers, so a selection made in code (Show in
Tracker, a new or renamed item, the selection put back after a reload:
`FolderWin::select_paths`) may name items not listed yet: those wait
for their own folder's listing (`pending_select`, by folder) and are
given up once it lands without them, never touching another column's
selection. In column view, `select_paths` on items deeper than the
window's folder opens the columns down to theirs, each selecting the
folder the next one shows, so a window comes back from a reload with
its columns. What such a selection selects scrolls into view, with
some of what's around it, in every view (`FolderWin::show`), and a
change of view keeps the selection in sight. → into a column not
listed yet selects its first item when it lands (`Pane::first`), as it
would have had the listing been there.

Tracker (`view.rs`: `Drag`, `DropTarget`, `take_drop`, `item_drop`):
files drag from every view and the desktop and drop onto folders (in a
view or on the desktop), into a folder window (anywhere in it; in the
column view, a column or past the last one), onto the Trash (moves them
there) or into another app. Within one file system they move, across
file systems they copy, ⌥ copies anyway; Tracker knows which before the
drop from `application/x-olo-device-N` in its own drags, and only its
own drags are moved (another program might delete what it was told was
moved). Text dropped on a folder becomes a clipping file named after
its first words. The desktop keeps icons where they are dropped
(`~/.config/olo/desktop.json`, `icons`: name or path → offset of the
cell from the screen's top-right, in logical px; things dropped onto it
from elsewhere land where they fell; a rename carries the place over);
the rest fill the grid around them, and Clean Up in its menu puts every
icon back on the grid. Terminal types dropped files as their
shell-quoted paths (and text as if pasted), bracketed when the program
asked for it: drag an image into Claude Code there.

### Move to Window: every tabbed app's tabs (`Menu::move_to_window`)

A pattern every app with tabs keeps (Ben, 2026-11-08: "a pattern and
works for all tabbed olo apps: if that app has multiple windows open i
should be able to right click on the tab or tab group and choose move
to window -> <window name>. if that leaves no more tabs in the origin
window then that window should close"). A tab's menu, and a tab group's,
has Move to Window ▸ (a group's: Move Group to Window ▸) built by
`Menu::move_to_window(title, others)`: the app's other windows by their
titles, in natural order, each with the command that moves it there, or
"No Other Windows", greyed. Moved there, the tab (a group's tabs, still a
group) goes in after the window's own tabs and shows; the window it left
closes if that was its last tab. The app's menu bar has the same under
its Tabs menu, for the tab showing. Terminal's tabs and tab groups
(`tab-to:SHELL:TARGET`, `group-to:GROUP:TARGET`, `move_group_to`) and a
window's own tab (the window menu: into another of its app's windows'
group where it shows, `GroupWindow`; a grouped window's whole group
too) use it. An app with tabs of its own uses it on its tabs' and
groups' menus.

### Show on AirPlay and Play On (`Menu::airplay`, `olo_kit::airplay`)

Wherever something can go to a television, its menu has it (Ben,
2026-11-12: "integrated airplay from relevant app menus and by right
clicking the window title / deskbar row / workspace etc."): Play On ▸
where a film is at hand, Show on AirPlay ▸ where a window or a screen
is. `Menu::airplay(title, paired, prefix)` builds it: each AirPlay
receiver paired with, by name, then AirPlay Settings… (Preferences ▸
AirPlay, to pair with another), with a greyed "No Receivers Paired"
above it when there are none. `olo_kit::airplay::paired()` is the list
to give it, read once and then followed (inotify), so a menu built
each time a window draws costs nothing more and a pairing made in
Preferences shows at the next draw; it never asks the network. The
items' commands are `prefix` and `airplay-on:KEY` (the receiver's id,
or its name if it announced none) or `airplay-settings`
(`olo_protocol::airplay::menu_command` reads them), and
`olo_kit::airplay::play_from_menu(command, file)` or
`show_from_menu(command, &Shown::…)` does what one says: a process of
its own (`olo-airplay play` or `show`, with `--notify`, so a receiver
that won't is said in a notification), shown in Deskbar's tray while
it goes, outliving the window that asked. Where it is now: Viewer's
File menu for a film, Tracker's menu for a film (its windows and the
desktop), a window's tab menu, Deskbar's app rows (one window: the
receivers; several: each window's own), Deskbar's workspace headings
(right button: that workspace, live though its display shows
another), the Agent Screens app's Screen menu (one running screen
chosen) and Deskbar's agent screens item (right button). An app with
something to send uses the same.

### Ad-hoc popup menus (`menu::context_menu`, `menu::popup`)

A context menu is `menu::context_menu(cx, menu, position,
on_choose)`; a menu under a button `menu::popup(cx, menu,
anchor, corner, on_choose)` (`MenuField`'s is one). `on_choose` gets the
chosen item's command: an app's own context menus use its menu bar's
command names and send them where the bar's go.

A menu taller than its display is as tall as the display allows (by
`olo_kit::display_height`: its window's display, else, before a popup is
told which it's on, the shortest the app knows of, else the smallest
screen; never unbounded) (24 pt
off its top and bottom, a whole number of items and one arrow, so
neither end shows half an item) and scrolls, as BeOS's did: an arrow at
each end there's more past, which scrolls it (480 pt/s, a tick every
8 ms only while the pointer rests there and there's more) with the item
under the pointer lit as they pass; the wheel scrolls it, and ↑↓ bring
the item chosen into view. A pop-up field's menu opens scrolled to the
item chosen, over the field. Agents read every item, shown or not, and
the arrows (Scroll Up, Scroll Down).

Every item with keys shows them, right-aligned, as the keyboard
profile's platform writes them (on a Mac in Mac order, "⌘O", "⇧⌘T",
"⌃⌘H"; on Windows "Ctrl+O"; on BeOS "Alt+O"), in context menus as in the
bar. Which keys an item has comes from the profile, by its command (see
"Keyboard profiles"): an app gives the Mac's (`Menu::item(…).key("o")`,
`.shift_key("t")`), and the menu bar gives each item the keys its
command has in `olo_protocol::app_keys` for the profile
(`menu::resolve`). A context menu gives each item without keys the
keys its command has in the window's menu bar, resolved
(`Menu::keys_from(&bar)` after `menu::resolve(&mut bar, raw)`), so a
context menu's Open shows ⌘O without the app saying so twice; keep
context menu commands the bar's. Keys that
aren't a ⌘ shortcut of the window's own (a desktop shortcut from
`olo_protocol::shortcuts`, a plain key such as Space for Quick Look)
are named with `.keys("⌃⌘H")` after the item (`Action::keys`); they are
only shown, whoever gets the keys acts on them, and shown in place of
the item's own shortcut if it has one. `Action::key_label()` is what's
shown, and agents read it as the item's `value`. A shortcut on = is
pressed with + too (⇧= types +), as ⌘+ zooms in on a Mac.

In a list of windows, `.minimized(true)` after an item marks a minimized
one: a hollow diamond where the check mark goes and a lighter label
(`style::diamond`), still enabled (choosing it brings the window back);
agents read `minimized` on its `MenuItem` node.

### Tips (`olo_kit::tip`)

A tip is a popup of its own, never drawn inside the window (in a
window smaller than what it says, it would be cut at the edge).
`tip::on(element, key, text)` gives an element one;
`tip::hover(cx, key, text, anchor, hovered)` is the same for a drawing
that follows the pointer itself (`WindowKind::Tip`: an xdg_popup
with no grab and an empty input region, so it takes no clicks; a
card's takes the pointer, below), below
the thing or else above it, slid to stay on the screen; it comes after
a rest, at once if another showed a moment ago, and not after a click
(`tip::pressed`). A text tip says at most 12 lines and 600 characters,
cut short with "…" past them: a tip is a glance, and a cut text's whole
(a file's line) can be any length. `tip::retext(cx, key, text)` changes what a
tip showing says (a live value: Deskbar's widgets' tips), resized and
placed again for it: a popup that changes size is placed again
(`xdg_popup.reposition`, version 3; one resized before its first
configure, as a tip opened at once and given its words straight after,
once that comes), so a tip that grows at the screen's edge stays on it.
So a tip can be wider or taller than its window: Deskbar's tray,
Terminal's sudo window's command.

A tip can be a card (`olo_kit::card`), for more than a sentence:
`tip::hover_card(cx, key, Rc<Card>, anchor, hovered)` and
`tip::recard(cx, key, card)` are `hover` and `retext` for one (a card
handed in while its tip waits to show replaces the one it would have
shown). A card takes the pointer (Ben, 2026-11-14: "i should be able to
move the cursor anywhere in the tip card without the tip card
disappearing -- it should require moving out of the tip card for it to
go away"; `WindowKind::Tip { takes_pointer: true }`, an input region
and no grab): it stays 450 ms after the pointer leaves its widget,
for as long as the pointer is on it, and goes 250 ms after the
pointer leaves it unless it's back on the widget. So a card must not
open over other widgets, which couldn't be reached past it:
`tip::hover_card_beside(cx, key, card, anchor, beside, TipPlace::Left,
hovered)` opens it at `beside`'s side (a row: Deskbar's, the bar's
width at the widget), its top level with it, flipped to the other side
if there's no room, slid to stay on screen (`TipPlace` is
`WindowKind::Tip`'s `place`). While a card lingers, a widget the
pointer crosses on its way there (between the widget and the card's
side) shows its own only if the pointer rests on it 300 ms; any
other takes over at once (Disk to the Token Pool widget under it).
**Things with tips inside one another** (a widget with a card, and in
it a name cut short, whose whole text is its tip: `cut`): the pointer
is on both, and one tip shows. `tip.rs` remembers every thing with a
tip the pointer is on (`Tips::over`, from its `hover(true)` to its
`hover(false)`). A card of what's around stands for all of it: words of
