  view's state): what it holds scrolled in a sunken frame with BeOS
  scroll bars (`horizontal`, `vertical`, `border`, `focused`,
  `background`, which runs under the bars too: they paint their own
  track over it, and stopped at a bar's edge, a point count off the
  device pixels, it left a pixel's seam at 1.75×);
  `ScrollBar::vertical(id, handle)` drives any
  `ScrollHandle` (a list's too): arrows that scroll on while
  held, a track click pages, the knob drags; agents read it as a
  `ScrollBar` with its position, 0 to 1. In a frame it places itself
  inside the frame's two lines on device pixels (`in_frame`).
  `auto_hide(true)` shows the vertical bar only while what it holds
  overflows (panes side by side); its content scrolls (clipped to the
  view, measured) with the bar hidden too, so the bar comes as soon as
  it overflows (not scrolling, a hidden bar's content ran past the view
  over what's below and never showed the bar). When what it holds starts
  or stops overflowing, the view that holds it says what it shows again
  (`invalidate_owner`): a second body. Where that body is costly, keep
  the scroll view in a view of its own (Calendar's preview pane is one:
  inside Calendar's body, every click between an event whose facts
  overflow and one whose facts don't ran all of Calendar's views twice).
- `widgets::SlimScrollBar::new(id, top, shown, total).on_scroll(|to,
  cx|)`: the slim one, there when wanted, for content a BeOS
  bar's column would cost (Terminal's scrollback; use the BeOS bar
  elsewhere). Laid over the box it's given: a thin rounded thumb at its
  right edge (`THUMB` 6, `THUMB_WIDE` 8 under the pointer, with a faint
  track), no arrows. It shows when the pointer comes within `SLIM_NEAR`
  (28) of the edge or the view scrolls (moved against both ends: not
  output added at the end it keeps to, nor a resize), stays while the
  pointer is near or the thumb held, and fades `LINGER` (0.9 s) after,
  over `FADE` (0.22 s): one timer, then the fade's frames, nothing while
  it rests. Hidden it takes no clicks. The thumb drags the view with
  the pointer, a click in the track pages (0.9 of what shows) towards
  it; `on_scroll` hears the top asked for, in the units it was given
  (lines, points). Agents read a `ScrollBar`, its value 0 to 1.
- `style::pill`/`pill_on_baseline`/`pill_width`/`pill_height` (a count
  or tag in a pill, its text on a label's baseline beside it),
  `baseline_at` and `label_on_baseline` (things of different sizes on
  one baseline), `card_ink`/`card_paper` (cards on a gutter).
- `widgets::StatusBar::new(fraction).label(..).trailing(..)` and
  `level_bar` (the bar alone). The trailing note is drawn whole and the
  label cut short ("…", its whole in a tip) to the room it leaves, so a
  label that changes as work goes on never runs into the note nor
  widens the bar's box.
- `copy::secret(text, clear_after)`: a password or one-time code on
  the clipboard, marked for clipboard managers to leave alone
  (`x-kde-passwordManagerHint`), and taken off after `clear_after` if
  it's still ours (nothing if something else was copied since). An app that quits
  while what's on the clipboard is its own runs on with its windows
  gone (`quit` closes them) until something else is copied or it
  takes its own off, so what it copied can still be pasted; launched
  meanwhile, it opens a window again and
  carries on.
- Pinches: `PinchEvent` (the Wayland client binds
  `zwp_pointer_gestures_v1` and turns its pinches into it: where, the
  scale since it began, `step` since the last event, the phase), and
  `on_pinch` on any element as `on_scroll_wheel`. A touchpad's pinch
  (with Preferences ▸ Touchpad's "Pinch to zoom") and a touch screen's
  two fingers on an Olo app both come so. `ImageView` (Viewer's
  pictures, Quick Look) and Viewer's PDF view zoom by `step` about the
  fingers.
- `widgets::ColumnListView::new(id, &model, columns, rows, cell)`:
  BColumnListView, its state in a `ListModel` entity the app keeps
  (`ListModel::new(cx, multiple)`; `state` is the shared
  `olo_kit_base::list::ListState`: its selection,
  anchor, cursor and sort). Only the rows in view are built
  (`uniform_rows`); `cell(&view, &mut Cell, g)` draws each
  (`cell.text(..)`/`text_with(..)`, cut short with "…"). A header
  click sorts (`on_sort`), the dividers drag; a title dragged sideways
  moves its column (past a neighbour once the pointer passes its
  middle, so the others make room as it goes, as BColumnListView's
  did), and the cells, the sort and `cell.column` keep each column's own
  index wherever it shows. The order and widths are kept for the app by
  the list's `id` and the columns' titles (`state/olo/tables/<app>.json`,
  written with the windows' sizes: a column added since goes where it
  was given), so the person's arrangement comes back; an agent reads
  the `ColumnHeader`s left to right and moves one by dragging it, an app
  with `ListModel::column_order`/`set_column_order`. A click, ⇧ and ⌘ clicks,
  a band, the arrows, Page Up and Down, Home and End (⇧ grows), ⌘A,
  and typing a name (`type_select`) select (`on_select`); a press on a
  selected row keeps the selection until the release (for dragging);
  **what's dragged over a list**: the view's `drop_over` asks the model
  what's under the point (`ListModel::row_under(at)`: None outside the
  rows, `Some(None)` over them on no row, the row) and says where it
  would go before it says the list (`ListModel::mark_drop`: a row
  framed, or the rows outlined), which the list draws over its rows
  with its band, at every scale (Tracker's list view: onto a folder's
  row, or into the folder shown; it took no drops at all before
  2026-11-17). A mark drawn through the list moves with its rows. (One
  laid over the list from outside was seen at 1× and 2× and not at
  1.25×, 1.5× or 1.75× that day, in Tracker's list view while a drag
  went over it; that code wasn't kept, and the kit draws such an
  element at every scale: `crates/kit/examples/overlay.rs`, a frame in
  an absolute canvas over a `ColumnListView` in the same box, inside
  it or at its edges, there from the first paint or coming a second
  after (`OVERLAY_EDGE`, `OVERLAY_LATER`), shows at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×,
  1.75× and 2×, each window fresh: so it was that code's.)
  double click or Return opens (`on_open`; **a double click opens at
  its release, where it wasn't dragged**: the second press of two quick
  ones that moves is a drag or a band, as any press is. It opened at
  the press, in the list and in Tracker's icon and column views and
  the Desktop, so a file clicked and dragged at once, within a double
  click's time, opened or did nothing and never dragged; Ben,
  2026-11-17, "it always works if i drag by icon but only sometimes if
  i drag by the name". Anything that opens on a double click and can
  be dragged does it so: the press is kept, `opens`, and the release
  opens); a right click keeps or
  makes the selection and calls `on_context` with where; `on_press`
  sees a left press first, with the row and where, and takes it by
  answering true (a tree's disclosure triangle, drawn by the cell: the
  press opens or closes the row and leaves the selection); a press on a
  selected row, or on a name, that moves three points calls `on_drag`
  with the row (for the app to carry it: DiskUsage's Collector). Columns
  wider together than the view scroll sideways under a horizontal bar.
  `ListModel::reveal(row)` scrolls a row selected in code into the
  middle (olo-kit: `reveal(cx, row)`, once the list is next laid out,
  `ScrollHandle::reveal_in_middle`: a list not yet shown has no view to
  centre it in, and a time zone's list opened at its top);
  `typing()` says a name is being typed (a space is part of
  it). Agents read `Row`s (named by their cells' text, selected or
  not) and `ColumnHeader`s (one scrolled out of view sideways is none
  wide at the view's edge, not clickable). `row_key(|view, row| u64)`:
  a number that changes when what a row shows does (its line's id and
  what a search marks in it): such a row whose key and look are as last
  frame's is kept, moved if scrolled, rather than painted again
  (Log Viewer's screen of 22,000 glyphs), and when the view says what
  it shows again it isn't even made (`Element::row_key_by`: a step of
  the selection makes the two rows it moves between, not the fifty
  kept round what shows), so the key covers all the row shows, what
  the cell painter captures included. Give it
  for any list of many rows, and for any list whose view says what it
  shows often (a selection moved, a folder changing, results coming
  in): without it every row near what shows is painted again each
  time (Tracker's list view, a step of the selection with 47 rows
  showing: 4.9 → 1.9 M instructions with a key). Keep a row's texts
  with what it shows (Tracker's `Entry::shown`, made the first time
  it's drawn) rather than formatting them at every paint, and hand a
  cell text that's shared already as it is (`SharedString::new(arc)`
  for an `Arc<str>`, `new_static` for a fixed word) rather than a
  `String`, which is copied again to be shared (Logs: 3,850 → 2,964
  allocations a step of a live resize, with the kit's own two below).
  `over_cell(row, column, element)` puts something over a cell, in the
  rows (it scrolls with them), in a box where the cell is and as big
  (`ListModel::cell_bounds(columns, row, column)`, as the person
  arranged the columns: keep it inside, a longer name scrolling in its
  field): a name edited in place. A press anywhere on that cell is its,
  not the list's (a click in the field puts the caret there and the
  keyboard stays in it). `no_header()` shows the rows
  alone (a list of things, not of columns: Passwords' items), its
  frame's line along their top; a cell drawn by hand (an icon and two
  lines) says its text to agents with `cell.say(text)`.
  `crates/kit/examples/list.rs` shows one.
- **A control that can't be used is dimmed once.** `Control`'s
  `.disabled(true)` has the element layer fade the whole of it
  (`DISABLED_OPACITY`, a half), so `control.rs` hands the widget's
  painter the state of an enabled control at rest and no widget picks
  a disabled colour of its own as well: a check box's label, a
  button's and a menu field's were dimmed twice, fainter than a
  disabled field's words beside them. What is drawn outside a
  `Control` (a slider's label and value, a field's text, a form's
  note) uses `style::disabled_text`, the panel's text as far towards
  the panel as the fade (`1 − DISABLED_OPACITY`), so the two are one
  grey side by side (measured in pictures: one pixel colour). A
  disabled slider's filled part is the track's own grey, not the
  accent (nothing to suggest it can be moved), and its bar and thumb
  fade as a control's do. `crates/kit/examples/controls.rs` shows
  each beside its live one.
- `style::label_fit` (a label cut short with "…" to a width, measured
  as shaped), `style::label_spaced` and `text_width_spaced` (letters
  spaced out, CSS's letter-spacing, kerning kept: small bold capitals
  such as a tab group's label; `ShapedLine::tracked`, the spaced line
  kept so it isn't shaped again), `style::selection_band`, `style::selection_wash` (a thing
  selected in place: the selection colour see-through, its edge
  inside) and `style::snap_centred`.
- `style::key_combo(g, right_center, keys, color)` and
  `key_combo_width`: keys as menus write them ("⇧⌘P"), each symbol
  laid out on its own a point closer to what follows; one about as tall
  as the capitals (⇧ ⌘ ↵ ⌫ ⏏) is set on their line by its outline
  (Noto's ⇧ sits a pixel low; kept per symbol). Where keys are listed
  one under another (a menu's items, the shortcuts lists, the command
  palette's rows), `style::key_combo_column` and
  `key_combo_column_width` instead: the last key at the left of a cell
  as wide as a capital W, the keys before it against the cell, so the
  modifiers stand in a straight column whatever the last key's width
  (right-aligned as one string each, "⌃⌥I" began five points right of
  "⌃⌥U"; a key wider than the cell, F12 or Space, takes what it needs).
  `key_combo` is for keys by themselves, flush right (a heading's). (A
  menu's frame with the pointer going over its items, release, 2× :
  0.27 ms before, 0.23 after, its `ui` 90 and 94 µs.)
  `style::DETAIL_SIZE`
  (11 points) is for secondary words (a row's subtitle and kind, a
  chip, a caption, a small button); `SMALL_SIZE` (10.5) for graphs'
  labels and headings in capitals. `style::soft_shadow` (an overlay
  panel's), `icons::paint_faded` (an icon of something unusable).
- `widgets::Graph::new(id, series, now)` (live series of timed samples,
  time running right to left, `now` at the right edge: lines drawn as GPU segments over faint
  fills, a grid in quarters and time lines that move with the samples,
  a hover readout, `on_click`/`on_hover` with the time, the next frame
  when the samples have moved a device pixel when `smooth`; agents read
  each series' latest value), `widgets::CellGrid` (Pulse's LED wells,
  `GridCell`s lit in colours, `on_click` with the cell; a click either
  takes is its own, not the clickable card's it's on), and
  `charts::paint_trace`/`paint_bars`/`paint_meter`/`paint_heatmap`/
  `paint_well` (small graphs painted in a canvas: Deskbar's widgets; a
  trace is timed points scrolled to `now`, its frames asked for with
  `charts::tick_within`, the window's one clock below; a heatmap is a
  cell a level, `heatmap_grid` laying them out as big as they go;
  `paint_heatmap_by` colours each cell from its level, as
  `usage_colour` does where full is what to watch: green at none,
  yellow at half, red at all),
  `widgets::legend`/`legend_height` (swatches, names and values, each
  name and value on one baseline: in one row where they fit, else in
  columns lined up, as many as fit, the rows filled evenly, four that
  don't fit a row two rows of two; the names quieter than the values
  but 4.5:1 on the card, as `style::secondary_text` is on a panel; laid
  out by their lengths, the review keeps them on a grid of their own,
  as it does a `TabView`'s tabs). A window's graphs move together on one clock,
  ticking at the finest step of those drawn (graphs of many sizes each
  on its own timer drew a frame for each: twice the frames); each
  graph's grid, fills (`paint_area`) and lines are one layer.
  `widgets::Spectrum::new(series, low, high)` is a `Graph`'s look for
  sound: each `SpectrumSeries` (a name, a colour, a level in dB a band,
  bands spaced evenly in log frequency from `low` to `high` Hz, a fill
  if asked) as a line, `floor(db)` at the bottom and 0 dB at the top,
  lines at 100 Hz, 1 kHz and 10 kHz named under the well
  (`SPECTRUM_LABELS` of its height) and every 20 dB; a silent series
  isn't drawn; agents read each series' loudest band. The levels are
  the app's (`olo_voice::spectrum` makes them from samples): it draws
  what it's given, so a live one is drawn each frame by a small view of
  its own, the rest of the window cached (Try Voice Processing).
  `GraphLayer::new(shelf, now)` draws graphs over a view that stays
  still: the view puts each with `graph.on_layer(&shelf)` (it keeps the
  graph's place and says where it is, and its clip, as it's laid out)
  and empties the `GraphShelf` as it renders; with both cached, a graph
  moving a pixel redraws the layer, not the cards, legends and figures
  around it (Activity Monitor's CPU section, while it was on this kit:
  4.2 ms a frame to 1.4; on olo-kit a `Graph::live` draws itself again
  alone, with no layer to keep).
- `widgets::Timeline::new(id, start, end, step, panels, key)` is a
  forecast's chart, read the other way from a `Graph`: time left to
  right from now, many things about one hour at once. `Panel::plot(title,
  height, Scale)` with `Track`s (`line`, `.thin()`; `columns`, each
  its own colour with `.colors`; `ranges` from lows to highs; `above`,
  each step shaded from its value to the plot's top with its edge
  solid, as a meteogram draws cloud over its base, so values that leap
  hour to hour read as clear air coming and going, not a zigzag;
  `quiet`, read out but not drawn: the cover that shades the cloud),
  `.alpha` for ranges and columns above, `.on_right()` and
  `Panel::right(Scale)` for a second scale, `.guide(value, name)` (a
  line named on a ground of its own: freezing, fog); `Panel::icons`
  and `Panel::arrows` are strips (a sky picture an hour, wind arrows),
  placed by their hours, so the review keeps them on a grid of their
  own. `Scale::new(say).range/.at_least/.from_zero` ends on nice
  numbers from what shows (not the hours past the end), two points in
  from the plot's top and bottom so a line at an end isn't halved, its
  values each on its line. Columns and ranges are drawn first, then the
  lines, the first named on top; each plot's legend is drawn only when
  it fits beside its title. `.now(t)` (a red line), `.nights(spans)`
  (shaded), `.spans(Span)` (an assistant's "dry and calm": yellow over
  every plot, named over the first, two rows of names so none runs
  into another), `.local(f)` (the place's clock, for the hours and day
  names, which may be another time zone's than the computer's).
  `.axis_on_top(true)` puts the axis over the panels (the days, then the
  hours by the plots, ticked down), where it's read first; `.axis()` is
  that axis alone, [`AXIS_HEIGHT`] tall, the same width and gutters as
  the chart, on the document's ground with a line under it, for a
  scroll view to keep in sight (`ScrollView::sticky`, Weather's: Ben,
  2026-11-15: "the timeline should be at the top and stay there as you
  scroll the data so that you always know when it is"). The
  pointer draws a line through every plot and a readout of every
  track's value then, kept inside what shows of the chart (its scroll
  view's, by `WindowCx::listener_shown`, exact, where the painter's
  visible bounds are rounded to bands); hovering draws the chart alone,
  one frame a pointer position (Weather: 0.4–0.9 ms a flush). Agents
  read each plot as a Figure: each track's first value, lowest and
  highest and when.
- `StringView::wrap(true)` (a paragraph, as tall as it wraps to),
  `StringView::cut(true)` (one line as wide as it's given, not as its
  text, cut short with "…" and its whole in a tip and to agents: a path
  that changes as work goes on, DiskBackup's "Now: …", mustn't make its
  window taller or wider), `StringView::size(points)` (a title's or lead's size, its row grown to
  fit), `StringView::beside(points)` (on the baseline of the text of
  that size beside it in its row: a small one centred by itself sits a
  point higher than the plain text beside it; a table's small column
  names on its heading's line, Preferences ▸ Notifications; drawn
  directly, `style::baseline_at` with `style::label_on_baseline`, as
  Backup's list rows' sizes beside their check boxes), `widgets::KeyHint::new("Space", "Next")` (a key's cap and what
  it does, `enabled(false)` dim: for views driven from the keyboard,
  where nothing needs the pointer; agents read "Space: Next"; the cap's
  text and what it does are drawn on one baseline, so they stay level at
  every scale; `level_with(size)` puts both on the baseline of text of
  `size` points beside the hint, the cap moved down with them, so a
  line of larger text and the hint after it read as one line: the
  command palette's 20-pt query and its "Ctrl Files", which centred
  each by its own capitals sat ~3 pt apart), `widgets::Banner::new(Tone::Success, title, line)`
  (news to be seen at once, not read in a status line: a box across its
  column tinted green or red, a large round check or cross
  (`widgets::verdict_mark`), a bold title, a line, `.trailing(…)` what to
  do next; `banner_height()` tall, and `banner_back(window, b, None, p)`
  draws a quiet box of the same shape for what stands in its place
  until it comes, so nothing moves when it does: the palm trainer's
  finished step and its summary),
  `widgets::heading(text)` (bold, a label row tall) and
  `widgets::separator()` (a groove across).
- `widgets::TabStrip::new(id, tabs, active)`: a row of document tabs
  under a menu bar (Terminal's shells), `STRIP_HEIGHT` (34) tall, each
  a `StripTab { label, icon, status, badge, group, faded }`, drawn as
  folder tabs (Ben, 2026-11-14: "folder tabs → labels"; the options page
  is in the journal): BeOS's slanted in Classic, Mac OS 9's rounded at
  the top in Platinum (`Shape`, from the look). The chosen tab is in
  the content's colours (`.content(fill, ink)`: Terminal's screen; else
  a document's), outlined as the window's frame is and open onto the
  content: the line along the strip's foot stops under it. The others
  are a shade off the panel behind that line, lighter under the
  pointer, their outline softer. Each tab is a 1-pixel outline, a
  bevel inside it (lit along its left and top, shaded down its right,
  a device pixel each at 1×, `scale.round()` at others) and its fill,
  every edge on device pixels (`folder`, `side_folder`; a tab's icon
  or badge painter can ask what it is drawn over,
  `strip::drawn_over()`: the tab's own fill, for a mark's rim), and ends
  where the strip does: its outline meets the line along the foot on
  the line's own last row (it ran a pixel past it, a tick under each
  lower corner and a row of a tab behind's colour under the line, at
  every scale: 143 to 290 stray pixels in the two rows under a
  two-tab strip, none now). The × shows on
  the chosen tab and the one under the pointer (red under it; a badge
  in its place otherwise). Each tab is as wide as its title needs in
  bold (between `TAB_MIN` 140 and `TAB_MAX` 250, or `max_tab_width`),
  the widest cut back alike when they don't all fit (`fit_widths`, on
  the 2-point grid, those under the cut rounded up so no title loses a
  fraction of a point), titles cut short with "…"; its icon only with
  room for it, its title only with room for a few letters.
  `.groups(vec![StripGroup { name, color }])` and each tab's `group`:
  a group is led by a label, a folder tab of its colour with its name in
  bold capitals spaced 0.6 points (`style::label_spaced`), the ink the
  look sets for it (`Palette::label_ink`); a gap between tabs (the
  look's, 2 or 3 points), more between groups (`GROUP_GAP`, 14). Group
  colours come from the look, never from the app:
  `Palette::group_colors()` (`GROUP_COLORS`, 8, in the same order in
  every look: red, orange, yellow, green, teal, blue, purple, grey, so
  the index an app keeps is the same colour after the look changes) is
  each colour's name, fill and ink. Platinum's are Mac OS 9's Finder
  labels, Classic's (and the BeOS colours') BeOS's bright even hues,
  every other look's its own hues; by day white names on deep fills
  (yellow and orange, and Mac OS 9's bright green and cyan, take the
  ink), at night lifted fills with a near-black name, as Chrome's tab
  groups are. With `.group_selection(chosen)` a label filled is a
  group chosen (or shown: Terminal fills every label while every group
  is tiled) and one on the panel, its name in its colour, not; a click
  gives `ToggleGroup(g)`, the right button `Group(g, pos)`. `chip(g, r,
  name, color, filled, hovered)` and `chip_width` draw a label anywhere
  else (Terminal's pane heads). `.closed()`: what's under the strip
  isn't the chosen tab's (Terminal's Tile All Tabs, every tab's pane),
  so the chosen tab stays closed, the line running under it. A tab with
  `faded: Some(why)` is left out of something the window shows
  (Terminal's Hide When Tiled): its icon and title drawn at
  `STRIP_FADED` (0.45), and agents read `why` in its name ("…, hidden
  when tiled"). `crates/kit/examples/tabs.rs` shows both strips, two
  groups and a tab view in the same look.
  `.side()` puts it down the content's left: rows on the panel, the
  chosen one a folder tab on its side open onto the content at its
  right (its outlines meeting the ends of the column's edge line), one
  under the pointer on a shade of the panel, a group's label above its
  rows (`STRIP_SIDE_HEADING`, 22), a gap between groups, New Tab a row
  after the last, the right edge dragged to resize (`Resize`). Its
  icons are at `WINDOW_INSET`, under the menu bar's first title
  (`SIDE_FACE`), and its first row is centred on `STRIP_SIDE_HEAD` (as
  a strip along the top: the pane heads beside it).
  Agents read a side label and New Tab as what shows (the label; the +
  and its name), though their whole rows take a click. A tab dragged rides as the chosen one under the pointer,
  its slot left empty, a caret over the gap where it would land (in the
  band above the tabs, or beside the rows: never under the tab riding
  there); out of the strip
  (`TEAR`) it's torn off (`TearOff`, `TearOffGroup` for a chip). A
  window of the app moved over the strip marks where its tabs would go
  (`strip::window_over`, from app_server's `WindowOver`: the strip is
  told which window it's in, `.in_window(cx.surface_id())`), and let go
  there `strip::on_window_dropped(handler)` gets the two windows'
  surfaces and the place (`strip_place`), on the commands socket's
  thread. It is one drawing: where everything goes is worked out as
  it's drawn and kept, with the press, the drag and what's under the
  pointer, in the element's own state (`node_state`), which its
  handlers go by; the pointer coming to a tab or leaving it (or the
  strip, for a menu over it) draws it again only when what it's over
  changes. An icon that turns (`PaintFn`, handed the painter) asks to
  be drawn again itself (`Painter::paint_again_within`).
  What the person did comes to `.on_action(|&StripAction, cx|)`.
  Agents read each tab as a `Tab` (its title, status and group in its
  name, `selected`), its close box, the chips and New Tab as buttons.
- `WindowOptions::max_size(w, h)` (xdg `set_max_size`): a window no larger along a side than its smallest is
  fixed along it, and app_server neither tiles nor groups it (Terminal's
  Find panel, fixed in height). `WindowOptions::under_pointer` and
  `olo_kit::begin_move(cx)`: a window torn off a strip opens with its
  tab under the pointer and moves with it.
- `MenuBar::raw(cx, menus)`: the bar's shortcuts as the app presses them
  (a terminal's ⌘ keys), not the profile's; `menu::resolve(&mut menus,
  raw)` gives a context menu the same keys (`Menu::keys_from(&bar)`
  after resolving the bar). `keys::unshifted(key)` maps the symbol a keystroke
  names for a shifted key ("_") to the key and Shift ("-", true);
  `olo_kit::right_control_held()` says whether the right Ctrl (the Mac
  profile's ⌘) is down, for a raw-keys window telling ⌘ from Ctrl.
- `widgets::Slider::new(id, value, range)`: BSlider (label and value
  above, the bar filled to a raised thumb, `limits` under the ends;
  `step`, `fill`, `width`); a press or a drag sets it, the arrows, Home
  and End once it has the keyboard; `on_change` gets each value. Its
  label gives way to its value, cut short with "…" (the whole in a tip)
  where the two don't fit: Performance's Watchdog pairs met in German,
  Spanish and French.
- `file_panel::show(cx, title, FilePanel::open(dir) / save(dir, name) /
  folder(dir), on_done)`: the shared Open, Save and folder panels (see
  "What every app does the same way"), in a dialog window of their own; `on_done` gets an
  `Answer` (the `PanelResult`, the filter and choices made, the folder)
  once, Cancelled if the window is closed. `types`, `filters` (a Show
  pop-up), `multiple`, and the app's `choices` (check boxes or
  pop-ups). Listing on a worker, following the folder as it changes;
  the folder pop-up goes up, to the standard folders, favourites and
  recent ones; Save asks before replacing; Space looks in the Viewer;
  an item's menu has Quick Look, Open With ▸ and Show in Tracker.
- `open_with`: Open With, the same in every app that shows files
  (Tracker's windows and desktop, Quick Look, the file panels).
  `open_with::kind_of(names)` is the kind a selection all is (None:
  mixed); `open_with::menu(kind)` the submenu, **always there for a
  file**: the apps worked out for it (`olo_xdg::open::offer`: as kept,
  else worked out then, 0.1 to 0.2 ms; warm the kinds where the files
  are listed, off the UI thread, `olo_xdg::open::warm`, so a menu finds
  them; what's kept holds while the person's choices and the installed
  apps are as they were, a few `stat`s to tell), the one it opens in
  marked "(default)", Other…, and Always Open With ▸ (the kind's
  checked) to make another its default; a kind no app knows gets Other…
  alone. (The submenu was missing for any kind not warmed: a file whose
  kind came after the listing, and every kind after an Always Open
  With, which forgot them all.)
  **What each of Olo's apps opens is said once, in
  `olo_xdg::open::OPENS`**: per app, `opens` (the kinds it is the app
  for: a type, or a family, "text/*"), `narrower` (kinds whose every
  narrower kind it takes too, by shared-mime-info's subclasses: a kind
  of text or XML is StyledEdit's, after any installed app that says it
  opens that very kind) and `also` (offered in Open With without being
  what the kind opens in: StyledEdit for a Word or OpenDocument text,
  the Viewer for text; Phone for a number to dial, `x-scheme-handler/tel`,
  as a link in a text view opens one). Open With, what a double click opens
  (`open::handler`) and the entries written for other programs
  (`open::for_others`, from `opens` alone) all read it, so **an app
  that learns a format is added there and nowhere else**; the test
  `what_olos_apps_open` holds every extension the Viewer and StyledEdit
  read to it (add the extension to the test's lists with the reader).
  A name two kinds claim alike (`*.json`: JSON and a JSON schema) is
  the broader of them (`mime::from_name`). `open_with::is_command(cmd)` tells its commands, and
  `open_with::run(cmd, kind, paths, cx)` does one: opens with the app
  (Always: and makes it the kind's, `open::set_default`), on a thread,
  or opens Other…, `OpenWithWin` (every app that opens files,
  `open::every_app`, read on a worker, found by typing part of its
  name; ↑↓ and Return; "Always open files like … with it"), a dialog
  over the window in front that closes itself
  (`open_with::window_options()` to open it yourself).
  A panel is
  a window on a looper of its own: `file_panel::show(title, panel,
  on_done)` takes no context, and `on_done` (`FnOnce(Answer) + Send`) is
  called once on the panel's looper, so it sends the asking view a
  message (`cx.messenger()`) rather than touching it, as a BFilePanel
  messages its target; `open_with::run(cmd, kind, paths)` likewise.
  The kit's `examples/panel.rs` opens each; `tools/dev/kit-compare
  OLD NEW --do "click 50 30" --then Open` compares, in two builds, a
  panel the steps open (`--then TITLE`).
- Menu items take icons (`Menu::icon(name)`, an item's or a submenu's):
  a column of them between the check marks and the labels, faded when
  the item can't be chosen.
- A button that opens a menu under itself: in its `on_click`,
  `cx.listener_bounds()` is where the button is (`menu::popup(cx, menu,
  bounds, Corner::BottomLeft, ..)`).
- `olo_kit::on_upgrade_due(f)` and `olo_kit::upgrade_waits_while(
  busy)`: a server finishes what is under way before it becomes its new
  version (Token Pool's drain); `busy` is asked four times a second
  while an upgrade is due.
- Tips are `olo_kit::tip` (the palette's tooltip colours, BeOS's pale
  yellow in light mode): see "Tips" above.
- `olo_kit::stay_resident()`: the app keeps running with no windows
  (an agent); otherwise it quits when its last window closes.
- `icons::paint(g, bounds, name)`: Olo's icon set (or a theme's,
  or a file's), from the bitmap made for the device size it's shown at,
  a texture pixel to a device pixel; decoded once, on a worker, the
  windows drawn again as each arrives.
- `app_menu`: every app's menus the same (the Olo Book, "Menus"; Ben,
  2026-11-13: "if there is one or more recommended settings apps/panels
  that are related then those should also be launchable from that
  app's menus. also standardize the olo apps menus"). The first menu
  starts with `Menu::app_items(&[panels])`: About *App* (`about-app`:
  an alert of the app's icon, its name from `olo_xdg::apps::OUR_APPS`,
  Olo's version, and About Olo Desktop…, Preferences' About), Keyboard
  Shortcuts (`keyboard-shortcuts`: `olo-palette --shortcuts`, the sheet
  of the front app's keys then the desktop's, showing the profile's
  keys for it), then a "*Panel* Settings…" item for each panel
  (`pref:PANEL` or `pref:PANEL/TAB`: `olo-preferences PANEL --tab TAB`,
  `app_menu::open_settings`; Deskbar's items use the same commands and
  labels, `settings_label`), and a separator. It ends with
  `close_quit()` (Close ⌘W, Quit ⌘Q) or, for a window of a program
  that keeps running, `close_item()`. `MenuBar` and agents' `invoke`
  run these three kinds of command themselves (`app_menu::run`) before
  the app's `command`. Each app's settings: Activity Monitor
  Performance; Doctor Performance, Power; DiskBackup Backup; Logs,
  DiskUsage, DriveSetup none; Notifications' History Notifications;
  Passwords Security ▸ Passwords; Token Pool AI, Deskbar; Agent Screens
  AirPlay, Terminal; StyledEdit Appearance, Default Apps; Telegram
  Integrations, Notifications; Terminal Terminal, Integrations; Tracker
  Tracker, Default Apps; Viewer Default Apps, AirPlay.
  `app_menu::review(menus)` is what the window review
  (`review::review_window`, so `tsession review`, the live and the
  built-in layout lint) finds wrong with a bar, as errors of kind
  `menus`: About not first, Quit or Close not last, a standard command
  (`STANDARD`: new, open, save, save-as, close, quit in the first
  menu; undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, select-all, find, find-again,
  find-previous, find-selection in Edit; zoom-in, zoom-out in View)
  in another menu or called otherwise ("Find…", "Find Again"), a
  settings item outside the first menu or not "… Settings…", two
  enabled items with the same keys. What a command is called is read in
  the English the app wrote (`Action::english`: kept by `Menu::item`, or
  said with `Menu::english` for an item whose label was made in the
  language already, as Undo's and Redo's are), the same in every
  language: in another, an item says it its own way ("Nueva ventana"
  doesn't begin with "Nuevo"), and one not translated yet is still
  English. A command that only looks like a
  standard one gets a name of its own (DiskUsage's Item ▸ Open is
  `open-item`; Tracker's Find…, a query of the disk, is in Edit as
  every Find… is, not BeOS's File). Windows without a bar (Preferences'
  panels, DeskCalc) aren't held to it.
- `menu`: BeOS menus (`Menu::new(title).item(label, command).checked(
  on).separator().submenu(m)`), shown as Wayland popups
  (`WindowKind::Popup`, an xdg_popup over the window at a corner of an
  anchor rectangle, flipped or slid by app_server to stay on screen):
  `menu::context_menu(cx, menu, position, on_choose)` and
  `menu::popup(cx, menu, anchor, corner, on_choose)`. Drawn as
  BeOS drew them; ↑ ↓ → ← Enter Space Escape; a submenu opens
  beside its item; items are `MenuItem`s to agents. `Menu::entries`
  flattens one for the palette (`agent::set_menus`). `Menu::sorted()`
  puts a list's items in alphabetical order by what they say (natural
  order, case aside), each run between separators on its own, its
  submenus' too, all the way down (Deskbar's Applications, Other
  Applications and Preferences). Keys are drawn as
  the kit's key combos (`style::key_combo`: each symbol on its own, ⌘
  and ⇧ tightened and lifted onto the capitals' line). `.minimized(on)`
  marks an item a minimized window (a hollow diamond where the check
  goes, a lighter label, `minimized` to agents), as a Mac's Window menu
  does. A menu shows no separator at either end or two together, so one
  built with items it has only sometimes needs no care with them (a
  menu field's, whose items are counted, is left as it is). A press anywhere in the window a menu opened over puts it away
  (the `Frame` sees it first: app_server's popup grab hands an app's
  own window the presses outside its menu), and that press doesn't
  open it again on what opened it, so a second click on a button
  closes its menu. `menu::popup_then(.., on_close)` is `popup` with
  word when it has gone, for what shows its menu open (Deskbar's rows).
  (Still to come: scrolling a menu taller than the screen, and
  press-drag-release choosing from the press that opened it.)
- `MenuBar::of(self, cx, |v, cx| v.menus(cx))` at the top of a window's
  view: the BeOS menu bar, **its menus asked of the view** at every
  body and again whenever they're used (a key nothing else took, a menu
  opening, the palette or an agent asking: `menus_now`), as BeOS's
  `MenusBeginning`: an item's `enabled`, check and label are right when
  it's chosen, whatever they go by, a child view's state too. Every
  window's bar is made so, and the window review fails one that isn't
  ("menus: … only as its body last said them"): `MenuBar::said` where
  the body already made them, `MenuBar::asked` for an app that keeps its
  windows' state itself and may be busy (Terminal, Passwords:
  `try_lock`, or they stay as said), `MenuBar::fixed` for menus that
  never change; `menu::offer` and `offer_asked` the same for a window
  with no bar. (`MenuBar::new` made them once a body: Viewer's Find
  Again goes by what its preview, a view of its own, has found, the
  window's body didn't run as that changed, the item stayed off and ⌘G
  did nothing; Ben, 2026-11-17. Quick Look's the same.) Saying them
  costs 30 to 90 µs a time (Viewer 29, Tracker 72 with 300 files,
  StyledEdit 92; release), at each key nothing else in the window took.
  **Find is the same everywhere**: `Menu::find_items(again)` (Find…,
  Find Again, Find Previous; the review fails a window with one of the
  last two and not the other; StyledEdit's and Terminal's Find Previous
  go the other way from their "Search backwards") and
  `Menu::find_selection`; a find bar's ⇧Return (the match before) is
  the bar's own (`widgets::find_bar`: a one-line field lets ⇧Return go
  on, so the views' "Entered with ⇧" never came).
  A press on a title opens its
  menu under it; with one open, sliding across the bar opens the
  others; a press on the open title puts it away (one that slid open
  stays for its first press, as on BeOS), and so does a press anywhere
  else in the window (`press_in`). The bar knows its menu by its popup,
  not its place: the popup a slide replaced goes after the new one
  opens, and taken by place the bar forgot the new menu and opened
  another over it, which xdg-shell forbids (a menu may open only on the
  topmost), so app_server ended the app's connection (Olo Doctor,
  2026-11-01). The Wayland client guards against any app doing that: before a menu
  opens, our menus showing outside its parent's chain are taken down
  (`withdraw_stray_menus`, with a warning). Items take keys with
  `Menu::key("w")` / `shift_key("z")` / `shortcut(..)` (a Mac's: the
  command key is Ctrl to an app), and `menu::resolve` gives every item
  the keys its command has in the keyboard profile (`olo_kit_base::keys`:
  Mac, Windows or BeOS keys and labels, followed live from app_server's
  settings). The window's `Frame` has the keyboard when
  nothing in it does and takes the bar's keys that nothing else took
  (a text field's ⌘C stays its own). With no `agent::set_menus`, the
  command palette reads and invokes the front window's bar. Titles
  that don't fit the window (tiled at its least width, a side of Main
  and Stack) go in a » title at the bar's end, its menu ("More Menus",
  to agents too) having them as submenus, as Qt's menu bar extension and
  the toolbar's » (`title_rects`, `toolbar::chevrons`); BeOS cut them
  off, and the live review called the cut title an error.
  `agent::invoking(cx)` says whether the command being run came through
  the commands socket (an agent's `invoke`, the palette) rather than a
  hand on the display (a click, a key): for the few a program mustn't
  give itself (Terminal's Auto Approve asks the person first then).
- A menu bar's menus are built when the view that holds it says what
  it shows (its `body`), not each time the window draws: a window
  whose picture moves (a video, a live agent screen, a scan's progress)
  draws that picture alone. (Building, resolving and copying the
  Viewer's menus each frame would be 32 µs of a 4K60 frame.) Opening
  a menu, a key the bar takes and an agent's or the palette's
  look read the menus the view last gave, so a view whose menus depend
  on its state invalidates itself when that changes.
  `Menu::keys_from(bar)` gives a context menu the bar's keys.
- `undo::History<C>`: Undo and Redo, one way for every app. A step is
  named for what it did ("Rename", "“Volume”") and holds what the app
  needs to take it back (`C`); `done` records one (`done_merging` folds
  a run of the same thing into one step: a slider dragged, a field typed
  in, while each comes within 1.5 s and nothing was undone); Undo takes
  the last off (`take_undo`), the app takes it back and records what that
  did with `Purpose::Undo` for Redo, and the other way round, so both
  lists hold what was done and a step goes back and forth; something new
  forgets Redo's. `edit_items(menu)` adds Edit ▸ Undo *name* and Redo
  *name* (commands `undo`, `redo`, the profile's keys). A window with no
  menu bar says its menus all the same (`menu::set_menus(cx, menus)`,
  as its view says what it shows): their keys work when nothing in the
  window took them (a text field's ⌘Z is its own), and agents and the
  command palette find Undo and Redo among them. (Any item's keys, as a
  bar's: `set_menus` gives them their keys from the profile, and the
  Frame chooses the item pressed, `menu::bar_shortcut`. Until 2026-11-16
  only Undo and Redo worked so, and a bar-less window's ⌘C did nothing:
  Tracker's Quick Look, Ben: "copy/paste doesn't work in quick look
  viewer -- it should". Its Edit menu is said that way: Copy, which is
  what's selected of a text and otherwise the file itself as Tracker's
  Copy copies it, Select All, Find…, Find Again and Find Previous.) Tracker (files: undo.rs) and Preferences
  (settings: undo.rs) use it. An app that keeps its steps its own way
  names them alike with `undo::edit_items_named(menu, undo, redo)` (each
  the next step's name, None for none; `edit_items_as` with commands of
  its own): StyledEdit's document (each step named by the command that
  made it, `Doc::name_next`, else by the edit: Typing, Delete, Move,
  Replace All, Table…), the Viewer's picture edits (`Op::name`: Rotate
  Left, Crop…), its video edits (Cut, Add Mark, Trim, Mute…) and its
  PDFs' (Typing, Check, Choice, Move, Resize, Drawing, Signature…); their
  toolbars' tips are the menus', so they say it too. A text field's own
  Undo takes back a run of typing at once (letters typed where the last
  went, within 1.5 s: one step, a space starting the next), as the kit's
  runs do; an app's own edit of a field is a step too when it should be
  (`TextField::replace_all`: DeskCalc's keys, Clear, a result, so ⌘Z
  after = brings the sum back), and its Undo and Redo can be an app's
  commands (`can_undo`, `undo_step`: DeskCalc's menu has them). What's
  left is in TODO ("Undo everywhere it makes sense").
- `WindowOptions::floating()`: the xdg-toplevel-tag `floating`, so
  app_server floats it over auto-tiled windows. `child()`: the window
  belongs to the app's window that has the keyboard (its xdg parent:
  a chat's Info over its chat), opening over it rather than as a tab
  beside it; `dialog()` is that and never a tab.
  `restore_key(key)`: what app_server knows the window by when its app
  comes back (a restart, an upgrade), the xdg-toplevel-tag word
  `restore:KEY`: its place, workspace, tab's place in its group and
  tile are this window's and no other's of its title. A key the same
  for the same window each time, unique among the app's (a document's
  path, a number kept in the app's saved state: Terminal's).
- What's kept between frames (the Olo Book, "Views", "Drawing",
  "Frames"): a view says what it shows only after `cx.invalidate()`;
  what comes of it is compared with what the window has, and an
  element that's the same keeps its layout and its drawing; a `canvas`
  with a key (`paint_key`, `key_by`) is drawn again only when the key
  changes. What agents read is kept with each drawing, so one that
  wasn't drawn again still says what it shows. A view's `body` runs
  whole when it's invalidated, so keep what changes often (a caret, a
  code counting down, a graph moving a pixel) in a small view of its
  own (a `Child`, invalidated alone) or in a drawing that asks to be
  drawn again in time (`Painter::paint_again_within`), beside what's
  costly, not around it: Passwords' item pane is a view of its own, so
  a one-time code counting down draws that pane alone, once a second.
- Glyphs a window will show are drawn ahead, off its looper: the text
  system does it for running text once it has drawn a few dozen of a
  face's glyphs (a glyph drawn the first time costs a frame ~12 µs; a
  chat of new text, 3 ms), and follows the window to another scale or
  text rendering.
- `WindowCx::warm_text(font, size, texts)` has the colour
  glyphs (emoji) of `texts` drawn ahead the same way, in the order
  given (shaped, then drawn on the warming thread without holding the
  text system, 16 texts at a time), kept for every window of the app
  after, and drawn again for a display of another scale the window goes
  to: the emoji picker's ~1,900 at open, so a search's first frame
  copies them (its slowest typing frame at 2×: 8.1 → 1.0–1.5 ms).
- `WindowCx::activate_window_with_token(token)` raises a
  window with an activation token another program gave (a notification
  clicked: `NoteEvent::Action`'s), which lets it take the focus.
- `WindowOptions::layer(namespace, layer, (top, bottom, left, right))`
  makes a layer surface (Deskbar, notifications, an overlay) instead of
  a window; `layer_options(|l| ...)` sets its exclusive zone, margins,
  keyboard (`LayerKeyboard::OnDemand` for the desktop, `Exclusive` for a
  modal overlay) and output; `no_panel()` leaves its background to it
  (transparent: what's under it shows). One anchored at both ends of
  an axis (across its output) is given its size there by app_server,
  so it opens with any size (1 × 1 is usual) and is laid out and drawn
  only once that comes (`PlatformWindow::awaits_size`, then
  `WindowEvent::Sized` from its stage's first frame), as is a lock
  surface: nothing is worked out at a size it never shows at, and its
  first frame comes no later for it (palette, picker, desktop, Rescue,
  greeter, screen saver measured). Menus open over it as over a
  window (`examples/layer.rs`); a layer that only carries a menu takes
  the keyboard `OnDemand`, as app_server gives every key to an
  exclusive one, past the menu's grab. `menu::context_menu_then(window,
  cx, menu, at, on_choose, on_close)` is `context_menu` with word when
  it has gone (to take such a layer away; `MenuPopup::close` puts it
  away, for a click on the layer, which the grab lets through as the
  same program's). A drawing can't open a window (it only looks): it sends its
  view a message, which does.
- `tip::hover(cx, key, text, anchor, hovered)` (from an
  element's `on_hover`) and `tip::pressed(cx, key)`: tips in a
  popup of their own (`WindowKind::Tip`, an xdg_popup that takes
  no input and grabs nothing), for a window too small to hold them
  (Deskbar's tray): after the pointer rests half a second, at once if
  one showed a moment ago, not after a press; below the anchor, else
  above, slid to stay on screen; in the tooltip colours, wrapping past
  360 points. `tip::on(element, key, text)` gives any element one.
  `tip::hover_card` / `tip::recard`: the tip a `card::Card` (a title,
  value and caption, then drawings, rows with bars and notes), which
  the pointer may move onto and rest on; `tip::hover_card_beside`
  opens it beside a row (`TipPlace::Left` / `Right`) so it covers no
  other widget: see "Tips" above.
- `dnd`: dragging out to another app or a folder
  (`WindowCx::start_drag`, Wayland's data source with a
  picture surface): `dnd::files(paths, copy, move)` (text/uri-list and
  the paths as text), `dnd::as_link` (Olo's make-a-link type, for an
  application dragged out of Deskbar), `dnd::picture(cx, icon,
  size, label, hotspot)` (the icon faded a little, its name below in
  the selection's colours, on whole device pixels; the name drawn on
  the CPU by `TextSystem::line_mask`), and `dnd::start(cx, drag,
  done)` while the press is down (`done` gets what it was dropped as).
  Ask for the icon's bitmap ahead (`icons::bitmap`) as the press comes,
  so it's decoded when the drag starts. Files dropped come to an element's
  `on_drop` (`ExternalPaths`; an app's own drag isn't dropped back on
  it); a window that takes what's dragged over it part by part says so
  (`View::takes_drops`, `drop_over`, `dropped`).
- `widgets::ImageView` (`image_view(cx, zoomable)`, `set_picture`): a
  picture (anything `Rgba`: its size and premultiplied pixels, as
  olo-preview's `Bitmap`) fitted to its view at a point a pixel at
  most, or zoomed (`zoom(Some(true))` a step in, `Some(false)` out,
  `None` to fit; `set_scale(1.0)`: Actual Size) and panned by dragging. Shown pictures are resampled exactly to
  their device size (Lanczos, `fast_image_resize`) on a worker, the last
  exact one standing in until the next comes; magnified, it is cut into
  512-pixel tiles drawn pixel for pixel, and a small one (256 pixels or
  less) is drawn with nearest sampling so its pixels stay sharp.
  Transparency shows over a checkerboard. `picture_bounds` says where it
  is drawn (an overlay's place), `set_still` stops pan and zoom,
  `on_drag_out` takes a drag where it doesn't pan; `resampled(src,
  size)` is the resampling alone (Lanczos made smaller, Catmull-Rom made
  bigger: a 1024 × 640 screen magnified to 1421 × 888 in 3 ms against
  9, `resample_timing`).
- A view that fills its box (`size_full`: a `ColumnListView`, a
  `ScrollView`) put in a plain `div` its flex parent stretches comes
  out none wide: make that `div` a flex column
  (`flex().flex_col()`, the view's place `flex_1`), as Agent Screens'
  History list sits.
- `style::spinner(window, centre, radius, colour)` (a busy spinner, a
  turning arc as a GPU ring slice; ask for the next frame while it
  shows),
  `widgets::check_box_look` (a check box's look alone, for one drawn in
  a canvas: a task list's), `TextField::font(font)` and `max_len(n)`.
- `TextRun::size` (a run at a size of its own in one line:
  code in a paragraph); `Painter::paint_image_nearest` (a picture drawn
  with nearest sampling); `WindowCx::set_keep_awake(on)` (idle-inhibit
  while the window shows); `WindowCx::display_bounds` is the display a
  window is on (`olo_kit::displays()` lists them all, to size a
  window for its content before it opens); displays' sizes are xdg-output's, in points,
  so right at fractional scales (wl_output's whole-number scale made a
  1.5× display 1280 points wide, not 1707), and an output's size and
  refresh are its current mode's (wl_output lists every mode).
- An overlay over something in the flow (a frame over a picture) is
  `.absolute().inset_0()`: an absolute element without insets sits
  where the flow would put it, after what it was meant to cover.
- `brand::wordmark_centred(g, bounds, dark)`: the wordmark (the
  brand's, light or dark; the same in every theme), decoded and trimmed once on a thread,
  averaged down to each height once, a texel to a device pixel;
  `Drawn::Loading` keeps its place, `Missing` asks for the name instead.
- `style::lit_ground`/`lit_edges`: a group current as a whole
  (Deskbar's workspace showing).
- `cx.close_window()` closes the window `cx` is in, from any of its
  handlers (its own button, key or menu command); `WindowHandle::close`
  from anywhere else.
- Keyboard hints: app_server asks by surface (`{"hints":[ids]}`); each
  window answers with its `WindowCx::surface_id()` and what can be picked
  in it. A layer surface's tree carries its namespace (`layer`). Picking
  a text field, a slider or a scroll bar (which a click would change)
  brings its window forward and asks the app to give it the keyboard,
  by its window's surface and its id in that window's tree
  (`{"focus_in":{"surface":S,"node":N}}`, `commands::focus_in`; an app
  from before it is asked `{"focus":N}`, for its window with the
  keyboard): `WindowCx::focus_agent_node` gives it to the element the
  node comes from, or to the nearest that holds it and takes the
  keyboard (an editor's text, said by its drawing). The kits had
  answered `focus` with nothing, so picking a field did nothing.
- Upgrades: when olo-session signals an upgrade (SIGURG) and the app's
  binary was replaced, or app_server restarts in place, `on_upgrade`'s
  state is saved and the app re-executes (as the new version), finding
  it in `restored_state()`. The Wayland client destroys
  every object it makes for a window with it (its fractional scale, its
  xdg-dialog, its idle inhibitor): one left alive names a surface that's
  gone, whose id goes to something else, and olo-wlproxy making it again
  on the new app_server named that (a protocol error that ended
  Notifications on a reload). The proxy now treats an object named in a
  recipe but made after it as gone, for programs that leak them.
  An upgrade restarts olo-wlproxy and app_server one after the other,
  so a program can lose its window's Vulkan surface mid-frame, or the
  compositor again while it reconnects: blade answers a lost surface
  (configuring, acquiring, presenting) with no frame rather than a
  panic, the renderer makes a new surface on the same window
  (`BladeRenderer::remake_surface`, at most every 2 s), and a program
  re-executing connects again if the compositor goes before its
  registry answers. (Telegram panicked on both, 2026-11-02, so an
  upgrade closed it; tried by replacing a copy of its binary, SIGURG
  and `tsession reload` together, twelve times running.)
- `WindowCx::activation_token(done)`: an xdg-activation token
  from the last click in the window, for another program to raise its
  window with (Notifications hands it to the app whose card was
  clicked); `done(None)` when the compositor has none to give.
  `WindowCx::export_handle(done)` (xdg-foreign): the handle another
  program's window can name as its parent (`foreign_parent`) to open
  over this one, exported on first asking and kept until the window
  closes; `done(None)` without xdg-foreign.
  `WindowCx::set_layer_keyboard(LayerKeyboard)` changes a layer surface's
  keyboard as it shows (`OnDemand` while a banner has a reply field,
  `None` otherwise).
- External pictures: another program's dmabuf shown in a
  window by the compositor itself, never copied (Agent Screens' Live).
  - `WindowCx::set_external_buffer(key, Some(ExternalBuffer))` sets the
    picture `key` shows: an id, size, DRM format and modifier, its
    planes' descriptors, and `released`, told the id once the compositor
    is done with it. It's made into a `wl_buffer` once per id (a few
    kept) and shows at once, with no frame drawn.
  - `Painter::place_external(key, bounds)` is called as its drawing
    paints, and kept with it, so a drawing that isn't made again still
    places it. A key not placed is hidden, and None lets it go
    with its buffers.
  - `Painter::external_bounds(bounds)` is where it shows, to the device
    pixel: corners at whole points, then the device pixels the compositor
    rounds them to. Draw round that.
  - `olo_kit::external_modifiers(fourcc)` lists the modifiers the compositor
    takes (linux-dmabuf v3's events). It's empty without a subcompositor,
    viewporter or linux-dmabuf.
  - On Wayland it's a desynchronized `wl_subsurface` with an empty input
    region (the pointer reaches the window under it), scaled by a
    `wp_viewport`. When the place changes with a frame, it's synchronized
    until that frame's commit, so window and picture move together.
- Ordinary hitboxes don't block what is under them: a `Button` or
  `TextControl` placed over something clickable (a card) needs
  `.occlude()` on its wrapper, or the click reaches both.
- `style::monogram(g, r, letter, fill)` (an app without an
  icon: its initial on its colour, `ink_on(fill)` black or white by
  contrast; a grid of its own for the review), `style::stop_mark`
  (BAlert's stop sign, small: an error's title), `style::latch` (a
  folding group's triangle), `style::close_box` (a ×, crisp at any
  scale). `CheckBox::height(h)` and `RadioButton::height(h)` give a
  check box or a radio button a row's height, so it centres on the same
  device pixel as a field, a button or a label beside it at fractional
  scales (elements of different heights centred in one row round their
  tops apart: a radio beside a button was a device pixel off at 1.25×).
  A `BBox` tells the review where its inset is on the device pixels
  layout rounds its children to; measured unrounded, anything flush
  with the inset (a full-width note, a button at the right) read as a
  point past it at 1.25× and 1.75×.
- Wrapping: a space after a word hangs past the edge rather
  than pushing that word down a row, as typesetters and CSS wrap
  ("…with Ann at" fits when "at" does); leading spaces still count. The
  multi-line field keeps its caret at the edge among hanging spaces.
- **A path through menus stays whole**: no line breaks beside its
  arrow ("Preferences ▸ Keyboard" goes down a line together:
  `LineWrapper::breaks_between`, in both wrapping paths), so a line
  never ends with ▸ nor begins with it, in any language and in text
  put together as it is shown, without no-break spaces in the words.
- **A paragraph's last line is never one word alone** where the word
  before can come down to it (`WrappedLine::keep_last_words_together`:
  both fit the last line, and the line they leave stays the longer, so
  a short line over a long one never comes of it; the number of lines
  is the same). Wrapping fills each line before the next begins, which
  left "…from Deskbar's / tray." in one language or another whatever
  the words said. For text set to read: an element's wrapped text
  (`StringView::wrap`, a note, an alert) and the kit's `Para`; not for
  text being typed (a word would jump as the next is begun), nor text
  cut to so many lines, nor a script that breaks anywhere (no spaces,
  no such word). Its decision is a function of the text and its
  glyphs' places alone (`last_words_break`, tested with a face of ten
  points a letter). To-Do's cards have their own, with their three
  lines (`board::wrap`).
- `WindowOptions::foreign_parent(handle)` (xdg-foreign): a window over
  another program's (a portal's dialog over the app asking; `wayland:`
  stripped, nothing if empty). `file_panel::window_options(title)` and
  `show_in(cx, options, panel, on_done)` open a file panel so;
  olo-print's `panel::view::show(cx, options, pages, on_done)` the Print
  panel.
- `widgets::MonthGrid::new(name, year, month, today)` (`widgets::month`):
  a month to pick a day from. Its name and year over six weeks of days
  (always six, so nothing under it moves as months turn), the weekdays'
  letters quiet and the days of the months either side quieter, today's
  box outlined in the look's highlight, the days `chosen(first, last)`
  bold on the list's selection (outlined is today, filled is chosen: a
  disc of the mark colour for today was louder than the day picked,
  To-Do's reviews), a dot under each day
  in `marked(days)` (sorted), weeks from `week_start(0 Monday … 6
  Sunday)`. It keeps nothing: `on_pick` says a day clicked, `on_turn`
  the month its arrows ask for, and its owner shows that. `month::Day`
  is a plain day (`number()` days from 1970, `plus`, `weekday`, `said`:
  "Wednesday, November 18, 2026"), so the widget ties no app to a date
  library; `month::turned(year, month, by)`. 168 × 174 points
  (`month::WIDTH`, `HEIGHT`). Agents: each day a Button named in full.
  Calendar's small month; `examples/month.rs`.
- `widgets::ArrowButton::back(name)` / `::on(name)`: a square push
  button with an arrow (`style::arrow`), for stepping through what a
  window shows, in a pair set flush. No words on it, so `name`
  ("Previous Week") is what agents read and its tip. A row's
  disclosure, where there's no room for a button's frame (Deskbar's
  folded workspaces), is `style::latch(g, r, open, color)`,
  BOutlineListView's: pointing right while what's under it is away,
  down while it shows (`PaneSwitch`'s too).
- `StringView::cut(true).beside(size)`: a line cut to its room sits on
  the baseline of the larger text beside it, as an uncut one does (a
  status after a title: it was half a point off, the layout review's
  "near-level").
- `widgets::ColorControl::new(id, rgb)` (BColorControl: grey, red, green
  and blue ramps with markers to click or drag, the lane pressed in
  keeping the drag, and Red/Green/Blue fields following the colour unless
  typed in; `on_change` gets each new colour) and `ColorWell::new(color,
  size)`, its sample; `color_control_height()` sizes a well beside it.
  `pictures::thumbnail(cx, path, px)`: a picture file no bigger than `px`
  device pixels, decoded on a thread of its own and kept by path, mtime
  and size; None until it's ready, then every window is drawn again (so
  a view just asks again). `icons::paint_in(window, b, theme, name)` draws
  in a theme other than the current one (Preferences ▸ Themes). `StringView::small`
  sets it in the small size.
- `widgets::ThumbnailPicker::new(id, thumbnails, selected)` (pictures
  to pick one from, wrapping in `width`, labelled under each, the chosen
  one on a `style::selection_plate`; a click chooses, a double click
  opens, or a click opens with `.click_opens()`; the arrows move it, and
  a choice's own key opens it; `RadioButton`s to agents; `height_for`
  sizes it) with `Thumbnail { picture, color, label, key }` (a picture
  made at the well's device size; `key`, "A", shown on the picture as a
  key cap). `style::key_cap(g, top_left, key, palette)` draws a key that
  chooses something as app_server's keyboard hints and Twitcher do: the
  focused tab's yellow, its bevel and frame, the key bold, 16 points
  tall. Live pictures of windows and screens for such a picker:
  `olo_capture::thumbnails::Live::start(items, send)` (a capture of each
  on a worker, a picture when one changed and its item's time has come,
  shrunk to its size in device pixels; `set_size` when the scale
  changes; stopped when dropped), which Share Screen's picker and Open
  in Which Window? use. Tell it whether anyone looks (`set_live(cx.
  is_window_active())` as the view draws): a picker behind other
  windows asks for nothing and keeps the pictures it has, and the
  worker sleeps until app_server answers, a picture's time comes or
  it is told something (two changing windows, release: 24.7 wake-ups
  a second before, looked at or not; 4.0 now while looked at, none
  while not, and no window read; `cargo run -p olo-capture --example
  live` measures it in a test desktop). `Cell::icon_text(g, icon, fallback,
  text)`: a list cell's 16-point icon and name, which names its row.
  `image_view::from_bgra` makes a picture of pixels in the kit's own order
  (a captured frame). A `TextControl` whose field is disabled
  (`TextField::set_enabled(false)`) is drawn faded, label and well, and
  takes no click. `paragraph` says its text to agents.
- A picture (`RenderImage`) is in the GPU's atlas while anything shows
  or keeps it, and leaves it when the last of it is dropped (its
  `Drop`: a frame and a kept drawing hold the pictures they show; no
  `drop_image` to remember). Its place is then the next picture's
  (`BladeAtlas::remove` gives the tile back to the texture's
  allocator): pictures replaced one for another (a live thumbnail, a
  preview) go round in the texture they began in. Before, a tile's
  place stayed taken until its whole texture went, so every eighth
  thumbnail replaced had a new texture made, 4 MB of the GPU's memory
  that the driver makes of 2 MB pieces it may wait for (kernel/
  TUNING.md): 26 textures for 200 pictures replaced, now 1, and a
  picture replaced in 93 µs where it took 292 (the atlas's test, which
  needs a GPU).
- A closed window lets go of its callbacks (and the views they hold) as
  it drops, not once the platform's tidying task runs: a view that
  answers something as it's released (a portal dialog cancelled) does
  so at once.
- What agents read of a window that isn't showing (on another
  workspace, minimized, covered) is as it is now, not as last drawn: it
  draws only when it shows, so the agent socket has each window draw
  what changed (`WindowCx::flush_now`, which doesn't show it; the next
  frame does) before it answers `tree`, `menus`, `invoke` or `review`.
- `widgets::Sidebar::new(id, rows, chosen).on_choose(f)` (a source
  list filling its box: `sidebar::Row::new(icon,
  label).value(v)` and `Row::heading(label)`, `sidebar::height(rows)`,
  its `ground` and `edge` colours for what sits on it; ↑ ↓ step over
  headings, rows past its height scroll, the chosen one is brought into
  view; `ListItem`s and `Heading`s to agents). `Row::dot(hue)` puts a
  dot of a hue where its icon would be (To-Do's lists; `paint_dot` for
  the same dot elsewhere). A heading after other rows has
  `HEADING_OVER` more over it, so its group stands apart from the one
  before (`tall_at`), and headings and values are in `secondary_text`.
  `Row::heading("")` is a
  short gap setting what follows apart, said to no one; `.bare()` drops
  its ground and edge, over what's behind it (a list's sunken well:
  Passwords' sources). Several chosen together, the app keeping which:
  `.also(rows)` draws those selected with the chosen one, `.on_pick(f)`
  takes ⌘- (or Ctrl-) and ⇧-clicks (the row and the modifiers),
  `.on_menu(f)` a secondary click (the row and where), and
  `.on_select_all(f)` ⌘A while it has the keyboard; a plain click with
  others chosen chooses that one alone (Agent Screens). Rows the person
  puts in their own order: `.on_reorder(f)` (Weather's places): a press
  on a row moved 4 points is a drag (followed anywhere in the window),
  a line in the accent shows where it would go among its section's rows
  (between its headings; on whole device pixels, 2 points), and the
  release tells `f` the row's index and the index it's to have
  (`drop_slot`, `moved_to`); the keyboard's and agents' way is the
  app's own (a menu's Move Up and Move Down, a command).
- `widgets::SidePane` and `side_divider(&pane, x, top, height, name,
  on_change)` (a pane beside the rest the person sizes and puts away:
  a chat list, a source list, an inspector): the view keeps a
  `SidePane` (`SidePane::new(width, min).restored(width, collapsed)`),
  lays its pane out `pane.shown(total, rest)` wide (0 put away), puts
  the divider at that edge, and says what it shows again when the
  divider says it changed (`on_change`); the divider sizes it
  (down to `min`), puts it away dragged on past half that, brings it
  back dragged out from the window's edge (a grip stays there), and a
  double click does either. View ▸ Hide/Show Sidebar is `toggle()`,
  its item `.key("s")` for every app's keys (`app.sidebar`: ⌥⌘S, as
  Finder's was; a kit app's keys have no Control of their own, so ⌃⌘S
  would be ⌘S). Agents read a Splitter (its width, or "hidden").
  Telegram's chat list (View ▸ Hide Chat List). In a window too narrow
  for both (a third of a screen: "Tiling layouts"), they show one at a
  time, never both squeezed: `pane.panes(total, rest)` says what shows,
  `Panes::Both(width)` side by side (the divider then), `Pane` the pane
  alone, `Rest` what's beside it alone (and put away, `Rest` too). A
  list to choose from shows first, what it opened once something is
  (`show_rest()` as a row is chosen), with a back arrow
  (`ArrowButton::back`) calling `show_pane()`; a pane that gives way (a
  sidebar of calendars, an assistant) has what's beside it first
  (`SidePane::new(..).first(Front::Rest)`), brought in front by its
  View ▸ Show (`toggle()`, which, one at a time, swaps them rather than
  put the pane away). `alone()` says they show one at a time (a back
  arrow wanted), `showing()` whether the pane shows (a menu's Show or
  Hide). Calendar's calendars and assistant; Phone's and Telegram's
  lists (a conversation opened comes in front; its header's back arrow,
  12 points before its picture, goes back).
- `widgets::TabView::new(id, labels, selected).on_select(f)` with the
  chosen tab's content as its child (BTabView: the tab strip's folder
  tabs, so there is one tab look, over a raised panel: outlined, lit
  along its top and left and shaded along its bottom and right; the
  chosen tab in the panel's colour and open into it, its name in bold,
  the others a shade off it; the content inside `WINDOW_INSET`; `Tab`s
  to agents). Each tab is as wide as its name in bold and its room;
  where they don't all fit the room either side shrinks first, then the
  widest are cut back (`strip::fit_widths`), short names keeping their
  width.
  Next and Previous Tab (`app::tab_step`: ⌃Tab, ⌃⇧Tab, ⌃Page Down and
  ⌃Page Up) step the window's first tab view from wherever the keyboard
  is, unless what has it stops them (a screen being controlled).
- `widgets::dashboard`: `Card::new(id, title)
  .figure(..).caption(..).selected(..).figure_ink(..).on_click(..)`
  holds its content as children under its head (`Card::height(content,
  caption)`), `Facts::new(rows)` (label: value rows, `.colors(label,
  value)` on a panel; `.label_width(w)` for several of them one under
  another with their values in one line, given `facts_label_width` of
  all their labels as shown; `.row_height(h)` for rows as far apart as
  a paragraph's lines, `style::PLAIN_SIZE * style::LINE_HEIGHT`, where
  boxes side by side hold a paragraph and facts each and should end on
  one line: Preferences' Kernel tab; the element is then its rows'
  height with a point over and under, not rounded up, or two such
  boxes would end a pixel apart), `meter`, `flow`/`flow_rows` for cards placed by
  hand, `across(width, least, most)` for a grid of them (`grid_cols`: as
  many across as fit, so they reflow in a third of a screen rather than
  be cut: Weather's), `GAP`, `FACT_ROW`, `gutter(p)`. Cards in a flex row
  are as tall as the tallest. `style::card(window, r, p, hover, selected)` paints a
  card's paper and shadow; `style::thousands(n)` writes "12,345".
- `menu::shortcut_command(cx, keystroke)`: the menu bar command
  a keystroke chooses, for a view that takes the keys itself and lets
  one through (Agent Screens' ⌘K while controlling). An item that's
  off has no shortcut, so the keystroke is the view's to do with as it
  would any other: the menus have to be as things are *now*. A window
  says its menus when its body runs, so whatever an item's `enabled`
  goes by must ask for that body when it changes (Terminal's Copy goes
  by the selection, which draws the screens alone: `Panes` says
  `Cx.redraw(window)` when there being a selection changes).
- `menu::menus_beginning(cx, menus)`: the bar's menus as things are
  now, said outside a body and without drawing it (BeOS's
  `MenusBeginning`), for just before `shortcut_command`: asking for
  the window's body isn't soon enough for a keystroke that follows the
  change at once.
- `code` (source code in the editor; see "Source code" above): `Code`
  (`spans`, `edit`, `reset`, `job`/`done`) and `code::parse`; re-exports
  `olo_syntax`'s `detect`, `by_name`, `Language`, `Edit`, `Class`.
- `editor` (StyledEdit's text; see "The text editor" above): styled
  text in paragraphs, laid out by `editor::layout` (shaped once by
  the text system, placed in rows: wrapping at spaces and hyphens,
  tab stops left, centre, right and decimal, alignment and
  justification, pictures as characters, emoji). The app keeps an
  `Editor` and its text behind the `Document` trait (`text`, `spans`
  each paragraph's styles, `paragraph` its format: indents, spacing,
  alignment, a list's marker, a table's row, pictures, a shade, bar or
  rule; `replace`, `copied`/`paste` for styles on the clipboard, `key`
  for Return, Tab and Backspace it has its own meaning for, as a list's
  or a table's, `types` for what Return and Tab type instead,
  `link_at` for a link under the pointer)
  and is its `EditorHost` (`editor(key, cx, f)` hands both over;
  `edited`, `context_menu`, `text_moved`, `open_link`: the command key
  and a click on a link opens it, the caret left where it was, and with
  the command key held the pointer over a link is a hand, drawn again
  as the key goes down or up in the focused editor, which is the only
  place a modifier's change reaches, and as the pointer moves with it
  held). `editor::view(host, key,
  options, cx)` is the element: a `ScrollView` that
  scrolls itself (a scroll alone, the wheel's, the fingers', their
  glide's, a bar's, lays out what shows and draws the text again in
  the handler, `scroll_alone`, without the host's body: StyledEdit's
  menus, tool bars and status line were a scroll's frame's
  millisecond; the host's body runs when the text moved across the
  window, on pages, or while a press selects), the caret, selection, input methods, the pointer
  (words and paragraphs on double and triple clicks, a selection
  dragged to move it or out to another app, a table's column rule
  dragged), keys (its own `on_key_down`, taken before the window's, so
  its Tab is its own) and `edit(host, key, Edit, cx)` for the Edit
  menu. `Options`: editable, wrap, alignment,
  justification, margins, background, `spelling` (misspelled words
  underlined, checked on a worker paragraph by paragraph, once until
  they change; `respell` after a word is learnt) and `pages` (set on
  sheets of paper down a desk as they print, rows that don't fit
  moved to the next page; `sheets()` for the app's header and
  footer). Only what shows is laid out, measured ahead a millisecond
  a frame; laid-out paragraphs are kept by their text, styles and
  width, and shaped ones by their text and styles alone, so a new
  width (a window being resized) places them again without shaping;
  each row's glyphs are painted from a `GlyphRun`. The paragraphs'
  heights are added up in a tree (`editor/heights.rs`: each node the sum
  below it and the widest), so one changing costs log n and so do a
  paragraph's top and the paragraph at a place; a new wrap width
  guesses again only the paragraphs wider than the narrower of the two
  widths (the rest are a row either way), found by going down the tree
  where something is that wide. (Each was a pass over every paragraph:
  on 100,000 lines of code a live resize spent two fifths of its time
  there.) On pages the tops are still worked out in order, a paragraph
  that doesn't fit at a page's foot moved to the next. Where each
  paragraph starts is kept apart from the rest of what's known of it
  (`starts`), so an edit moving every later one along is a pass over
  those alone (it went through 8 MB on 100,000 lines, every key). The
  text agents read (its node's value) is copied once at a change,
  into what it's shared as. The
  view is kept on the paragraph at its top through edits above it and
  relayouts; at the very top it stays there (on pages, the first
  sheet's top). On a dark document the text's own colours are made
  lighter until they read (4.5:1, as `olo_theme::readable`; printed and
  saved as they are).
- `widgets::Ruler` (StyledEdit's, after Gobe Productive's and
  ClarisWorks', `ruler::HEIGHT` 26 points high): a paragraph's indents
  (first line, left, right) and tab stops in inches or centimetres
  (`ruler::metric()`, as the locale measures), dragged
  (`RulerEvent::Changed`; snapping to sixteenths of an inch or quarter
  centimetres), a stop added with a click and taken off by dragging it
  away, a double click or a right press for a stop's kind, a line down the text where the marker held goes (`guide()`).
  `set(setting, origin, width)` from the text's place across the
  window, and `follow(origin, width)` from `EditorHost::text_moved` as a
  frame is laid out (scrolled sideways on pages), so it moves with the
  text in the same frame.
- `spell::checker(cx)`: kit-base's checker (`olo_kit_base::spell`, the
  dictionary of the person's language and the words they taught it),
  read on a worker the first time one is wanted; `loaded(cx)` once in.
- Every scroll view's ends are elastic, as on a Mac (`Elastic`): fingers
  pull past an end and it springs back, a glide
  bounces off it, a wheel stops there. A view that scrolls itself keeps
  an `Elastic` too (`scroll` from its wheel handler with the event's
  `kind` and `touch_phase`, `offset` where it draws, a frame asked for
  while it springs back), as the editor does.
- `workspaces::follow(cx)` (an app that keeps a window per thing on
  each workspace, as Tracker's folder windows): a thread follows where
  the app's windows are (app_server's events for its own windows and
  the workspaces, nothing polled); `workspaces::here(window)` or
  `here_surface(id)` (a window's surface as its view last saw it, from
  outside its update) says whether it's on the workspace the active
  display shows.
- `icons::paint_tinted(g, b, name, tint)`: an icon with its
  colours multiplied (a selected one darkened, as Tracker's), still a
  texture pixel to a device pixel (two image triangles).
- A window is never opened smaller than 1×1: a layer anchored to every
  edge (the desktop) is given 1×1 and app_server sizes it; asked for
  0×0, a buffer of nothing was made, and app_server ended the
  connection.
- `olo_kit_base::clipboard::files`/`copied_files`/`FILES` (files as file
  managers copy and paste them) and `olo_kit_base::files::named_file`/
  `moz_url` (a picture dragged out of a web page, a browser's link)
  are kit-base's.
- A single-line `TextField`'s Return is the window's default button's,
  as BeOS's (the field doesn't see it); `keeps_enter()` keeps it for a
  field whose Return means something else (a first password field going
  on to the second). A default button that can't be clicked takes no
  Return.

## The session and in-place reload

Olo upgrades without logging out. `olo-session` (what the login
screen runs) owns the Wayland socket (`wayland-N`) and the IPC socket and
hands both to app_server, so clients never see the sockets disappear.

**The displays' modes at a restart** (`display.keep_modes` in
app_server.json, or `OLO_KEEP_MODES=1`; off unless set, until tried on
the real displays). As ever, app_server opens each GPU with every
connector switched off (Smithay's `reset_state`) and modesets each
display from dark, and the app_server going puts back the state it
found: each display dark a second or two, twice, at every upgrade.
Kept, in Olo's Smithay (`backend::drm::keep_current_modes`): the
device isn't reset, only its cursor and overlay planes switched off in
a commit that needs no modeset (refused, it's reset as ever); a surface
whose CRTC already shows the mode asked for (`same_timings`: a CRTC's
mode and its connector's listed one differ in their type bits and
name) on the connectors asked for starts from that state, so its first
