opened at never becomes the group's. Sizes wait only while a window's
edge is being dragged (a resize grab), not for any pointer grab: a
menu's lasts until the pointer next moves, and a held button is one. A window
that joined a group on arriving keeps the frame it came with
(`WindowMeta::joined`): sent on to a workspace where it is on its own,
untouched, it has that frame again, so a window taken to another
workspace and back comes back as it was. A group that comes apart
around it while it shows (the others closed or gone) leaves it the
group's frame as its own: it isn't put back in the one it came with
the next time it comes back (mode-fuzz found one jump after a Focus
round trip and a workspace switch). Only the
front window is drawn whole and takes input over its frame: the ones
behind it show just their tabs (`mark_behind`, before every frame,
`Decoration::behind`), so they never show around it while it is sized
smaller; a capture for an agent draws a window whole. Being behind, a
window gets frame callbacks once a second (Smithay throttles a surface
on no output), so its last buffer may be that old: one brought to the
front while its client waits to draw (`waiting_to_draw`) is told to
draw at once and shows only its tab, the old front still drawn, until
it commits or `FRONTING` (100 ms) passes (`Decoration::fronting`): a
Terminal tab clicked showed what it had printed a second before, then
jumped to now. It waits once: one new to its group waits so too, till
it has been the front (`Decoration::fronted`), and a wait ended by its
drawing counts as that (`drew_while_fronting`): a commit asks for the
next frame, and taken for one still to come to the front, a busy window
was held back after every frame it drew, the old front showing for
seconds (a Terminal with an agent streaming, after an upgrade, when no
window has been the front; `top_turn`,
`a_window_brought_forward_waits_once`). Moving, resizing,
rolling up and tiling (one cell per group) act on the whole group; an
arranging command on a window behind brings it to the front first
(`front_of_group`). A
window leaving a group gets its own tab back and steps out by `CASCADE`
so it isn't hidden. Grouping is on for every app; the ones a person
turns off are `TilingSettings::ungrouped_apps` (app ids), toggled by
Group Windows in Tracker's menu for an app
(`olo_kit::settings::groups_windows` / `set_groups_windows`). Deskbar's
team menu says what its windows are, not the setting (Ben, 2026-11-08:
"it should not be checked unless they are all grouped … no checks/ticks
just the option changes based on the state"): Ungroup All Windows when,
wherever two or more of them show together, they're all in one group
(with fewer showing, as the setting is), else Group All Windows.
`Request::GroupApp` does it (`group_app`): grouped, every one of the
app's windows groups by itself again (`Auto`, wherever it was: taken out,
or put in another group by hand) and the setting goes on; ungrouped,
each is taken out (`Alone`), the group's front window staying where it
is and the others stepped out a `CASCADE` each, each brought in front
of the last so every tab shows, and the setting goes off. Before this,
the menu's tick was the setting alone, so it showed ticked with a window
taken out by hand. A group's
frame is never smaller than any of its windows can be (`least_frame`).
A window that joins a group it can't be as small as draws bigger only
on that side: `keep_on_screen` fits to the screen only the sides an app
chose itself, never one it took as asked, so a Tracker put in a Terminal
group sized by hand taller than its display is wider, as tall, and
doesn't pull the group back onto the screen. A window brought back into
its group (from hidden) likewise only grows it to that window's least
size, where it is. Tiled (by a tile shortcut), a group grown past its
tile for a window that needed it is its tile's size again once that
window has gone (taken out, dragged out, closed): `back_to_tile` in
`sync_groups`, by `tile_frame`, where `retile` would put it.

Only an app's own windows group by themselves, but any windows can be
grouped by hand (`WindowMeta::grouping`: `Auto`, `Alone` once taken out,
`With(key)` once put in one; `tab_order` places each tab). ⌘-dragging a
tab (shell/tabdrag.rs) works as Haiku's Stack & Tile does, with ⌘ for
its Option key: along its group's tabs it reorders them, the others
making room where it would go; pulled `TEAR` px above or below the tab
row (or `TEAR_SIDE` past its ends) the window comes out and follows the
pointer on its own (`Alone`, so it doesn't just join its app's group
again); held within `NEAR` px of another group's tabs, or a lone
window's, it folds into just its tab in the place it would take, and
that group's tabs and frame light up in the focus blue
(`Decoration::target`); let go there, it joins at that place
(`put_in_group`, showing only its tab for up to `DOCKING` while it draws
at the group's size). Back over its own group, it goes back in. A plain
drag still moves the whole group. The window menu (the palette's) has
Remove from Group, and Move to Window ▸ (its app's other windows where
it shows, a group's once: into its group) and, in a group, Move Group to
Window ▸ (every window of its group, `GroupWindow` each) and Close
Others after its Close (Ben, 2026-11-09: every other window of its
group, `Close` each, as its close box does: one that asks first still
asks). Dialogs, fixed-size panels and fullscreen windows
never group (`groupable`). Agents do the same with `GroupWindow { id,
with, index }` (into `with`'s group, or a new one with it), `UngroupWindow
{ id }` and `MoveTab { id, index }`; `WindowInfo` says `group` (a number
its members share), `tab` (its place), `groupable`, `output` (the
display it is on, or was on while hidden) and, in `Reply::Windows`,
`tab_frame` (where to click or ⌘-drag its tab).

A window moved by hand over another of its own app's windows' content
(`own_window_under`: the top window there, not covered, same client) is
drawn see-through (`WindowMeta::ghost`) and its app is told where, and
where it is let go (`window_drop.rs`: `{"window_over":…}` and
`{"window_dropped":…}` lines on the app's kit socket, from a worker
thread that keeps only the latest place, so the compositor never waits
on an app): a kit app's tab strip marks the place, and a window let go
on it becomes tabs there (`widgets::strip::on_window_dropped`). A move a client asks
for with the press of another of its windows (a tab torn off a strip,
`olo_kit::begin_move`) starts from the pointer, not from that press; one
asked for before the window has shown (Vulkan's present commits its
first buffer on its own, after the request) waits till it is placed
(`WindowMeta::pending_move`). A window tagged `under-pointer` opens
with its tab under the pointer, alone (`place_under_pointer`).

Other programs arrange windows through two requests: `Arrangement`
answers the active display's connector, its tiling area (global logical
pixels) and its windows on this workspace, front first, with frames;
`Arrange { windows: [Placement { id, x, y, w, h }] }` puts the listed
ones in those fractions of the area (`arrange`), as Tile All does its
cells: undoable, and tiled as `Tile::Cell` so their edges move together.
It is for an arranger outside app_server (an agent, a script; the
window-manager fuzzer does it): Smart Tiling, a model that looked at
the screen and arranged it, was its first user and is gone (Ben,
2026-11-16: "it never worked well and is, frankly, silly").

## Shortcuts of two parts (olo_protocol::shortcuts::Keys, app_server chord.rs, the palette's chord.rs)

A shortcut's keys are one chord, or two pressed in turn (Ben,
2026-11-18: "you do the first part to start Float/Move/etc and then the
second part to select the specific option. this chord support must be
made native to olo, supported and customizable in keyboard shortcut
prefs"). `Keys { first, then }`, written with a space between
("Ctrl+Alt+Cmd+Z V") wherever keys are written: a profile's
`shortcuts`, the tables' defaults; shown (`Keys::label`) with room
between the two ("⌃⌥⌘Z  V", two spaces: with one, "⌃⌥⌘Z Z" read as a
letter said twice at 1×), and several keys for one thing with a comma
and more room (`Keys::labels`: "⌃⌥↵,   ⌃⌥⌘Z  Z"). BeOS had none; Emacs's prefix keys
and VS Code's chords are the model, with which-key's panel for what the
second can be. (In Olo's code a "chord" is still one key with its
modifiers, `Chord`: the two-part kind is `Keys` with a `then`.)

**The groups that come with Olo**, the same keys in every profile (on
⌃⌥⌘, where Olo's own extras are): ⌃⌥⌘Z begins Zoom's (Z zoom, V
vertically, H horizontally, B back to its own size), ⌃⌥⌘F Float's (F
the window, with its group; W the window alone; A its application
always), ⌃⌥⌘V Move's (1 to 9 a workspace, ← → the one before or after,
N P the next or previous display). They are second keys of those
shortcuts: each keeps the chord it had (⌃⌥↵ still zooms). Float's ⌃⌥⌘F
was a shortcut by itself; F again does what it did. A group is nothing
but the shortcuts whose keys begin with one chord
(`shortcuts::begun_by`): give any shortcut keys of two parts in
Preferences and its first chord begins a group, named (`menu_of`) if
all of it is one of the window menu's submenus.

**Clashes** (`Keys::clashes`): two shortcuts can't have the same keys,
and a chord that is a shortcut by itself can't begin another. `assign`
takes keys from whatever they clash with, as it always did;
`bindings` gives what the person chose precedence over what comes with
the platform, so a chord given to a shortcut before a group began with
it stays that shortcut's.

**In app_server** (`keymap.rs`, `chord.rs`): the keymap takes a
group's first chord (`Action::ChordBegun`: it reaches no program) and
waits (`pending`); the next key that isn't a modifier picks from the
group, pressed alone or with the first's modifiers still held
(`Keys::picked_by`: ⌃⌥⌘Z then V with the fingers still on ⌃⌥⌘ is ⌃⌥⌘Z
V), or lets go of it (Escape, any key that's none of its own), and
reaches no program either way (`ChordEnded`, then the shortcut). Left
waiting, it's let go of after `CHORD_WAIT` (5 s), and by a press of the
pointer. A key costs the keymap what it did (0.13 to 0.25 µs down and
up, release, before and after: `what_a_key_costs`), and nothing ticks
while a group waits (release, 2560×1600 at 2×: app_server 0.0% of a
core and its two wakeups a second at rest, as before; the panel's
program 0.0%).

**What's shown while it waits**: `olo-palette --chord FIRST OUTPUT`,
started once a group has waited `SHOW_AFTER` (350 ms: keys typed
straight through show nothing), handed to the running palette: a panel
at the foot of the display, as wide as what it says (220 to 420
points), with the group's name, the chord that began it, each second
key on a cap with what it does (the shortcuts' titles, as Preferences
and the shortcuts sheet list them, through the words layer), and "Esc
cancels" under a rule. What it lists is what can be done here, as a
menu would (`chord_info`): the workspaces there are, another display
only where there is one, the number keys first as Move's menu has its
workspaces, and what's so already checked and stepped back
(`ChordOption::current`: the workspace the window is on, as its menu's
item is). It takes no keys
and no pointer; it goes at `Event::Chord` with no first (or when a
group can wait no longer). Agents: `{"type":"chord"}` answers the group
that's waiting (`ChordInfo`: first, name, each option's keys, id and
title), or with `"first":"Ctrl+Alt+Cmd+Z"` what that chord begins;
`Event::Chord` (by name) says when one begins and ends; the panel is a
kit window, read as any. `tools/dev/chord-check` goes through all of it
in a headless session (a group begun, picked from with the modifiers
let go of or held, let go of by Escape, another key, the pointer and
the wait; the panel; Move's and Float's; a second key of the person's
own), 41 checks.

Not done, to decide (both reviewers asked for it): the panel says what
each shortcut is, in the words Preferences and the shortcuts sheet use
("Float over the tiles, or tile"), not what its key would do now, in
the menu's words ("Unfloat"). TODO, "The chord panel in the menu's
words".

**An app's commands** can have keys of two parts too. The app never
sees them: app_server takes both (`app_chords`, the profile's entries
for the app that has the keyboard, told the keymap when that app
changes; an empty list, as profiles come, costs a key one test) and
chooses the command from the app's menus over its commands socket, as
an agent would (`window_drop::invoke`, the kit's `invoke_in`, from the
worker thread that already tells apps where a window was dropped);
Chrome's is pressed as what Chrome takes for it (`CHROME_NATIVE`). The
kit shows such keys beside the item (`keys::Known`: words, and no
`Shortcut` to press).

**In Preferences ▸ Keyboard ▸ Shortcuts**: a shortcut's keys read
"⌃⌥↵,  ⌃⌥⌘Z Z" (a comma between its keys, a space between the two
parts of one). Click a shortcut and type a chord, as ever; Add a Second
Key then records the chord to press after it. It's asked for, not
waited for after every chord: the next key typed after giving a
shortcut its keys is as likely the shortcut being tried. The shortcut
last changed stays lit, faintly, till another is clicked (the one Add
a Second Key is for, at the left under the note about it); while the second
key is waited for its row reads "⌃⌥⌘J  …", the ellipsis where the key
will be. The note is the list's caption: a line of its own right under
it (`TIGHT`), over the buttons (beside both it had half the width, and
wrapped in English too), dimmed only as the idle hint. All Default Keys
(it was Default Keys, read by both reviewers as the lit shortcut's
alone), at the right, gives every shortcut the profile's own keys
again. The profile row's Save As… and Delete are as wide as their
words (`Button::min_width`): at the kit's least width they left the
menu six points short of "Mac (Customized)".

## Menus in groups (the window menu, Deskbar's; every menu of Olo's)

Ben, 2026-11-18: "group the 3 zoom options under a "Zoom ->" parent and
the 3 float options under a "Float ->" parent, the move options under a
"Move ->" parent, and anything else that makes sense to be grouped …
similarly clean up the deskbar right click menus and any other menus
that are unwieldly. try to make everything follow consistent
patterns/groupings where appropriate". The pattern, top to bottom:

1. **What it is**: the windows of an application, a state said in
   words (Deskbar's rows).
2. **What's done to it at once**: Hide, Show, Roll Up, Send to Back.
3. **Its size and shape**: Zoom ▸, Float ▸, Tile ▸ (and Make Main,
   where the tiles have a main window).
4. **Where it is and shows**: Pin ▸, Move ▸ (workspaces first, each
   display's with a line between; then Next Display and Previous
   Display; then elsewhere: Agent Screen ▸, Another Window ▸), Show ▸
   (Always on Top, On All Workspaces, In the Scratchpad, On AirPlay ▸).
5. **What it is to others**: its group, its file (Show in Tracker).
   Deskbar's Group All Windows goes with where they go: a line round
   one item makes a slab of it.
6. **Closing and quitting**, last, under a line of their own; a tray
   menu's Settings… after even those.

A submenu is named for the verb alone (Zoom, Float, Tile, Pin, Move,
Show; Move All where it acts on several), and its items for where the
thing goes or what with, without saying the verb again (Move ▸
Workspace 2, Next Display, Agent Screen; Show ▸ On All Workspaces;
Tile ▸ With Another Window). An item says the verb only where it is the
verb, or the verb and how (Zoom ▸ Zoom, Zoom Vertically; Float ▸ Float
Its Group). Three of a kind make a submenu; two stay where they are.
An item in a group shows its keys of two parts, the ones that begin
with the group's chord; at a menu's top it shows its one chord. What's
said of one thing is said in the singular (Deskbar's Show, Hide, Move
and Close for an application with one window; Show All, Hide All, Move
All and Close All with several).

Held by: the kit's `menu::review_groups` (a submenu's item or submenu
that says its verb again before "to", "on", "in", "with"…: "Move ▸ Move
to Workspace 2: the verb is the menu's, say “Workspace 2”"), which the
window review runs over every window's menu bar (`app_menu::review`,
kind `menus`) and the window menu's test over the popup; and that test
(`apps/palette/src/window_menu.rs`, `asks_and_items`), which has the
menu's top level and each group item by item. The window menu went
from twenty-odd items to ten; Deskbar's application and workspace
menus (`team_menu`, `heading_menu`) have Show All and Hide All, Move ▸
or Move All ▸, Show on AirPlay ▸ and grouping, and Close All last.
Items' keys stand in a straight column (`style::key_combo_column`).

## Windows snap into place as they're dragged (app_server shell/snap.rs, shell/glide.rs)

A window moved by its tab can be let go into a place (Ben, 2026-11-18:
"if i drag to different areas of the screen it takes that tile location
while dragging but isn't "saved" until i let go … show each hotspot as a
semi-transparent overlay with a letter in each … or they can just press
the letter"). How Windows 11, macOS Sequoia, GNOME, KDE, Rectangle,
FancyZones and BeOS/Haiku's Stack and Tile do it, and why Olo's is as it
is: [reports/window-snapping.md](reports/window-snapping.md).

**The places** (`snap::pads`, a pure function of the display, its tiling
area and the other windows' frames, tested on its own): nine, a map of
the screen on the nine keys at a keyboard's left, and one for each other
window there.

    Q  top left quarter      W  top half          E  top right quarter
    A  left half             S  the whole screen  D  right half
    Z  bottom left quarter   X  bottom half       C  bottom right quarter

Each has a pad where a hand goes for it: the quarters' at the tiling
area's corners, the halves' at the middle of each side, the whole
screen's a bar along the very top between the corners ("very top of the
screen anywhere should be full screen"), the top half's under it in the
middle. A pad at the area's edge counts out to the display's edge
(`Pad::hot`): the pointer stops there, past the windows' margin and
whatever Deskbar takes. Another window's pad is at its middle, not the
whole of it (a window dragged across a screen of windows passes over
others all the way), lettered from the right hand's keys (J K L H U I O
P …, the front window first); one whose middle would lie under a pad
already there has none, nor has a window of the dragged one's own app
(let go on one of those, it becomes its tab: `window_drop`). The letters
are keys' places, as keyboard hints' are (`hints::letter`): the same
keys on every layout.

**What's seen.** The pads come up as the move begins (past a click's
distance, `PointerMoveSurfaceGrab::started`; a finger's move too) on the
display the pointer is on, and go as it ends. With the pointer in a pad
the window itself is in that place, not an outline of it, and the other
pads step back (`OTHERS`); out of it again, it's under the pointer at
its own size. On another window's pad the two are shown swapped: the
other one where the dragged one was. Let go in a pad, it stays, as a
tiling command would have put it (tiled there, or zoomed; its own frame
kept for Restore; a swap gives each the other's frame, tile and zoom:
`Arranged`). Let go anywhere else, it's where it was let go: a window
taken out of a tile or a zoom is its own size from the moment it's
taken, its tab still under the pointer, and that is its own frame now.
Escape puts everything back as it was, the other window of a swap too.
A letter pressed is the window let go in that pad (`snap_key`: the move
ends; its letting up types nothing; with ⌃, ⌥ or ⌘ held it's a
shortcut's key).

**Which windows.** Those that tile: not dialogs, alerts, windows of one
size, full screen ones (`snaps`). A tile of an auto-tiled display's tree
keeps what dragging does there (onto a tile: swap; beside one:
`auto_dropped`). Preferences ▸ Windows ▸ Dragging a Window turns it off
(`TilingSettings::snap`).

**A pad** (`pad_pixmap`) is a plate raised as Olo's panels are, with
the highlight's edge and a point of shadow; on it a small picture of the
display in a sunken well, the place filled with the highlight behind a
line of the screen's white (another window's: a small window, raised,
its yellow tab and close box on its top edge, and under it that window's
title, so a pad over a covered window says whose it is), and the
letter's key cap as keyboard hints draw theirs (`hints::key_cap`). Three
looks (`Look`): at rest; with the dragged window in it, the selection's
ground, an edge twice as wide and the cap pressed in; and stepped back,
while the window is in another: its key cap alone, on a collar of plate,
where it was. Everything on whole device pixels, a line `floor(scale)`
of them. The plates are opaque (`PAD_ALPHA`): Ben asked for see-through
hotspots, and so they were first, but a pad is a small plate over
whatever is there, a window's words more often than not, and at 80%, 92%
and 95% those words still read through it as the pad's own (Astra's and
Opus's reviews, each time). What's see-through now is the screen: with
the window in a place, every other pad is no more than its letter. The
other window of a swap glows while it's shown swapped, as a new window
can (`glow`, at its own place among the windows), and the glow fades
once it's let go or put back. The pad a move begins in (a window at the
top is taken by its tab inside the whole screen's bar) counts only once
the pointer has left it and come back (`Snap::began_in`).

The pictures are made when the pads change (`snap_show`, kept by scale
and look), not in a frame: a frame places them (`snap::elements`, under
what `showing` draws). The scale or the look changing while they're up
makes them again (`snap_tick`).

A key cap's letter (keyboard hints' and Twitcher's caps too) that hangs
below the line, Q's tail and J's hook, is raised until a point of the
cap's face shows under it (`hints::cap_raise`: found by drawing it, as
the face's metrics say only where capitals stand); every other capital
is where its capitals' height centres it (tested at every scale).

**For agents**: `{"type":"snap"}` answers the window being dragged, the
display, and each pad's letter, place (`TopLeft`, `Left`, `Whole`,
`Window 7`…), rectangle and whether the window is in it; dragging is
the pointer's (`synthetic` button and moves), a letter a key. Without
dragging: the tiling shortcuts (`run_shortcut`) and `place`.

**Gliding** (`glide.rs`; Ben: "windows should smoothly animate when they
move not jarringly just redraw somewhere else"). A window put somewhere
at the person's word glides there: a place taken while dragging, a drop,
the other window of a swap, Escape; a tiling shortcut, Zoom (the key,
the tab's box, `toggle_zoom`), Restore, Centre (`glided`, which makes
`set_frame` a glide for what it wraps). Not what arranges many windows
at once (auto-tiling, Tile All: those show every window's new size in
one frame, `rounds`), nor `place` over the socket, whose asker reads
the frame back.

It's the window itself at each size on the way, drawn by its app as when
its edge is dragged (`tiling::follow`: asked a size, put where that size
belongs when it draws it, told it's being resized so it keeps room in
its buffers): nothing is stretched. Each step is where the glide has got
to by the clock, closing on its target as a critically damped spring
does (`RATE`: half way in 30 ms, there in 0.28 s), so a slow app takes
fewer steps and arrives when a fast one does, and a target that moves
(the pointer, as a window goes back under it) is followed without a
jump. `glide_tick` is each frame's (`pre_repaint`), a test for an empty
list when nothing glides; frames are asked for only while something
does.

A gliding window that something else places is that thing's: a layout or
a drag that asks it a size (`ask_to_follow`, when the asking isn't the
glide's own, `glide_stepping`) and a zoom end the glide; what needs the
window where it belongs first (an edge taken in hand, its workspace put
away: `park`) has it there at once (`glide_finish`); another frame given
it (`set_frame`) is where it glides to instead. A zoom at the end of a
glide (`glide_then_zoom`) leaves what the window unzooms to as it was
(`zoom_there`: `zoom_window` would take the zoom's own frame for it).

Measured (release, 2560 × 1600 at 2×, 120 Hz, Kache and Weather; the
machine busy with other builds, two runs): at rest 0 ms of CPU and 20
wakeups in 10 s, before and after; a window dragged in the open for 4 s,
ten pads up, 230 to 290 ms of app_server's CPU against 240 before, a
frame's work 0.30 to 0.37 ms (slowest 0.9) against 0.30 (1.05); into the
left half and back out, eight times: in place 271 to 276 ms after the
pointer enters the pad, the first step 5 to 10 ms after, Weather
drawing 26 frames of its own on the way at 0.9 ms each (slowest 1.7),
app_server's frame 0.25 to 0.28 ms (slowest 2.2) of the 8.3 it has,
`pre_repaint` with the glide's step in it 25 µs; onto another window's
pad and off, eight times, the other gliding and glowing: 0.56 to 0.61 ms
a frame (slowest 3.0). (A stepped-back pad's picture is its collar, no
bigger: as eleven pad-sized pictures, the frame that first showed a
place was 5.7 ms, handing them to the GPU.)

`tools/dev/snap-check` drags a window through every way a drag can end
in a session of its own (a corner, out of a tile, Escape from each
state, a letter, the whole screen, a swap and its preview, the
shortcuts' glides and one given while the last still glides, the
setting off) and reads the frames and tiles back.

## Keyboard hints (app_server hints.rs, Preferences ▸ Keyboard)

Opt-in (`KeyboardSettings::hints`). Pressing Control twice quickly
(either Control, or Caps Lock when it is one), with nothing else down or
typed in between, is the keymap's `Action::Hints`: the second press must
come within `KeyboardSettings::double_press_ms` of the first (Preferences
▸ Keyboard ▸ Double-press speed, 400 ms by default) and each press be
shorter than that. A yellow key cap with a letter goes on everything
that can be picked, as Vim's EasyMotion does. Typing a letter picks it; Backspace goes back a level;
Esc, Control (tapped once: on its release, and it still goes on to be
Control), a click or any other key (which then does what it does) puts
them away. A letter typed with Control held picks it as ever, but
another window's (on its tab) makes it its tiles' main window where
they are Main and Stack's (`make_main`), and the hints go (Ben,
2026-11-14: "if i hold down ctrl and type the letter of a window it
makes it main"). Letters are by key position, as on a
US keyboard, home row first (`LETTERS`).

They must show at once, however busy the screen. What can be picked
comes from the kit's trees, asked for only the surfaces showing
(`{"hints":[surface ids]}`, which answers once those have drawn, with
only what can be picked: see the commands socket): the focused window's
controls, the other windows (by their tabs, which app_server knows
itself; picking one brings it forward and letters its content next)
and every layer surface on screen (Deskbar, the desktop's icons,
notifications; not one hidden behind windows, which draws once a second).
Each app is asked on a worker thread of its own, which also reads and
`build`s its answer (`ask_and_build`), 500 ms at most; the event loop
only prunes and letters. The asking starts ahead: Control let go on its
own is the keymap's `Action::HintsAhead` (`hints_ahead`), and the
second press shows the level asked for then (`Hints::ahead`, good for
`AHEAD`), or shows it the moment it is in; the gap between two presses
is longer than the apps take to answer, so the letters are there as
Control goes down. An app from before `hints` hangs up on it
and is asked `{"tree":true}`. How long they took is logged at debug
(`keyboard hints shown`). `build` turns a tree into `Node`s: what is clickable,
enabled and shows in the window, less a nameless area behind others (a
list's background) and the outside of a control around its own inside;
boxes (a widget's own nesting) are `Group`s. With a menu open, only its items,
the last opened (a submenu) first. `prune` drops what a click wouldn't
reach (a window in front: `clicks_reach` follows the surface under the
middle up to its window or layer). A level never has more than 26
letters (`expand`): all of it when it fits; else groups opened smallest
first while they fit, outlined in navigation blue, and what's left
after 25 letters in runs. Picking a leaf clicks its middle (the pointer
goes back after `SETTLE` if untouched) and then looks for a menu it
opened, whose items are lettered next; sliders, text fields and the
like are given the keyboard instead (`{"focus":ID}`), as a click would
change them. The badges are memory buffers in front of everything
(`Hints::elements`, from both backends), cached per letter, scale and
theme.

Agents read the letters showing with `{"type":"hints"}` (label, global
rectangle, name, role: AccessKit's, `Window` or `Group`) and type them
as keys.

## AI features (crates/ai, Preferences ▸ AI)

Preferences ▸ AI (`olo-preferences ai`) holds `Settings::ai`
(`AiSettings`). Its Claude Code box is the model (`CLAUDE_MODELS`: Opus
5.5 by default, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Fable 5.1) and effort (`AI_EFFORTS`,
Claude Code's own levels; Medium by default) Olo starts Claude Code with
for a task in a Terminal window (`AiSettings::claude_code`: `claude
--model … --effort …`; DiskBackup's Agent Setup; Ben, 2026-11-08: "have
the claude code model selectable in the ai prefs, default to opus 5.5 on
medium"). Each feature is an `AiFeature { enabled, model, effort }`,
the model one of `AI_MODELS` and the effort one of `AI_EFFORTS`; the
panel's `feature()` draws its switch and choosers, so the next feature
is a struct field and a BBox: Ask, Weather (its
assistant, Astra 6 at Medium by default: "Weather (apps/weather)"), and
Emoji (the emoji picker's ⌘↩, low effort by default: it's asked while
the person waits); Weather's sits in the left column with Ask. `AI_MODELS` is OpenAI's current Codex
models (Astra 6, the default; Sol 6.1, Terra 6.1, Luna 6), reached
through the Token Pool's gateway (`http://127.0.0.1:{OLO_POOL_PORT or
17891}/codex`) and its Codex accounts. A model no longer listed (a
Claude model chosen before they were dropped) is read as the default
(`AiFeature::model_id`), keeping its effort. Claude is still spoken by
`olo_ai` for when it is offered again: through the pool's `/claude`
with `use_pool`, otherwise straight to Anthropic with
`olo_ai::saved_key()` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/olo/anthropic-key` or
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`).

Every call introduces itself as `olo-ai/VERSION` (the pool lists its
requests by it) and is tried up to 4 times while the answer is 429,
503 or 529: after the `retry-after` it asks for, else 2, 4, 8 s plus up
to a quarter at random. Asked to wait over a minute (a quota resetting
later), it gives up with the server's message.

`olo_ai::ask` sends one question and returns the answer's JSON. For
Claude it is the Messages API (`anthropic-version: 2026-10-21`): the
system prompt, one user turn of content blocks (`png_block`,
`text_block`), `output_config: {effort, format: {type: "json_schema",
schema}}` (structured output), thinking left to the model (adaptive;
Opus 5.5 can't turn it off), and `fallbacks: "default"` with the
`server-side-fallback-2026-07-01` beta on every model but Haiku, so a
declined request is retried on another. `stop_reason` "refusal" and
"max_tokens" are errors. OpenAI's (`gpt-*`) go to the Responses API as Codex sends it
(`instructions`, `input_text`/`input_image`, `reasoning.effort` with max
as xhigh, `text.format` json_schema strict, streamed, not stored);
`openai_answer` reads the stream's text deltas or the completed
response. `OLO_AI_BASE_URL` sends every call to a fake server instead:
**tests never call a real model**.

## Power (crates/app_server/src/power.rs)

**Power modes** (`olo_system::power_profile`, Preferences ▸ Power,
Deskbar's battery menu): Performance, Balanced, Power Saver, through the
power profiles daemon's D-Bus API (`org.freedesktop.UPower.PowerProfiles`:
power-profiles-daemon, or Fedora's tuned-ppd; `net.hadess.PowerProfiles`
for older daemons), which makes each what the machine has: the
processors' energy/performance preference and governor (intel_pstate,
amd-pstate), the firmware's platform profile (a ThinkPad's power limits
and fans), tuned's settings. `power_profile::watch` follows the daemon's
signals (a ThinkPad's Fn+L/M/H change the platform profile, and the
daemon follows), so the panel and the menu show the mode in use and
why Performance is held back (on a lap, running hot). Setting it is
polkit's `switch-profile`, allowed to the person at the computer.
Performance has a button to Power, where people may look for it.

**The battery's charge limit** (Preferences ▸ Power ▸ Battery, where the
battery has one: `olo_system::battery::charge_limit`): UPower's charge
threshold (`EnableChargeThreshold`, polkit's to the person at the
computer): charging stops at its end (80 % on a ThinkPad) and starts
again below its start (75 %). Power is two columns (the power mode and
the battery; when idle and caffeinated), to fit 1280 × 800.

app_server owns idleness: any input (or a synthetic event) is activity; a
5 s tick turns the displays off (`settings.power.display_off_minutes`) and
then asks logind to suspend (`sleep_minutes`). Caffeinated mode
(`Request::SetCaffeinated`, the Deskbar cup), apps holding a
zwp_idle_inhibit inhibitor, and IPC connections that asked
`Request::KeepAwake` (for as long as they stay open: olo-portal holds one
for each app's wake lock, through the Inhibit portal or
`org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver`, `apps/portal/src/inhibit.rs`, released
when the app lets go or leaves the bus) count as activity. `Request::PowerStatus` and
`Event::PowerChanged` report it all, with the built-in display's brightness
(`Request::SetBrightness`, perceptual 0–1). Brightness, volume and
microphone keys are taken by app_server (the microphone key, a
ThinkPad's F4, KEY_MICMUTE: the microphone in use muted or unmuted,
`audio::toggle_input_mute`, a microphone on screen, slashed while
muted; when that's Olo's voice processing, the microphone it records
from too, so the sound stops at the hardware and the key's light, the
kernel's `audio-micmute` trigger on the card's capture switch, comes
on), as are a laptop's display, airplane and notification keys (a
ThinkPad's F7 KEY_SWITCHVIDEOMODE opens Preferences ▸ Display; F8
KEY_RFKILL turns every radio off or back on, `olo_system::rfkill`,
`/dev/rfkill` being the session's, an airplane on screen; F9
KEY_NOTIFICATION_CENTER opens the notifications' history, as Deskbar's
bell does; the phone keys, F10 and F11, and the star, F12, go to the
app in front and can be shortcuts); the brightness keys act on the
display under the pointer when its brightness can be set, else the
built-in one.

**A display's brightness in HDR is SDR's white** (Ben, 2026-11-17:
"the brightness settings on my builtin monitor are broken i can't turn
them up or down ... it's like i change it and then it just goes back
to what it was"). In HDR a display shows light as it's sent and a
panel's backlight does nothing (the ThinkPad's OLED ignores it), so
its brightness is where SDR's white is, everything that isn't HDR:
`power::sdr_level` and `sdr_nits_at`, even steps of light on a log
scale from 80 cd/m² (level 0) to 600 (level 1). Everything that sets
a brightness sets that for a display in HDR (`set_sdr_level`: the
keys, `step_sdr_white`; `SetOutputBrightness`, Preferences ▸ Display's
Brightness slider; `SetBrightness`), and everything that says one says
it (`OutputInfo::brightness`, `PowerStatus::brightness`); Preferences'
"Everything else's brightness" is the same thing in cd/m²
(`ConfigureOutput`'s `sdr_nits`, which brings a panel that was off
back on: `sdr_white_set`). Three things were wrong, and each alone put
a brightness back: in HDR the slider and the IPC moved the backlight
while the keys moved SDR's white; setting the built-in display's
brightness told subscribers the power status changed but not the
displays (`OutputsChanged`), so Preferences' slider, which shows the
display's own level, went back to the one it had after its 600 ms
hold; and SDR's white, unlike the backlight's level, was taken from a
client's copy of the settings (`desktop::keep_brightness` kept only
`brightness`), so Preferences' older copy, given back with any other
setting changed, undid what the keys had done. `tools/dev/brightness-
check` holds all of it: a headless session whose screen stands in for
the built-in panel and does HDR, the slider's request, an agent's, the
keys, a subscriber's events, an older copy of the settings, the bottom
and back; it fails eleven ways on the build before.

**The bottom of the built-in display's brightness is off** (Ben,
2026-11-12: "putting the screen on min brightness should turn the
screen off: right now it just gets dim but not off"), as a MacBook's.
The last step down (`power::off_at`: level 0, from the keys, a slider
or an agent's `set_brightness`) switches the panel off, and the
indicator says "Display off"; it stays off until its brightness is
raised, when it's back at the first step. Off lasts while whoever
chose it is there: once the displays have slept for idleness (or
the computer was put to sleep for it), the first touch brings the panel back
at the first step too (`panel_back_on`), so nobody comes back to a
dark screen and can't tell why. It isn't the displays asleep: nothing locks, its windows stay where they are (it's still
the display it was), other displays are untouched, what mirrors it
goes on drawing. In HDR, where the keys move SDR's white and not the
backlight (`step_sdr_white`), the bottom step is off the same way,
the least of SDR's white being still light. A brightness kept as off
isn't how a session starts (`power::starting_level`: the first step),
so nobody sits down to a dark screen and can't tell why.
`PowerStatus::panel_off` says so to whoever asks. The backend does it
(`Backend::set_output_on`): on DRM, the same call that puts displays
to sleep for idleness, for the one display (its planes cleared, which
turns the CRTC off), nothing drawn on it meanwhile
(`UdevData::outputs_off`, looked at in `render_surface`), and the
next frame drawn on it turns it back on. In a test session the
built-in panel is whichever headless screen `OLO_INTERNAL_OUTPUT`
names, and the backend only says what it would do ("a display
(simulated)"): 16 steps down from full reach it, another changes
nothing, one up brings it back at 1/16; left off for a minute's
idleness (the displays asleep), a key brings it back at 1/16. On a
real panel it hasn't been tried.

A **human presence sensor** (a ThinkPad P1 Gen 9's, in its camera
module: the HID sensor hub's IIO device "prox", `proximity0` someone
there, `attention` looking; `olo_system::presence`) locks the screen
when the person walks away (`PowerSettings::lock_when_away_seconds`)
and wakes the displays, asleep for idleness, when they come back
(`wake_on_return`), and dims the built-in display while someone in
front of it looks away (`dim_when_looking_away`: `attention` 0 for
`DIM_AFTER`, 8 s, then the panel at `DIM_TO`, 30%, of its level; back as
they look again or touch anything; `PowerStatus::dimmed` says so). All
three are in Preferences ▸ Power ▸ Presence, shown only on a computer
with one. All three are off by default. `SyntheticEvent::Presence` gives app_server
a reading as the sensor would (tests, agents: it wakes nothing by
itself). app_server watches the sensor only while one is on
(`presence_settings`): a thread waits on its buffer
(`/dev/iio:deviceN`, which carries a sample only as either changes),
`_raw` read once at the start (each read asks the sensor). Walking away
arms a one-shot timer, not a poll. `data/udev/73-olo-presence.rules`
(Olo Doctor's "rule:presence", and `tools/install-session.sh`) gives
the session the device and turns its buffer on, at 1 Hz.

Each display's brightness is `OutputInfo::brightness` (None: can't be set)
and `Request::SetOutputBrightness { name, level }`. Besides the built-in
backlight, monitors that take it over USB (Apple Studio Display and Pro
Display XDR, LG UltraFine: the USB Monitor Control class) are driven
through hidraw (`olo_system::hid_monitor`), matched to their connector
by the EDID maker; `data/udev/70-olo-displays.rules` (installed by
`tools/install-session.sh`) gives the session's user the device. DDC/CI
isn't reachable on Apple Silicon. app_server keeps each display's level in
`OutputConfig::brightness` and sets it when the display appears; with none
kept, every display starts at full brightness. Brightness belongs to
app_server: `SetSettings` keeps its own copy of these levels.

Hardware is touched only when app_server is the session
(`Backend::IS_SESSION`), from a worker thread: the backlight through
logind `SetBrightness` (no root needed), USB monitors, the inhibitor,
suspend, the sound server. Headless sessions simulate a backlight and a
USB brightness control on every display (all starting full) and only log
"would sleep", so tests can drive all of it safely.

## The screen saver (crates/screensavers, apps/screensaver, app_server saver.rs)

The modules are R5's own list, in its order (Blackness, BuyNow, Flip,
Icons, Lens, Lissart, Message, Spiral, Spots, StringTheme, SuperString;
from period screenshots of R5's ScreenSaver preferences). Each is a
`olo_screensavers::Module` that draws a whole frame into a rect on a
`Canvas` (rectangles, lines, polylines, discs, rings, triangles, text,
icons and the desktop picture, whole or as textured triangles; points
and colours are the crate's own `geom` types), so the same code runs
full screen and in the preview monitor of Preferences ▸ Screen Saver.
Both draw on the kit (`kit_canvas`, feature `kit`): it keeps
what a module draws and paints it at the end of the frame, a run of the
same kind of thing to a `paint_layer`, since hundreds of crossing lines
each inserted in the scene's bounds tree made Lissart and SuperString
two to three times egui's CPU. Size things with `Frame::k()`, step motion
with the fixed 60 Hz `Clock`, and add settings as `Opt`s (stored as strings
in `settings.screen_saver.options[module]`; Preferences builds their
controls). Modules with `uses_desktop` (Flip, Lens) get a picture of the
desktop that app_server takes as the saver starts.

app_server starts `olo-screensaver` after `screen_saver.run_minutes`
idle, from `Request::StartScreenSaver` (Test) or when the pointer enters
the "Fade now" corner, on a private connection (`spawn_private`, like the
lock screen); the "Don't fade" corner and caffeinated mode hold it off. Any
input disconnects it (after 1.5 s grace for a deliberate start). With
`screen_saver.lock` it locks underneath after `lock_minutes`, and keeps
drawing over the lock screen (`Lock::over`) until the first input. The
displays turning off ends it. app_server hides the pointer while it runs
(`saver::shown_cursor`, in every backend and in screenshots): the
saver's own `CursorIcon::None` only counts once the pointer is on its
surface, which takes a move, and a move ends it.

**A program hiding the pointer** (`crates/app_server/src/pointer_hide.rs`;
Ben, 2026-11-18: "the cursor shouldn't disappear when over a video at
all, it should only ever disappear if in full screen and hasn't moved
for 5s and then come back if it moves again"). A program may ask for
no pointer; app_server weighs it (`SeatHandler::cursor_image` →
`client_cursor`; `AnvilState::cursor_status` is what's shown,
`pointer_hide` what was asked):
- hidden **while it rested** (the program had shown one since the
  pointer came to it, and it hadn't moved for a second,
  `Kind::Resting`: a video's player): shown all the same in a window;
  over a full-screen window hidden once it has been still five seconds
  (`STILL`; one timer, set when it's asked), and shown again the moment
  it moves (`pointer_moved`, from every motion: a clock read and a
  compare), whatever the program then says or doesn't;
- hidden **as it came in or while it moved** (`Kind::Own`: the program
  draws its own): hidden, as asked;
- **held** by its window (locked or confined: a game): hidden, as asked.
The look shown in place of "none" is the last the program asked for
(the arrow if its cursor surface has gone). The reason for the second
part of the first rule: in Chrome and Slack a pointer hidden over a
video sometimes stayed gone until it left the window and came back
(Chrome sends a cursor only when it changes or the pointer enters, so
one request refused or lost leaves it wrong till then). **Its cause
was the proxy's**, found with the `olo-debug-help` skill the same day:
after app_server restarts (every upgrade), olo-wlproxy dropped the
cursor shapes of a Chrome or Slack that had lived through it ("An
object is made again…", under the proxy above). In a test session
without a restart Chrome asks with the right serial and is obeyed in
every case tried (a click, the wheel, a key, a context menu, full
screen and back, a window opening over the still pointer), which is
why it wasn't seen there. Olo's Smithay also says when it refuses a
cursor from the very program the pointer is over
(`allow_setting_cursor`: log target `cursor`, "a cursor from the
program under the pointer was refused", with both serials, once an
enter). Measured (release, 20,000 synthetic moves over the
desktop, `perf stat --no-scale -e instructions:u`, three rounds each):
206.6–206.8 M instructions before, 207.2–208.1 M after (25 to 70 a
move), 1.30–1.46 µs → 1.32–1.36 µs of app_server's CPU a move.
Tried with Chrome on a test page (a looping video whose player hides a
rested pointer; `tsession shot --pointer` against a plain shot says
whether the pointer is drawn): in a window the pointer stays; in full
screen it goes at 5 s and is back on a move, again and again; a page
that never asks for it back gets it back; a box with `cursor: none`
keeps it hidden.

Test headless: `tsession ipc NAME '{"type":"start_screen_saver"}'`, or set
`screen_saver.module` with get/set_settings first.

## A new size is committed with its frame (olo_interface, the Wayland window)

A window given a size (a configure) acknowledges it and sets its
viewport to it at once, and the frame at that size is drawn when the
looper's layout for it comes (`Stage::draw_frame` draws nothing until
then, for `SIZE_WAIT` at most). Nothing of that is committed until that
frame is (`FrameLoop::size_undrawn`): the viewport's new size with the
buffer before it is that buffer stretched to the size. `frame()` used
to commit what was acknowledged whenever it drew nothing, so a size
that came just before a frame's callback (the two in one read) showed
the old picture stretched until the next frame: a pixel or two in a
resize by hand, a whole frame of a zoom or a tile, and every step of
app_server's glide, which sends each size as a frame begins (found
2026-11-20 with `WAYLAND_DEBUG=1` on the app: `set_destination`,
`ack_configure`, `commit` with no `attach` between). With the commit
held, the stage asks for the frame itself when the wait is over
(`frame_after`), as no callback is on its way.

## Fractional scaling (app_server render.rs, shell/deco.rs; the kits)

A screen can be at 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75, 2, 2.5 or 3 (Preferences ▸
Displays; each is a whole number of 120ths, as wp-fractional-scale
sends it). At every one of them, nothing Olo draws is resampled, and
every line and edge is a whole device pixel. This is how modern
compositors and toolkits do it (KWin's pixel-grid snapping, Mutter,
Chrome, GTK 4.16 text), and how Olo does it:

- **Sizes in a row on the 4-point grid.** 4 points is a whole device
  pixel at 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75 and 2×; 2 points only at 1, 1.5 and 2×. A
  fixed width, a label column's divider, or an inset that the next thing
  starts after, if it's off the 4-point grid, starts everything after it
  on a half pixel at 1.25× and 1.75×. Layout and painting then round it
  apart, a pixel at a time. Found so at 1.25× and 1.75×, and fixed
  (2026-11-08):
  - Power's grid of menus: gaps 11.2 and 12.8.
  - Network's columns: a menu's text a pixel off a field's under it.
  - Telegram's panes: laid out as roots of their own, a pixel past the
    window.
  - A 20-point check box centred beside a 24-point menu: their labels a
    pixel off level. In a row, a check box takes the row's height (the
    form's `row` does it).
  - Right-aligned labels: `style::label` rounds their left edge down, so
    they never run past their anchor.
  - The review measures a text field by its frame.
  `tools/dev/ui-lint --review --scales 1,1.25,1.5,1.75,2` checks every
  app at all five.
- **Clients draw at the device size.** The Interface Kit asks app_server for
  wp-fractional-scale-v1 and wp-viewporter on every surface, draws into
  a buffer of `round(size × scale)` pixels and sets the viewport's
  destination to the logical size (a window's scale is the fractional
  one, never an integer scale set over it). app_server
  places each window on a whole device pixel
  (`to_physical_precise_round`), so a buffer lands one to one. Programs
  without fractional scale get the next whole scale and are scaled down.
- **app_server's own pictures go pixel for pixel**
  (`render::exact`, `render::picture`). smithay sizes a memory element in
  whole logical points, so a picture drawn at its device size `w` came
  out `round(round(w / s) × s)` wide: 2561 pixels for a 2560 wallpaper
  at 1.5×, softly resampled. Wrapped in `render::Exact`, it fills exactly
  the rectangle it was drawn for. Every app_server picture goes through
  it: the wallpaper, tabs, the ⌘Tab switcher, the level indicator,
  Identify and the keyboard hints' badges. Lines (the hints' group
  outlines) are hairlines between corners rounded to the nearest pixel.
- **The decorator works in device pixels.** The frame is drawn outward
  from where the content lands: a border's width (`px(BORDER)`, the
  content's own offset) on every side, the same on all four.
  - *Its lines* are `deco::lines(scale)`. The outline is a hairline,
    `floor(scale)` (as olo-kit's `style::line_pixels`). The bevel's light
    and shadow are each `round(scale)`. The flat middle takes the rest.
  - *At 1.5×* that gives 1, 2, 3 and 2 pixels. Rounding each logical line
    from the window's corner gave 2, 1, 2, 1 and 2 on one side, and
    mirrored it differently on the other.
  - *Where the frame reaches:* it can end a pixel past `px` of its logical
    right and bottom. A tab ending there ends on it.
  - *The tab* is drawn the same way, its boxes inset equally from its own
    two ends, so every tab looks the same wherever it sits.
  - `frame_bands_at_every_scale` pins the bands at each scale.
- **The kit snaps what it works out.**
  - *Sizes* are on the 2-point grid (whole pixels at 1×, 1.5× and 2×).
    Positions it works out go through `style::snap` or `snap_centred`.
    Lines are `style::line_pixels`.
  - *A box's border* (olo-kit: `.border_1()`, `.border(…)`) is whole
    device pixels, laid out, drawn and clipped the same
    (`Style::border_pixels`, `style::border_device_pixels`: a point is
    `floor(scale)` pixels, never less than one, as the kit's lines). A
    one-point border was a pixel and a half at 1.5×: a line with a smear
    beside it, and where its clip's edge fell on the pixels' centres the
    smear ran along part of an edge only (sudo's command box).
  - *What's scrolled is on whole device pixels* (olo-kit). Where a
    scroller is is read by what draws its rows, by agents and by the
    review, so it's kept on the scale's pixels wherever it comes from:
    asked to go somewhere once laid out (`ScrollHandle::settle`: a
    view needn't be whole points tall, nor half of what's left of it
    round a row), when the scale changes, and when a node takes a
    scroller its view kept while it wasn't shown (`ScrollHandle::snap`,
    from `follow_scroll`). A list on a tab that wasn't showing when the
    scale changed came back a third of a point off, every row between
    pixels (the live lint, Date & Time's Time Zone list, which centres
    the zone in use).
  - *A scroller shown again scrolls from where it was*
    (olo-interface). Its place is kept twice: by the looper, which
    makes the rows near it, and by the display thread, which moves it
    under the wheel and fingers and says where it got to, each word
    marked with the looper's last move of it (`ScrollHandle::put`'s
    epoch) so one from before that move is dropped as stale. The
    display thread lets go of a scroller a commit leaves out (its tab
    isn't chosen), so every scroll layer carries where its looper has
    it (`Layer::at`, `set` when the looper moved it since it last
    said), and one the display thread hasn't starts there. It started
    at the top: the looper's rows were at the end, the list blank, and
    every word of it after carried an old mark, the wheel's too
    (Agent Screens' History back from Stats, Ben 2026-11-14;
    `ui_lint_a_list_shown_again_scrolls_from_where_it_was`).
  - *A drawing kept lands where a fresh one would* (olo-kit). What a
    node drew is kept and moved with it when layout puts it elsewhere,
    if that's by whole device pixels; a drawing of the app's own (a
    canvas) only if by whole points too, else it's drawn again
    (`WindowCore::place`). What a drawing rounds to a point (a check
    box's square: its middle less 6.5 points, rounded) comes out a
    pixel elsewhere half a point along at 2×: moved, a square sat a
    pixel off its label until something drew it again. (What scrolls
    moves as one in its layer, by device pixels, and isn't drawn again:
    nothing in it jitters.)
  - *A window's viewport* (olo-kit) is its own size in points, while
    what's laid out is its buffer's (`round(size × scale)` pixels over
    the scale). Set from the buffer's size cut to whole points, a
    window whose buffer rounded down was a point short (487 points at
    1.75× are 852 pixels, 486.86 points: 486), and app_server drew its
    852 rows in the room of 850.5.
  - *The text caret*, menus' and tips' outlines are hairlines at each
    scale (`style::hairline`): a one-point stroke would be a pixel and a
    half at 1.5× and smear over two.
  - *An icon* is drawn at its texture's size from a whole pixel. A bitmap
    with no size of its own (ours come at 16, 24, 32 …, so 20 at 1.25×)
    is averaged down to exactly the device size once, when it loads (as
    Chrome scales its icons), instead of being stretched by the GPU
    every frame. Pictures are resampled exactly to their device size on
    a worker (`ImageView`).
  - *Viewer's pages* are drawn pixel for pixel once rendered for the
    current zoom and scale.
  - *An app that caches anything measured in pixels* keys it by the scale,
    as Terminal's cell metrics are (`Metrics::ppp`); a window can move to
    a display at another scale.
  - *At 1.25× and 1.75×* two points are 2.5 and 3.5 pixels. Edges are
    still crisp there (each is rounded), but spacing may differ by a
    pixel.
- **A picture made for the device is drawn at its own size whatever the
  float noise of its bounds** (`sprite_bounds`, interface painter.rs).
  A picture's bounds reach the painter as logical pixels and are
  multiplied by the scale; its corner is floored and its size ceiled,
  as a picture covering part of a pixel must be. But 968 / 1.5 × 1.5 is
  968.00006, and ceiled as it came a 968-pixel tile was drawn 969 wide,
  every texel blended with the next (Viewer's PDF pages at 1.5×: soft
  across the second tile, a seam where the tiles met). A bound within a
  hundredth of a whole device pixel is now that pixel, before the floor
  and the ceil; its test tries every size to 4096 at 1.25×, 1.5× and
  1.75×.
- **Text** is drawn by the Interface Kit at the device size, each line's
  baseline on a whole pixel, as each display's text rendering says
  (Preferences ▸ Display): at most hinted vertically
  ("light", as FreeType, GTK 4.16 and Chrome do it) and positioned
  across in subpixel steps, so stems and baselines sit on pixels while
  shapes and spacing stay as designed. Which step and which pixel come
  from where the glyph is to the nearest 64th of a device pixel
  (`painter::glyph_at`), not the bare float: a place in points is added
  up from everything that holds it, and at 1.25× a glyph a quarter into
  its pixel came out 126.24999 one way and 126.25 another, a quarter
  pixel apart drawn afresh and moved there kept. Tab titles (cosmic-text and swash)
  are hinted, on a whole-pixel baseline.
- **The pointer** is a vector drawn at each screen's exact scale (see the
  next section).

To check: the layout review flags fills, icons and outlines off the
pixel grid (`off-pixel`, `blurry-icon` with an icon a pixel off its
texture's size, `blurry-outline`). For the decorator, zoom into a
corner at each scale (`$T zoom NAME OUT X Y W H 8`), with the window at
an odd x so it sits between pixels.

## The pointer (crates/hvif, app_server cursor.rs)

Where it is drawn: a frame draws the pointer where the last reports say
it will be at the frame's vblank (`cursor::Track`, from the velocity of
the last two reports, at most a frame ahead and only while reports keep
coming and nothing warped the pointer; kept on the display). A mouse
reports at its own rate (125 Hz, 1000 Hz) against the display's (60,
120 Hz): drawn at the last position, one frame got two reports' worth
of motion and the next three, and the pointer moved unevenly though the
hand didn't (Ben, 2026-11-01: "jittery/off"); as `pace.rs` does for
scrolling, the frame clock gets the position for its time: where it was
4 ms before the vblank, interpolated between the reports either side of
then, or past the last report along the velocity of the last 6 ms of
reports by at most 4 ms (a frame's extrapolation at the last two
reports' velocity overshot every turn and was noisier than the real
position with a 1 kHz mouse: measured, `{"type":"pointer_trace",
"output":"DP-1"}` answers the last 120 frames that drew the pointer,
vblank, real and drawn position, the last report's age and interval).
Hit-testing, focus and what clients get use the real position.
`OLO_POINTER_AHEAD=0` draws the real position.

What the pointer is in follows what is under it, not only its moves
(Smithay looks again only on motion): a window that opens, closes,
comes forward or moves under a still pointer (Space in Tracker opening
Quick Look under it) takes the scroll or the click that comes next
(Ben, 2026-11-05: Quick Look didn't scroll until the pointer moved).
Before a scroll and a button press, `repoint` enters what is under the
pointer if that isn't what it is in, or is but moved (about 2 µs a
scroll event, 300 wheel notches measured, and no motion sent when
nothing changed); not while a grab has the pointer (a button held, a
drag, a menu). A window or layer that comes on screen, a window
brought forward, minimized, restored or closed asks for it once that
turn of the loop is done (`repoint_soon`), so the window under the
pointer has it, its cursor and its hover, without a move. The kit takes
the place it is entered at as a move (`wl_pointer.enter` dispatches a
`MouseMove`): otherwise a window entered without a move kept the
last cursor and hover until the pointer moved.

The pointer's reports themselves are watched (`Track::health`,
`PointerHealth` in `{"type":"frames"}`, Activity Monitor ▸ Inputs'
Pointer card): reports a second, the device's interval (1 ms for a
1 kHz mouse), gaps over 5 ms within a run of motion in the last minute
and the longest. A gap is the mouse's, not a frame's: a receiver asleep
(USB autosuspend; `data/udev/95-olo-input.rules`, installed by
`tools/install-session.sh`, keeps every USB device with a HID
interface awake) or a 2.4 GHz link dropping packets (Ben's Razer receiver on a
hub, 2026-11-01: frames of 67, 10, 50 px with reports 1 ms apart, and
"stuck for a second" after a pause). No frame can make up for a report
that never came.

The touchpad's reports are watched as they reach app_server
(`touch_health::Track`, `TouchHealth` in `{"type":"frames"}`, Activity
Monitor ▸ Displays' Touchpad card): reports a second and, over the last
minute, each one's latency from the kernel's time on it to app_server
handling it (libinput's work, Olo's touch filter and its palm model,
and any wait for the main thread, which draws too), typically, at the
99th percentile and the longest; whether the filter and the person's
palm model are in use (its training date and test numbers); and the
main thread's nice, realtime or not and `uclamp.min`. Noting a report
is 21 ns (`note_cost`; 15 on a performance core); the minute's figures, 44–68 µs on the ThinkPad (one computation, cold; 33 when first measured, 2026-11-03, the code the same), are made when
asked. A 99th percentile over 4 ms (half a 120 Hz frame) is shown red:
touches waiting on frames being drawn.

The pointer is Haiku's system cursor set (`crates/hvif/cursors`, from
Haiku's CursorData.cpp, MIT; see the LICENSE there). `olo-hvif` reads
the Haiku Vector Icon Format and draws it as Haiku's IconRenderer does
(shapes in order, 2.2-gamma blending, level-of-detail, stroke and contour
transformers); `olo_hvif::cursor::render(shape, scale)` draws a cursor
as Haiku's CursorManager does: 22 logical pixels, the icon's top-left
32 × 32 region, a soft shadow, the hotspot scaled. app_server's
`cursor.rs` maps CSS cursor names (from its own decorations, or clients'
cursor-shape-v1 requests) to them, caches each shape per scale and
hands the backend a buffer whose pixels land one-to-one on the screen.
Clients that set a cursor surface still get theirs. To see every cursor:
`OLO_CURSOR_SHEET=/tmp/c.png cargo test -p olo-hvif sheet`.

When the displays sleep for idleness, `Backend::set_displays_on(false)`
clears every CRTC on DRM (DPMS off) and rendering stops, since any frame
would turn them back on; input, waking from sleep or a returning session
calls it with `true` and renders again.

### The pointer on a thread of its own (app_server input_thread.rs)

Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ Scheduler ▸ Pointer, "Move the pointer on a
thread of its own" (`Settings::input_thread`, off until tried on Ben's
ThinkPad; `OLO_INPUT_THREAD=1` or `0` overrides it): libinput is read on
a thread of its own, `olo-input`, at nice −15 (the most rtkit gives) and
realtime above the loop (12; guarded, as "Realtime threads and the kept
core" says: rtkit's limit on a realtime thread that spins would end
app_server and the whole desktop with it, and the guard puts it back to
its nice first), on the kept core beside the loop, and while app_server's loop
is held, that thread moves the cursor itself. Why: the loop does
everything (clients' requests, every display's frames), and under load
it was seen held 78 and 142 ms in the GPU driver waiting for a buffer's
lock (2026-11-12); with libinput on the loop the pointer stood still
that long, and worse, the kernel keeps only 64 events of a device
unread (about 30 ms of a 1000 Hz mouse) and drops the rest, so the
pointer also ended up short of where the hand took it.

- libinput's context and devices live on the thread (they aren't
  `Send`). Its events are made owned (`input_thread::Threaded`, smithay's
  `InputBackend`: every event kind, with its device's snapshot `Dev`)
  and sent to the loop a batch a read, numbered; the loop handles them
  exactly as libinput's own (the handling is generic), then says which
  it handled and where the pointer is (`View`). Settings, the keyboards'
  lights, a restart for the touch filter and the session pausing go the
  other way as `Command`s. Devices are opened by the session, the loop's
  alone: the thread asks (`contacts::Request`) and waits; the loop never
  waits on the thread.
- The pointer must be on the display's cursor plane for any of this:
  on an HDR display it wasn't until 2026-11-13 (composed into the HDR
  frame; HACKING, "HDR"), so on Ben's OLED the thread never had a plane
  to move (the log's `the pointer is on a plane of the display's own`
  never came for eDP-1; `{"type":"frames"}` says `cursor_plane` for
  each display).
- After each frame the loop says where the cursor plane is (smithay's
  `DrmCompositor::cursor_plane`) with the pointer where that frame drew
  it, on the CRTC's own cursor plane only (not an overlay standing in for
  one), and not while a window locks or confines the pointer, a finger is
  the pointer, a drag shows its icon, a mirror shows the display, the
  displays are off or the session is another's.
- A motion the loop hasn't handled after 12 ms (`TAKE_OVER`): the thread
  moves the plane to where the loop will put the pointer (its last place
  and the motion since, kept on the screens as the loop keeps it, on the
  display it's on, turned as the display is) with the kernel's legacy
  cursor move, which keeps the plane's buffer and takes the CRTC's locks
  and none of the GPU's; at most every 4 ms (it shows at a vblank). The
  loop catches up from the same events and draws it there; when it has,
  it wakes the thread, which lets go ("the loop caught up: the input
  thread had moved the pointer while it was held ms=388 moves=60").
- The switch takes effect at once, both ways (`start_libinput`): on,
  the loop's libinput is dropped (closing its devices) and the thread
  started; off, the thread is told to quit and libinput starts on the
  loop again only once the thread says it has closed every device
  (`contacts::Request::Stopped`, on the same channel as its closes), so
  no device is ever open twice. Either way the devices come back as
  new, with their settings.
- What it costs (vkms, a 1000 Hz mouse, each thread's time on a CPU from
  its schedstat, six runs of each, 2026-11-13): idle, nothing (0 wakeups:
  the thread sleeps in its poll, with no timer unless a motion is
  waiting on the loop); moving, one more wakeup a report and about 3% of
  a core more: the loop 4.6% and the thread 3.8%, against 5.4% on the
  loop alone (about 30 µs a report, so 0.4% for a 125 Hz mouse or
  touchpad). Most of it is the second wakeup itself; calloop's own
  calls (5 of the thread's 9 a report: its timerfd and notifier, re-armed
  each wait) are under 0.2% and were left.

`tools/dev/cursor-thread-check` tries it on a real seat of its own:
asks sudo once for a virtual display with a cursor plane (vkms) and a
virtual mouse (uinput) on "seat-olotest", which the person's session
never sees (`tools/dev/cursor-thread-seat`: a udev rule, checked before
anything moves, all undone at the end), runs a test app_server there
(`OLO_TEST_SEAT`, libseat's noop session, a sandbox home, drawing in
software) with libinput on the loop, then turns the switch on as
Preferences does (`set_settings`) and again off, and each way reads
the kernel's cursor plane every 5 ms while the loop is held 400 ms
(`{"type":"hold_loop","ms":400}`, which only a test app_server
honours). vkms shows its 512 px cursor plane only while all of it is on
its 1024 × 768 display, so the check starts the pointer near the top
left each time. 2026-11-13: on the loop, the plane stood still 260 ms
(all the motion there was) and the loop, catching up, put the pointer at
162 px of the 302 the mouse had moved it to; on the thread, it never
stood still more than 20 ms (12 to take over, 4 between moves, 5
between reads) and the loop put it exactly where the thread had; turned
off again, the plane followed the mouse on the loop. `--hdr` does it
all with the display drawn as an HDR one (a test seat's app_server
takes `OLO_HEADLESS_COLOR` as a headless one does; vkms takes no HDR
signal, but it's drawn as one) and HDR switched on as Preferences does:
the same, 129 px while held, 21 ms at most still. Moving the pointer
there (three runs each, alternating, the machine busy) cost app_server
12.4–15.3% of a core and 6,700 wakeups a second while the pointer was
composed into the HDR frame, and 3.2–4.0% and 800 on the cursor plane;
a frame's drawing 478–571 µs (median) against 117–138.
Left: the first frame after a hold may have been drawn before it, so
the pointer can step back to there for a frame (seen once, 1 px); and Ben's Intel panel
(PSR2) may take the kernel's slow path for a legacy cursor move, a
commit a move, which only his machine shows.

## Windows' buffers stay in memory (kernel/gpu-memory, apps/gpu-memory; Olo Doctor; tools/dev/gpu-holds)

The desktop stood still for up to two seconds under a build, keys and
all (Ben, 2026-11-16: "i just had a responsiveness stall when i was
typing and it actually even repeated a letter eg "sunbursst" please
root cause and fix", then "i don't ever want it stalling … go as low
level as you need to"). His log had 126 holds of 100 ms or more in a
day, every one in the same place: app_server handing a frame to the GPU
("slow frame: finishing it took_ms=1916", "input (key) came 2045 ms
late: the loop was held by look (whole)"). A key pressed just before a
hold had its release delivered after the client's repeat delay (300 ms),
so the client typed it twice.

**What held it**, traced in the kernel (bpftrace, as root; kept as
`tools/dev/gpu-holds`):

* Intel's xe driver takes, for every GPU submission
  (`DRM_IOCTL_XE_EXEC`), the lock of every buffer its client shares
  with another (`drm_gpuvm_exec_lock`: each "external object" bound in
  its address space). app_server shares every window's buffers with the
  app that draws them: 221 buffers, 3.4 GiB, on his desktop; 15,000 lock
  takes a second. Whatever holds one of those locks holds the
  compositor's loop (`drm_exec_lock_contended`).
* TTM, the memory manager under xe, backs GPU buffers up to swap when
  the kernel is short of memory (`xe_shrinker_scan`, called by kswapd as
  any shrinker is: 138 times in 30 s of a build), were it only short of
  file cache, which a build's output always makes it. Over 1 GiB of 101
  programs' buffers were out; an idle app's, all of them.
* A buffer backed up comes back inside its program's next submission
  (`xe_exec_ioctl` → `xe_vm_validate_rebind` → `ttm_tt_restore` →
  `ttm_pool_restore_commit`: pages copied back one by one, their
  caching changed, each a round of every processor), under that
  submission's locks: its window's buffers', which app_server's every
  submission takes too. The lock's owner during his compositor's waits
  was an app's `display` thread in exactly that stack (Tracker's,
  Terminal's, Chrome's GPU process). And every buffer of every window
  sits in app_server's own address space too, so its own next frame
  brought back the ones it shares.

The same from-scratch build of three apps (6 to 9 minutes; app_server's
own log, and every lock its loop took, traced):

| | slow frames (4 ms or more handing over) | keys late | lock waits of 20 ms or more |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 GB of zram swap, as Fedora sets it | 47 (12 over 100 ms, the worst 951 ms) | 3 (149, 188, 887 ms) | 30 |
| swap off | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| swap on, Olo's patch in | 0 | 0 | 0 (of 9.5 million takes, one of 1 ms) |

**The gate.** TTM backs a buffer up only while there is swap space free:
`ttm_backup_bytes_avail()` (free swap, in bytes) is the one question
(`ttm_pool_backup` refuses without it, and xe's shrinker then counts
nothing it could shrink but what programs have given up: purgeable
buffers, still freed). No setting turns it off, a program can't pin its
buffers (xe has no such call), and the kernel's swappiness doesn't
govern it: it is asked for whenever kswapd runs. With no swap at all the
answer is zero, which is why turning swap off cured it.

**Olo's patch** (`kernel/gpu-memory/olo_gpu_memory.c`, GPL-2.0 as the
kernel is): a live patch that replaces that one function in the running
kernel with one that says none. GPU buffers are never backed up; the
computer keeps its swap for ordinary memory (Ben: "is there a way to
just prevent stuff that is going to be used with the gpu from going
into swap?"). One function, no restart, undone by unloading it; not a
replacement of the driver (which could only be tried by restarting the
session, and would be the whole driver's to carry for each kernel).

A module is built for one kernel. **`olo-gpu-memory`** (apps/gpu-memory;
root, systemd's `olo-gpu-memory.service`, at every start) builds the
patch for the running kernel where it hasn't yet (a new kernel's first
start: three seconds, with the kernel's own build system, `make` and
the compiler: one of the few places Olo runs another program, there
being no other way to build a module for a kernel; its headers are
`kernel-devel`'s, which `kernel-devel-matched` brings with each new
kernel), installs it to `/lib/modules/KERNEL/extra/olo/` (where locally
built modules go, and the one place SELinux lets a service load a
module from: from /var/lib the kernel refused it, "Permission denied")
and loads it (`finit_module`). Its work is in
`/var/lib/olo-gpu-memory/KERNEL`; what it built for kernels since
removed, it removes. It says how it went in `/run/olo-gpu-memory/status`
("patched", or "failed: " and why), and `olo-gpu-memory --status`
prints what there is as JSON (anyone); `--remove` takes the patch out
(its service's stop; an upgrade's restart takes an older patch out and
puts this one in). Where it can't (no headers, no live patching in the
kernel, Secure Boot refusing an unsigned module), the kernel is as it
was and the service ends failed.

**Olo Doctor** (`graphics_swap` in checks.rs): where xe drives a display
and swap is on, "Windows' graphics memory is moved out to swap"
(Problem), whose fix, **Keep Graphics Memory in Memory**, installs the
service (root's copy of the program in /usr/local/libexec/olo, its unit,
enabled and started; what building needs installed first where it's
missing). Where the kernel can't take the patch (Secure Boot; no live
patching) or the service tried and couldn't, the fix is **Turn Swap
Off** instead: zram-generator told to make none (an /etc file naming no
device), /etc/fstab's swap lines commented, systemd reloaded *before*
the areas are turned off (`Step::SwapOff`: `swapoff(2)` each).
That order matters: turned off alone, an area is back within minutes,
as swap's target still wants its unit and the next system service to
start brings the target's wants up again (measured: off at 11:47, on
again at 11:58 as PackageKit started). The patch loaded but its service
not installed (or an older build's): "kept out of swap only until the
next start", **Keep It at Every Start**.

**Looking again** (`sudo tools/dev/gpu-holds [SECONDS]`): whether swap
is on, how much of each program's GPU memory is out of memory now
(fdinfo's total less resident), then, on the compositor's loop, every
wait of 20 ms or more on a buffer's lock with the lock's owner and its
kernel stack, display commits that waited, and at the end all its lock
waits by length, how often xe's shrinker ran and who brought buffers
back. It needs bpftrace (`dnf install bpftrace`); with the patch in,
the kernel's own probes on xe and TTM still attach.

Not the cause, though each looked it: the scheduler (the loop is
realtime, and waited on no run queue), the GPU being busy (the wait is
for a lock, before anything is submitted), memory running out (40 GB
were available; file cache alone makes kswapd run).

### The core stays in memory (`olo_app::realtime::lock_memory`; Olo Doctor's Keep the Core in Memory)

A page of app_server's own moved to swap, or its code dropped and read
back from disk, is a wait for everything on screen as surely as a lock
is (Ben, 2026-11-16: "is there a way or anything we could/should do to
also prevent the latency-sensitive olo processes from being swapped
out? … and any realtime/rtkit type processes e.g.
libinput/pipewire/etc … even if it isn't being swapped out right now i
think it'd make sense to keep all those core "responsiveness" processes
out of swap always"). It had taken 7,669 major page faults in 2 h 20
min.

**Olo's own.** The programs that are realtime for as long as they run
lock their memory as they start: app_server (libinput's thread is in
it), the session (its watchdog), the supervisor, Deskbar, the proxy
(`olo-wlproxy`) and the voice service
(`olo_system::realtime::keep_in_memory`, where realtime is `wanted`:
not on an agent's screen, nor a headless app_server). `mlockall` with
`MCL_CURRENT | MCL_FUTURE | MCL_ONFAULT`: everything mapped now and
later, each page from when it's first touched, so nothing is read in
for it and room only reserved takes none; what's locked is never
swapped nor dropped. Not an app's: apps' memory is the bulk of what the
desktop holds, and locked it could never be given up (swappiness keeps
it in RAM while there's cache to drop, below). Not inherited: what
app_server starts isn't locked.

Only where the account may lock without limit (`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`
unlimited; a login's is 8 MB): with a limit, `mlockall` is refused when
what's mapped is over it, and were it under, whatever the program
mapped past it later would fail to map, and the program end for want of
memory that was there. So a limited program doesn't lock, and says so
("app_server's memory isn't kept in RAM: the account may lock 8 MB, not
all a program has").

**Olo Doctor** (`memory_kept`): "The desktop's core can be moved out of
memory" (Recommended), **Keep the Core in Memory**:

* `memlock unlimited` for the account, in the limits file Allow Realtime
  writes (`/etc/security/limits.d/80-olo-realtime.conf`: in force at
  every login);
* the same for the programs running now (`Step::LetSessionLockMemory`:
  `prlimit(2)` on each of the account's processes), so what starts from
  them has it without a new login: app_server started again by an
  upgrade locks its memory at once;
* the sound server kept out of swap: `MemorySwapMax=0` for PipeWire, its
  PulseAudio side and WirePlumber (drop-ins in /etc/systemd/user, read
  at once by the person's manager, `after_fix`: a running unit takes the
  setting on its manager's reload, tried on a unit of the test's own).
  Not PipeWire's own `mem.mlock-all`: it locks without `MCL_ONFAULT`, so
  each of the three read in everything it had mapped, 40 MB become 260
  to 310 (measured in a private sound server, `tools/dev/pw-sandbox`,
  with the limit raised). On Fedora their memory is shielded from being
  reclaimed at all besides: uresourced gives `session.slice`, where
  they run, 250 MB that is never taken (`memory.min`, handed down:
  `memory_recursiveprot`); PipeWire's group had no page reclaimed in 22
  hours.

Then "The desktop's core keeps its memory from Olo's next start" until
the person's app_server has locked its own (`VmLck` in its status), and
fine after.

### Swappiness and the size of swap (Olo Doctor)

`vm.swappiness` is how readily the kernel moves programs' own memory to
swap rather than dropping file cache: 60 as the kernel has it. Doctor's
**Keep Programs in Memory** sets it to 1 where swap is on
(`/etc/sysctl.d/80-olo-memory.conf`, and now): cache goes first, and
swap is used when memory is truly short (Ben, 2026-11-16: "could we
just make it set swapiness to 1 … without losing the benefits when
it's really needed?"). It doesn't govern the graphics driver's shrinker
(above), which is asked whenever kswapd runs. Measured little either
way once the patch was in: in 26 minutes with a whole release build,
