7.8 MiB of programs' memory went to swap at 60 (the 16.8 GB written to
swap in the 21 hours before were with windows' buffers among them).

**That is as far as swappiness goes, and nothing here may go further.**
Under Fedora's multi-generational LRU, 1 is "the files' cache first" of
each generation, not of the whole, so a computer whose agents build all
day still writes to swap with memory free (102 GB in three days on
Ben's, 2026-11-20: "i want the swap to only get used when absolutely
necessary"). A setting that made it so, **Swap used last**
(swappiness 0 with the kernel's older reclaim and more room kept free:
kernel/TUNING.md, "Tried and withdrawn"), was built, measured in the
guest, put on on that computer the same day, and withdrawn within the
hour: with nothing going to swap until the cache was all but gone,
memory ran short at a peak, a driver's own allocation failed
(NVIDIA's: drivers ask in a way that may be refused, where a program's
waits), its card's power management failed after it, and the card
stopped answering ("just remove that particular swap setting it's
obviously dangerous"). What it taught: the computer needs its swap at
its peaks, and a kernel that swaps only at the last has nothing ready
for an allocation that may be refused. So **what is swapped may be steered, never whether**: which
programs' memory goes first is for control groups to say (docs/TODO.md,
"Background work is swapped first"), and the amount the kernel may
reclaim or swap is left whole.

With graphics memory kept out of it, more swap costs nothing until it's
used but its tables, and gives what should be moved out somewhere to go
before the largest program is stopped. Doctor **suggests** swap as
large as memory (Ben: "have olo doctor suggest a swap size equal to the
ram size, e.g. 64gb for this machine, and have it offer to set it"):
**Make Swap as Large as Memory** writes zram-generator's size
(`zram-size = ram`), reloads systemd and makes the device again
(`Step::RemakeZramSwap`). Only for the generator's swap in compressed
memory (a disk's size is a partition's), and only where xe can't take
the room for windows' buffers (Olo's patch in, or another driver). Not
free: the kernel's tables for a swap area are there used or not, 222 MB
for 62 GiB of zram on Ben's computer (`VmallocUsed`, 216 to 438 MB), a
third of a percent of its size, which the suggestion says.

`RemakeZramSwap` does the making itself: the swap turned off
(`swapoff(2)`: what's in it comes back into memory), the device reset
(`/sys/block/zramN/reset`, asked again for up to ten seconds while the
kernel says busy), its swap unit started afresh
(`olo_system::systemd::start_afresh`: its failures forgotten first),
and the swap looked for in `/proc/swaps` before the step is done.
Restarting zram-generator's own units, the first try, left his computer
with no swap and both units failed while Doctor said "done": udev has
the device open for a moment after its swap goes, the generator's reset
asks once ("Device or resource busy"), and its next start then can't
set a size ("Cannot change disksize for initialized device"). And
Doctor's unit steps now fail where the unit stands failed after its
start (`systemd::failed`), where before any start that systemd took
was called done.

## No program held for large pieces of graphics memory (kernel/gpu-pages, apps/gpu-pages, crates/kmod; Olo Doctor; tools/dev/memory-holds, gpu-pages-check, gpu-pages-try)

Ben, 2026-11-20: "something is really broken my desktop is lagging";
and of whatever it took: "if you need to write a new kernel module as
part of olo or anything to fix bugs or make it work properly that's
also on the table if it can't be done through standard linux
mechanisms. if you do that, work with astra 6.2 max on the design and
implementation and review".

**What was found** (`sudo tools/dev/memory-holds`; kernel/TUNING.md,
"Graphics memory in 2 MB pieces", has the figures and the account).
The GPU drivers' memory pool (TTM, under Intel's xe) fills every buffer
with the largest pieces of memory it can get, and since Linux 7.3 tries
hard for the size xe names, 2 MB: where none is free it compacts
memory and reclaims on the thread that made the buffer. Those threads
draw. With memory in small pieces and a build running, kit apps'
drawing threads and Chrome's GPU process were held a third to half of
a second at a time, app_server's loop up to 8 ms, with tens of
gigabytes to be had. No setting of the kernel's turns it off.

**The module** (`kernel/gpu-pages/olo_gpu_pages.c`): a kprobe at
`ttm_pool_alloc_page()`'s entry that takes `__GFP_DIRECT_RECLAIM` off
its gfp argument for that one try (the pool's own "beneficial" size,
2 MB, from the page allocator, for one PCI device bound to xe, named
as it loads: `bdf=`), the kernel's own function then running: a free
2 MB piece is taken, the kernel's threads are woken to make more, and
the pool goes on with smaller pieces as it does whenever a size is
refused. Nothing of the kernel's is replaced or copied.
`/sys/module/olo_gpu_pages/parameters`: `on` (root's to write), `bdf`,
whose load it is (`service_id`, `trial_id`), and for anyone `changed`
(tries made with no waiting allowed, whether or not they would have
waited: not waits spared) and `missed`.

**How it is kept from being wrong**, each way from a review with Astra
that broke the one before in a guest (five reviews: the design, and
four of what was built):

1. *It checks itself as it loads, before it touches anything real.*
   Until the check has passed its probe looks only at a pool of the
   module's own, owned by the device (so the check goes the way real
   buffers will), comparing the pool's address before reading anything
   of it. That pool is filled twice while the page allocator's
   tracepoint is watched: as the kernel has it the 2 MB try must be the
   hard one and the 1 MB try must not reclaim; with the change the 2 MB
   try must differ by the one flag. Otherwise it says why in the
   kernel's log and its load fails. (A probe registers and does nothing
   where probes are disarmed for the whole kernel; kernels before 7.3
   wait at other sizes too.)
2. *It is loaded only into a kernel it was checked in*
   (`kernel/gpu-pages/QUALIFIED`, a line a build: release, the
   kernel's build ID, its ttm module's, and the build of Olo's live
   patch `olo_gpu_memory` that was beside it; `olo_kmod::builds` reads
   the IDs from `/sys/kernel/notes` and the modules' notes). Where a
   build keeps the function's arguments is nothing a module can check
   as it loads; and a live patch changes the kernel under the same
   notes, so the module loads with none in the kernel or with exactly
   that one, settled. **A new kernel is not on the list**: the module
   stays out of it, which Olo Doctor and the Kernel tab say, until an
   Olo with its line is installed.
3. *No tool says a build is good.* `tools/dev/gpu-pages-check
   --qualify` runs the guests on the very build and reads what it can
   of the function's machine code; a review showed that reading passes
   shapes the probe would misread. It prints the build's words and
   "pending a person's review" (exit 2) or "listed". **To qualify a
   kernel**: run it; run `--qualify`; then read, in that build, what
   the list's header sets out (the caller's setting up of the three
   arguments and the callee's use at the probe's site, the function's
   range and clones, every relocation against it in code and data, the
   pool's layout, the falling back on refusal), with Astra; add the
   line, and say in the commit who read what.
4. *One loader at a time, each with its own.* The service gives each
   load a name (`service_id`), loads it switched off, and switches on
   only what carries that name, for the device, in a kernel still as
   checked; it removes only its own, switched off first. A trial's
   load carries the trial's (`trial_id`) and is on only while the trial
   holds `/dev/olo_gpu_pages_trial_switch` open: writing `on` does
   nothing for it, and whatever ends the trial, a kill too, puts the
   kernel's own behaviour back. Both take `/run/olo-gpu-pages.lifecycle.lock`.
   (The service had switched on a module it never loaded, on a build
   not listed; the trial's first form could leave its module in and
   on.)
5. *It is not offered until it has been tried on a real computer, and
   nothing switches it on before* (`kernel_tuning::GRAPHICS_PAGES_OFFERED`,
   false; a made-up computer, `OLO_KERNEL_ROOT`, always has it, for
   tests and pictures; no switch in the environment does it on a real
   one). The guests show what it does in the kernel and can't show
   what it does to frames. `sudo tools/dev/gpu-pages-try
   --on-this-computer`, with the computer's owner's word and never
   without, runs matched phases off and on by turns and takes the
   module out again whatever happens; TUNING.md has what else is owed
   before the offer.

**The service** (`apps/gpu-pages`, `olo-gpu-pages.service`; as
olo-gpu-memory's): at each start, where a device is on xe and the
kernel is as it was checked, it builds the module for that very build
where it hasn't (`olo_kmod`; a kernel of the same name rebuilt isn't
given the last one's), loads it as 4 has it for the device (the one
the computer started on where xe has several), and says how it went in
`/run/olo-gpu-pages/status`: "in force", "not needed" (no xe), "not
checked" (this kernel's build, or its live patches), or "failed: "
with why, which for a kernel the module stayed out of is the module's
own words from the kernel's log. A module in the kernel that isn't its
load is left alone, and that is a failure said. `olo-gpu-pages
--status` says what there is as JSON, to anyone (in the kernel, ours,
in force, for which device, the builds, whether this one and its live
patches are as checked, the counts); `--remove` takes its own out.

**Olo Doctor** (`graphics_pages` in checks.rs; `olo-doctor --kernel
graphics-pages on|off`, which refuses `on` while it isn't offered):
where the module is in, "No program waits for large pieces of graphics
memory", with its count for what it is; in by hand without its
service, that it goes at the next start; chosen and out of this
kernel, why (a build not checked yet; Secure Boot; the module's own
words), with nothing to press, since there is no other way to it. The
offer itself ("Drawing waits for large pieces of graphics memory",
Never Wait for Large Pieces) only once it is offered;
`OLO_DOCTOR_DEMO=1`'s report has the card, and
`OLO_DOCTOR_DEMO=pieces-out` the card for the module out of this
kernel, where Preferences' button leads.

**Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ Kernel**: the sixth box, Drawing, under
Window Buffers (the box that was "Graphics": each named for what it
keeps, since both are of Intel's graphics memory). Shown where the
module is in the kernel or its service installed (and, once offered,
wherever xe is). Its switch, its paragraph and its rows keep their
places in every state. The rows say what is so, each by itself: the
module in the running kernel, in it and switched off (a trial between
its phases), or not in it; whether this kernel's build was checked;
whether it is kept at every start. Out of the kernel, the paragraph
says why in place of what it does (and Open Olo Doctor where Doctor
has the module's own words). The switch shows the person's choice,
which they can always take back; it can't be pressed on where that
would do nothing or isn't offered yet, whatever is in the kernel.

**Checking it** (`tools/dev/gpu-pages-check`; no GPU in a guest, so
`kernel/gpu-pages/check` has a PCI driver named "xe" for QEMU's host
bridge, a pool with xe's flags filled while the kernel's tracepoints
are watched, and a fixture that keeps one page of every free 2 MB
piece): the module builds with no warning; loads beside Olo's live
patch in the same module; changes xe's 2 MB try by the one flag and
nothing else's; `on` 0 and unloading put the kernel's own behaviour
back; with probes disarmed it refuses; and in memory left in small
pieces 64 buffers are filled with the thread never compacting or
reclaiming for a large piece, where the kernel's own way did 113 and
56 times. A kernel warning in a guest ends it. `--trial-tool` runs
`gpu-pages-try` itself in four guests, with the real bpftrace and
journalctl: to its end, then in the same guest what must stop it
before it loads anything (tracing that fails or lacks a probe, a
warning in the phase with nothing loaded) and another's load that got
in first (left as it was); and stopped three ways while its module is
on (a warning of the driver's own that doesn't call itself one, a
SIGTERM, a SIGKILL): off within milliseconds each time, and out of
the kernel but after the kill, where it stays in, off, the trial's
own. Run all of it
(`--qualify --trial-tool`) after any change to the module, the
service's loading or the trial tool, and through the tool's own
command: a part of it tried by hand had hidden that the whole
couldn't finish.

## BBRv3 for TCP (kernel/bbr3, apps/bbr3, crates/kmod; Olo Doctor; tools/dev/bbr3-check, kvm-guest)

How fast TCP sends is its congestion control's to decide. Linux's
default, CUBIC, sends faster until a buffer along the way overflows: an
upload keeps the slowest link's queue full, and everything else waits
behind it. Its own `bbr` is BBRv1. BBRv3 (Google's) keeps the queue
short, takes a fair share beside CUBIC and loses a twentieth of what
BBRv1 does; it isn't in Linux, where Google's is a kernel with patches to
TCP itself (Ben, 2026-11-16: "i also want olo doctor to offer to set the
tcp congestion control algo to BBRv3 if it's not. if BBRv3 is not
shipped with fedora then vendor the kernel module/patches and adapt if
needed and then have olo doctor take care of doing everything needed to
switch to BBRv3").

**The module** (`kernel/bbr3`, `tcp_bbr3`, the congestion control
`bbr3`; [kernel/bbr3/README.md](../kernel/bbr3/README.md) is its whole
account: read it before changing it). Google's `tcp_bbr.c` kept
untouched beside it (`upstream/`), and `tcp_bbr3.c` made of it for the
kernel as it comes: the algorithm unchanged, and what it needs of
Google's patches made in the module from what any congestion control is
given. The packets in flight and lost when each packet was sent, which
the patches record in the packet, are looked up in a log of snapshots
taken wherever TCP calls the module before it sends (`bbr3_olo.h`);
each retransmission and each lost packet is told by a probe (ftrace's
fprobe) on the function that does it; its state, too big for the room a
socket has, is allocated. Not a patched kernel: TCP is built into the
kernel, so the patches mean rebuilding the whole kernel at every update,
and running one that isn't Fedora's.

It is shown, not assumed, in a KVM guest (below), by
**`tools/dev/bbr3-check`**: a build that also takes the true figures
where the patched kernel records them, and compares every one looked up
(1.3 million over 25 links: all the same; every loss told; tail-probe
recoveries the kernel's own count); `--compare` beside Google's real
BBRv3 in a kernel built for the guest with its patches (15 links three
times each: the same within the runs' spread), and beside this kernel's
CUBIC and BBRv1; `--timing` for what it costs (333 ns an ACK at
50 Mbit/s, 226 of them BBR's own; 0.10% of a core there, 0.36% at
500 Mbit/s; nothing while a connection is idle). Run it after any
change to the module, and on each new kernel series before the module
is trusted with it (the README's "A new kernel" lists what it leans on;
the build itself stops if the two probed functions are declared
otherwise).

**`olo-kmod`** (crates/kmod) is what Olo's kernel modules' services
share: a module's source carried in its service's program, built for
the running kernel with the kernel's own build system (`make` and the
compiler: one of the few places Olo runs another program, there being
no other way), in `/var/lib/STATE/KERNEL`, installed to
`/lib/modules/KERNEL/extra/olo` (the one place SELinux lets a service
load a module from), built again for another source or a kernel of the
same name rebuilt, and removed with its kernel (`tidy`).
`olo-gpu-memory` ("Windows' buffers stay in memory") is on it too.

**`olo-bbr3`** (apps/bbr3; root, systemd's `olo-bbr3.service`, at every
start) builds the module where it hasn't yet (a new kernel's first
start: two seconds), loads it, and makes `bbr3` what new connections
use (`net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control`; what it was is kept in
`/var/lib/olo-bbr3/was`). Connections there already keep theirs; a
network namespace made later begins with the system's. Where the
kernel's own `bbr` is BBRv3 already (a kernel built with Google's
patches: told by what it answers for a socket,
`olo_net::tcp_info::kernels_bbr_version`), that one is chosen and
nothing is built. A module built from another source (Olo upgraded)
while the old one is loaded is built at once and loaded from the next
start: a module can't be changed under the connections that run it. It
says how it went in `/run/olo-bbr3/status` ("bbr3", "bbr", or "failed: "
and why); `--status` prints what there is as JSON (anyone); `--remove`
(its service's stop) gives new connections back what they had and
unloads the module once none runs it. Where it can't (no headers, a
build that fails on a kernel whose TCP has changed, Secure Boot refusing
an unsigned module), connections go on with what there was.

**Olo Doctor** (`tcp_bbr3` in checks.rs): "TCP could send with BBRv3",
a suggestion, whose fix, **Use BBRv3**, installs the service (root's
copy of the program in /usr/local/libexec/olo, its unit, enabled and
started; what building needs installed first where it's missing). Its
text says what the congestion control in use does and what was measured.
Fine once new connections use it and its service is this build's;
"only until the next start" where it's in use without the service.
Nothing is offered with Secure Boot on (unless the kernel has BBRv3
itself). The default qdisc is left as it is: BBR paces by TCP's own
timers where the qdisc doesn't (`fq`), which Wi-Fi's has none of
anyway, and the measurements with and without `fq` don't differ.

**A kernel to test with** (`tools/dev/kvm-guest`). Nothing of a kernel
module is tried in the person's own kernel: a fault in one stops the
whole computer. `kvm-guest SCRIPT` starts this computer's kernel (its
image is in `/lib/modules/RELEASE`, so a module built for this kernel
loads) in a KVM guest whose root is an initramfs made on the spot of
this computer's programs (bash, ip, tc, ss and what's named, with the
libraries they load) and the kernel modules named; runs the script as
its root; and gives back its output and exit status. No root is needed
(QEMU with `/dev/kvm`), nothing is installed, and it's gone when it
ends; a start takes under a second. `--kernel` runs another kernel (the
reference one with Google's patches). `olo_net`'s `tcp-flow` (crates/net
examples) makes the flows and reads what the kernel says of each.

## The kernel's settings (`olo_system::kernel_tuning`, Olo Doctor's kernel.rs; Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ Kernel; tools/dev/kernel-check)

Ben, 2026-11-16: "research what other linux kernel patches are
recommended for high performance, responsive desktop operating systems
and if you find any that are win-win over the fedora 45 kernel and would
be a win for olo users then also integrate them into olo like bbr3 so
that olo doctor can offer them. let's also have a new tab in the
performance prefs for kernel tuning where this stuff can live and be
configured and show any stats/details/data in there about the running
patches too".

[kernel/TUNING.md](../kernel/TUNING.md) is the whole account: what the
desktop kernels (XanMod, Zen, CachyOS) carry and where Fedora 45's
kernel stands on each, what was measured, and what was measured and left
alone. Read it before adding a setting. The rule it goes by: **a setting
is offered only when it was measured here, off and on, and gained
something with nothing given up**; a trade isn't offered (dm-crypt
without its work queues: small reads 2.5× quicker, large ones a quarter
slower), nor is anything taken on another distribution's word, or on
its first runs: MGLRU's thrash protection (`min_ttl_ms` 1000, the
kernel's own advice for a desktop) looked like a clear gain until the
same run was made nine times, in three of which it ended a program
that fitted in memory.
`tools/dev/kernel-check` makes every measurement again, in a KVM guest
on this computer's kernel (`kvm-guest` has `--disk SIZE[,OPT…]` for it:
an empty disk, slow with QEMU's `throttling.bps-write=`; and `--module
"NAME PARAM=VALUE"`), with `kbench` (crates/system/examples/kbench.rs:
disk latency, wake latency alone and from another thread, compute, pipe
chatter, a memory hog, a working set in use, saves, a copy).

Three settings there are (two came of that research, the third of a
day of looking at why the desktop lagged under agents' builds,
2026-11-20):

- **Preemption: full** (`preempt=full`). A program woken while the
  processors are busy runs at once, where Fedora's lazy kernel has it
  wait for the next tick: with every processor computing at nice 19, 99
  in 100 wakes within 4 µs where they took 950; computing, pipes and
  contended writes got as much done (0.998× to 1.04×).
- **Removable disks: 16 MB may wait** (`bdi/strict_limit`,
  `bdi/max_bytes`, by a udev rule). Of 600 MB copied to a disk that
  takes 10 MB a second, 14 MB were still in memory when the copy ended
  where 280 were, and it was all on the disk 1.5 s later where it took
  28 s; the whole took as long, and a disk that takes 400 MB a second
  loses nothing to the limit, busy computer or not (one that takes
  1 GB a second loses a fifth to two fifths while the computer is busy,
  so a disk on a USB link of 10 Gbit/s or faster is left out).
- **Short turns: 0.7 ms** (the scheduler's base slice,
  `/sys/kernel/debug/sched/base_slice_ns`). How long a busy program
  keeps a processor before one that is waiting gets it. The kernel
  lengthens it with the number of processors (0.7 ms for one, 2.8 ms
  for eight and more); kept at 0.7, what waits under load waits a
  fraction as long: on Ben's computer beside fifteen more busy
  programs, the kernel's own workers (which hand every frame to the
  GPU and every byte through a terminal) waited over a millisecond
  six times less often (0.45% of their wakes to 0.07%), Terminal's
  threads seven times (2.0% to 0.28%, the worst 29 ms to 4), and the
  compositor's GPU jobs were handed on in 5.7 ms at the worst where
  it had been 14.5. Why it matters though Olo's own threads are
  realtime: what they hand work to in the kernel isn't (HACKING,
  "Realtime threads and the kept core").

What isn't among them, having been one for an hour: **Swap used last**
("Swappiness and the size of swap", above; kernel/TUNING.md, "Tried
and withdrawn"). Nor **huge pages made behind the program that asks**
(`transparent_hugepage/defrag`: defer), which was measured both ways
in the guest (`tools/dev/kernel-check huge-pages`, with `kbench
fragment` and `kbench huge`) and on the computer itself with nothing
of it changed (a real link over and over, as it is and with huge
pages off for that one process): the linker that asks is a seventh
quicker for its huge pages and waits for them itself, and what runs
beside it waits a few milliseconds more at the worst. A trade
(TUNING.md, "Huge pages when asked for").

**Read** (`olo_system::kernel_tuning`; anyone, no root):
`look(&Places::here())` gives a `State` of `Preemption` (what the
kernel was built to start on, from its build options, read once; what
it was started with, `/proc/cmdline`; what the next start has,
`/etc/kernel/cmdline` or GRUB's defaults; a switch since the start,
which the kernel tells only root, so Olo notes it in
`/run/olo-kernel/preemption`; whether the running kernel can be
switched, which a locked-down one, Secure Boot's, can't), `SlowDisks`
(Olo's rule; each removable disk here with its limit; what waits now
and what may), `Turns` (what the kernel starts on for its processors, counted from
`/sys/devices/system/cpu/online`; what it was set to since, Olo's
note in `/run/olo-kernel/turns`; whether Olo's unit keeps it), and Olo's own
pieces in the kernel: `Bbr3` (the congestion control, the module, and the connections on it now: how many
of all TCP's, their round trips' middle, the share of their segments
sent again, from `olo_system::netdiag::flows`, one walk of the kernel's
table of connections, `sock_diag` with each one's `tcp_info` and
congestion control), `GraphicsMemory` (the live patch) and
`GraphicsPages` (the module: in force, kept, whether this kernel's
build is one it was checked on, its count, what its service said;
None where it isn't offered and nothing of it is here: "No program
held for large pieces of graphics memory").
`OLO_KERNEL_ROOT=DIR` reads a made-up computer under DIR (its
connections from `proc/net/olo-flows`: lines of "control state rtt_us
sent sent_again").

**Set** (apps/doctor/src/kernel.rs; root, through the helper):
`kernel::steps(setting, on, &places)` gives the steps that put a setting
on, now and at every start, or back as the kernel comes; only what
isn't so already.

| | on | off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| preemption | `Step::AddKernelArgument` `preempt=full`; where the kernel isn't locked down, `full` written to `/sys/kernel/debug/sched/preempt` and noted | `Step::RemoveKernelArgument` `preempt` (new: an argument taken out wherever one is put); the running kernel back on what it was built with |
| slow-disks | `/etc/udev/rules.d/61-olo-slow-disks.rules` (data/udev); each removable disk here without a limit given `strict_limit` 1 and `max_bytes` 16777216 (which reads back a little under: the kernel keeps a share of its whole limit) | the rule removed; each back to `strict_limit` 0, `max_ratio` 100 |
| short-turns | `/etc/olo/short-turns.conf` (two lines in tmpfiles' form: the scheduler's file, and Olo's note of it) and `olo-short-turns.service`, enabled, which has systemd's own tool apply them once debugfs is mounted (among /etc/tmpfiles.d's they could run before it is; tried as a service under SELinux: it may write there); where the kernel isn't locked down, 700000 written and noted now | the unit disabled and removed with its lines; the running kernel back on what it comes with for its processors |
| bbr3, graphics-memory, graphics-pages | Olo Doctor's own fix for each (its service installed, enabled, started) | its service stopped (which takes its work out of the running kernel) and disabled |

The kernel-argument steps carry the file system's root, so a test's tree
is written like the real one. `olo-doctor --kernel` prints what there is
as JSON (every setting's `on`, what it is now, its figures; null where
the computer has nothing to set), for anyone; `olo-doctor --kernel
SETTING on|off` sets one, asking for an administrator's password once.
Under `OLO_KERNEL_ROOT` it writes the tree as the person, with no
password and nothing of systemd asked (the unit, the link systemd would
make, and what the service would leave in the kernel stand for a
service chosen): how the tab's switches are tried in a test session.
The steps themselves were done to this kernel in the guest: `full`
written to the switch took 99 in 100 wakes from 942 µs to 7 in the same
boot, and the rule, run by udev there on a USB stick
(`kvm-guest --usb-disk`), limited it and left the guest's own disk
alone.

**After a kernel update** (Ben, 2026-11-16: "make sure all these kernel
tunings/mods will continue to work properly after doing os updates that
update the kernel"; kernel/TUNING.md, "After a kernel update", and
kernel/README.md). The start argument: Fedora's kernel-install makes a
new kernel's entry from `/etc/kernel/cmdline`, unless that is older than
GRUB's defaults; the kernel-argument steps write the defaults first and
leave the command line no older than them (`edit_kernel_arguments`, its
test). A start made without the argument though it was kept before that
start (`Preemption::lost`: the kept file's time against the computer's
start, `/proc/stat`'s `btime`) is said by Doctor ("The kernel was
started without full preemption") and its fix puts it in every entry
again. The udev rule isn't the kernel's version's. The two modules are
built for the new kernel by their services at its first start
(`olo_kmod`; both services' `built_for_the_kernel_an_update_brings_…`
tests), and the live patch now refuses to build where the function it
replaces has gone or changed shape. BBRv3's module is built for any
kernel; the series its full self-check has passed on are
kernel/bbr3/CHECKED, and where the running kernel's isn't one of them
Doctor's "TCP sends with BBRv3" and the tab's Network box say so.
**`tools/dev/kernel-next`** checks all of it on the newest kernel
Fedora's repositories have, before it's installed (its packages
unpacked in scratch, the kernel run in the guest: the settings, BBRv3's
self-check there through `bbr3-check --on RELEASE --root DIR`, the live
patch loaded and taken out, the services' own builds): run it when a
new kernel is on its way, and add a series BBRv3 passes on to CHECKED.
On 2026-11-16 it passed on 7.3.3-300.fc45, with BBRv3's full self-check
(1,265,738 figures over 25 links).

**Offered** (apps/doctor/src/checks.rs, `kernel_settings`): the
suggestions `kernel:preemption` (Preempt at Once) and
`kernel:slow-disks` (Limit Removable Disks), and, recommended,
`kernel:short-turns` (Keep Turns Short), each with what was
measured, where the kernel has the setting and it isn't on. A `preempt=` of the person's own choosing is theirs (nothing
is suggested), and nothing is suggested while a scheduler loaded over
the kernel's is chosen or scheduling: it asks for each switch itself,
so the setting changes nothing (measured with LAVD: the same wakes
either way), which the tab's Preemption box says too. A locked-down kernel with the argument kept is fine,
"from the next restart". A stick plugged in before the rule was there
is offered its limit.

**Shown and switched** (Preferences ▸ Performance ▸ Kernel;
`olo-preferences kernel`, or `performance --tab Kernel`): a box for
each, the kernel's own settings on the left (Preemption, Processor
Turns, Removable Disks) and Olo's pieces in it on the right (Network,
Window Buffers, and Drawing where its module is: three a side, 717
points on the smallest screen's 760): four on one side were taller
than the smallest screen, and no other split keeps what belongs
together. Each has a check box (`kernel-preemption`,
`kernel-short-turns`, `kernel-slow-disks`, `kernel-bbr3`,
`kernel-graphics-memory`, `kernel-graphics-pages`), what
it does in a sentence that ends with the kernel's own name for it,
and its figures as facts, every box's values in one line
(`Facts::label_width`: one width for the tab's labels) and its rows
as far apart as the paragraph's lines (`Facts::row_height`, whose
height isn't rounded), so boxes side by side with as many lines and
rows between them end on one line: Processor Turns and Window Buffers
do. The columns stand as far apart as boxes stand over one another,
their titles' room included (twice `STACK`; at `SPACING` the two read
as one wall of boxes), and each column's last box takes what height
its column has to spare (`Ui::growing_bbox`), so both end on one line.
The note that says whose the settings are is under both columns,
across the tab, as far under them as boxes are from each other (not
`Ui::note`, which sets a note close under its control): with three
boxes a side neither column is the shorter one it used to stand
under; a switch's result takes its place. A sentence with the
setting's own figures
in it says "With this on," so it reads right while the box is
unchecked. The facts: what the kernel is on now and at the next
start; what may wait for a removable disk, what waits now, and the
disks here with whether each is limited; what new connections use, how
many connections are on BBRv3 now, their round trip and the share of
their segments sent again, and whether its module was checked on this
kernel's series; whether the patch is in the running kernel and at
every start. A switch runs `olo-doctor --kernel` on a thread
("Setting it: an administrator's password is asked…", every box
dimmed; refused or failed, as it was, with why in red). The figures are
read every two seconds while the tab is shown, by a thread that sleeps
(parked, not polling) on any other tab and ends with the panel. A
setting the kernel hasn't says so in place of its switch; the Window
Buffers box is there only where Intel's xe driver is, and Drawing as
"No program held for large pieces of graphics memory" says.

## Every frame on time (app_server frames.rs; Activity Monitor ▸ Displays)

A display's frames are paced by app_server from each vblank: it waits,
then draws, so that clients told to draw at the vblank have time to hand
in their buffers and still make the next one. Smithay waits 60% of the
frame and draws in the last 40% (6.7 ms at 60 Hz, 3.3 ms at 120 Hz),
whatever the frame costs. A 5K frame with a video playing cost 5–9 ms of
CPU on asahi (2026-11-01), so a third of the Studio Display's vblanks
were missed, each a frame shown twice: the pointer jerked and scrolls
stuttered, and on the 120 Hz built-in display the 95th-percentile frame
(2.9 ms) was within a hair of the budget.

`frames::Pacing`, one per display, sets the split from what its frames
cost. Forward: the budget is at least the 95th percentile of the last
120 frames' CPU time, and a quarter more, plus 0.5 ms for the GPU. Back:
the vblank's hardware timestamp against the vblank the frame on its way
was drawn for says whether it made it; a frame or more late is a drop,
and a drop widens the budget by a quarter frame at once, since the GPU's
share isn't measured. Six hundred frames on time in a row narrow it by a
sixteenth, down to Smithay's split, because a narrower budget is a later
draw and less latency for everyone. The pacing costs nothing while a
display rests, and a look of a display's own (woken, or its idle look)
isn't judged, since it wasn't drawn for a vblank.

The pointer goes on a plane of the display's own where there is one.
Apple's display controller (apple-drm) has no cursor plane, so every move
of the pointer was a frame of the whole screen, and when one ran long the
pointer waited with it. It has two overlay planes a CRTC that take
ARGB8888 (how macOS shows its pointer): the topmost becomes the cursor
plane, and Smithay draws the pointer into a 64×64 buffer of its own and
moves that, the frame underneath untouched. The log says
`no cursor plane; an overlay plane holds the pointer` when a display is
set up so, and `the pointer is on a plane of the display's own` the first
time it goes there; a pointer the plane refuses (bigger than 64 px, a
client's cursor it can't hold) is drawn into the frame as before.
`OLO_CURSOR_PLANE=0` keeps the overlay planes as they are. Olo's Smithay
keeps the plane on the display (clipped at an edge; apple-drm refused a
plane hanging off the display with EINVAL on the page flip, and the
first try took the desktop down with it), and a display that refuses a
frame's commit draws everything from then on (`planes_refused`), the
pointer too: a refusal costs a frame, never a restart.

Olo's Smithay also checks every rect in `Rectangle::
subtract_rects_many_in_place` (which the damage tracker uses to find
what an opaque region stopped covering): swapping the last rect in for
one taken out could bring in a piece made in the same pass and leave an
earlier rect unchecked, so a frame's opaque regions weren't all taken
from themselves and the same strip was damaged every frame: with any
window floating over Focus's, app_server drew 60 frames a second while
nothing changed (2026-11-02; `subtract_rects_many_checks_every_rect`).

Where a frame's time goes: measured on Ben's session (2026-11-01,
read-only stack samples of app_server's main thread, and Smithay's
phases through `PHASE_HOOK`), the 5 ms a 5K frame costs is all
`render_output`, and inside it the GPU submit (Mesa's asahi driver
flushing the batch for the fence Smithay makes finishing a frame) and
syncobj waits: app_server sits in the kernel handing the composite to
the GPU, about 3 ms a frame, 48 times a second for a video call, which
is its 20% of a core. Plane assignment and the atomic test cost 0.0 ms.
So the way out is fewer composites: the pointer on its plane, and a
window whose buffer changes every frame (the call) straight to an
overlay plane, which Olo's Smithay now tries for every window's own
surfaces (`Kind::ScanoutCandidate`); the display's "scan-out" record
(`DisplayFrames::scanout`, Activity Monitor ▸ Displays) says how many
elements went to a plane and why the rest were drawn ("overlaps": an
element above it on the primary plane; "format": its buffer isn't one
the plane takes; "the driver refused": the atomic test failed; "not
tried": not a candidate).

`{"type":"frames"}` (`tsession ipc NAME '{"type":"frames"}'`) answers
each display's record (`DisplayFrames`): frames a second, dropped in the
last minute and in all, the draw's percentiles, the budget and delay,
whether the pointer is on its own plane, resting. Activity Monitor's
Displays section shows it, a card a display with graphs of its frames
a second, drops and the 95th percentile of drawing over the span
chosen, asked every second while the section (or Inputs) shows and
never otherwise; the answers are kept for the graphs
(`Activity::frame_history`, half an hour). Its Inputs section has the
pointer's and the touchpad's cards (each with a graph: reports a
second, the touchpad's latency typically and at the 99th) and What
You Did: clicks, scrolling steps, gestures begun and keys pressed in
the last minute (`InputActivity`, app_server's `input_counts`: a time
noted per event as it's handled, real or synthetic, how many and never
which key), with a graph of each. Its check box, "Capture debug
information whenever a frame drops" (`{"type":"capture_drops","on":true}`),
has app_server log every drop as a `frames` record: how late, how long
the draw took and its parts (gathering, `drm render_frame`, …), the
budget, and what else held the loop meanwhile (the slowest request,
input event or commit since the last vblank); Logs filtered for
"frames" shows them. It stays on until app_server restarts.
`OLO_ACTIVITY_DEMO_FRAMES=1` gives Activity Monitor made-up displays to
look at in a headless session, which has none.

## Caffeinated mode and the level indicator (power.rs, osd.rs)

Caffeinated mode holds a logind block inhibitor ("sleep:idle", plus
"handle-lid-switch" when asked to survive the lid) and keeps idleness at
bay; `Request::SetCaffeinated { on, minutes, lid }` sets it, the power
tick ends a timed stretch, and `PowerStatus` carries `caffeinated_until`
and `caffeinated_lid`. Deskbar toggles it from the cup (right-click, or
Olo ▸ Stay Awake, for durations and the lid); Ctrl+⌘A toggles it from
the keyboard. The keyboard backlight (`olo_system::backlight::keyboard`, an LED
class device set through logind) follows its keys and Preferences ▸
Keyboard, and goes off with the displays. The brightness, keyboard and
volume keys and Ctrl+⌘A show `osd.rs`'s
panel low on the screen under the pointer for 1.6 s (in a real session
the worker reports the volume it set; headless simulates a volume).
`OLO_OSD_SHEET=/tmp/o.png cargo test -p app_server osd_sheet` draws
every state.

## Approving without asking (app_server approve.rs, Deskbar approve.rs)

For a while (5 minutes to a day), requests that would ask for the
account password are approved without asking: sudo in Terminal's window
and Passwords' unlock and `op` access. Deskbar's key in the tray turns
it on (a click: for 15 minutes, `approve::USUAL`; right-click or Olo ▸
Approve Without Asking: the lengths) in a small window that takes the
password; the key is gold while it is on, its tip saying until when,
and a click (or Ask Again) turns it off.
`Request::SetAutoApprove { minutes, password }` (`minutes: None` turns it
off; while on, a new length needs no password) checks the password
through PAM on a thread and replies once it has ("That password isn’t
right."). app_server keeps the password (`Zeroizing`) only while it is
on: the power tick ends it at its time, the lock ends it (sleeping locks
first), and app_server's restart ends it; `PowerStatus` carries
`auto_approve_until`. Terminal's sudo window, before showing, asks
`Request::AutoApproveSecret` (answered only to a peer that is Olo's
olo-terminal, `Conn::peer_is_ours`) and gives sudo that password;
Passwords asks `PowerStatus` (on a thread) and unlocks, or lets a
terminal's `op` in, without its window. Each says so in a quiet
notification ("Approved without asking", "Passwords unlocked without
asking"). Never test with the real PAM: debug builds take
`OLO_PAM_CONFDIR`/`OLO_PAM_SERVICE` (a stand-in `pam_exec` check),
Terminal's sudo `OLO_SUDO_REAL`, and `OLO_NO_FINGERPRINT=1` leaves
fprintd alone.

## Security keys (olo-fido; Preferences ▸ Security ▸ Sign In; app_server security_key.rs)

A security key set up (a YubiKey: any FIDO2 key with `hmac-secret`) is
touched instead of typing the account password once the person is
signed in: Terminal's sudo window, Passwords' unlock and the polkit agent
(for the person's own identity). Never the lock screen or the login
screen: those are the doors to the computer, and a key is usually left
in it (Ben: "if someone found the laptop and got the login screen we
can't have them just pressing the yubikey to get access"); a face, a
finger or the password open them. Natively, as the person, no root: `olo_fido` speaks
CTAPHID to the key's FIDO interface (its hidraw node, found by usage page
0xF1D0 under /sys, open to the person at their seat by systemd's
uaccess) and CTAP2 itself (GetInfo, ClientPIN's key agreement in PIN
protocol 2 or 1, MakeCredential, GetAssertion with `hmac-secret`).

* **Setting up** (Preferences ▸ Security ▸ Sign In ▸ Security Keys, `security_keys.rs`):
  the box says the steps first (the password, then a touch when the
  key's light blinks, of its gold contact, on a Nano the gold edge at its
  end; a touch before it blinks types a code, which app_server swallows,
  so nothing happens), then what to do as each touch is waited for, with
  the touches had. A key stops waiting for a touch after about 30 seconds
  (a YubiKey answers "operation denied"): each touch is asked for again,
  three times in all (`olo_fido::TOUCH_TRIES`, `Asked`), saying so, and
  one never touched is "The key wasn't touched in time." (Ben's first
  setup ran out while he touched the wrong part of his key: the box
  said only "touch the key twice".)
  The password is checked through PAM, then two touches: a credential
  made for Olo (relying party `olo.local`, not discoverable,
  `hmac-secret` on), then its secret for a random salt, which seals the
  password (XChaCha20-Poly1305 under HKDF of it, the user and credential
  as associated data). Kept in `security-keys.json` in the config
  directory (0600): useless without the key. A second key set up the same
  way is a spare; Remove forgets one. The box follows keys plugged in and
  out from udev's own announcements (`olo_fido::hid::watch`, netlink
  group 2: sent once the node's permissions are set; no polling), asking
  each what it is and whether it's one set up without a touch
  (GetAssertion with `up` off). A key with a PIN set that wants it for a
  credential isn't supported yet (it says so).
* **Unlocking** (`olo_fido::touch`): each window, as it asks for the
  password, starts a wait on a thread of its own (alongside the finger
  and the face: in sudo's window and the polkit agent a second PAM
  conversation takes the key's password while the first listens for a
  finger, so Touch ID set up doesn't hold the key back; see Terminal's
  sudo and the polkit agent): if a key set up is
  plugged in it says `olo_fido::TOUCH_OR_TYPE` ("Touch your security key,
  or type your password.") beside the field, and the password the touch
  unseals goes where a typed one would (sudo's prompt, the polkit
  helper's, PAM through `olo_system::auth::check_password` for Passwords,
  so a password changed since setting up fails as a wrong one would). The
  wait is dropped with the window (CTAPHID_CANCEL), and Passwords waits
  only while its window has the keyboard. The lock screen (olo-lock) and
  the login screen (olo-greeter, its PAM services `data/pam/olo-login*`)
  have no key code at all, and nothing in the system's PAM stack (no
  `pam_u2f`) gives them one.
* **Stray touches** (app_server `security_key.rs`): a touch with nothing
  waiting types the key's one-time code through its own USB keyboard.
  app_server knows that keyboard by the device as it's added
  (`olo_protocol::keyboards::security_key`, by its USB id from then on)
  and passes its keys to nobody; three touches in a row (each within
  three seconds of the last) type the third's code into the focused
  window as the key would have (`SecurityKeySettings::three_touches_type`,
  on by default: Preferences ▸ Security ▸ Sign In ▸ Three touches type a code).
  While a window waits for the key a touch answers that instead (FIDO),
  typing nothing at all.
* **Testing**: never with the person's key or password. Debug builds take
  `OLO_FIDO_SOFT=FILE`, a software key (`olo_fido::soft`: the same
  CTAPHID and CTAP2, its master secret in FILE so a credential made in
  one process opens in another) that touches itself
  `OLO_FIDO_SOFT_TOUCH_MS` (400) after it starts waiting, or never
  ("never"), with a PIN if `OLO_FIDO_SOFT_PIN` is set (eight tries); with
  the PAM stand-in (`OLO_PAM_CONFDIR`/`OLO_PAM_SERVICE`, given to
  `tsession run` itself: it doesn't pass them on), `OLO_SUDO_REAL` and
  `OLO_POLKIT_HELPER` the whole thing runs headless. `cargo run -p
  olo-fido --example soft-set-up [PASSWORD]` (with `OLO_FIDO_SOFT` and
  the session's `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`) sets the soft key up as Preferences
  does, sealing PASSWORD ("test"), for a window to wait on it.
* **A key with a PIN**: setting it up asks for the PIN beside the
  password, once (Preferences knows from the key's info). `olo_fido::pin::
  token` gets a token for it (CTAP 2.1's with the make-credential
  permission where the key offers `pinUvAuthToken`, else 2.0's
  getPinToken), and makeCredential carries its proof. The secret after
  needs no PIN: the `hmac-secret` assertion is made without user
  verification at setup and at every touch alike, so it is the same
  secret. A wrong PIN says how many tries are left. A key that wants
  its PIN at every use (`alwaysUv`) is listed as unusable: a touch
  couldn't stand for the password.
  `cargo run -p olo-fido --example info` asks every key plugged in what it
  is, without a touch; `--example touch` runs setting up's two touches on
  the first key plugged in (nothing kept, no password), every CTAPHID
  message printed with when, to see what a key does. `cargo test -p olo-fido` (both PIN protocols
  against the soft key, cancelling, sealing).
* **Olo Doctor** (`security_keys`): a key plugged in whose FIDO node isn't
  the person's to open is a finding, its fix
  `/etc/udev/rules.d/74-olo-security-keys.rules` (systemd's `fido_id`
  and `uaccess`, for systems whose own rules don't), applied to the keys
  there with a `change`; one that is, a fine line.

## Face unlock (olo-face, olo-faced, pam_olo_face; Preferences ▸ Security ▸ Sign In)

A look at the infrared camera stands for the account password: sudo
(Terminal's window, any terminal), polkit's requests, Passwords' unlock
and the lock screen. Natively and in process: no howdy, no OpenCV
binaries, no linux-enable-ir-emitter.

* **Only infrared counts.** The camera is the one whose node gives only
  grey (`camera::infrared`: the ThinkPad's "Integrated IR Camera",
  640×360 GREY at 15 frames a second), read over V4L2 by raw ioctls
  (`camera::Camera`: S_FMT, memory-mapped buffers, poll and DQBUF). A
  face on a screen isn't there at all in infrared, displays giving off
  none. A face must be near (80 pixels wide), lit by the flood, and its
  relief (the middle of the face against its sides, which turn away from
  the light) like the one enrolled, since a print is lit evenly; two
  frames must match (`look::verify`). With no face at all for 2 s the
  look ends.
* **The emitter** (`emitter.rs`): a camera that waits to be told to
  light it (Chicony's, as Windows Hello's driver does) is told through a
  vendor control in one of its UVC extension units (`UVCIOC_CTRL_QUERY`).
  Olo finds it once, at the first enrolment, as Windows' setup would:
  each control of the infrared interface's units (read from the USB
  descriptors; on the ThinkPad units 10, 13 and 14) that can be both
  read and set, each value its range suggests, set while the frames are
  watched for the flood. The one that lights it is kept per camera (by
  its USB id, in `emitters.json`) and set each time the camera opens;
  everything else tried is put back as it was.
* **The models** (`model.rs`, `data/face`, Git LFS): YuNet (OpenCV
  Zoo's detector, MIT) finds each face and its five landmarks in a
  640×640 letterbox (its three strides decoded and overlaps dropped, as
  OpenCV does); SFace (OpenCV Zoo's recogniser, Apache 2.0) turns the
  face, aligned to its template by those landmarks (a least-squares
  similarity), into 128 numbers, compared by cosine similarity (a match
  at 0.42, above SFace's own 0.363, for the margin infrared and a lock
  want). The grey goes into all three channels. On the public-domain
  NASA portraits (`OLO_FACE_SAMPLES=DIR cargo test -p olo-face
  recognises -- --ignored`): two photographs of Armstrong five years
  apart 0.59, other men 0.09 to 0.26; 25 ms to find a face, 28 to
  recognise it.
* **olo-faced** (root, the system bus's `org.olo.Face1`, started by
  systemd when first asked) alone opens the camera, runs the models and
  keeps each person's enrolled looks (`/var/lib/olo-face/UID.json`,
  root's only), so nothing running as the person can read the faces or
  skip the look. Who asks is known from the bus
  (`GetConnectionUnixUser`): a person may ask about themselves, root
  about anyone. `Status`, `Verify(user, ms)`, `Enroll(user, password)`
  (with `Progress` signals) and `Forget(user, password)`; enrolling and
  forgetting check the password through PAM first, so something running
  as the person can't put its own face in. No password is kept anywhere:
  a look doesn't unseal one, it answers PAM. The camera is opened for a
  look and closed after it.
* **The PAM module** (`pam_olo_face.so`, `auth sufficient` first in
  `/etc/pam.d/sudo` and `/etc/pam.d/polkit-1`): asks the service (on the
  system bus, as fprintd is reached: polkit's helper runs as
  `policykit_auth_t` under SELinux), says "Looking for your face…"
  through the conversation, and succeeds on a match. Anything else (no
  service, nobody enrolled, no camera, not them, a remote login) goes on
  to the password: it never fails a login, it only spares the typing.
  It links libpam by file name (`+verbatim`), so it builds without
  pam-devel.
* **Passwords and the lock screen** ask the service themselves
  (`olo_system::face::verify`): Passwords once each time its locked
  window takes the keyboard, the lock screen when someone is there (a
  key, the pointer) at most every 5 s, so the camera's light isn't left
  on.
* **Installing** (Preferences ▸ Security ▸ Sign In ▸ Face Unlock ▸ Install…):
  `pkexec olo-faced install --models DIR --pam FILE` (Olo's polkit agent
  asks) copies the service to /usr/local/libexec, the models to
  /usr/local/share/olo/face and the module to /usr/lib64/security,
  writes its systemd unit, D-Bus activation and bus policy, puts the
  module's line in sudo's and polkit's stacks (polkit's from
  /usr/lib/pam.d copied to /etc/pam.d, which wins), and has systemd and
  the bus read theirs again; `uninstall` (Remove) takes it all out. The
  service and module come from beside Preferences or the tree it was
  built in (`share/olo/build-dir`). Set Up… takes the password and five
  looks (each a little turned), Set Up Again replaces them, Forget… drops
  them.
* **Testing**, without root, a camera or anyone's face: a private bus
  (busd), a debug `olo-faced serve --bus A --root DIR --models DIR
  --camera-dir FRAMES` (pictures for frames: only on its command line,
  never from its environment; a debug build takes the PAM stand-in,
  `OLO_PAM_CONFDIR`), and `cargo run -p olo-face --example client
  status|enroll|verify|forget|pam` with `OLO_FACE_BUS`; `pam` runs PAM's
  check with the module first in a stand-in stack. Tried so: a wrong
  password refused; five looks enrolled from crops of one portrait in
  1 s; another photo of him matched in 0.7 s, another man "not you",
  empty frames "no face"; through PAM, his face let in a wrong password,
  the other man's didn't, and the right password still did after the
  look.

## A display that leaves without a word (app_server udev.rs)

app_server looks at a card's connectors when the kernel says something
changed there (`device_changed`: a forced probe of each, as the DRM
master), and lets a display go when it's found gone. The kernel doesn't
always say. Ben's ThinkPad (xe, kernel 7.2.15), 2026-11-10: a
Thunderbolt dock pulled out with a Studio Display (DP-2) and a Dell
(DP-3) on it. Two events came within 0.3 s; the scan found DP-2 gone
and DP-3 still there. Eleven seconds later the kernel logged
"[CONNECTOR:549:DP-3] … Failed to enable link training" and sent no
event after it. For five minutes DP-3 was `connected` in sysfs with the
Dell's EDID, Olo had a desktop on it that nobody could see, and logind,
which counts connected connectors, said `Docked` (so a lid shut
wouldn't have suspended). `echo detect >
/sys/class/drm/card0-DP-3/status` as root cleared it.

So app_server looks again when it has reason to doubt, and at no other
time (no timer runs while nothing has happened):

- **After a display leaves a card**, the card is looked at again 1.5,
  4, 10 and 20 seconds after (`LOOKS_AFTER_LEAVING`, `look_again`),
  and those start over if a look finds another gone: a dock's displays
  don't all leave in the one event, and the last look is after the
  kernel has given up on a link.
- **When a frame can't be put on a display** (`frame_finish`'s
  error), its card is looked at 0.3 s later, once in ten seconds for
  that display however many frames fail.

A look is a probe of every connector of the card on app_server's own
thread (some milliseconds each; a hitch after an unplugging, not in a
frame's ordinary way). Not tried on a dock: a test's session has no
connectors, so this is by reading and by the kernel's log of that day;
TODO has what Ben is to try, and what isn't known (whether a forced
probe says "disconnected" before the kernel gives up on the link).

## Each display on its own GPU (app_server udev.rs; Preferences ▸ Display ▸ Graphics)

Each display is composed by the GPU it is wired to (`render_surface`:
the surface's own render node), so no display's frame crosses between
GPUs (a window's picture may: below): on a
hybrid laptop the built-in panel and the USB-C ports are Intel's and
the HDMI port NVIDIA's, which wakes only while a display is plugged in
there. Composing the panel on NVIDIA's had every frame copied to
Intel's through the CPU (NVIDIA can't render into the linear buffers
Intel can import: `--probe-gpus` says which formats each GPU can render
and import linear), 11 ms a frame: 30 Hz (Ben: "we should just use
whatever the native one is they need to use"). Only a display device
that can't render (a USB adapter) has its frames composed on the
primary GPU (the one the computer started on) and copied. A second
GPU's own displays are composed at 8-bit (10-bit there is untried).
Windows' buffers from another GPU are copied to the one that shows
them (below). Display's Graphics box (two or more GPUs,
`Request::Gpus`: `olo_system::gpus`) says what each drives.

### A window drawn by one GPU, shown by another

Apps draw with the primary GPU (Intel's), so a window on the HDMI
display has its picture made by one GPU and composed by another, and
the two share no layout of a buffer but the plain one, linear (NVIDIA
can't draw into linear and can read it; Intel does both:
`--probe-gpus`). So at each commit the GPU that drew the window copies
its picture into a linear buffer of its own (Smithay's
`dma_shadow_copy`, kept for the window and drawn into again where the
commit's damage says), and the composing GPU reads that as a texture.

**NVIDIA's driver reads a linear buffer from another GPU as if each
row were the picture's width rounded down to 8 pixels** (32 bytes),
whatever row length the import names: a window 964 pixels wide came
out sheared four pixels a row, and so did every window whose width
wasn't a multiple of 8 (Ben, 2026-11-12, a television on HDMI: "all
messed up / scrambled"; driver 615.71). So:

- **The copy has rows of a whole multiple of 16 pixels**
  (`SHARED_ROW`): it's made that much wider than the picture, the
  picture drawn at its left, and its last column repeated into the
  spare ones so that a window shown scaled blends at its right edge
  with itself. The composing GPU's texture is wider than the window,
  and is sampled over the window's part (texture coordinates are by
  the texture's own size).
- **A linear buffer NVIDIA would misread is never read by it directly**
  (`GlesRenderer::reads_rows_of`, `linear_rows`: 32 bytes for NVIDIA's
  driver, by its vendor string; any length for others): the import
  refuses it, and a buffer a client said was for that GPU
  (`set_sampling_device`) is then read on the GPU that can and copied
  as any other (`import_on_src_node`).
- **Apps aren't offered linear buffers for such a GPU's displays**
  (`get_surface_dmabuf_feedback`): an app drawing with Intel's would
  take the offer (linear is the one layout both know), draw slower for
  it, and gain nothing.

**`olo-app-server --probe-shared [FOLDER [SIZES]]`** is how it was
found and is how to check it, with no display plugged in: for each pair
of GPUs, a pattern is drawn into a buffer as an app's would be (in the
drawing GPU's own layout; linear; linear and said to be for the
composing GPU), imported by the other GPU's renderer as a window's
buffer is, drawn there, read back and compared pixel by pixel; then
another picture drawn into the same buffer, and then a part of it,
imported again into the texture the frame before made with only that
part said to have changed. It says "the same, all three pictures" or
what differs, and keeps the pictures in FOLDER. It opens the devices
unprivileged and touches no display (safe beside a running desktop; a
sleeping GPU is awake while it runs). On the ThinkPad: before the fix,
right at 1920 and 1408 wide, wrong at 964 and 333, and over 91 widths
right exactly at the multiples of 8; after, 175 tries the same. **What
it can't see** is the frame NVIDIA sends to the display (a display
needs to be plugged in for that): the fix wasn't seen on a television.

### Variable refresh rate (VRR)

A display that can vary its refresh rate (the kernel's `vrr_capable`
and the CRTC's `VRR_ENABLED`: a ThinkPad P1 Gen 9's panel, 40–120 Hz)
says so in `OutputInfo::vrr` (None: it can't; `Backend::vrr`, from
Smithay's `vrr_supported`), and Preferences ▸ Display shows "Variable
refresh rate" under its refresh rate. It's the person's: off unless
turned on (`OutputConfig::vrr`, kept per display and set again as the
display appears), through `Request::ConfigureOutput`; app_server asks
Smithay (`use_vrr`), which changes it without a modeset where the
driver can and with the next frame's otherwise. Headless screens
simulate one, so the switch can be tried and reviewed.

### The discrete GPU stays asleep

NVIDIA's GPU on a hybrid laptop sleeps (D3cold) while nothing uses it,
and whatever loads NVIDIA's drivers wakes it and waits for it, ~2.3 s:
every Olo app's start took 2.5 s instead of 77 ms (DeskCalc, its
first window), Chrome's GPU process the same, and each app_server start
(a reload's too) opened it. Nothing routine may wake it:

- app_server leaves NVIDIA's card unopened while nothing is plugged
  into it (`left_asleep`: its connectors' status, as sysfs keeps it,
  read without asking the GPU), and opens it when a udev change says a
  display is.
- Olo's apps are handed the one Vulkan driver of the GPU they draw on,
  so the loader never loads NVIDIA's ("One Vulkan driver, handed to
  the loader"); they draw on the GPU the displays use, and a window on
  NVIDIA's HDMI display is imported there.
- Programs Olo starts get `olo_kit_base::gpu::asleep_env()` (Vulkan's
  loader and glvnd's EGL without NVIDIA's): `olo-chrome` does.
- **A headless app_server loads Mesa's EGL library alone**
  (`app_server::egl_vendor`, `olo_kit_base::gpu::mesa_egl_alone`).
  glvnd asks every maker's library in turn for a display, NVIDIA's
  first: each agent's screen's app_server, and the person's, had
  NVIDIA's nine EGL libraries loaded (found 2026-11-20 by reading
  `/proc/PID/maps`: twelve app_servers, the card's driver stuck in the
  kernel that day). Where NVIDIA's card only sits beside the GPU the
  computer started on, app_server gives glvnd Mesa's vendor file
  first thing in `main` (glvnd reads only the environment; set before
  any thread, marked as its own so an in-place restart decides again,
  and taken out of what it starts, `realtime::start_off_kept`: a
  program put on NVIDIA's card on purpose needs NVIDIA's library). A
  headless one always does, and draws on the GPU the computer started
  on whatever its node's number (`headless::render_node`); the
  person's own does only where NVIDIA's card has its DRM device and
  no connector at all, since a display plugged into the card later
  needs NVIDIA's library and the choice can't be changed once made
  (on a laptop whose HDMI port is the card's, it loads it as before).
  An agent's screen's app_server: no library of NVIDIA's (9 before),
  6.7 MB less of its own memory (70.8 → 64.1 MB), 11 ms sooner to its
  EGL display (30 → 19 ms); whether loading the library ever woke a
  sleeping card isn't known (it didn't when `left_asleep` was
  measured), so this isn't claimed to save a wake.
- Activity asks NVIDIA's library only while the GPU is awake, Doctor
  and `olo_system::gpus` read sysfs attributes only (never a PCI
  device's `config`, which wakes it), and no local model (voice,
  palm, olo-complete) has a GPU to run on: the CPU's SIMD.

The person decides otherwise by setting Vulkan's or glvnd's variables
themselves, or `__NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1`: those are left alone. To
check: NVIDIA's `power/runtime_status` stays `suspended` and its
`power/runtime_active_time` doesn't move through a launch.

### Power modes (Preferences ▸ Power, Deskbar and `olo-gpu-follow.service`)

Power uses the shared kit's `RadioButton::description` and `CheckBox::description` for wrapped notes aligned with their mark labels. A menu can use `Menu::note` for a readable, non-interactive status line, as in Viewer's Decode With menu.

Power has two tabs. **Power Mode** offers Battery Saver, Adaptive Performance
and Low Latency. Choosing one in Preferences or Deskbar applies it immediately.
The same stable IDs work with PPD, the ThinkPad's firmware shortcuts and
app_server's agent API. `{"type":"set_power_mode","mode":"balanced"}` selects
Adaptive Performance. `power_status` and `power_changed` include `policy`,
with available modes, the active mode, supply, percentage, any restore-on-AC
mode and selection errors. Modes unavailable on the machine are disabled.

| Mode | Processors | Graphics and cooling |
|---|---|---|
| Battery Saver (`power-saver`) | Low-power chassis profile, energy-first EPP, turbo off on hardware that supports it. A supervised background build service can use up to half the CPU capacity. | Conservative Intel graphics ramp and clock ceiling, reduced NVIDIA ceiling on first use. Firmware fans. The built-in panel uses an offered mode at its existing resolution at or below 60 Hz, and dims after 30 idle seconds. |
| Adaptive Performance (`balanced`) | Low native floor, full turbo, balanced chassis profile. Performance-biased EPP on AC and energy-biased EPP on battery. | Driver-managed range and demand-based discrete graphics. The ThinkPad's Cool curve anticipates heat. |
| Low Latency (`performance`) | Full turbo and performance EPP with a low floor. Intel HWP dynamic boost covers I/O wakeups. Registered foreground window threads get a temporary utilization hint for the interaction and 200 ms afterwards. | Full operating range. Where supported, the GPU runtime-PM delay spans at least 250 ms during this mode. The ThinkPad's Cooler curve starts earlier. |

**Each mode can be changed** (Ben, 2026-11-20: "2 columns and the second
column has the customization options specific for each mode … if i change
the options for one of the modes then it persists for that mode but says
customized or something with a revert button … let me customize all the
things that the mode does"). Beside the modes is a box named for the one
in use (`power.rs`, `mode_box`), with everything it sets as a control,
and what is chosen there is that mode's alone:
- What root's follower does for a mode is the plan's "MODE/…" entries
  (`gpu_tuning::Plan`, in `/etc/olo/gpus.json`): the processors' preset
  and each GPU's (`mode_cpu`, `mode_gpu`), each one's top speed in
  percent of its fastest, 100 down to 50 in tens (`mode_cpu_top`,
  `mode_gpu_top`: a ceiling only, `with_top`; the lowest clock stays the
  driver's and is never raised to meet it), whether the GPUs are kept
  ready between tasks (`mode_gpu_ready`), the fans' profile
  (`mode_fans`) and each NVMe drive's power. A choice equal to what the
  mode does anyway isn't kept, so a mode never touched follows Olo's own
  as that changes. Changed in the box, they wait ("Not applied yet.")
  until Apply… hands the whole plan to `olo-gpu-tune set` through polkit,
  once, off the window's thread; the follower then follows it.
- What the session does for a mode is `PowerSettings::modes`
  (`ModeChoices`): the built-in display limited to 60 Hz, dimmed when
  idle, the front app favoured after input. These take effect at once
  (app_server's `apply_mode_choices`, also when the mode changes), and
  say so in the box.
- The box's last line says how the mode stands (defaults, customized,
  not applied yet) and Restore Defaults clears both kinds for that mode;
  a customized mode says so beside its name in the list, whichever is in
  use.

Battery Saver temporarily selects the nearest offered refresh at or below
60 Hz at the current resolution. A lower refresh already in use takes
precedence. Display settings made while in Saver become the preferred mode
when it ends. Idle dimming uses the panel's backlight in SDR and its SDR white
in HDR. Input restores the chosen brightness. Display sleep, Caffeinated and
application inhibitors use the ordinary idle policy.

The automatic choice is Off, 10%, 15% (default) or 20%. app_server's
`power_modes` worker follows UPower and PPD, remembers the previous mode
and restores it when power is connected. A choice made above the threshold
keeps automatic Saver armed. A manual choice at low charge, including a
firmware shortcut, takes precedence until AC returns. The episode survives a compositor reload in
the user's runtime directory. Supply changes settle for two seconds. An
adapter that reports four switches within half a minute is treated as
battery until stable. Agent screens simulate mode choice locally.

**Current hardware state** reads the actual CPU performance limits and
turbo, active display connectors, discrete GPU runtime state and cooling.
Opening it, Refresh, and changes to the follower's report refresh the
readback on a worker. NVIDIA is never queried through NVML for this panel.

**Battery & Idle** offers the charge threshold reported by UPower and
independent display-off and suspend times for battery and AC. Never
disables that timer. Earlier shared timers and battery-only sleep retain
their effective values on each supply. The first edit materializes the
two columns. Lock and presence are under the disclosure and temporary
Caffeinated mode is available in Deskbar. Screen Saver's display timer
edits the current supply. The location `olo-preferences gpus` still
opens Power with the hardware disclosure expanded.

**Hardware ownership.** Olo Doctor installs or updates the privileged
follower and, on supported ThinkPads, its fan service. The three named
modes supersede the old per-mode CPU, GPU and fan grid. Legacy tuning
files remain readable for backup, including existing per-drive NVMe
and SATA choices. Unconfigured drives use the controller or link's
normal policy. Fedora's stock Performance mapping can use the
`olo-low-latency` TuneD profile based on its laptop Balanced policy.
A custom distribution or administrator mapping is respected. TuneD's
`profile_changed` completion signal synchronizes the follower with its
asynchronous writes. The follower releases Intel's global minimum
before setting the maximum, reads the result back and records refused
writes. Generic CPUFreq drivers use a demand-based governor when
available.

`/run/olo-gpu-follow.json` records the applied mode, supply, CPU floor
and ceiling, GPU requests, deferred devices, drives and errors. A sleeping
RTX receives its pending settings when a client opens its device. Native
inotify observes device opens and additions. Only a pending open gets a
bounded recheck of runtime status. The NVIDIA clock lock is held by the
follower's NVML context. Fine-grained runtime D3 remains available. On
resume the follower reconciles hardware state again. `olo-gpu-tune show`
reports GPU readback as JSON. `--wake` explicitly queries sleeping devices.

**Not done from here: keeping a card awake while memory is short.**
A runtime suspend of NVIDIA's card failed for good on 2026-11-20 with
memory short ("A graphics card that stopped answering": its last
check was made against a deadline already three seconds past; that
memory being short is what spent it is likely, not shown). The
follower was made to hold an awake card awake while programs were
being held for memory, by writing "on" to its `power/control` at each
telling of the kernel's (`olo_system::memory_pressure::watch`, a
pressure-stall trigger), and "auto" again after two calm minutes. It
was withdrawn on review before it ever ran, for what that write is:
the kernel's `pm_runtime_forbid`, which resumes the device then and
there. A card that went to sleep between Olo's look at it and its
write was woken, under the very pressure it was to be spared
(reproduced on this kernel in a guest, with a USB hub); one in the
middle of suspending is waited for with no limit; and the one policy
bit can't be shared with the person's own "on", the udev rules that
write "auto" as a card is bound (Olo's and NVIDIA's), or a follower
started again in the middle. Measured on this computer besides: the
mark it used (100 ms of stall in two seconds) was met in 315 of 891
two-second spans of three ordinary minutes with 17 GB and more to be
had, so the card would have been held awake most of a working day.
User space has no way to keep a device from suspending without
resuming it; the place for it is the driver's own suspend, which can
refuse before it has touched anything (docs/TODO.md, the patched
driver). The watcher itself is kept (`memory_pressure`, with what it
costs the kernel), and `kbench pressure` measures it.

And **only a card that says it is awake is asked**
(`gpu_load::askable`: `runtime_status` exactly "active", and no
module of NVIDIA's on its way out): the panels' figures
(`nvidia_now`), the processes on it (`procs`), and the follower, which
leaves a card that stopped answering wholly alone (nothing written,
nothing counted as refused) and sets one that is going to sleep or
waking at its next open. A caller that means to wake a card may ask
one asleep (`not_failed`: Preferences, `olo-gpu-tune show --wake`),
never one that failed or whose driver is being unloaded. NVIDIA's
video encoder and decoder ask the kernel's files the same before
anything of NVIDIA's is loaded or started (`olo_video`'s
`nvidia_card::usable`), so the menus don't offer what can't work.
What still isn't done: NVIDIA's library, once started in a program,
is held for the program's life with the card's device open
(`gpu_tuning::nvml`): TODO.

**Thermal headroom.** The fan service uses its existing sensor samples
and the hardware's individual trip points. Within 8 °C it signals
background work to ease off. Within 5 °C for eight seconds it also asks
the follower to trim the CPU performance ceiling to 80%. The ceiling
and background budget recover after 15 seconds with at least 12 °C of
headroom. User-service build quotas are temporary and explicit quotas
are respected. Existing foreground scheduling and firmware protection
remain in force. These are control thresholds to validate on each
platform. A headless run can exercise the policy and deadlines but does
not measure a laptop's thermals or battery life.

**Media choices.** Screenshot's Record menu has Encode With and Video
Format, filtered by the available engines. Automatic recording tries the
integrated VA-API hardware path for H.264 and AV1 on either supply.
Viewer ▸ View ▸ Decode With selects the decoder for the current video and
future videos. Its Automatic option prefers the integrated decoder and
can use NVIDIA on battery when enabled. Explicit device selection,
capture commands and codec arguments remain available.


## The touch screen (app_server input_handler.rs)

A touch screen (a laptop's, as the ThinkPad P1 Gen 9's Wacom panel) is
mapped to the built-in display (eDP, else the first). Where a finger
comes down on a client that has `wl_touch` (Chrome, GTK), it gets
touch; anywhere else (every Olo app, and app_server's
own frames, tabs and menus) the finger is the pointer (`takes_touch`,
`touch_pointer`, `TouchPointer`): a tap clicks where it lands, a finger
that moves past 6 points drags (its button pressed where it came down),
so windows move, menus open and buttons click as with a mouse; a second
finger before the first has pressed makes the two scroll what's under
them (their middle's movement as a finger scroll, inverted: the content
follows the fingers; a lift stops it), or, once they've moved 8 points
and their distance apart changed more than their middle moved, pinch
(the pointer's pinch gesture, `zwp_pointer_gestures_v1`, as a
touchpad's). The pointer hides while a finger
is it, and shows again as a mouse or touchpad moves
(`touch_hides_pointer`).
The pen is a tablet tool (`zwp_tablet_v2`). Agents and tests touch with
`SyntheticEvent::Touch { slot, phase, x, y }` (`tsession touch NAME X Y`,
`tsession touchdrag NAME X1 Y1 X2 Y2`), which goes the same way.
A display's touch screen can be turned off (Ben, 2026-11-06):
Preferences ▸ Display's "Touch screen", shown for the display a touch
screen is on (`OutputInfo::touch`: Some while app_server counts a touch
device, `touch_screens`, on `touch_output`), on by default and kept off
by its key as its other settings are (`OutputConfig::touch`,
`DisplaySettings::touch_for`; on isn't written). Off, a finger coming
down or moving on it is ignored (`touch_on`); one already down still
lifts, the pen goes on working, and agents' synthetic touches are taken
whatever it says (they drive it, not the hardware). Agents set it with
`ConfigureOutput { touch }`.

## The touchpad (app_server udev.rs, momentum.rs, touch_filter.rs)

[TOUCHPAD.md](TOUCHPAD.md) has the measurements and the reasoning.
Preferences ▸ Touchpad & Mouse has four tabs (Touchpad, Touch, Gestures, Mouse)
and a tuning profile (protocol `touchpad.rs`: `PROFILES`,
`apply_profile`; changing any tuning by hand makes it "custom"); the
pad and the profile it suits come from `Request::InputDevices`
(`DeviceKind::detect`), and again from `Event::InputDevicesChanged`
whenever a pointing device comes or goes (`EventKind::InputDevices`:
the panel waits on it, nothing is polled). Headless, a test names the
devices in a JSON file (`OLO_HEADLESS_INPUT_DEVICES`, as
`Reply::InputDevices` lists them).

**Mice** (protocol `mice.rs`, the Mouse tab): each mouse is named by
maker and model (`mice::identify`: its USB or Bluetooth ids first, then
the name its driver gives it, with the maker's vendor id; `MODELS` holds
only ids seen on real devices and names as drivers give them; `maker`
names the rest by vendor), with its sensor and resolution, the
hardware database's `MOUSE_DPI` (read from udev's database by
`device_facts`, with the bus and whether its USB device may sleep), and
its quirks (`Quirk`: buttons on its motion node, which key remappers
grab; a receiver that must stay awake; a report rate above the
displays'; free-spinning and thumb wheels; a touch surface). A mouse
follows the other mice (`Settings::mouse_speed`,
`touchpad.mouse_accel_profile`), its model's profile
(`Settings::mice[key] = MouseTuning { profile: "recommended" }`:
`Class::Gaming` no acceleration, `Class::Everyday` adaptive), or its
own speed and acceleration (`profile: "custom"`); app_server's
`configure_pointer` takes `mice::effective`. What gets in a mouse's way
(a remapper's virtual pointer in the list, a receiver allowed to sleep)
is shown with a button that opens Olo Doctor, which fixes it.
A **pointing stick** (`InputDeviceInfo::pointing_stick`: named so,
scrolled on a held button by libinput's own default, or the PS/2 mouse
on a ThinkPad's keyboard controller, `isa0060/serio1`, which is its
TrackPoint when the kernel didn't know it as one: the P1 Gen 9's comes
as "PS/2 Logitech Mouse") is shown as the TrackPoint, at the top of the
second column, and scrolls while its middle button is held
(`TouchpadSettings::pointing_stick_scroll`, on: libinput's
`ScrollMethod::OnButtonDown` on BTN_MIDDLE, which it gives only the
sticks it knows).

On MacBook pads (Apple MTP) app_server loads
**Olo's touch filter** into its libinput: `touchpad.lua`, a libinput
1.30 Lua plugin written with the settings filled in to
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo/libinput-plugins` (`touch_filter::install`). It
counts a touch only while it presses, reports palms and hovering
fingers with no size, and makes the click from the fingers' pressure
alone. libinput drops pressure on pressure pads, so with the filter on
`install` also writes a quirk, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/libinput/olo-touchpad.quirks`,
that takes `INPUT_PROP_PRESSUREPAD` away, and the plugin clears the
pressure axis's resolution (docs/TOUCHPAD.md). Plugins and quirks are
read when libinput starts, so `start_libinput` makes a new libinput
context when the filter's settings change.
`cargo test -p app_server touch_filter` runs the plugin in mlua against
scripted frames; `examples/touch_filter_probe.rs` runs it on a real
device (root, read-only).
The filter also runs a **palm model** (`use_palm_model`, on by default;
`touch_filter::model_in_use`): the person's, trained on their hands
(`TouchFilter::palm_model`), or else Olo's own, made from real hands
(`olo_palm::default_model`, written by `make_default_model` from the
trainer's kept runs; crates/palm, `olo-palm`; docs/TOUCHPAD.md "Palms
told apart by a model"). Its live samples come
from app_server's `contacts.rs`, which reads the pad's slots with
`EVIOCGMTSLOTS` on a copy of libinput's descriptor while anyone
subscribes to `EventKind::TouchContacts` (only by name), for every
touchpad libinput opens (`INPUT_PROP_POINTER` without
