Ben, 2026-11-18: "we should add a language setting and also let's
translate all olo apps and prefs and ux to support all the major
languages (defaulting to us english)". **The layer and the choice are
in; the translations are under way** (docs/TODO.md).

**Preferences ▸ Language & Region** (`apps/preferences/src/language.rs`;
its icon `language`, a globe with a speech bubble standing before it,
drawn as the clock and calendar of Date & Time are): Olo's language,
each language by its own name ("Deutsch (German)"; never translated),
saying how much of Olo is in it so far (`words::covered` against
`words::english()`, the list in `data/words/en.txt`), and
that other programs take it as they next start: `LANGUAGE` (gettext's,
"de_DE:de") in the person's own `~/.config/locale.conf`
(`olo_xdg::locale::set_language`, the rest of the file kept), which
`locale::give` hands every program Olo starts, over what the starter
had. Formats (dates, numbers) follow the system's region for now.

**The lint in a language**: `OLO_LANGUAGE=de cargo ui-lint` draws every
window in German (`lint::program` starts the words layer; before, a run
"in German" checked English), so a translation is held to the same
rules as English: nothing past its room, no field's column too narrow,
every window within 1280 × 800. German's first run found 307 things,
which came to: label columns sized for English (a field's `divider` is
now where it starts at the least, in `MenuField` and `TextControl`: a
wider label pushes the field over instead of being drawn under it;
`divider_for` measures labels as drawn); words built with `format!`,
so never translated (Undo and Redo are `tr!("Undo {}")` with the step's
name looked up, durations `words::count("1 second", "{n} seconds")`,
sentences `olo_kit::tr!`, and anything handed on as owned text goes
through `words::of_text`); the menu check comparing translated menus
with English (it compares with the same words translated); and German
too long for its room, put right with shorter German where the English
is right. The kit's own lint tests look for words as drawn
(`words::tr("Revert")`), and the settings index is drawn in English
whatever the lint runs in (`ui_lint_settings_index`, under the lint's
one-window lock). German (`words/de.txt`), Spanish (`words/es.txt`,
Spain's, "tú", sentence case as Spanish menus have it) and French
(`words/fr.txt`, "vous", sentence case, a check box's words in the
infinitive; a narrow no-break space before `:` `;` `?` `!` and
no-break spaces inside « », as French sets them) have every one
of Olo's words: those the same as in English (names, paths) as
themselves, so coverage says all. Each is clean in the layout lint and
the live one in its language (`OLO_LANGUAGE=es cargo ui-lint
--no-fail-fast`, `OLO_LANGUAGE=es tools/dev/ui-lint --no-cache`): where a
translation ran past its room it was said in fewer words, measured
against German, which fits (a long note under Power's modes is 480
characters in German, 498 in Spanish). **What the lint can't see**: a
line cut short by design (a headline `.cut(true)`, a status line an app
paints and cuts) passes it, so a translation cut there is found only by
looking: DiskBackup's "Sicherung nicht abgeschlos…" and Disk Usage's
hint were (2026-11-19). Measure such a line's translations against its
room (Noto Sans at the line's size and weight; DiskBackup's headline is
24 pt bold beside its buttons), and picture the app in each language.

The words stay in the code, in English, as they always were. Each
language has a catalog of them (`data/words/CODE.txt`): blocks
apart by an empty line, the English then the
translation; a sentence that counts something has the English with
`{n}`, then a line for each form the language has (`one:`, `few:`,
`many:`, `other:`; `Counting` is CLDR's rule for each language). `\n`
is a new line, `#` a comment.

- **The catalogs are data, read at start** (`words::text_of`): a
  program reads its language's catalog from Olo's data
  (`olo_xdg::data_dirs`: the tree's `data/words` beside a build or
  under cargo, `OLO_DATA`, the installed `share/olo/words`, then the
  tree an install was built from) the first time a word is wanted, and
  keeps it; none found, its words stay English and the log says so. A
  first install copies them (`tools/install-session.sh`) and each
  upgrade brings the new or changed ones before programs start again
  (`upgrade::sync_words`, each moved into place whole); an upgrade
  made by a session from before they were data doesn't know to, and
  programs then read the tree's until the next one does. They were
  compiled into olo-kit-base until 2026-11-20 (another agent's study
  of kache's misses, which Ben passed on: "packaging catalogs as
  separately updatable resources is worth measuring … a one-string
  edit is a good benchmark"). Measured, release, this computer: one
  word changed in the German catalog built 48 crates again, 2 min 35 s
  for the workspace (and the same again for whoever builds dev), and
  38 of the 81 programs each carried all twelve catalogs, 3.5 MB; now
  it builds nothing. Against that, a program starting in German reads
  268 KB, 0.2 ms, before making the same table as before (1 ms:
  `what_a_catalog_costs`); one in English reads nothing, as before.
  A catalog is matched to the code by the English itself, so a
  program a build behind or ahead of its catalog shows English for the
  words the other lacks, nothing worse. Tests and the lints read the
  tree's (`cargo` names the package's folder at run time, so a build
  kept elsewhere, `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, reads the tree's too).
- **A literal handed to a widget is translated with nothing said**
  (`olo_kit::words::of`, called where the kit's widgets take their
  words: a button's label, a menu's title and items, a check box, a
  radio button, tabs, a menu field's label and choices, a box's
  title, a `StringView`, a field's hint, a tip, a window's title, a
  list's column, an empty state, a sidebar's rows, a banner, a card).
  A literal is told from what's made as the program goes by
  `SharedString::as_static`: `Button::new("Save")` is looked up, a
  file's name, an event's title or a `format!` never is. A
  translation is no literal, so it's never looked up twice.
- **Words given as plain text but always the app's own** (an alert's
  title, message and buttons; a Preferences box's title) are found by
  what they say (`of_text`).
- **A sentence with parts**: `tr!("Updated {} ago", when)` (the
  catalog's translation may order them, `{1}` before `{0}`);
  **one that counts**: `words::count(n, "{n} window", "{n} windows")`.
- **What an app paints itself** (`style::label`) is its own to ask
  for: `tr!("…")`. The kit doesn't translate at the paint, where a
  width measured from the English would no longer fit.
- **Words another crate keeps in English** (a shortcut's title and its
  group, `olo_protocol::shortcuts` and `app_keys`; a windowing mode's
  and a layout's sentence; a Bluetooth device's kind, `olo_system`)
  are asked for where they're shown: `words::tr(title)` for a
  `&'static str`, `words::lookup` for one that came over a socket as
  text (the chord panel's rows, from app_server). They are in the
  catalogs like any word (`words gather` doesn't find them: add them
  to `en.txt`). Until 2026-11-20 none was: Preferences ▸ Keyboard ▸
  Shortcuts, the shortcuts sheet and the chord panel were English in
  every language, 207 titles.
- **A sentence put into a sentence** is asked for too
  (`tr!("{} Choose a workspace's own from Deskbar's tray.",
  words::tr(what))`), and a name is never put into a sentence that
  would want it in another case: two whole sentences instead ("Tap the
  Windows key…", "Tap ⌘ (the Super key)…").
- **A panel that shows the computer's own devices** has a demo for
  pictures, as the lint's fixtures: `OLO_BLUETOOTH_DEMO=1` (Preferences
  ▸ Bluetooth), `OLO_PHONE_DEMO=1` (Phone, connected; `=connect`: its
  first step), `OLO_KEYBOARDS_DEMO=1`, `OLO_POWER_DEMO=1`. A test
  session shares the system's Bluetooth, so without them a picture
  shows the person's phone by name, and a button there is the real
  adapter's.
- In English nothing is looked up or read: one load of a flag.

The language is `Settings::language` ("de", "pt-BR"; empty: English;
`words::LANGUAGES` lists them: Chinese simplified and traditional,
Dutch, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Brazilian
Portuguese, Russian, Spanish; Arabic waits for right-to-left layout),
applied by the kit to every running app as the look is
(`theme::init`, `look`: the windows say their words again);
`OLO_LANGUAGE=de` for a test or a picture. `OLO_WORDS_SEEN=FILE`
writes every word asked for to FILE, each once (literals, and in
English too what's otherwise left as it is: a tab view's tabs, a menu
field's choices, a box's title, an alert's words: `words::note`).

**Olo's word list** (`data/words/en.txt`, 4,083 words on
2026-11-19) is what `tools/dev/words gather --write` finds: both layout
lints run with `OLO_WORDS_SEEN` (`cargo ui-lint` opens Preferences',
DiskBackup's and the kit's windows; `tools/dev/ui-lint` every app's,
and their menus, built as an app starts), and the literals handed to
widgets in the apps' code that no window either lint opens shows
(`Button::new("…")`, `.note("…")`, `.item("…", …)`, `tr!("…")`: a
pairing dialog, a first-run window, an error's note; ids and a
service's log words left out), and what agents call a field with no
label shown (`.name("Range")`, looked up as `words::of_name`; one with
a capital: a thread's `.name("pty reader")` isn't a word. Sixteen were
never gathered before 2026-11-19, so no language had them). A word only seen as the lints ran counts
if the code holds it as a literal outside its tests and comments: what
this computer shows the lints (its displays, its graphics card, its
disks, its Wi-Fi card) is data, and once came into the list that way
(removed 2026-11-19), as did the lint fixtures' made-up names. It never
takes a word out. The list was
first made from the unit lint alone (1,161 words): every app's menus
and windows but Preferences' and DiskBackup's were missing, so German,
Spanish and French left them in English. Sentences made with `format!`
or owned copies of literals (`"…".into()` to a `String`) aren't looked
up and aren't in it until they're `tr!` or `words::of_text`.
**What Olo shows that never asked**: `tools/dev/words unasked` runs the
live lint with `OLO_WORDS_UNSEEN`, under which the layer keeps every
word it hands back (`tr`, `lookup`, `count`, `fill`, `note`) and the kit
writes down text a widget is handed that isn't a literal (`words::of`
given a `String`) or that an app paints itself (the review's drawn
labels), less what the layer made: by program, the sweep's list of
words made at run time (1,136 on 2026-11-19, 378 of them Preferences').
It catches what no scan of the code can: a helper that takes `&str` and
copies it into a `String` (Network's text fields' hints, "Each
network's own"). Data shows among them (a network's name, a file's),
told apart by eye; what agents call a control, made from its label, is
handed on with `words::of_name`, not flagged. Watching costs one load
when nothing watches (Preferences over 180 keys typed: the same within
the rounds' spread, before, after and with it hard-wired off).
`tools/dev/words sweep FILE…` converts what it can by itself: a
`format!` sentence to `olo_kit::tr!` (its number formats moved into its
parts), a literal of two words or more copied into a `String` to
`words::tr("…")` copied; its diff is read by eye, since a command it
runs, a file's or a keyring item's name, a fixture's data and an
agent's command-line output must stay as they are. A helper that takes
a label as `&str` hands it on with `words::of_text(label)`, by what it
says. A sentence spliced from parts moves its leading space or comma
outside the `tr!` (`format!(", {}", tr!("of {}", …))`): a catalog line
keeps no leading space. Preferences was swept so on 2026-11-19 (468
places, 461 new words); its unasked list went from 378 to 258, the
rest data and what's drawn by name.
**Whose words are they.** A window's words are the person's: through
the layer. A program's words for another program stay English: a
service's state another window reads (`why` DiskBackup isn't backing
up, which its window and Deskbar compare: "turned off" is Paused), what
it answers (Passwords' `Response::Error` to whichever program asked),
what a command line prints and what an agent is told (an MCP reply,
the context Terminal's palette or Calendar's assistant gives a model)
and a log. Agents and programs read them, and a program that doesn't
start the kit's app speaks English anyway: the language is chosen as
the kit starts (`theme::init`), so a command line's `tr!` was English
all along, and converting it only gave translators words no one sees.
Where a window shows a service's words, the service marks them
`words::en("turned off")` or `olo_kit::en!("the keyring can't be read:
{}", e)`: English as before, but gathered into the catalogs, and the
window gives them in the person's language with `words::of_said(text)`,
which finds the sentence by its words, whole or around the parts put
in it (a path, a number, the system's own message), and puts the parts
in the translation's places (of two that fit, the one with more words
of its own; a count's `{n}` must be a number; too few words of their
own, "{}: {}", is no sentence). What it finds is kept (a window shows the
same few at each progress tick). A service whose own words reach the
person (Calendar's reminders, a notification) chooses the language
before it makes them: `words::choose()` asks the window server for the
setting (Calendar's service does at each waking; it had taken it only
as a side effect of its first `palette()` call, and never again).
The kit's glance server (`glance::serve`, Deskbar's glances: Weather's,
Calendar's, kache's, Notifications') chooses the language as it starts
and again when the settings' file changes: before, a glance's words
were English whatever the setting, as its process never started the
kit's app.
**What the kit asks for itself**, besides the widgets above: a
dashboard card's title and caption (`Card::new`, `caption`), a fact's
label (`Facts::new`'s pairs), a chart legend's names, a timeline's
tracks' names, panels' titles and guides: a literal looked up as each
is made (`words::of`). What an app paints itself is its own to ask for
(Weather's next-hour axis, a day's "Today"). **A phrase mid-sentence**:
`words::mid_sentence("Partly cloudy")` makes its first letter small,
as English and French do in a sentence, and keeps it in a language that
writes every noun with a capital (`Language::capital_nouns`, German:
"44°, Regen"); `to_lowercase()` on a translation would make German's
nouns small. **One English word, two things**: a key means one thing in
every language, so where English says two things alike the code says
one of them differently: Weather's sky is "Clear sky", not the button's
"Clear" ("Leeren", "Borrar", "Effacer").
**Saying a sentence whole.** A word spliced into a sentence ("in this
{}" with "tab" or "window"; "{} items" with "Its" or "Their"; "Started
{} ago" with "5 minutes") can't be translated: languages decline,
agree and order differently. Each is its own sentence
(`if tabs > 1 { tr!("… in this tab. …") } else { tr!("… in this
window. …") }`), and a number with its noun is `words::count`, whose
forms may leave the number out ("Every day" for one of "Every {n}
days"; merge and `the_catalogs` allow it). `tr(if a { "x" } else { "y"
})` hides both from the gatherer, which looks for a literal right after
`tr(` (or `count(`): write two calls, and a helper handed its words
gets each as its own `tr("…")` or `count(n, "…", "…")` at the call
(DiskBackup's "one a day for ever" came in only so). The converter
leaves a sentence with one word around its parts ("Gusts {}", "Sun
{}–{}", "Temperature ({})"): convert those by hand. A word held in a
table (Weather's sky phrases, from tomorrow.io's codes; a menu's
choices in a `const`) is looked up as it's shown (`words::tr(describe(
code))`) and put in en.txt by hand: the gatherer finds a literal by the
call it's in. It knows a dashboard's: a card's title, a caption, a
pair's first (`("Entries".into(), …)`, a pair's parenthesis, not a
call's). The gatherer skips
a lint's fixtures, the settings index written from them, a block only
tests and demos take (`if cfg!(test) …`, and the item after any
`#[cfg(test)]`), comments (in the code scan too: a doc comment's example
had come in as a word), strings of numbers alone ("+1 555 123 4567"),
names in capitals (PATH), in camel case (an API's fields:
dewPointDepression) and a search's syntax (program:all). The sweep skips a thread's name and a line that
already says `en!`.
`tools/dev/words missing LANG` lists what a catalog lacks, and `words
merge LANG PAIRS…` puts translations in (written as "English |||
translation"; it refuses unless every word is there and each keeps its
English's parts, and sets French's spaces). A catalog's entries are by
that list's English. Tests run in English. Tested: `words`' `a_catalog_read`, `a_sentence_filled`,
`counting`, `the_catalogs` (every translation keeps its English's
parts), `words_in_a_language_and_back`; Preferences ▸ Power looked at
in German with a few words (`OLO_LANGUAGE=de`): tabs, radio buttons,
menus and buttons in German, the layout following their widths.

## Google accounts (crates/google, `olo_google::accounts`; Preferences ▸ Integrations ▸ Google)

Ben, 2026-11-18: "we need a Google Workspace integration where for each
google workspace account you add you setup the "Olo" google app …
that should handle DiskBackup, Email, Calendar, anything else we add
later … for each google workspace we should have it be e.g. "Olo
([an address])" so that it is separated for the user … add as
many google workspaces as we want in prefs -> integrations and then
choose which ones are enabled for mail, calendar, diskbackup in like a
grid". (And not a published app of Olo's own: Google's review of mail
and calendar scopes is a yearly cost, and an organisation still has to
let a third party's app in.)

**Why an app per account.** Google lets only a registered app (an OAuth
client in some Google Cloud project) sign someone in, and an
organisation's accounts are let into an app of its own where another's
is refused: a Workspace account signing in with the app another
account made (DiskBackup's, in a Gmail account) got "Access blocked:
Your institution's admin needs to review … Error 400:
access_not_configured". So each account Olo connects has an app of its
own in a project of its own, named "Olo (its address)" (several people
of one organisation each have theirs): a Desktop app client, its
consent screen Internal for a Workspace account (no publishing, no
warning, never signed out) or External and published for a Gmail one
(Google shows "Google hasn't verified this app" once: Advanced ▸ Go to
Olo), the Gmail, CalDAV and Drive APIs on, and the three scopes.

**One sign-in, every service.** `olo_google::accounts`: the list
(`~/.config/olo/google-accounts.json`: each account's address, the
services ticked, the scopes its sign-in was allowed; nothing secret)
and, in the login keyring, what signs each in (its app's client and
the refresh token: `application=olo service=google account=ADDRESS`).
`sign_in` asks for everything Olo's services use at once (`openid
email`, `https://mail.google.com/` for IMAP, `…/auth/calendar` for
CalDAV, `…/auth/drive.file` for DiskBackup's own files only), going to
the account meant (`login_hint`) or asking which (`prompt=select_account`,
never whichever the browser is signed in to); what Google says was
allowed is kept (its consent page lets some be left out: a service
not allowed can't be ticked until the account signs in again).
`token(address, fresh, agent)` gives an access token, kept while good
(an hour less a minute), a new one where a server refused the one in
hand. `Service::{Mail, Calendar, DiskBackup}` (DiskBackup is one
account's: ticking it for one unticks the rest, `tick`). Mail, Calendar
and DiskBackup each read the list and take their sign-in from here:
none keeps one of its own. Tests: `OLO_GOOGLE_ACCOUNTS` (a list),
`OLO_GOOGLE_SECRETS` (**a test's own keyring**: without it a test's
sign-in goes in the person's), `OLO_GOOGLE_API` (a Google of its own),
`OLO_GOOGLE_CONSENT=self` (the consent page fetched, nothing opened).

- **Mail** (`olo_mail::accounts`): the Google accounts ticked for Mail,
  then those added with an app password (`own_accounts`, `mail.json`:
  Fastmail's, and Gmail ones from before, which go on as they were).
  A Google one signs in to IMAP with `AUTHENTICATE XOAUTH2` (its
  address and a token; refused, the server's line of why is answered
  and the refusal said: is Mail allowed, and IMAP on in its Gmail
  settings?), `auth_of` choosing.
- **Calendar** (`olo_calendar::account::accounts`): the Google accounts
  ticked for Calendar (`Provider::Google`, the id `google:ADDRESS` as
  before, so what was kept of their calendars stays theirs), then
  Fastmail's and other CalDAV servers' (`calendar-accounts.json`).
  Calendar's window, reminders and widgets follow both files
  (`account::watched`). Calendar's own Google sign-in is gone.
- **DiskBackup** (`target::google_for`): the account it backs up to
  signs in through its app where it's connected; DiskBackup's own
  sign-in from before (`DISKBACKUP_GOOGLE`) is used only where it
  isn't. `olo-diskbackup --set-up-drive-account ADDRESS` backs up to a
  connected account's Drive (the folder found or made, a backup there
  opened with its key or made, the settings saying so, the account
  ticked for DiskBackup); `--disconnect-drive` stops (no target, the
  account unticked; the backups in Drive left as they are). Back Up To
  ▸ Google Drive… chooses among the connected accounts (none: it says
  to connect one, Open Integrations…). **`drive.file` files are seen
  only by the app (the project) that made them**: a backup folder made
  by one project's app is invisible to another's, so moving DiskBackup
  to another app would start a fresh, empty backup there. That's why an
  account whose DiskBackup app came first keeps that app (below).

**Preferences ▸ Integrations ▸ Google** (`apps/preferences/src/google.rs`;
the panel is a tab a provider: Google, Fastmail, CalDAV, GitHub,
Telegram; with the grid it was 868 points tall in one, past a 1280 ×
800 screen): the grid, each account with a tick for Mail, Calendar and
DiskBackup (one not allowed can't be ticked; DiskBackup's tick runs
`olo-diskbackup --set-up-drive-account` or `--disconnect-drive`, and
the grid follows only once it's done), how its sign-in stands (a token
asked for on a worker as the panel opens), Sign In Again (the
account's own app, in the person's browser; with none kept here, the
by-hand form, saying where its client is) and Remove (what signs it
in forgotten; DiskBackup stopped first if it backs up there). The list
is followed: an agent's finished account shows at once.

- **Add a Google Account…** (the agent; it was DiskBackup's Agent
  Setup, moved here and made the account's: `olo_google::setup`): the
  account's login chosen from Passwords (its `Shares`: those that say
  Google, else every login; no secret read), an agent screen of its own
  (`google-setup`) started and the login shared with it, and Claude
  Code opened in a Terminal window (Preferences ▸ AI's model and
  effort; `--allowedTools` olo-screen and the done command, `--add-dir`
  the screens' pictures and ~/Downloads, `--no-chrome`; it works in
  `~/.local/state/olo/google-agent-setup`, the task kept there as
  TASK.md). The task (`setup::brief`): sign in to Google Cloud there
  with the shared login without seeing its password, then the steps
  (`setup::steps`: a project named "Olo Desktop", as Google refuses a
  name under four letters ("Olo", Ben, 2026-11-18); the three APIs; the consent
  screen "Olo (its address)", Internal for Workspace; the three scopes;
  publish if External; a Desktop app client, its JSON downloaded),
  first looking for a set-up begun before; and the finish:
  `olo-preferences --google-setup-done ~/Downloads/client_secret_….json
  --screen google-setup`, which signs Olo in with Google's consent page
  opened on the agent's screen for it to allow, lists the account
  (ticked for Mail and Calendar where allowed; DiskBackup where it backs
  up to that Drive already), and tries each service, saying how each
  went for the agent to read (Mail: its inbox opened; Calendar: how
  many calendars; DiskBackup: whether the app sees the backups there,
  `accounts::sees_drive_file`). The person follows along in Terminal.
  Or **Set Up by Hand…**: the steps, the client's ID and secret, Sign
  In with Google in the person's browser.
- **Bring It Into Olo…** (shown while DiskBackup backs up to an
  account's Drive with its own app from before, and that account isn't
  connected): the agent brings **that** app up to date instead of
  making another (`setup::Task::Extend`: rename its consent screen
  "Olo (its address)", turn on the Gmail and CalDAV APIs, add their
  scopes; told never to make another project or client), then
  `--google-setup-done --account ADDRESS` signs in again with that
  app's client (DiskBackup's, from the keyring) and checks the app
  sees DiskBackup's folder. DiskBackup goes on backing up throughout:
  the same client, the same folder, the same key and settings.

Tested: `olo_google`'s `ticks_and_what_is_allowed`, `setup`'s
`the_brief_says_where_what_and_how`, `google_logins_first`,
`shared_once`; Calendar's `signing_in_to_google` (Olo's sign-in against
Calendar's stand-in Google: every scope asked, the account named, its
calendars listed); Mail's `a_google_token` (XOAUTH2 against the
stand-in IMAP server, refused said); DiskBackup's
`set_up_drive_account_then_disconnect`; Preferences'
`tests/google_setup.rs` (the done command against DiskBackup's stand-in
Google: the browser played, the account listed and ticked, its sign-in
kept, each service tried; signed in again with the app it has; an app
that doesn't see DiskBackup's folder said; an account with no known
app refused). Looked at headless (made-up accounts; a stand-in
Passwords socket, `OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET`, as a test session shares the
person's runtime directory): the grid, the Add flow's login chooser,
the by-hand form and Sign In Again with no app kept, each tab, at 1×
to 2×. **Not tried against Google itself**: that's Ben's accounts (the
agent's run is his to start).

## The fans (apps/fans, `olo-fans`)

**Four profiles** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "default is Auto, but then have
Cool, Very Cool, Coolest where Cool is about +10% more aggressive than
Auto at ramping up fans, Very Cool is +20% and Coolest is +30% …
maybe we use Auto/Cool/Cooler/Coolest"): Auto, the firmware's own
curve, and Olo's at three strengths (`olo_system::fans::Profile`;
`/etc/olo/fans`: `auto`, `cool-1`, `cool-2`, `cool-3`). Each strength
starts the fans, and has them at full speed, a step earlier than the
one before: a step is a tenth of a sensor's room from a warm idle
(40 °C) to its limit (`span`: for a processor that throttles at 100 °C,
from 61 °C to full speed at 95 for Cool, 55 to 90 for Cooler, 49 to 84
for Coolest; for the board's sensors, throttled at 65 °C, from 52.5,
50 and 47.5), and the processor's power asks for the fans at 15% more
watts for Cool and 15% fewer for Coolest (`level_for_power`). Full
speed always comes before the limit. **Cooler's is the curve there was
before** (it was called Cool, and its word, `cool`, still means it:
nothing chosen before changes). The steps are a design, by where each
sensor is throttled: **not yet measured against the firmware's own
curve on this computer**, which needs the fans' profile changed under
a steady load (the fans' file is root's, and the person's to change).
`olo-fans --status` says what each of the three would set now.
The three Power modes select these curves automatically (see Power
modes above). Olo Doctor installs the fan helper alongside the power
follower on supported ThinkPads. The stand-alone fan tools still accept
the four profile names and the previous `cool` spelling.



A ThinkPad's fans run ahead of the heat, so the computer isn't slowed
down for it: the firmware's own curve waits for the processor to be
hot, falls behind, and the board's sensors pass the temperature at
which the firmware throttles the processor (their zones' passive trip,
65 °C on a P1). `olo-fans` is a root service (systemd's
`olo-fans.service`; the fans are root's to set, through
`/proc/acpi/ibm/fan` of thinkpad_acpi loaded with `fan_control=1`).
`/etc/olo/fans` holds the profile, one word: `auto` (the firmware's
own curve: nothing read or written, asleep until the file changes) or
`cool` (the firmware's curve while everything is cool, the fans raised
early as anything warms, up to full speed). The current three Olo curves use the same controller at different strengths.
In `cool` it watches every sensor the computer has (each core and the
package, the firmware's own readings, every thermal zone with a trip,
the SSD, the memory), each with where the fans start for it and where
they're at full speed (`Sensor::span`, from its own limit), and sets
the level by the worst of three things: how near a sensor is to where
it would be throttled, how fast it's rising, and how much power the
processor draws (heat that hasn't reached a sensor yet). It comes down
a step at a time, after a hold. It is safe by the firmware's watchdog:
while it holds a level it says so every few seconds, and if it stops
the firmware takes the fans back within 30 seconds; ending, it hands
them back itself. `olo-fans --status` prints what it reads and would
do, changing nothing (as anyone); `/run/olo-fans/status` is a line of
`level=… why=…`, there from the service's start to its end and
written again when the level or the profile changes. Its source's doc
comment has the rest. Never run the service, or write a fan level,
from a test: `--status` and its unit tests only.

**It never ends for something it can't do**, and what it can't do is
said where people look. Two things went wrong on Ben's P1 on
2026-11-12, both from one cause: levels had been turned on by loading
thinkpad_acpi again by hand (`fan_control=1`), which that morning's
restart undid, and nothing kept the setting.

- The driver refuses every write then ("Invalid argument"). The
  service ended at its first, twice; systemd started it a third time
  into a cool moment, and it sat there, running, setting nothing and
  saying nothing (its status was written only when the level changed).
  Three ends in two minutes and systemd would have given it up for
  good. Now: where the driver doesn't take levels (`CONTROL`) nothing
  is tried; the fans are the firmware's; the service says so; it
  writes the file that turns levels on at the driver's next loading
  (`MODPROBE`: `olo_system::fans::CONF`, the same Olo Doctor's helper
  writes), and looks again once a minute, for a driver loaded again by
  hand. A level refused for any other reason is said once and tried
  again 30 seconds later (`Fans::refuse`).
- "Running" is the service's folder in /run (`Places::running`:
  systemd's `RuntimeDirectory`, there for the service's life and no
  longer), not its having said something. `State::amiss` is why a
  chosen Cool isn't in force (`Amiss`: the driver doesn't take levels
  and will from the next start; doesn't and nothing tells it to; the
  service isn't running), `State::level` the level held ("auto" for a
  running service that has said nothing), and `State::now` and
  Activity Monitor say those. A driver that doesn't take levels comes
  first: whatever the service says, nothing is set.

Olo Doctor finds each (`checks::fan_profile`, only where Cool is
chosen): "The Cool fan profile isn't in force" with Repair the Fan
Profile (the driver's file) or Start the Fan Service, "…starts with the
computer's next start" (nothing to fix), and "Olo's fan service runs
an older version" with Update the Fan Service, since root's copy is
one an upgrade doesn't replace. Its fix is `fans::steps`, the same
steps choosing Cool runs. Loading the driver again, which would put
levels in force without a restart, is not something Olo does (a
driver that didn't come back would take the Fn keys and the battery's
limits with it until the next start): by hand, as root,
`modprobe -r thinkpad_acpi && modprobe thinkpad_acpi`, then
`systemctl restart olo-fans`.

**Choosing the profile** (Ben, 2026-11-10: "have in the power prefs
the option for the default auto and this new cooler/louder auto
profile"). Three parts, each knowing only its own:

- `olo_system::fans` reads what there is, as anyone: whether the fans
  can be set at all (`look` is None without a ThinkPad's
  `/proc/acpi/ibm/fan`), the profile in force (`/etc/olo/fans`' while
  the service is installed, else the firmware's), whether
  thinkpad_acpi takes levels (`fan_control`), and the level the
  service holds and why (`State::now`: "Now: level 4 of 7, for 19 W.").
  It changes nothing.
- Olo Doctor sets it (`apps/doctor/src/fans.rs`), as it does the login
  screen's parts: `fans::steps(profile, bin, places)` are root steps
  for only what isn't so already. Cool: `olo-fans` copied from beside
  Doctor to `/usr/local/libexec/olo` (root's copy: an upgrade replaces
  the person's programs, not it, so choosing Cool again brings it up
  to date) with its SELinux label put right, its unit
  (`data/systemd/olo-fans.service`, carried in the program),
  `/etc/modprobe.d/olo-fans.conf` (`options thinkpad_acpi
  fan_control=1`), kept whether or not the driver takes levels now (it
  may only because someone loaded it again by hand) and, where it
  doesn't, in force from the computer's next start and said so, the
  word, and the unit
  enabled and, if its program or unit changed, started again (running
  already, the service reads the word by itself). Automatic: the word
  alone, and only where the service is installed. `olo-doctor --fans`
  says what there is; `olo-doctor --fans auto|cool` sets it, through
  the helper and pkexec (the password asked once), or there under
  sudo: the way in for a person at a terminal and for an agent. It is
  asked for only in the person's own session (`helper::run_as_root`
  goes by `helper::way`): from a test session or an agent's screen it
  says so and does nothing.
- Preferences ▸ Power ▸ Battery & Idle has the Fans box, only where
  `look` finds fans to set: "Fan profile:" (Automatic, Cool), what the
  chosen one means, and what the fans are doing now, read with the
  battery every five seconds while the panel is open. Choosing one
  runs `olo-doctor --fans WORD` on a thread ("Setting it: an
  administrator's password is asked…", the menu dimmed); refused or
  failed, the menu is back on the profile in force with why in red.
  It's in the settings index (`olo_xdg::settings`: "Fan profile").

`OLO_FANS_ROOT=DIR` puts every one of those places under DIR, for
tests: a made-up ThinkPad is two files (`proc/acpi/ibm/fan`,
`sys/module/thinkpad_acpi/parameters/fan_control` holding `Y`), Doctor
writes its steps there as the person with nothing of systemd's asked,
and a status written by hand (`run/olo-fans/status`) shows in the box.
The whole of it was driven so (2026-11-12): Cool chosen from the menu
(the program, unit and word written under DIR), the status following,
Automatic refused by a folder made read-only (said in red), the panel
reviewed at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75× and 2×, light and dark. On the
real computer it has not been chosen from the panel yet. Activity
Monitor's Fans card and Doctor's finding were looked at the same way
in each state (2026-11-12: a driver that takes no levels, kept and
not; the service stopped; running and silent; a level held; a level
refused), the card at 1×, 1.5× and 2×.

## Realtime threads and the kept core (`olo_app::realtime`, `olo_xdg::realtime`, `olo_system::cores`)

Nothing anyone runs may hold the desktop up (Ben, 2026-11-15: "nothing
should ever be able to impact the responsiveness of olo"; "any audio i/o
and other stuff like that should be realtime too"; "an option -- enabled
by default -- to reserve a cpu core just for olo's most important
threads"). A nice isn't enough, measured: under others' builds and a
GPU job, app_server's loop at nice −10 waited on a run queue 100–300 ms
of every second and the display stalled for up to 2.5 s under scx_lavd
(which gives a nice little weight), and still 8 s in 80 under the
kernel's own. Two reasons a nice can't help: the processor is shared out
between sibling cgroups by their weights before any nice counts (below),
and a nice orders shares, not who runs first.

**Realtime, never ended for being busy.** The threads someone waits on
are SCHED_RR, set by the program itself (`olo_xdg::realtime`,
`sched_setscheduler`), above every normal and sched_ext thread under any
scheduler:

| Thread | Priority | Made realtime by |
|---|---|---|
| The session's watchdog, the Performance supervisor's look (`SUPERVISOR_RT_PRIORITY`) | 21 | itself |
| PipeWire's data loops | 20 | libpipewire, as a stream starts |
| A player's, recorder's or AirPlay's sound (`SOUND_PRIORITY`) | 15 | itself, `olo_xdg::realtime::promote_if_wanted` |
| app_server's input thread (`olo-input`) | 12 | itself |
| app_server's loop | 10 | itself |
| The keyboard's program's display thread, and the proxy's loop | 9 | app_server (`realtime::focus`); olo-wlproxy itself |
| The keyboard's program's windows' loopers (`w>…`), and Deskbar's | 8 | app_server (`realtime::focus`, `realtime::always`) |

The watchdog and the supervisor are above the rest (Ben, 2026-11-15:
"give the olo supervisor thread(s) slightly higher priority than the
other olo stuff"): a realtime thread is never put back for running
long, so they must always get to run, whatever the others do; each
mostly sleeps. Only the person's own: a headless app_server, an agent's
screen (`OLO_SCREEN`) and `OLO_REALTIME=0` leave everything at its nice
(`OLO_REALTIME=1` makes a headless one realtime, to measure). A window
that loses the keyboard goes back to its nice; nothing goes back for
being busy.

A thread is made realtime only where the account lets a program do it
itself (RLIMIT_RTPRIO, from the login's limits): Olo Doctor's **Allow
Realtime** writes `/etc/security/limits.d/80-olo-realtime.conf` (the
account by its uid: `rtprio 70`, `rttime unlimited`), in force from the
next login; without it threads keep their nice. Never through rtkit:
rtkit gives realtime only to a process whose hard limit on realtime time
without sleeping (`RLIMIT_RTTIME`) is 200 ms at most, and the kernel
ends the process at that (SIGKILL), busy or not. app_server was, at
13:29 on 2026-11-15, three seconds into a live lint's dozen sessions,
most likely inside a GPU driver's wait where no signal could be taken
(Ben: "there should never be short kill rule and we should NEVER drop
priority down"). Before, a guard put a thread back to its nice at 50 ms
and a keeper made it realtime again two seconds on; both are gone.

The guard (`olo_app::realtime`, every Olo program, plain system calls)
now only ends a thread truly stuck: `RLIMIT_RTTIME` soft 30 s (realtime
processor time without once sleeping), whose SIGXCPU it turns into an
abort (a crash report, as any crash, "stuck" said on stderr), and hard
31 s, the kernel's SIGKILL for a thread stuck inside the kernel all that
while. A limit lowered below the guard's by something else in the
process (libpipewire's realtime module, where it went through rtkit)
can't be raised again: then nothing there is made realtime. app_server
makes another program's threads realtime only when its limits are the
guard's (`olo_app::realtime::guarded`, from /proc) and the thread is
marked as registered (`marked`: SCHED_RESET_ON_FORK on its class,
which threads it starts don't have, though they take its name; on
whichever normal class it has, batch and idle too, as a program a
build started is in the build's class and olo-supervisor lowers builds
to batch: marked only from "other", such a program's loopers were never
marked, and olo-app's own test failed whenever the tests ran from a
build long enough to be lowered, the whole workspace's and not one
crate's). The kit
registers each window's looper and its display thread as they start
(`guard_ui_thread`), and a registration is forgotten as its thread ends
(a thread-local's destructor: the kernel gives the id to new threads).
Put back (a window that lost the keyboard) with `SCHED_OTHER |
SCHED_RESET_ON_FORK`: the kernel refuses (EPERM) an unprivileged caller
that would clear the flag. Tests: `a_stuck_thread_ends_its_program_with_a_report`
(olo-app: SIGXCPU, the program aborts) and `a_busy_thread_stays_realtime`
(olo-xdg, ignored without the account's leave: 1.5 s of work, still
realtime).

**The kept core** (`Settings::keep_core`, on by default; Preferences ▸
Performance ▸ Scheduler ▸ Kept Core). One core, the fastest
(`olo_system::cores::kept`: ACPI CPPC's `highest_perf`, else the highest
clock; all its hardware threads; never CPU 0; only with four or more
online; `OLO_KEPT_CORE` chooses another), has app_server's loop and
input thread to itself: they are homed there alone (single threads: one
core is all either can use), and nothing else of the person's runs
there. With the person's own programs it needs no privilege: app_server
(the person's only, never a headless one, even realtime) sweeps every
thread of the account off it as it starts and as the setting changes
(`cores::sweep`, on its realtime worker, once: on the ThinkPad about
1,900 threads, whose affinity read takes 8.5 ms even from Python), and every program started later inherits a parent's
affinity. Threads already realtime are left as they are (PipeWire's;
what they are for is never waiting), as is an affinity a program chose
for other cores; one pinned to the kept core alone is moved off, as
that was inherited from a homed thread. The homed loop's own children
would inherit the kept core alone (the kernel copies a thread's
affinity to the threads and programs it starts), so every program
app_server starts begins where the person's run
(`realtime::start_off_kept`, `cores::start_off`: the affinity set in
the child before it runs, 7.5 µs to work out), and app_server's other
threads (its own, and those zbus and the compositor start as they go)
are swept off on its realtime worker at each focus change
(`kept::sweep_own`, 35 µs for 25 threads, never on the loop). Before
(2026-11-15), Palette, started by app_server, started Terminal, and
every shell, build and agent in it ran on the kept core alone: one
processor for all of it, and the desktop's at that (Ben: "wait why is
the shell limited to one [cpu]???? that should never happen!"; "we
want the core olo threads for responsiveness to stay on that one core
but nothing else"). `cores::tests::a_program_started_from_a_pinned_
thread_begins_off_it` starts a program from a thread pinned to one
processor, with and without it. The system's
services are root's: Olo Doctor's "Keep Them Off" (`olo-doctor
--keep-core on|off`, Preferences' button beside the setting) writes
systemd's own `CPUAffinity=` (`/etc/systemd/system.conf.d/50-olo-kept-core.conf`),
inherited by everything systemd starts from the next boot, and sweeps
what runs now as root (`Step::KeepOffCores`). Affinity, not a cgroup's
cpuset: Intel's low-power daemon (intel_lpmd, running on the ThinkPad)
sets the slices' `AllowedCPUs` itself, and the two combine (a thread
runs where both allow; under its low-power mode, the kept core isn't
among the low-power cores, and the loop runs where the cgroup allows).

Measured (`tools/dev/loadtest`, a test session's app_server with
Charts animating, eight burners at nice 10 on the E-cores 4–11, the
person's session keeping the rest; 30 s each, 2026-11-15):

| app_server's loop | Waited for a processor | Worst 50 ms | Heartbeat latest |
|---|---|---|---|
| nice 0 | 61 ms | 4.8 ms | 3.45 ms |
| realtime | 0.1 ms | 0.03 ms | 0.34 ms |
| realtime, on a kept core (CPU 11) | 0.6 ms | 0.01 ms | 0.27 ms |

Realtime alone takes the waiting away, under any scheduler; the kept
core adds nothing measurable to that here. What it adds is beside the
waiting: the loop's frames on the fastest core at its full clock, its
caches its own, and a core free when other realtime work (PipeWire's at
20, other programs' sound) is on the rest.

**The GPU has priorities too**, and they are not what they seem
(measured 2026-11-20, on Intel's xe, Linux 7.2, Mesa's iris and anv;
`tools/dev/gpu-priority-check` measures them again, and with `asked`,
as root, shows what each program really asks the driver for):

- **Nothing of Olo's asks for less than the ordinary priority, ever.**
  The firmware's scheduler (GuC) runs strictly by priority: a queue
  below ordinary gets the GPU only when no ordinary queue has work. One
  ordinary program kept the GPU busy for 2.0 s and a low context's
  0.2 ms draw waited 2012 ms, all of it (12 ms at the ordinary
  priority). And xe takes a job that hasn't started five seconds after
  it was handed over for the firmware having failed, and resets the
  whole GPU (`check_timeout` in xe_guc_submit.c: "GuC never scheduled
  this job - let the caller trigger a GT reset"); the reset then times
  out other programs' work in flight, a dozen and more: their Vulkan
  device is lost and the kit starts them again, with the person's
  screen still meanwhile. From 2026-11-15 a headless app_server (an
  agent's screen, a test session) asked EGL for Low, and a kit program
  on an agent's screen for Vulkan's lowest global priority, so that
  agents' screens drew after the person's desktop. On 2026-11-20 that
  reset the person's GPU fifteen times, each time under a push's live
  lint, each begun by a headless app_server's job "not started" (Ben:
  "something is really broken my desktop is lagging", "deskbar keeps
  crashing"). A headless one asks Medium now (`headless::gpu_priority`,
  with a test), and the kit asks nothing (blade's Olo change for it is
  gone).
- **What a context is granted isn't what EGL says.** The person's
  app_server asks for High (udev.rs) and EGL reports High; Intel's
  drivers grant it only to a process with CAP_SYS_NICE
  (`xe_exec_queue_device_get_max_priority`), Mesa finds that out and
  asks the kernel for the ordinary priority instead, silently. Seen
  from the kernel, the person's desktop has drawn at the ordinary
  priority all along. With the capability it is granted (2), and beside
  six ordinary programs drawing a probe's draws waited 22 ms at the
  99th percentile where an ordinary one's waited 49 (TODO: the
  capability from Olo's login, to the person's app_server alone).
- `OLO_REALTIME=1` on a headless one asks High as the person's does,
  to measure.

**One Vulkan driver, handed to the loader** (vendor/blade-graphics,
`vulkan/direct.rs`; Olo's change to it). The Vulkan loader finds its
drivers by loading every one installed and asking each what it has:
on a desktop with Mesa a dozen libraries, and NVIDIA's where its
driver is installed, which wakes its card to answer (2.3 s a start on
a ThinkPad P1 Gen 9 whose card slept, 2026-11-04, and the card kept
awake for a GPU the program never draws with). Olo first kept
NVIDIA's out with the loader's own variable, set while the context is
made (`VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE`), where there was a DRM card of
NVIDIA's beside another. That told NVIDIA's card by its DRM card, and
on 2026-11-20, with its display module stuck unloading and that card
gone, every program loaded NVIDIA's driver again, for a card that no
longer answered: a window 684 ms after its program started, and the
kit's tests crashed in NVIDIA's library as they exited.

A program is given the one driver of the GPU it draws on instead, the
one the computer started on (the device the renderer always took
first), which depends on nothing else that is installed: its kernel
driver read from sysfs (`boot_driver`: the card whose device says
`boot_vga`, or the only card), the Vulkan driver's library for it
found in the loader's own manifests (`libraries_of`, `installed`:
Mesa's by kernel driver; two for i915, where the GPU's generation
decides and each driver knows its own; not NVIDIA's own driver,
untried on a computer that draws with it: there the loader does as it
always did), loaded, and handed to the loader with
`VK_LUNARG_direct_driver_loading`, exclusively: the loader then loads
no other. What the driver has is asked of the driver (the loader
can't say before the instance exists, and asking the loader is what
loads every driver). The library is asked for the loader's interface
first, as the loader would ask (version 7, which handing a driver over
needs), and the manifests are read as the loader reads them (JSON,
`ICD.library_path`, the library's bits, every candidate kept until one
loads).

Where it steps aside (`find` says None), the loader does as it always
did: the person or the compositor chose a device or drivers
themselves (a loader variable, as a test session's lavapipe; PRIME
offload, `__NV_PRIME_RENDER_OFFLOAD=1`; Mesa's device selection; a
render node named for the session, `ANVIL_DRM_DEVICE`,
`OLO_RENDER_NODE`); a device forced by its id; the program runs with
privilege or in a Flatpak, or the loader has a settings file (the
loader's to decide then); a loader from before it took drivers
(`loader_takes_drivers`: 1.3.240; an older one loads every driver
while refusing); no one GPU the computer started on; a kernel driver
not in the table; no manifest for it; a library that won't load or
doesn't speak the interface. Where it was tried and came to nothing
(the instance can't be made, or has no device that will do: one with
none is destroyed now, and so is one whose device can't be made), on
a computer with a card of NVIDIA's beside the GPU it started on
(`needs_scoped_retry`), Mesa's software driver is handed over the
same way (`software`: slow, and it draws), since the loader's own
search there is what loads NVIDIA's driver; on any other computer,
the loader's own search, as before. **No variable is set in the
running program any more** (the older filter set and took back
`VK_LOADER_DRIVERS_DISABLE` around the context's making: whatever
else read the environment or started a child meanwhile saw it).
`OLO_VULKAN_SOFTWARE=1` has one program drawn by Mesa's software
driver, to tell a fault of the GPU's driver from one of Olo's. The
log says which way was gone ("Vulkan: libvulkan_intel.so alone,
handed to the loader directly").

What it is on trust for, and what it doesn't do (Astra's review,
2026-11-20, /var/tmp/claude-blueferry/review2/answer.md): it was
tried on Intel's driver and on lavapipe; RADV and the rest of Mesa's
speak the same interface by their source, untried here. The GPU the
computer started on is not always the one the compositor draws with
(a mux, an external GPU, a render node chosen for the session):
where one of those is said in the environment it steps aside, and
the compositor's own answer (`Request::Gpus`) is what it should go
by (TODO). And Mesa's Intel driver itself opens every DRM render
node there is to see whose it is, NVIDIA's among them, before it
looks at the vendor (the loader's way did the same): whether that
wakes a sleeping card isn't known, and the mend is Mesa's (a patch
is drafted: TODO).

Chrome, which Olo starts with NVIDIA's drivers left out
(`olo_kit_base::gpu::asleep_env`: the loader's variable and glvnd's,
given to the child as it is started), now knows NVIDIA's card from
the PCI bus too, beside a GPU the computer started on that has a
render node, and sets each of the two unless the person set that one
themselves.

Measured (2026-11-20, release builds, a test session on the GPU, ten
starts each, the two builds in turn, a load of 18; the build before
with NVIDIA's driver left out, as it was on a healthy computer):
DeskCalc's window is listed by app_server 23 ms after it starts where
it took 55 (the least 20 where 47), StyledEdit's 30 where 58 (to the
window's being there, not to its first picture on the screen); a program has 3 MB
less of its own written to (10 and 13 MB where 13 and 16) and 28 MB
less resident, lavapipe and LLVM no longer mapped beside the driver
in use (shared between programs, so each one's share is as it was);
a start's processor time is as it was. Against the state of that
afternoon, NVIDIA's driver loaded for a dead card: 71 and 49 ms
where 684 and 339.

**Groups' weights.** The processor is shared between sibling cgroups by
weight first. Fedora's uresourced raises the active user's manager
(`user@UID.service`, where GNOME's shell runs) to 500; Olo runs in
logind's scope for the session (`session-N.scope`: app_server, every
app, the terminal's jobs), at 100. Whatever ran as a service of the
person's (a browser's scope, a build service, kache's daemon) had five
times the whole desktop's share, and no nice reached it. Olo Doctor's
"Give the Desktop Its Share" gives every session's scope the manager's
weight (`/etc/systemd/system/session-.scope.d/50-olo-weight.conf`, and
this session's cgroup now); the supervisor lowers a build service as a
whole (below).

`tools/dev/loadtest HOME SECONDS [--cpus 4-11] [--burners N] [--kept
CPU] [--session NAME]` measures a test session (`OLO_REALTIME=1
tsession start NAME --home HOME` for a realtime one; an animating client
in it): its loop's run-queue waits every 50 ms, the heartbeat's
lateness and its slowest step, with burners like a build's beside it on
`--cpus` only, so the person's session keeps the rest of the computer.

## The scheduler (`scx_lavd`, tools/build-scheduler.sh)

Which scheduler the computer runs under is the person's to choose
(Ben, 2026-11-10: "add to olo the ability to pick a custom scheduler in
preferences -> performance and the recommendation should be scx_lavd
and if the user enables it then olo should handle installing"): the
kernel's own (EEVDF), or LAVD, `scx_lavd` of sched-ext/scx (GPL-2.0;
the Latency-criticality Aware Virtual Deadline scheduler), loaded over
the kernel's through sched_ext (Linux 6.12 and later). LAVD is made
for a computer someone is sitting at: what it judges is being waited
for runs first, long work around it. If it stops, or the kernel puts it
out, the kernel's own takes over again by itself.

The kernel's own is the one recommended now (2026-11-15). Measured under
others' builds and a GPU job, app_server's loop (at nice −10) waited on
a run queue 23.8 s of 80 under LAVD, which gives a nice little weight,
and 8.3 s under the kernel's own; Ben went back to the kernel's. Olo's
threads someone waits on are realtime since ("Realtime threads and the
kept core"), above either scheduler's normal threads, so what the
scheduler decides is how the rest share what's left.

It is built as the fans' profile is, in the same three parts:

- `olo_system::scheduler` reads what there is, as anyone: whether the
  kernel can load one at all (`look` is None without
  `/sys/kernel/sched_ext`), what starts with the computer (LAVD when
  its program and unit are installed and systemd's link to the unit
  is there, `multi-user.target.wants/olo-scheduler.service`), and what
  is loaded now, whoever loaded it (`state`, `root/ops`: "Now: LAVD
  1.1.4 is scheduling."; another's is named and said to be not Olo's;
  chosen but not loaded is said, with where to look).
- Olo Doctor sets it (`apps/doctor/src/scheduler.rs`):
  `olo-doctor --scheduler` says what there is, `olo-doctor
  --scheduler kernel|lavd` sets it, through the helper and pkexec, in
  the person's own session only. LAVD: the `olo-scx-lavd` beside
  Doctor copied to `/usr/local/libexec/olo/scx_lavd` (a root service
  must not run a file the person can write), its unit
  (`data/systemd/olo-scheduler.service`, carried in the program),
  enabled, and started (again, if either changed). With no
  `olo-scx-lavd` beside Doctor, root's copy serves if there is one;
  else it says LAVD isn't with this copy of Olo. The kernel's own:
  the unit disabled and stopped (LAVD unloads itself as it ends), its
  parts left for the next time.
- Preferences ▸ Performance has a Scheduler tab: the two as radio
  buttons, each with what it's for, what is scheduling now (read
  again every five seconds while the panel is open), and that it's
  the computer's, so choosing asks for an administrator's password
  ("Setting it…", the buttons dimmed; refused or failed, back on
  what's in force with why in red). Where the kernel can't load one
  the tab says so. `olo-preferences performance --tab Scheduler`
  opens it there.

**The program isn't Olo's and isn't in Olo's workspace.**
`tools/build-scheduler.sh` builds one named version (1.1.4) from its
published source (`cargo install --locked`, with the lock file it was
published with: it carries its own libbpf and vmlinux.h, and wants
clang and libelf's headers, which tools/setup.sh installs) and puts it
in `target/release` as `olo-scx-lavd`, so what carries Olo's programs
carries it: tools/install-session.sh and an upgrade from the Deskbar.
Nothing runs it from there. Two minutes the first time (1 min 47 s
here), and 4 GB while it builds (removed after); nothing when that
version is built already. Olo builds and runs without it. A release doesn't carry it
(`tools/release.sh` leaves it out): a GPL program is passed on with
its source, which is the publisher's to arrange (TODO).

`OLO_SCHEDULER_ROOT=DIR` puts every one of those places under DIR,
for tests: a made-up kernel is one file (`sys/kernel/sched_ext/state`
holding `disabled`), Doctor writes its steps there as the person (an
empty file stands for systemd's link), and `state` and `root/ops`
written by hand show in the panel. The whole of it was driven so
(2026-11-12): LAVD chosen from the panel (the built program, the unit
and the link under DIR), chosen-but-not-loaded said, then loaded,
the kernel's own again; the tab reviewed at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75×
and 2×, light and dark. **Never choose a scheduler on the real
computer from a test**: it is the whole machine's, and everything
running on it (the person's work, every measurement) changes with it.

## Olo Doctor (apps/doctor)

Looks the computer over for what gets in Olo's way, and for what Olo
suggests for the best of it (below: once an app of its own, Olo
Suggestions, folded in on 2026-11-14: Ben, "just have it be one unified
olo doctor app where each item has a type showing whether it's e.g. a
suggestion or something critical and any of them can be put on the
ignored list"), and fixes or applies each with a button: each finding's
own, or one for all that's checked (one password for everything that
needs root).

**A fix under way says how it goes** (`app.rs`: `status`, `still`).
Beside its card's buttons: what it is doing, as its steps say; "Waiting
for another fix to finish…" where another fix as the administrator is
ahead of it (the helper does them one at a time); and how long it has
been at it once that is 15 seconds ("Installing kernel (40 s)", by
five seconds, then by the minute: a count that moved every few seconds
would move the words' wrap). The header says the same of the longest
("Fixing… (3 min)"), for a card out of sight. And a fix run as the
administrator that has been at it three minutes says, on a line of
its own under the finding's words, that it is still going, that other
fixes wait until it's done, and that if it never finishes restarting
the computer stops it. Those are the fixes that call into the system,
and one of them never came back (2026-11-20, a driver's unload: "A
graphics card that stopped answering"): the window said "Fixing…" for
hours, under a finding whose own fix was only waiting behind it. Told
again by a timer only while a fix is under way (five seconds, then
twenty). `OLO_DOCTOR_DEMO=slow` makes the demo's fixes take four
minutes and say what they do, to look at it. What is not done: the
fixes still go one at a time, so one that never returns holds the
rest (TODO).

Every finding has a kind (`Severity`, its tag's word `label()`):
**Critical** (something the person relies on doesn't work or is at risk
now: the last backup not whole, no driver for the built-in sound),
**Problem** (gets in Olo's way now), **Recommended** (`Advice`: better
changed) and **Suggestion** (none of it needed: `suggest.rs`).
`checks::look` takes the checks' report and the suggestions' as one
(`Report::merge`), sets aside what's ignored and lists the most pressing
first (`Report::sort`, by kind, each kind in the order found). The
window (`app.rs`) says what was found by kind at the top ("1 critical, 2
problems, 1 recommendation and 2 suggestions.", how many things were
looked at, fine and ignored), then one list on a card gutter: a card per
finding, its kind's `Tag` (red, orange, blue, green) level with its
title, what it is, and under it Ignore (a quiet link) and its fix (the
button), with how the fix goes or why it failed (Try Again) at the left;
at its top left, before the tag, a check box (`CheckBox::mark_only`,
named by its title, id `choose-ID`; a finding with no fix keeps its
room, so the tags line up; a fix that is never done with the others,
`Fix::batchable`, has its mark greyed, with a tip saying so: the room
left empty read as a mark that hadn't drawn). A finding's words may be
paragraphs (a blank line between them in `detail`): the card sets them
`metrics::TIGHT` apart, half a line, so the room over the buttons stays
the largest in the card.
Then three latches (`PaneSwitch`), each over a card of lines: Fixed (this
time; open), As It Should Be (folded while anything is found: it's the
long part; open when nothing is; what's applied can be undone from its
line) and Ignored (folded: it isn't to draw attention). Check Again and
the button for what's checked are under the list, as a dialog's
buttons: the kit's pattern for acting on what's chosen
(`olo_kit::chosen`, "Acting on what's chosen" above; Ben, 2026-11-14:
"the fix all button only fixes all problems but there's no way to
apply all suggestions. we need a way to do both and either/or"). The
problems (Critical, Problem, Recommended: kind
`NEEDED`, "Fix") start checked, the suggestions (`SUGGESTED`, "Apply")
don't; what the person checks is kept (`Chosen`, in the saved state,
for findings still listed). "Choose: All · Problems · Suggestions ·
None" checks every one of them, of a kind, or none, and the default
button does what's checked and says so: "Fix 2 Problems", "Apply 1
Suggestion", "Fix 2 and Apply 3" (⇧⌘F, `fix-all`; dimmed with nothing
checked). The Fix menu has the same (`chosen::menu`): the button's
item, Choose All (⌘A, Doctor's `choose-all` in `app_keys`), Choose
Problems, Choose Suggestions, Choose None. A finding being fixed is
out of what's chosen and its box dimmed until it's done. Which latches
are open, and what's checked, come back after an upgrade. `OLO_DOCTOR_DEMO=1`
(`demo.rs`) shows a made-up report, one of every kind, a fine list with
an undo, an ignored finding, without looking at the computer it runs on
or telling its Deskbar; its fixes change nothing (one fails, to show a
failure), so the window can be tried headless.

`checks.rs` finds; each `Finding` carries its `Fix` as
`Step`s (`fix.rs`: write a file, set a sysfs knob, remove a file, start,
stop, enable or disable a system unit through `olo_system::systemd`,
signal a process), all done in process. From a terminal or an agent:
`olo-doctor --report` (the findings as JSON, each with its `severity`),
`olo-doctor --fix` (those with a fix, by id, each with its kind, and
what can be undone), `olo-doctor --fix all|suggestions|ID…` (what the
buttons do: `all` is what's checked to begin with, every finding's fix
but the suggestions', `suggestions` every suggestion; root
steps through the helper and pkexec, or, under sudo, run there with the
scan made for the sudo user), `olo-doctor --fans [auto|cool]` (the fan
profile: "The fans", above), `olo-doctor --scheduler [kernel|lavd]`
("The scheduler", above).

**Everything it does can be undone** (applied.rs; Ben, 2026-11-16:
"everything in olo doctor that it does must be reversible, e.g. for any
fix/suggestion applied i should be able to undo/restore to the previous
behavior"). Each step says, just before it runs, what puts back what
it's about to change (`Step::inverse`, asked by whoever runs the step:
the root helper for root's files, which only it can read): a file's
words as they were (or the file removed, if it wasn't there; a program
or a picture copied back from a kept copy, root's under
/var/lib/olo/doctor/kept), a unit stopped that it started and started
that it stopped, enabled or not as it was, a sysfs value, a kernel
argument, a login shell, the packages it added removed and those it
removed added, a folder it made removed if still empty. What only makes
a change take effect (systemd reading its files again, a service
started again, NetworkManager's settings read, the start-up images
made) is done again after everything is put back, once
(`fix::undo_of`: put back last-changed-first, then those). What can't
be put back is said, in the step's own words (an update of packages; a
kept build removed; a repository's release package), and what changes
nothing that stays (a process ended, hardware started again) has
nothing to undo. The helper answers with the undo of the steps that ran
(`FromHelper::Done`'s `undo` and `kept`), and it's kept with Doctor's
state (`~/.local/state/olo/doctor/applied.json`: the finding, its
title, the button's words, when, the steps). The window lists them
under **Fixed**, each with when and what undoing does, and **Undo**;
`olo-doctor --fix` lists them as `applied:ID`, and `--fix applied:ID`
undoes one. Undone, an entry goes; one whose finding is found again
goes too (the fix isn't in force), as does one a suggestion has an undo
of its own for. A fix that fails part way keeps the undo of the steps
that ran. Tested on files (applied, undone: as they were), in the
helper's protocol, and in the window against a made-up entry. Fixes
applied before this (2026-11-17) left nothing to undo by.

What it looks for:

- **DiskBackup** (`diskbackup`, from its settings and its service's
  state file): not set up ("Nothing is backed up": said, no button,
  since where backups go is the person's to choose); its service not
  running (a problem: Start It); paused (Resume Backups); nothing whole
  for three days or three of its intervals (a problem, the last's reason
  said: Back Up Now); the last backup not whole (critical: what's
  backed up may not come back; Back Up Now); its key only in this
  computer's keyring (Keep Key
  in Passwords); else when it last backed up, as fine. Each fix is
  DiskBackup's own command line (`Step::StartProgram`: one of Olo's
  programs, `olo-…`, started as the person, never as root).
- **Input remappers** (keyd, xremap, Input Remapper, evremap, kmonad,
  Interception Tools): they grab the keyboards, and any mouse whose motion
  node has keys (a Logitech G309), and type through a virtual device, so
  Olo's key mapping and its per-mouse settings never reach them. Fixed by
  stopping and disabling the unit (or signalling a copy started by hand);
  one installed by hand under /usr/local is removed too (its /etc
  configuration is left).
- **Another desktop's daemons** in this session (GNOME Shell, Mutter,
  KWin, gsd-*): quit. Never another login's: a desktop shell of this user
  in another `session-N.scope` means that desktop is logged in there, and
  everything of it is its own.
- **GNOME's services Olo has its own in place of** (`GNOME_SERVICES`:
  dconf-service, GNOME's and GTK's portal backends, gvfs's daemons and
  volume monitors, GNOME Online Accounts, and GNOME Keyring while Olo's
  keyring answers), running in this session or as the user's services
  (not when GNOME is logged in elsewhere, nor an agent screen's:
  `OLO_SCREEN` in its environment, `on_a_screen`, its own session's,
  which starts its services again; the same for another desktop's
  daemons and old versions): advice, quit by the fix (what
  asks for dconf, a portal or the keyring reaches Olo's). None, and
  nothing of another desktop either: "Nothing of GNOME's runs".
- **USB input devices allowed to sleep** (an interface of class 03 with
  an input node under it, a receiver's paired devices a level down;
  `power/control` not `on`), and **Olo's udev rules** (95-olo-input,
  70-olo-displays; the Doctor carries them with `include_str!`) missing or
  out of date: installed and applied to what is plugged in now.
  The input rule is numbered to come *after* the smart-card readers'
  (`92_pcscd_ccid.rules`), and applies at every event of the device,
  not only as its interfaces come: that rule turns autosuspend on for
  anything with a smart-card interface when the device's driver
  binds, which the kernel says after the interfaces, so a YubiKey (a
  keyboard, a FIDO device and a smart card) was back to `auto` at
  every start and every plugging in, whatever Olo's rule (then
  71-olo-input) had set, and Doctor's fix lasted a day (`udevadm test
  --action=bind /sys/bus/usb/devices/PORT` shows which rule writes
  what, changing nothing). Where it was is taken away as the new one
  goes in.
- **A fix lasts.** What Doctor fixes stays fixed through a restart and
  a replugging, with nothing to press again (Ben, 2026-11-10, of a
  finding back after every reboot: "olo should just set ephemeral
  stuff like that as needed on startup"): a fix installs what makes
  the thing so (a rule, a unit, a file, a daemon told to remember),
  and writes today's value only beside that. `Step::WriteSysfs`
  alone is for nothing; it says so. Every fix was gone through
  (2026-11-12): three didn't last, the security key's (above), the
  Thunderbolt 5 ports' USB (below) and a Thunderbolt device let in
  (boltd is told to remember it, `Step::AllowThunderbolt`, where the
  kernel's `authorized` was written for the once).
- **rtkit** not running (the supervisor's priority tiers need it).
- **Your own services get five times the desktop's share of the
  processor** (a problem, where the login session's scope weighs less
  than the person's manager, `user@UID.service`, which uresourced raises
  to 500): Give the Desktop Its Share writes
  `/etc/systemd/system/session-.scope.d/50-olo-weight.conf` (every
  session's scope at the manager's weight, CPU and I/O) and this
  session's cgroup's `cpu.weight` and `io.weight` now.
- **Builds can't be kept apart from the desktop** (advice, where the
  drop-in that has systemd leave a login session's scope to what Olo's
  login makes in it isn't written): Let Olo Divide Sessions writes
  `/etc/systemd/system/session-.scope.d/50-olo-groups.conf`
  (`Delegate=cpu memory`), in force for sessions started after it.
  Fine, and said to be for the next login, once it is written; fine in
  a session that is divided and whose programs are in its desktop
  group.
- **Allow this account to request high GPU priority** is an individual
  administrator action on Intel systems. Doctor reports the configured
  UID and the running seat compositor's credentials separately. The
  graphics driver determines the actual queue priority.
- **The system's services can run on the window server's core**
  (advice, with the kept core on and systemd's drop-in missing or for
  another core): Keep Them Off writes it and moves what runs now
  (`apps/doctor/src/kept_core.rs`); with the kept core turned off and
  the drop-in still there, Let Them Back removes it.
- **Bluetooth not listening for the AirPods** (only with AirPods
  paired): BlueZ started without its experimental interfaces, where its
  advertisement monitor is. Fixed by a drop-in
  (`/etc/systemd/system/bluetooth.service.d/olo.conf`, `--experimental`)
  and Bluetooth restarted.
- **A USB 2 device in a Thunderbolt 5 port may go unseen** (advice, where
  Intel's Barlow Ridge USB controller, 8086:5782, is present): Ben's
  YubiKey in such a port wasn't seen at all (2026-11-04; the kernel heard
  nothing) while USB 3 drives were and the key worked in another port.
  It says to use another port meanwhile, and Keep It Awake installs
  `75-olo-thunderbolt-usb.rules` (the controller's and its root hubs'
  `power/control` `on` at every start) and writes them now, so
  plugging the device in again tells whether the sleeping controller
  misses the plug; once awake, it's fine, and Let It Sleep (the way
  back) takes the rule away.
- **Voice processing's sound not realtime**: a voice service's PipeWire
  thread that rtkit refused (its processes-per-user limit reached).
  Fixed by an rtkit drop-in (`/etc/systemd/system/rtkit-daemon.service.d/olo.conf`:
  64 processes, 256 threads a user), systemd reloaded, rtkit restarted;
  then Doctor itself, as the person (rtkit gives only to a thread's own
  user), asks it again for those threads before it looks
  (`checks::after_fix`, a fix's after-step, off the UI thread). Left to
  the supervisor's retry a minute on, the look just after the fix still
  found them refused and the finding came back after "Fixed.".
- **Frames kept off the fast cores**: `kernel.sched_util_clamp_min`
  below 1024 caps the `uclamp.min` app_server's and the windows' threads
  ask for (rule 9): set to 1024, now and at boot (/etc/sysctl.d/
  80-olo-uclamp.conf); a kernel without `CONFIG_UCLAMP_TASK` is advice.
- **Olo programs on an old version** (their `exe` is a replaced file in
  ~/.local/bin; never the session, app_server or the proxies): quit. Not
  one finishing what it has before it goes (`finishing`: marked in
  `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-upgrade-waits`, the mark no older than the
  process, as olo-session leaves it): Quit Them stopped Token Pool's
  copy the session follows while it streamed its last answers after an
  upgrade, which left Token Pool running twice for two days (Ben,
  2026-11-07). Nor one another program started
  (`olo_system::procs::started_by_another`, the session's own rule: a
  command in a shell, an agent's tool), which ends with what it's doing
  and which nothing would start again: those are said among what's
  fine, each with who started it.
- **Token Pool running twice, or without its gateway** (`token_pool`:
  this session's olo-pool processes on the gateway's port, `OLO_POOL_PORT`
  or 17891, and which of them hold its listening socket, by
  `olo_system::listening`). A copy that serves nothing beside the one
  that serves ("Token Pool is running twice", its window showing no
  requests and taking the launches): Quit It (the session starts it
  again, and it keeps the one serving). None serving: "Token Pool's
  gateway isn't running", Start It Again (the same signal). Another
  program on the port: said, no button. Never the keeper
  (`OLO_POOL_KEEPER` in its environment), a copy finishing after handing
  over, a launch younger than 15 s, the command line's own (`--status`),
  nor one on a port of its own (a test's). Else which serves, as fine.
- **Software can't be installed here** (`package_services`, on Fedora):
  PackageKit or dnf's service (`dnf5daemon-server`) missing, as on a
  minimal Fedora, so Olo's fixes that install something and OS Updates
  can't; a problem; Install Them puts them in place with Fedora's own
  dnf, this once (`Step::InstallPackageServices`; every package step
  does it first where they're missing).
- **The build cache** (`kache`, where kache is used: its store,
  `~/.cache/kache`, there). Its daemon not running (no `kache-engine
  daemon` process of this user's) with its service installed
  (`~/.config/systemd/user/kache.service`): "The build cache isn't
  running", advice, Start It (`olo-kache --start`: the unit started over
  systemd's D-Bus). Running, its last clean-up (`gc_stats.json`) held
  back more than its limit by builds' target folders (`bytes_held`; the
  limit its settings' `local_max_size`, else as kache sets it, 5% of the
  store's disk from 5 to 100 GiB; only from a clean-up that looked at
  entries): "The build cache can't keep under its limit", advice, Open
  Kache; no clean-up takes those while the
  folders are there (counting them toward the limit only evicts others
  harder). Else running, as fine.
- **The login screen's entry** (/usr/share/wayland-sessions, or
  /usr/local/share's on an atomic system) missing or pointing at
  nothing.
- **Olo's own login screen** (`own_login_screen`, where Olo's build has
  olo-login and olo-greeter; not on an atomic Fedora, whose /etc and
  /usr/local Setup doesn't change; Ben, 2026-11-07: "the login screen
  should come up in olo doctor as something it can do for me"):
  another display manager's (`display-manager.service`'s link,
  `login_screen::display_manager`) is advice, "The login screen is
  GNOME's (GDM), not Olo's own", and Use Olo's Login Screen runs what
  the Installer's login-screen stage runs (`login_screen::steps`, the one
  list both use: programs copied to /usr/local/libexec/olo, data to
  /usr/local/share/olo, PAM, `pam_olo_keyring.so`, sysusers and
  tmpfiles, its user and folders, SELinux's labels, its unit, the other
  disabled and olo-login enabled), from the next start. Olo's already:
  fine, with Go Back to GDM (or SDDM) beside it as its undo
  (`login:own-undo`), unless a copy in libexec is older than the build
  in ~/.local/bin (an upgrade replaces those, not the copies:
  `login_screen::stale`), which is advice, Update the Login Screen
  (`login:own-older`).
- **Olo's start-up screen as the computer starts** (`start_up_screen`;
  suggestion, Use Olo's Start-Up Screen; out of date, Update It; not in
  the start-up image, Make It Again; fine, Use the One Before) and
  **Olo's chime as the computer starts** (`start_up_chime`; suggestion,
  Play It as the Computer Starts; an older copy, Update It; fine, Play
  It as You Log In): "The login screen and boot splash" has both.
- **Olo's Wi-Fi healer** (below) missing, out of date or stopped, on a
  machine whose Wi-Fi chip needs it (brcmfmac): installed as a root-owned
  copy, with its unit and NetworkManager's setting for the chip.
- **A second graphics card kept awake** (NVIDIA's, AMD's, not the one
  the computer started on; `power/control` "on", as it stays with no
  driver: nouveau failing on a new card): Let It Sleep installs
  `data/udev/72-olo-idle-gpu.rules` (runtime power management for such
  cards, at every start) and sets it now. On the ThinkPad P1 Gen 9 the
  RTX PRO 2000 went from D0 to D3cold.
- **NVIDIA's console on cards with no display** (`nvidia_console`:
  `nvidia_drm`'s `fbdev` reads Y, as it comes, on a laptop's second
  card, there to compute). The console shows nothing there, and
  giving it up as the module unloads is one place the driver can wait
  for ever on a card that stopped answering (below; not the only
  one, and nothing to do with why a card stops answering: the words
  claim no more). Recommended, Turn Off the Console:
  `/etc/modprobe.d/olo-nvidia-console.conf` (`options nvidia_drm
  fbdev=0`: the module's option, so for every card of NVIDIA's at
  once), read as the module loads, so from the next start. Offered
  only on what is known for certain: the module loaded and running
  with modesetting (one on its way out has taken its cards' DRM
  devices away already, and nothing can be told of them: it was
  first offered in exactly that state, from a card whose connectors
  could no longer be read); every display device of NVIDIA's its
  driver's, not the one the computer started on, with a DRM card of
  its own and no connector on it (one that can't be read isn't
