  known); another display device the computer did start on. Then
  the running module's own word decides: off, fine; the option kept
  since this start, fine, "from the next start"; kept from before
  this start and still on, said ("isn't in force": another option
  says otherwise, or the driver is loaded from the start-up image).
- **Olo's own build of NVIDIA's modules** (`olo-nvidia`, apps/nvidia;
  the patches, the designs and what was shown of them are in
  kernel/nvidia, its README first): **a prototype, held.** It fetches
  NVIDIA's source by hash, applies the prevention patches at their
  exact lines, compiles as a user with no privilege, and checks what
  it built against the stock set; `status --json` says, for each
  kernel, which set is chosen and which is loaded, by build ID. It
  refuses to change a real root or to run as root: Astra's review
  found that the way it made its set the chosen one (a folder under
  `updates/` and an index from depmod) could publish an index with
  other drivers missing, kept the version rule only when its check
  ran, and could be undone by any other depmod. That part is being
  designed again (README, "The builder"). Its tests run under a
  made-up root (`OLO_NVIDIA_ROOT`, as the program itself takes it);
  those that compare with NVIDIA's source take checkouts from
  `OLO_NVIDIA_BASELINE` and `OLO_NVIDIA_PATCHED` and are skipped
  without them. Nothing of it touches the running driver, and nothing
  is installed or loaded on the person's card without their word.
- **A graphics card that stopped answering** (`gpu_stuck`: its
  `power/runtime_status` "error", the kernel's word for power
  management that failed, its driver not answering after: NVIDIA's
  when memory ran short while it suspended, 2026-11-07 and
  2026-11-20). Said, with what brings it back, a restart of the
  computer, and **no fix: Olo doesn't start such a card again in
  place.** It did (Ben, 2026-11-07: "i don't want you to restart the
  machine just fix the card/driver or whatever"): the programs with
  its nodes open quit, the services that hold it stopped, NVIDIA's
  modules unloaded, the card reset and found on the bus again, its
  driver loaded. That worked once. On 2026-11-20 the first unload
  (`delete_module("nvidia_drm")`) never came back: NVIDIA's display
  module, giving up a console it had taken on a card that drives no
  display, programs the card's display engine and waits for it to
  take the commands (`nvEvoMakeRoom`), with no time limit, no look
  at a signal, and its own lock held; the card's firmware had been
  told to stop by the failed suspend and took nothing. From there
  nothing ends it but a restart: the module stays "going" (it can't
  be loaded again, and what it uses can't be unloaded), the thread
  spins on a processor and can't be killed, the computer can't sleep
  (the thread never freezes), and Doctor's helper, which made the
  call, said "Fixing…" for ever. Read against the driver's source
  and the kernel's (an investigation with Astra at max,
  2026-11-20): no other order is safe either. A reset under the
  bound driver leaves its objects pointing at a reset chip;
  unbinding or removing the device waits without limit on a
  reference the stuck teardown holds; a live patch can't reach a
  thread already inside the loop, and the loop is in NVIDIA's
  prelinked core, which has no entry to patch at; and nothing that
  can be read beforehand (the PCI state, the driver's link, NVML's
  cache) tells the state that hangs from the one that doesn't. So
  the finding offers nothing, and says why, in the kernel's terms
  ("The NVIDIA graphics card's power management failed": that state
  alone doesn't say every use of the card is gone, nor that a restart
  is sure to mend it). A module of NVIDIA's that stays on its way
  out (`/sys/module/NAME/initstate` "going", and still so three
  seconds on: every unload passes through "going" for a moment) is
  said as "NVIDIA's graphics driver is stuck", by the module's name,
  with what it costs until the restart: the card can't be used, a
  processor may stay busy, and putting the computer to sleep may
  fail or hang (the stuck thread can't be frozen, and NVIDIA's own
  preparation for sleep waits, with no limit, for a lock it holds).
  `Step::RestartGpu` is kept only to be refused: a request holding
  it (a Doctor window from before an upgrade) is turned down whole,
  before its first step (`fix::refused`: the old request quit the
  card's programs first). What would make an in-place restart
  possible is in the driver, not in the order of calls: docs/TODO.md,
  "The NVIDIA card stopped answering". A stuck thread like that one
  can be put out of the way meanwhile, not ended: the idle
  scheduling class and one slow core (`chrt --idle -p 0 PID`,
  `taskset -pc CPU PID`: 91% of a performance core to 6% of an
  efficiency core at a load of 22, as it was seen then, not a cap); a
  CPU quota does nothing to it,
  since this kernel throttles a thread only as it returns to user
  space (kernel/sched/fair.c, `throttle_cfs_rq_work`), which it
  never does.
- **A graphics card with no working driver** (NVIDIA's, no driver
  bound; nouveau loaded and gone says it tried): NVIDIA's driver
  (`akmod-nvidia`, built for each kernel) installed from the system's
  repositories when one has it (Fedora's NVIDIA repository, RPM
  Fusion's), else what to turn on; with Secure Boot, its key to enrol.
- **Intel graphics that can't decode H.264 and HEVC** (`intel_video`:
  an Intel GPU on Fedora, whose iHD leaves them out, and no full driver
  in `/usr/lib64/dri-nonfree` or `dri-freeworld`): RPM Fusion's
  `intel-media-driver` installed, its free and nonfree repositories
  added first where PackageKit doesn't find it (`Step::InstallRepository`:
  the release package downloaded from mirrors.rpmfusion.org, installed
  as a package file, the lists read again); on an atomic Fedora, what
  to do by hand. Fine once it's there ("Intel graphics decodes every
  video"). Olo's player decodes all four codecs there then
  (`olo_vaapi::decode`).
- **Built-in sound with no driver** (critical: no sound at all, nor
  calls; Intel's SOF bound, no sound card made of it: a new laptop's SoundWire codecs, named from
  `/sys/bus/soundwire/devices`): a newer kernel and firmware installed
  when PackageKit has updates for them (`DRIVER_PACKAGES`: the kernel,
  linux-firmware, alsa-sof, Cirrus and Intel audio firmware, GPU and
  Wi-Fi firmware), else said plainly that there isn't one yet.
- **Temporary files in memory** (`temp_files`, Ben 2026-11-05): /tmp a
  tmpfs (`olo_system::env::in_memory`, statfs) and the session's
  `TMPDIR` (systemd's user manager's, `env::manager_environment`, else
  Doctor's own) unset or in memory too. The fix (not root) writes
  `~/.config/environment.d/60-olo-tmpdir.conf` (`TMPDIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP` =
  /var/tmp; removing it undoes it), which the user manager reads at each
  login, and sets them in the running manager and D-Bus activation
  (`Step::SetSessionEnvironment`) for what starts from now on;
  olo-session takes them from that file as it starts, before any thread
  (`take_tmpdir`), so Deskbar's apps and Terminal's shells have them.
  Programs already running keep theirs until they start again.
- **The power button's helper** (`power_now`, on a computer with an
  ACPI power button, `Power Button` in /sys/class/input): Olo's
  `olo-power-now@.service` and its polkit rule (carried with
  `include_str!` from data/systemd and data/polkit) missing or out of
  date (advice: Install the Helper, Update the Helper): written, and
  systemd reloaded. It's what lets Preferences ▸ Keyboard ▸ Power
  Button's "immediately" restart or shut down at once.

Drivers and firmware come through PackageKit (`olo_system::packages`,
its D-Bus API: resolve, refresh, install, update, install a package
file; each a transaction waited on off the UI thread, its progress
followed): `Step::InstallPackages`, `Step::UpdatePackages` and
`Step::InstallRepository`, run as root by the helper, telling how they go (`Step::run_with`,
`FromHelper::Progress`) under the finding in the window ("Installing
akmod-nvidia: Downloading 42%") and on the command line. `Roots`'
`packages` and `updates` answer for the system's packages (tests: made
up).

Root is reached as Activity Monitor's is: the program run again through
pkexec (`olo-doctor --helper`, JSON lines of `ToHelper::Run { id, steps }`
and `FromHelper::Done`), asked for only in the person's own session;
`OLO_DOCTOR_HELPER=direct|off` as `OLO_ACTIVITY_HELPER`. After a fix the
report is taken again; what was fixed and is gone is listed under Fixed.
Scans run on a thread; nothing is polled: Check Again (⌘R), a fix, or
the app opened again looks again. What can't be found out says nothing,
never a problem: systemd's user manager busy past its 10 s (as it was
while memory ran low on 2026-11-07) left the watcher, started at login
before Doctor's TMPDIR fix, judging by its own environment, and the
tray said "Temporary files take memory" while the window said all was
well (Ben: "seems like some of the checks are flaky"). The session's
TMPDIR is the manager's, else what Olo's environment.d file sets, only
then Doctor's own (`session_tmpdir`); a unit systemd didn't say the
state of (the Wi-Fi healer's, rtkit's) is left until the next look.

`olo-doctor --report` prints the report as JSON (agents, scripts).
`olo-doctor --watch` is one of the real session's services
(`REAL_SHELL`, with no window: it is never a running app in Deskbar):
after 20 s it looks, and every 15 minutes after (Ben: "run periodically
like on startup and then maybe every 15 mins"; a look is a few hundred
milliseconds of a background thread), and a problem not told of before
(critical or not; remembered in `~/.local/state/olo/doctor.json`; one
fixed and back is told again) is told in a notification whose click
opens Olo Doctor, and so is each new suggestion, once ever (below);
then it follows the Wi-Fi healer's report by inotify and tells of each
reset and what came of it (`--notify` is the look alone). Every look
(the watcher's, the window's, the command line's: `checks::look`) writes
what it found that gets in the way, or is recommended and has a fix
(not the suggestions: `tell_tray`;
`olo_protocol::doctor::DoctorFound`, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-doctor-found.json`);
Deskbar follows it by inotify and shows Olo Doctor's bag in the tray
while there is something, a click opening it. Tests build a
machine in a folder (`Roots { fs, bin, uid, scope, units }`) and check
the findings and their steps exactly.

Any finding can be ignored (Ben, 2026-11-07: "each item can be ignored
which puts it into an ignored section and also has a button for each
ignored item to still fix it if the user changes their mind but it
won't alert about ignored items or draw attention to them"): its
Ignore link, before its fix, keeps its id in
`~/.config/olo/doctor-ignored.json` (`ignored.rs`, one list, a
suggestion's id as any other's; the file's old `suggestions` list, from
when Olo Suggestions was an app of its own, is read with it and written
into it at the next change), and every look sets those aside
(`checks::look`: `Report::set_aside` moves them from
`findings` to `ignored`), so the counts, what's checked and Choose,
the tray's bag, the watcher's notifications and `--fix all` leave them
out. The window lists them last, under Ignored, folded: each with its
kind's tag in grey (the tags in one column, so the titles line up), its
title dim, Stop Ignoring (a link under it) and its own fix button, which
fixes it as ever. From a terminal or an agent: `olo-doctor --ignore ID…`
and `--unignore ID…` (with no ids, the ignored listed), and
`--report`'s `ignored`; `--fix` lists them as "ignored" and fixes one
only when it's named. A process list says each program once with its
processes ("GTK's portal backend (xdg-desktop-portal-gtk, processes
1625065 and 1625111)", `by_program`), and the title counts programs:
D-Bus had started GTK's portal backend six times, said six times over.

## Olo Doctor's suggestions (apps/doctor, suggest.rs)

What Olo suggests for the best of it, none of it needed (Olo works the
same without): each with what it does and why, a button that applies it,
a check box to apply it with others (unchecked to begin with: Fix ▸
Choose Suggestions, or the link under the list, checks them all), and,
once applied, a button that
undoes it (its line in As It Should Be). Until 2026-11-14 they were an
app of their own, Olo Suggestions (`olo-suggestions`, the same body by a
`Kind`); now they're findings of kind `Suggestion` in Olo Doctor's one
list, ignorable as any other. A suggestion is a `Finding` whose `Fix`
is applied by the same steps and root helper, what's applied is a
`Fine` with an `Undo` beside it (`Report::undo`, found by
`Report::action` as a fix is), and `olo-doctor --report` and `--fix
[suggestions | ID…]` do from a terminal or an agent what the window does
(an undo only when named). `suggest.rs` has them (`scan`), with
`before` keeping what an apply changes, for its undo. The upgrade takes
the old `olo-suggestions` program away (`upgrade::RETIRED`, and
tools/install-session.sh's list: cargo leaves its last build in the
build tree, which mustn't be installed again).

- **brush as the login shell**: brush (github.com/reubeno/brush), the
  bash-compatible shell in Rust, is built with Olo (`apps/brush`,
  `olo-brush`: `brush_shell::entry::run`, installed and upgraded with
  Olo's programs). Applied as root: Olo's build copied to
  /usr/local/bin/brush, listed in /etc/shells (`Step::AddShell`), tried
  (`Step::TryShell`: it runs `-c 'exit 0'`), and made the login shell
  through AccountsService (`Step::SetLoginShell`,
  `olo_system::accounts::set_shell`); the shell it was is kept first
  (`~/.config/olo/suggestions.json`) for the undo, else bash. A copy
  older than Olo's build is suggested again (Update brush). Terminal
  starts the account's shell as it is now (`pty::shell`: the password
  database first, `$SHELL` from login after), so its next window is
  brush at once.

- **olo-brush's process goes where the shell is**: brush keeps its
  working folder for what it runs, not as its own process's, so its
  `/proc/PID/cwd` stayed where it started, and Terminal (which reads a
  tab's folder there: its repository, worktree and PR, where a new tab
  opens) saw a tab `cd`'d into a worktree as still in its first folder.
  olo-brush's `prompt` hook (vendor/brush-interactive's, called as each
  prompt shows) moves the process there, as other shells move on `cd`.
- **Programs worth having** (`TOOLS`, `tool_list`): just, uv, mise and
  worktrunk (`wt`), each suggested while it's on no folder of PATH nor
  in ~/.local/bin or ~/.cargo/bin (where installers put them, which a
  session's PATH may not have), else said to be installed, and where.
  just and uv come from the system's repositories (`Step::InstallPackages`
  as root, PackageKit); mise and worktrunk, which Fedora doesn't carry,
  from their makers' latest GitHub release (`Step::InstallRelease`, as
  the person, to ~/.local/bin): `releases.rs` asks GitHub's API for the
  latest tag, downloads the asset (`{tag}` filled in: mise's bare
  `mise-{tag}-linux-x64`, worktrunk's `…-unknown-linux-musl.tar.xz`)
  and the SHA-256 its maker published (a SHASUMS256.txt, or the asset's
  own `.sha256`), refuses it if they differ, takes the program out of
  the archive (tar with liblzma or flate2) and puts it in place whole
  (written beside it as `.partial`, 0755, then renamed). Nothing is
  shelled out to; the download's share shows under the suggestion as it
  goes (`Msg::Progress`: a fix run as the person tells how it's going as
  the root helper's does). Olo doesn't take them away again. `cargo test
  -p olo-doctor installs_from_github -- --ignored` installs both, for
  real, into a scratch folder.
- **A build kept from before the kits, removed** (Ben, 2026-11-16:
  "the doctor should handle removing that pre-kits login fallback"): a
  build kept to fall back to (`tools/keep-build.sh`, ~/.local/olo-kept)
  whose login entry says it was made before 2026-11-11, when Olo's own
  kits replaced GPUI, runs GPUI, which is gone for good: suggested for
  removal ("Remove “Olo Desktop (before the kits)” from the login
  screen", its size said), unless it's the session running. As root,
  `Step::RemoveKeptBuild { home, name }` does what `keep-build.sh
  --remove` does and nothing more: the folder `home`/.local/olo-kept/
  `name` (a plain one-word name, not a link; `remove_dir_all` follows
  none inside) and `olo-kept-NAME.desktop` in /usr/share/wayland-sessions
  or /usr/local's, then the kept builds' folder if it was the last.
  Not undone: it's gone.
- **worktrunk's worktrees where Terminal makes them** (with `wt`
  there): its `worktree-path` in ~/.config/worktrunk/config.toml
  (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`'s if set) set to Terminal's place
  (`settings.terminal.worktrees`, asked of app_server) as worktrunk's
  template, `<place>/{{ repo }}/{{ branch | sanitize }}`: the folder
  Terminal's New Worktree… makes for any name it allows (no `/`, so
  `sanitize` changes nothing). Written with toml_edit, the rest of the
  file (comments too) as it was; the value it had is kept in
  suggestions.json for the undo (none: the key taken out again).

Each new suggestion is told once, ever, in a notification from Olo
Doctor (`notify.rs`, the session's `olo-doctor --watch`, from the same
look as the problems), the suggestion box its picture: "Olo has N
suggestions" with their titles, a click (or Show in Olo Doctor) opening
its window. What's
told is remembered by id and title (`Told::suggested` in
~/.local/state/olo/doctor.json, never forgotten, so one not taken isn't
told again, and Update brush after Use brush is), and one with nothing
to apply yet (brush before Olo's build of it) waits until it has. A look
costs under 10 ms, four times an hour.

`--fix` with an id that isn't there (mistyped, or an option it doesn't
take) does nothing at all and exits 1, rather than fixing the ones it
knows.
- **brush's suggestions from Olo's model (olo-complete)**: with
  Preferences ▸ Terminal ▸ Command Suggestions on
  (`~/.config/olo/complete.json` `enabled`, read by brush and the daemon
  with or without Olo's session), the grey hint after what's typed in
  brush is the model's.
  - `crates/complete` (`olo-complete`), the model and its arithmetic:
    `history` reads `.bash_history`/`.brush_history` (with `#<secs>`
    times) and Olo's record (`~/.local/state/olo/complete/
    history.jsonl`: each command with its folder, time and shell);
    `index` keeps per command its counts, folders, hours, weekdays,
    exit statuses, what follows what (one and two back) and each shell's
    last commands, offers the candidates that start with the line
    (at most 32) and gives each 16 features (`FEATURE_NAMES`). `kernels`
    is the model: 16 → 16 (ReLU) → a score, 289 numbers, a candidate's
    softmax over the line's candidates; scalar reference, NEON, AVX2+FMA
    (SSE2 without), each tested against the reference. (A GPU kernel was
    tried and dropped: 258 µs a suggestion through blade against 1 µs in
    NEON.) `Weights::baseline` is written by hand (the features weighed
    as they're meant). `train` replays the history as typing (examples
    at a few points in each command, from what was known before it) and
    fine-tunes with Adam pulled toward its start: the newest tenth of
    what it learns from checks each pass and the best pass is kept (the
    start among them), and the newest tenth of all, held out, judges the
    result, kept only if it ranks them as well (MRR; top-1 reported).
  - `apps/complete` (`olo-complete`, the daemon): one a person, on
    `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-complete.sock` (`OLO_COMPLETE_SOCKET` instead,
    for tests: a test session shares the runtime folder with the
    person's), JSON lines, one request a connection (`protocol::Request`:
    suggest, ran, ended, accepted, continues, stats, learn, reload). `learn` is the
    first fine-tune, from the hand-written weights over everything; a
    second after the first new command (Ben, 2026-11-15: "it should
    retrain pretty often when there are new commands, like once a second
    or something"; it was a minute) a quick one from the current
    weights over the newest, on its own thread (the model locked only to
    copy the examples and to put the weights in). Asleep otherwise (a
    condvar, and poll on the socket and an inotify watch of its folder:
    it exits when its socket is removed, as at logout, and when `reload`
    finds it off). `stats` is its account: suggestions offered and
    taken, latency from the question read to the answer sent (p50, p95,
    worst of the last 512), what it knows, the last fine-tune's report.
  - brush: `vendor/brush-interactive` adds `hooks` (`set_hooks`: the
    hinter, and each line entered with the folder and last status).
    `apps/brush` asks the daemon for a hint with 8 ms to answer, else
    shows brush's own; tells it each line entered, how the last ended
    and whether the hint was taken (whole, `complete_hint`, or a word);
    starts it, once a minute at most, when nothing answers. Its binary
    holds `protocol::HINTER_MARK`, by which `protocol::asks_for_hints`
    tells a brush that asks from one built before it did.
  - Preferences ▸ Terminal (`apps/preferences/src/complete.rs`): the
    checkbox (`protocol::OPTION`), usable when the login shell
    (`olo_system::accounts::login_shell`) is Olo's brush. On a worker:
    turning it on saves the setting, starts the daemon and waits for its
    first fine-tune ("Learning from your history…", then how it did);
    off saves and sends `reload`, and the daemon goes. Another shell, or
    a brush without the mark, gets a note and Open Olo Doctor….
    `complete::lint_states` are linted (`ui_lint_command_suggestions`;
    the pane is the tallest's size).
  - Activity Monitor ▸ AI (`sections::ai`): `model_poller` asks `stats`
    once a second while the section shows, nothing otherwise; its
    latency is graphed (`ai.p50`, `ai.p95`). `OLO_ACTIVITY_DEMO_AI`
    shows `protocol::demo_stats` to look at headless.
  - The session and the screen (Ben, 2026-11-05): in Olo's Terminal a
    shell's session is its shell id, not its process (olo-termd sets
    `OLO_SHELL_ID`, and `OLO_SHELL_RESTORED` with the id of the shell a
    restored tab's stands in for; brush reads both as it starts, before
    it takes the environment into its variables, `protocol::shell_id`,
    and says `continues` once, `Index::continue_session`), so a tab's
    last ten commands (`SESSION_LAST`) carry on across a restart, from
    the record if the daemon started again too. olo-termd writes each
    shell's last 80 lines as text (`protocol::tail_path`, in the runtime
    folder, wrapped rows joined, `tail_text`) 300 ms after its output
    stops (`TAIL_AFTER`: nothing while idle), a restored tab's
    scrollback among them, and removes it as the shell or olo-termd
    ends. The daemon reads it when the file changed (`named`, cached by
    its time, and again after each command run) for the commands it
    names (`output::named`: what was run at a prompt, a line or
    backquoted text starting with a program the person runs, or what
    follows a colon after words saying to run it: "Resume this session
    with:" and the command after it, "To continue this session, run:
    codex resume …", `git push --set-upstream origin topic`, "run `cargo
    fix`"; not "error: cargo build failed"; the prompt being typed at
    left out), and the latest one that fits what's typed comes first,
    ahead of the model's
    (`output::tests::bens_restored_tab_suggests_the_resume`: Ben's
    restored tab, `cl` typed, his `claude … --resume 00000000-…`).
  - A printed command, with how its program was started (`carry`; Ben,
    2026-11-15: started as `codex
    --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, codex prints `codex
    resume 01a1ddfb-…`, and "what i want is `codex
    --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox resume 01a1ddfb-…`. but
    don't like hardcode that rule for codex/claude or anything"). Each
    printed command knows its start: the command at the prompt above it,
    the same program (`Named::start`), else the shell's last run of it.
    `carry::Habits`, kept by the index from every command as it's run,
    knows of each program's options which take a value (never seen
    without a word after: `-m o3`), which come before its first other
    word (the program's own, not a subcommand's), and which the person
    gives it in most runs. `Habits::carry` puts into the printed command
    the start's options it hasn't (by name: its own `--resume NEW` keeps
    over the start's `--resume OLD`), each where it was: before the first
    other word, or after a word the printed command has too (`git push
    -f`'s after `push`); one belonging to a word it hasn't (`cargo build
    --release`'s, for a printed `cargo fix`) isn't carried, nor a value of
    more than one word (a prompt), nor the printed command's own
    subcommand taken for a value. With no start shown, the options the
    person gives the program in most of at least three runs. Both are
    offered, the carried one first; typing the printed one's own words
    (`codex r`) gets it as printed. What the person runs next votes
    (`carry.json`): the carried one, or the printed one as printed; two
    more as printed than carried and that program's are left as
    printed. olo-termd gives each shell its own `OLO_SHELL_ID` only
    (`shell_env`: a Terminal started from a Terminal shell had both
    ids). Tried
    headless: a command printed by `printf`, `git l` typed in brush, the
    hint `og --oneline -3`. The installed `/usr/local/bin/brush` is the
    copy Olo Doctor's suggestion put there, brought up to date by its
    "Update brush".

**A welcome in a new shell** (`welcome`, termd.rs; Ben, 2026-11-17: "olo
doctor should offer a suggestion to install an olo greeter/welcome
message for the terminal that shows the olo logo in full color ascii";
"should also show some slick colorful stats/info etc. like is the trend
with these greeters in modern OSes"; "have the greeter show a random
haiku … a loose theme of humans and ai working together but not in your
face cliche"). On while `~/.config/olo/terminal-welcome` is there
(`olo_xdg::terminal_welcome_path`): Olo Doctor's suggestion "A welcome
in Terminal" writes it, and removes it (no shell's files are touched,
and it shows only in Olo's Terminal). A new shell, not a command nor
one restored, opens with it as part of what the terminal shows (the
bytes go to the screen before the shell's own, as a restored shell's
scrollback does; nothing is typed). **The ring** is Olo's own drawing
(`olo.svg`, rendered at 192 pixels and averaged down to 24 by 24, a
pixel a half cell: an upper half block in the upper pixel's colour on
the lower one's, a pixel under 43% there left the terminal's own
background; `ring_cells`), not characters shaded to look like it:
"ASCII" as these greeters are, in the terminal's cells and its full
colour. **Beside it** (`facts`): who and where, then the system, the
computer's model, its processor and GPUs (found once a daemon,
`fixed_facts`: the GPUs' names alone took 4 ms), memory, disk and
battery as bars (green, amber, red as they fill or empty) with their
figures, how long it's been up, the shell, and the terminal's sixteen
colours; names in the terminal's own blue, so each theme colours it.
**Under it**, one of twenty-four haiku (`HAIKU`), picked by the clock.
A window too narrow for the facts gets the ring and a line; too small
for the ring, the line or nothing; too short, no haiku. Measured
(release, `welcome_costs`): the first 15 ms (the ring rendered, once a
daemon), then 1.2 ms a shell, most of it the battery's reading.
  - Measured (M2 Max, release, 640 commands): a suggestion 1 µs in the
    daemon, 2 µs at p95 (26 µs round trip from a client); with a shell's
    tail (ThinkPad, 2026-11-05) 2 µs at the median, 3 at p95, as without
    one, and 40 µs once each time its tail changed; the first
    fine-tune 5 to 11 ms, a quick one about 2 ms; idle 0% of a core, 0
    wakeups a second; while Activity Monitor's AI shows, one a second
    in the daemon and 3 in Activity Monitor's poller (0.1% of a core).
    With carrying and learning a second after (ThinkPad, release, 600
    commands, a shell's tail with a printed resume, 2026-11-15): a
    suggestion 4 µs at the median and 5 at p95 in the daemon, as the
    build before it on the same history; a command learned 1.00 s after
    it ran, its quick fine-tune 1.2 to 1.3 ms on about 2,000 examples;
    idle 0 context switches and 0 CPU over 10 s.

## The Installer (apps/installer, tools/release.sh)

**On a Fedora with no desktop** (a minimal install; Ben, 2026-11-15:
"we should be 100% independent of gnome"): `olo-installer --console
[--yes] [--login-screen] [--boot-splash] [--rpm-fusion]` (`console.rs`)
runs the same plan in the terminal, its stages and progress written as
lines, the licence agreed to by typing "agree"; the administrator's
helper is started through sudo (`helper::Way::Sudo`, `OLO_SETUP_HELPER=
sudo`), which asks on the terminal (no polkit agent there, polkit maybe
not installed yet); with no display manager at all, Olo's own login
screen is chosen too. A minimal Fedora has no PackageKit or dnf's
service either, which Olo installs software through: the package stage
first puts them in place with Fedora's own dnf, this once (Ben: "just
have olo installer and olo doctor install the needed packagekit/dnf
stuff", choosing one dnf call over a package manager of Olo's own:
`olo_system::packages::bootstrap`, Doctor's `Step::InstallPackageServices`,
which every package step takes first where they're missing), then asks
the bus to read its activation files again. Tried on a minimal Fedora
45 (2026-11-15, a `@core` install in a VM: no desktop, no display
manager, no PackageKit, no graphics drivers): the console installer
over SSH with a terminal, the password typed when sudo asked, then the
machine started again with a 3D GPU: Olo's login screen, and the
password into Olo's desktop. What it found, each fixed: Wayland's
server library missing (app_server opens it as it starts: "NoWaylandLib";
every Workstation has it, so the package list never named it: the list
is Doctor's now, `olo_doctor::needs`, with each library Olo's programs
open checked against that machine, and Doctor's "Olo needs …" installs
what's missing); SELinux's `semanage` missing for the login screen's
labels (installed first where SELinux is on and it isn't); the
computer set to start to its console (`multi-user.target`: the
login-screen steps make `graphical.target` the default where it
isn't, `UnitAction::MakeDefault`, systemd's `SetDefaultTarget`); GDM
named as the display manager to turn off where there's none; and Olo
not made the person's session (the test-run guard took the console's
`OLO_SETUP_HELPER=sudo` for a test's `direct`).

One program a person downloads from Olo's releases and runs on a stock
Fedora Workstation (Ben, 2026-11-06: "a full screen gui app that
\"olo-fies\" their fedora"; first made as Windows 95's Setup in BeOS's
look and called Olo Setup, a wizard of five pages; then, 2026-11-11:
"redo the installer to be reminiscent of the beos installer instead of
windows 95"). `olo-installer`, full screen, is BeOS's Installer for Olo
(`ui.rs`): the plain blue of BeOS's desktop (51, 102, 152: its
Installer ran on the bare desktop of the CD it started from), and on it
one window drawn as BeOS draws them (the yellow tab with its title, the
grey panel and its frame, from the palette; as tall as what it holds,
its top fixed, so it grows downwards).

First "Licence", as BeOS showed its own before anything else:
`licence.txt` (Olo's MIT terms, as Cargo.toml says, and the others'
work it carries) in a white scroll box, Disagree (quits) and Agree.

Then "Installer", the one window everything happens in. Olo's mark at
its top left where BeOS's had Be's, and beside it a white box of words
that says what to do and then what is being done: what installing
does and that the password is asked for once (why this computer can't
have Olo, in red, if it can't: `plan::unsuitable`, not Fedora 44 or
newer, an atomic Fedora, root, under 9 GB free; Begin is dimmed), then
the stages and their notes as they come, a failure in red with what to
do, and at the end "Installation completed" and how to get to Olo.
Under it
"Install from:" and "Onto:" as pop-ups, as BeOS's chose a CD and a
volume: here there is one of each (Olo's newest release, or
`--bundle`'s archive; this computer's Fedora, for this person), so they
say what will happen. "More Options", a latch (the kit's `PaneSwitch`;
"Fewer Options" while open), opens the optional parts under it and the
window grows to hold them: Olo's login screen, its boot splash and RPM
Fusion, each a check box with its words under it (BeOS's showed what a
part was only under the pointer: no use to whoever reads the window
without one), what the computer has already chosen again and said so
("Installed already: it's brought up to date": `Choices::
installed_under`, Olo's login screen as `display-manager.service`,
Plymouth's theme `olo`, RPM Fusion's repository file; the login screen
runs copies of its own in `/usr/local/libexec/olo`, which an update
leaving it out kept old), and "Disk space required", as BeOS's pane
ended. It starts open when something in it is chosen. While it works, a
BeOS status bar (the stage over it and "n of m" at its right, what
it's doing under it) and everything that chooses dimmed. Along the
bottom, About… at the left (where BeOS's had "Setup partitions…") and
Begin at the right, which is Stop while it works: stopped, the window
is as it was with "Installation stopped" in its words, and Begin goes
on from there. A failure leaves Quit and Try Again; installed, Log Out
(Restart when the login screen or splash changed) and Quit, which is
what Return does: leaving the desktop it runs in is asked for with a
click of its own. The whole of it, More Options open and at work, fits
1280 × 800. About comes in front, alone on the desktop until OK (one
surface has no windows to stack: a window drawn over another reads, to
the layout review and to an agent, as its parts among the other's),
with what Olo is. None of Olo is installed when it
starts, so it carries what the kit draws with (build.rs: Olo's fonts,
its icons at every size, the wordmark), unpacks it into the runtime
folder and points the kit there (`OLO_DATA`).

`OLO_SETUP_DEMO=done|restart|fail` is for looking at it on a computer
that mustn't be changed (a test session, the layout review): Begin
installs nothing and plays an install's events instead (`ui::pretend`:
the stages, a wait for the password, progress, notes, and its end),
and Log Out and Restart only print what they would do. Without it,
Begin installs for real (PackageKit, the helper) and Log Out and
Restart end the session of whoever started it: never click them in a
test.

The work (`plan.rs`) runs on a worker, each stage told to the window
(`Event`), each doing only what isn't done, so it can be stopped
(Stop) and begun again: checking the computer; what Olo needs from
Fedora (`PACKAGES`: what its programs link, `ldd` on every program,
22 packages, and the services and fonts a session uses) through
PackageKit; RPM Fusion's two repositories if chosen (Olo Doctor's
`InstallRepository`); Olo itself (`olo_release`, `crates/release`, shared with
the upgrader: the newest GitHub
release's `olo-VERSION-ARCH.tar.zst` of `benmyles/olo`, or `--bundle
URL|FILE`, downloaded into `~/.cache/olo-installer` and kept, its
published SHA-256 checked, unpacked (zstd, tar; nothing outside `olo/`)
and put in place as tools/install-session.sh does: each program beside
its old self then renamed over it, the data copied over, `op`, `pbcopy`
and `pbpaste` linked, the version in `~/.local/share/olo/version`);
Olo on the login screen's menu (its session entry naming
`~/.local/bin/olo-session`, Olo's udev rules, the devices they're for
told to look again by their `uevent`); and if chosen, Olo's login
screen (tools/install-login.sh `--switch`'s work: its programs in
/usr/local/libexec/olo, Olo's data in /usr/local/share/olo, the PAM
services and `pam_olo_keyring.so`, its user and folders made by
`systemd-sysusers` and Setup itself, its unit, the display manager
it replaces disabled (GDM's) and olo-login enabled: Olo Doctor's
`login_screen::steps`, which its "Use Olo's Login Screen" runs too) and boot splash
(the theme drawn by `olo-app-server --plymouth-theme` as the person,
then put in /usr/share/plymouth/themes/olo with plymouthd.conf kept
beside as `.before-olo`, and the start-up images made again:
`Step::RebuildInitramfs`, dracut). Two steps run another program,
each the system's own and with no other way in: dracut, and
`systemd-sysusers` on the login screen's own file
(`Step::MakeSystemUsers`: systemd's sysusers service runs only after an
update, `ConditionNeedsUpdate=/etc`, so restarting it made no user);
the tmpfiles entry's folders are made by Setup itself (`Step::MakeDir`:
systemd refuses to restart its tmpfiles service by hand). What
needs root is Olo Doctor's privileged helper (`helper.rs`, the same
`Step`s, two added for Setup: `CopyTree` and `RebuildInitramfs`), this
program run again through pkexec (`--helper`), asked for once: the
password goes to the desktop's own polkit agent, GNOME's on a stock
Fedora; `OLO_SETUP_HELPER=direct` runs it as the person (tests: what
needs root then fails, safely). PackageKit's lookups now find what is
installed first and only look for the rest in this architecture
(`olo_system::packages::resolve`: asked for the newest alone, an update
waiting showed as not installed, and installing what was missing
became an update, which asked for a password). `--yes` agrees, begins
and quits by itself, a step every four seconds (`--login-screen`,
`--boot-splash`, `--rpm-fusion` choose), for tests and agents; `--check`
says as JSON whether this computer can have Olo and opens nothing.

The release (`tools/release.sh [OUT]`, from a release build): every
`olo-*` program stripped (300 MB with line tables to 30 MB; a third of
that compressed), `pam_olo_keyring.so` and face unlock's
`libpam_olo_face.so`, Olo's data as an upgrade installs it
(`upgrade::sync_data`: the icons' and themes' sizes, the brand, the
fonts, the models that read text in pictures and that know a face;
never a data folder whole, which also holds what its pictures are made
from) and what goes outside the home folder (`system/`: the session
entry, udev rules, PAM services, the login screen's unit, user and
folders), and `VERSION` (the date and the commit) in
`olo-VERSION-ARCH.tar.zst` (zstd -19, 567 MB), and the installer
stripped beside it, each with its `.sha256`. **The wallpapers are a
part of their own**, `olo-wallpapers-VERSION.tar.zst` (1.67 GB, any
architecture; `olo/share/olo/wallpapers`): GitHub takes files under
2 GiB, and with the lossless pack Olo was 2.2 GB (4.7 with the
wallpapers' sources, which the script copied too until 2026-11-17).
The archive's `.sha256` names both; Setup takes every other `.tar.zst`
named there as a part (`bundle::parts`), fetches it from beside the
archive (`Origin::beside`: the same release, or folder), checks it and
unpacks it over the first (`bundle::fetch`, `bundle::unpack`); the
script stops if either is 2 GiB or more. A Setup from before the parts
installs such a release without its wallpapers. `cargo test --release
-p olo-installer a_real_release -- --ignored` with
`OLO_RELEASE=OUT/olo-VERSION-ARCH.tar.zst` finds, checks and unpacks
what the script made as Setup does (into a folder beside it, removed)
and says what's missing. Publishing them (a GitHub release with the
five files) is a separate step.

`tools/dev/installer-check` tries it all in a virtual machine (KVM, a
virtio GPU, no window, driven through QEMU's monitor; `boot --gl
RENDER` gives it a GPU with 3D, virgl through one of this computer's
render nodes, as Olo needs one to draw: Fedora's GNOME draws in
software on the plain one, Olo can't and its login screen steps aside;
its screen is then read through a VNC socket of its own, as QEMU's
screendump has no picture of a 3D scanout, and here only through the
NVIDIA node's EGL): `install` puts a
fresh Fedora Workstation on a disk from Fedora's own network installer
(a kickstart choosing Workstation's package set; for the test alone,
GDM logs the tester in and GNOME's first-run tour is skipped), `boot
--serve DIR` starts it with the release served to it at
`http://10.0.2.2:8642/`, and `shot`, `type`, `key` and `click` look and
act. Everything is kept in /var/tmp/olo-installer-check.

## The Wi-Fi and Bluetooth healer (apps/wifi-heal)

**Bluetooth** (`bluetooth.rs`): a controller that stops answering is
reset: its driver unbound, the device reset where it can be (PCI's
function reset, `reset`), and bound again; BlueZ takes it up as before.
On 2026-11-09 Intel's PCIe Bluetooth (`btintel_pcie`, a ThinkPad) failed
every command from the morning on ("Bluetooth: hci0: sending frame
failed (-19)", ENODEV): AirPods sat at Connecting…, and rfkill's off and
on didn't reach it (its driver couldn't send even the reset). What says
so: the kernel's messages (`/dev/kmsg`, read as they come; root only, as
`dmesg_restrict` is 1), a send failing with ENODEV, a command timing out
or a hardware error, three within a minute (from before start only the
last ten minutes'); and at start, BlueZ's adapter powered with its power
off or the other way round (`Adapter::not_answering`), twice five
seconds apart. Limited as Wi-Fi's resets are, apart from them; 15 s
after one it looks whether BlueZ has it on again, and says so in the
report (`interface` "hci0"), which Olo Doctor tells the person of ("Olo
fixed Bluetooth"). Doctor installs the healer on any machine with
Bluetooth (not only a Mac's Broadcom Wi-Fi), finds a controller that
doesn't answer (`bluetooth-stuck-hci0`, from BlueZ: the person can't
read the kernel's messages) and fixes it with `Step::RestartBluetooth`
(as root, asking for the password), and Preferences ▸ Bluetooth says so
over its list, with Open Olo Doctor.


The Broadcom chips in Apple machines (brcmfmac; BCM4388 here) can get
stuck in their firmware: every join fails without associating
(wpa_supplicant's `ASSOC-REJECT status_code=16`, which brcmfmac reports
for any failed join), address changes are refused (`-52`, NetworkManager's
"failed to set MAC address"), and scans stick ("Reject scan trigger since
one is already pending"); NetworkManager then asks for the password again
and says it was wrong. It lasted 38 hours on 2026-10-31. Resetting the
device (the driver unbound and bound again, which reloads the firmware)
joins at once, measured; a run of failed joins can bring it on (it did,
in testing, after two resets and four refused joins). Joining early
after the firmware starts, and a regulatory change, were measured not to.

`olo-wifi-heal` is a root service (a root-owned copy in
/usr/local/libexec, never the person's own file, which anything running
as them could replace) that follows NetworkManager's device states and
wpa_supplicant's interface states as D-Bus signals, nothing polled.
When a join fails after two or more tries to associate with none getting
further, or a scan runs two minutes, it resets the chip and joins the
same network again. On this chip a wrong password fails the same way
(the firmware does the handshake), so the reset is the test: if the
join after it fails alike, the chip wasn't at fault, which is recorded
("its password is most likely wrong"), and that network isn't reset for
again until it has joined. One reset in three minutes, four an hour,
only for drivers known to recover so (`DRIVERS`). Each goes in the
journal and `/run/olo/wifi-heal.json` (`olo-wifi-heal --status`), which
`olo-doctor --watch` tells the person of. `OLO_WIFI_HEAL_DEBUG=1` logs
every event. Test it as root with a copy in /var/tmp and a profile with
a wrong password (the chip may stick after; the healer frees it).

`data/NetworkManager/80-olo-brcmfmac.conf` (installed with it) keeps the
chip's own address while scanning, so NetworkManager doesn't change it
every few minutes while idle; each network still gets its own address.
Olo's join (`olo_system::network::join`) asks for the security the access
point offers (`key_mgmt`): WPA3 alone is "sae" (asking for WPA2 was
refused before it began: "Access point does not support PSK"), Enhanced
Open "owe".

## Voice processing (crates/voice)

`olo_voice::Voice` processes one microphone, a 10 ms frame (480 samples
at 48 kHz) at a time: `render` takes what the speakers play, `capture` a
microphone frame and gives it back processed; `latency_samples` says what
it adds (30 ms with noise suppression, 10 ms with echo cancellation
alone, 0 with neither). `Settings` (mode, echo cancellation, noise level,
normalization) choose the chain; build a `Voice` off the real-time thread
(loading the model takes a moment). In order:

1. **Echo cancellation** (`echo.rs`): finds where the echo is (coherence
   over 0-500 ms, moved only when clearly better than where it is), then a
   partitioned-block frequency-domain Kalman filter, 120 ms of room, over
   the whole band, in two paths (Speex's: a foreground copy the output
   comes from, kept safe while both people talk). Then residual echo
   suppression: a Wiener gain per frequency from the filter's own
   uncertainty, applied to the noise model's input spectrum (so it never
   hears the other person's voice, which would make it turn yours down).
   No delay of its own. About 30 µs a frame.
2. **Noise suppression**: DeepFilterNet3, one of two models
   (`Settings::model`, Preferences ▸ Sound ▸ Noise model): DeepFilterNet3
   itself, two frames of look-ahead (the voice 30 ms behind), or its
   low-delay version DeepFilterNet3-LL, none (10 ms; both tarballs
   built in from LFS, the second's pages read only when it's chosen).
   Measured against each other (tests/least_delay.rs, chain.rs): as much
   room noise out between words, a voice in a noisy room 1-2 dB less
   clean with the low-delay one, and it keeps more of a quieter voice
   (another person's, or what the canceller leaves of the far end's: 34
   dB down where DeepFilterNet3 takes 57); its estimate of a frame's SNR
   runs about 10 dB under DeepFilterNet3's, so fewer frames of noise
   alone are gated to silence. Thresholds: noise-only frames go down to
   the limit, both decoders always run otherwise (the library's defaults
   chop clean speech).

   The GRUs' matrices (512 wide in the low-delay model: twelve 1536 ×
   512, read whole every frame for one vector each) are 8-bit
   (`deep_filter::q8`): a byte a weight scaled by its row, the vector as
   15-bit integers, summed as integers by AVX-VNNI (`vpdpbusd` on the
   vector's high and low bytes: the same sums as 16-bit, to the bit),
   else AVX2 (`vpmaddwd`), else a plain loop. The rest of the weights
   are f16 (`deep_filter::tract::half_weights`: each matmul's constant
   f32 weights swapped for an f16 copy before optimizing, so tract runs
   its f16-weights, f32-activations kernels; translating the whole model
   to f16, activations too, had wrecked it). The time a frame is the
   time to stream the weights: in f16 a GRU matrix took 58 µs (27 GB/s
   on one core); in 8 bits 10.5 µs from L2, 18 from L3, 34 from memory.
   A frame back to back, x86 with AVX-VNNI (2026-11-07): DeepFilterNet3
   318 → 232-260 µs, the low-delay one 850-1458 → 405-441 µs; one every
   10 ms as live, the low-delay one's median 1.5-1.8 → 1.0 ms and its
   99th 2.4-5.5 → 1.5 ms; every voice trial's SDR within 0.4 dB of f16.
   `OLO_VOICE_F16=1` leaves out the 8 bits, `OLO_VOICE_F32=1` asks for
   f32, to compare. Where a frame's time goes, model by model and node
   by node, paced or not: `vendor/deep_filter/tests/profile.rs`
   (`OLO_DF_MODEL`, `OLO_DF_NODES`, `OLO_DF_PACED`; `q8_speed` times the
   8-bit product hot, from the cache and from memory).
3. **Level normalization**: AGC2 (adaptive digital gain from a neural
   voice detector, then a limiter), allowed to turn loud talkers down as
   well as quiet ones up: speech lands within half a dB of -24 dBFS rms
   from anywhere between -40 and -1 dBFS peaks.

`Mode` (Calls, Recording) doesn't change the processing, only the
buffering around it. The FFTs are rustfft's (NEON, AVX, SSE at run
time), the model runs on tract's NEON/AVX kernels, and the canceller's
per-frequency math is laid out as separate real and imaginary arrays in
straight loops, which compile to vector code (check with objdump: `.4s`
instructions in `EchoCanceller::cancel`). A GPU doesn't fit: a frame is
well under a millisecond of work, shorter than a round trip to a GPU
queue, and every frame depends on the one before.

`cargo test --release -p olo-voice -- --nocapture --test-threads=1`
prints what each stage does on synthetic speech (CMU Flite voices,
`tests/data`), room noise, music and the other person's voice over a
synthetic echo path: noise and echo taken out, the voice's level kept
(frame by frame, so that a high-pass filter's harmless phase shift
doesn't count as damage), delays as stated, and the time a frame takes.
Don't judge a speech model with tones: DeepFilterNet takes a synthetic
buzz for noise.

## The voice service (apps/voice, `olo-voice --service`)

Every microphone through voice processing (`crates/voice`, above). The
service puts a source of its own, named after the microphone it listens
to ("AirPods (Voice Processing)", `Config::description`, renamed live
as the microphone changes: `pw_stream_update_properties`, which every
list of devices, PipeWire's and its PulseAudio server's, follows;
`olo_protocol::voice::NODE`, `olo_voice`), in front of the microphone
the person chose and makes it the default input, so anything that
records gets the processed voice, and the processed device and the raw
one are always told apart:

- **Which microphone**: whatever becomes the default input that isn't
  its own (Preferences, Deskbar, AirPods' choice, any program) is the
  one it listens to, and it is the default again. Device lists
  (`olo_system::audio::devices`, `watch_devices`) leave its source out
  and show that microphone as the default; `devices_raw` has both.
  Turned off, stopped or quitting, the microphone is the default itself
  again; if it crashes, WirePlumber falls back to the microphone.
- **Its mute is the microphone's** (`main.rs`, `follow`), both ways:
  muted on the source (an app, the microphone key), the microphone is
  too; on the microphone (Olo's controls, which show the microphone in
  the source's place), the source follows. WirePlumber keeps nothing of
  the source's own (`state.restore-props` false). (Ben, 2026-11-09:
  Chrome said the processed microphone was muted and couldn't unmute
  it, while Preferences said it wasn't: muted once, the source came
  back muted at 69% at every start, out of sight.)
- **Its volume is the recording app's**, for its automatic gain
  control: applied by PipeWire after the processing, as any source's
  is, and put back to 100% as the source is made and whenever nothing
  records from it any more (`reset_volume`), so what one app's gain
  control left it at isn't the next recording's. The microphone's own
  volume is the person's (Olo's controls), untouched by apps. It used to
  be the microphone's too, the engine making up what PipeWire took off:
  an app's gain control then never heard its change take effect, and
  WebRTC's (Chrome's, every call app's on it) stepped the microphone
  down 6% every few seconds to its floor, 71% to 29% on a call of
  Ben's on 2026-11-09 (its clipping step, 15 of 255, and floor, 70),
  while the level stage made the loss up digitally, noise and all. In a
  pw-sandbox, speech recorded from the source as an app set it to 50%:
  before, the microphone went to 50% and the recording from −27 dBFS to
  −42 and back up to −31; now the microphone stays at 100% and the
  recording at −42 (0.5³, −18 dB), the source back to 100% once the
  recording ends; mute across both ways in both.
- **What's behind the source** (`engine.rs`, PipeWire's thread): the
  microphone's capture and, for echo cancellation, the default output's
  monitor, only for an output the microphone can hear (not
  `Device::private`: Bluetooth, a headphones or headset port or form
  factor). Made inactive, switched on only while something records from
  the source: idle, nothing runs and the microphone isn't open. What
  records is the links from the source (a registry listener on Link
  objects whose output node is the source's), not its state: it's one
  group with the captures, so once they ran it ran whether anything read
  it or not, and after the first call it never paused again: the
  microphone stayed open and the processing ran for good, 11.5% of a
  core (568-582 ms of CPU every 5 s in a pw-sandbox, 8 s after the
  recording ended; now 0, and the microphone suspended). A new
  microphone or new settings rebuild only the captures, so a call keeps
  its device. The captures and the source are one group (`node.group`:
  one driver and clock) and the source a triggered stream, run from the
  microphone's process as its frames are done; calls force the graph to
  a frame a cycle while something records (`node.force-quantum` 480), so
  nothing is held back for the frames' fit, and with a quantum another
  program forces only its misfit is (`misfit`: `FRAME - gcd`, 448 samples
  for a power of two), exactly, from the start (silence before the
  sound); recordings 2048 samples and four frames more. Triggered, the
  source gives each cycle's frames in that cycle, so an app recording
  through Pulse (Chrome's, every call app's: PipeWire schedules them in
  the cycle) gets the voice with nothing added but the processing's
  delay and what's held; only a client PipeWire schedules asynchronously
  (pw-record, pw-play: `node.async`, `=` in pw-top) reads it a cycle
  late, as it reads any source that isn't a device. What the service
  says it adds is that. `tools/dev/voice-latency` measures it in a
  private PipeWire graph of its own (no hardware; its own WirePlumber
  with every monitor off, runtime, config and state folders): speech
  into a test microphone, the microphone and Olo Voice's source recorded
  side by side by a synchronous probe (a realtime `pw_filter`, as
  Pulse's streams are scheduled), and the lag between them
  cross-correlated (`--settings`, `--quantum`, `--probe async` for
  pw-record, `--signal clicks`, `--other loopback` for PipeWire's own).
  2026-11-07: the processing off 0.0 ms, a forced 256 or 1024 quantum
  9.33 (the frames' misfit), the low-delay noise model 10.0, DeepFilterNet3
  30.0, each said as measured, no dropouts. (Measured with pw-record
  before, every figure had a quantum more: not Olo's.) Don't judge the
  delay with clicks in silence: the level stage boosts and limits them,
  and a speech model takes them for noise.
- **Settings** `voice.json` in the config folder
  (`olo_protocol::voice::Settings`: enabled, mode, echo cancellation,
  noise, normalize), followed by inotify. **State** `olo-voice.json` in
  the runtime folder: the microphone, recording or idle, echo cancelling
  now, the delay it adds, a frame's processing time, dropouts.
- **A quiet microphone's boost** (Ben, 2026-11-16: "some inputs like
  airpods are not loud enough on microphone input. add the ability in
  voice processing to optionally boost the input level to some target
  level and have it suggest the ideal level"). Each microphone's own
  (`olo_protocol::voice::Boosts`, `voice-boost.json` beside the
  settings, by its node's name: AirPods' boost isn't the laptop
  microphone's), in 3 dB steps up to 30, a gain on each frame before
  the chain (`olo_voice::boosted`, kept within full scale): evening out
  the level alone doesn't do it, as that stage raises its gain only
  while it's sure it hears speech, which a quiet microphone is where
  it's least sure. **Suggested from what's heard**: while something
  records, the service measures the voice as it comes in, before any
  boost (`olo_voice::SpeechLevel`: the active speech level, the mean
  power of the frames someone speaks in over the last three seconds,
  those within 15 dB of their mean, as ITU-T P.56 states speech levels;
  a frame is speech when it's 12 dB over the microphone's own noise
  floor), and says it in its state (`speech_db`, kept for each
  microphone heard; `boost_db`). `suggested_boost` is what brings that
  to -26 dB (`AIM_DB`, the level speech is nominally stated at), to the
  nearest step. Preferences ▸ Sound ▸ Voice Processing: "Microphone
  boost:" (None, +3 dB … +30 dB), **Use Suggested** when the measured
  voice wants another, and the line under it ("Your voice comes in at
  -34 dB: +9 dB brings it to the -26 dB aimed for."). Measured in a
  private sound server (`tools/dev/voice-latency --level -20 --boost
  9`, which says the levels too): speech played 20 dB quieter read
  20.4 dB lower (-13.4 and -33.8 dB; a first measure, the mean of the
  frames' levels in dB with a fixed gate, read 13 lower: the quiet
  one's soft frames fell under the gate), 9 dB suggested, and the
  source 8.9 dB over the microphone with it set, 9.3 with noise
  suppression and levelling on; no delay added. A frame costs 0.9 µs to
  measure and say, 0.08 to boost (`speech_level_cost`, ignored).
- **Command line**: `olo-voice --status [--json]`, `olo-voice --set
  KEY=VALUE…` (`enabled`, `echo`, `normalize`: on/off; `mode`:
  calls/recording; `noise`: off/moderate/strong/full). Deskbar's menu
  uses it too.
- **None as the output** (Preferences ▸ Sound, first in Play sound
  through; first in Deskbar's speaker menu): sound goes nowhere rather
  than to the only device there is (a network speaker in another room).
  It's a silent sink of Olo's (`olo_system::audio::NO_OUTPUT`, PipeWire's
  null sink, loaded over the PulseAudio protocol: `set_no_output`) made
  the default, never listed as a device (`Devices::no_output`).
  `olo_protocol::sound::SoundChoice` remembers it, and Deskbar makes it
  again at login (the sound server forgets it).
- **A Bluetooth device that plays nothing** (Ben's AirPods, 2026-11-04:
  an input, but no output): `Devices::unplayable` lists each Bluetooth
  card (`api.bluez5.address`) with no output of its own, why
  (`Silence`: its profile `off`; no music or call profile available, its
  Bluetooth audio not connected; or one chosen yet no output) and the
  profile that plays (an available `a2dp-sink*`, else
  `headset-head-unit*`). Preferences ▸ Sound names it under Output ("…
  is connected but plays no sound: its sound is turned off.") with Play
  Sound Through It (`set_card_profile`). The watcher follows cards too
  (`SubscriptionMask::CARD`), so it goes as the profile comes up.
- **UI**: Preferences ▸ Sound's Voice Processing box (and what it's
  doing in a line); Deskbar's speaker menu: "Clean Up Microphone Sound"
  and a Voice Processing submenu.
- **Try It…** (Preferences ▸ Sound ▸ Voice Processing,
  apps/preferences/src/voice_try.rs): six seconds recorded from the
  microphone the service listens to (`State::microphone`, not its own
  cleaned-up source) with `olo_system::recording::Recording` (the
  PulseAudio protocol's record stream, mono 48 kHz float, in memory
  only), then put through each setting worth comparing on a worker
  (`variants`: as set, each other noise level, the level the other way,
  the other mode; `olo_voice::trial`, after a short untimed one: a
  process's first chain sets up what the rest share, a 27 ms first
  frame against 0.4), each listed as it's done: the delay it adds, its
  time a 10 ms frame (median and worst), what noise suppression and
  levelling did (`Stage::change_db`) and what ran it
  (`accelerated_by`). Played with `recording::Player`, the original or
  the chosen setting's sound, switching at the same place (one stream,
  the take chosen by an atomic; 60 ms ahead at most, so a switch is
  heard at once), with a live spectrum of both (`olo_voice::spectrum`,
  under 40 µs a call). "Use This Setting" saves it. The recording's
  own speech level is measured the same way (said under the list: "Your
  voice came in at -35 dB; voice processing aims for -26 dB."), and
  where it wants another boost than the microphone has, that's tried
  too ("Boosted +9 dB (suggested)"; "Not boosted" for one that has a
  boost), every row with the boost it would run with; using a row sets
  its boost as well. Echo cancellation
  isn't tried: a recording has no speakers' sound beside it. Tested in
  a `tools/dev/pw-sandbox` (`recording::tests`, whose "talk" sink the
  "mic" source hears: two tones played, switched halfway, recorded
  back). Measured: 292 µs a frame while playing (the whole window
  drawn each frame was 1.8 ms), 252 µs while recording, nothing idle.
- **Running it**: olo-session starts it in a real session (`REAL_SHELL`)
  and restarts it if it exits; an upgrade installs the new `olo-voice`
  and sends SIGURG, on which it starts again as the new version (the
  source comes back, the default stays); SIGTERM gives the microphone
  back. The supervisor never lowers it and keeps it in the audio tier
  (above). Olo Doctor checks its sound is realtime.
- **Testing**: in `tools/dev/pw-sandbox`, never the person's sound
  server: `OLO_VOICE_DIR=DIR` keeps its settings and state apart, and
  `pw-cat --playback --target talk speech.wav` talks into the made-up
  microphone while `pw-cat --record` records the default input. Measured
  there: the voice comes through with no dropouts; another voice on the
  speakers with its echo in the microphone goes from −24…−63 dBFS
  (processing off) to −89…−99 dBFS; idle 0% and 0 wakeups, recording
  5.8% of a core (388 µs a frame).

## AirPods (apps/airpods, olo_system::airpods, Preferences ▸ AirPods)

Olo talks to AirPods itself, in Rust, as Apple's devices do. Their
sound is BlueZ's and PipeWire's like any headphones' (AAC at music
quality; the headset profile for calls); everything else is Apple's
accessory protocol (AACP), written from the protocol's public notes
(LibrePods' docs, the apple-wireshark dissector), not from anyone's code:

- `olo_system::airpods::proto`: the messages, both ways. `04 00 04 00`, a
  16-bit opcode, its bytes: the hello (nothing is answered before it),
  host features (Conversation Awareness while sound plays, Adaptive),
  notifications, the broadcast keys; levels (left, right, case, or
  over-ear headphones' one), where each bud is, every setting (opcode 9:
  listening mode, the modes press and hold cycles through, Conversation
  Awareness, Personalized Volume, Adaptive's strength, ear detection,
  one-bud Noise Cancellation, volume swipe, case sounds, which bud's
  microphone, press speed and hold duration), Conversation Awareness's
  levels, who they are (model number, serial, firmware), renaming.
  Unit-tested against documented captures.
- `link`: the L2CAP channel (PSM 0x1001, a SEQPACKET socket through
  libc), opened once BlueZ has connected them.
- `adv`: their LE proximity broadcast (Apple's manufacturer data, kind
  7): model, levels, ears, connected or not, and the block sealed with
  their encryption key (levels to the percent); `resolves` checks their
  rotating private address against their identity key (tested on the
  Core Specification's sample).
- AirPods are known by BlueZ's Modalias (`bluetooth:v004Cp2024…`:
  Apple, product 0x2024, AirPods Pro 2 USB-C); `Model::of` says what
  each can do.

`olo-airpods --service` is a real session's service (`REAL_SHELL`). It
follows BlueZ by its signals (`bluetooth::watch`: connections, pairing,
names; a search's signal strengths ignored), opens the channel to each
pair connected (a thread each, asleep on it; tried again for a few
seconds while their profiles come up), and follows the sound server
(`audio::watch_devices`; a Bluetooth device's address, codec and
profile come with it, `audio::Bluetooth`, and cards and their profiles,
`audio::cards`). What it does, by Olo's settings (`airpods.json`,
`AirPodsSettings`, followed by inotify): pauses what plays (MPRIS,
`olo_system::media`) when a bud comes out, if the sound is going to
them, and plays it again when it's back (within ten minutes); turns
their output down while Conversation Awareness says the wearer speaks,
and back after; keeps the computer's microphones as the input (an input
of theirs that has just come and been made the default is undone), so
they stay at music quality, unless the person chose theirs. It keeps
their broadcast keys in `~/.local/state/olo/airpods-keys.json` (0600).

Their broadcast (`olo_system::bluetooth::watch_apple`: BlueZ's
advertisement monitor, passive, its devices' ManufacturerData followed
by signals) is resolved to a pair by its key, gives their levels while
they aren't connected here, and says whether they're nearby and
connected elsewhere (`AirPods::nearby`, `elsewhere`). With it: **connect
automatically** when a bud is put in an ear and they're connected to
nothing; **switch automatically** when something starts playing here
(`audio::watch_playing`) while they're in an ear on another device (the
phone takes them back itself when it plays). **Never a tug of war**:
once they stop being connected here (a phone took them, or the person
disconnected them), nothing is taken by itself until their broadcast has
said "connected to nothing" for 60 s (`may_take`, tested), and one try
every 15 s at most. BlueZ 5.87 has the monitor among its experimental
interfaces: without `bluetoothd --experimental` the state says so
(`AirPodsState::not_listening`), Preferences greys the two settings, and
Olo Doctor offers to turn it on.
It publishes `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-airpods.json` (`AirPodsState`) on
every change, and answers `Request`s (JSON lines) on
`olo-airpods.sock`; after an upgrade (SIGURG from olo-session) it
starts again as the new binary. Idle it is asleep on BlueZ's signals,
the sound server's events and the channels: nothing is polled.

**Where recording comes from** with a pair connected is the person's
choice (`MicrophoneChoice`, Preferences ▸ Sound and ▸ AirPods: This
Computer's Microphones, AirPods (High Quality): their own stream's
source below, AirPods (Call Quality): Bluetooth's headset input). The
service makes that the input: as the pair's source or headset input
comes (`sound_changed`, once: the person may choose otherwise after),
and at once when the choice is changed while a pair is connected
(`follow_settings`, `input_for`: theirs if it's there and not the one
in use already; back to the computer's, the one last in use, only when
theirs is in use). It was only kept before, to be acted on when a
device next came or went, and the headset choice never was: with
"AirPods (Call Quality)" chosen the computer's microphones went on
being recorded from, and the voice service's processed microphone,
named for what it listens to, read "Core Ultra … Microphones (Voice
Processing)" beside two unprocessed AirPods ones (Ben, 2026-11-18, of
Teams in Chrome: "it still doesn't show the airpods device as 'Airpods
(Voice Processing)'"). The voice service follows whichever real
microphone is made the default input and puts its own source back in
front of it (`olo-voice`, "The person (or something) chose a
microphone"), so the processed one is then the AirPods', named so.

**Their own microphone** (`mic.rs`): while a pair's channel is open,
the service has a PipeWire source for it ("… Microphone",
`airpods_mic.ADDRESS`, made in process with pipewire-rs on a thread of
its own, `priority.session` 100 so it is never the input by itself). It
starts the AirPods' wideband stream (`proto::start_microphone`) only
while something records from it (the stream streaming) and stops it
1.5 s after recording stops, so idle it costs nothing, nor their
battery; Conversation Awareness is off meanwhile (speaking would duck
the sound), and their sound stays at music quality (A2DP AAC; checked
by ear on a lossless stereo track). Their frames (AAC-ELD, four of 480
samples a message at 64 kHz, though the config says 48) are decoded by
`olo-eld`; frames lost on the air (a gap in the frames' 24 kHz
timestamps, 180 a frame) are decoded empty, so the sound dies away
through the filter bank rather than stopping. `resample.rs` takes them
to 48 kHz (windowed sinc, Kaiser, 32 taps, 512 interpolated phases),
its ratio steered within ±0.5% to keep 60 ms waiting (the AirPods'
messages come every 31 ms on median and up to 53 ms apart, measured;
150 ms when voice processing is tuned for recordings, read as the source
starts streaming):
the two clocks' difference is followed, never by dropping or repeating
samples, and a source run dry fades out over 5 ms and back in. Each
cycle is given exactly what it asks for (`Buffer::requested`). Checked
on AirPods Pro 2: 12 s recorded, no gap, never dry, none lost, the
largest step between samples −50 dBFS (room noise); sound begins
320 ms after recording does (the AirPods' start, then the 60 ms).
`OLO_AIRPODS_CAPTURE=FILE` keeps the raw frames (to test `olo-eld`
against). `--microphone on|off` drives it by hand.

The command line asks it, for people and agents: `olo-airpods`
(`--status [--json]`), `--mode off|transparency|adaptive|anc`, `--set
SETTING VALUE`, `--rename NAME`, `--connect`, `--disconnect`,
`--quality music|calls`, each with `--address` for one pair of several.

Where they show: Preferences ▸ AirPods (`airpods.rs`, opened from
Bluetooth's "AirPods Settings…", Sound's and Deskbar's: name, levels
with a picture of each bud and the case, noise control, press and hold,
listening features, the microphone, and On This Computer); Bluetooth's
list (their model, their lowest level); Sound (under the output: model,
codec, music or call quality, noise control; in the input: where to
record from while they're connected); Deskbar's tray while they're
connected (`status::draw_airpods`, amber at 20%, red at 10%; its menu
has their levels, noise control, Conversation Awareness, Disconnect and
both panels), and the speaker's right-click menu (`sound_menu`, for any
device: every output and input, mute, voice processing (on or off, and
its settings in a submenu), and while AirPods play, their levels, noise
control, Conversation Awareness, Personalized Volume and music or call
quality). Deskbar follows the sound server's whole device
list (`audio::watch_devices`), the volume being the default output's. Their icons are `airpods`, `airpods-case`, `airpod-left`
and `airpod-right`, in every theme.

**Tests only look: never pair, connect or disconnect real AirPods.**
`OLO_FAKE_AIRPODS=1 olo-airpods --service` pretends a pair (AirPods Pro
2 USB-C, connected, taking every change); `OLO_AIRPODS_DIR=DIR` keeps
its state and socket in DIR rather than the runtime directory, so give
it to the service and to what reads it (Preferences, Deskbar: start the
session with it in the environment). `olo-fakesound` with
`FAKESOUND_AIRPODS=AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF` adds their output (AAC, music
quality, the default) and card, for Sound.

## The phone (apps/phone, olo_system::phone, olo_protocol::phone; Preferences ▸ Phone)

An iPhone's or an Android phone's messages, contacts and one-time codes,
on this computer. **Olo speaks to the phone itself**, in Rust, in
process, as it speaks to AirPods; nothing else is installed.

(It began, on 2026-11-16, as a front end to BlueFerry, a Python backend
over BlueZ's obexd that Olo Doctor installed. That evening its unit
wouldn't start, and Ben: "i don't love this blueferry dependency it's
going to be too flaky. get rid of blueferry and build everything we need
in rust ourselves and make the pairing/setup process much nicer and
intuitive and visually well designed", then "and also include support
for android too". BlueFerry's protocol notes remain the best account of
what an iPhone does over Bluetooth, and are where the iPhone's habits
below were learnt; none of its code is in Olo. Where it's still
installed, Olo Doctor offers to remove it: "BlueFerry is installed, and
Olo no longer uses it" (`Step::RemovePackages`, and Olo's Bluetooth
drop-in back to what AirPods alone need), since its obexd would hold the
profiles Olo's own then can't register: `Link::Taken`.)

**The protocols** (`olo_system::phone`, written from the Bluetooth
specifications):

- `obex`: OBEX's packets and headers, a client's session (Connect, Get,
  Put, SetPath, Disconnect; an object in as many packets as the other
  side takes, 32 MB at most) and a server's (`Server::next`: one whole
  operation at a time), over anything that reads and writes.
- `map`: the Message Access Profile's client side. `Mas`: a session in
  the phone's `telecom/msg`: `listing` (the inbox), `message` (one whole,
  a bMessage), `mark_read`, `send`, and `notify`, after which the phone
  connects back to **Olo's own Message Notification Server**
  (`serve_notifications`) and tells it of each message as it comes
  (`Event::New`, a handle to fetch it by). `BMessage::outgoing` makes a
  message to send: a recipient is structure in a bMessage, so one that
  would break out of its line (a line end, a second `@`, anything but a
  number or an address) is refused, never escaped; a line of the text
  that reads `END:MSG` is. Handles are hexadecimal and nothing else
  (`is_handle`), checked before one goes back to the phone.
- `pbap`: the phone's contacts in one pull (`contacts`: names, numbers
  and addresses only, by the filter; the owner's own card, entry 0,
  passed over), vCards 2.1 and 3.0 read (`parse`), and whose a number is
  however it's written (`key`: its last ten digits; `name_of`). **A
  phone's book has the same person more than once** (a card from each
  account it syncs; of Ben's 428 numbers, 68 were in several cards, 63
  of them under one name), so cards with one name (its letters and
  digits, any case) are one person; two or three people who share a
  number are all said ("Dad or Home"), and a number in more cards than
  that (a caller-blocking app's lists: four cards of 146 to 231 numbers
  each) is nobody's. Until 2026-11-17 a number in two cards was nobody's,
  and such a conversation showed as its number (Ben: "it is just showing
  numbers not contact names").
- `link`: **the link is BlueZ's**. Olo registers three profiles
  (`ProfileManager1.RegisterProfile`): the client's side of the phone's
  messages and of its contacts, and the Notification Server, with its
  service record (what a phone looks for to know this computer wants to
  be told). BlueZ finds the phone's channel for a profile, opens it and
  hands over the socket (`Profile1.NewConnection`: `Opened`, a `Stream`
  with a patience of 30 s); `Profiles::open` asks for one
  (`Device1.ConnectProfile`); `phones` lists what's paired and offers
  its messages (an iPhone by Apple's vendor id in its Modalias; its
  battery when BlueZ has it); `watch` tells when that changes, and when
  BlueZ itself goes or comes. **A BlueZ started again has forgotten
  every profile and says nothing of it** (an update; Olo Doctor
  changing how it's started; a crash): `ensure` registers them again
  with the BlueZ running now (known by its name on the bus), and the
  service calls it whenever BlueZ says anything and before every try.
  (Found on Ben's computer, 2026-11-16: Doctor's removal of BlueFerry
  restarted Bluetooth, and the phone stayed "isn't in reach" while
  connected, Try Again doing nothing, until the service was started
  again.) `solicit` advertises to an iPhone (below). No root, no obexd.

**What phones do** (kept true in `standin`, the stand-in phone):

- An **iPhone** refuses its messages (OBEX Forbidden) until its owner
  turns on Show Notifications for this computer (Settings ▸ Bluetooth ▸
  ⓘ), and its contacts until Sync Contacts; turning them on says
  nothing, so they're asked for again (below). An SMS and an iMessage
  both come as `SMS_GSM`; a listing's `subject` is the text's first
  128 bytes whatever length is asked for (taken for the whole text until
  2026-11-17: Ben's long messages ended mid-word, "call us using
  Contac"); its sent folder is empty (what's sent from here is kept here); it often
  gives a time with no zone (taken as this computer's). A message is
  sent with an empty originator, the recipient's `TEL` or `EMAIL`, and
  `TYPE:SMS_GSM` whichever way the phone then sends it.
- An **Android** phone asks on the phone, as it pairs or as the profile
  first opens, whether this computer may see messages and contacts. Its
  listing has only a message's first words (so a message that comes is
  always fetched whole), and what was sent is in its sent folder.
- **An iPhone shows its switches for a computer only while the
  computer advertises for them** (BlueFerry's notes, iOS 26: asking for
  its messages alone, refused, never brings them; Ben, 2026-11-16: "i
  never get these options"). So while an iPhone that's connected
  refuses its messages, or hasn't given its contacts in the first
  minutes, the service broadcasts a low-energy advertisement soliciting
  Apple's Notification Center Service (`Profiles::solicit`:
  `LEAdvertisingManager1`, `SolicitUUIDs` ANCS, discoverable for three
  minutes, a manufacturer id that claims to be nobody's), for fifteen
  minutes from when the phone first refused or Try Again was pressed
  (`ALLOW_FOR`), and never while pairing (two records for one computer
  on the phone, the notes say). After the fifteen minutes it asks every
  five, with no advertisement. The stand-in iPhone refuses to have its
  switches turned on while nothing is advertised.
  (Ben's, 2026-11-17: with it, Show Notifications appeared.)
- **Sync Contacts appears only for a computer that says it's a phone
  book client**: one with the Phone Book Access *client's* service
  record (0x112e). The contacts profile was registered under the
  phone's own service (0x112f) as a client, for which BlueZ publishes
  no record, and Ben's iPhone showed Show Notifications "but no sync
  contacts". It's registered as the client now (`registered_as`), with
  no role: BlueZ publishes the client's record from its own table
  (`get_pce_record`, version 1.2), listens on nothing, and connects it
  to the phone's 0x112f still. The stand-in iPhone refuses Sync
  Contacts to a computer without that record.
- **The computer says it's a hands-free device** (Ben, 2026-11-17:
  "have it identify as blueferry suggests"): Class of Device major 4
  (Audio/Video), minor 2 (Hands-Free, the byte 0x08), as BlueFerry's
  notes found an iPhone wants. Olo Doctor offers it wherever there's
  Bluetooth, a problem with an iPhone paired and a suggestion before one
  is, judged by the class the adapter says now (`Roots::bluetooth_class`)
  (`phone_class`: `Class = 0x000408` in /etc/bluetooth/main.conf, and
  Bluetooth started again), which bluetoothd applies itself at every
  start: nothing has to put it back. **BlueZ's hostname plugin puts its
  own class over it** when the chassis is one it knows ("laptop":
  Computer, Laptop): Ben's adapter stayed a laptop with the class set.
  So the fix also starts bluetoothd without that plugin (`-P hostname`,
  in Olo's drop-in, which the AirPods and BlueFerry fixes keep), and,
  since the plugin also named the adapter after the computer, writes
  that name in main.conf (`Name`: pretty, static, then transient
  hostname, as the plugin chose; one set there already is kept), or the
