  adapter would be "BlueZ 5.87". Preferences ▸ Phone's first step
  says so while the adapter isn't (`Adapter::hands_free`), with Open Olo
  Doctor: it must be so *before* the iPhone pairs. (At first Doctor said
  it only with an iPhone paired, and Ben, who had unpaired to pair
  again, heard nothing of it.) (Not Car Audio, the other class an
  iPhone gives a car's features to: it can turn on the iPhone's Driving
  Focus.) What the computer said as they paired is what counts, so a
  phone paired before may need pairing again.
- **A phone is paired from its side** (`bluetooth::pair_phone`, the
  Phone panel's Pair): `Device1.Connect` on it unpaired; the phone,
  refusing to be connected to without security, starts pairing, and
  leading the link it derives the low-energy keys as well: one bond for
  both radios, one entry for this computer on the phone. A `Pair` from
  here gave an iPhone a Classic bond only on an Intel controller (the
  notes). Where the controller ends the connection first, `Pair`; a
  code said to differ isn't tried again.
- **With a real iPhone** (Ben's, iOS, 2026-11-17, an Intel controller,
  BlueZ 5.87; the service's log): connected; BlueZ busy with it, asked
  again in 3 s; a channel to its messages open (a stream: RFCOMM) and
  refused; the advertisement begun; twenty seconds on, its owner having
  allowed it, its messages open (10 in its inbox), and three seconds
  later its contacts (355); the advertisement ended. Paired from the
  phone's side it has one bond for both radios (BlueZ's `Bearer.BREDR1`
  and `Bearer.LE1`). An Android phone has not been tried: BlueZ would
  connect its messages over L2CAP (packets), in basic mode where OBEX
  over L2CAP means ERTM, which may want Olo to open the channel itself.
  Groups' names (ANCS), and a store of conversations that outlives the
  service, are also to come.

**`olo-phoned`** is the service (service.rs, in the crate's library;
a real session's, `REAL_SHELL`): a program of its own, with nothing of
a window in it. It was `olo-phone --service` until Phone had a window:
the kit linked beside it cost it 3.5 MB at rest (8.7 to 12.2 MB,
measured; 9.3 MB as its own program). An `olo-phone --service` still
running from a version before starts again so across an upgrade, and
the session then ends it (`retire_dropped`) and starts `olo-phoned`.
With a phone paired, it asks BlueZ for a channel to its messages and
opens a session on it, on a thread of its own (`session`: it waits on
the phone, the service's loop never does). Refused: `Link::Allow`, and
tried again every ten seconds (`ALLOW_EVERY`; an iPhone advertised to
meanwhile, above). A channel BlueZ can't open while the phone is
connected says why, as BlueZ does, in the panel (`trouble`) and the log
(`ConnectProfile` waits on the phone, up to half a minute, so it's
asked from a thread). Open: `Link::Ready`; the
phone is asked to tell of messages, the newest 60 of its inbox are read
(what's there is history; an unread one that came within five minutes
is fetched whole and told of, as one that comes), and its contacts are
asked for, and again every 15 s for five minutes and then every five
minutes until they come (`ask_contacts`). A message that comes
(`FromSession::Came`: its listing's row for when, itself whole for its
text) goes in its conversation (`thread_for`: one for each number or
address, named by the contacts, else as the phone names the sender,
else the number). **A message read from a listing whose text may be
only its beginning** (`may_be_cut`: none, or 125 bytes and more: an
iPhone's 128 cut where a character ends, an Android's 255) **is asked
for whole**, once (`Cmd::Whole`; the ones kept from before too, the
newest first), and its text put in place of the beginning
(`FromSession::Whole`); which messages are known whole is kept with
them (`Kept::whole`), so none is asked for twice. Asking doesn't change
whether a message was read. The conversations kept from a run before
are named again by the contacts as the service starts (`name_threads`). A phone out of reach (`Link::Away`: BlueZ says it
isn't connected, or the channel can't be had) is tried when BlueZ says
anything of it and otherwise after 15 s, 30 s, then every minute for
its first half hour away (`AWAY_A_WHILE`: it doesn't connect by itself
when it's back, it's found by being asked for), and after that 2 and
then every 5 minutes (`AWAY`, `away_wait`); a session whose link drops
is tried again after 2 s, once. Another phone, or none: what the last
had is let go.

**A flaky phone** (Ben, 2026-11-17: "harden it as much as possible …
assume the phone connection is flaky and needs to be constantly
monitored … so that to the user it 'just works'"). What a night of his
iPhone showed in the service's own log, and what's kept true since
(`apps/phone/tests/service.rs`, `a_flaky_phone`, against a stand-in
phone that does each: `--tell set asleep`, `classic-gatt`, `deaf`,
`quiet`; `--tell asked` and `acquired` count what was asked of it):

- **A phone asleep takes the channel and says nothing.** 71 sessions
  of 78 ended on the 30 s a read waited ("Resource temporarily
  unavailable"); the phone dropped the link twenty seconds after each,
  the next asking paged it back, and round it went, a minute a round
  for hours. An answer did come at 50 s once. Now its first answers
  are waited for 3 minutes (`FIRST_ANSWER`; later ones 45 s, `ANSWER`:
  `Stream::patient` changes a channel's patience from outside what
  speaks on it), while the link stands (its end ends the wait at once).
  Silence past that is the phone asleep (`FromSession::Silent`), not
  the link gone: asked again after 30 s, 2, 5, then every 15 minutes
  (`SILENT`), and the panel says "connected but isn't answering (it may
  be asleep)". A phone that connects by itself (not paged from here in
  the last 20 s: `paged_at`) is awake and asked at once; after
  silences, no sooner than 30 s or 2 minutes.
- **Nothing is asked again at once for ever.** BlueZ busy with the
  phone (`InProgress`) is asked again in 3 s five times, then as a
  phone out of reach (`BUSY_SOON`); a phone that closes the channel
  within 10 s of its coming three times running, further and further
  apart (`hangs`, `HELD_UP`).
- **BlueZ stuck busy with a phone that isn't connected is told to let
  go** (Ben, 2026-11-17: "after leaving the room and coming back it says
  my phone is out of reach and doesn't seem to have auto reconnected").
  Out of reach, the link dropped; BlueZ's own reconnecting tried its
  hands-free side, which failed ("Host is down"), and BlueZ 5.87 never
  ended that connecting (profiles/audio/hfp-hf.c's `connect_cb`, on an
  error, never calls `btd_service_connecting_complete`), so the
  device's pending list stood for good and every asking after was
  refused `org.bluez.Error.InProgress: br-connection-busy`
  (src/device.c's `device_connect_profiles`: `pending || connect ||
  browse`): 52 minutes and counting, the service asking every 5
  minutes, each refusal unlogged (the same as the last), with the
  phone back in the room. Now three busy answers running with the phone
  not connected (no connecting takes six seconds: a page times out in
  five) have the next asking begin with `Profiles::unstick`, the
  device's `Disconnect`, which on a device that isn't connected only
  drops what's pending, answers an unanswered Connect and cancels a
  lookup (`device_request_disconnect`), and the asking after it pages
  the phone afresh; no more than every 2 minutes (`UNSTICK_AFTER`,
  `UNSTICK_EVERY`), and once a spell of busy answers
  (`tried_unstick`), said in the log. A failure the same as the last is
  logged again every 10 minutes with how many times it has been
  (`SAY_AGAIN`), so a service that keeps trying never reads as one that
  stopped. The stand-in plays it: `--tell set stuck yes` (refused busy
  until `Disconnect`; `--tell unstuck` counts), `--tell set in-reach
  yes` (not connected, but connected by the next asking, as a phone
  back in the room). BlueZ's own fix is upstream's to make (the failure
  passed to `btd_service_connecting_complete` in `connect_cb`).
- **Its other notifications are taken over low energy only.** BlueZ
  shows an iPhone's characteristics over the classic link too, with
  `org.bluez.Bearer.LE1`'s `Connected` false, and takes a subscription
  there; the phone tells nothing that way and BlueZ closes the socket
  at once. The service took the characteristics for the link, and
  opened it again the moment it closed: 4667 times in twelve minutes
  after one upgrade, until BlueZ refused ("Notify acquired"), after
  which it was never tried again. `Profiles::notifications` now gives
  none while that bearer is down (`low_energy`; a BlueZ too old to say
  is taken at its word), the bearer's coming is news
  (`Change::Link`), the phone is asked to connect that way every 5
  minutes while they're wanted (`LE_ASK`), and a link that closes
  within 30 s without a word, or can't be opened, is tried again
  after 5 s, 30 s, 2 and then every 10 minutes (`OTHERS_AGAIN`,
  `others_failed`), one line in the log, not one an opening. A link
  that held and went is asked for again at once.
- **A message sent while the link is down waits for it** (25 s,
  `HOLD`, the phone asked for at once), and goes when the session is
  up: a drop of a second or two no longer answers "The phone isn't
  connected". One whose sending broke off is still said to have
  failed (it may have gone: sending it twice would be worse).
- **A phone that doesn't connect back to tell of messages is looked
  in on**: its inbox's newest read every minute (`CHECK_UNTOLD`,
  `Cmd::Check`; it's asked once more to tell, `Cmd::Notify`), what's
  new taken as what's told of is. A phone that tells isn't looked in
  on: its session sits idle for hours, and a phone asleep that's
  asked something doesn't answer, which would end the session.

Measured (release, the stand-in phone): at rest with a session open,
with the phone's services showing over the classic link, and with the
phone asleep and its channel waited on: 0.0% of a core, 0 wakeups a
second each; subscribed to 0 times where it was 13 times a second.
A test's waits are a thirtieth of these (`OLO_PHONE_PACE=30`: `paced`).

**Nothing in it waits for good, and what goes wrong is seen** (Ben,
2026-11-17, his iPhone paired and the panel still at "Waiting for the
phone": "olo needs to supervise/monitor it and make it bulletproof").
What his phone showed, and what's kept true since:

- **BlueZ's sockets are non-blocking** (it reads them from its own
  loop; the flag is the socket's, so the descriptor it hands over has
  it): the first read failed at once with "Resource temporarily
  unavailable", and every session ended as it began. `Stream::adopt`
  makes it blocking, with its patience. **And of packets** where the
  phone offers OBEX over L2CAP (an Android; an iPhone offers RFCOMM
  alone), which BlueZ then connects by (profile.c, `record_cb`): each
  read one whole OBEX packet, read so and handed on as a stream; a
  write is a whole packet already. The stand-in BlueZ hands over
  sockets the same (non-blocking; packets for the Android's messages
  and contacts): with the fix taken out, the link's test fails as his
  phone did.
- **Every wait has an end.** Asked for a channel, BlueZ has a minute to
  answer (`OPEN_ANSWER`) and, once it has said yes, five seconds for
  the channel to come (`OPEN_COMES`): it says yes and opens nothing
  when it takes the profile for connected already, which left the
  service at "connecting" for good. Past either the asking is given up,
  BlueZ is told to let go of the profile (`Profiles::let_go`:
  `DisconnectProfile`) and asked again in three seconds. BlueZ busy
  with the phone (`InProgress`: connecting, pairing) is asked again in
  three too.
- **A phone that closes the channel is known of at once**, not when
  next something is asked of it: its end is waited for, asleep
  (`Stream::gone`: a `poll` for hang-up that nothing arriving wakes),
  and the session asked for again a second later. A session shuts its
  channel however it ends (`Shut`).
- **The service's own loop is watched** (`watchdog`): told as the loop
  takes something up and as it's done, and if it isn't done in 90 s
  (`STUCK`: it asks BlueZ what phones there are, and BlueZ can stop
  answering) the service ends, and the session starts it afresh. Two
  messages a turn of the loop; nothing at rest.
- **Every deadline the loop wakes for is acted on** (`deadlines`, each
  by name; `tick` acts on each that's past: moves it or lets it go). One
  that `tick` left as it was would have the loop turn without waiting,
  a core's worth: asking the phone again over low energy (`le_ask_at`)
  was waited for while a try of its other notifications was set for
  later, which `others_link` waits for, and the service spun ten minutes
  at a time for hours (2026-11-19: Olo's supervisor said "Seems stuck",
  141 % of a core). Both now ask `le_ask_due`, which isn't due while a
  try is pending, and a failed try ends the asking. A deadline found
  still past after a turn is said once, by name, as an error ("… is
  past and nothing moved it").
- **The pairing agent is BlueZ's default while a panel has it**
  (`Agent::register`: `RequestDefaultAgent`), so a pairing the phone
  starts is asked about too (BlueZ had "No agent available" for his
  iPhone's), and it's registered again with a BlueZ started since
  (the bus's word of its new owner).
- **It says what it does**: each change of how the phone stands is a
  line in the log (`olo-logs --print --program olo-phoned`): the profiles
  registered, the phone and whether it's connected, a channel open and
  of which kind, refused, its messages open, its contacts come, why a
  channel couldn't be had or a session ended; `PhoneState::trouble` the
  last of those while the phone is connected, `since` when the link
  came to stand as it does.
- **Olo Doctor watches it** (`phone_link`): with a phone paired, the
  service not running (the session leaves one stopped that ended again
  and again), or its profiles not registered (`PhoneState::profiles`:
  another program has them; Bluetooth not answering), or the phone
  connected and its messages not opened for three minutes
  (`phone-messages`, with why; its fix ends the service for the session
  to start afresh) is a problem it says; all well, it says so among
  what's fine.
Conversations are kept in memory only: **nothing a message says is
logged or written to disk**. It publishes
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-phone.json` (`PhoneState`: the phone's name and
kind, the link, whether its contacts came, its battery, how many
conversations and unread, a count of codes; never a sender, a number, a
text or a code) before it answers a request that changed it, and
answers on `olo-phone.sock` (0600): `Status`, `Conversations`,
`Contacts`, `Send` (to a number, an address or a conversation's key;
answered when the phone has taken it), `MarkRead` (on the phone too),
`Reconnect`, `Code`. Everything but `Status` is refused to a program on
an agent's screen. Each message is told of in a notification of Olo's
own, in the Message style, answered in place (the answer sent through
the session; a failure said in the notification), with Mark as Read
and, for one with a code, Copy Code. Settings are
`~/.config/olo/phone.json` (`PhoneSettings`, followed by inotify). At
rest it is asleep on its channel: 0 wakeups a second.

**One-time codes** (codes.rs). `find` is a heuristic: a number of four
to eight digits ("123-456", "123 456" and "G-123456" are 123456; right
after "code", letters and digits too) is a code only when a word for
one is said with it, in the same sentence: strong words ("verification
code", "OTP", "Bestätigungscode", "验证码", …) by themselves; "code",
"PIN", "password" only in a sentence about signing in or right beside
the number ("code: 4829", "482913 is your code"). Never amounts, dates,
times, decimals, phone numbers, order and tracking numbers, or codes
people and shops tell each other ("my code", door, Wi-Fi, promo). A
last line `@site #code` binds the code to that site. `service` reads
who it says it's from ("Your Acme Bank verification code…", "[Acme] …",
"… for Acme"). Tested on 30 messages that are codes and 18 that aren't;
`olo-phone --find-code` reads a message from standard input and says
what it finds. A code is kept in memory only, for five minutes
(`CODE_LIFE`), wiped (zeroize) when it's used or too old.

**Which tab it's for** (as macOS offers a code from Messages, but
choosing the tab). Every browser's extension host stays connected to
the service's socket (`Request::Browser`; apps/chrome/src/codes.rs). When
a code comes, the service asks them all which tabs are waiting
(`ToBrowser::Any`, which says nothing of the code); each extension asks
every tab's frames (`chrome.scripting.executeScript`, content.js's
`codeWaiting`: a field for a one-time code, shown and empty) and answers
with what it knows of each (`Waiting`: host, title, whether the field
has the focus, its tab shows and its window is in front, whether the
field declares itself `one-time-code`, how many digits it takes, whether
the page says the code was sent by text or by mail or comes from an
authenticator app, how long ago the field was first seen). After every browser has
answered, or 700 ms, `codes::choose` takes the best (`score`: bound to
its site +100 and to no other; the service the message names in the
tab's host or title +40; focus +25, text +20, showing +15, front +10,
declared +10, fresh +15; a field of another length, or a page that asks
for an authenticator's code and isn't the service's own, is out; of two
as good, the one whose field came up last) and **only that browser is
given the code** (`ToBrowser::Code`). A code field that comes up, or
takes the focus, after the code came says so itself
(`FromBrowser::Waiting { id: None }`) and gets one still good. In the
person's own browser it is **offered**: "Fill code 482913 / From Acme
Bank, by text message" under the field, in a closed shadow root (the
page can't read it; built with `textContent`, since a sender's words
are a stranger's), taken with a click, or ↓ then Return in the field;
Escape, or typing a code oneself, sends it away. Filled, it is spent:
gone from every other tab it showed in.

**A tab on an agent's screen** is known by its Chrome's environment
(`OLO_SCREEN`, read by the service from the connecting process, not
taken on its word). By Security ▸ Passwords' "In an agent's tab": **Fill
It In** (the default: Ben's "it should go to the agent's tab not the
user"): put in at once when the code is surely that tab's (`sure`: bound
to its site; or of the service the message names; or a field no older
than ten minutes on a page that says a text was sent), the person told
in a notification ("Code given to Agent Screen “agent”": who from, at
which site), and it goes in that screen's history (`kind: "code"`,
among Keys and Typing: who from, the host and the page's title, never
the code); when it isn't sure the person is asked; **Ask Me First**
(a notification on their screen, Give Code or Not Now); **Never**
(agents' tabs aren't candidates). The doubt it guards: a page on an
agent's screen that merely has a code field must not be handed the code
of a sign-in the person began elsewhere.

**Codes sent by mail** (Ben, 2026-11-17: "the extension should see that
the user is on a page waiting for a one time password, so it should
check the configured email accounts to see if a new message has arrived
with the code and keep looking for up to 60s until one arrives from
phone/email and then offer to fill it"). The phone service is where
every code goes to the browsers, so it reads the mail too (it runs
whether or not a phone is set up). When a code field comes up or takes
the focus (`FromBrowser::Waiting { id: None }`) and no code had is for
it, on a page that says the code was mailed (content.js's `by_mail`:
"email", "inbox", an address, masked or not) or says nothing of a text
or an app, every mail account set up and not left out
(`PhoneSettings::unwatched_mail`) is watched for a minute (`MAIL_FOR`;
`olo_mail::Watch`, a thread each): signed in with its app password from
the keyring, what came in the last five minutes read (of the inbox's
newest five, by INTERNALDATE), then each message as it comes, the
server telling (IDLE; one without it asked every five seconds), until
the minute is up (signed out) or a code is given to a tab (the watch's
connection shut: over at once); another field coming up watches
longer. **Where else mail lands is watched beside the inbox**
(`Session::elsewhere`; Ben's code that a rule filed away, 2026-11-18):
Gmail's All Mail (every label's and an archived message's are there)
and its spam; another account's every mailbox but sent mail, drafts and
the trash (by their special-use flags), its junk and archive first, 30
at most. What came to them in the last five minutes is read as the
inbox's is, then what each will number next is asked every five
seconds (`ELSEWHERE_EVERY`; in one asking where the server lists with
it, LIST-STATUS, else STATUS each), and what came to one that grew is
read, the inbox opened again where it had got to (`read_from`), so
nothing that came there meanwhile is missed. Each message goes on with
a key of its own, its Message-ID (else its mailbox and UID), so one in
two mailboxes (Gmail's inbox and All Mail) is one. A message's code
(`codes::find_mail`: in its subject, else in
its words read after the subject; who it's from, its sender's name if
the words don't say) becomes a pending code as a texted one does
(`mail_came`; each message once, the same code had already not again)
and goes to the tab by `choose`, scored by where the page says the
code comes (+20 when the page says mail and it came by mail, or text and
it came by text; `sure` takes a page that says mail as one that says
text). Mail's way of showing a code, alone on a line of its own under
"Your verification code" with a footer's year and address about it, is
`find`'s too: a message that says it's a code and has one number alone
on a line has that number. Nothing of a message is kept or logged.
Tested end to end (`a_code_from_mail_to_the_tab_waiting_for_it`: the
service against `olo_mail::standin`, an IMAP server of the test's own
reached through `OLO_MAIL_IMAP`, and a stand-in browser) and on the
mail of eleven services that are codes and three that aren't.

**A link to sign in with, sent by mail** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "i tried to
login to claude and it didn't manage to find the verification code in
my email", then "the ones that send links -- support that too by
having olo passwords extension offer to navigate to the link
received"). Some services mail no code but a button: Claude's "Your
secure link to Claude is here", "Click the button below to finish
signing in", whose page meanwhile shows a field for the code the link
gives when opened elsewhere. The button's address is only in the
message's HTML, so `olo_mail::Message` keeps a message's links
(`links`: what each is shown as and where it goes, `https` only:
`mime::html_links`; the addresses written out in a plain message
otherwise). A message with no code is looked at for one
(`codes::find_link`): it must say it carries a link to sign in with
(`LINK_SAYS`: "secure link", "magic link", "finish signing in", "link
to log in", …; a notice of a sign-in doesn't), and the link is the one
shown as the signing in ("Sign in", "Log in to Acme", "Continue":
`LINK_DOES`), else its only link that isn't something else (help,
privacy, unsubscribing: `LINK_NOT`). It becomes a pending offer as a
code does (`mail_link`; `Pending::link`) and goes to the tab it's for
(`codes::choose_link`): one of the person's own browsers, never an
agent's screen (a link signs whoever opens it in), at the link's own
site, or of the service the message is from, or whose page says
something was mailed and came up in the last ten minutes; once (it's
for the page that asked, not for whichever page waits next; an offer
that couldn't be shown may be made again). `ToBrowser::Link { url, to,
from }` → the host → the extension: background.js keeps the address
(`linkOffers`; the page is told only the host it goes to) and has the
page show the offer under the field as a code's is, "Open sign-in
link at acme.example / From Acme, in mail to ada@example.com" (the
link's site, `codes::site_of`, not its whole host: a long host's end
is what tells whose it is); taken (a click, or ↓ and Return), the
page says so (`link-take`, its id only) and the extension takes that
tab, and no other, to the address (`chrome.tabs.update`). A code's
offer says how it came too now, and to which account ("From Verda
Cloud, in mail to ada@example.com"; `ToBrowser::Code::mail` and
`account`: it said "by text message" for both; Ben: "it should say
from <email address> if it's from email"). Extension 1.15.5. Tested: `codes::tests`
(`a_sign_in_link_by_mail`, `whose_tab_a_link_is`), `mime`'s
`a_messages_links`, the service end to end (the mail test above: a
page waiting, the message delivered, `{"say": "link", …}` to its
tab), and in Chrome in a test session (the phone service, `cargo run
-p olo-mail --example imap_standin` as the mailbox, a page with a code
field: the offer shown, and taken, the tab at the link's address).
**Check for Codes** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "if i don't want to wait i can
right click in the field and in the olo extension menu choose to
'Check for OTPs' to make it check immediately"): the field's menu,
Passwords ▸ Check for Codes, on any page (whatever Passwords knows of
it). The extension says its tab's waiting again with `now`
(`FromBrowser::Waiting { now: true }`): the service gives a code or
link it already has that's for the tab, else reads the mail afresh at
once, whatever the page says of how its code comes (the watches under
way are ended and begun again: a new one reads what came in the last
five minutes before it waits; one under way only waits for the
server's word of a new message). Tested in the service's mail test (a
page that says "authenticator": the mail left alone; checked: signed
in to at once).

**The toolbar button's list** (popup.html/js/css): this page's logins,
one chosen (a click, the arrows; the first to begin with), then Fill
(the default: Return, or a double click) or Open Passwords, which
shows that login in Passwords (`popup-open` with its vault and id →
`Request::Show`, Passwords started first if need be; with no login to
choose it only brings Passwords forward). Ben: "if i click the
extension icon and click on one of the login items and then click open
passwords it should open or activate the passwords app and take me to
that specific login". (A click used to fill at once, so there was
nothing to choose and then open.) Extension 1.15.5.

**How well codes are found in real mail**: `cargo run --release -p
olo-phone --example mail_codes [MONTHS] [--misses]` runs
`find_mail` over every message of the accounts set up that says it
carries a code (any mailbox, read only: `Session::mailboxes`,
`look_in`, `search`, `read`), and prints counts by sender's domain
and, for a miss, its subject and the sentence that says so. On a year
of two accounts: 254 found; what wasn't found carried no code. A code
sent to an address that isn't an account set up can't be found: the
address a sign-in mails is the account's to give.

**What's looked in, and where codes go, is Security ▸ Passwords'**
One-Time Codes box (`phone::codes`; Ben: "move the phone prefs
one-time codes stuff into prefs -> security -> passwords and change it
up a bit so that you can choose what to monitor"): "Look for codes in:"
the phone set up ("Text messages to “Mira's iPhone”", `codes`) and
each mail account ("Mail to ada@example.com (Gmail)", not in
`unwatched_mail`), then Offer a code in the browser tab, In an agent's
tab and Copy a code no tab is waiting for, as before. Saved in
`phone.json`, which the service follows. Phone's panel says where they
went, with a Security… button (Security on its Passwords tab). The
palette's index names the sources by kind ("Text Messages", "Mail"),
and the spotlight lights their box (`spotlight::show`: no control so
named, its box).

**A phone asked for once at a time** (2026-11-20; Ben: "a problem
with the phone service reconnecting to my phone after i was away for
the night … try again doesn't do anything either"). Three faults, found
with a second investigator who reproduced each on a private bus:
- *The service asked over its own asking.* `devices` (the survey BlueZ's
  every announcement runs) took a phone not connected with an opening
  under way for a session gone: it dropped the opening and began
  another. But a phone being paged is not connected, and BlueZ
  announces every device to everyone: with some program holding a
  search, strangers come and go several times a second. So each
  asking was abandoned mid-page, the next was answered
  `br-connection-busy` (BlueZ busy with the first), and the first's
  real answer, a page timed out, was thrown away as an old one's. The
  service heard "busy" for five hours, took it for stuck, and its
  remedy (`Disconnect`) cancelled the one attempt that was real, every
  two minutes; `tries` was set to nought at each announcement, so it
  asked every fifteen seconds for good. Now an opening is its phone's
  until BlueZ answers it or its time is up (`OPEN_ANSWER`); a session
  ends when its phone goes from connected to not (`went`); what's
  counted (`tries`, `busy`, `hangs`) is kept through announcements and
  short drops and begun again for another phone, a long absence
  (`lost_at`) or messages open.
- *The notifications' waits were forgotten at every drop.* Their
  asking again goes 5, 30, 120, 600 seconds (`OTHERS_AGAIN`), but a
  survey that found the phone not connected set the count and the wait
  to nought, so a link that came and went every six seconds was asked
  at once each time: 2,400 times in four hours. The wait is kept
  across a drop (not woken for while the phone is away,
  `others_due`), and begun again only after a link that held or said
  something (`others_lost`). The two threads that read its sockets
  kept them when the link was let go (BlueZ then answered "Notify
  acquired"): the sockets are shut, which wakes and ends them
  (`link::shutdown_socket`).
- *Try Again threw its answer away.* It joins the asking in flight or
  begins one, says "Connecting to …" (`Link::Connecting`), and what
  comes of it stays in the notice until the phone works again
  (`report_retries`): Bluetooth's word where the phone is there, and
  where it answered no page, "… isn't in reach. Is it nearby,
  unlocked, with Bluetooth on?". An asking the service couldn't be
  given is said too (`Msg::RetryFailed`).
`Profiles::unstick` looks at `Connected` itself just before
(`Disconnect` on a phone that has connected meanwhile would drop it).
Phone's demo has the two states for pictures (`OLO_PHONE_DEMO=away`,
`=connecting`). Why the phone answered no page that morning isn't
known (TODO).

**Connecting a phone is Preferences ▸ Phone**, three steps each seen to
happen (phone.rs, `connect`; Ben: "make the pairing/setup process much
nicer and intuitive and visually well designed"; then, of a first
rework with a large title in a narrow centred column: "ewww it was
better before": it is a Preferences panel like the others, the kit's
heading and group boxes at full width, with room between its rows): a
drawn stepper (`stepper`: a numbered disc each, ticked green once done,
the one being done blue and bold); 1. **Find your phone**: the phones
Bluetooth sees nearby (a search started as the page shows), each with
Pair (one already paired with this computer for something else:
Connect); 2. **Confirm the code**: the six digits large, in two groups
(`code`), "Does “Mira's iPhone” show this number?", It Matches (Return)
or It's Different; 3. **Allow it on the phone**: the phone's own
switches for this computer drawn as the phone shows them (`switches`:
an iPhone's Show Notifications and Sync Contacts; an Android's Text
messages and Contacts), each turning green as the phone turns it on
(the service's state), the page following by itself. Pairing is the
Bluetooth panel's own watcher and agent (`bluetooth::link`): one
pairing, wherever it's started. (**Found building it**: the pairing
agent asked BlueZ for the device's name with a blocking call from
inside its own handler, on the connection's own thread, which never
gets its answer: every question a device asked while pairing, a phone's
"does it show this number?" among them, hung until BlueZ gave up.
`AgentObject::name` now asks on the handler's connection, awaited.)
Connected, the panel is how the phone stands, what is told of, and
One-Time Codes. A phone's row in Preferences ▸ Bluetooth has Messages
and Codes…; `olo-preferences iphone` (or `messages`, `codes`, `sms`)
opens the panel.

**Archived conversations** (Ben, 2026-11-17: "in the phone app the
ability to archive messages. if this can't be done for real on the
phone due to protocol limitations then at least let me archive them in
the phone app and have it remember. show the archived ones like we do
in telegram. and i also need to be able to multi-select the threads
from the messages list and bulk archive / unarchive"). The phone can't
be told: MAP reads and sends, and an iPhone's has no archive (nor
deletes). So Phone keeps its own (`~/.local/state/olo/phone/
archived.json`: each conversation's key and when it was archived,
written off the looper), and a conversation is archived until a
message comes after that (`archived_in`): it's back among the rest, as
Telegram's are, and leaves the file. As in Telegram: the archive's row
at the top of the conversations ("Archived", a few names, the unread
among them), clicked for the archive with a band back over it
("‹ Archived Conversations"), View ▸ Archived Conversations; ⌘-click
chooses a conversation too (the one open with it), ⇧-click every one
from the last chosen; a right-click is for the conversation or, on one
of several chosen, all of them ("Archive 3 Conversations", "Unarchive",
"Mark All as Read"), Conversation ▸ the same for those chosen or the
one open, Edit ▸ Select All Conversations. A search finds archived
ones too. Agents: `archive:NAME[,NAME…]` and `unarchive:…` (by key or
name) through the menus' socket.

**Elsewhere.** Deskbar's tray (`status::draw_phone`: a slab with its
screen, dim out of reach, amber at 20% and red at 10%, a blue dot while
messages are unread), shown while the phone is connected, has unread
messages or a code still good; its menu says how it stands, copies the
code that just came, tries the phone again, and opens the panel. The
command line, for people and agents: `olo-phone` (`--status [--json]`),
`--conversations`, `--read WHO`, `--send TO TEXT…`, `--mark-read WHO`,
`--contacts [QUERY]`, `--reconnect`, `--code`, `--copy-code`,
`--find-code`, `--settings`, `--set SETTING VALUE`; with nothing asked,
or `--open WHO`, it is Phone, the app.

**Its other notifications** (an iPhone's: `olo_system::phone::ancs`,
`apps/phone/src/others.rs`; Preferences ▸ Phone's "Show the phone's
other notifications", `PhoneSettings::others`). Apple's Notification
Center Service, which an iPhone offers over low energy to a paired
computer its owner allowed (its Show Notifications switch): every
notification on the phone as it's added, changed and removed, what it
says when asked, and its actions. Three characteristics: the
Notification Source (eight bytes a notification: event, flags,
category, count, its number), the Control Point (written: ask what a
notification says, ask an app's name, do an action) and the Data
Source (the answers, cut into as many packets as the link needs).
`ancs.rs` is the bytes (`told`, `get_notification`, `get_app`, `act`,
and `Reader`, which splices an answer from its packets: whole when
every attribute asked for has come), written from Apple's
specification. `link.rs` has the characteristics from BlueZ
(`Profiles::notifications`: found under the phone's device by their
UUIDs once BlueZ shows them; the two notified ones taken as sockets
with `AcquireNotify`, a packet a read, since two changes of a `Value`
property in one turn of BlueZ's loop would merge; the Control Point
written with `WriteValue`, type request, on a thread of its own, as a
write waits for the phone). `others.rs` decides, as a state machine
with no I/O (`Others`: `told`, `data`, `act`, `tick` return
`Effect`s: write this, show that, close that): what a notification
says is asked for one question at a time (answers share one stream),
given up on after 5 s; an app's name is asked the first time it's met;
then it's shown (the app as the subtitle, its title and text, its
actions' buttons: an incoming call's Answer and Decline, sticky; a
notification's Clear), shown again when it changes, and closed when
the phone removes it. Not shown: what was on the phone before the
link opened (old news, but for a call ringing), and text messages
while they come whole the other way (the Message Access Profile, with
their own notification: `messages_elsewhere`). Dismissing one here
does nothing on the phone (a call isn't declined by closing its
notification): only its buttons act. The link (`Service::others_link`):
opened whenever BlueZ shows the service on a connected iPhone, closed
when it goes (a call still shown ringing goes with it) or the setting
is turned off; while the phone is connected without it, BlueZ is asked
once to connect it over low energy too (`Bearer.LE1.Connect`) and the
computer advertises for the service for 15 minutes (`solicit`, the
advertisement an iPhone's switches need anyway: an iPhone connects
that way by itself to a computer advertising for its notifications).
`PhoneState::others` says they come; `PhoneState::model` is what the
phone says it is over that link (its Device Information's model
number, "iPhone17,3"). The log says which app a notification shown was
of, never what it said.

The stand-in has it all (`--tell set notifications yes`: its owner
allows them, and it connects over low energy to a computer advertising
for them; `--tell notify APP NAME TITLE MESSAGE [call|silent]`,
`--tell unnotify NUMBER`, `--tell acted`, `--tell set low-energy
no`): BlueZ's objects for the services and characteristics, answers in
20-byte packets, what was there before told as such at subscribing,
a malformed command and an unknown number refused. Tested against it:
the integration test (the link, a notification told of, asked, spliced
and cleared, the link gone), `others.rs`'s and `ancs.rs`'s own, and the
service in a headless session with the notification service: a mail
and a call shown, Answer pressed (done on the phone, the notification
gone), a mail read on the phone (gone here), Clear pressed, the link
dropped and back (the ringing call shown again), the setting off and
on. At rest with the link open: 0.0% of a core, 0 wakeups a second.
**Not tried with a real iPhone** (nothing is connected to one in a
test): on Ben's, read only, the phone was connected over the classic
link alone, bonded for low energy and not connected that way.

**Its calls, taken here** (`olo_system::phone::calls`,
`apps/phone/src/calling.rs`; Preferences ▸ Phone's "Take calls on this
computer", `PhoneSettings::calls`). The hands-free profile, which the
sound server speaks: PipeWire, as the hands-free unit of a phone
connected that way, runs the profile and carries the call's sound (the
far end to the output in use, the microphone in use to the phone), and
says what it knows on the session bus, `org.pipewire.Telephony`: an
object manager at `/org/pipewire/Telephony`, a gateway for each phone
connected hands-free (`…/agN`, `AudioGateway1`: `Address`,
`Dial(number)`) and under it its calls (`…/agN/callM`, `Call1`:
`State` (incoming, waiting, dialing, alerting, active, held),
`LineIdentification`, `Name`, `Answer`, `Hangup`); read from the
interfaces PipeWire 1.6's Bluetooth plugin declares (on this computer:
the service is there and the hands-free unit's record is offered).
`calls.rs` reads and drives it (`Telephony::survey`, `dial`, `answer`,
`hang_up`, `watch`: its signals, nothing polled). **A phone connected
hands-free sends every call's sound to the computer, as to a car,
wherever it's answered**, so Olo connects it that way only for a call
answered or made *here* (`Profiles::hands_free`: BlueZ's
`ConnectProfile` of the phone's audio gateway, 0x111f) and lets go
when no call is left; a call answered on the phone stays there, and a
phone that connected hands-free by itself is left as it is.
`calling.rs` decides, with no I/O (`Calling`: `answer`, `dial`,
`hang_up`, `survey`, `tick` return `Effect`s): Answer on a ringing
call's notification (the phone's own, above), `olo-phone --answer` or
Deskbar's Answer connects the hands-free side, waits up to 8 s for
the telephony service to have the phone and the call ringing, and
answers it there; Call on a contact's number in Phone, or `olo-phone
--call NUMBER|NAME`, connects, dials when the gateway is there, and
waits for the call to show. If the hands-free side doesn't come, a
call being answered is answered on the phone instead (its
notification's action: its sound stays on the phone), one being made
isn't (said). While a call is on, a sticky notification says who (the
phone's contacts by the number) and how it stands, with Hang Up; a
ringing call has one notification, the phone's own where there is one
(whichever word of it comes first). `PhoneState::call` says how a call
stands (ringing, calling, active, held; never who), for Deskbar's menu
(Answer and Decline, or Hang Up) and `olo-phone --status`;
`Request::Call`, `Answer` and `HangUp` (not from an agent's screen).
With calls turned off, Answer answers on the phone.

The stand-in is the telephony service too (its gateway while its
hands-free side is connected, `--tell call NUMBER NAME`, `picked-up`,
`hung-up`, `set hands-free yes`: connected by itself, `set
refuses-hands-free yes`). Tested against it: `calling.rs`'s own tests
(answered here, a phone connected by itself, made here, the hands-free
side never coming), the integration test (ring, answer, end, dial,
pick up, let go), and the service in a headless session: a call rung,
answered here (hands-free connected, the call's notification with Hang
Up), hung up (let go); one made, picked up, ended by the other end; a
phone that refuses hands-free (answered on the phone after 8 s); one
declined; a phone hands-free by itself (one notification, its Answer
pressed, left connected). **Not tried with a real phone**, and no
call's sound was heard: that part is PipeWire's.

**Its own picture** (`olo_protocol::phone::picture`,
`data/icons/phones.txt`; Ben, 2026-11-16: "generate theme styled icons
for the top 10 most popular android and iphone models and show the
closest matching icon for a paired phone based on what it is"). Twenty
pictures in both icon themes (docs/ICONS.md): the ten commonest iPhones
(17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, Air, 17e, 16, 16 Pro, 16 Pro Max, 16e, 15) and
Android phones (Galaxy S26 Ultra, S26, S25 Ultra, A56, A17, A07, Pixel
10, Pixel 10 Pro, Redmi A5, Redmi Note 14; Counterpoint's best-sellers
of 2026 and their makers' lines), each seen from behind. Which is
nearest: an iPhone by its model number ("iPhone18,1": the 17 Pro; a
Plus as its plain one, a 15 Pro or 14 Pro as the 16 Pro, older ones as
the 15), which it says only over low energy (`PhoneState::model`, read
when its other notifications' link is up); one that hasn't said, or a
newer one than any drawn, is the commonest (the 17). An iPhone's
Bluetooth product id doesn't say: no table of them is public. Any
other phone by its Bluetooth name, its model's until its
owner changes it ("Galaxy S24 Ultra": the nearest Ultra; "SM-A566B":
Samsung's own number; "Pixel 9 Pro XL"; "Redmi Note 13"); `phone` for
one that matches none. Shown in Preferences ▸ Phone (beside the phone's
state, and in the list of phones found, by their names), Deskbar's
phone menu, Phone's empty pane, and `olo-phone --status` names it.

**Kept between runs** (`apps/phone/src/kept.rs`). The service keeps the
phone's conversations, the handles of the messages it has seen and its
contacts in one file, `~/.local/state/olo/phone/kept.json` (the
person's alone: 0600 in a 0700 folder; what a message says is in it, as
in the phone's own store), so they are there the moment it starts again
(an upgrade, a restart, the next login), before the phone has been asked
anything and while it's out of reach, and what was sent from here (an
iPhone keeps nothing of it) isn't lost with the service. Written two
seconds after the conversations or contacts change (`KEEP_AFTER`: once
a burst has come, not at each; whole beside the file and moved over
it), and at once when a message is sent; read when the phone is found
(`devices`), for that phone alone (its address); another phone's
replaces it, and a phone unpaired has it removed (its device gone while
BlueZ still has its adapter, `Profiles::has_adapter`: with the adapter
gone too, switched off or unplugged, nothing was unpaired). Tried
against the stand-in: a message sent, the service killed, the phone out
of reach, the service started: the conversations with what was sent and
the contacts were there; unpaired, the file went. (The stand-in now
forgets what a departed program registered, as BlueZ does: the killed
service's profiles had stood in the next one's way.)

**Its music** (`olo_system::phone::music`; found 2026-11-17 on Ben's
iPhone). A connected phone is a player and the computer its remote
control (AVRCP), which BlueZ already keeps as a `MediaPlayer1` under the
phone's device (`MediaControl1.Player` says which: `…/avrcp/player0`),
with its `Status`, its `Track` (Title, Artist, Album) and `Play`,
`Pause`, `Next`, `Previous`. The service publishes what's playing
(`PhoneState::music`: title, artist, album, playing or not; a song's
name, unlike a message's, may be in the state) and takes
`Request::Music` (play, pause, toggle, next, previous; not from an
agent's screen). It follows BlueZ's signals: `Profiles::watch` now says
what kind of change came, `Change::Link` (devices, pairing, BlueZ
itself: the phone is tried) or `Change::Detail` (the battery, the
track, playing or not: read again, and no try made, so a new song
doesn't set off connecting), and never the position, which moves all
the while. `olo-phone --music [play|pause|toggle|next|previous]`;
Deskbar's phone menu has the track with Play or Pause, Next and
Previous; Phone has it under the list, with a Music menu
(`music:toggle|next|previous`). The stand-in has a player (`--tell
music playing|paused|none TITLE ARTIST`, `--tell pressed`: what its
remote control was pressed). Seen on the real phone, reading only: the
player's properties and methods are those. Not pressed on the real
phone.

**Phone, the app** (window.rs; Ben: "did you already build an app for
working with the messages, contacts etc? if not we need that too", and
"make sure the messages/contacts/etc app is really nicely styled, the
weather and telegram apps are good examples"). As Telegram's: a list
down the left, sized and put away by its divider (the kit's
`SidePane`), of the conversations (who, their latest words, when, how
many unread) or the contacts, with a search over both; beside it the
conversation as balloons (ours on the right in a tint of the keyboard's
blue, theirs on the card colour, a run of one side's joined, a heading
for each day, the time at each balloon's foot), a one-time code with
Copy under it, a balloon's own menu to copy its words; under it the
field to write in, as tall as its lines (six at most), and Send. A
contact with one number is written to at a click; with several, their
card has each. A number or an address typed in the search can be
written to with no contact. People are their initials on a colour of
their own (`olo_kit::person`; a head and shoulders for a bare number).
With no phone connected it says what to do (Connect a Phone…:
Preferences ▸ Phone); a phone refusing or out of reach is a line over
the conversation, with Try Again. A message's notification, clicked,
opens it at that conversation (`--open`); Deskbar's phone menu has
Open Phone. **A `tel:` link** (a number in an event's notes, clicked:
Phone is the app for `x-scheme-handler/tel`, `olo-phone tel:NUMBER`)
opens it at the number's card on the Contacts tab: its contact's, or
one of its own (`Shown::Number`: the number, Call and Message), the
number written as a phone's contacts write it (`+1 (646) 555-0100`;
another country's groups a space apart, E.123's `+44 20 7946 0018`),
the one the link gave in bold among its contact's others; Call there
calls it, as a click on a link calls nobody by itself. A number given as Phone starts is matched to its
contact once the contacts come (`contact_with`, by `pbap::key`).

It holds nothing of its own: it asks the service on its socket, off
the UI thread (`cx.work`), whenever the published state says something
changed (`PhoneState::changes`; the file followed with inotify, never
polled), and sends through it. Agents drive it by command (`open:KEY`
or a name, `to:ADDRESS`, `send:TEXT`, `tab:contacts`, `new-message`,
`mark-read`) and read it as its tree: each row is a button named by who
it is (its value their latest words), each balloon a list item ("Mira
Kovač: Here now"), the header a heading. `OLO_PHONE_DEMO=1` is made-up
people and no service (`=2000`: that many conversations and contacts,
and 600 messages in the one open: the benchmark's); the layout lint
(lint.rs: five states) and the live lint and bench use it.

*Fast, measured* (`tools/dev/bench --apps phone`, release, 120 Hz, the
2,000-conversation demo, at 1×, 1.5× and 2×): at rest 0 frames; the
pointer over it 0.5–0.7 ms a frame; the list scrolled 0.5 ms (p99 0.8,
worst 1.1); the conversation scrolled 0.2 ms (worst 0.9); typing 1.1 ms
(worst 2.0); the window resized live 0.8–1.0 ms (worst 4.0); every
frame within the 8.3 ms budget. What that took:
- The lists and the balloons are each one drawing that paints only what
  shows, found from where the scroller is scrolled to (`in_view`), not
  from the drawing's clip, which isn't narrowed to the scroller: by the
  clip every row of 2,000 was painted each frame (5.7 ms a frame).
- The conversation is laid out only when it, the width, the look, the
  clock or the day changes (`lay`, `LaidFor`), and wrapping its text is
  never all done in one frame: what shows is wrapped at once, the rest
  2.5 ms a frame from what shows outwards (`shape_more`, on
  `on_next_frame`: asked for with a zero timer, the slices ran back to
  back inside one frame), a message not yet wrapped taking the size it
  had, or a guess by its length, and what shows held where it is as the
  ones above it settle. Wrapped all at once, a resize with 600 messages
  took 46 ms in one frame. The wrap width moves in steps of 16 points,
  and not at all once the pane is wide enough for the widest balloon.
- What the search finds is kept until the words or the data change.

**Tests never touch Bluetooth, a phone or anyone's messages.**
`phone-standin` (olo-system's) is a stand-in BlueZ
on a bus of the test's own (`org.bluez`: its devices, profiles
registered, a profile's channel opened as a socket pair handed over the
bus, discovery, pairing through the agent with a code) with a stand-in
phone behind it (`olo_system::phone::standin`): an iPhone with made-up
people in it, or with `--android` a phone with an Android's habits;
`--unpaired` for one nearby and not paired. `--tell receive NAME ADDRESS
TEXT…` has a message arrive (the phone opens a channel to the
Notification Server and tells it), `--tell set messages|contacts|
connected|paired yes|no` turns the phone's own switches and takes it
out of reach, `--tell sent` prints what was sent through it.
`OLO_PHONE_BLUEZ=ADDRESS` points the link at that bus
(`DBUS_SYSTEM_BUS_ADDRESS=ADDRESS` the rest of Olo's Bluetooth: the
panel's pairing), `OLO_PHONE_DIR=DIR` keeps the service's state and
socket in DIR, `OLO_PHONE_SETTINGS=FILE` its settings; the service's
own `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` must be the private bus too, or its
notifications go to the person's. End to end with
`OLO_TEST_BUS=unix:path=…` (an `olo-bus` of the test's):
`crates/system/tests/phone_standin.rs` (the link and the profiles, for
both kinds of phone) and `apps/phone/tests/service.rs` (the service:
not allowed, allowed, the inbox and the contacts; codes to stand-in
browsers, one on an agent's screen; sending by name and by number; out
of reach and back; unpaired). The panel's steps were gone through in a
headless session against the stand-in (find, the code, the switches
turned on one at a time, connected), the review clean at 1×, 1.5× and
2×. The extension was tried in a copy of Chrome in a scratch
`XDG_DATA_HOME` on a page served from 127.0.0.1.

**The classic link has a word of its own.** BlueZ's `Device1.Connected`
is of any link: with the low-energy one up (an iPhone's notifications),
the classic one its messages need comes and goes without `Connected`
changing, as when the phone connects back by itself. Where BlueZ says
of each link (`org.bluez.Bearer.BREDR1.Connected`, 5.8x:
`Phone::bredr_connected`, None on an older one), the service counts
that link's coming as the phone's coming and its going as its going
(`came_or_went`, with a test), and watches both bearers for changes.
A phone that is connected and answers no page for its messages is said
so, plainly, and nothing is asked of the person ("… is connected, but
its messages aren't answering. Olo keeps trying."): why a phone doesn't
answer isn't to be known from the computer.

## The supervisor (apps/supervisor, Preferences ▸ Performance)

Keeps the desktop responsive; off by default. `olo-supervisor` is one of
the real session's services (`REAL_SHELL`): it waits, following
`performance.json` (`olo_protocol::performance::PerformanceSettings`),
until turned on in Preferences ▸ Performance, by Deskbar's gauge (a
click; its menu has the findings, Show in Activity Monitor and
Performance Settings…) or `olo-supervisor --on`. Then every two seconds
(about 4 ms on its own thread; each command line read once a process)
it looks at the person's own processes in /proc (`sample.rs`: told
apart by their folders' owner, a `stat`, not each one's `status`, ten
times the cost; a folder is its process's effective user's, so root's
are read once, in case one is the person's running as root, and kept by
the folder's change time, `Owners`; each file in one read) and:

- **Tiers first** (`olo_protocol::performance::tier`, Ben, 2026-11-01):
  what keeps the desktop responsive runs above everything else, always,
  supervisor or not: app_server's main thread (every input event and
  frame) at nice −10, olo-session, Deskbar and olo-wlproxy at −5, each
  asking rtkit for itself as it starts; olo-termd's threads every key
  typed in Terminal and its echo pass through (a client's reader and
  writer, each shell's PTY reader and writer) at −5 too, each asking as
  it starts (rtkit's high priority is reset in what a raised thread
  starts), and a shell termd starts put back at 0 before it runs, so a
  build in a tab never inherits it (measured, a byte through four
  processes' pipes as the echo goes, beside eight nice-0 burners on the
  same cores: p99 2.1 ms and worst 31.7 ms at nice 0, p99 0.75 ms and
  worst 2.8 ms at −5); Terminal's own three on that path at −5 as
  well (its writer to termd and its reader from it, `termd writer` and
  `termd reader`, and each shell's `shell output`, which reads what
  the shell prints into the screen before any of it is drawn): left at
  0 until 2026-11-21, they waited 113, 117 and 70 µs a run beside two
  burners a processor, with 27 of 495 twentieths of a second holding
  over a millisecond of waiting among the three, and 42, 35 and 15 µs
  with 3 at −5 (two runs each of 25 s, a key every 80 ms, release
  builds, four processors); a raise rtkit refuses is asked for again
  (`priority::raise_self_patiently`: rtkit gives 25 raises in 20 s for
  all of an account's programs, a session coming back starts more
  threads than that at once, and one refused stayed at 0 for as long
  as it lived: a helper thread asks again every seven seconds for a
  minute, and ends when nothing is left to ask for); in the person's
  own session only
  (on an agent's screen, `OLO_SCREEN`, and in a headless app_server they
  stay at their nice and leave cores to the scheduler: three agent
  screens' compositors at app_server's own −10, on fast cores at full
  clock, had competed with the person's desktop)
  (`olo_system::priority::raise_self`:
  `org.freedesktop.RealtimeKit1`'s `MakeThreadHighPriorityWithPID`, the
  one way an unprivileged process gets a negative nice, down to its
  `MinNiceLevel`, −15 here), and each frame's thread on a fast core
  (its `uclamp.min`, rule 9; no privilege needed). The supervisor
  re-asserts a tier for a
  program found above it (rtkit refused at its start, or a thread made
  since; `priority::raise_process`, every thread), on every pass: one
  lowered since (reniced) is raised again, one rtkit refused is asked
  again a minute later. app_server's main thread matters most: it reads
  the pad and Olo's touch filter judges palms on it (the palm model, as
  each frame comes), and it draws. It publishes what it raised
  (`SupervisorState::raised`; Activity Monitor's "Olo's own" row) and
  notes once a program it couldn't. Only then the focused app over
  background work, which is the lowering below.
- **The voice services** (olo-voice, olo-airpods: the audio tier,
  `AUDIO_NICE`, −10 as app_server's): raised as they start, their
  processing thread on a fast core (`AUDIO_UTIL_MIN`). PipeWire's thread
  for their sound (`data-loop`, `AUDIO_THREAD`) should be realtime:
  libpipewire asks rtkit as a stream starts. The supervisor looks: one
  that isn't is asked for again (`olo_system::priority::realtime`: a
  200 ms RLIMIT_RTTIME set first, which rtkit wants), and a minute after
  each refusal. rtkit gives realtime to 15 processes a user by default;
  a desktop's programs use that up, and Olo Doctor offers more.
- **Priorities** (`priority.rs`): background work, known by name (the
  settings' list: compilers, linkers, build tools, indexers) or a
  terminal's job busy for a minute and more, has every thread lowered:
  nice up to the setting's (never down: unprivileged, it couldn't come
  back), `SCHED_BATCH`, idle I/O priority. Never a realtime thread (a
  program's sound), and putting back only touches threads at batch, so
  one made realtime meanwhile stays so (it once put every thread to
  `SCHED_OTHER`). A class is set with the thread's mark kept (`policy`:
  SCHED_RESET_ON_FORK, which a window's looper has once registered,
  "Realtime threads"): the kernel lets nobody without privilege take
  the mark off, so set without it a marked thread was neither lowered
  nor put back. A nice orders threads only inside their cgroup: one
  running in a unit of the person's own manager (a build service, a
  `systemd-run` scope; `olo_system::systemd::user_unit_of`, from its
  cgroup) has the unit lowered whole as well (`CPUWeight=idle` for as
  long as it runs, its cgroup's `cpu.idle`: it gets the processor only
  when nothing beside it wants it; `priority::unit_lowerable`: never an
  app the person started, `app-…`, nor a unit with a weight of its own),
  put back as its last lowered process ends or the supervisor is turned
  off. That's why lowering a build's compilers didn't help before: in a
  service of the user manager they were in a cgroup with five times the
  desktop's weight ("Realtime threads and the kept core", Groups'
  weights); Activity Monitor says when a unit was lowered. Never the active window's app
  and what it started (followed from app_server's `WindowsChanged`), and
  never Olo's own programs (by name, or beside the supervisor). One
  lowered and then brought to the front (a program started from a
  terminal and busy for its first minute, whose window the person
  then turns to) is put back as it becomes the active window's, and
  lowered again once it no longer is, if it still counts as
  background: it used to stay lowered until the supervisor was turned
  off (found in review, 2026-11-20). Put back, or turned
  off, batch and the I/O priority are put back (a raised nice stays until
  its process ends: the account may not lower one, `RLIMIT_NICE` 0); a new supervisor (an upgrade) takes over what the
  last one lowered from its published state, or puts it back if off.
- **The background group** (`group.rs`; `olo_system::background`,
  `olo_system::session_groups`; "Give compilers and linkers only spare
  memory", off as it comes; kernel/TUNING.md has the measurements and
  the three reviews that shaped it). Linux has no link between a
  process's priority and what is taken from memory first: it chooses by
  control group. Olo's login divides a login session in two before the
  desktop starts (`desk`, and `bg` beside it: "The session divided",
  under the login screen), and here:
  - **Who goes in `bg`**: compilers and linkers by their own name
    (`olo_protocol::performance::COMPILERS`, of the names the person
    has in the Background list; every one of them is in that list as
    it comes, which a test keeps so: Rust's own linker, gcc's link
    driver and mold as a driver starts it, `ld.mold`, were in the
    first and not the second until 2026-11-21, and so were never moved
    by name). Never what starts them: cargo, make,
    a cache's server, a shell start programs someone is waiting for (a
    window, a server an editor asks, a helper asking for a password),
    and what a process starts is born in its group. Found at the
    supervisor's look and moved by one write, the process checked to
    be the one seen before and after (`background::move_to`); only out
    of the desktop's own group. What a compiler held until then stays
    charged where it was (up to two seconds of its life).
  - **The allowance** (`background::allowance`, `memory.high` of `bg`,
    which is the person's file by the login's doing): what the group
    holds plus what is to be had for nothing, less a reserve
    (`background_reserve`, 12% of memory). To be had for nothing: what
    is free, and a credit (`Credit`) of the cache the kernel has down as
    unused that is neither the group's own nor mapped by a program.
    The credit is all of it while the desktop's own group isn't seen
    to wait on memory (`desk/memory.pressure`), halves between two
    readings in which it waited more than 1% of the time (each reading
    against the time since the one before, kept while the group is
    empty), comes back at a tenth of it a second, and is nothing where
    the desktop's waiting can't be read: the kernel's "unused" is a
    guess, and the desktop's waiting is the fact. Never under what the
    group's programs themselves hold
    at the deciding look, unless little is available. Droppable file
    cache is no more than is on the group's two file lists, nor than
    its files less its memory files. What the rule forbids is kept by
    the kernel, not by the keeper being quick: the group's swap
    ceiling (below).
  - **One keeper** (`background::Keeper`): a lock for the session
    (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-background-session-N.scope.lock`), so a
    second supervisor reaching the same session neither keeps nor
    lifts; a thread at the background's own priority, asleep on the
    group's `cgroup.events` while it is empty and looking four times a
    second while it isn't; the allowance read back at every look
    (nobody else's figure stays); lifted when the group empties, when a
    figure can't be read (said once), and when stopped (read back).
    A look never waits, not for memory to come back and not for a
    process: the allowance is written without waiting (O_NONBLOCK,
    Linux 6.16; on a kernel before it nothing is kept, and said why),
    and what the group then holds over it is taken back by a second
    thread, the taker (`memory.reclaim`: its droppable cache first,
    then its programs' own), for the look that decided it and no
    other. And what the rule forbids, the kernel refuses while there
    is memory to spare: at every look, before the allowance, the
    group's swap ceiling (`memory.swap.max`) is closed if the look
    leaves its programs what they hold; so whoever takes memory back
    (the group's own programs as they ask for more, the taker, a part
    asked for a moment too late) swaps nothing of theirs, and a
    program that outgrows its allowance is slowed until a look gives
    it more. When the computer is short the background's is meant to
    go first: the ceiling is open (not a figure) at a look that puts
    the allowance under what the programs hold or comes within half a
    gigabyte of it (the band), looks come every 50 ms from far enough
    off that the band isn't crossed between two (`near`: within 3 GiB
    of the line), and what of the desktop's own went to swap lately
    (`Lately`: its group's swap seen to grow, a fall paying back, half
    as much every five seconds) counts as needing its room back first
    (a ceiling kept closed had the kernel meet a desktop's sudden
    need out of the desktop's own memory). Open, which the kernel
    takes first is its own choice: the allowance and the taker's
    asking lean it towards the background's, and in the guests it
    mostly was the background's that went. The price is
    within the band, where a build that outgrows its allowance has
    its own swapped with memory to spare. The login hands the keeper
    `bg/memory.reclaim` and `bg/memory.swap.max` for it; a session
    without them is kept by the allowance alone, only while memory is
    short, and says so. kernel/TUNING.md, "The keeper's own write",
    has the six forms this took, the reviews that faulted the first
    five, and how far each sentence here goes.
    A
    guard (`olo-supervisor --background-guard`, a process waiting on a
    pipe the supervisor holds the other end of) lifts both and moves
    what is in the group back if the supervisor ends by any other
    road; a guard that can't be started, and there is no keeping; one
    that ends while the keeper keeps is replaced on a thread of its
    own (starting a program can wait on the kernel), the group
    without allowance and ceiling until the new one says it is there.
    Nobody
    keeping, nothing stays in `bg`: stopped, ended or killed, what was
    there goes back among the desktop's. The lock is *let go* when its
    holder is done (`LOCK_UN`), not only closed: it belongs to the open
    file, and a child of the supervisor being born at that moment has a
    copy of every open file until it becomes its program, so a lock
    that was only closed stayed with it and the next to ask was told
    another keeps (the keeper's test, under load; then a test of just
    that, which failed at once: four threads starting programs, the
    lock taken and dropped 20,000 times). For the same reason the
    guard, who comes after a keeper that died, asks for the lock over
    a second before it takes it that another keeps.
  - **Nothing of it on the supervisor's realtime thread** but a filter
    of the process table it already has and a list sent over a
    channel: a worker thread starts and stops the keeper, reads where
    a process is and moves it, and tries a refused move again after 2,
    8 and 32 seconds, then says so once.
  - **Off**: the allowance lifted and read back and everything still
    in `bg` moved back to `desk` (off the idle processors), by the
    keeper under its lock, and what came of it noted (how many were
    left, or that the list couldn't be read). A supervisor that starts
    with the choice off, or turned off altogether, clears what one
    before it left the same way, if nobody keeps. While another
    supervisor keeps the group, this one puts nothing in it and asks
    again at every look. A compiler the active window's app started
    is left where it is while that window is in front, as the
    priorities leave it. In a session that isn't divided there is
    nothing to do, and Preferences says what it takes.
  Tests: the rule, the credit, the keeper on groups of plain files (one
  keeper, read-back, lift), the move, the choosing, the worker thread
  with a made-up compiler; against the kernel itself in a guest:
  `tools/dev/kernel-check session-groups` (the login's steps as root,
  then what the person may and may not do: 51 checks), `keeper` (a
  group asleep, a file locked in memory, a session from before the
  login's hand-over, a program growing with memory to spare, a
  desktop that suddenly needs more than there is (four ways), swap
  on a slow disk: 37 checks; on a kernel before 6.16,
  that nothing is kept) and
  `groups` /
  `groups-cold` with the case `olo` (this keeper as the one that
  keeps). `OLO_KBENCH=` names another build of the keeper, to
  measure two in turn; `OLO_GUEST_KERNEL=` another kernel for the
  guests (one from before 6.16: its packages unpacked in scratch).
- **Watchdog** (`detect.rs`), each from several signals, with a
  confidence and its evidence: stuck in a loop (busy at least `spin_cpu`
  of a core in every sixth of `spin_minutes`, waiting on almost nothing,
  almost no I/O, its memory unchanged); leaking (anonymous memory and
  swap, one sample a minute for three hours, rising by a least-squares
  fit at least `leak_fit` R² over `leak_minutes`, by `leak_rate_mb` a
  minute and `leak_growth_mb` in all, most of its steps up); too much
  memory (`memory_share` of RAM while less than `memory_available` is
  free, or tasks stall on memory (PSI) more than `memory_stall`, worse
  if it's growing or the system swaps); zombies (a parent leaving
  children unreaped `zombie_minutes`, urgent at `zombie_count`). Every
  number is in `Thresholds`, tuned in Preferences.
- **Urgent findings** (stuck for sure, memory that runs out, many
  zombies) ask once a process and kind in an alert (`olo.supervisor`,
  named "Performance"): Ignore This Process (into the settings'
  `ignored`, by name or command), Show in Activity Monitor (`--inspect`),
  Stop Process (TERM, then KILL after 3 s). Not asked again after an
  upgrade.

**The embedded controller, watched** (`ecwatch.rs`,
`olo_system::ec_storm`; always on, whatever Performance says: it isn't
about the person's programs). Ben, 2026-11-17, his brightness keys dead
for two hours and the battery running down on its charger: "add
something to olo's supervisor to do this if an unsustainable backlog
builds up". A laptop's embedded controller tells the kernel of each
thing that happens to it with an interrupt, and the kernel queues a
handler for each without limit; a controller repeating itself (a
ThinkPad P1 Gen 9's: its charger coming and going 23 times a second)
fills that queue faster than its handlers run, and the keys' and the
ports' handlers wait behind (AGENT-NOTES, "The embedded controller's
event storm"). From outside the kernel a storm is two things at once,
neither alone: the ACPI interrupt held at 8 a second or more
(`interrupts`, the `acpi` line of `/proc/interrupts`; the P1's: 46) and
workers of the EC's query queue standing blocked (`waiting`:
`kworker/…+kec_query` in state D, six or more; a key or the lid: one,
for a moment). `judge` takes two readings four seconds apart.
Measuring means reading every process's `stat`, so it's done only with
reason: `follow` sleeps until UPower says the power supply changed
(its `PropertiesChanged`, any of its objects), and looks only when that
has happened ten times in fifteen seconds (`Watch`: a charger plugged
in makes a handful, a battery in use one every half minute); a look
that finds nothing rests two minutes. In a storm it looks every twenty
seconds, and three looks without one end it. At rest the supervisor,
this included, is at 0.0% of a core and 0 wakeups a second (20 s, a
test session).

A storm found, the supervisor says so: a notification that stays
("The laptop's controller is flooding the system": what may stop
working, and that a full shut-down clears it; its click opens Olo
Doctor), and `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-state/ec-storm.json`
(`performance::EcStorm`: since when, events a second, handlers
waiting) for as long as it lasts, which Olo Doctor reads as a Critical
finding with the whole account (`checks::ec_storm`). Over, the file
goes and the notification closes. It says, and mends nothing: keeping
the queue short is the guard's, below.
`OLO_EC_STORM_DEMO=SECONDS olo-supervisor` says a made-up one for that
long, to see it; in a test session give it a runtime folder of its own
(`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR=/var/tmp/… WAYLAND_DISPLAY=/run/user/UID/wayland-N`,
the display by its whole path), or the person's own Olo Doctor reads
the file: test sessions share `/run/user/UID`.

**The guard** (kernel/ec-storm, `olo_ec_storm`; apps/ec-storm; Olo
Doctor's "Guard the Keys", a suggestion on a computer with an embedded
controller). The kernel's EC driver looks up a query's handler in a
list, and a handler a module adds (`acpi_ec_add_query_handler`,
exported) goes first in it, before the firmware's own for the same
query. The module walks the controller's ACPI methods as the driver
does, and for each `_Qxx` adds a handler that counts
(`olo_ec_storm_count.h`): the first event of a kind to come runs the
firmware's method; one that comes while that runs is only counted, up
to eight owed, and the one running runs the method again for each. An
event carries nothing but its number, and its method reads what is so
now, so nothing is lost but repetitions; a flood of one event costs a
counter's change a time and one worker running its method back to
back, the queue never grows, and the keys' handlers run as they come.
Nothing of the driver's is read (no structure, no probe: the first try,
by hand on the night, read three private structures by their offsets).
It prevents a backlog; one already there (handlers queued before it
was loaded) it doesn't shorten, so it is loaded at every start
(`olo-ec-storm.service`, as Olo's other kernel services: built for the
running kernel by `olo_kmod`, said in `/run/olo-ec-storm/status`),
and only on a kernel series in `kernel/ec-storm/CHECKED` (the driver's
functions are declared in its own header: nothing at build time says
if they changed; `tools/dev/ec-storm-check --series vX.Y` compares the
driver with the one it was written against, 7.2 and 7.3 the same).
`/sys/module/olo_ec_storm/parameters/stats` says what it has done
("guarding 64 ran 812 counted 0"), which Olo Doctor shows. Checked:
its counting from sixteen threads (32,000 events of a flood: 2,111
runs, never two at once, a run after the last event; 5,000 one at a
time: 5,000 runs; five in a burst: five), its build for 7.2.15, and in
a KVM guest (no controller: refused, "No such device", the kernel none
the worse). **Not tried with a real controller's events**: that takes
a computer with one and its owner's word.

It publishes what it does in `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-supervisor.json`
(`SupervisorState`: on, its pid, what it favours, findings, what it
lowered and why, the last 50 things it did, memory); a state whose
supervisor has gone reads as off. Activity Monitor's Supervisor section
shows it as cards (and turns it on or off), each process's inspector a
Supervisor tab; Deskbar's gauge (`status::draw_gauge`, shown when it is
installed) counts the findings, red when one is urgent. Agents read
`olo-supervisor --status [--json]` and drive the same controls.
**Test it with a private `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` and
`OLO_SUPERVISOR_ONLY_UNDER=PID` (only that process and what it started
are looked at), never on the person's own processes; and give every
program it may start `OLO_ACTIVITY_HELPER=off`.**

## DriveSetup (apps/drive-setup, olo_system::disks, udisks-fake)

BeOS's DriveSetup with Haiku's disk map: the chosen disk drawn to scale
(`map.rs`: every stretch at least 48 px so small partitions keep their
labels, coloured by family: Linux, Windows and everywhere, encrypted,
swap; an unlocked volume shows what is inside under a purple band; free
space hatched) over a `ColumnListView` of every disk, its partitions
(logical ones under their container, unlocked contents under what holds
them) and its free space. The Disk and Partition menus and the context
menu act on the selection; double-click opens, mounts, unlocks or
creates, whichever fits.

`olo_system::disks` is the UDisks2 client (blocking, so call it from
a worker): `status()` reads `GetManagedObjects` into `Disk`s, `Volume`s
and `Job`s (all `Serialize`); each mounted volume's
`space` (`Space`: size, used, free, from statvfs at its first mount
point) comes with it; `watch(f)` calls `f` after each burst of
UDisks signals; the operations (mount, unlock, format with an optional
LUKS passphrase, create/delete/resize partitions, label, new table,
eject, SMART update, cancel a job) map UDisks errors to words with
`error_text`. `release(volume)` unmounts and locks what is in use before
a format or delete. `write_image` streams a file onto the fd from
`OpenForRestore`; `benchmark` reads spread samples and random 4 KiB
blocks from `OpenForBenchmark` (read-only). UDisks itself asks polkit.

The list's Free column shows a mounted volume's free space after a
small bar of how full it is (red past 90%), and the status line says
"N free of M"; while the window is open the app re-reads every 5 s,
since writing files sends no UDisks signal.

The app runs one step at a time (`DriveSetup::run`: a worker, reporting
progress; Stop sets its flag, or cancels the UDisks job), shows UDisks'
own job progress in the status line, and re-reads on every change.
Destructive steps are behind an alert or form naming the disk and
device; nothing destructive is offered for the disk or volumes holding
the running system (`Volume::system`, `Disk::system`). On Olo's own kit
(olo-kit): the window is a `DriveSetup` view on its own looper, told
what the disks are by workers (`cx.work`, and UDisks's news and a
step's progress through `cx.messenger()`); the forms (Format, Create,
Resize, Rename, Unlock, New Partition Table) are `Form` views in
windows of the main one's (`open_window_here`), made from plain data
(`FormSpec`: their fields are made in their own window) and handing
back what was typed (`Msg::Submit`), drawn as alerts with fields
(`AlertFrame`, `paragraph`, `button_row`; Return submits, also from a
field, and Escape cancels, the keyboard kept in the form), each window
as tall as what it shows as fields come and go (`fits_content`: an
`AlertFrame` lays what it holds out in flow, so its window knows how
tall that is, or Format's form would be cut off at its Encrypt box); a
resize's form asks what the file system allows on
a worker of its own; the benchmark is a window on a looper of its own,
told its samples by its own thread; the map is one canvas keyed by a
count of what it shows changing, a click found again from the same
arithmetic that drew it (`map::item_at`), and its segments after the
first are their own grid for the layout review. A periodic re-read that finds nothing
changed draws nothing. Agents: `--list` prints
`Status` as JSON; `--mount`, `--unmount` and `--eject DEVICE` do the safe
steps.

**Never test on real disks.** `OLO_UDISKS_BUS=ADDRESS` points the
client at another bus, where `udisks-fake --address ADDRESS` (in
olo-system) plays UDisks2 with four made-up disks (an NVMe system
disk, an empty SD card, a USB stick, an encrypted USB disk whose
