  the line is let go, and followed by every Tracker window as the
  settings change (`columns::follow_settings`); agents read each line
  as a Splitter "Column width" whose value is the width, and set it
  through the settings. In a window, a column is never wider than the
  window less the start of the next column (`BESIDE`: its line always
  shows, with the next column's icons, which say a folder opened
  there), by the window's width as it is at render time
  (`fit_columns`, `cx.viewport_size()`: by the scroll view's bounds of
  the frame before, a window just tiled narrow kept the wider column),
  and a whole number of device pixels (a width of 221 points is 331
  and a half at 1.5×). The line is one line (a quarter of the way from
  the document's ground to its text, so it shows in every look), the
  last of its column, which the rows on both sides meet at every
  scale: it was an etched pair whose second half doesn't show on a
  list's ground (a selected row stopped short of the line one saw)
  and which left a device pixel of ground before the next column at
  1.5× and 1.75× (the layout review's seam; `style::Rule::Etched` is
  for a panel's ground).
  Editing a name is a `TextField` over the label (items.rs `Rename`);
  Return or a click elsewhere renames, Escape doesn't. In the list view
  it's over the Name cell (`ColumnListView::over_cell`), no wider than
  the column (`Rename::element_within`): a name longer than the column
  scrolls in it. The list view, Find's results and Go To's names key
  their rows by what each shows (`folder::row_key`: the path, size,
  date, kind, icon and backup mark), and an entry's texts in a list
  (`Entry::shown`: name, size, date, kind) are made the first time it's
  drawn and kept with it (an item changed on disk comes as a new
  entry), with what it is hashed once (`Entry::look`). The icon views
  draw a row of the grid at a time and the column view a row of a
  column (`uniform_rows`, rows and drawings keyed by what they show,
  `FolderWin::icon_row_key`, `column_row_key`): a step of the
  selection makes and draws the row it left and the one it's on, a
  scroll makes only the rows it brings near. The band and a drop's
  outline are a drawing over the rows, in the content's own
  coordinates. Where the content is in the window comes from where it's
  scrolled to (`icon_geo`, `col_geo`: the scroll handles' place and
  offset), never from where it was last drawn: a drawing is laid out
  where its content would be unscrolled, and the stage moves it.
  The column preview is keyed by its file and the thumbnails made
  (`thumbs::made`).
- **A picture's icon is the picture, a video's a frame of it** (the
  icon view's big icons and the desktop's; `items::small`, `thumbs.rs`;
  Ben, 2026-11-17: "in tracker's icon view the icons should show
  preview thumb of images/videos"). Asked for as a row is drawn
  (`thumbs::of`: so only what's in view), made on the thumbnails'
  thread, the last asked for first (what has just scrolled into view;
  no more than 240 wait, the oldest askings let go), and the kind's own
  icon shows until it's made (a row with a picture in it is drawn again
  as pictures come: `thumbs::made` in its key). Kept in memory (900 at
  most, those asked for longest ago let go) and on disk where every
  desktop keeps them: the freedesktop thumbnail cache,
  `~/.cache/thumbnails/normal` (128 pixels a side; `large`, `x-large`
  and `xx-large` for the column view's bigger previews), a PNG named by
  the MD5 of the file's URI that says the file and its date
  (`Thumb::URI`, `Thumb::MTime`), the person's alone (0600 in 0700
  folders), so a folder of photographs is decoded once, by whichever
  program shows it first, and other programs' thumbnails are used.
  What's drawn is made from that at the exact device size (`drawn`: the
  picture fitted to the 48-point box at the scale, its shape kept; one
  smaller than the box in points is a point a pixel, as big on every
  display), a texture pixel a device pixel, in a hairline frame, and
  darkened as an icon is when selected. A video's frame is the
  preview's (`olo_preview::media::video`). What decoding took goes back
  to the system when the queue is empty (`malloc_trim`). Measured
  (release, a folder of 35 pictures and a film, icon view, three runs):
  resident 84 to 91 MB against the installed build's 74 to 75, of which
  7 MB is the bigger program's own pages (the recogniser linked for
  Quick Look: file-backed, 58 → 66 MB with an empty folder, where
  what's private is 14 → 15 MB) and 2 MB its four threads; at rest
  0.0% of a core and 1 wakeup a second, as before. Looked at 1×, 1.5×
  and 2×.
- `Desktop` (desktop.rs): a background layer anchored to every edge;
  icons placed by hand kept in `desktop.json`, the rest on the grid.
  Each icon is a drawing of its own keyed by what it shows, laid out
  again only when its cell, name, selection or the scale changes
  (`laid`); the band is a drawing over them. So a band's sweep draws
  the band and the icons it takes in or lets go.
- Drops come through the kit's (`View::takes_drops`, `drop_over`,
  `dropped`): each part says whether it takes what's dragged
  over it (`items::take_drop`, BeOS's rules: move within a
  file system, copy across, ⌥ copies, the secondary button asks;
  `items::Spring` opens a folder a drag rests on), and the window's
  drop handler gives the Tracker the drop. Drags out carry Olo's own
  types (the folder and file system they're from, whether to ask).
- Paste reads the clipboard off the looper (`olo_kit::clipboard::paste_as`).
- **Edit ▸ Undo and Redo** (undo.rs; ⌘Z and ⇧⌘Z, `app.undo`/`app.redo`,
  named for the step: "Undo Rename", "Undo Move to Trash"), one history
  for every window and the desktop, as Finder's. A step is what was
  done, as done: items moved from where to where (rename, move, put
  back), put in the Trash or restored from it (from where, to where in
  it), or made (copy, duplicate, new folder, links, a paste or drop of
  text or a picture), or desktop icons placed (dragged, Clean Up: each
  one's place before and after, put back at once, no job). Each job reports that (`ops::Outcome::moved`,
  `created`); a rename or a new folder records it at once. Undoing runs
  what takes it back as a job like any other (on a worker, progress,
  Stop): moved items go back to exactly where they were
  (`ops::Kind::PutBack`), trashed ones are restored, restored ones go
  back in the Trash, made ones go in the Trash (Redo restores them from
  it, to the byte). What that job did is the step Redo takes back, and
  the other way round, so a step goes back and forth as often as wanted,
  many files as one; a job stopped part way records what it did. When a
  step can't be any more (an item gone, the Trash emptied, something new
  where it would go back to), the job says why and the step goes. A
  name being edited keeps ⌘Z for its text (a menu's keys reach the
  window only when nothing in it took them). Emptying the Trash isn't
  undone.
- `quicklook.rs`: olo-preview's `PreviewView` with the footer and keys;
  its window opens when the preview comes (or after 120 ms with a
  spinner) and has the keyboard.
- **Open With ▸** on a file's or folder's menu: the kit's
  (`olo_kit::open_with`, see "The kit"), for what's selected when it's
  all one kind (`folder::open_with_menu`, the kinds warmed as the
  folder is listed); on the desktop's items too, and on Quick Look's
  Open button (its secondary click). Its commands go through
  `Tracker::open_with`, which opens Other…'s window itself (to keep it
  in its windows' list) and hands the rest to `open_with::run`.
- `goto.rs`: Go ▸ Go to File or Folder… (⇧⌘G, Finder's Go to Folder;
  `tracker.go-to` in the keyboard profile, so Preferences ▸ Keyboard
  lists and changes it): the kit's window (`olo_kit::go_to`, shared
  with the file panels, "File panels" above) with Tracker's own names
  in its list (`goto::Names`: its icons, marks and a link's slant),
  a dialog over the folder's window: the field holds a path copied
  (absolute, `~/…` as written, a `file://` URI's:
  `olo_kit_base::files::written_path`, which takes quotes and a
  trailing newline too, as the palette's Go to does), selected, so Return goes; the
  names its folder has that what's typed could be listed under it,
  each folder read once on a worker; Tab completes (the chosen name, or
  as far as they agree, case aside) where there's one to complete to,
  else moves on as Tab does (`capture_action` of `FocusNext`); ↑↓
  choose, and Return then puts the name in. Go reveals (`Tracker::
  go_to`: a folder opens, a file is selected in its folder's window); a
  relative path is from the folder it was asked in; nothing there, it
  says so and stays. Agents and the palette: `go-to` opens it,
  `go-to:<path>` goes straight there.

## Archives (crates/archive, `olo-archive`; Tracker's Compress and Extract)

Every archive read and written in Rust, in process, never a program run
(Ben, 2026-11-14: "olo's tracker should have native support for
compression/archives … support all the common formats including zip,
tar, gz, tar.gz, bzip, 7z, rar, iso and so on"). `olo_archive::kind`
says what a file is by its first bytes (inside a compression, by what
the compression holds: a tar, a cpio, or one file), then its name;
`list` what's in one; `extract` everything out; `compress` files and
folders into a new one. Written: zip (deflate; AES-256 with a password),
tar plain or with gzip, bzip2, xz or zstd, 7-Zip (LZMA2; AES-256, its
names hidden too, with a password). Read, also: RAR (RARLAB's own
unpacker, the `unrar` crate, built from its source: reading only, as
its licence has it), disc images (its own readers: ISO 9660 in
`iso.rs`, Rock Ridge's names, permissions and links where the image has
them, else the UDF tree where there is one, else Joliet's names, else
the 8.3 ones; UDF 1.02 to 2.60 in `udf.rs`, the file system of DVDs,
Blu-ray discs and Windows' install images, whose ISO 9660 tree holds no
more than a note to read the UDF one: a 2.50 metadata partition, a
write-once disc's virtual allocation table, strategy 4096's chains of
entries and continued allocation descriptors followed, a file streamed
from its extents, a directory at a time in memory; a tree walked once,
its loops and depth bounded), cpio (newc and odc,
`cpio.rs`: initramfs, RPM's payload), and a single file in gzip, bzip2,
xz or zstd. (The `cdfs` crate was looked at for ISO and left: it
requires FUSE, clap and a logger.)

**Nothing outside.** Extraction goes into a hidden folder of its own in
the destination (`.olo-extracting-PID-N`) through one `Sink`: every
name a `safe_path` (no `..`, nothing absolute, no drive letter, a
backslash a separator), every file made new (`O_EXCL`, `O_NOFOLLOW`),
every folder on the way one it made itself, and links made last: a
symbolic one only when what it points to stays inside (never absolute,
never more `..` than it's deep), a hard one only to a file it wrote; so
an entry "through" a link to a folder lands in a real folder, never
where the link points. setuid, setgid and sticky are dropped;
permissions and times kept (a folder's set at the end, deepest first,
so a read-only folder is still filled). Then what came out is put in
place as Finder's Archive Utility does: one thing at its top as it is,
beside the archive; several in a folder named for the archive
(`base_name`: "photos" for photos.tar.gz); a name taken gets a number
("report 2.pdf", `unique`). Made archives are written beside their
place under a hidden name and renamed into it at the end. Stopped or
failed, nothing is left: not the hidden folder, not a half-made archive.

**Progress and Stop.** Each takes a `Control`: how far (bytes of how
many: the entries' sizes, or for a stream how much of the file has been
read; at most twenty reports a second, and always one per item) and a
flag that stops it between reads. A password-protected archive says so
(`Error::Password(false)`), and a wrong password (`true`) is told apart
where the format can (zip's check, 7-Zip's, RAR's).

**In Tracker** (archives.rs, ops.rs `Kind::Compress(Format)` and
`Kind::Extract`): Compress ▸ (Zip; Tar, gzip; Tar, xz; Tar, zstd; Tar,
bzip2; Tar; 7-Zip; Compress As…) on any selection's menu and in File,
Extract Here and Extract To… (a folder chosen in the kit's panel) when
everything selected is an archive (by its kind: nothing is read on the
UI thread to decide). They're jobs like Copy's: on a worker, in Tracker
Status with its bar (bytes) and Stop, what they made selected after,
and Edit ▸ Undo puts it in the Trash (`undo::Change::Made`); a long one
says it's done in a notification. Compress names its archive "photos.zip"
for one item and "Archive.zip" for several; Compress As… (a dialog:
Name, Format, Protect it with a password, which only Zip and 7-Zip
take) names it and chooses. An archive wanting a password brings up a
dialog asking for it (the job's `Outcome::needs_password`; "That
password isn't right. Try again:" when it was wrong), and the job runs
again with it (`ToHub::ArchiveJob`). Passwords is offered there: Use
Saved Password reads the one Passwords keeps for that archive (a
Password item titled "Archive: NAME", `archives::saved_password`,
`Request::Secrets`: asked only when pressed, as it may bring Passwords
up to be unlocked), and Keep It in Passwords keeps the one typed
(`Request::KeepSecret`) once the job has worked (the hub's
`keep_password`, by job: never a wrong one); Compress As… keeps a new
archive's password, on by default (an archive's password is easy to
lose). The archive's own window offers both too. Tested with a
stand-in for Passwords on a socket of the test's own
(`OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET`; `archives::tests`), and in a test session: a
zip made with a password kept, then extracted with Use Saved Password. Commands, for agents and the
palette: `compress:zip`, `compress:tar.gz` (any `Format`'s ending),
`compress-as`, `extract-here`, `extract-to`.

**Looked into as a folder** (archive_win.rs): opening an archive Olo
reads (`fs::open`; an .rpm or .deb opens as it always has) shows a
window of what's in it, a level at a time, as a folder's list (folders
first, then by name; size, modified; `children` makes the levels from
the entries' paths, folders implied by what's deeper): a folder in it
opens in the same window (Enclosing Folder, Go ▸ Enclosing Folder,
back out to it selected), a file opens with what opens its kind, taken
out first into Tracker's cache (`~/.cache/olo/tracker/archives/<the
archive's path, size and time>/`, once: opened again, it's there).
Extract Selected… takes what's selected out into a folder chosen
(`olo_archive::extract_some`: only those entries, the folder being
looked at taken off their paths; on a worker with the window's bar;
Undo's, as `Extract`), Extract All everything beside the archive
(Tracker's job). A password is asked for in the window when listing or
taking something out needs one.

**Quick Look** lists what's in any of them (`olo_preview::archive`,
through `list`), says when one is protected by a password, and for a
single compressed file what it unpacks to and how big.

**Tests.** `cargo test -p olo-archive`: every format written round
trips (contents, the executable bit, links but in 7-Zip, times), a
password asked for and checked (zip, 7-Zip), a tar made by hand to
write outside (`../`, absolute paths, links out, a file through a link)
writes nothing outside, a single gzip, a cpio and an ISO 9660 made in
the test, UDF images made by real tools (genisoimage's 1.02 beside an
ISO 9660 tree, its long and Unicode names, a file of 300 KB and an empty
one; mkudffs's 1.02 in 512-byte blocks with strategy 4096, 2.01 with
the root's names in its entry, 2.50 with a virtual allocation table)
and one of them given a metadata partition in two runs, RAR read (the `unrar` crate's sample archives, one with a
password), Stop leaving nothing. Tracker's `ops::tests::compress_and_extract`
runs them as jobs. Tried in a test session: Compress ▸ Zip of two items
(Archive.zip, selected), Extract Here (a folder "Archive"), Undo (it went
to the Trash), Compress As… 7-Zip with a password, its Extract asking,
a wrong password asked again, the right one; the dialogs reviewed at 1×,
1.5× and 2×, light and dark. Nothing per frame changes.

## Agent Screens (apps/screen)

Agents get screens of their own: `olo-screen start [NAME] [--size WxH]
[--scale N] [--sound]` starts a headless Olo session (`olo-session
--headless`, in its own process group), a whole desktop with its own
Deskbar, windows, pointer and keyboard focus, so nothing an agent does
there moves the person's pointer or takes their focus. It runs the
person's programs and files (their HOME), but with app_server settings
of its own (`OLO_APP_SERVER_SETTINGS`, a copy of the person's at 1×
unless asked, with no lock, screen saver, display sleep or system
sleep; app_server on a screen, `OLO_SCREEN` set, is never idle
whatever its settings say: the "agent" screen once started its saver
after an in-place restart and locked itself, 2026-11-07; it locks only
when asked, `Request::Lock`, and its lock screen leaves the person's
fingerprint reader, security key and camera alone, as everything
outside their own session does: `olo_system::env::readers_here`, from
`at_the_computer`, which the lock screen, Passwords' lock and Allow
alert, Terminal's sudo and the polkit agent all ask; Passwords' lock,
sudo's and polkit's waits didn't until 2026-11-08),
silent unless `--sound` (`PULSE_SERVER` pointed at nothing),
without `DISPLAY` (X programs would show on the person's screen), and on
a D-Bus session bus of its own (below, "A screen's own bus"). Screens
are listed in `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-screens/NAME.json` (the session's
pid, its sockets, the size); `screens.rs` checks the pid is still that
session before trusting an entry, by the `OLO_SCREEN=NAME` it was started
with (`is_session_of`: kept across an upgrade's re-execution; its command
line, which a session re-executed bare before 2026-11-07, isn't, so
every upgrade had `list` drop each running screen, and starting it again
by name made a second, ten left running unknown). An entry is dropped
only once its session has ended (`running`), `stop` ends the session's
whole process group if it hasn't ended 5 s after being asked (and keeps
the entry while it runs), and `start` and `stop` end any screen's
session nothing lists (`strays`: of that name whatever its age, others
once two minutes old so one being started isn't; never a session
inside a screen's, and never one started under another runtime folder,
`listed_in`: its screen is listed there. An olo-screen given a runtime
folder of its own, as tools/dev/readme-shots gives its screens, saw
every other running screen as a stray and ended them all at each start
and stop, another agent's in the middle of its work, 2026-11-16). The
rest is the screen's own app_server
IPC (`Client::connect_to`): `run` (a program with the screen's
`WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, `OLO_SOCKET` and `OLO_SCREEN`), `look` (a PNG,
`--window ID` for one), `windows` (`Reply::Windows`, whose `WindowInfo`s
carry `frame`, their place on screen, and `content`, where the app's
drawing is inside the tab and border; the `WindowsChanged` event leaves
them out, or a drag would send one every frame), `tree` (each kit app's
`commands::tree`, matched to its windows by title and size (Chrome's by
the page title its window's title starts with: see "Chrome's widget
tree") and moved by
`content`, so every node is in screen pixels, ready for `click`; an
outline, or `--json`; a program not on the kit, GTK 3 or 4, Qt, gives
its tree over AT-SPI instead, `atspi.rs`: its connections to the
accessibility bus found by its process id, each window's accessibles
walked while they show, roles named as AccessKit names them, a "push
button" a `Button`, states as the node's flags, a field's text and a
slider's number as its value, containers and a button's own label
left out, and places from the window's geometry, as GTK gives them;
each question has 1.5 s, so a hung program can't hold `tree` up.
olo-session sets `QT_ACCESSIBILITY=1`, as GTK is always there.
Tried with GNOME Calculator (GTK 4): its buttons clicked by name, its
display set by typing, `wait --text` on the answer. To try one
headless, the accessibility bus must be dbus-broker (registryd crashes
on busd): `dbus-broker-launch --scope user --config-file
/usr/share/defaults/at-spi2/accessibility.conf` given a listening
socket as fd 3 (`LISTEN_FDS=1`), `at-spi2-registryd` and the program
with `AT_SPI_BUS_ADDRESS` set to it, and a screen entry in a private
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`), `menus` and `invoke` (a window's app's menu bar
and choosing from it, `commands::menus`/`invoke`), `click`, `move`,
`down`/`up`, `drag`, `scroll`, `wheel`, `key` (chords as people write
them: `Cmd+S`, `Enter`, `Esc`; parsed by `olo_protocol::Chord` with
aliases) and `type` (what a US keyboard types as keys, anything else
— é, emoji, CJK — put in whole with `Request::InsertText`, in order),
all as `Request::Synthetic`, in the
screen's logical pixels. `stop` ends the session, and with it the
programs on it. `olo-screen --help` lists it all. Each action on a screen
(`history::ACTIONS`: `start`, `stop`, `run` and every input, find and
window command; not the reads) goes in its history,
`$XDG_STATE_HOME/olo/screens/NAME/actions.jsonl`, a JSON object a line
as each ends: when, how long, its arguments, its answer (what `print_json`
printed: what it matched, where it clicked, the focus after) and its
error, kept under 8 MB by dropping the oldest half and outliving the
screen until `history NAME --clear`. `history NAME` lists it (`--kind`,
`--search`, `--last N`, `--json`); `stats [NAME]` sums it
(`history::stats`: first start and last use, time running from each start
to its stop or now, time in use as the actions and the gaps under a
minute between them, actions by kind, failures, programs run) with
whether each screen runs now and its windows. Beside it are the frames
the screen drew (`record.rs`): `olo-screen record NAME`, started with
each screen in its process group (one a screen: it holds `recorder.lock`
in the history's folder for its life, `screens::take_recorder_lock`;
when an upgrade replaces its file it becomes the new version between
two frames, the same process, and starts a segment of its own; and a
running screen found with none, at an agent's next action on it, is
given one, `screens::ensure_recorder`), takes the screen's picture (as the
viewer does, RGBA) when the screen has drawn something new (its
app_server says so, `EventKind::Painted`, to a thread of the recorder's:
at most eight times a second for five seconds after each action, the
history's file changing, and once a second otherwise; what is drawn
between two looks is told again, so the last thing drawn is always
kept), and keeps the 64-pixel tiles that changed since the frame
before, zstd-compressed, with a whole keyframe where the last is 30 s
old, in five-minute segments (`frames-START.olof`; the format is in the
module's comment), the oldest dropped past 512 MB. A screen that draws
nothing isn't looked at and nothing is written for it: the recorder
sleeps on its app_server's word (it took every screen's whole picture
every second whatever it showed, read back from the GPU and compared,
5.2 MB a second a screen; **an agent's screen sitting still** was 1.9%
of a core between its app_server, Deskbar and recorder, 90 wakes a
second, and is 0.1% and 8, measured on release builds, 2026-11-20:
see "An agent's screen sits still" under Deskbar's widgets). Each picture comes through a file in the
runtime folder (`screens::recorder_frame`, 5 MB at 1440 × 900, in
memory): the recorder removes it as it ends, `stop` does for one ended
with its screen's process group, and `start` and `stop` sweep those of
screens not running (six stopped screens' were left, 31 MB, until
2026-11-18). `record::index` reads the records'
heads, `frame_at` builds the screen as it was at a time from its
keyframe; `history NAME --look N [OUT.png]` writes it as it was when
action N ended. In the window, History (a tab beside Live and Stats;
`replay.rs`) lists its actions as they come: a worker follows the
history's folder (`olo_kit::watch`) and reads only what was added
(`history::Reader`, from where it last read to the end of its last
whole line; all again when the file was cut down or replaced) and the
frames' segments that changed (`record::index_known`; records still
being written wait), at most four times a second and the frames alone
once a second, with each action's search text made there. A search and
the kit's filter menus narrow the list (`kind:` Pointer, Keys and
Typing, Menus and Choices, Windows, Programs, Start and Stop, or a
command's own name; `result:failed|ok`; `since:5m|1h|today`), picked
within 2 ms a frame however long the history (`go_on_picking`), the
count of shown and all at the right. It shows the screen as it was at
the action chosen or wherever the scrubber is (in a sunken well,
`picture::PictureWell`), what the action was and what came of it under it
(what it matched, the program's pid, the window in front after, or why
it failed), and plays it back in time with them (Play/Pause, 1× to 8×,
◀ ▶ action by action among those shown; stretches of more than 3 s with
nothing in them skipped), each click a ring where it went and the
newest key or text a caption under the picture. Playing draws again
only when something shown changes (`Replay::play_on`: the next frame or
action, the scrubber's next device pixel, the time's next second;
every frame only while a ring grows or a caption fades), so a long
history plays at a few frames a second. At the newest action it
follows the screen (Live, or Latest for a stopped one, pushed while it
does): each new action is chosen as it comes and brought into view
once, so the list scrolls freely otherwise, and rings and captions fade
on the clock. Narrow, the scrubber goes over the buttons. Frames are
built on a worker, the latest asked for winning, played on from the
last (`record::Player`) rather than from a keyframe each time.
`history NAME --export OUT.mp4 [--from N] [--to N] [--zoom 1|2|3]
[--encoder auto|cpu|nvidia|vaapi]` (`export.rs`) makes it a video in
process, of what the agent did: each action from 0.8 s before it to
1.5 s after it ended (a wait over 10 s: its start and its end), played
as it went at 10 frames a second; gaps under 3 s play through, and the
rest is skipped, the screen playing on as it went for 5 s more before
each skip and after it (time to read what's on it), then shown across
the skip quickly: under 30 s in half a second, longer in 1.5 s, racing
on, always under the small ⏩ badge at the top saying how long, never a
card over the screen (Ben, 2026-11-16: "never use the large overlay
one it's too intrusive"; "add an extra 5s delay before and after each
fast forward"). While it runs, the window's Export Video… button
shows how far (`Button::working`, told by History's `ExportProgress` as
each percent passes) and History its bar and Cancel. The screen
changing by itself (a page's
animation, a spinner, a clock) isn't something happening: counted so,
real histories were busy nearly every second. The work follows what's
kept, not the history's length: `record::Player` plays forward once
(each record applied once, a record found by halving, a jump ahead
from the nearest keyframe, the segment's file kept open, `applied`
saying whether the picture changed); a picture is encoded only when it
changed (one that didn't is the one before, its MP4 sample longer); it
goes to the encoder in BGRA, zoomed in the same pass (each pixel z × z,
crisp; as far as H.264 goes, `export::zooms`); a skip's screen is drawn
once a sample, its badge over it. The encoder is
`olo_video::Encoder`, chosen by the work (`open_encoder`: up to about
600 million pixels, the built-in GPU's or the processor's, at once;
more, NVIDIA's, whose start takes two seconds). Measured 2026-11-15
(release, real histories): 9 hours, 71 actions, 2.5 min of video, 195
pictures, 1.8 s (Intel's); 16.5 hours, 3.2 min, 554 pictures of 2160 ×
1350, 6 to 8 s (NVIDIA's); 51.5 hours, 2,209 actions, 86 min, 6,747
pictures, 25 s; before, the first of these ran for minutes, every
keyframe a stretch of activity. Its MP4 is Olo's own (`olo_video::Mp4`:
`ftyp`, `mdat`, `moov` with the parameter sets; `co64`, one chunk).
`progress` gets how far it is and can stop it. Olo's Viewer plays the
result. In the window, History's Export Video… asks where (the kit's
Save panel, `NAME.mp4` in ~/Videos, its Size: Actual Size, 2× or 3×,
the last chosen again) and exports on a worker, the bar saying how far
it is with Cancel, then an alert with Open in Tracker
(`Replay::start_export`). What it exports (`Replay::export_part`): the
rows chosen when there are several (⇧ or ⌘ in the list), else what the
list shows when a search or filter leaves some out, else all; the file
says a part ("NAME (12 actions).mp4"). **Take Screenshot…** (beside it,
and Screen ▸, ⇧⌘E; Ben, 2026-11-17: "a "Take Screenshot..." button
that takes a screenshot at the current time point and saves it and the
user should be able to choose the size like they can for the video"):
the screen as it was at the time shown (the playhead, `Replay::now`),
"NAME at 1.42.png" in ~/Pictures by the same Save panel and Size
(Actual Size, 2×, 3× as far as fits, each pixel that many times over,
the last chosen again), decoded from its keyframe and written on a
worker (`save_shot`: through a `.png.part` renamed once whole), then
the same alert. The header leaves the screen's name out where a narrow
window leaves it no room (it drew an "…" over the buttons at 2×). The sidebar (the
kit's `Sidebar`) has every screen running and every one stopped, under
Running and Stopped, by last use (`viewer::rows`,
read on a worker; every listed one's as it acts: its history's folder
watched, `follow_use`, a file's time read as an action is added, so a
row's time is right without being chosen: it used to change only when
clicked), each with how long ago (`olo_kit::ago`, following the clock),
and New Screen under them. A screen can be given a name of its own
(Screen ▸ Rename…, or a click on its title in the header: a field over
it, Return keeps it, Escape puts the old back; `olo-screen rename NAME
[TITLE]`): kept with its history (`history::title`, a `title` file
beside its actions, gone with it), shown in the list and the header,
and in `olo-screen list` as `title`. Screens are chosen together with
⌘-click (adding or taking one away), ⇧-click (the run from the last),
⌘A in the list or Edit ▸ Select All Screens; a secondary click opens
the menu for all of them (for the one clicked alone if it isn't one),
as the Screen menu has it too, each item saying how many it acts on:
Rename…, Start, Archive, Unarchive, Stop… and Delete… (asked once for
all). Every screen is kept from its start, not only once an agent has
acted on it: `screens::start` writes what it was started with
(`screen.json`: size, scale, sound) beside its history, which is what
lists a stopped one (`history::names`: a folder with `screen.json` or
`actions.jsonl`) and starts it again as it was (`screens::kept`; Start,
the Start Screen button in a stopped one's header, `olo-screen start
NAME`, which take it out of the archive too). Before, one made with New
Screen and stopped before an agent did anything on it went from the
list altogether. Archived screens (stopped ones, `history::archived`,
an `archived` mark beside the history) are listed under Archived
unless View ▸ Show Archived is turned off; Delete moves each screen's
folder (its history, recordings, title, Chrome profile and the
passwords shared with it) to the Trash (`history::trash`,
`olo_xdg::trash::move_to_trash`, with its .trashinfo to put it back).
The same for agents: `olo-screen list` gives each screen's `state`
(running, stopped, archived; a stopped one with its kept size),
`archive`, `unarchive` (`screens::archive`, a running one refused) and
`delete` (`screens::delete`, stopping it first). The chosen screen's
header names it and says how it is (running and its size, up for how
long, its actions, the last how long ago), with Export Video… and Stop
Screen… (for a stopped one Clear History…, which deletes its actions
and the frames kept with them and nothing else, and Start Screen). Stats (`stats.rs`) are the kit's dashboard
cards: its use (started, last used, ran for, in use), its actions by
kind with bars and how many failed, actions a minute over the last hour
of use, and the programs run on it (`history::stats`, worked out again
as the history grows or once a second while it runs). View ▸ Live,
History, Stats (⌘1–3), Find (⌘F), and Playback's Play, Previous and
Next Action and Go Live drive it from the menus.
How much is kept, and how long, is Preferences ▸ AI's Agent Screens
(`AiSettings::screen_history_mb`, `screen_history_days`; 512 MB a screen
for a month): `history::limits` asks the person's app_server, else the
screen's own, and each screen's recorder applies them as it starts
(`history::prune`: actions and frame segments older than that go, and
histories left empty; segments past the size, oldest first).

Input that plays out over time is paced, a batch per IPC request with
waits between (`Screen::input_paced`): `drag` presses, moves in steps
and lets go over ~300 ms (a knob or a window's corner needs to see the
movement); `scroll` moves in ≤20 px steps every 8 ms and rests 80 ms
before the fingers lift, so app_server doesn't glide on (a lift arriving
at speed is a flick) and the lift ends the gesture (a list pulled past
its end springs back); `wheel` sends one notch at a time. `find.rs`
finds elements by what they are (`--name`, exact before partial, values
counting; `--role`; `--match ROLE:TEXT`; `--text`; `--index`;
`--window`) for `click`, `set` (click in, checking it took the focus,
then ⌘A, Delete and the text), `select` (open the dropdown, wait for the
`MenuItem`, click it), `wait` (until it shows or `--gone`; `--idle`: two
outlines a quarter-second apart the same, and no window settling) and `scroll-to` (wheel until it
shows whole and in view: straight toward it when the tree already has
it out of sight, a web page's below the fold; else to the top, then
down; then read again until it stops moving, as a browser's smooth
scroll glides on). `click` and `set` scroll what they find into view
first (`into_view`: its middle within its window's content and the
screen): a web form's field listed at y 1045 of a 900-point screen was
clicked where nothing is, and `set` failed 14 times on one screen. A
point is `X Y`, `X,Y` or `--at X,Y`, `scroll` takes `--dx`/`--dy` and
`--at`, and keys go by X11's and the web's names too (`Page_Down`,
`Next`, `ArrowDown`, `KP_Enter`): what agents write, which failed
"x must be a number" and "unknown key" 21 times on that screen.

**Every action says how the screen is after it** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "i
want the agent to always know what the latest state is"; `afterwards`
in main.rs). Its answer's `after` is read once the screen has settled:
nothing in the windows or the focused window's tree changed for a
quarter of a second (`QUIET`, as `wait --idle` has it), no window still
drawing a size it was given, no page loading (`UiNode::busy`: the
extension marks a tab's `Document` busy while `tab.status` is
"loading"); at most 2 s, or 8 s while a page loads, `settled` false if
it was still changing. Then: the focus (`find::focus_of`, from what was
read), `picture` (the whole screen, a PNG among the screen's pictures,
`history::dir(NAME)/pictures`, the newest 20 kept; on disk, as the
runtime folder is memory, and `look` without a file writes there too),
`windows`, and `tree`, the focused window's outline as `tree
--visible-only --max-len 80` gives it, its first 150 lines. `run` waits
first for what it starts to show (the windows or the focused tree
changing, at most 5 s: `shown`), and prints JSON now, its pid with it.
The history keeps the answer without the picture, tree and windows (the
frames are kept), with `settled` and what it took (`ms`); History says
"still changing" where it was. Before, an action said only the focus,
read as soon as the app had taken it in: a click whose page answered
300 ms later, or a link's new page, was answered with the page before.
Measured (release, a 1280 × 800 screen, StyledEdit): an action takes
~305 ms (~295 settling, 5 for the picture) against 76 ms quick; the app
~1 ms more CPU an action (the reads; 2.1 ms against 1.1 ms over its
threads), olo-screen 13 M instructions against 9 M; the answer ~3.8 KB.
In Chrome, a click on a button whose text changes 300 ms later: 610 ms,
with the new text; on a link to a page that takes 1.5 s: 1.8 s, with
the new page. `--quick` (anywhere after the name; for `run`, before the
program) or `OLO_SCREEN_QUICK=1`: the focus alone, at once, as before.
Popups are in the trees: a kit program
gives an open menu or dropdown as a window's tree of its own (a menu's
with no title, a submenu's titled by its item; its nodes placed within
the popup), and `olo-screen` puts each under the window it opened from
(`with_popups`: the program's trees no window took, matched to the
window's `WindowInfo::popups` by size, never one titled as another
window; its root a `Menu`, its items moved to the popup's place on the
screen), so `tree` lists a `Menu` with its `MenuItem`s, `click --role
MenuItem --name …` chooses one, and `--visible-only` keeps them though
a popup hangs outside its window. (With Olo's own kits a popup became a
window of its own in the program's answer and was dropped, as no
window of app_server's matched it: an open menu wasn't in `tree` until
2026-11-17.) `WindowInfo::popups` gives
every window's open popups' frames, GTK's too (smithay's
`PopupManager::popups_for_surface`, from the client's geometry). Table
rows carry their place (`UiNode::row`/`rows`, printed `row 13/61`)
and whether they're `selected`, as tabs and column headers do. `focus`/`close`/`minimize`/`zoom` are the window
requests; `resize` and `place` are `Request::Place` (a frame, as
`set_frame` gives tiles). `look` writes among the screen's pictures
when given no file (above), and `--crop` cuts an RGBA picture down in
process (png crate).

The person's side is the window (`olo-screen`, or `olo-screen
watch NAME`; on the kit): the screens in a sidebar and the chosen
one's Live tab, the screen with the agent's pointer drawn in and its
latest action under it. Live shows the screen's own frames as it draws
them, never copied (`viewer::stream_live`, `olo_capture::live`):
- The screen's app_server captures each frame on the GPU into one of
  three dmabufs in turn. Frames come only when the screen changed, at
  its refresh (agent screens start at 120 Hz, `screens::fastest`).
- The viewer hands each buffer to its window (olo-kit's
  `WindowCx::set_external_buffer`, `ExternalBuffer`), and the person's
  app_server shows it in the well's place as a subsurface
  (`Painter::place_external`, `picture.rs`).
- A buffer is captured into again once the person's app_server lets it
  go (`wl_buffer.release` → `Waker::released`).

The window draws nothing for a frame, and nothing is read back. Dragging
a window on the screen for 5 s: the viewer used 0.6% of a core for
~60 frames a second (120 at 120 Hz). Picture by picture it used 30% for
8 a second and missed pointer-only changes.

The picture's corners sit at whole points (subsurfaces can't be placed
finer). `Painter::external_bounds` gives the device pixels the compositor
rounds them to, so the frame line drawn round it is flush at every
scale; measured at 1, 1.25, 1.5, 1.75 and 2×, resized to odd sizes.

Where the two app_servers share no dmabuf layout
(`olo_kit::external_modifiers(fourcc)` empty, asked of the display thread
once as the viewer starts; or `OLO_SCREEN_PICTURES` set to compare), it
takes pictures as before:
- one worker follows the screen's `EventKind::Painted`; another asks for
  a `format: "rgba"` picture then, at most eight a second, and reads it
  back (an app_server from before `Painted`: eight a second);
- each picture is resampled on a worker to the device size it's shown at
  (the last stands in until it's made).

Either way only while Live shows, so a screen at rest costs nothing to
watch. A live view that ends (the screen's app_server restarting) starts
again every half second. Take Control (⌘K) steps in: the person's pointer,
wheel and keys over the picture go to that screen through another worker
over a connection kept to it, moves run together to the last (keys by
their evdev codes on a US keyboard, the agent's, from the keys the kit
names; Ctrl, Shift and Alt pressed and let go as each key event says, a
held key repeated by the screen, Tab and ⌃Tab to the screen too, ⌘K
still stopping), with a ring in the keyboard-navigation colour round
the picture, until Stop Controlling (everything held let go). New Screen starts one that is new: its name is the first of "agent", "agent-2", … that no screen there is has, running, stopped or archived, and that nothing is kept under (`screens::new_name`; with `free_name`, which looks only at the running ones and is what `olo-screen start` with no name uses so that an agent gets its stopped "agent" back, New Screen started a stopped or archived screen again, its history and Chrome profile with it); Stop
Screen… ends one after asking. A viewer running on an agent screen
leaves that screen out of its list. While any screen runs (other than
the one a Deskbar is on), Deskbar's tray shows a monitor with a pointer,
and their count when there are several (`status::agent_screens` reads
the same listing as a screen's file comes or goes, `olo_kit::watch`, and
every 30 s while there are any for one killed without a word, judging
entries as `Screen::alive` does; a viewer's frames go in `views/` beside
them, so they don't wake whoever follows the listing);
clicking it runs `olo-screen watch`. Test it in a sandbox: a private
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, a fixture HOME and XDG dirs (the screen runs the real
programs), and a second screen to run the viewer on.

Agents learn all this from the **`olo-screens` skill**
(`apps/screen/SKILL.md`): a real session (`--tty-udev`, at start and
after each upgrade; `crates/session/src/skills.rs`, on a thread) puts it
in `~/.claude/skills/` (or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/skills/`) when Claude Code
is there and in `~/.agents/skills/` when Codex is, replacing only a copy
that still has Olo's marker line. **Change SKILL.md with the CLI**:
it is the agents' manual. Headless sessions never write it, so tests
don't touch the person's home.

The same way goes the **`olo-hardware` skill**
(`docs/skills/olo-hardware/SKILL.md`; Ben, 2026-11-16: "add an agent
skill in this repo that a new olo user can call that asks the agent to
analyze their hardware and add first-class support for it in olo like we
have done with the thinkpad p1 gen9"): how a coding agent, on a computer
Olo wasn't developed on, reads what the computer has, compares it with
what Olo supports (by this document's sections), agrees with its owner
what to do, and does each piece properly (keyed by the hardware, tested
on a stand-in, measured, documented, an Olo Doctor fix for what needs
root). The README and the website's install page say how to ask for it
(`/olo-hardware` in Claude Code), under the warning that Olo is beta and
tested on few computers. **When a kind of hardware gets a new home in
Olo (a new section here, a new place per-machine data lives), say so in
that skill**: it is the map a stranger's agent follows.

**The `olo-debug-help` skill** (`.claude/skills/olo-debug-help/SKILL.md`,
the repository's own, for whoever works on Olo; Ben, 2026-11-18: "if
you need help root-causing a bug like this you can launch in a subshell
a codex instance running gpt-6.2-astra on max effort in headless mode
with auto approve -- actually add a skill for doing that in this repo")
is for a cause that won't be found: a written brief (the symptom, the
evidence, what was tried and ruled out, the code on the path, how far
it reproduces) goes to `tools/dev/codex-help BRIEF.md`, which runs
`codex exec -m gpt-6.2-astra -c model_reasoning_effort="xhigh"
--approve-for-me` (xhigh since 2026-11-20, Ben: "whenever you use astra
6.2 it should be on xhigh not max") in the repository with the rules in front (the
working tree unchanged, no commits, the person's session left alone,
headless tests under a `codex-` name, scratch in the brief's folder,
no helper of its own), in the background, and writes `answer.md` and
`log.txt` beside the brief. What it says is a lead: checked, then
fixed by whoever asked. It is one of the Codex helpers CLAUDE.md's
"Subagents" allows. `.claude/` is ignored but for `.claude/skills/`.

**A second look at every change's pictures** (`tools/dev/codex-look`;
Ben, 2026-11-18, after a status line set right under its paragraph
reached him on every Integrations tab: "provide all screenshots of
changes to a codex agent … using astra 6.2 on medium for a second
review / set of eyes to identify anything you missed"): `codex-look
--about "WHAT CHANGED" PICTURE.png…` hands the pictures to `codex exec
-m gpt-6.2-astra -c model_reasoning_effort="medium" -s read-only` with
a designer's brief (spacing, alignment, text cut or crowded, what's out
of keeping), prints what it finds and keeps it as `codex-look.md`
beside the first picture. It takes a minute or two. Its first look,
at the Fastmail tab and Calendar's notes, found four things: one fixed
(CalDAV's empty list worded as Google's), three judged and kept (a
scrolled view's partial lines at its edges, as the kit's other views
have them; Integrations' one height for every tab; a refused
connection's wording, seen only against a made-up server). What it
says is checked against the picture, as the debug helper's is.

**And a designer's review of them** (`tools/dev/opus-look`; Ben,
2026-11-19, of To-Do's first pictures: "omg so much is ugly make sure
you get visual design reviews from opus 5.5 and astra 6.2"): `opus-look
--about "WHAT IT IS, WHAT CHANGED" PICTURE.png…` hands the same
pictures to Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude -p --model claude-opus-5-5
--effort high`, the Read tool alone, run from the pictures' folder so
nothing of the project is loaded and nothing can be changed) with a
product designer's brief: composition, hierarchy, rhythm, colour, what
looks amateur or unfinished or out of keeping with the desktop, and
what to do about each, the most important first. It keeps its review as
`opus-look.md` beside the first picture. It can only look, so give it
whole windows and enlarged crops. Every change's pictures go to both
before a commit, and something new goes to both early, before it's
built out: codex-look is for what's wrong by a pixel, opus-look for
whether the design is any good.

**Codex subagents** (`tools/dev/agents`, the `olo-codex-agents` skill;
Ben, 2026-11-19: "you now have permission to utilize subagents for
narrow, targeted work items that can be parallelized. they must be able
to work in this same worktree without clobbering each other, ideally
with their work scoped to a single crate that only one agent is working
in at any given time … use codex via a subprocess to do the work with
astra 6.2 on xhigh … in interactive mode via e.g. tmux … where you can
monitor its output and get notified when it needs you … the codex
subagents themselves should NOT be allowed to launch more subagents …
review their work carefully, especially any visual design … up to 5 at
once"; and "the codex agents should run on auto approve for most things
only the super risky stuff should come to you"): `agents start NAME
CRATE BRIEF.md` starts an interactive Codex (gpt-6.2-astra, xhigh,
`--approve-for-me`, its multi-agent features off) in a tmux session of
its own (`tmux -L olo-agents`) on one crate no other agent is in, with
its rules in front of the task (that crate only, no git that changes
anything, no new dependencies, no agents, nothing on the person's
screen, `report.md` and DONE when finished); `agents watch`, in the
background, returns as soon as one needs its lead (an approval its
reviewer won't pass, a finished turn, an exit, 15 minutes with nothing
new); `peek`, `say`, `approve`, `stop`. Each builds in its own target
folder. Its work is reviewed, pictured and committed by its lead.

While the person controls a screen (Take Control), the viewer writes
`NAME.control` (its pid) in the screens' folder, and `olo-screen`
refuses every action on that screen (`history::ACTIONS` but `start`,
and `maximize`) with "the person is controlling screen NAME …: nothing
was done. Wait until they hand it back (olo-screen wait NAME --free)",
kept in the screen's history like any action; reading it still answers.
Stop Controlling, a quit or another screen chosen removes it; a viewer
that has gone (its pid not an `olo-screen`) controls nothing, and one
re-executed by an upgrade forgets its own (`clear_controlled_by_me`).
Two hands on one pointer made a mess before (Ben: "all kinds of weird
stuff happens").

While the person controls a screen, its clipboard and theirs are one
(`clip.rs`): what they copy on the screen is on their clipboard and what
they copied on their own display pastes on the screen, every form of
it (text, pictures, files), both ways, each side's clipboard watched
(`clipboard::watch`) and what came from the other side not sent back
(by a digest of it). Handed back, what of theirs is on the screen's
clipboard is taken off it (an agent's screen never has the person's
clipboard on its own); what they copied from the screen stays on
theirs. It's joined off the UI thread (two displays' connections).

### Moving windows to and from screens (apps/screen/src/moving.rs)

The person can put any of their windows on an agent screen (for an agent
to work in it: a Terminal tab, a Chrome window, a document), and give a
screen's windows to themselves; the program keeps running as it goes.
`olo-screen take NAME|--new --window ID…` moves the person's windows
(ids on their display) onto a screen, and `olo-screen give NAME
[--window ID…] [--workspace N] [--display OUTPUT]` the screen's (all of
them by default) to the person's display, onto one of its workspaces;
both answer JSON (`went`: each program, how it went and its windows'
new ids; `stayed`: what didn't, and why), go in the screen's history,
and are allowed while the person controls the screen (they're the
person's moves). `moving::move_windows` groups the windows by program:
- An app on Olo's kit is asked over its command socket (`{"move":…}`,
  `olo_kit_base::moving::MoveTo`: the window's surface, or none for the
  whole app, and the environment of the display it goes to). Its only
  window, or all of them, and it re-executes there with its state
  (`on_upgrade`'s), as for an upgrade, keeping its pid
  (`upgrade::move_to`). One window of several, or an app that is also
  part of the desktop (a layer: Tracker's desktop; resident), goes by a
  copy of the app started there with that window's state
  (`on_move_window`, `moving::start_copy`) and let go here: Tracker's
  folder and Find windows, Terminal's windows. Otherwise it says why it
  stays.
- Any other program is moved by the olo-wlproxy holding its connection
  (`move PID PATH`, above). A program's connection is all its windows,
  so they all go (`went` says so).

A moved kit app is started with `OLO_MOVED` (claimed as it starts), so it
never hands itself to a copy already running there (`instance::forward`
is skipped, and `instance::listen` leaves that copy its socket). The
person's app on a screen carries `OLO_HOME` (`moving::env_for`: what its
environment was, a `MoveTo` back); dropped as it goes back. It goes back
when the screen stops (`screens::stop` first runs `moving::send_home`:
each proxy's `home`, then each kit app with an `OLO_HOME` asked to move
back, and a moment for them to go) or ends without a word (a kit app
whose compositor is lost while its screen's session or socket is gone,
`upgrade::going_home`, waits up to 2 s to tell an end from a restart; the
proxy's `AWAY_GONE`). A program started on a screen and given to the
person stays theirs when the screen stops (a kit app re-executed with
their environment; another program served on by the screen's forked
proxy). Terminal: its shells live in the olo-termd of the display it
started on, which a moved Terminal keeps talking to (`wire::display`
reads `OLO_HOME`), and a window or tab goes by a Terminal on the screen
attaching its shells (`Saved::moved`: taken from the other Terminal,
whose tab goes as olo-termd detaches it, never hung up; no other shells
opened); a Terminal started on a screen stays there
(`refuse_moves_while`: its shells end with the screen).

Where it's offered (`olo_kit_base::moving::screens()` lists the screens
running, by the name the person gave each; only on the person's own
display, `menus_offer`, and only for windows whose program can move,
`WindowInfo::kept`; each runs `olo-screen take` on a thread, a
notification saying why if nothing moved, `take_to_screen`):
- the window menu (a window tab's right-click): Move to Agent Screen ▸
  each screen, New Agent Screen (`Menu::agent_screens`);
- Deskbar's app menu: Move (All) to Agent Screen ▸; a workspace
  heading's menu: Move All Windows to Agent Screen ▸;
- Terminal's tab menu: Move to Agent Screen ▸ (the tab alone, by a
  Terminal on the screen: `moving::copy_to_screen`);
- Agent Screens, beside Take Control: Move Windows To… (and Control ▸
  Move Windows To ▸): every window on the screen to one of the person's
  display-workspaces (`moving::give`, on a worker; an alert says what
  stayed).

Tested in a private world (its own `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, HOME and bus, a
stand-in person's `olo-session --headless` and a screen beside it):
DeskCalc and GNOME Calculator there and back (the calculator took input
on the screen), each coming home when the screen stopped and when its
session was killed without a word; a screen's DeskCalc and zenity given
to the person outliving the screen (its stop 0.05 s with the forked
proxy, 3 s before); a Tracker folder window and a Terminal window and
tab moved by copies, the Terminal's shell the same process on the
screen (`echo $$`), all of them back when the screen stopped.

### A screen's own bus (crates/bus, crates/session/src/own_bus.rs)

On the person's session bus, a program started on a screen found the
person's copy of itself by its name (GTK's GApplication) and had it open
the window on their display, a portal dialog it asked for (Chrome's
upload, Open With) showed on their display, and its notifications popped
up there. So each screen's session runs a bus of its own: `olo-screen
start` passes `olo-session --own-bus unix:path=$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/
olo-screens/NAME.bus`, and the session starts `olo-bus` there before
anything else (waiting for its "ready"), points its environment at it
(`DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS`), and looks after it with the shell (started
again if it ends; ended with the session, and with `--with-parent`
however the session ends). A bus that ends takes every connection with
it, and GLib programs (Chrome, GTK's) quit with their session bus: so an
upgrade leaves it the old version until the screen restarts (`check_stale`;
restarted 90 s after the upgrade of 2026-11-14, it took a screen's
Chrome and its pages with it, and left Olo's portal and notification
centre there on the bus that had gone), and if it ends anyway, the
services the session runs on it are started again on the new one
(`restart_bus_services`: tried by ending a screen's bus, its portal,
notification centre and xdg-desktop-portal back on the new bus within
a second, every name answering). The listing has it (`Screen::bus`), so `run`
and moves give programs the screen's bus (`moving::bus_env`), and a
move back gives the person's back. A screen from before has none and
stays on the person's.

What the person's session has on their bus, the screen has on its own
(`own_bus::services`, with the shell): its own notification centre
(`olo-notifications --bus`, shown on the screen: agents see their
programs' notifications, the person doesn't get them), Olo's portal
backend (`olo-portal --bus`) and GTK's (Settings: the colour scheme),
behind xdg-desktop-portal, so Open and Save panels and the rest show on
the screen. Nothing on the screen's bus starts on demand, so `olo-bus`
stands in for what the frontend needs (a permission store in memory, so
the person's on-disk one is never written by two; the document portal's
mount point, the person's: sandboxed programs' file sharing isn't
offered on a screen) and waits for the backends the session is starting
when they're asked for (`--expect`). The keyring isn't there: the
person's secrets reach a screen only through Passwords' grants
("Passwords for agent screens"). The accessibility bus stays the
person's (`olo-screen` asks theirs for its address: `OLO_A11Y_BUS` to
the session, `AT_SPI_BUS_ADDRESS` to programs, and `org.a11y.Bus` on
the screen's bus answers it), so `tree` reads GTK and Qt programs there
as before.

`olo-bus` is busd 0.5.0's broker (MIT; `crates/bus/LICENSE-MIT`) on
async-io and smol rather than tokio (zbus's `tokio` feature would have
turned every Olo program's zbus to tokio: Cargo unifies features), Unix
sockets only, lenient about match rules as dbus-daemon and dbus-broker
are (spaces, `eavesdrop`: Chrome's, `fdo::dbus::lenient_rule`), and it
answers a call to a name nobody has at once (`ServiceUnknown`;
`Peers::answer_unknown`), where busd left the caller waiting out its own
timeout (GLib's 25 s: GTK programs on test buses took that long to show).
And a call whose recipient goes without answering it is answered by the
bus, `org.freedesktop.DBus.Error.NoReply`, as dbus-daemon and
dbus-broker answer it (`Peers::answer_for`: each call delivered is kept
until its answer passes, by who has it, who asked and its serial), where
busd answered nothing: a zbus caller has no timeout of its own and
waited for good (Preferences ▸ Network's worker, its stand-in
NetworkManager stopped mid-call; `crates/bus/tests/no_reply.rs`). It
costs nothing measurable: `cargo run --release -p olo-bus --example
calls -- ADDRESS` times calls through a running bus (about 110 µs to
the bus and 140 µs to a peer here, before and after, 20,000 each), and
the bus stays at 7.5 MB through 400,000.
tsession's sessions use it too, when built.

An Electron app (Slack, VS Code, Discord) finds its running copy through
a lock in its config folder, not the bus, so one started on a screen
gets a config folder of the screen's own (`XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, beside its
history as Chrome's profile is: `olo_xdg::electron`, known by its
`resources/app.asar` or a launcher script naming one), from `olo-screen
run` and from anything a screen's own programs start (`olo_xdg`'s
`spawn`, `spawn_app`, `spawn_detached`, which see `OLO_SCREEN`): signed
out, its own. Tested with Slack running for a stand-in person and
started on the screen: two Slacks, each on its display.

Tested in a private world and on a real screen: the portal's Open panel
asked on a screen shows there; GNOME Calculator runs on the person's
display and on the screen at once (before, the screen's handed itself
over); a notification sent on the screen is the screen's centre's; Olo's
Chrome opens in half a second with no match rule refused; `tree` reads
GNOME Calculator's buttons on a screen with its own bus; the bus ends
with the screen.

### Passwords for agent screens (apps/screen/src/shares.rs)

Agents on a screen get the passwords the person chose, and only those:
items shared with every screen (Screen ▸ Passwords for Every Screen…)
and, in each screen's Passwords tab, more or fewer for that screen. Both
lists are every item Passwords has (titles, usernames, vaults, kinds: no
secrets), searched and filtered in the kit's language (`vault:`,
`kind:`, `shared:yes`), several chosen at once (⇧, ⌘, ⌘A) and shared
or not with Share and Stop Sharing. The tab says how each stands: Every
screen, This screen (besides), Not here (every screen's, taken away
here).

The choice is kept in the person's store, sealed with it
(`vault::Shares`: `everywhere`, and each screen's `ScreenShares { add,
remove }`), and asked and changed over the keychain socket
(`Request::Shares`, `SetShares`), which waits for Passwords to be
unlocked and refuses a program on an agent screen (`OLO_SCREEN` in its
environment, `shared::on_a_screen`), so an agent can't share itself
more. After anything that changes the store, Passwords writes what each
screen has as a store of its own (`Vault::write_copies`): every
screen's in `~/.local/state/olo/screens/passwords.vault`, and one in
`screens/NAME/` for each screen given more or less (gone again when it's
back to every screen's), each sealed with a key kept beside it (0600),
an unchanged copy not written again. This is the person's choice
(2026-11-03) over sharing only while their Passwords is unlocked: a
screen's items are there whether or not their Passwords is open or
unlocked, and are readable by anything that can read the screen's key.

Passwords started on a screen (`OLO_SCREEN` set) opens its copy, or
every screen's, with that key alone (`Vault::open_shared`): no lock, no
setup, no syncing, read only (no New Item or Edit; the store refuses
changes), the person's settings left alone, `op` answered without asking
(what's there was given to the screen's agents), and the copy followed:
shared more or less, it opens again (`SharedChanged`). Its status line
says "N items shared with this screen". A passkey shared with the
screen is used there without asking (Ben, 2026-11-16: "they should NOT
require a tap / user approval to use the passkey, it should be approved
automatically but logged in the agent history"): a page's sign-in
request for a site with one passkey here is signed at once
(`unasked`), where the person's own Passwords asks in an alert; with
several for the site, which is the agent's to say, in the question on
its own screen. Each use is written in the screen's history
(`olo_keychain::shared::log`, from the store as it signs, so however it
was chosen): a line of `screens/NAME/actions.jsonl` as `olo-screen`'s
own, `passkey example.com "Title (user)"`, which Agent Screens' History
and `olo-screen history` show. A passkey not shared with the screen
isn't there to use: the page gets Chrome's own way. Making one is
refused as any change (the copy is read only). Tried headless
(Passwords started as on a screen, a fixture store, `olo-keychain-ask`
asking as Chrome's extension does): one passkey, an assertion at once
and the line in the history; two, the question; the build before, the
question for one. To try it: `cargo test -p
olo-passwords fixture -- --ignored` writes a store with a few items
(`OLO_FIXTURE_VAULT`, `OLO_FIXTURE_KEY`).

**What real agents tripped on** (Ben, 2026-11-17: "go through the agent
screens history for a sample of the real agent screens that have run
and identify any problems the agents hit ... and fix what we can").
Read from every screen's `actions.jsonl` (61 screens, 66 000 actions,
500 refused; counted and shaped, never their words), and each kind
reproduced on a screen with a page made for it. What was fixed:

- `set` "didn't take the focus; nothing typed" (60, all but two in
  Chrome): a field that moves as it takes the focus (a label floating
  up, a page scrolling it in) was compared by its exact place.
  `find::focus_in`: the same kind of thing by the same name, or one
  that takes typing where it was.
- `select` "its menu has no item (or didn't open)" (31, all in Chrome):
  a page's `<select>` menu is the browser's, with no items in any
  tree. The Olo extension now lists a select's options on its node
  (`UiNode::options`, tree.js; extension 1.13.0; 1.14.0 says a page's
  code was mailed, `by_mail`; 1.15.1 opens a link in the window chosen,
  `open_in_front`), the outline shows
  them (`options=[…]`), and `select` chooses by the keyboard, by the
  option's words (`find::option_meant`: the same, else the only one
  starting so, else the only one holding them), then checks the value.
  A kit pop-up whose menu opened without the item says so at once with
  what it has (it waited three seconds).
- A miss by name (215 clicks and sets; after most the agent tried other
  words, coordinates or a key): names now match but for case, quotes
  and dots (`find::plain`), what's asked for on a screen still changing
  is looked for again for up to 1.5 s (a screen at rest answers at
  once), and a miss says the same words under another role ("there is
  a Link with those words") and lists the names most like it first
  (`find::likeness`), with how many there are.
- `invoke` given a control's name (10): says it's for menu commands and
  what presses a button; given an item's label, chooses that item; a
  command it hasn't names the nearest; one that's off says so.
- `scroll-to` given the words alone (7 of 8 of its refusals): takes
  them as `--text`.
- Every action's `after` waited a flat 150 ms: it now reads as soon as
  the focus has settled (two reads alike, 30 ms apart, from 40 ms; at
  most 0.4 s). Measured on a screen: a kit app's click 160 → 76 ms, a
  key 160 → 82 ms, a page's `set` 312 → 161 ms (its first click had
  taken the focus all along; the second was the miss above). At the
  histories' rate (9 000 clicks, 9 000 keys, 2 800 types) that is about
  half of the time agents spent in `after`.

Already fixed before this look, and gone from the recent histories: key
names as X11 and the web write them (`Page_Down`), points as `X,Y` and
`--at`, scroll's `--dy` alone, `stop` of a screen already gone.

## Google Chrome (apps/chrome)

`olo-chrome` is Google Chrome in Olo's applications (`OUR_APPS`).
With Chrome installed it execs Chrome's own launcher
(`~/.local/share/olo/chrome/current/google-chrome`) with its arguments,
adding `--ozone-platform=wayland` under Wayland (Chrome otherwise goes by
`XDG_SESSION_TYPE` and falls back to X11). Each profile it starts gets
Olo's defaults once (`prefs.rs`: Olo's title bar, the GTK theme, no
password saving of Chrome's own) and Passwords' extension, the first
start after installing too. On an agent screen (`OLO_SCREEN`) a profile
starts ready for an agent: Chrome's `First Run` mark written in its
folder, so no terms of service window, first-run or welcome pages (a new
screen's profile showed Google's terms, which agents couldn't get
past), `session.restore_on_startup` set to the New Tab page (no
"Continue where you left off" bar) and `--no-default-browser-check`;
the person's own first Chrome still shows them Google's terms. Without it, it offers to
download it in a window on the kit (an `AlertFrame` with the
installer icon: the offer, the download's `StatusBar` with Cancel, or
why it failed with Try Again; Return and Escape as an alert's; 54 MB
against egui's 77) (`install.rs`, on a worker thread, cancellable): Google's rpm
repository for this CPU (`repomd.xml` → the primary index → the newest
`google-chrome-stable`), the package downloaded with live progress and
its sha256 checked against the index, then unpacked natively (the rpm
lead and headers, the payload's compressor from tag 1125, a cpio
stream: "newc", or rpm 6's stripped form, `07070X` and a number for
each file, its place in the header's own list of files, which gives
its name, mode and size, `Header::files`; Google's packages since
157.0.8103.78 are built with rpm 6.0.1, and until 2026-11-17 the daily
update said "in a form Olo can't unpack" and Chrome stayed as it was;
only `./opt/google/chrome/`, no setuid bits, no `..`) into
`<version>/`, with `current` switched over by a rename and older versions
removed. It installs Chrome's icons into the hicolor theme and a
`google-chrome.desktop` that starts it through `olo-chrome` (NoDisplay,
as Olo lists it itself; rewritten when it isn't ours). Nothing needs
root. Once a day (`.checked`), a start also runs `olo-chrome
--olo-update` in the background: a newer version is put in beside the
running one and becomes `current` for the next start (the one it
replaced is kept, as Chrome reads its files as it runs; older ones go;
`.updating` keeps it to one at a time). Test it with a fixture HOME (`tsession run NAME HOME=… XDG_DATA_HOME=…
target/debug/olo-chrome`), never Ben's profile.

With a Chrome already running on the profile folder (its
`SingletonLock`, `host-pid`, naming a live process on this computer),
`olo-chrome` hands it the command line itself (`singleton.rs`) instead
of starting a second Chrome only to do that: Chromium's process
singleton protocol, `START`, the current folder and the arguments (the
program first), each after a NUL, written to `SingletonSocket` in the
profile folder, the write side closed, answered `ACK` (or `SHUTDOWN`: that
Chrome is going, so start one). The activation token goes along as
`--xdg-activation-token=…`, as Chrome's own hand-over passes it, so the
window comes forward. A link from `xdg-open` (a CLI's sign-in) so opens
in a millisecond and says nothing on the terminal, where a second Chrome
printed "Opening in existing browser session." and its zygote's
"Failed sending zygote boot message: Broken pipe" as it went. No Chrome
running, or no answer: Chrome is started as before.

**Open in which window?** (`choose.rs`; Ben, 2026-11-17: "when something
is opening with the default app, e.g. a url opening in chrome, and that
app has > 1 windows open and the url would normally open as a tab in
that app, then i want olo to show me a dialog where i can choose which
window to open it in -- each window should have a live thumbnail ... as
well as the window title ... and it should also have a kb shortcut for
each one"). A web link (http, https: `link_of`, nothing said of a new
window) handed to a running Chrome whose browser process has two
windows or more on this display (app_server's: its own, `google-chrome`,
not Slack's or another app's, not DevTools or a picture in picture,
the one in front first) asks first, in a dialog that is olo-chrome's
only window: "Open the Link in Which Window?", the windows as live
thumbnails (`olo_capture::thumbnails`, a picture a second when one
changed, while the dialog is the active window: behind others it
keeps the pictures it has and asks for none) titled by their page
(" - Google Chrome" left off), each with
its letter, A, B, …, as a key cap on its picture (`style::key_cap`,
keyboard hints' and Twitcher's look). Its letter (wherever the keyboard
is) or a click on it opens the link there; Return, in the one chosen
(the one in front at first); New Window, in a new window; Escape or
Cancel, nowhere. Agents read the windows as radio buttons. The window
chosen is brought forward (`Request::Activate`, waited for until
app_server has it focused), then Olo's extension opens the link in a
new tab of it (`open_in_front`: the host's `open-in-front {url, title,
width, height}` command on Chrome's socket, `{open_in_front}` to the
extension, which finds the window by its page's title and its size, as
Agent Screens pairs them, and of two alike takes the one Chrome has the
focus in). Chrome's own hand-over won't do: tried on an agent screen,
it opened every link in the window it had last opened one in, whatever
was in front, though Chrome's windows API had the one brought forward
as focused. A file isn't asked about (an extension can't open one in a
tab); without the extension, Chrome's hand-over as before. Tried on
agent screens with Chrome's own windows on pages of a loopback server:
eight links each in the window chosen by its letter (two of them with
both windows on one page at one size), a click, Return, Escape, New
Window; reviewed at 1×, 1.5× and 2×.

**One window: the link goes to it. And a window is a profile's.** (Ben,
2026-11-18: "it's not opening in my existing single chrome window it is
opening a new chrome window. if there is one existing chrome window it
should always open in that, and if more than one it should show the
picker".) With one browser window the link was handed to Chrome, and
**a running Chrome opens a handed-over link in the profile it used
last, making a window for it if that profile has none** (one of its
windows was open and has been closed since): a second window beside
the one that was there. Reproduced in a test session with a Chrome and
a profile of its own in scratch: a window of "Profile 1" opened, used
and closed, then a link: a new window, with Default's window sitting
there. (Which display or workspace the window is on, and whether it's
minimized, made no difference: each tried.) So with one window Olo no
longer leaves it to Chrome: the window's own profile is asked to open
the link (`choose::open_in_window`), then the window is brought
forward.

A Chrome with several profiles open has Olo's extension, and a host,
for each, and a window is one profile's: its extension is the only one
that can put a tab in it. The socket agents ask Chrome's trees on
(`commands::serve` for Chrome's pid) is one, taken over by the host
started last, so a link sent there reached whichever profile that was
(the picker too, with windows of two profiles). Each host now also
listens on a socket of its own (`host::hosts_dir()`:
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-chrome-hosts/CHROMEPID-HOSTPID.sock`; a host
sweeps those of Chromes that have gone as it starts), once its
extension says it can be asked so (`{can: ["open_in_window"]}`: an
older extension opens a link whatever it's asked and never answers).
`open_in_window` asks each host of that Chrome in turn `{url, title,
width, height, must_match, focused}`; the extension opens the link only
in a window of its own that matches, makes none, and answers
`{opened_in_front: n, ok}`. After the picker (the window brought
forward) the hosts are asked first for the window Chrome has the focus
in, then for it wherever it is; with one window, once. None did (a
private window, an older extension until Chrome is started again and
takes the new one, 1.15.3): the picker's old way, then Chrome's
hand-over. Chrome's own record of which profiles have windows (`Local
State`, `profile.last_active_profiles`) was tried as a way to tell
Chrome the profile (`--profile-directory`) and dropped: Chrome writes
it when it suits it, and in the trial it named the profile whose window
had gone. Tried in the test session: the failing state made again, the
link in the one window; then windows of two profiles, the picker, each
window chosen in turn by its letter, each link in the window chosen.

The trees too (2026-11-20): `olo-screen tree` of a Chrome with two
profiles' windows read only the windows of the profile whose host had
the agents' socket, and none at all once that host had gone with its
profile's last window (the socket was left with nobody behind it). Now
every host listens on its own socket from its start (`host::
own_socket_answered`), and answers `{"tree": true}` there with its own
profile's windows; the host that has the agents' socket asks its
extension and, at the same time, each other host of that Chrome
(`others_trees`: all at once, each given as long as an extension has,
a host that has gone or says something else adding nothing), and
answers with them all. A host takes its own socket away as it ends
(`OwnSocket`), each host follows the hosts' folder (`keep_answering`:
one inotify watch, asleep until it changes, nothing asked on a clock),
and one that finds the agents' socket unanswered (`commands::answered`)
takes it, ending what it answered it with before
(`commands::Serving::stop`: a host that takes the socket again and
again keeps one listening thread, not one more each time). A host
killed outright leaves its socket file, and nothing is told: the next
host to start or end puts it right, as does the extension, which
starts its host again when its port drops. Tried in a test session
(a Chrome and profile in scratch, its runtime folder its own): two
profiles' windows in one answer; the second profile's window closed
and opened three times, one window then two each time, the first host
at one `trees` thread throughout and 0 wakeups a second at rest; a link
asked of each host with `must_match` opened by the one whose window it
was. Tests: `the_other_profiles_trees_are_gathered`,
`a_served_socket_stops_when_told`. (One-time codes never went through
that socket: each host is the phone service's own "browser", `codes.rs`.)
To try Chrome in a test session: its own copy of Chrome
(`cp -r --reflink=auto ~/.local/share/olo/chrome/VERSION` into the
session's home, with `current` and a fresh `.checked`), a
`--user-data-dir` in scratch, pages from a loopback server.

**A code texted to the phone** is offered in the tab waiting for it
(see "The phone"): `src/codes.rs` keeps the host connected to the phone
service, `background.js`'s `codeTabs` asks every tab's frames, and
`content.js` says whether a frame's code field is waiting (`codeWaiting`)
and shows the offer under it (`showOffer`), or puts the code in on an
agent's screen.

**An authenticator's code, offered** (Ben, 2026-11-17: "when a login
asks for a one time code from the authenticator app and the passwords
item has it then olo passwords ext should be smart enough to offer to
auto fill it like it does for when they come via sms"). A code field
that comes up or takes the focus (`code-field`) is also looked at for
Passwords' own code (`background.js`, `codeFromPasswords`): where a
login for the site has a one-time code, the same offer shows under the
field, "Fill code 123456 / From Passwords, for ann". Which login: the
one filled in this tab (`filledIn`), else the one last used on this
site in this profile (`chosenFor`), else the only one with a code; with
several and none of those, none (the menu's One-Time Code has each).
Not where the page says its code was texted (`by_text` without
`by_app`), not while a sign-in under way will fill its own (`nextStep`),
and, sent away, not on that site in that tab for ten minutes. The code
alone is asked of Passwords, never the login's password
(`Request::Code { url, vault, id }`, answered `Response::Code { code,
seconds }` only for a site the login is for; it doesn't wait: locked,
nothing is offered and nothing asks to unlock), as it's offered and
again as it's taken (`code-fresh`: a code changes every half minute,
and what's filled is the one good then). Tested: the request in the
store (`a_logins_code_alone`: the right code, refused for another site
or a login with none, nothing else of the login in the answer), and in
a headless session with a Chrome of its own and a Passwords on a
fixture vault (`otp_fixture`; as on an agent's screen, the one way a
test's Passwords is unlocked: `OLO_SCREEN` and the vault as that
screen's shared copy): offered on a page asking for an authenticator's
code; taken half a minute later, the field had the code good then, not
the one offered; Escape, and not offered again; nothing offered on a
page saying the code was texted, nor with two logins that have codes.

**Passwords in Chrome** (`extension/`, `src/extension.rs`, `src/host.rs`).
Each start (before exec) packs `apps/chrome/extension` (built into the
binary, plus a `palette.css` from Olo's palette, light and dark) into
a CRX3 signed with a P-256 key of this user's own
(`~/.local/share/olo/chrome/extension-key.der`, 0600; the extension id
comes from it), and writes `<chrome>/extensions/<id>.json` naming it:
Chrome on Linux installs such an extension at start without asking, and
takes a higher `version` as an update, so **raise `version` in
`manifest.json` whenever the extension changes**. The listing is the
