install's, so one extension serves every profile and user data folder
that Chrome runs (each gets it once): only an olo-chrome whose own
`~/.local/share/olo/chrome` holds the Chrome it runs writes it, and it
takes out any other Olo Passwords listing (a `*.json` naming an
`olo-passwords.crx` or `tabula-passwords.crx` signed with another key)
from every version folder, which Chrome uninstalls as it next starts.
One with a home of its own running another home's Chrome (a test's,
through a `current` link) lists nothing there and registers its host for
the install's extension, read from that install's key: listing its own
copy put a second Olo Passwords in each of the person's profiles. The worker reloads on
`onUpdateAvailable` (Chrome would otherwise wait for it to go idle,
which the open native port prevents) and puts `content.js` into the tabs
already open on install or update. Beside the profile goes
`NativeMessagingHosts/com.olodesktop.passwords.json`, naming `olo-chrome`
itself: started as `olo-chrome chrome-extension://ID/`, it is the
native messaging host (length-prefixed JSON on stdin/stdout), passing
only `logins`, `fill`, `check`, `save`, `unlock`, `show` and the
passkey requests on to Passwords over the keychain socket (`{id,
request, start}`; `start` starts Passwords and waits out its unlock;
`{cancel: id}` ends a waiting request's connection, which Passwords
sees as `Incoming::gone`) and `{open: true}`. The
extension: a field's context menu has "Autofill with Passwords (the best
login)" and Passwords ▸ each login ▸ Autofill, Username, Password,
One-Time Code (when it has one), and Open Passwords (Unlock Passwords…
while locked); Chrome puts an extension's items under its name when it
has more than one, so they show under Olo ▸. The best login is, in
order: one whose username the page shows (`seen` in content.js: its
text and fields' values, an account chooser, "signed in as"), the one
used on this site (its registrable domain, roughly) before in this
Chrome profile (`chosen` in `storage.local`, which is the profile's:
set by an autofill, or by a login signed in with by hand, found by its
username, a hidden username field or the one account the page shows),
the profile's own account (who is signed in to Chrome there), then
Passwords' order; the popup lists them so too. Which profile: the
extension keeps a random token in its storage, and the host finds the
profile whose `Local Extension Settings/<id>` holds it (`profile.rs`;
among those whose storage Chrome, its parent, has open, since Chrome
rewrites its command line into one string, else every profile of the
user data folder) and reads who is signed in from `Local State`. The
menu is rebuilt when a field gets the focus or the pointer comes over
one (Chrome shows it as it is when the button goes down). Fields are
found in open shadow roots too; the password is the focused one, else
`current-password`, never a `new-password`; the username the text field
before it (one that says it's for the account first); one-time codes by
`one-time-code` or what the field says (never a card's "security
code"), split over one-digit boxes when the site does; each filled as
typing does (keys, `input`, `change`). A sign-in in steps (the account,
then the password, then a code) gets the rest as it comes: after an
autofill that didn't fill everything, the tab is watched (a
`MutationObserver`, and the next page on the same site, for 3 minutes)
and a password or code field that turns up is filled from the same
login. A fill goes only to the frame it was asked from and only while
it is still at the origin the login was asked for. The
toolbar button lists the page's logins (Enter or a click fills one). A
password sent with a form (submit, a button, Enter) is checked, and a
new or changed one offered in a notification (Save/Update, Not Now; the
pending login is kept in `storage.session` only). Passwords names the
waiting app from the keychain caller's program (`Incoming::from`). Test
with a throwaway `--user-data-dir` (DevTools needs a non-default one:
`--remote-debugging-port`), the fake 1Password and a localhost page; the
fake's "Olo Test Site" login (`http://localhost`, jane) has a TOTP.

**Credit cards** (keychain `Cards` and `FillCard`; `card_fields` in
Passwords' `store.rs`; `cardKind`, `fillCard` in `content.js`). A card
form's field (by its `autocomplete` token, `cc-number`, `cc-name`,
`cc-given-name`, `cc-family-name`, `cc-exp`, `cc-exp-month`,
`cc-exp-year`, `cc-csc`, else by what it says: "card number", "CVC",
"expiry month", "name on card"…) tells the menu so as it gets the focus
or the pointer: "Autofill Card (Travel Visa •••• 1111)" on top, and under
Passwords ▸ every card ("Travel Visa (•••• 1111, 08/2029)"), then the
logins as ever. `Cards` gives what may be said of each card (title,
name, brand, last four digits, expiry; never the number or the code),
doesn't wait, and is kept like a page's logins; it is every active
Credit Card item, as a card isn't kept for a site. `FillCard` waits
for an unlock and answers only for a card (the candidates are the one
chosen, if it is one): the number (digits), name, month, year and code,
from 1Password's built-in fields (`ccnum`, `cardholder`, `type`,
`expiry`, `cvv`), else by their types and labels; wiped from the
response once sent. So any page can be given a card, but only by the
person choosing it in Chrome's menu, which a page can't trigger. The fill
goes to the frame the menu was opened in and to the tab's frames that
are the same site's or a payment provider's (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen,
Checkout.com, Square, PayPal and others, whose fields shops put in
frames of their own: `PAYMENT_HOSTS`), never another site's; each fills
the card fields of the form the person was in (else its own), typed as
a person would, selects chosen by value or text ("8", "08", "Aug",
"August"; "29" or "2029"), an expiry field in its own shape (its
placeholder's "MM / YY" or "MM/YYYY", else 4 or 6 long, else "MM/YY"),
a name split where the form asks for given and family names; the frame
the menu was opened in is filled last, so its field keeps the focus.
Tested end to end in a test session: the fake 1Password's Travel Visa
into a checkout page (one form by `autocomplete`, one by its labels with
month and year selects, a same-site frame and another site's frame),
through DevTools (`Runtime.evaluate` in the extension's worker: `cards`,
`buildMenu`, `fillCard`) and through the real menu: only the form the
person was in filled, the same-site frame too, the other site's never.

**Passkeys** (`extension/passkeys.js`, `relay.js`; Passwords'
`passkey.rs`; the keychain's `Passkeys`, `PasskeyCreate`, `PasskeySign`).
Passwords is the page's passkey authenticator in Chrome. `passkeys.js`
runs in the page's own world (`"world": "MAIN"`, `document_start`, every
frame) and answers `navigator.credentials.create`/`get` for
`publicKey` requests (an iframe only where its permissions policy lets
it); `PublicKeyCredential.isUserVerifyingPlatformAuthenticatorAvailable`
and `isConditionalMediationAvailable` say yes, so sites offer passkeys.
Its credentials are objects on `PublicKeyCredential.prototype` (and the
response types') with their values as own properties, so `instanceof`,
`toJSON()` and `getPublicKey()` work as on Chrome's. It talks through
`relay.js` (the isolated world, `postMessage` on its own window) to the
worker, which builds the client data from the frame's origin as Chrome
reports it (`sender.origin`, never the page's word), hashes it, and asks
Passwords, which checks the relying party fits the page
(`olo_keychain::rp_id_fits`: the page's host or above it, a secure
page, never a public suffix or an address). Making one: Passwords asks
in an alert in front ("Save a passkey for “ann@…” on example.com in
Passwords?", naming the login it joins), Use Another Device… / Cancel /
Save Passkey; it joins that account's login, else gets a login of its
own, in a "Passkey" section (P-256 key, attestation "none", the
backup flags set since 1Password syncs it, sign count 0); the item view
shows only its site and user. Signing in (`get`): when Passwords has
none the page may use, Chrome's own way at once (its sheet: a phone's
passkey by QR code, a security key); else an alert, with a radio
button per account when there are several, and Sign In signs. "Use
Another Device…" hands over to Chrome's own sheet; Cancel gives the
page `NotAllowedError`; the page giving up (an `AbortSignal`, leaving)
takes the alert down. Locked, Passwords answers from the index it keeps
while locked: none here means Chrome's way without an unlock; else it
comes forward to be unlocked ("Google Chrome is waiting for a passkey")
and then asks. A sign-in that suggests passkeys in its account field
(`mediation: "conditional"`) gets Chrome's own suggestions and, in the
field's context menu, Olo ▸ "Sign In with Passkey (who)" (the others
under Passwords ▸), which signs at once (the click is the consent);
whichever is chosen first wins and the other is let go. Passwords
filters items with a passkey (`has:passkey`). Test with a localhost
page that checks what a site would: the client data, the
authenticator data's site hash and flags, the attestation, and the
signature with WebCrypto.

**A one-time code a page shows to set up** (Ben, 2026-11-16: "olo
passwords and its chrome extension should be able to scan/detect a qr
code shown on a page for mfa setup and offer to add/update the mfa one
time code stuff in the associated passwords item"; `content.js`'s
`qrShown`, `background.js`'s `otpShown`, the keychain's `OtpScan`,
Passwords' `qr.rs`, `store::otp_read`/`otp_save`, `OtpAsk`). A site
setting up two-step sign-in shows a QR code to scan with a phone, an
`otpauth://totp/…` URI; Passwords takes it for the site's login
instead.
- The content script looks for one where a page shows it: as the page
  has loaded, and 0.9 s after a click or Return (set-up steps open on
  those); it never watches the page. What looks like one: an `img`,
  `canvas` or `svg` in view, square (within an eighth), 90 to 600
  points a side, with words about it in what it's in (a few levels up:
  authenticator, two-factor, 2FA, one-time, QR code, scan the…) or in
  its own `alt`. Each picture is looked at once.
- The worker then takes a picture of the tab
  (`chrome.tabs.captureVisibleTab`, a JPEG; only the tab in front, no
  oftener than every five seconds a tab) and sends it to Passwords
  (`{type: "otp_scan", url, title, image}`, which the host passes on;
  Passwords isn't started for it).
- Passwords reads it natively, on the store's thread (`qr::otpauth_in`:
  the `image` crate and `rqrr`, every QR code in the picture, the first
  that is a time-based `otpauth://` URI with a secret; nothing of the
  picture is kept). None: `NoCode`. A login for the site has that very
  secret: `Known`, nothing asked. Locked, or on an agent's screen
  (read only): `Locked`, an error; nothing shown, and the extension
  looks at the same picture again another time (`qr-again`).
- Else it asks, in an alert in front (`OtpAsk`): "Add the one-time code
  this page shows to your login “Title” (user)?", or "Replace the
  one-time code of your login …" when it has another; the login is the
  one whose username the code names (its account), else the site's
  only one (`qr::joins`), else chosen among them with radio buttons;
  with no login for the site, "Save a login for HOST with the one-time
  code this page shows?" (titled by the code's issuer, its account the
  username). Return adds, Escape doesn't; the page going closes it.
  Added, it's the login's One-Time Password field (the URI whole, so
  its digits, period and algorithm are kept), the first one's value
  replaced if it has several.
- Tested: codes read from pictures as PNG and JPEG, big and small, and
  not other QR codes or `hotp`; which login a code goes with; the
  store's part on a store of its own (found, added, known, replaced, a
  new login). Tried headless end to end: a test Passwords (set up to
  keep only on this computer, a login saved for the site), this
  build's `olo-chrome` in a scratch home with a copy of Chrome's
  install (so it packs and lists this build's extension; end that
  Chrome by its program's path, `readlink /proc/PID/exe`, as a start
  with one running only hands it the page), and a localhost page that
  shows a QR code when its button is clicked: the question came 2 s
  after the click, Replace put the code in the login, and the page
  loaded again asked nothing. `qr_fixture` (ignored) writes a code's
  picture for such a page.

**Downloads** (`background.js`'s Downloads, `downloads.rs`). The
extension (with the `downloads` permission: Chrome only asks again for
a permission an extension it installed itself gains, never for one in
its install's `extensions` folder) tells the host of Chrome's downloads:
`{downloads: [...]}` with those under way (id, file, received, total,
paused, url), on each start or stop and every half second while there
are any (Chrome says nothing as one goes), and `{downloaded}` when one
finishes or fails (with Chrome's `InterruptReason`). The host sends
Deskbar a `com.canonical.Unity.LauncherEntry` update for
`application://google-chrome.desktop` (the count, and the progress of
them all once each knows its size: Chrome itself would only through
libunity), marks the file being written (`NAME.crdownload`) with the
size it will be (`olo_kit::files::set_expected_size`, the
`user.olo.expected_size` attribute), and shows an Olo notification for
a finished one (the picture, if it is one; a click or Open opens it,
Open in Tracker shows it; one that failed for a reason other than being
cancelled says why). Tracker shows a `NAME.crdownload` as `NAME`, of the
kind it will be, with a bar under its icon (icon views, the column
preview) and "3.1 of 10 MB" / "Downloading, 31%" in its Size and Kind
(`Entry::downloading`, `label`, `size_text`, `kind_text`); Chrome renames
it when done, and the bar goes. In olo-slack's Chrome, Chrome's own
download UI is off (`chrome.downloads.setUiOptions`, the `downloads.ui`
permission, set as its host says it's Slack's, at each start): Slack's
window is an app's, without Chrome's toolbar, and Chrome's bubble,
anchored to the toolbar's hidden button at the window's corner, opened
at its top left and over the display beside it (Ben, 2026-11-19;
Chromium has since anchored it to the window's edge). Olo's notification
is the download's there. A download Chrome holds there until the
person keeps or deletes it (its `danger`, not safe or accepted) is told
of (`{held}`): Olo's notification says so, and Show Downloads opens
Chrome's Downloads page (`{show_downloads}`), where that's done. (Not
seen in a test: no kind of file served from loopback was held by a
scratch profile's Chrome on Linux.) A normal Chrome window keeps
Chrome's bubble, by its toolbar's button.

**Chrome's widget tree, for agents** (`extension/tree.js`, `host.rs`).
The extension (named "Olo": it does more than passwords) connects to
its host when its worker starts and stays connected (reconnecting after
10 s), so a host runs beside every Chrome. The host answers a kit app's
`tree` socket for its parent, Chrome's browser process (the Wayland
client app_server names in `WindowInfo::pid`), with
`commands::serve_trees`: each question goes to the extension as
`{tree: n}`, which injects `tree.js` into every frame of each window's
active tab and answers `{tree: n, windows}` within `TREE_WAIT`.
(A Chrome with several profiles open has a host for each: the one that
has the socket gathers the others' windows with its own, above.)
**Iframes**: in each frame, `tree.js` tells every iframe element a token
of its own (kept per element in the extension's isolated world, posted
to the iframe's window each time, since it may have navigated); the
frame inside keeps it (`content.js` listens; a frame not told yet waits
up to 150 ms) and reports it with its nodes. An iframe's node carries
its token and content box (its rect less border and padding), and
`stitch` (background.js) puts the frame's nodes under it, offset to that
box and clipped to it (and to every iframe around it), cross-origin
frames and nested ones alike, so `click`, `set` and `wait` work inside
embedded sign-ins, payment forms and consent dialogs as on the page. `tree.js`
walks the page (shadow roots too, at most 4000 nodes) as assistive
technology sees it: ARIA roles, else the element's (Link, Button,
TextInput, PasswordInput, CheckBox, ComboBox, Heading, Image, List, Row,
Cell, Dialog, …), "Clickable" for script-made buttons (an `onclick`, a
`tabindex`, or where the pointer cursor starts), and "Label" for text
not inside anything named; names from `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`,
the control's `<label>` (which is then left out), `alt`, `placeholder`
or the text; values, checked, selected, disabled and the focus.
Passwords' values are never read (`••••••••`). Places are the viewport's
CSS pixels times the tab's zoom, the page set at the bottom of the
window below Chrome's tab strip and toolbar (`window.height − page
height`); a `Window` node and a `Document` node (title, URL) hold it.
Agent Screens matches a tree to its window by the page title the
window's title starts with. Chrome's own tab strip and toolbar aren't in
the tree. Test on an agent screen with a private `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, a
copy of Chrome in a fixture `XDG_DATA_HOME` (`olo-chrome` writes into
the install's `extensions` folder) with a fresh `.checked`, a throwaway
profile and a page served from 127.0.0.1.

## Slack (apps/slack, olo-slack)

`olo-slack` is Slack, Olo-fied, as `olo-chrome` is Chrome: Slack's web
app in Olo's Chrome, as an app window of its own (`--app`), on a Chrome
profile of its own (`$CHROME_CONFIG_HOME`, else the config folder, then
`olo-slack`: an agent screen has its own), so Slack's sign-in and data
are Slack's alone and the person's Chrome is untouched. It is one of
`OUR_APPS` ("Slack", Olo's `slack` icon). Chrome names an `--app`
window's Wayland app id after the URL and the profile folder
(`chrome-app.slack.com__client-Default`); app_server reports it as
`olo.slack` (`olo_xdg::apps::WEB_APPS`, `WindowElement::app_id`), so
Deskbar, the palette, Twitcher and agents know it as Olo's Slack. Its
keys are Chrome's as the keyboard profile has them ("Keyboard
profiles": on a Mac ⌥← and ⌥→ a word, ⌘[ and ⌘] Back and Forward,
whatever Chrome's are set to in Preferences). It
always starts on the same page (the app id comes from it) and goes to a
link once in: `olo-slack LINK` (a `slack://channel?team=T&id=C`, `open`,
`user` link, or a Slack page) leaves it in the profile folder (`Olo Slack
Link`) for the extension's host to take once. With Slack open,
`olo-slack [LINK]` brings its window forward (app_server's `Activate`)
and hands the link to it (the kit's commands socket: `open URL`), never
a second window. Chrome starts with `--no-first-run
--no-default-browser-check`: the first-run dialog's "Make Google Chrome
the default browser", ticked, would have made Slack's Chrome the
person's browser. `slack://` links open in it (`open::ours_for`).

The joining is the Olo extension's (apps/chrome: `slack-page.js`,
`slack.js`, background.js's "olo-slack" part) and its host's (`slack.rs`),
only in olo-slack's Chrome: olo-slack gives Chrome `OLO_SLACK_URL` and
`OLO_SLACK_PROFILE`, which reach the host as Chrome starts it; the host
takes them out of its environment at once (nothing it starts, a link's
browser, inherits them) and tells the extension `{slack: {url, open}}`.
The extension then registers its two Slack scripts for Slack's address
(`chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts`, kept by Chrome between
starts; the first time, Slack's page is reloaded so they are in from its
start):

* **Notifications** (`slack-page.js`, in the page's own world before its
  scripts): the page's `Notification` (and a service worker
  registration's `showNotification`, and `permissions.query`) is
  answered there, always granted; each goes to the host, which shows it
  as an Olo notification of Slack's (`Notifier`, "Slack", `olo-slack`:
  Message style, Slack's aubergine edge, the sender's face as its icon,
  fetched by the extension with Slack's sign-in and kept in
  `~/.cache/olo/slack/faces`; silent, as Slack plays its own sound; a
  tag's later one updates it in place). Olo's Notifications keeps its
  history and its Do Not Disturb. A click on one brings Slack forward
  and is the page's `click` (Slack goes to the conversation); its going
  is the page's `close`.
* **Unread count** on Slack's Deskbar row: the page's app badge
  (`navigator.setAppBadge`, answered in the page) once Slack sets one,
  else what its title says (`(3) …`: 3; `! …`: at least one), as a
  `com.canonical.Unity.LauncherEntry` count for `olo-slack.desktop`,
  sent only when it changes (and again to a new host). Slack's Chrome's
  downloads show only their progress there (`downloads::SLACK`): the
  count is Slack's.
* **Links**: a link out of Slack that would open a tab (a click on a
  `target=_blank` link, a middle click, Ctrl and a click: `slack.js`; or
  `window.open`: background.js's `tabs.onCreated`, the tab taken back)
  opens with Olo's default app for it, the person's own browser, not
  Slack's Chrome. Slack's own pages (its sign-in, `*.slack.com`) and a
  sign-in's popup stay.
* **Pictures**: a picture's context menu has Open in Viewer: the
  extension fetches it with Slack's sign-in and the host writes it to
  `~/.cache/olo/slack/pictures` and opens it in Olo's Viewer. The cache
  keeps faces and pictures 30 days.
* **The palette**: the host answers the kit's commands socket for
  Chrome's process (`commands::serve`, `Served`: menus and invoke beside
  the trees) with Slack's commands, asked of the page as the palette
  asks (nothing is watched between): Jump To… and Search… (Slack's own
  Ctrl+K and Ctrl+G), and each conversation in Slack's sidebar under
  Channels (`#name`) or Direct Messages, which goes there through the
  sidebar's own link (no reload). Only `jump`, `search` and `open http…`
  pass the host. 3 ms from asking to answer.
* **Agents and Passwords**: as in any of Olo's Chrome's windows (the
  extension's trees, Passwords and passkeys).

* **Status**: Slack's follows Olo's. The host follows the screen's lock
  (app_server's power events), Do Not Disturb (Notifications' state
  file, by the kernel's events; until when, from its settings, if it
  was turned on for a while) and calls (an app recording from a
  microphone, `olo_system::audio::watch_listening`: not Olo's own, not
  a monitor; for 20 s before it's a call, a voice clip isn't, and over
  after 10 s with none), and tells the extension `{slack: {status:
  {away, dnd, dnd_until, call}}}` when it changes (`status_of`); the
  background keeps the latest for a page that comes later. The page
  (slack-page.js) calls Slack's web API as its own client does, with
  each signed-in workspace's token from `localConfig_v2` and the page's
  sign-in: `users.setPresence` away while locked and automatic after,
  `dnd.setSnooze` for Do Not Disturb's time (a day at a time when it
  has no end) and `dnd.endSnooze`, and "In a meeting"
  (`users.profile.set`, :spiral_calendar_pad:) during a call, only when
  the person has no status of their own, cleared after only if it is
  still ours. What Olo set is kept in the page's `oloSlackStatus`, so
  only that is undone, after a reload too. Checked: `status_of`'s test
  (a lock, Do Not Disturb, a voice clip that isn't a call, a pause
  that doesn't end one), and the page's calls against a fake Slack in
  node (`node tools/dev/slack-status-check.mjs
  apps/chrome/extension/slack-page.js`: each case's calls, a status of
  the person's own left, ours changed by them kept), and
  `watch_listening` against a private PipeWire (a virtual microphone
  recorded counts; a speaker's monitor recorded doesn't); not yet against
  Slack itself, which would change the person's status where others
  see it.

Idle, nothing runs (the host 0% of a core, 0 wakeups a second, its
watchers asleep on their sources; the page watches only its
`<title>`). Test with a stand-in page served from
127.0.0.1 (`OLO_SLACK_URL=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/client`: a sidebar of
`/client/T/C` links, buttons that make a `Notification`, change the
title and call `setAppBadge`, a `target=_blank` link, a picture), a copy
of Chrome in a fixture `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `CHROME_CONFIG_HOME` and
`XDG_CACHE_HOME` in `/var/tmp`, in a tsession with its own bus and
`olo-notifications --bus` (its app id is the stand-in's there: check
`olo.slack` against Slack's real address, which shows its sign-in).

## Log Viewer (apps/logs)

`olo-logs` shows every Olo program's log in one place: what they
write to stderr goes to the user's journal (through the session's
journal stream, or, for a program started by another with its stderr
on /dev/null, its own: "Crash reports"), and Log Viewer reads that
journal natively. `olo-logs --query TEXT` opens it on that search (and
a running one takes it: Olo Doctor's "Viewer crashed" does). Kit apps
log `warn,usvg=error,olo=info` unless `RUST_LOG` says otherwise
(`olo_kit::run`; tsession starts clients with `RUST_LOG=warn`): Olo's
own crates keep their info for what is rare and worth knowing after
the fact (a reconnect, an upgrade, why a close was asked about: the
Terminal's `asking before closing` names the program and where the
close came from, app_server's `asked to close a window` and `close box
clicked` the window and who), dependencies only their warnings.

Logs an app writes beside the journal are read too: File ▸ Agent Screen
Logs lists the Agent Screens' (`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-screens/logs`, a
folder of their own so that Deskbar, following the screens listed
beside it, doesn't wake for each line: a
screen's own `NAME.log` and each program run there, `NAME-PROGRAM.log`,
the latest written first), File ▸ Open Log File… (⌘O) any other, and
`olo-logs FILE` (or Tracker's Open With) opens one; File ▸ Journal goes
back. The window then shows that file, titled by it, with the same
search, filters and live tail (`reader::run_file`: read whole, then
followed as it grows, from the start again if it is cut short, as a
screen started again under its name does). Its lines are parsed as the
journal's (`model::file_line`: tracing's time and level, Chromium's
prefix, GLib's words, a panic as an error, indented lines going on with
the one before); those without a time of their own take the file's.
Changing what is read restarts the reader with a new generation
(`Logs::start`): the old one stops, what it already sent is dropped, and
the list's kept cells (keyed by line) are keyed by the generation too.
`olo-logs --print --file LOG` prints one for agents.

- journal.rs: systemd's journal file format (JOURNAL_FILE_FORMAT.md): the
  header, entries through the chain of entry arrays, fields in data
  objects (zstd, xz or lz4; the regular and the compact layout). Data
  objects are cached by offset (most are shared between entries). A
  file still being written is read on from where it was left, and
  across journald rotating it (the open file is finished, then the new
  one opened). `user_files(uid)` finds `user-UID.journal` and its
  archives in /var/log/journal (or /run/log/journal), oldest first.
- reader.rs: on a worker thread, every file in batches, then the active
  one read on as it changes (`olo_kit::watch`: journald truncates the
  file to its own length after each write so that readers hear of it;
  every 30 s anyway, every ½ s without inotify); `Update::Lines` carries
  new lines and more text for lines sent before.
- model.rs: an entry as a line: the program (`_EXE`'s name, else
  `_COMM` made whole from a longer name seen, else the identifier;
  Chrome's lines, which Google's launcher passes through `cat`, as
  chrome), the level and text without terminal colours and without
  `tracing`'s time and level (or Chromium's `[pid:tid:time:LEVEL:file]`),
  GLib's `-WARNING **` and panics recognised, and Olo's own stderr
  lines Info unless they say otherwise (the session's stream files all
  of stderr as warnings). Continuation lines (a pretty debug print, a
  backtrace) join the line before from the same process. `Query`, made
  from the search's text (`Query::from_text`, the kit's language,
  `olo_kit::search`): `since:` (10m, 2h, 1d, today, boot, all; since
  startup if not said), `level:` (the least: debug, info, warning, error;
  info if not said), `program:` (several, any of them, matched by their
  start while one is typed; `all` for every program; none: Olo's),
  `-program:` (left out), `pid:`, and words, phrases and `-words` in the
  message or the program.
- highlight.rs: syntax highlighting as spans: the target `tracing` puts
  first, `key=value` keys, strings, numbers, paths and URLs, type names,
  trouble words; the list and the detail pane colour them from the
  palette.
- main.rs, on Olo's own kit (olo-kit): one `Logs` view on its window's
  looper, told each batch of lines by the reader's thread
  (`cx.messenger()`), filtering a slice at a time by a message to
  itself (`Msg::FilterOn`: everything else in the looper's queue gets
  its turn between slices); the kit's `SearchField` and a `FilterBar` (Program, with
  each program's lines in the query's time and Olo's first; Level; Time)
  above a `ColumnListView`, in one row when the window has room for the
  field, else the menus under it (their text over the list's first
  column; the Message column as wide as the list allows, beside its
  scroll bar); what the words find is marked in the messages
  (`search::runs`: the syntax colours, the marks behind; `Cell::text_runs`).
  The selected line in full (highlighted, selectable, a `TextView`)
  below; Live keeps the list at its end as lines arrive while it is
  there (`ListModel::at_end`); a new query is gone through 2 ms at a
  time between frames (a task yielding to them), and a sliding time
  ("Last 10 Minutes") is chosen again every five seconds only while
  it's asked for. Loading 160,000 lines its worst frame is 3 ms
  (egui's 34), a live line one frame of under 1 ms to 3 (egui drew
  three a line), and it holds 17 MB less. Show in Context
  (⌘K, or a line's context menu) shows every line around one
  (`program:all level:debug since:all`), and Back returns to the search
  before. Show Only (a line's menu) sets `program:` to its program. The
  search's filters are kept from one run to the next, its words aren't
  (`search::filters_only`); settings from before (a menu each) become
  the text once.

For agents, the same query from the command line, reading the journal
directly: `olo-logs --print [--query TEXT] [--since
10m|2h|1d|today|boot|all] [--level debug|info|warning|error] [--program
NAME | --all-programs] [--find TEXT] [--json] [--follow]`, `--query` as
typed in the window's search and the others its filters (JSON lines:
time in UTC, program, pid, level, message). Tests: `cargo test -p olo-logs` (synthetic journal files
in both layouts); `-- --include-ignored` also reads this machine's
journal and highlights every line in it.

## Deskbar (apps/deskbar)

The Olo menu, the tray and the running applications, in the top-right
corner of every display (a layer surface each, namespace `deskbar`, no
keyboard: its menus take the keys as they open), on olo-kit. One
model (`Deskbar`: app_server's windows, workspaces and displays as
events say, the tray's status, other programs' tray items and launcher
badges) behind a lock (`Model`), kept by the app's looper (`Hub`:
what app_server, the status watchers and the tray say comes to it
through the app's proxy, `Msg`), that every display's bar (`BarView`,
on its window's own looper, which keeps only what the pointer is doing
over it) draws: a bar draws again when the hub says the model changed
(`BarMsg::Changed`; a bar that changes it, `Model::update`, has the
hub tell them all), the pointer moves onto something else in it (only
that bar), a dot shakes or drains, or the clock's minute (or second)
comes (a thread of its own, asleep between); idle, nothing runs. What
asks the person first (Restart and Shut Down, the upgrade) is the main
display's bar's to open (`Effect`), so there's one of each; Approve
Without Asking's window is the app's. The lock is held while a bar is
drawn: nothing a drawing calls may take it again (its closures do
later, as the pointer acts). Each bar is painted in one `canvas` (the egui drawing,
moved over: the tile and wordmark, the tray's well, headings, rows,
the lit workspace), with transparent hit areas over it for the pointer:
a left click as a click, the right and middle buttons as they're
pressed (menus open on the press, as BeOS's), hovering that lights and
a tip in a popup of its own (`olo_kit::tip`: the bar is narrower than
what its icons say). A tray icon opens its menu on either button (Ben,
2026-11-06), each menu ending with the app that tells more (Network's,
Displays', Power's, Sound's, Notifications' and Security's preferences,
Activity Monitor, Screenshot); one with no menu (Olo Doctor, the agent
screens, an upgrade) does what its click does on either; another
program's item shows its menu on either button, with "Open NAME" (its
activation) last, or is activated if it has none. The volume's wheel
still sets the volume; Mute is in its menu. The tray's glyphs (status.rs) are exact-coverage
paths and the GPU's discs, rings and arcs (`paint_sector`), straight
lines on device pixels. An application dragged out is a link to its
program (`olo_kit::dnd`, its icon and name under the pointer); files
dropped on one open with it, its row lit as they come over it. A
click on a running application's row with ⌘ held (Super on a Mac's
keys; Control too), or ⌘ held as an application is chosen in the Olo
menu (`run:` and `desktop:` items), starts it again as a process of its
own beside the one running (`launch_again`,
`DesktopEntry::launch_new_instance`): Olo's apps are started with
`OLO_NEW_INSTANCE=1` (`olo_xdg::NEW_INSTANCE`), for which the kit's
`instance::forward` hands nothing over (and clears it; `spawn_detached`
never passes it on), so the copy opens its own window and leaves the
launch socket to the first; another program does as it does (Chrome
opens a window in the one it has). Deskbar never has the keyboard, so
Wayland doesn't say what's held: it asks app_server at the click
(`Request::HeldModifiers`, the seat's keys as pressed). Tried headless:
⌘-clicking Terminal's row, and ⌘-choosing Terminal in Applications,
each started a second olo-terminal with its own window; plain, a
window in the one running. Bars
for displays that come are opened once the model's update is over (a
window draws as it opens, and its bar reads the model), before those
going are closed, so the app always has one. Approve Without Asking's
window (approve.rs) is the kit's alert frame with a `MenuField` and a
`ConversationField`. Release build, against the egui one: first frame
58–73 ms (egui 69–87), 57 MB resident (141), 30 pointer moves across it
32 frames, 0.8 ms each (egui drew 150). The tray's items are counted
before they're placed (one more than counted is drawn nowhere and
logged, never a crash: Olo Doctor's bag, uncounted, took Deskbar down
on its first start after an upgrade, 2026-11-04). The battery: a click
opens Preferences ▸ Power, a right-click the power mode (Performance,
Balanced, Power Saver, checked as the daemon says) and Power
Preferences…. Olo Doctor's bag shows while its last look found
something to fix (`olo_protocol::doctor::DoctorFound`, followed by
inotify); a click opens Olo Doctor. (A recording going wasn't counted
either, until 2026-11-07: the last item went undrawn while one was.)
DiskBackup's item shows once it's set up (and `in_deskbar`, the app's
Show in Deskbar): a drive in a circular arrow (`status::draw_backup`),
the arrow and the drive's light green while it backs up, tidies or
restores (green, not the selection's blue, so it shows with its menu
open), all dim while it isn't backing up (off, on battery, the service
not running), a red dot when the last didn't finish and an amber one
when nothing finished for three days (or three of its intervals). Its
status (`status::Backup`) holds only what the glyph and tip say, so the
state file's progress every 2 s while it runs draws nothing (measured:
5 frames in 20 s with a write every 2 s, 3 without, 0.0–0.1% of a
core); the menu reads the state as it opens: what it's doing, in
DiskBackup's own words (`Progress::lines`, `olo_protocol::diskbackup::
words`, the window's too; Ben, 2026-11-08: "it's also not entirely clear
to me what it means … what is read vs new and i'm backing up my whole
home dir which is hundreds of gigs so why doesn't it say anything about
that"): what it backs up (your home folder), how far through how much
and how long is left, files of files, what's new to the backup and
sent; counting what's there first; a stop finishing the pack it's
sending; a stop said calmly, with what it got through; deleting, how
many of how many; the last and the next, Back Up Now or Stop (Stop
Tidying, Validating, Deleting), Pause or Resume
Backups (`olo-diskbackup --now`, `--stop`, `--set enabled=…`), Restore
Files… (`olo-diskbackup --restore-window`) and DiskBackup…. The speaker's menu has None first
among the outputs (below). The tray's battery and links
follow UPower's display device and NetworkManager's signals
(`olo_system::battery::watch`, `network::watch_links`, each on a thread
that sleeps until one comes; the links on a bus connection of their own
that the bus sends only device state changes, NetworkManager's own (the
default route moving), and for each link connected its properties, its
addresses' and its access point's: a scanning adapter's access points
come and go several times a second here, and aren't asked for), so idle
it wakes 0 times a second (it was 7–9, polling every 4 s). A signal
that says only the access point's strength or the adapter's rate (what
comes every few seconds) is taken from the signal's own values
(`network::quick`); anything else reads the links again (about two dozen
calls, 3.5 ms here) and asks for the signals of what's connected again
only if that changed. Measured beside the old Wi-Fi-only watch over
60 s, idle on Ben's machine (Ethernet and Wi-Fi both up): under one
wakeup a second, against about two.

**Captive portals** (Ben, 2026-11-13: "when a connection requires
portal signin the link is available to click in the network settings
and also a tray icon + notification should appear about it"): a network
that wants its sign-in page first is NetworkManager's own connectivity
check finding it (`Connectivity` = portal, its request answered by
someone else), heard in the same signals as the links, so nothing is
polled. `network::Links::portal` and `Status::portal` (a
`network::Portal`: the network, by its SSID for Wi-Fi, its link, the
page and whether the network named it) read the computer's
`Connectivity` first, one call that is all a read costs while there's
no portal (the links' read went 4.56 → 4.65 ms median, 3.48 → 3.61 ms
best, 30 reads each, interleaved, against `nm-fake`), then the link
whose own check says so (`Ip4Connectivity`/`Ip6Connectivity`, else the
default route's), and the page: the one its DHCP names (option 114,
RFC 8910, NetworkManager's `captive_portal` option; only an `http` or
`https` address), else the check's address
(`ConnectivityCheckUri`, Fedora's when it gives none), plain HTTP the
portal answers with its own page or sends on to it. Deskbar shows a
globe (`browser`) at the head of the links, whose tip says the network
wants you to sign in and whose click opens the page; the link's menu
says Sign-In Needed and has Open Sign-In Page; and it posts one
Important notification (Network, "Sign in to “…”", with an Open
Sign-In Page action), once per network, taken back when the portal
goes. Preferences ▸ Network says "Connected to “…”: sign-in needed"
(Ethernet's Status too) with an Open Sign-In Page button, and the page
as a link when the network named it. Opening it (`network::open_portal`:
the default browser, `olo_xdg::open`) has NetworkManager check again
(`CheckConnectivity`) every 5 s for at most 5 minutes, one round at a
time and stopping as soon as it's through, so the globe goes as you
sign in, not at NetworkManager's own next check five minutes later.
`nm-fake --tell portal [URL]` puts it behind one (the URL as its DHCP's
option 114), `--tell "portal off"` signs in, `--check-uri URI` is its
check's address, and its state says how many checks were asked for;
`crates/system/tests/nm_portal.rs` runs it end to end
(`OLO_TEST_BUS=unix:path=…`).

**AppImages** (`olo_appimage`, crates/appimage, shared with Tracker):
with a `~/AppImages` folder, the Olo menu has an AppImages item under
Applications, each AppImage in it by the name its own desktop entry
gives (else its file's, a version and machine trimmed:
"Obsidian-1.5.12.AppImage", Obsidian) with its own icon. A type 2
AppImage is an ELF runtime with a SquashFS image after its section
headers; that's read in process (`backhand`, no mounting), for the entry
and `.DirIcon` (followed through links), else the entry's `Icon=` by
name (at the top, or the largest in its hicolor theme). What was read is
kept in `~/.cache/olo/appimages` (the icon, PNG or SVG as given, named
by its bytes so copies share one, and `apps.json`, by path, size and
time, changed under an `flock` as Deskbar and Tracker both write it), so
each version of an AppImage is read once, by whichever app comes to it
first. The folder is followed (inotify, `olo_kit::watch`: made later,
removed, renamed back too), and a change lists it again on a worker, one
scan at a time with one more after it if it changed meanwhile (an
AppImage still downloading). Chosen, it runs; one not executable yet
(just downloaded) is made so first.

AppImages are themselves wherever an app shows (Ben, 2026-11-09: "if an
appimage has an icon in it for the app show that icon in the tracker,
when running in the deskbar apps, and anywhere else an icon is shown for
the app"). For each AppImage known, a desktop entry is kept in
`~/.cache/olo/appimages/applications`
(`olo_xdg::desktop_entry::appimages_dir`, the last of `app_dirs()`, so
an installed app of the same id wins): named by the AppImage's own
entry's id (`dbdelve.desktop`), `NoDisplay` (the Applications menu, the
palette and Open With leave it out: `~/AppImages` is listed on its own),
with `Exec` the AppImage (quoted for `sh -c`, its own `%f`/`%U` kept),
`Icon` the file taken out of it, its `StartupWMClass` and
`X-Olo-AppImage`. So every lookup of an app id (`find`, `find_among`,
`icon_for_app`) finds a running AppImage's name and icon as it finds an
installed app's: Deskbar's running apps, the Twitcher, the window
menu's Quit, notifications, the palette's windows. Of two with one id,
the one in `~/AppImages` is named, then the newest; an AppImage gone is
let go of (entry and icon) at the next change, and only entries that
changed are written. A window whose app id no entry gives is looked at
once by Deskbar, on a worker (`ask_processes`, each id once, not on
every window event): if its process is an AppImage's
(`olo_appimage::of_process`: the runtime's `APPIMAGE` and `APPDIR` in
`/proc/PID/environ`, and the program in that mount, so a program an
AppImage started isn't taken for it), that AppImage is read, and an id
its own entry doesn't give is kept for it (`learn`: another entry by that
name). The Twitcher, which looks each app up once, looks those no entry
gave up again as it's shown, on a worker, if an applications folder
changed since (`twitcher::recheck`, `desktop_entry::stamps`): an
AppImage's entry is made a moment after its first window. Tracker shows an AppImage's file (`.AppImage`, or an
extension-less program with the AppImage mark) with its icon
(`apps/tracker/src/appimages.rs`): asked for as an item is drawn,
read on a thread of its own (`olo_appimage::info`), the windows drawn
again only when an icon came; the kind's icon meanwhile. Third-party
PNG icons decode whatever their format (`olo_xdg::decode_png`
normalizes to 8 bits a channel: palettes, 16 bits, a transparent
colour): of the 3,980 PNG icons on Ben's machine (ours, /usr/share's,
the cache's), the 3,836 that decoded before are byte for byte the same,
and 144 more (palette ones, Adwaita's 16 px among them) now decode.
Tried in a tsession with a real AppImage (DBDelve) in `~/AppImages`,
in Downloads (with and without its extension) and in a folder nothing
looked at: Tracker showed each with its icon, and run from any of them
Deskbar listed it as DBDelve with its icon and the window menu said
"Quit DBDelve", at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75× and 2×, light and dark.

### Folded away (the button at its top right)

Ben, 2026-11-18: "add a little icon button to the top right of the
deskbar to be able to collapse it (collapses to the right) and expand
it and when it collapses and expands the windows on the screen should
expand/collapse to fill the space too". At the Olo tile's right end, a
small button of two chevrons (`paint_fold`; quiet until the pointer is
on it, "Hide Deskbar") folds every display's Deskbar away to the right;
folded, a Deskbar is that button alone (22 × 20 points at the screen's
top right corner, "Show Deskbar"), no taller than a window's tab, so
it sits in the row of tabs over no window's content. It is a setting
(`DeskbarSettings::folded`, `deskbar.folded`; `set_folded` reads the
settings, changes that and writes them), so it stays so across a
reload, and an agent folds it with `set_settings`; a Deskbar's layer
surface is anchored at the top right and takes its new width
(`BarView::width`). **From the keyboard and the palette** (Ben, 2026-11-18:
"ctrl+cmd+d by default (but customizable). it should also be available
in the command palette"): the shortcut Hide or show Deskbar
(`Shortcut::ToggleDeskbar`, `toggle-deskbar`, in the Desktop group:
⌃⌘D in the Mac and Windows profiles, ⌥⌘D in BeOS's, whose ⌃⌘D is its
left third), changed in Preferences ▸ Keyboard ▸ Shortcuts as any
other; app_server flips `deskbar.folded` (`set_settings`, so every
display's folds and it's saved). The palette has it as a command said
as Deskbar stands, "Hide Deskbar" or "Show Deskbar", found by "fold",
"collapse", "taskbar" too.

**Other workspaces' applications, collapsed** (Ben, 2026-11-18: "add an
option in deskbar prefs (disabled by default) to default to showing
other display's apps collapsed in the deskbar with an icon button to
expand them (down) and collapse them again (up)"; 2026-11-19, in its
place: "change this existing option to Other workspaces' applications
start collapsed and it should apply to every other workspace when
checked regardless of what display they are on (same or other) so that
only the active workspace for a given display is the one expanded by
default"). A display's Deskbar lists its own workspaces and
applications, then the other displays'. With Preferences ▸ Deskbar ▸
Applications ▸ "Other workspaces’ applications start collapsed"
(`DeskbarSettings::others_collapsed`, `deskbar.others_collapsed`, the
key the other displays' rows had: a box ticked stays ticked; off unless
turned on), each display's Deskbar has the workspace its own display
shows open, and each other workspace with applications only its
heading, the ones other displays show too (`fold_of`, by the bar's
display: on D0's, D1's showing workspace stayed open, Ben, 2026-11-19:
"it needs to be display aware too e.g. on D0 only D0 Workspace 1 should
be expanded … each display needs its own state for this"): how many applications it has while they're put
away, then a latch just before its windowing mode, pointing right
while they're away and down while they show under the heading
(`style::latch`, BOutlineListView's, as BeOS has it; it pointed down
then up, an accordion's way, until Ben, 2026-11-19: "I'd use ▸ when
collapsed and ▾ when expanded"; the modes stay in one column, the
latches in another); while they're away,
the heading ends its group with the rule its last row would have (two
headings ran together). A click on the arrow
or its count folds; anywhere else on the heading goes to the workspace,
as ever (the arrow's hit is over the heading's, as the mode's is).
Which are open is Deskbar's own (`others_shown`, by `fold_key`: the
bar's display, then the workspace's display and number, so an arrow
opened in one display's Deskbar leaves the others' as they were), until
Deskbar starts again: they start collapsed, as asked. Agents: a Button named
with what a click does ("D0 Workspace 2: 1 application. Click to show
it."), its value "collapsed" or "expanded". Tried in a test session of
two displays (`tsession start NAME 2560x1600,2560x1600 --session
--shell`; `tsession shot NAME FILE --output HEADLESS-2` for the second):
both Deskbars with it off and on, an arrow clicked open and shut, light
and dark at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75× and 2× (the arrow on whole pixels at
each); Preferences' pane clean in the review at 1×, 1.5× and 2×.

The windows follow in app_server. `usable_area` leaves out a Deskbar
only if it is wider than `DESKBAR_FOLDED` (48): a folded one takes no
room. And whenever a Deskbar's surface draws, `deskbar_drew` (called
from every commit; 3.6 µs on average, most of them not a layer's and
answered at once) compares the room beside it with what it was
(`usable_was`, by display); if it changed, `tiling_space_changed` has
the zoomed and tiled windows of the workspace take their places again
in it (the others as they come back, `welcome_back`), as when the
space around windows is changed in Preferences. Tried in a test
session: a zoomed Tracker 1088 points wide beside Deskbar, 1264 with
it folded, back and forth by the button and by `set_settings`; the
button looked at in light and dark at 1×, 1.5× and 2×.

### Live widgets (widgets.rs, Preferences ▸ Deskbar)

Ben, 2026-11-07: "add a preferences app for the deskbar and in it
support configuring/adding live performance widgets into it e.g. cpu,
gpu, disk, network monitors etc. -- it should all be very customizable
in terms of where they appear on the deskbar, how they look, how often
they update, exactly what to show and so on". As BeOS's Pulse and
ProcessController put their bars in its tray.

* **Settings**: `Settings::deskbar` (`olo_protocol::deskbar`), kept by
  app_server, so Deskbar follows a change at once (`SettingsChanged`)
  and agents read and set them (`GetSettings`/`SetSettings`; a widget
  with only `id`, `measure` and `place` takes the rest as it comes).
  Each `Widget`: an `id`, what it measures (`Measure`: CPU, all or each
  core; memory, and swap; a GPU by PCI address; a disk's reads and
  writes; a volume's fullness; an interface's down and up; a hwmon
  temperature, "chip/label"; battery power), where (`Place`: an icon's
  place in the tray, a row under the tray, a row at the foot under the
  applications), its look (`Look`: graph, bars, heatmap, meter,
  number), its row's size, its name and value shown, how often it's
  read (`every_ms`, 250 ms to a minute), how far back its graph looks
  (`span_s`), its colour (a `Hue`, or the accent), whether it's
  `beside` the one before it, sharing its row, and its own `name`
  (Ben, 2026-11-14: "let me provide a custom name for the widget if i
  want to override/customize the name"): None or blank, it's named by
  what it measures (`Widget::default_label`, "CPU", "Claude 5-hour");
  given, it's its label in a row and beside others (`Widget::label`,
  `short_label`: the name as it is, cut with "…" where even beside the
  shortest value it doesn't fit, never left out), its card's title
  (what it measures leading the caption, "CPU · over the last
  minute"), the start of its tip and its name for agents.
* **Readings**: `olo_system::meters` (Preferences' list of what there
  is too, `sources`: cores, GPUs, disks, volumes, interfaces, sensors,
  a battery): `/proc/stat`, `meminfo`, `diskstats`, `net/dev`, statvfs,
  hwmon, the battery's `power_now`, and the GPUs through
  `olo_system::gpu_load` (Activity Monitor's, moved there for both: a
  GPU asleep is never asked, an idle NVIDIA one only every 20 s, each
  question being use that keeps it awake, but every time for 8 s
  after it wakes, when what woke it is about to show). **A GPU is as
  busy as its busiest engine** (`gpu_load::busiest`): NVIDIA's
  graphics engine, encoder and decoder (`NvidiaNow::total`: its
  library counts NVENC and NVDEC apart from "GPU utilization", so a
  screen recording encoding on the card read as an idle GPU, and as
  one not worth asking; a 4K encode is graphics 14%, encoder 50%), and
  xe's render and media GTs' idle residencies. Activity Monitor has a
  series for each engine beside the card's own (`gpu-render`,
  `gpu-media`; `gpu1-render`, `gpu1-encode`, `gpu1-decode`), and a
  program's share of an NVIDIA card is the most of the three it
  uses. `cargo test -p olo-system watch_nvidia -- --ignored
  --nocapture` prints the card's engines a line a second, to run
  beside something that encodes on it (olo-video's
  `nvenc_cost_by_codec`); it never wakes a sleeping card. A worker (`deskbar-widgets`) reads each widget when
  it's due and sends them together (`Msg::Meters`); with no widgets
  there is no thread, and with the displays asleep or the screen locked
  nothing is read (`Live::pause`). **An agent's screen sits still**:
  the Deskbar of a screen nobody sits at (`OLO_SCREEN`,
  `on_an_agents_screen`) shows none of the person's widgets and its
  clock has no seconds (`widgets_here`, `settings_msg`). They were all
  that ever changed on an idle agent's screen, and kept the whole of it
  at work: its Deskbar woke 38 times a second, its app_server 47 times
  to draw what Deskbar drew, and its recorder kept every change, ten
  screens a fifth of a processor and gigabytes of recorded meters a day
  (Ben, 2026-11-20: "they also should be more efficient beyond that
  too"). And **a status holds only what the bar draws**
  (`status::Status`, `publish`): a status that differs is every bar
  drawn again, on every screen, so what a tray item's glyph and tip
  don't show isn't kept there but read when its menu opens (a small
  file, or what the watcher last heard). DiskBackup's progress, the
  supervisor's state (`Supervisor::shown`: on or off and how many it
  found; which processes it lowered changes with every build's) and the
  Wi-Fi's signal (`Wifi::bars`, the arcs its glyph lights, held until
  the signal is clearly past a mark, `wifi_bars`; the figure is in the
  link's menu) each drew every bar again every few seconds for
  something it didn't show (the last two 47 times in 90 s). Which parts
  of a status changed is logged at debug level
  (`RUST_LOG=olo_deskbar=debug`: "status changed=[…]", and "told" for
  each message), the way to find the next one. What a widget draws is made once a
  reading (`Shown`: each series' levels over its history, rates against
  the highest in it, its value in words), not each frame.
* **Drawing**: tray widgets take the tray's first slots (a graph, bars,
  a heatmap or a meter in a sunken well, or the value in small
  figures); a row of its own has the name at the left and the value at
  the right (shortened, "↓27K ↑102K", or without the name, when both
  don't fit), the drawing between them in a small row and under them in
  a medium or large one. Widgets `beside` one another share a row
  (Ben: "more than 1 widget per row, e.g. a more compact representation
  of a combination of things", as iStat Menus' labels over little
  meters): equal cells `TIGHT` apart, each its name (shorter, "Mem",
  where the whole doesn't fit) over its drawing, its value beside the
  name only if it fits whole (a number's under it), the row as tall as
  its tallest. A tip says what it measures in full and each series'
  value; a click opens Activity Monitor; the other button, Activity
  Monitor and Deskbar Preferences…. Agents read each as a `Meter` with
  its value.
* **Motion** (Ben: "make the graphs etc in the deskbar widgets all
  animate smoothly like in activity monitor"; "even if e.g. something
  only updates once per second it still smoothly animates, including
  e.g heatmap the tiles should animate to the next state"): each
  reading is timed (`widgets::clock`), and a graph's right edge is an
  interval behind the latest (`graph_now`, Activity Monitor's `now`),
  so its line runs into the edge a device pixel at a time and stands
  still once readings stop; bars, meters and heatmap cells move from
  where they're drawn to each reading over the time between readings
  (a second at most), still at each end so one move runs into the next.
  Frames follow the pixels: a graph's when it has scrolled one, a
  level's when it has moved one (a heatmap's: a sixteenth of its
  colour), at most 60 a second, all on the window's one clock, none once
  nothing moves. They're drawn by a view of their own over the bar
  (`widgets::Layer`, a child of the bar's view): the bar lays them
  out (`Shelf`) and draws their ground, tips and clicks, the layer
  draws them; a reading or a step of motion draws the layer alone (the
  bar too only while a widget's tip is up, for its words).
* **Cost** (release, 2× headless, five widgets: a tray's bars and
  number, two graphs and a meter, 20 s, `tools/dev/cost`): 0.7% of a
  core, 78 wakeups a second, 12.8 frames a second at 307 µs, 107.5
  MB. With no widgets, on two displays at 1.5×: 0.0%, a frame each few
  seconds as the status watchers say something new (10 in 30 s), 452
  µs each.
* **Tips' top five** (Ben: "for relevant widgets like cpu, gpu,
  memory, network make it so that hovering over the widget also shows
  the top 5 highest consuming processes"): with the pointer on a CPU,
  memory, GPU, network or disk widget, the worker looks at every
  process (`olo_system::procs::Sampler`, Activity Monitor's reading,
  ranked by `Rank`), twice 350 ms apart for a first rate, then every
  second, and the tip says them under its reading ("Using the most:",
  CPU as a share of the whole processor as the widget's, GPU as its
  share of that GPU, memory resident, network and disk a second), kept
  up to date as it shows (`tip::recard`, its reading too). No tip, no
  look, and the sampler (its memory of every process) goes as the
  pointer leaves. A look, 827 processes: 10 ms (disk counters only for
  a disk widget's, a second file each), 5 ms more for the sockets, and
  20 ms for who has each, at most every 3 s; the worker's share of a
  core while a tip shows: CPU 0.8%, network 1.2%, none after.
* **Tips are cards** (Ben, 2026-11-14: "improve the popovers so that
  they can have rich widgets/designs inside of them and then update
  the ones for the deskbar widgets so that all their popovers are
  nicely designed and visually show the data better"): a widget's tip
  is an `olo_kit::card` (`Shown::card`, `Live::card`): what it
  measures as its title, its value at the top right, what it is and
  its span under them ("Each core · over the last minute"); then its
  last span as a graph 64 points tall (a volume's fullness as a
  meter), each core's bars now under "Each core now", each series
  against its colour's swatch (Down and Up, Memory and Swap), what the
  reading notes ("14.4 GB of 66.8 GB"), and "Using the most" as rows
  with bars (of the whole processor or GPU; else against the first).
  A Token Pool widget's: the provider as its title, what's left in
  green to red, "Token Pool · each account · what holds it back"; all
  the accounts together, a graph of its span; its summary lines; then
  each account (the account answering now: each quota) with what's
  left as a bar in the usage colours, when it resets, the one
  answering now in bold, one out until a reset at 0% with why and when
  it's back, one turned off without a bar (`Reading::summary`,
  `Reading::rows`: `meters::DetailRow`). The card is made as the
  pointer comes and again with each reading or look at the processes
  (`BarView::retip`, by the widget's id), never as the bar is drawn;
  it opens to the left of the bar, level with the widget
  (`tip::hover_card_beside`), so it covers none of the others, and the
  pointer can move onto it and rest there: it keeps updating while
  it's on it (`Live::pointer_on`; the processes looked at until no
  card shows);
  its drawings paint the widget's own `Shown` (`paint_drawing`, in
  another look), so a graph scrolls as the widget's does. Release, 1×,
  three bars and nine widgets: idle unchanged (no card is made);
  while a CPU card shows, its window 13.9 frames a second at 215 µs
  mean (0.3% of a core), the process 2.3% against 1.8% idle. A
  widget's label too long for its cell is cut with "…" (its card says
  it whole).
* **Backups** carry them with app_server's settings; from another
  computer, a widget measuring a GPU, disk, interface, sensor or volume
  this one hasn't measures its default instead, said
  (`backup::widgets_here`).
* **Token Pool** (`Measure::Pool`; Ben, 2026-11-13: "a deskbar widget
  for showing the token pool usage / quotas … aggregate availability
  for each provider x quota type and any other options/views", then
  "make the quota type a multi-select and then in e.g. heatmap show
  each selected quota type as a different color with the color
  representing usage where red is 100% used and green is 0% used"):
  a provider's quotas across its accounts, from the meters the pool
  writes (`olo_protocol::pool`: `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-pool-meters-
  DISPLAY.json`, by the copy serving, half a second after a burst of
  changes and only when what it says differs; `crates/pool/src/
  meters.rs`). Its options: the provider; any of its quotas (`quotas`,
  each a series; none: whichever holds each account back now; a single
  `quota` as first written is read too); All accounts together (what's
  left of the accounts' worth, `availability`, accounts turned off or
  signed out counted as having none if asked), Each account, or The
  account answering now; used rather than left; orange under a quarter
  left and red under a tenth (`warn`, on the least left of its
  quotas); and a notification when a quota is out on every account
  and when it's back (`notify`: as Token Pool's, Open Token Pool on
  click; one a widget, updated in place). It's read a minute apart and
  again as the file changes (`olo_kit::watch`, only while a Pool
  widget is shown); its tip says each quota's share left, its
  accounts, the next reset and the pace over the last hour. In a
  heatmap each quota (each account's, in Each account) is a cell
  coloured by how used it is, the palette's green at none through
  yellow to red at all (`charts::usage_colour`,
  `charts::paint_heatmap_by`), so its own colour and "Orange, then
  red" are dimmed in Preferences ("Coloured by use"). Of several
  quotas its value is each one's ("24% · 46% left"), and where that
  doesn't fit beside its label, shorter ("24% · 46%", then the least,
  "24%", `Shown::shorter`); a row tries its label with each, then its
  short label ("Claude 5h/Wk") with each, then the shortest alone. A
  click opens Token Pool. Tested on made-up meters
  (`meters::tests::a_pool_reading`, `pool::tests`) and in a headless
  session with a made-up meters file for its display (two Claude
  accounts and a Codex one, two quotas each: a heatmap of four cells,
  "Claude 5h/Wk 24% · 45%", at 1×, 1.5× and 2×, light and dark).
  Its quotas are a `MenuField::many` ("Quotas:", "Whichever holds each
  back" when none is chosen; Preferences' `Ui::choose_many`): first a
  row of check boxes, which a real Claude account's quotas ("Weekly",
  "Weekly Fable", "Weekly Overage Included", "Overage") ran past
  Preferences' right edge (Ben, 2026-11-13: "why didn't the lints pick
  this up?"). They didn't because the made-up meters had two short
  quotas and the Preferences lint drew Deskbar's panel with no widget
  in it; `lint::ui_lint_deskbar_widgets` now draws the editor for every
  kind of widget, a Pool one with seven Claude quotas and five Codex
  ones of the longest names the services use, and long device names
  (with the row of boxes back it finds 54 errors). The pool names a
  quota as people say it (`upstream::claude_label`, `words`): each
  word capitalised, `seven_day` "Weekly", `oi` "Overage Included",
  the same quota from the usage endpoint, a header and a rejection
  one name (`pool::quotas` merges names that differ only in case),
  and `seven_day_breakdown`, which is no limit, isn't a quota.

**A divider** (`Measure::Divider { line, reach }`; Ben, 2026-11-17: "a
spacing/divider widget (with plenty of visual customization options)
for the deskbar widget section for when the user wants to break stuff
up") is a widget that shows nothing of the computer: room, a line, or
a heading, to set groups of widgets apart. It is a row of its own
(`rows`: nothing is beside one), as tall as its size says (`Room:` in
Preferences: 7, 13 or 25 points; 19 at least with a heading), read
nothing (it isn't in the readings, so a Deskbar with only dividers is
at rest: 2 frames in 8 s), and has no tip, no card and no click (its
menu has only Deskbar Settings…). `paint_divider` draws it with the
kit's `style::rule(g, x0, x1, y, Rule, color, palette)` (every part on
whole device pixels at any scale: `Hairline`, a device pixel; `Etched`,
the panel's shade over its shine, as BeOS's separators; `Bold`, two
points; `Dotted`, a device pixel in three; `Dots`, round ones two
points across, centred in the reach), or nothing (`DividerLine::None`:
room only), as far as its reach says (edge to edge, as wide as the
widgets' own words and drawings, or the middle third). Its colour is
the widget's hue, or with none the look's own: the panel's shade where
it's etched, else the secondary text's grey at 0.55 (the shade is near
black on a dark panel: dots of it were lost there). Given a name, it
is a heading: the name small and bold at the left, where the widgets'
labels start, the line going on from it. For agents it is a
`Separator`, named by its heading. Seven meters with six dividers
among them cost what the meters alone do (0.6% of a core against
0.7%; a frame 417 µs against 394).

Preferences ▸ Deskbar (`deskbar.rs`) lists the widgets in order (Add
one of a kind after the chosen one, Remove, Move Up, Move Down; a named
one's row starts with its name, "Build box: CPU, a graph under the
tray") beside the chosen one's settings (what it shows and which of it,
its Name: a field whose hint is its name by what it measures, emptied
to go back to that; where, look, size, name and value shown, beside
the one before it, how often, how far back, colour), each changing the
Deskbar at once; Defaults has none. A divider's settings are its own:
Line, Reaches, Name, Where, Room and Colour ("The look's own" first);
its row in the list says "Divider: a dotted line under the tray", or,
named, "Tools: a heading under the tray".

### An app's widgets (glances.rs; olo_protocol::glance, olo_kit::glance)

Ben, 2026-11-15: "the weather app should make available a deskbar
widget that is customizable and can show useful stuff ... it should be
able to render a customizable type of widget e.g. that shows visually
with rain/clouds/sun etc ... make sure it looks beautiful and any new
support/functionality you need try to add to the kit in a way that can
be reusable for future apps that want to provide rich olo widgets for
the deskbar". BeOS's replicants were an app's own view running in
Deskbar; here the app says what to show and Olo draws it (as iOS's
WidgetKit), so it looks like Olo's, agents read it, and it needs the
app only to make what's next.

* **What apps give** (`olo_protocol::glance::PROVIDERS`): each app's
  program and its no-window argument (`olo-weather --glance`), its
  kinds (`Kind`: an id, its name in Preferences' menus, a line about
  it) and their options (`Opt`: a menu of values, the first the one it
  comes with). A widget of one is `Measure::App { app, glance,
  options }` (`Measure::app`, `same_kind`; `kinds()` lists them after
  the meters). Weather gives Now, Next Hours and Next Days; Kache, Build
  Cache; Calendar, Next Event and The Day Ahead (`apps/calendar/src/
  glance.rs`, `olo-calendar --glance`: from what's kept on this
  computer, nothing asked of a server nor of the keyring
  (`sync::kept`: what signs an account in is for asking its server);
  an entry wherever what it says changes, an event starting or ending
  and midnight, for a day ahead; made again as the accounts' files,
  Calendar's settings' file or what's kept change (`sync::
  kept_folders`: the folder of accounts and each account's, a
  calendar being a file in its account's), and every six hours; a
  declined invitation left out. Next
  Event: "2 PM Design review / Today · Room 2", "Now … until 3:30 PM"
  while it's on, and what's after it time first, "Then 3 PM ·
  Interview", as a Deskbar is narrow and what's cut is the end. The
  Day Ahead: "Wed 18 · 3 to come" over 3, 5 or 8 lines, another day's
  by its weekday with its time in the tip. Tested: `glance::tests`.
  At rest the provider wakes 0 times a second.)
* **What one shows**: a `Timeline` of `Entry`s, each a `Glance` from a
  minute on (`Timeline::at`): a headline (icon, value, title, detail),
  a note, a `Body` (`Slots` across: label, icon, value, level, drawn
  as small columns in the body's hue; `Spans` down: label, icon, low
  to high on the body's scale, coloured cold to warm, blue to orange in
  the look's hues; `Lines` down: a label, a mark in the line's hue and
  its words, a day's events), and its tip in words. `plain` gives it a
  headline of ordinary words (a 16-point icon, the value bold and the
  title on one line, the detail quieter under it) for what isn't a
  figure to read from across the room (Ben, of Calendar's with the big
  one: "that calendar icon and heading on the widget is ginormous").
  `open` is what a click opens: its app run with those arguments
  (Calendar's `--show HREF START`: the event shown), where a bare
  click runs the app as it is (`Glances::opens`).
* **How it gets there**: a folder a display, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/
  olo-glance/DISPLAY/` (`glance::dir`; a folder of its own: a watch
  follows a folder's parent too, and the runtime folder changes
  several times a second, each a wake for nothing: the provider woke
  4 times a second in it, 0 out of it). Deskbar writes each app's
  `Requests` (`APP.requests.json`, only as they change: each widget's
  id, kind, options and size) and starts its provider with
  `OLO_GLANCE_DIR` set, on a worker: one from before (a lock, its pid
  in it) is ended first, so after an upgrade the provider is the new
  program; ended by itself, it's started again a minute after it last
  started at the soonest. The provider (`olo_kit::glance::serve`)
  holds the lock, makes every widget asked for, writes each one's
  timeline (`ID.json`, whole: a rename) only when what it shows
  changed (its entries: when it was made is news to nobody; and
  again if its file has gone), and sleeps until its requests' file,
  the desktop's settings' file or one of the app's own paths changes,
  or the time it asked for comes; none asked for, it ends. It follows
  those files themselves, never the widgets' folder nor the settings'
  folder: every provider writes in the first and every program in the
  second, and a provider woken by either made its widgets again for
  each write, its own too (2026-11-21: the Inbox's and Calendar's
  kept each other at it twelve times a second, "A change is news only
  to who shows it" above). An app whose paths come and go says which
  to follow before each making (`serve_following`: Calendar's
  accounts' folders, To Do's lists'; before it, neither widget heard
  of a calendar or a to-do changed, a watch of a folder telling of
  its items and not of theirs). Deskbar follows the folder (one
  inotify watch), reads a widget's file as it changes, takes it for
  another only when its entries are, and switches each to its entry
  for the time as its clock's minute comes (`Glances::turned`: the
  layer drawn again only if one turned).
* **Drawing** (`olo_kit::glance`, the same in a preview or an app's
  window): in a row of its own, as tall as what it shows
  (`glance::height`: small, one line, its icon, value and title;
  medium and large, the headline (a 32-point icon, 40 large, the value
  at 21 points, 26 large, the title on its baseline, the detail under),
  the note, the body); beside other widgets, its icon and value over
  its title (`paint_cell`); in the tray, its icon (`paint_tray`). Words
  in the panel's text, quieter ones in `style::secondary_text`; icons
  at their device size, each column and bar on whole device pixels.
  Each line is recorded for agents as a label, each slot and span as a
  list item with its value ("14, 46°, 60%"; "Tue, 40° to 52°"), and
  the widget as a Meter whose value is its tip. Slots with no icon
  among them (Kache's hours) drop the icon row: the label over the
  value (`SLOTS_PLAIN`). Its tip is a card
  (`Glances::card`: its title and detail, its value, the body as rows,
  the note); a click opens its app (`glances::opens`); the other
  button, its app and Deskbar Preferences.
* **An inbox** (`Body::Inbox`, Notifications' "Inbox": Ben,
  2026-11-17, "a notifications widget in the deskbar … a stack of cards
  that you can flip through, with two actions for each one: Dismiss and
  Snooze. use a small icon button for each. the idea is to be able to
  rapidly work through them to empty it out … clicking on the card
  should take you to the relevant app-window-tab. and it should include
  both the "red dot" ones and the "blue dot" ones"). The card on top is
  the one to deal with, the edges of two more under it while there are
  more (`style::card`'s paper; each under one a shade darker and 4
  points narrower a side, 3 lower). On it: its app's icon and name and
  "2 of 5"; a dot of its kind, red or blue, draining as a notification
  fades (the card itself stays whole); its title; its text, a line
  (two, large; none if the widget's Text is "Title only"); then
  Previous and Next at the left and Snooze and Dismiss at the right,
  drawn marks (`inbox_mark`) on a plate under the pointer. Small: one
  line, the dot, the title, Snooze and Dismiss. Empty: "Nothing new".
  Its height doesn't change with how many there are (the room for the
  cards under is kept), so the buttons stay under the pointer as cards
  go. `glance::inbox_laid` is where the card and each button are, for
  the painting and for Deskbar's hits both. In Deskbar
  (`Glances::inbox`, `inbox_shown`): a click on the card opens the item
  (`olo-notifications --invoke ID`: its action at its app, or what it
  said shows it, or its app brought forward), the wheel or the arrows
  turn the cards; Dismiss and Snooze take the card away at once
  (`Glances::dealt_with`: the service's answer comes a quarter of a
  second later, and the next card is under the pointer meanwhile) and
  ask the service (`--dismiss`, `--snooze ID MINUTES`); one that
  arrives goes on top, whichever was chosen ("if newer ones arrive
  they should be added on top of the card stack too, not the bottom");
  a card stays until it's read or cleared (it once left when it
  "faded away", which took unread things out of sight: no more), its
  dot draining with its age to the floor ("the dot should animate …
  like we do in deskbar"). Its options: what it shows (everything, red, blue), the
  order, how long Snooze snoozes, and whether cards show their text.
  Agents read the top card as a list item ("Slack: Dana: lunch?", "2 of
  5, waiting in its app") and each button by name. The layer over the
  bar is drawn again when a widget's data changes
  (`Taken::Widgets`: it showed a card dismissed elsewhere until the
  pointer moved).
* **Preferences ▸ Deskbar**: the Add menu has each app's kinds ("Weather:
  Next Hours"); an app widget's settings are what it shows, its kind's
  line about it, a menu for each of its options, its name, where, its
  size, beside the one before it (not look, words shown, how often or
  colour: it looks as the app made it). Its list row: "Weather: Next
  Hours, the next 6 hours, chance of rain, under the tray".
* **Cost** (release, 2× headless, 60 s idle, `tools/dev/cost`): Deskbar
  with Weather's three widgets, 0.0% of a core, 1 wakeup a second, 8
  frames a minute at 762 µs (no widgets: 9 at 712 µs, 3 wakeups a
  second, its status watches in the runtime folder); the provider,
  0.0%, 0 wakeups a second, 14 MB resident.

## The lock screen (crates/app_server/src/lock.rs, apps/lock)

`lock_screen()` (Ctrl+⌘Q, Deskbar ▸ Lock Screen, `Request::Lock`, the
display turning off for idleness when `power.lock_on_display_off`, logind
`PrepareForSleep` and `Lock`) covers every output in black at once, takes
keyboard focus away and starts `olo-lock` on a socket pair of its own
(WAYLAND_SOCKET): ext-session-lock is offered to that one client only. The
locker is restarted if it dies (at most every 2 s); the screen stays
black meanwhile, so the lock never fails open. While locked, input reaches
lock surfaces only, keybindings are off, and the displays sleep after a
minute. A marker, `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-locked-$WAYLAND_DISPLAY`
holding olo-session's pid, makes an app_server that reloaded or crashed
come back locked (only in the same session: display names get reused). Before sleep,
app_server holds a logind delay inhibitor until every output shows the lock
surface (or 3 s).

`olo-lock` (on olo-kit) uses `olo_kit::lock_session(app, build,
on_event)` (a window from `build` on every output, each on a looper of
its own, and on any added while locked; `on_event`, on the app's
looper, hears `Locked` once, `Outputs` when the windows covering
outputs changed, `Finished` if refused, each with those windows) and
`olo_kit::unlock_session()` (app_server has been told by the time it
returns; then quit). The lock itself (who is asked, what was answered)
is kept on the app's looper, apart from any window: each screen is told
what to show (`ScreenMsg::Shown`) and says what was typed through
`olo_kit::proxy()`; the first open window has the panel, and the next
one takes it if that window goes with its display. The Interface Kit
takes app_server's `WAYLAND_SOCKET` as a Wayland connection, and a lock
surface makes no commit before its first configure and checks the password with `olo_system::auth` (PAM via
libpam, on a thread) while listening for Touch ID with
`olo_system::fingerprint` and looking for the person's face
(`olo_system::face`). A security key doesn't unlock it (see "Security
keys": a key left plugged in mustn't open a computer someone found). Debug builds take `OLO_PAM_CONFDIR` +
`OLO_PAM_SERVICE` (passed through by tsession), so tests use a private
pam_exec service and never a real password; then (or with
`OLO_NO_FINGERPRINT=1`) it leaves the fingerprint reader alone, which is
the person's own:

```sh
printf 'auth required pam_exec.so expose_authtok quiet /path/check.sh\naccount required pam_permit.so\n' > $dir/exec
OLO_PAM_CONFDIR=$dir OLO_PAM_SERVICE=exec tools/dev/tsession start lk --light
tools/dev/tsession ipc lk '{"type":"lock"}'; tools/dev/tsession type lk secret; tools/dev/tsession key lk 28
```

## Olo Rescue (app_server rescue.rs, apps/rescue, `olo_protocol::rescue`)

Holding Ctrl+Shift+Super and pressing Delete (or Backspace, a Mac's
delete; either side's modifiers), from anywhere, whatever has the
keyboard, brings Olo Rescue: for when something has gone wrong and the
person can't see or can't drive the desktop. app_server reads the chord
