- **Where to-dos are kept: a vdir**, the layout vdirsyncer and todoman
  use, so other programs read it and a CalDAV sync can be put under it
  with nothing moved: `$XDG_DATA_HOME/olo/todo/` (`store::root()`;
  `OLO_TODO_DIR` instead, for tests and pictures), a folder a list
  (`displayname`; `color`, `#RRGGBB`, read back as the nearest of the
  look's `Hue`s; `olo-sections`, a section a line, in order), in it a
  file a to-do (`UID.ics`: a VCALENDAR of one VTODO), and what's
  attached to a to-do copied into `LIST/.files/UID/`.
- **`item`**: `ToDo` (uid, title, notes, `Status`, when it was made,
  changed and done, its due as Calendar's `When`, `Remind`, section,
  order, `Attachment`s) read from a VTODO and written into one through
  `olo_calendar::ical`, so what Olo doesn't know of a to-do survives its
  changing one (`write_into(was, component, now)` writes only what
  changed; `rewrite(text, was, todo, now)` a file's text). SUMMARY,
  DESCRIPTION, STATUS with COMPLETED and PERCENT-COMPLETE, DUE; a
  reminder is a VALARM, `TRIGGER;RELATED=END` so long before it's due
  (`Remind::Before(seconds)`: negative, into the day, for one due on a
  day) or `TRIGGER;VALUE=DATE-TIME` at a time of its own (`Remind::At`);
  `X-OLO-SECTION`; `X-OLO-ORDER` (whole numbers 1024 apart, so one is
  put between two without the rest written again); `ATTACH` (a link, or
  a `file:` address with FMTTYPE and FILENAME). `remind_at(todo, zone)`
  is when it reminds.
- **`store`**: `Book` (every list and to-do; `load`, and `refresh(root,
  changed)` reading only the folders and files that changed),
  `create_list`, `change_list`, `trash_list` and `untrash_list` (a list
  deleted is moved aside whole, to be put back by Undo), `create`,
  `change(item, todo)` (the file read again and only what the person
  changed written over it, so two programs changing different things
  of one to-do both keep theirs; it returns the text there was, which
  `put_back` writes again: Undo), `remove`, `move_to` (another list:
  its file and its attachments), `attach` and `attach_bytes` (a file
  copied, or what was pasted written, into the to-do's own folder, a
  name already there numbered), `sweep` (folders of attachments whose
  to-do is gone).
- **`quick`**: a line typed, read: `read(text, now, month_first)` gives
  its title and, where its last words say one, its due (`Typed`:
  "Call Ann tomorrow at 3pm", "Book flights Friday", "Pay the rent by
  Dec 1", "in 3 weeks", "11/24 at 9:30", "2027-04-15", "tonight": its
  tests are the list), with the words it read as the due
  (`said`), so the window can show which they are and keep them as
  words if they were meant so ("Read Tomorrow and Tomorrow and
  Tomorrow": a day's word after `and`, `of`, `the`… stays in the title).
  A time typed gives a reminder at that time (`Typed::to_do`).
  `fields(day, time, …)` reads the details pane's two fields and says
  which one it couldn't.
- **`view`**: what each place shows, in order (`rows(book, place, now,
  done)`: `Place::Today`, what's overdue then today's by time;
  `Upcoming`, by day; `All`, a list after another, each by when its
  to-dos are due and those with no due after, in the list's order;
  `Done`, by the day done on the person's clock, the newest first;
  `List`, its sections in order, then, with `done`, what's done of it),
  a list's board (`columns`: a lane a section, what's in none first;
  `done_of`, its last lane), where a to-do dropped among others goes
  (`place`: the orders to write, its neighbours' too only where there's
  no room between them), `overdue`, `due_day`. Each of `rows`,
  `columns` and `done_of` has a `_where` that takes what counts as
  still to do, for the window's to-do just checked off, kept where it
  was a moment. A sort asks when a to-do is due of a table made once,
  not of each pair it compares.
- **`demo::fill(root, now)`**: made-up lists for pictures and the
  layout lint (`OLO_TODO_DEMO=1` with an empty `OLO_TODO_DIR`).

## To-Do (apps/todo, `olo-todo`)

One window of three panes (`view.rs`): the places and the lists down the
left (the kit's `Sidebar`, each list a dot of its colour, how many each
has to do; New List at its foot), the chosen place in the middle under
its header, and the chosen to-do's details at the right (`SidePane`s:
in a window too narrow for all three the details give way, then the
sidebar, each brought back in front with a way back; `ui-lint --tiles`
shows every layout).

- **A place as a list** (`list.rs`): the row a new to-do is typed in
  first (not in Done), then headings and to-dos, made as they come near
  what shows (`sized_rows`: a heading after the first is six points
  taller, the more over its words, so groups stand apart; every row a
  whole number of device pixels tall at the scale it's shown at). A
  row: its check circle in its list's colour, its title, quiet marks
  for what it has (notes, attachments, a reminder: `marks.rs`, drawn on
  whole device pixels), and at the right its list (where a place mixes
  lists) and its due, in columns as wide as the widest of each, on its
  title's baseline. A heading counts what's still to do under it; a
  day's says its name and its date. A to-do checked off is struck
  through where it was for two seconds (`lingering`), then goes where
  done ones are.
- **A list as a board** (`board.rs`, View ▸ As Board, kept by list): a
  lane a section, sunken wells with cards in them, and last the lane of
  what's done (a card dropped on it is checked off; one dragged out of
  it is to do again). A card is its title on up to three lines, under
  it when it's due (red: overdue) or when it was done, and its marks at
  its right edge on its last line. A press moved four points is a drag:
  the card stays faint where it was, its copy follows the pointer, a
  line shows where it would drop. A lane's + (and New To-Do) puts a
  card at the lane's top to type the new one in. Each lane's cards are
  laid out once for the board as it is and the lane's width
  (`lane_layout`: laying a card out measures its title's words) and
  only those that show are made (`sized_rows`); a card is found by its
  place among the book's to-dos, never looked for by its name. With
  900 cards, choosing one took 40 ms a frame before that and takes
  under 1 ms.
- **What's typed for a new to-do** is read as it's typed (`quick`): the
  words read as its due turn blue in the field, the due they say shows
  beside them (the row's right end; a card's own foot) with an × that
  keeps them as words.
- **The details** (`details.rs`): its title, typed in where it is; its
  list and section; its due as a day and a time, typed ("friday",
  "nov 21", "3pm") or picked (the calendar button: the usual days, or
  the kit's `MonthGrid` in a well); its reminder (the usual ones for
  one due at a time or on a day; none to offer once it's done); its
  notes, in a well as tall as what's written; and what's attached, a
  row each (a file from a panel, a link typed, what's on the clipboard,
  or files dropped on the pane or on a row). Delete and when it was
  made, and done, at its foot. Every change is kept as it's made, on a
  worker (`Job`, one at a time), and can be undone (`History<Back>`:
  the file's text as it was, put back).
- **Kept on this computer only** for now: no account, nothing asked of
  a server. The store's folders are watched (`olo_kit::watch`), so what
  another program, `olo-todo --add` or the palette writes shows at
  once; the window's own writes aren't read back as news.
- **The day turning, what becomes overdue**: one timer (`Due`) for the
  next moment something changes (midnight, a to-do's due passing); at
  rest the window wakes 0 times a second.
- **For agents**: everything in its menus by name through its socket
  (`{"invoke": "check"}`; `new`, `new-list`, `new-section`,
  `rename-list`, `delete-list`, `delete`, `attach-file`, `attach-link`,
  `paste-attachment`, `undo`, `redo`, `show-done`, `sidebar`, `details`,
  `place:today|upcoming|all|done|LIST`, `layout:list|board`,
  `due:today|tomorrow|next-week|none|month|YYYY-MM-DD`, `move-to:N`,
  `select:UID` (`select:` alone: none) and `add:WHAT TO DO WHEN`), its
  rows, cards and fields in its tree (a to-do a ListItem named by its
  title, its value what it's due and what it has; its check a CheckBox),
  and without a window: `olo-todo --print [today|upcoming|all|done|LIST]`
  (JSON: uid, title, list, section, done, due, reminder, notes,
  attachments, file), `--add "WHAT [WHEN]" [--list NAME]` (as typed in
  the window; prints its uid and file), `--done UID`, `--show UID`
  (opens it in the window, the running one's if there is one). The
  palette offers "todo …" (or "to-do …") to add one, and finds to-dos by
  their titles (`apps/palette/src/sources.rs`).
- **Reminders** (`service.rs`, `olo-todo --service`, started with the
  session): one `olo_kit::clock::Alarm` for the next reminder, the store
  watched; a notification with Done, In an Hour and Show (its title the
  to-do's, under it when it's due and its list). What fired and what
  was put off are kept (`todo-reminders.json` in the state folder), so
  a reminder isn't shown twice across a restart, and one whose time
  passed while the computer slept shows on waking (unless long past:
  `STALE`); a to-do done or gone meanwhile takes its notification with
  it. At rest: 0 wakeups.
- **Deskbar widgets** (`glance.rs`, `olo-todo --glance`; the `todo`
  provider in `olo_protocol::glance::PROVIDERS`; it follows the folder
  of lists and each list's, as the window and the reminders do): Due
  Today ("3 due
  today", "1 overdue" under it; a line a to-do, a ring in its list's
  colour, `Line.ring`, red where it's overdue, its time or its day
  before it) and Coming Up (the next days'), 3, 5 or 8 lines; a click
  opens the first of them in the window.
- **Words**: through the words layer; a day said inside a sentence
  ("Done today", "Was due yesterday, 3 PM") has its own entries in
  small letters (`words::in_words`). Weekdays' and months' names are
  English still, as Calendar's (docs/TODO.md, Language).
- **For tests and pictures**: `OLO_TODO_DIR` (the store), `OLO_TODO_NOW`
  (`2026-11-19T10:30`: the clock the window, the widgets and the
  reminders go by, and what a to-do is stamped done and made with, so
  a picture's "today" is one day everywhere), `OLO_TODO_DEMO=1`.
- **Measured** (release, a store of 5,000 to-dos, 2026-11-20): read and
  printed in 45 ms; the window at rest 0.0% of a core and 0 wakeups a
  second, 74 MB; scrolling All's 4,500 rows 60 frames a second at
  0.34 ms a frame (slowest 3.0); a step of the selection 0.9 ms;
  checking one off 2.7 ms (slowest 5.7); a letter typed 0.7 ms; on a
  board of 900 cards, choosing one 0.9 ms.

## Passwords (apps/passwords, crates/onepassword)

**Undo** (undo.rs, `olo_kit::undo`): Edit ▸ Undo and Redo for items
changed (put back as they were), made (deleted) and deleted (made again:
a new item, every field as it was; `Vault::delete` gives back what it
deleted). Each is a save, a creation or a deletion like any other, so a
sync with 1Password takes it as one; the store's jobs carry a `Tag` (what
for, the step's name, an edit's item as it was) that its reply gives
back, and the reply records the step. An item with files attached can't
be made again (its files went), so its Delete still says it's for good;
the Archive isn't undone (nothing takes an item out of it yet). Steps
hold secrets: they go when Passwords locks (and when the store changes).

**Searching**: the toolbar's `SearchField` and a `FilterBar` over the
list (Tag, Has) share one query (`olo_kit::search`). Words find an item
by its title, username, websites, tags, kind, its sections' titles, its
fields' labels (a secret's too), the values of those that aren't secret,
and its notes; with words, the best come first (title 4, username and
site 3, tags 2, the rest 1), else by title; what was found is marked in
each row, whose second line is the username (else the site), or, when
the search found it inside the item, where: "Admin Console › region:
eu-west" (the field with most of the words; `found_in`, worked out with
the list, once per change). The item pane marks it too (section titles,
labels, and values that aren't secret). Filters: `type:` (login,
secure-note…), `vault:`, `tag:`, `site:`, `user:`, `has:` otp, password,
website, files, reused (its password is another item's too), weak (under
12 characters, or of one kind), and `section:` and `field:` (by title or
label, suggested with how many items have each), which narrow the item
pane as well to just those sections and fields (`-section:` and `-field:`
leave them out), saying so under its header. The vault worker sends a
`Searchable` for every item with the list (`store::index`, again after
each change): the username, each field as `FieldText` (its section's
title, its label, its value unless secret), that and the notes as text,
and flags; never a password, code, card number or key, and of a
password only whether it is weak or reused. So searching finds usernames
of items never opened.

**Editing**: the editor shows the fields as the item pane does: the
built-in ones and untitled sections' first, then each titled section
under its heading (one with no fields yet too); each group ends with its
own Add Field…, whose field goes at the end of that section (the first
group's in the untitled section custom fields go in, made when first
needed; `Editor::groups`, `add_field`) and is focused: its label if it
has none yet, else its value. A passkey's section has none.

`crates/onepassword` (package `olo-onepassword`) is a Rust 1Password SDK
modelled on the Go one: the same `Client` (`Secrets`, `Items`, `Vaults`,
`Groups`, `ItemShares`, `ItemFiles`, `Environments`), the same types and
JSON shapes (camelCase, tagged enums), `op://` references, the password
generator (random, memorable from the EFF word list, PIN) and TOTP. It
talks to the 1Password desktop app's SDK integration, as the official SDKs
do, over the abstract unix socket `@1PASSWORD_SDK_INTERGATIONS` (sic): one
connection per call; frames are a u32 LE length (counting the flag byte),
a flag byte (2 = more, 1 = last) and up to 499,999 bytes of a JSON request
`{kind: init_client|invoke|release_client, account_name, payload: base64}`;
the reply is `{success, payload: base64}` whose payload is the result's raw
JSON (or `{name, message}` on failure). 1Password asks the user to allow
each app and unlocks itself; users turn on Settings ▸ Developer ▸ Integrate
with other apps. Service-account (token) access is not implemented: that
needs 1Password's closed core.

`onepassword::accounts::local()` lists the accounts signed in to the
app (name, email, sign-in address, UUID) from the summaries in its
`1password.sqlite` (`~/.config/1Password`, or the Flatpak's;
`OLO_1PASSWORD_DATA` overrides), read-only and nothing else from it.
Passwords' setup offers them as a choice and keeps the UUID, which the
SDK integration takes as the account's name.

Tests never touch the real app. `onepassword-fake [--account NAME]
[--socket NAME] [--data FILE] [--accounts DIR] [--items N]` (DIR gets a
`1password.sqlite` listing it) serves an in-memory account (two vaults of
sample items, item versions, OTP codes; `--items N` adds N made-up
logins, to measure Passwords with a vault the size of a person's) over
the same protocol;
`tests/desktop.rs` drives it. Apps take `OLO_1PASSWORD_SOCKET` to use it.

Passwords is the app: sources (vaults, categories, Archive), a two-line
item list and the selected item's fields (hover for Copy/Show; one-time
codes count down), an editor with templates per category, a Password
Generator panel, and File/Edit/Item/View menus (⌘C username, ⇧⌘C password,
⇧⌘O one-time code, ⌘0 All Items, ⌘1–⌘9 the vaults by place, as
`app_keys` has them). Secrets go to the clipboard with
`olo_kit::copy::secret` and leave after `clear_seconds` (quit before,
Passwords runs on without its windows until they do: `Passwords::quit`
closes them and ends at the next thing due, the secret's time; opened
meanwhile, it carries on). A field (or website) drags out as text onto
another app's field (`Detail::drag`, what goes `Passwords::dragged_field`:
a one-time password's current code;
the picture shows the field's name, never the value). It opens locked and locks after
`lock_minutes` idle, and when the screen locks if `lock_with_screen`
(`lock.rs`): Touch ID through fprintd, claimed only
while the locked window has the keyboard, or the account password through
PAM. Those, and `auto_sync`, are Preferences ▸ Security's
(`Settings::security.passwords`, followed live through
`olo_kit::settings::watch`; the screen locking comes from
`settings::watch_power`, `PowerStatus::locked`; View ▸ Lock After writes
the same setting with `settings::update`). Its own settings (accounts,
the generator) live in `passwords.json`.

It is on olo-kit. Passwords runs with no window (started at login as
the SSH agent and the keychain, locked) and its window comes and goes,
so its state and what it does are the app's, not a window's: one
`Passwords` behind a lock (`app()`, `main.rs`). The app's looper takes
what the proxy brings (the store's replies, the lock's, other
programs' requests, settings) with `Passwords::message`; each window's
view locks it while it says what it shows and again to act, and
`Passwords::changed` tells the windows to say what they show again.
Nothing that waits is done under the lock, and nothing calls `app()`
while holding it (it isn't re-entrant: a handler takes what it needs,
lets go, then calls the kit). What only a window has (its text fields,
its list, its scrollers) is its view's; what the app wants of those
(the password field emptied, the search field given the keyboard, the
editor's form made again for fields that came or went) it leaves in
`Ui`, which the views take as they next say what they show
(`take_asks`). The main window is `view::MainView` (the setup, lock and
connection panels; the toolbar, sources, items under their filters and
the status line); the selected item or its editor is a view of its own,
`view::Detail`, so a one-time code counting down (the pane says what
it shows again on the second, only while one shows), the pointer
moving over the fields and typing in the editor draw that pane alone.
Nothing ticks: the app's looper keeps one timer for the next thing due
(a sync, the auto-lock, the status line clearing, a copied secret's
time when it's closing), set again whenever the app changes
(`next_due` lists only what `tick` would act on, so a time gone by
never spins), and the main window one for when "Synced a minute ago"
next reads differently. The list is worked out once for each change to
the items, the source or the search (`visible`), and its rows keep
their drawing by what they show (`row_key`). Review Sync, Sync
Problems, the generator (a panel: it floats, never a tab) and the
passkey question are views in windows of their own that read the app;
alerts are the app's (`open_app_alert`, answered on the alert's
looper); a passkey question closes itself when the page gives up.
Debug builds only take the PAM test
service, so a release build can't be unlocked in a test session: to
measure one, build it with `CARGO_PROFILE_RELEASE_DEBUG_ASSERTIONS=true`
in a scratch `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`. Tests give it a keychain socket of its
own (`OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET`; the default is the person's Passwords') and
a fake 1Password on a socket of its own (`onepassword-fake --socket
NAME --accounts DIR`, `OLO_1PASSWORD_SOCKET=NAME`,
`OLO_1PASSWORD_DATA=DIR`). `olo-keychain-ask` (an example of
olo-keychain: `cargo build -p olo-keychain --example olo-keychain-ask`)
asks a test's Passwords one thing as Chrome's extension would (a
passkey to make or sign with) and prints the answer's kind alone; it
wants `OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET`, so it never reaches the person's.
A test session keeps what its Passwords kept (its dir's `config`), so a
second start is a locked one; remove `config/olo/passwords.*` and
`passwords.key` for the setup again. Return on the item list opens the
item's website in a browser: tests press it only with an alert up.

**Its own store** (`vault.rs`). Every vault and item lives on this
computer, so the app, Chrome's extension and the palette never wait on
1Password: `passwords.vault` in the config directory, "TABV", a format
byte, a 24-byte nonce and the JSON sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305 (header
as associated data), written whole and atomically (0600) after each
change. The key is 32 random bytes in the login keyring
(`olo_system::secrets`, a Secret Service client that first checks a
keyring owns, or can start, `org.freedesktop.secrets`, so with none it
answers "nothing" at once; the session bus's calls time out after 10 s;
PAM unlocks the
keyring at login, so Touch ID still opens Passwords). A store whose key is
missing is never overwritten with a new one. `OLO_PASSWORDS_KEYFILE`
keeps the key in a file instead; tsession sets it for every session, so
test apps never touch the real keyring. The worker (`store.rs`) owns the
store: it opens it at the unlock, lets it go at the lock (after a running
sync), and answers the UI, Chrome's extension and op from it. Items keep 1Password's
types; each entry also records what 1Password last had (version, update
time, archive state), whether it changed here, and a revision; deletions
of synced items leave tombstones. Without an account (Keep Only on This
Computer) items live in a local "Personal" vault.

**Syncing with 1Password** (`sync.rs`, optional: the setup panel or File ▸
1Password Accounts…) never changes anything, on either side, without the
person's approval. It runs in two steps, each on its own thread:

* `sync::plan`, from a snapshot (`Vault::snapshot` changes nothing, even
  for an account switch), only reads. Down: vaults whose
  `content_version` moved are listed (both states); new or changed items
  (update time or state) are fetched fifty at a time with `get_all`;
  items gone there are noted. 1Password refuses to give apps archived
  items ("item is not in an active state"), and one archived id fails a
  whole `get_all`, so only active items are fetched: an item archived
  there since is archived here from its listing (`Change::Archived`),
  archived items never synced are left out with a note, and whatever a
  batch didn't bring is fetched one at a time, so a bad item costs only
  itself. A field 1Password's SDK names but won't give the value of (its
  `Unsupported`, with no value and no section: an older card's expiry,
  three of Ben's cards) is asked for by its secret reference
  (`op://vault/item/field`, `resolve_unread`, all of a batch at once,
  else one by one), which 1Password answers: a card's expiry or
  valid-from that reads as a month and year becomes a `MonthYear`
  ("MM/YYYY"); any other keeps its value. An item synced before that
  with such a field empty is fetched again, once, its vault changed or
  not (`has_unread`). `cargo run -p olo-onepassword --example
  card_shapes [VAULT ITEM]` shows what the 1Password app gives for each
  card (or one item): every field's id, label, type and section, and its
  value's shape only ("NN/NNNN"), never a value or a title, and how its
  unsupported fields resolve. Up: 1Password's copies of items changed here
  are fetched to compare (their unread fields asked for the same way). The plan is the store's `Change`s, what to send,
  and a `Row` for every change either side would see (add, change with the
  parts that differ by name, never values, archive, delete, keep both).
* The store keeps the plan and the UI shows its rows in Review Sync. Only
  `Job::Approve` with that plan's id runs `sync::apply`, which makes
  exactly those changes. A changed item is put against the version that
  was reviewed, and a deletion checks it first, so anything changed in
  1Password meanwhile is refused (reported) rather than overwritten, and
  comes up in the next review. A plan nobody would notice (nothing but
  what was looked at) applies without asking.

With `auto_sync` (the default), plans are made at the unlock, every 5 minutes, 3 s after a change here
(the status line then says "3 sync changes to review"; a click opens
them), and on File ▸ Sync Now or the setup panel's Sync (the review opens
at once). Automatic plans wait while Review Sync is open. Cancel leaves
"Not synced: changes not applied". Changed on both sides: 1Password's copy
stays as the item and ours is kept beside it as "… (conflict)", to be
reviewed next time. A push that lands after another edit here keeps the
edit pending (revisions). The first sync with an account brings in
everything; local-only items move to its Personal (or first) vault.

**Several accounts.** The setup ticks any of the 1Password app's accounts
(`Settings::accounts`, `Linked { id, label }`; the first takes items made
here; an id is the UUID, or a name typed by hand, which the app also
answers to and which is kept). The store keeps which account each vault is
in (`Data::vault_account`); `Vault::snapshot(account, home)` holds only that
account's vaults (and, for the first, the local vault), so one account
never sees another's vaults as gone. `Job::Sync { accounts }` plans each
in turn into one `Plan` of per-account parts, one review: with more than
one account a vault is named "Personal (Work)" there, in problems, the
editor and the item's header, and the sidebar lists each account's vaults
under its name (as Tracker lists volumes). An account that can't be
reached is a problem, not a failure, unless none can be. Unticking one
asks first, then `Job::RemoveAccount` drops its vaults and items here
(never-sent items stay, in the local vault). Stores and settings from the
one-account days carry over (`Data::account`, `Settings::account`). The
fake serves more signed-in accounts on one socket (`FakeAccount::others`). Files attached in 1Password aren't copied (their metadata
is), so they aren't shown.

**Vaults** (Ben, 2026-11-14: "olo passwords should support
creating/managing new vaults") are made, renamed, described and deleted
here, as items are: at once in the store, and in 1Password at the next
sync, once reviewed. File ▸ New Vault…, Vault Info… and Delete Vault…, and
a vault's right-click in the sources (`vault_menu`), are commands
(`new-vault`, `vault-info[:ID]`, `delete-vault[:ID]`); New Vault and
Vault Info are one small dialog (`vaults.rs`, Name: and Description:,
saying where it goes), Delete asks first, naming how many items go with
it. `Vault::create_vault` makes a `local-…` vault (in the first account,
listed after 1Password's and chosen), `edit_vault` and `delete_vault` the
others; each is a `VaultChange` in `Data::vault_changes`, counted in what's
pending. Only vaults the person made can be deleted (`vault::deletable`:
`UserCreated`, never Private, Shared or the vault kept here before any
account); one never sent just goes. A sync shows each as a row of Review
Sync with the vault's icon ("Make this vault in 1Password", "Renamed (was
“X”)", "Its 4 items too") and, applied, makes vaults first and gives
their items 1Password's id (`Change::VaultMade`, then `apply_made`; an
item of a vault that couldn't be made waits for it); a vault being
deleted isn't listed. The fake makes, changes and deletes vaults as
1Password does (`VaultsCreate`, `VaultsUpdate`, `VaultsDelete`, only
`UserCreated`). Tests: `vaults_made_renamed_and_deleted_here`,
`vaults_made_here_before_a_sync`.

**Problems** are `sync::Problem`s (vault, item or none, a reason in plain
words from `sync::reason`, and whether it's only a note), never joined
text. The status line counts them ("Synced just now · 2 problems", red
only for failures); the review shows one line ("⚠ 2 problems reading
1Password…"). Either opens Sync Problems: grouped by vault
(`sync::grouped`, repeats dropped), a warning or info icon, the item and
its reason under it, with Copy (`sync::as_text`) and Sync Again. The fake
behaves as 1Password does: archived items can't be read, and a vault with
`"no_access": true` can't be listed.

**Reset** (File ▸ Reset Passwords…, after an alert) erases the store here
(`Vault::reset`, or the file if it can't be opened) and the account
choice, back to the setup panel. It never touches 1Password: pending
deletions go with the rest.

`cargo test -p olo-passwords` covers the store (sealing, wrong keys,
conflicts, races, accounts, reset) and syncing against the in-process fake
(both ways, conflicts, nothing to do, 1Password down, that a plan
changes nothing and names every change, archived items and an
unlistable vault, and several accounts in one review). The Secret Service
client has an ignored test for a private keyring:
`tools/dev/private-keyring start` (busd if installed with `cargo install
busd --root /var/tmp/olo-dev/busd`, else dbus-daemon, plus its own
gnome-keyring), then
`DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS=unix:path=/var/tmp/olo-dev/keyring/bus cargo test
-p olo-system secrets -- --ignored`; it refuses any other bus.

```sh
target/debug/onepassword-fake --socket olo-fake --accounts $acc &
tools/dev/tsession start pw 2560x1600 --light --home $home
tools/dev/tsession run pw HOME=$home OLO_1PASSWORD_SOCKET=olo-fake OLO_1PASSWORD_DATA=$acc \
    OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET=$sock OLO_NO_FINGERPRINT=1 \
    OLO_PAM_CONFDIR=$dir OLO_PAM_SERVICE=exec target/debug/olo-passwords
```
(`run` doesn't pass `OLO_PAM_*` on by itself; give them as above, with
`$dir` set up as for the lock screen; `$acc`, `$home` and `$sock` are
scratch paths of the test's own, under `/var/tmp`.) Account: `Olo Test`
(choose Sync in the setup, then Apply in Review Sync); password:
whatever `check.sh` accepts. Pass `--data FILE` to the fake to see what
reached "1Password". The same line again while it runs is handed to
the one running (its window comes back). `olo-op item list` with the
same `OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET` brings the Allow alert; `olo-keychain-ask`
a passkey's question.

### op: 1Password's command line (apps/op)

`olo-op` stands in for 1Password's `op` so scripts that use it (`op
inject`, `op read`, `op run`, `op item get`, `op whoami`, `op account
list`, `op signin`) work from Passwords. It is installed with an `op`
link to it beside the other binaries (`~/.local/bin`, ahead of
`/usr/bin` on the PATH); `olo_xdg::link_op` makes the link only where
there is no `op` already and removes only its own. app_server keeps the
link in step with Preferences ▸ Security ▸ "Answer 1Password's op
command" (`PasswordsSecurity::op_cli`, on by default) at startup and on
each change, skipping `target/` builds; Passwords refuses `op` while it
is off.

Passwords is the session's SSH agent (`agent.rs`; Preferences ▸ Security
▸ "Be the SSH agent", on by default): the agent protocol
(draft-miller-ssh-agent: identities and signatures; adding, removing
and locking refused, Passwords keeps the keys) on
`olo_xdg::ssh_agent_socket()` (one a display), which olo-session puts in
`SSH_AUTH_SOCK` as a login starts (unless the login gave one) and
exports to systemd and D-Bus activation. olo-session starts `olo-passwords
--agent` at login (`REAL_SHELL`): Passwords without a window, staying
when its window closes (`stay_resident`), opened by a launch as before;
off, it exits `SERVICE_NOT_WANTED` and isn't started again. Each request
of a program of the person's own (`SO_PEERCRED`) is a keychain request
(`Request::SshKeys`, `SshSign`, made in process with
`Incoming::local` and the program's pid), so it's answered as `op`'s:
once unlocked (an agent-only Passwords opens its window to be unlocked),
a signature once that terminal session is allowed ("Allow “ssh …” to
sign in with your SSH keys?", one grant with `op`'s), the keys read and
used only on the store's thread (`agent::keys`, `agent::sign`): SSH Key
fields of active items, OpenSSH text or PKCS#8 (Ed25519, RSA with
SHA-256/512 as asked, ECDSA P-256), through RustCrypto's `ssh-key`.
`~/.ssh/config` naming another agent (1Password's app writes
`IdentityAgent ~/.1password/agent.sock`) is said in Security, with "Use
Passwords for ssh" once this session's `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` is Passwords'
(`olo_keychain::ssh_config`: `IdentityAgent SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, the old line
kept as a comment). Tried headless with a store shared to a screen
(`ssh_fixture`): `ssh-add -L` lists its key, `ssh-keygen -Y sign` through
the agent makes a signature `ssh-keygen -Y verify` accepts. Idle, agent
only: 59 MB, no CPU.

`op` asks over the keychain socket (`Request::Cli { query: CliQuery }` →
`Response::Cli { json }`, in 1Password's JSON shapes), starting Passwords
if it isn't running; the shapes, field types and `op://vault/item/[section/]field[?attribute=…]`
references are `apps/passwords/src/cli.rs` (`cli::reference`, one
function for `op item get`'s and for Passwords' Copy Reference: an
item's right-click menu and Edit menu copy its main field's,
`cli::main_field`, its password else its first secret; a field's own
right-click menu, that field's; tested by resolving each back,
`copy_reference_resolves_back`). Account questions (`op
account list`, `whoami`) are answered from the linked accounts without
unlocking. Anything else waits for an unlock, then for the person's say:
an alert names the command, the program that ran it and its folder, and
Allow covers that terminal session (the caller's session id and
terminal, from `/proc/PID/stat`) until Passwords locks or for 10 minutes
after its last use (12 hours at most); Deny answers "not allowed".
What unlocks Passwords allows it too (`apps/passwords/src/allow.rs`):
Touch ID, a touch of a security key set up, or a look, each waited for
on a thread of its own while the alert is open (the look once, up to
3 s, as it opens; the sensor and the key 40 s at most, so an alert left
open holds neither from sudo) and stopped as it's answered. What there
is is found on the worker that asks app_server first (`Ways::find`:
fprintd's and olo-faced's lists over D-Bus, the key's file and /sys;
nothing asked of the sensor, key or camera themselves), and the alert
says it ("To allow it, you can also touch your security key."). Allowed
so, the alert goes, a quiet notification says how ("Allowed with Touch
ID"), and the request goes on. None of the three where nobody sits at
the computer (`olo_system::env::readers_here`: see Agent Screens); a test's soft
key or face service (`key_here`, `face_here`) does. Tried headless: the
soft key set up in the session (`cargo run -p olo-fido --example
soft-set-up`), Passwords debug with it and the PAM stand-in; `op item
list` showed the alert with the sentence, the key's touch 2.5 s later
took it away and op printed the list; with a key that never touches,
Allow still answered it and the key's wait ended with it. A look and
Touch ID through stand-ins on the session's own bus (`cargo run -p
olo-system --example fake-readers -- --bus ADDRESS --finger
match|no-match|none --face match|no-face|none`, with `OLO_FACE_BUS` and,
debug builds, `OLO_FPRINT_BUS` at that address: it prints what it's
asked): with no finger enrolled the alert offered the camera and a
matching look allowed op with no click; with the look finding no face,
the finger's match did (Claim, VerifyStart, VerifyStatus match,
VerifyStop, Release).
`op run` passes the values in the environment and masks them in the
command's output (`<concealed by 1Password>`, `text::Masker`) unless
`--no-masking`; `inject` writes files 0600. Commands that change items,
vaults or accounts say Olo's op doesn't do them, and errors look like
op's (`[ERROR] date time message`, exit 1).

`cargo test -p olo-op -p olo-passwords` covers templates, env
files, masking, arguments, references and item JSON. To try it, run
Passwords as above and `op` from `target/debug/olo-op` through an `op`
link in a scratch folder with the session's `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` and
`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`.

### The keychain (crates/keychain)

While Passwords runs it serves other Olo programs (Chrome's extension
host, the palette, `op`) on
`$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-keychain-$WAYLAND_DISPLAY.sock`
(`OLO_KEYCHAIN_SOCKET` overrides): one JSON request, one JSON reply per
connection, and only for our own uid running an `olo-*` program
(SO_PEERCRED + `/proc/PID/exe`); what's shared with agent screens
(`Shares`, `SetShares`) never to a program on one ("Passwords for agent
screens"). `olo_keychain::call` blocks, so call
it from a thread. One Passwords serves a display: `serve` refuses ("already
served") where another answers, and takes a socket nothing answers. So
a Passwords that quits lets go of its sockets first, the keychain's and
the SSH agent's (`Served` in main.rs: removed if still the files it
bound, never another's): the kit runs a program on after it quits for
what it copied, giving up its launch name, and a Passwords opened
meanwhile found the old one serving, served nothing, and went on so
once the old one had gone. Chrome's passkeys and logins then answered
"Passwords isn't running" and Google showed its own QR sheet (Ben's
google-setup screen, 2026-11-18; found by the second investigator,
made to happen and stop happening in a test session: text copied in
Passwords, Quit, Passwords again, the clipboard taken). Requests: `Logins {url}` (title and username of each
login whose website fits the page, honouring 1Password's autofill
setting; `Locked` if locked), `Fill {url, vault, id}`, `Check {url,
username, password}` (`Known`, `New` or `Changed`), `Save {…, replace}`,
and `Unlock`. Fill, Save and Unlock wait while Passwords is locked: it
comes forward and answers after the unlock. `olo_keychain::matches`
is the site rule, as 1Password's: the same registrable domain (the `psl`
crate's public suffix list, so mail.google.com's login fills
accounts.google.com but alice.github.io's never fills bob.github.io), the
same host where there's none (localhost, addresses), and never an https
login into a plain-http page (localhost aside). Every login that fits is
listed, nearest first (`olo_keychain::closeness`: the page's own host,
then its parent domains from the nearest, then the site's other hosts),
then by title; an item that can't be read is logged, not hidden silently.

An Olo program's own secrets: `KeepSecret {title, secret, note}` keeps
one as a Password item of that title (DiskBackup's key, Weather's
provider key; left as it is if that title and secret are there) and
`Secrets {title}` reads them back. `Reference {reference, purpose}`
reads the secret an `op://vault/item/[section/]field` names, for a
program the person gave the reference to (Weather's key, kept in
Passwords already): resolved as `op read` resolves it (`cli::resolve`:
vault and item by ID or name), once the person allows that program
that secret. Passwords asks per program (by `/proc/PID/exe`) and
reference ("Allow “Weather” to use the “password” of “Weather:
tomorrow.io API key” in Personal (for tomorrow.io’s forecasts)? Always
lets it have it whenever it asks, until you take it back (File ▸ Apps
Allowed…).": the item, field and vault by name, not the reference):
Deny (Escape), Approve Once (this request, and any waiting with it) or
Approve Always (the default, Return). Always is kept in the vault
(`Data::allowed`: the program's file, the reference, since when), so
it holds across restarts and upgrades (Ben, 2026-11-15: "once i allow
the weather app to use the passwords item it should keep that approval
forever, not until the next restart"; before, an Allow lasted until
Passwords quit); File ▸ Apps Allowed… (`allowed.rs`) lists each with
Take Back. On an agent screen, what it was given is the agents' there,
so it isn't asked. Requests waiting for the same answer share one
alert. Apps read a secret this way with `olo_keychain::read_reference
(reference, purpose)`, which blocks while Passwords asks and gives the
secret or a `ReferenceError` whose text is for the person (Weather's
key does); any app taking a key or a login from Passwords should, so
it's asked the same way. Tested headless with a stand-in vault (debug builds only: the
stand-in PAM, `OLO_PAM_CONFDIR`, is compiled out of release builds,
which check the real account).

## Token Pool (apps/pool, crates/pool)

(Its windows are on olo-kit. What outlives them is a `Hub` on the
app's looper, `ui.rs` (the gateway serves with no window open): which
clients use the pool, a sign-in being waited for, the last thing
said. Each window is a view on a looper of its own, reading the pool
itself and told the rest by the hub: `ui.rs` the main one,
`clients_window.rs` the Clients window. Both carry the app's menu
bar.)

Several Claude and ChatGPT subscriptions shared by Claude Code and Codex
on this computer, the way Token Pooler's Local mode does it on macOS
(written fresh; no team or cloud gateway). The session's real shell
runs `olo-pool --service` (no window; launching `olo-pool` again
opens it), which listens on `127.0.0.1:17891` (`OLO_POOL_PORT`), and
on `127.0.0.1:17892` (`OLO_POOL_PROXY_PORT`) as the clients' proxy.

- **Proxy** (`intercept.rs`, `authority.rs`, `peer.rs`): Claude Code
  and Codex run as on their own subscriptions, signed in as they are
  and talking to their own hosts, with `HTTPS_PROXY` set to the pool (no
  API mode, no other endpoint). It takes CONNECTs only. A connection to
  `api.anthropic.com` or `chatgpt.com` is opened with a certificate for
  that host from the pool's own authority (`pool-ca.pem` and its key,
  0600, in the config directory; name-constrained to those two hosts and
  issuing nothing further, so even its key vouches for nothing else),
  and on it the model requests (Claude's `/v1/messages…`, Codex's
  `/backend-api/codex/…`: `intercept::pooled`) are served as the gateway
  serves them; everything else on those hosts goes through untouched
  (the client's own sign-in, every header and byte, its compression,
  WebSockets and other upgrades joined byte for byte after the 101), and
  every other host is a plain tunnel. Only the clients themselves are
  opened: the program on the other end is read from /proc (the socket's
  inode in `/proc/net/tcp`, the process holding it; `peer::program`),
  and one that isn't Claude Code or Codex (a script one of them runs,
  which inherits the setting but needn't trust the certificate) is
  tunnelled, as without the pool. Codex's Responses over a WebSocket
  (Codex 0.170 asks for one first) are the pool's too
  (`gateway::serve_socket`, below); it was answered 426, Codex's sign to
  use HTTPS for the rest of its session, which Codex left to itself never
  does. A Claude model request asking for one still gets 426 (Claude
  Code never asks). A provider with no usable account is tunnelled, so its client runs
  on its own sign-in. A request body compressed (Codex's zstd on
  ChatGPT's backend) is sent on as it came and read decompressed for its
  model (`gateway::plain`). The client's own account's headers
  (`x-organization-uuid`, `chatgpt-account-id` and the like) are the
  pool account's, or none, on a pooled request.

- **Gateway** (`gateway.rs`, axum): `/claude/v1/*` goes to Claude's API,
  `/codex/v1/*` to Codex's Responses API, each with the chosen account's
  OAuth sign-in in place of the client's (its `authorization`,
  `x-api-key`, cookies and hop-by-hop headers are never passed on;
  Claude gets the `oauth-2025-04-20` beta added). Only loopback `Host`s
  and no `Origin` (no web page can use it). An account's sign-in is
  refreshed within a minute of expiring, one refresh at a time per
  account, the rotated refresh token kept; a 401 is refreshed and
  retried once, then the account is marked signed out and the next
  tried; a 429 that says a meter ran out (Claude's
  `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-status: rejected`; any 429 from Codex)
  marks the account (or, for a per-model meter, just that model family)
  out until its reset and the next is tried. Claude's other 429s (a
  burst limit, or a request it won't serve on that account) are the
  request's: passed back as they came, the account left in use. Both happen
  before anything is passed back; a network failure is a 502 and never
  replayed. With none left, a 429 shaped as the provider's with a
  `retry-after` of the soonest reset (the clients are set to retry ten
  times). `x-olo-pool-account` names who answered. `/pool/status`
  is the state without sign-ins. Its own `/claude/v1/*` and
  `/codex/v1/*` remain for programs pointed at it by address (Olo's AI
  features).
- **Order** (`schedule.rs`): earliest-expiry-first. The account whose
  usable quota resets soonest serves, since quota that resets unused is
  lost; ties go to the older account, then the id. The account serving
  keeps serving unless another resets more than five minutes sooner.
  Windows can be model-scoped (Weekly Opus, Weekly Fable): a request
  for another model isn't held up by that model's meter, and one for
  that model goes to another account before it's even tried (Ben,
  2026-11-08: "make sure too that token pooler switches accounts when
  the model in use is the one that the limit hits"; `tests/gateway.rs`
  `switches_by_the_model_whose_meter_ran_out`: an account whose report
  says its Fable week is used up is never asked for Fable but still
  serves Opus; one refused for Fable, claim `seven_day_fable`, waits for
  Fable only; with none left Fable waits while Opus is served).
- **Usage** is read from the answers as they stream through: only
  `usage` objects (SSE lines containing "usage", or a JSON body's), the
  content discarded as it passes. Quota comes from every answer's
  rate-limit headers and the providers' usage reports, read for each
  account every five minutes (`SYNC_EVERY`; reset credits every 30) and,
  when a report answers 429, at twice the last wait up to 30 minutes:
  reading them twice a minute per account was itself rate limited.
  Every meter there is (Ben, 2026-11-08: "make all the quotas for an
  account show up e.g. i think anthropic has a special fable quota and
  codex might have a 5 hour quota … right now i only see weekly for
  everything"; `upstream::parse_usage`): Claude's report's `limits`, the
  server's list of every meter (kind, group, percent, reset, a model's or
  a surface's scope), as Claude Code's own `/usage` reads it (2.1.319):
  the session as 5-hour, the week as Weekly, a model's as "Weekly Fable"
  for that model alone, a surface's (Cowork) shown and limiting nothing
  here, one not known yet by its own words; the older fields for what the
  rows don't say, one not started yet (`utilization: null`, how the
  session showed before its first request: it had been left out, so
  only Weekly showed) at 0%, "not started"; every
  `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-*-utilization` header, not a list; Codex's
  `rate_limit` windows, each `additional_rate_limits` entry's (a model's
  own, "GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark 5-hour", for its requests) and code
  review's. A window's length comes from what it's called (Codex's
  primary can be a week), else its name. `examples/seed_vault.rs
  --meters` makes accounts showing each kind, for the window.
- **Store** (`store.rs`): `pool.vault` in the config directory, sealed
  as Passwords seals its own (XChaCha20-Poly1305, header as AAD); the key
  is 32 random bytes in the login keyring (`OLO_POOL_KEYFILE`: a file
  instead, for tests). It is the pool's own, rather than Passwords'
  1Password-backed store, because the gateway must work, and save the
  refresh tokens providers rotate, while Passwords is locked. The vault
  is opened on a worker thread, retried every 30 s while the keyring
  is shut, and nothing is saved until it has been read.
- **Adding accounts** (`import.rs`): *this computer's* sign-in is read
  from `~/.claude/.credentials.json` (`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`) or
  `~/.codex/auth.json` (`CODEX_HOME`). The pool then refreshes it, so
  the client's own copy goes stale: point the client at the pool.
  *Separately* runs the official client's own sign-in in Terminal with
  its config in a private directory on the runtime tmpfs (`claude auth
  login`, `codex login` with file storage), takes the result and deletes
  the directory. The same email again updates that account's sign-in.
- **Clients** (`clients.rs`): "Claude Code uses the pool" sets
  `HTTPS_PROXY`, `NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS` (the authority's certificate,
  added to what it trusts) and `NO_PROXY` (loopback) in Claude Code's
  `settings.json` `env`; "Codex uses the pool" sets `HTTPS_PROXY`,
  `SSL_CERT_FILE` (`pool-ca-bundle.pem`: the system's roots and the
  authority's, since Codex's setting replaces the roots) and `NO_PROXY`
  in Codex's `~/.codex/.env` (`CODEX_HOME`), which Codex reads as it
  starts. What was there before is kept in `pool-clients.json`.
  Unchecked, a client is only paused (`pool-clients.json`'s `paused`,
  mirrored in `Shared::paused`): its settings stay pointed at the proxy,
  which decides for each request (`Shared::routes`: not paused, and an
  account to serve it) whether the pool serves it or passes it through
  on the client's own sign-in (`intercept::through`; a new connection
  for it is only tunnelled). So checking and unchecking takes effect
  from the client's next request, with nothing restarted (Codex's
  service neither) and nothing under way cut. `olo-pool --put-back
  claude|codex` (`clients::put_back`) takes a client off the proxy
  altogether, its settings exactly as before the pool (from its next
  start). A client set up the old way (an endpoint of the
  gateway's own: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and the rest, or an `olo_pool`
  model provider in `config.toml`) is moved over as the pool starts
  (`clients::migrate`).
- **Codex's daemon** (`codex_daemon.rs`): Codex's interactive sessions
  run their turns in a daemon of Codex's own (`codex app-server`, pid in
  `~/.codex/app-server-daemon/daemon.pid`), which lives for days and
  reads `.env` only as it starts, so a window opened after the change
  still talks through a daemon from before it. Every 10 s, and right
  after the checkbox changes, the pool looks for a daemon that started
  before `.env` last changed (its start in ticks from `/proc`, which the
  pid file records too, so a reused pid isn't taken for it) and
  restarts it at once, even in the middle of a turn (an agent's turn can
  go on for hours, all of it straight to OpenAI; waiting for one to end
  once meant never), with Codex's own `codex app-server daemon restart`
  (its start, pid file, locks and updater are Codex's), run from the
  daemon's directory with its environment (its sessions' commands get
  theirs from it) less the pool's settings, which the new one reads
  from `.env` as it is now. Codex's windows reconnect to the new daemon
  by themselves and carry on with the conversation; a daemon merely
  stopped leaves them "Reconnecting to server…", since nothing starts
  another. Its conversations, and whether each is in a turn, are asked
  over its control socket (the app-server's JSON-RPC over a WebSocket:
  `initialize`, `thread/loaded/list`, `thread/read`: `threads()`).
  Since unchecking only pauses, a restart is needed only when `.env`
  first points Codex at the proxy (or `--put-back` takes it off).
- **Upgrades of the pool itself, without a gap** (`ui::hand_over`,
  `drain.rs`; Ben, 2026-11-06: "it should serve new requests in the new
  process but allow old requests to finish in their existing process so
  that nothing errors"). olo-kit tells the app a new olo-pool is installed
  (`olo_kit::on_upgrade_due`), and the same when app_server restarts (an
  upgrade's reload, a crash: the compositor gone, `lost_compositor`,
  which hands over first and waits while it's busy, rather than
  re-executing at once: it had cut every agent's stream at each reload,
  "API Error: Connection lost mid-response", Ben 2026-11-07; a tunnel
  through the proxy with a ping every half second across `tsession
  reload` broke a second in before, and answered 50 of 50 after). The app starts a copy of the new version
  beside itself with the listening sockets (copies kept at bind,
  `Drain::keep`; made inheritable for it alone, `Drain::for_a_copy`, and
  named in `OLO_POOL_LISTENERS`, `PORT=FD`), the windows' state (the
  kit's `restore::hand_over`; its own windows close and the copy opens
  them), its launches (`instance::close`, then the copy listens:
  `OLO_NEW_INSTANCE=1`) and the read end of a pipe (`Drain::finishing`,
  `OLO_POOL_FINISHING`) whose other end it keeps until it has finished.
  The kernel
  gives each new connection to whichever process accepts on the shared
  socket, and the old one stops (`Drain::retire`), so the copy answers
  every new request at once. The old one finishes what it has under way
  (`Underway`, held by an answer's body until it has gone: `Counted`;
  the proxy's requests and the gateway's own `/claude/v1`, `/codex/v1`
  alike), closes connections as they fall idle (a client's next request
  opens one to the copy), and saves nothing (no quota reads, no activity,
  no whole-file writes: the copy owns the file). **What finishes there
  is booked by the copy** (Codex's fourth review: a turn that ended in
  the old copy was counted in its memory only): each turn it finishes,
  and what an answer or a socket tells it of an account (its meters, a
  refusal's cooldown), goes to the copy as a line of JSON on the pipe
  it's known to be finishing by (`gateway::Late`, `Drain::tell`: written
  whole or not at all, never waiting), and the copy reads them on a
  thread of its own (`follow_predecessor`) and books each as its own
  (`book_late`), then saves it; what the old one saw before a reset the
  copy confirmed since is old (`reset_at`) and let go. A copy from
  before reads none (they fill the pipe, then are dropped). **No reset
  claim is under way across a handover**: before starting the copy the
  old one takes every provider's claims (`Shared::claims_closed`, on the
  kit's upgrade thread, which waits: a claim being made finishes first,
  its result saved with the flush that follows; two minutes at most),
  and holds them until it has retired, when none can be made there (a
  claim asked for meanwhile finds it retired). Else a claim made as the
  copy started was left there unclear, its intent saved but not how it
  went, for the copy to make again (Codex's third review). A sign-in either renews
  meanwhile goes under the store's lock file (`store::lock_at`), after
  reading the file again for one the other renewed (`newer`: another
  token lasting longer), so it's renewed once; the old writes only that
  sign-in in (`Store::put_credential`), and the copy's saves keep a newer
  one from the file (`adopt_newer`) while its predecessor is still
  finishing (`Drain::overlapping`). Claude rotates refresh tokens:
  renewing twice would sign the account out. Two rules there, each
  learnt from a pool that stopped answering for six hours until it was
  killed (Ben, 2026-11-18; every agent's request "timed out"). **The
  lock file is taken before the pool's `store`, never with it held**
  (`Shared::store_lock`): its holder takes the store next (to read the
  file, to write it), and each opening of the file is a holder of its
  own, two tasks of one copy as much as two copies, so a renewal holding
  the lock and wanting the store to save, with a request holding the
  store and wanting the lock, waited on each other for good, and every
  request after behind them (olo-sync's cycle check doesn't see a lock
  file; `renewals_and_saves_while_two_copies_overlap_dont_lock_each_
  other_out` in `tests/drain.rs` does, hanging on the old order). The
  lock is waited for 60 s at most (`store::LOCK_WAIT`, twice a renewal's
  own limit; said in the log, then on without it). **And a predecessor
  is one at work only until it has finished, not while its pid lives**:
  the copy olo-session started stays for good as the keeper (below),
  same pid, same start time, and the copy that knew it by those ran
  every request under the lock file, reading the sealed file again each
  time, for the rest of its life, which is what gave the two above hours
  to meet. The pipe closes as the old copy finishes
  (`Drain::finished`), ends or becomes the keeper (close-on-exec), and
  the new one sees it hung up (`poll`, not waiting) the next time it
  asks; a copy from before the pipe still names its pid, believed for
  the 20 minutes it can take at most. `/pool/status` says it (`drain.
  beside`). Tried with two real processes in a test session (the old
  one stopped mid hand-over: `beside` true; let go: false half a second
  on, its pid there or not). Once nothing is under way (20 minutes at
  most: past the provider's read timeout), the old one goes: the
  olo-pool olo-session started becomes the **keeper** in place (same pid:
  `OLO_POOL_KEEPER`, `main`'s `keeper`), a subreaper (`PR_SET_CHILD_
  SUBREAPER`) asleep in `poll` (a signalfd, and a pidfd for each copy it
  follows), about 8 MB, that passes SIGTERM, SIGINT and SIGHUP on to the
  copies that serve and ends once none is left, with how the last of its
  own ended (so a crash restarts the pool as before); an upgrade makes it
  the new version's keeper in place. A later copy (`OLO_POOL_KEPT`) just
  exits, and its successor goes to the keeper. The copies it follows
  are its children running olo-pool and whichever olo-pool holds the
  gateway's listening socket (`drain::serving`, from `olo_system::
  listening`: the socket's inode in `/proc/net/tcp`, then the
  processes whose descriptors say `socket:[inode]`), its own or not.
- **One Token Pool, whatever happens to the copy the session started.**
  The session's `olo-pool --service`, finding another copy already
  serving the port as it starts (and not handed the sockets itself:
  `OLO_POOL_LISTENERS`), becomes the keeper of that one (`main`, before
  anything else; it asks it to open its window if its own was open)
  rather than running beside it with no gateway, or ending. Ben,
  2026-11-07: Olo Doctor's Quit Them stopped the session's copy while it
  finished handing over to a copy of the new version (it ran a replaced
  binary); the copy ran on alone, each `--service` olo-session started
  forwarded its launch to it and exited, until olo-session gave up
  ("keeps exiting"), and the next upgrade's restart came in the moment
  the launch socket was between copies, so it ran as a second Token Pool
  that couldn't listen (its window, which took the launches, said
  "Can't listen on 127.0.0.1:17891" and showed no requests) for two
  days. Upgraded, that copy found the one serving and became its keeper,
  as it should. A launch that finds no copy taking launches while one
  serves (`main`) asks it over the gateway instead (`POST /pool/open`,
  loopback only: it opens its window and takes launches again, if no
  copy does), and only a copy from before that waits for its launch
  socket. Olo Doctor leaves programs finishing what they have
  (`olo-upgrade-waits`) out of Quit Them, and says when Token Pool runs
  twice, has no gateway, or another program has its port (its
  `token_pool` check). `/pool/status` says the serving copy's `pid`.
  Tested end to end in a test session (test ports, a scratch home, a key
  file, a fake upstream): a second `--service` became the keeper of the
  first; a launch with the launch socket gone opened the serving copy's
  window, which took launches again; the serving copy, upgraded, handed
  over to its own child, and the adopting keeper followed it; SIGTERM to
  a keeper ended the copy it followed and then itself; a copy forced to
  start beside the serving one was found by Olo Doctor, and Quit It
  ended it.
  While the old one finishes, the kit marks it waiting
  (`restore::mark_waiting`: `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/olo-upgrade-waits/PID`),
  and olo-session's stale check leaves it alone rather than stopping it
  90 s after the upgrade. If no copy can be started, the old way: no new
  connections (they wait in the kernel's queue), what's under way
  finishes, then the process becomes the new version with the sockets
  (`hand_over`, `drain::listen`); 10 minutes at most, and an upgrade that
  never comes ends the drain (`Drain::end`). `/pool/status` says which
  (`drain`: `draining`, `retired`). Tested against a fake provider
  (`tests/drain.rs`: a new copy answering at once while the old streams;
  two copies renewing a sign-in once against a provider that refuses a
  reused refresh token) and end to end, real processes in a test session
  (`examples/seed_vault.rs` makes a made-up account; `OLO_POOL_UPSTREAM`,
  `OLO_POOL_PORT`, `OLO_POOL_PROXY_PORT` keep it apart from the person's
  pool; the binary run from a scratch copy, replaced and sent SIGURG as
  olo-session would): a 20 s stream under way finished whole while new
  requests were answered in the fake's own second; the old pid became the
  keeper; a second upgrade went to a third copy under the keeper; the
  window came back once; SIGTERM to the keeper ended all; a copy killed
  ended the keeper with it.
- **The Clients window** (Pool ▸ Clients, ⌘L, or the Clients button;
  `apps/pool/src/clients_window.rs`): the pool's activity over time, a
  line each for Claude Code and Codex in requests a minute over the last
  hour, six hours or day (the kit's `Graph`, stepped a minute or a few
  at a time, hovering says each one's rate; totals, failures and tokens
  in the legend), from `activity.rs`: each minute's requests by client,
  counted as each request ends and kept for a day in a plain file of its
  own (`state_dir()/pool-activity.json`, only counts, so not in the
  sealed vault), written at most once a minute. Below it, Codex's
  service (`running::scan`): its version, since when, whether it is on
  the current settings, where its connections go, its conversations
  (title, folder, working or waiting for you), and **Restart**
  (`codex_daemon::restart_now`, on a worker thread); then each Claude
  Code and Codex running (from /proc: `peer::Program::is_client`), its
  folder, since when, and where its connections go: to the pool's
  proxy, straight out to port 443 elsewhere, or none open (a Claude
  Code going only straight out while it should use the pool shows red;
  one with an MCP server can have both). What's running is read every
  two seconds while the window is open, off the UI thread. For agents:
  `olo-pool --clients [--json]` (the same, without the window),
  `olo-pool --restart-codex-service`, and the activity in
  `--status --json` (`activity`: the day's minutes).
- **As the clients send** (`capture.rs`, `likeness.rs`; Ben,
  2026-11-19: "all requests from the pool need to be exactly the same as
  if they came from claude code / codex"). Every request the pool makes
  for itself (a quota read, a reset credits read, a reset's claim, a
  sign-in's renewal) is sent as the account's own client sends it:
  built from what that client was captured sending for that account,
  byte for byte (each header's name in its case, its order, its value;
  the body as the client writes it; HTTP/1.1 written as is, or HTTP/2
  where the client's offer has it and the host agrees; the client's ALPN
  offer), the account's own values in place of placeholders (its
  sign-in, organization, ChatGPT account id, the cookies ChatGPT set for
  it, kept in a jar the way Codex keeps them). Sent the pool's own way
  (reqwest), the credit read was refused by Claude as the wrong
  "surface" for every account, where sent as Claude Code it lists each
  account's resets.
  **Capture** (`capture::capture`, blocking a minute or two): the
  installed client (`capture::installed`: `claude` or `codex` on PATH,
  symlinks followed, its version from the install's folder) is run in a
  sandbox (a scratch home in Olo's cache folder, removed after; nothing
  of the person's but PATH and language) holding the account's access
  token and a made-up refresh token (a real one never goes there),
  through a proxy of the capture's own (its own authority, trusted only
  by the sandbox, made each time) that writes down every request as it
  came and every TLS ClientHello's offer, even one the client then
  refuses. The client can reach nothing but that proxy: Landlock's
  network rules let it connect over TCP to the proxy's port alone
  (`capture::confine`, between fork and exec; no Landlock, no capture),
  whatever it makes of its proxy settings. The proxy passes on only the
  reads named in `capture::reads` (each client's profile, flags, limits
  and settings), and only with the account's own sign-in (or none): a
  model request, a reset's claim, a sign-in's renewal, logging and
  analytics are answered there and never sent (no quota spent, no reset
  used, no sign-in rotated), and a request carrying anything made up
  never reaches a provider (Ben: "we don't want to make requests to the
  real api with fake data though that is not polite"), nor one whose
  body didn't come whole or came chunked, nor Codex's TUI asking for
  Reserve. Each `Sent` says whether it was passed on. A capture uses the sign-in as the pool keeps
  it, never renewing it (one due within a quarter of an hour waits);
  its client's process has its own session, nothing of the pool's open
  in it, ends with the capture's thread, and its group is ended when it
  stops; a sandbox names its owner (its process id and when it
  started), and the pool removes only those whose owner is gone (as it
  starts, its own earlier one too: an upgrade in place keeps the
  process's id). Only a pool talking to the providers' own hosts
  captures (a test's never runs a client). Claude Code is run in a
  terminal of its own first (a pseudo-terminal, typed into: `/usage`, a
  message), then as `claude -p hi` and `-p /usage` (in that order:
  print mode's `/usage` left its usage kept, and a session after showed
  that rather than ask), at its used-up limit where the account has one
  (its model request answered with the 429 Anthropic sends there,
  `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-*`, then `/limit-reset`), and with its
  sign-in expired (its renewal);
  Codex through its app server (`account/rateLimits/read`,
  `account/rateLimitResetCredit/consume`), as `codex exec`, in its TUI,
  without the sandbox's authority (its native TLS: OpenSSL's, where a
  custom authority makes it use rustls), and with an expired token made
  up for its renewal (every request carrying it answered by the capture).
  What's kept (`capture::path`: Olo's state folder, `pool/captures/
  ACCOUNT.json`, readable by the person alone) has every secret and the
  account's ids as placeholders (`{{access_token}}`, `{{organization_uuid}}`,
  `{{cookie}}`…), and a body only where the pool makes the request
  itself (a claim, a renewal); a removed or re-signed-in account's goes
  with it, and a capture that ends after that isn't kept. The pool
  reads each account's once and keeps it (a request never waits on the
  disk). Captured when the pool starts (a minute in, each
  account whose capture is of another install), when a client changes
  (the folder `claude` and `codex` are found in, watched: an update
  points them at another version), and by hand (Pool ▸ Capture Client
  Requests Again, `olo-pool --capture`): one account at a time, on a thread at
  idle priority (what it runs too); `capturing` in `--status --json`.
  Found so: Claude Code 2.1.329 speaks over three stacks (its API client
  for `/api/*`, axios under Bun: no ALPN, `Connection: close`; the SDK
  for `/v1/messages`, Bun's fetch, ALPN `http/1.1`; Bun's fetch for
  flags and logging), names its entrypoint in its User-Agent (`cli` in a
  terminal, `sdk-cli` in print mode), and its interface offers no
  `cedar_ember` reset to claim (`/limit-reset` is `juniper_tide`'s 5-hour
  one; at the limit only "Stop and wait"). Claude answers a credit read
  in print mode's name (`sdk-cli`) as the wrong surface: where a
  capture's session missed its read, print mode's goes with the
  session's `cli` (`likeness::as_session`). Its claim is made as its API
  client makes it (`Xt.post` with the program, grant and request ids),
  the quota read's head as a POST with `Content-Length` where that
  client puts it (`likeness::claude_claim`). Codex 0.170.0 speaks
  HTTP/2, names its front end in its User-Agent (`codex-tui`; its app
  server the client's name) and adds `x-openai-codex-luna-reserve: 1` to
  its TUI's quota read; its claim (`{"redeem_request_id": …}`, the credit
  left to ChatGPT) is answered `{"code": "reset"|"nothing_to_reset"|
  "no_credit"|"already_redeemed", "windows_reset": n}`; the pool takes
  Codex's own requests from its app server (its TUI's quota read asks
  for Reserve, which the pool can't use). Cookies are kept per account
  and host. The TLS handshake under them: what the pool offers a host
  (`relay::tls_offer`: rustls with aws-lc-rs, the client's own ALPN)
  is what Codex itself offers when it trusts an authority of the
  person's, as it does through the pool: the same suites and signature
  schemes in the same order, held to the captures' by a test
  (`the_pools_offer_is_codexs_under_an_authority`). It is neither of
  Claude Code's two (BoringSSL's, Bun's), nor Codex's with only its own
  roots (OpenSSL's): docs/reports/token-pool-tls.md says what each
  offers and what matching would take. A capture keeps each client's
  whole ClientHello (`hello.rs`: read off the connection before the
  recorder's acceptor has it, then put back, `Prefixed::unread`;
  `capture::Hello::offer`: suites and extensions in the client's order
  with what's in them, and nothing that is one connection's alone: no
  random, keys, tickets or name), and says in the log, once a capture,
  where it and the pool's own for that host and ALPN differ
  (`relay::own_offer`, `Offer::differences`: "pool: Claude Code's TLS
  offer to … and the pool's differ in N things (the client's | the
  pool's): …"). rustls writes its extensions in a new order at each
  connection, so that order is said apart and never counts between
  two rustls programs (`hello::ORDER`).
- **Passed on exactly** (`relay.rs`): a Claude model request goes on as
  Claude Code sent it, byte for byte: each header's name in its own
  case (hyper's server writes it down, its client writes it back:
  `preserve_header_case` on both, the case map in the request's
  extensions, which the proxy carries over), in its order, its value,
  the account's own in the client's places (its sign-in; the
  organization headers; the `account_uuid` in `metadata.user_id`'s
  string and nowhere else, the account's as its capture has it, the
  body's length to match; the account's cookies, `likeness::Jar`, never
  the client's, and what a host sets kept for the account, not passed
  back, as Codex's cookie store keeps and sends them, RFC 6265's rules:
  a cookie's Domain to its subdomains, a host's own to it alone, within
  its Path (else the request's, to its last `/`), until its Max-Age or
  Expires, replaced by name, domain and path, the longer path first),
  over HTTP/1.1 as Claude Code speaks to Anthropic (HTTP/2 if a
  client offered it and the host chose it), offering in its TLS what
  the client offered the proxy (`relay::ClientOffer`). The pool's
  connections follow the client's (`relay::ClientConn`): for each
  connection a client opens to the proxy, one of the pool's for each
  account its requests go on for (and one for its own sign-in's, passed
  through, one for each sign-in: a hash of its credential, in memory
  alone; ChatGPT's passed through on a client of the sign-in's own),
  kept between its requests and closed with it; none made before an
  account left or signed in again, or before the network changed, is
  kept. The pool's own reads for an account go on that account's own
  connections, a capture or not. A request a kept connection never sent goes again
  on a new one; one that may have reached the host is never sent again
  by the pool, which answers 502 (once there's a network) for the
  client's own retry, as a dropped connection would; a redirect goes
  back to the client, never followed (followed, a failure after it had
  the request sent again). Each step has a deadline (a connection 20 s,
  a kept one ready 5 s, an answer's head and each next piece 15
  minutes; the client's request head 30 s and its body 60 s, at most
  64 MB). The client's `accept-encoding` goes
  on, Codex's too, and the answer comes back as it came (its status
  line's reason, each name's case, its length, compressed as it came;
  a length beside chunking dropped, as the chunks frame it), the pool
  reading a decoded copy as it streams (`Decode`: usage counted only
  from an answer that decoded whole, its compression's own end and
  check reached; an empty answer, a HEAD's, ends at once). To the gateway's own address (no proxy)
  the `Host` is the host's. What isn't kept: a header's spacing, and a
  header repeated with another between (hyper groups a name's values);
  no client sends either. Codex's go on in their order, the account's
  own in place, HTTP/2 as Codex would get it (reqwest, per account).
  Codex's sockets (its Responses over a WebSocket, `serve_socket`): the
  account chosen at the handshake, which goes on as Codex sent it but for
  the account's own (its sign-in, its ChatGPT account, its cookies), on a
  connection of its own offering what Codex offered (no `h2`: HTTP/2 has
  no 101); one refused there (a 429, a sign-in refused) gives way to the
  next before Codex hears a thing, and the 101 comes back as it came
  (Codex's key accepted, each name in its case). Switched, the socket is
  passed on both ways as it came, the server's side read as it passes
  (`socket::Reader`: each message whole before it goes on, a moment, its
  `permessage-deflate` inflated for the pool's own reading with the
  server's context kept from message to message; one it can't read goes
  on unread): each turn counted from `response.created` to its end with
  its usage (an incomplete or failed turn's too, counted as not passed),
  the account's meters taken from `codex.rate_limits` as from an
  answer's `x-codex-*` headers, a meter of another name (a model's own,
  `metered_limit_name`) kept as its own. An account that runs out inside a
  socket (an `error` event with status 429 and `usage_limit_reached`, of
  the account's own limit, which Codex takes as final) is marked until
  its `resets_at`, and the socket closed both ways with that unsaid
  (what came before it in the same read still goes): Codex takes a
  socket that broke as a stream to ask again for (its first retry
  unshown), and the pool gives that another account. Once anything of
  the turn has reached Codex, the refusal goes to it as it came instead
  (asked again, the turn would be said twice). Another 429 (a burst's
  `rate_limit_exceeded`, its retry advice with it) goes to Codex as it
  came and marks nothing. A refusal at the handshake is read for its
  `resets_at` (a small JSON body, a second at most; anything else goes
  back whole); a renewal the sign-in service can't give is a 502, which
  Codex tries again, not the pool "out of quota", which it never does.
  Each new turn on an open socket (its first data frame,
  `socket::ClientFrames`) is the pool's to give again: with Codex paused
  in the pool, the account out, signed in again or reset since the
  handshake, or the pool handing over, it isn't passed on and the socket
  closes, so Codex asks again. A turn holds a handover from its first
  frame to its end, however quiet (a socket alone counts only while
  something crosses it, ten seconds); the handshake's hold passes to the
  socket as it switches. A clean end of one side lets the other finish
  (Codex done sending still hears the rest, a frame the server broke
  off included), a Close five seconds for its answer; a reset or a
  failed write ends both. Codex keeps a socket for a turn and continues
  on it (`previous_response_id`), so a socket stays on one account; a
  continuation another account doesn't know is answered "previous
  response not found", which Codex asks again in full. The reader
  passes a ping or a Close at once with the frames before it (a server
  waiting for its pong mid-message waited for ever), reads a message
  that ends one DEFLATE stream and goes on with another (RFC 7692; the
  window kept across it), bounds what it holds and inflates as it goes,
  and stops reading (all still passed on) at anything not a server's
  (a masked frame, reserved bits, text that isn't UTF-8). Reading a
  turn of 303 messages: 50 µs (59 before Codex's fourth review's fixes;
  1.75 billion instructions for 2,000 turns, from 2.34). Checked
  against ChatGPT itself: a prewarm turn (`generate: false`), its six
  messages compressed with the server's context, each read, all 2,020
  bytes passed on as they came.
- **Reset credits** (some subscriptions get a few, to reset their quota
  early): read with each sync (Claude's `cedar_ember` grants in the
  usage report, `?cedar_ember=1&skip_spend=1`, each read whole: its kind
  (`session`, `weekly`, `full`), the limits it `clears`
  (`seven_day_overage_included` is Fable's week), when it starts and
  ends, whether it waits for a limit; ChatGPT's
  `/wham/rate-limit-reset-credits`: `reset_type`, `title`, `expires_at`)
  and shown on the card. A Claude reset fills a limit up again and
  leaves its reset day as it was ("Your weekly limits still reset on
  their usual day and time"); a Codex one starts a new week at the next
  request and loses what was left of the old (OpenAI's help, for bought
  resets). One is spent
  automatically when no account can serve a request (`redeem_for`): one
  that clears every limit that's out for it (`Account::claim_for`; a
  Fable-only reset never for a request the week stops too), the
  narrowest of those, then the soonest to expire, on the account where
  it gives back most, never for under 5%; one refused (nothing spent),
  the next (the same account's others too). Claims are made one at a
  time for each provider, every way in (a request turned away, one by
  hand, one about to expire) through the same gate, and before each the
  pool looks again whether an account can serve (two turned away
  together once claimed two; a refusal as the account wasn't out after
  all had another's claimed). Each account's resets are counted (a
  revision): a request remembers the one it was sent at, so a 429 for a
  request sent before a reset, coming after it, is stale and marks
  nothing (it once had a second credit claimed), and an account reset
  after a request tried it is tried again; a quota read that a reset
  overtook is let go. What a reset gives back follows each provider's
  rule (`Window::reset_worth`): Claude's, the use to come before the
  limit resets by itself that a refill lets through past what's left
  (so it's worth most once the limit is out, and next to nothing just
  before its reset); Codex's, what's used less the part of the week
  gone. A credit due to expire within 48 hours is claimed at its best
  moment of those left (`Account::expiring_claim`, every expiring one
  weighed; one that only works at a limit, only then); by hand (Account
  ▸ Use a Reset Credit…) the one that gives back most now. A claim's
  intent (its credit and request id) is kept on disk before the
  provider is asked, or it isn't asked; one left unclear is made again
  first, the same under the same id (its credit gone from the list, it
  went: nothing more), and no other credit is claimed while one is
  unclear, by any way in, by hand too (it may have gone through); one
  that can't be made again now (its sign-in not renewed) stops claims; an automatic one is checked again
  under the lock, and a copy of the pool that has handed over makes
  none (checked again just before it's sent). The intent and every
  save are written by one writer that takes its snapshot after the
