  store (an older snapshot written later once dropped an intent),
  synced with its folder; while another copy is at work, never without
  the store's lock (a claim waits rather), and never by a copy that
  handed over. After
  a claim only what it reset starts again, and only the waits it lifts
  end; a Claude 429 marks the meter it names used up until its reset.
  Claude's claims need the account's organization (`organizationUuid`,
  read at sign-in). Codex's count is ChatGPT's (`available_count`),
  either way: its list of details shorter at times (the rest ChatGPT's
  own choice), or longer (the soonest to expire of them). The pool's
  polls of Codex's quota are the reads Codex makes on its own (its app
  server's), never its TUI's, which asks for Reserve.
- **Activity** (a heatmap, after Token Pooler's menu, drawn as Pulse's
  LEDs with the kit's `CellGrid`): the requests open now are lit cells
  under the header (`Pool::open`, blue, marked C or X for Claude or
  Codex), and each card has a strip of the account's latest 25
  (`Account::recent`, saved): green completed, yellow rate limited (the
  next account took it), red failed (refused, a server error, a broken
  answer), grey cancelled (the client went away before the end). Each
  *try* is one cell: a request that moved on is yellow on the first
  account and green on the next. A finished answer is told from a
  dropped one by a marker chained on the end of its stream (`respond`).
  Clicking a cell shows its account, model, client (from the user
  agent), time, duration, status and tokens on the line under the grid,
  which is always there, so nothing moves.
- **Agents**: `olo-pool --status [--json]`, or `GET /pool/status`
  (`open`, each account's `recent`, and `served`, each try with its
  `outcome`).

Tests: `cargo test -p olo-token-pool` runs the gateway and the proxy
against a fake provider (`Upstreams::fake`, standing in for every host;
`OLO_POOL_NO_TUNNEL` refuses tunnels, so nothing reaches the network).
`tests/clients.rs` runs the real Claude Code and Codex through the proxy,
signed in with fake subscriptions: `CLAUDE_BIN=$(readlink -f
~/.local/bin/claude) CODEX_BIN=$(readlink -f ~/.local/bin/codex) cargo
test -p olo-token-pool --test clients -- --ignored --nocapture`
(`CODEX_LOG` for Codex's own log). Run it when either client updates:
Codex 0.166 asks `/backend-api/wham/accounts/check` before a turn (the
fake answers as ChatGPT does), and both must come out as their own
programs to `peer`. `codex_daemon_follows_the_pool` starts Codex's
daemon on a proxy that goes nowhere, changes `.env`, and checks the pool
restarts it, sees it busy in the middle of a turn, and that the new one's
turn goes through the pool. For the window, start a session with a fixture `--home`
holding fixture credentials, a fake upstream
(`OLO_POOL_UPSTREAM=http://127.0.0.1:PORT`: its `/oauth` takes
refreshes), `OLO_POOL_PORT` and `OLO_POOL_KEYFILE`, and a fake
`claude` or `codex` on `PATH` for separate sign-ins. Never real accounts.

## Telegram (apps/telegram, crates/telegram)

A Telegram client of Olo's own: MTProto in process through grammers
(`olo-tg`), no Telegram Desktop and no tdlib.

* **olo-tg** (`crates/telegram`): `model` is chats, messages, topics,
  folders and contacts as plain data; `backend` the commands the app
  sends (`Cmd`) and the events it hears (`Event`) over channels, from
  `net` (the real account, on a tokio runtime of its own thread: raw TL
  for the dialogs, history, replies, forum topics, folders, search,
  read state, drafts, pins and archive, notify settings and typing;
  grammers' client for sending, editing, deleting, forwarding,
  reacting, pinning, uploads and downloads; updates converted as they
  come) or `demo` (a pretend account answering as the real one would,
  with no network: people, groups, a channel, a forum, folders and the
  archive, every kind of message; `OLO_TELEGRAM_DEMO=N` adds N more
  chats, `OLO_TELEGRAM_DEMO_EVERY=S` a message every S seconds).
  `account` keeps the API ID and hash and the session's secrets (home
  datacenter, authorization keys) in the login keyring and the rest
  (peers' access hashes, update state, cached chats, messages and media)
  in a folder only the person can read; signing out clears both.
  `OLO_TELEGRAM_SECRETS=DIR` and `OLO_TELEGRAM_CACHE=DIR` keep them in
  folders instead, so tests never touch the keyring. `signin`: the
  phone code, the QR code (`auth.exportLoginToken`) and the two-step
  password.
* **Setting it up** is in Preferences ▸ Integrations ▸ Telegram: the
  API ID and hash the person registers at my.telegram.org (never
  Telegram Desktop's), then signing in by phone or QR, the password if
  asked; Sign Out. The app is told (`--reconnect`) and picks the
  account up.
* **The app** (on olo-kit: see "On olo-kit" below). `store` is what is known,
  kept up to date from the events (the list's order, each thread's
  loaded messages with a version bumped on change, our messages still
  sending, who's typing); `pics` asks for pictures the first time they
  are drawn and decodes them on two workers into the kit's pictures (BGRA).
  `list` is the chat list (the search field, asking Telegram after a
  pause in typing; folders as chips with the rest under More, pinned
  chats, the archive's row and Unknown Senders', unread and mention
  counts, typing in place of the preview; while searching, matching
  chats then Telegram's people, chats and messages): its rows are
  painted in one canvas, only those near the view, and found under the
  pointer by arithmetic (60 pt each, the picture 40 across). The list
  comes as the main list (folder 0) then the archive (folder 1), each
  chat's place as Telegram has it; once it's whole, chats it no longer
  gave go (`Store::whole`: left, deleted, cached from before). A page
  that fails is asked again (`dialogs_retrying`: after the FLOOD_WAIT
  Telegram asks for, shown as Waiting, else 2, 4, 8… s; six tries), one
  load at a time, so a list never stops halfway with the rest as the
  cache had it. The cache (`chats.json`, read first for an instant list)
  follows the list as it changes, not only after a whole load: a second
  after the person's own change (a chat archived, pinned, muted,
  deleted) or a whole list, else within 30 s (messages coming in; about
  1.3 ms for 1,500 chats, on a blocking thread). Archiving or
  unarchiving takes the folder from Telegram's answer
  (`updateFolderPeers`), else asks for the chat's dialog
  (`getPeerDialogs`), and shows where Telegram has it, saying so if
  that isn't where it was asked to go. Each load ("telegram: the chat
  list: N in the main list, M archived, in P pages"), each page asked
  again and each move are logged (`olo-logs --print --program
  olo-telegram`).
  **The person's changes reach Telegram** (`outbox.rs`): archiving or
  unarchiving, pinning, muting, reading and marking unread go into an
  outbox written to disk (`outbox.json` in the cache, whole then moved
  into place) before they're sent, and leave it only when Telegram has
  them; until then the chat shows the change over whatever Telegram or
  the cache still say (`Outbox::apply_to`, in `put_chat` and on every
  page of the list). A later change to the same thing replaces one
  waiting. A task sends them: archive moves together, up to 100 to an
  `EditPeerFolders`, the rest one by one; a refusal (4xx) drops the
  change, says so and reads the chat again; a FLOOD_WAIT, an outage or
  a chat not known yet waits (Telegram's wait, else 5 s doubling to a
  minute) and goes again, at once when the connection is back or
  another change is made; a change for a chat gone from a list read
  whole is dropped. What's left goes when the app starts again: never
  lost to quitting, a crash or a kill. `Event::Sync { pending, total,
  waiting }` drives a line under the chat list ("Sending 3 changes to
  Telegram…", a bar, "2 of 5 sent", Telegram's asked wait, or offline),
  and quitting with changes on their way shows them going and quits once
  they're sent, or after 30 s, or at Quit Now (`QUIT_WAIT`; whatever's
  left is kept). (Before, each change was a request of its own that
  nothing kept: quitting dropped those in flight, and "Unarchive 40
  Chats" sent 40 at once, which Telegram throttles.) The demo account
  shows it with `OLO_TELEGRAM_DEMO_SEND_MS=1500` (each change "sent"
  that long after).
  **Updates, each applied once.** Every update in an account's sequence
  has its place in it (pts; each channel its own), and grammers fills
  gaps and drops repeats within a run but keeps where it got to only
  when asked (`UpdateStream::sync_update_state`, "not automatically
  done"): it's asked after every update handled, and the session saves
  it with the rest every 10 s and on quitting. (It never was, so every
  start replayed everything since signing in, onto the fresh list: old
  messages counted unread again, old moves to the archive undoing
  later ones.) Starting again catches up from there when that's under
  six hours old (`CATCH_UP_SECS`), else starts from now (the list is
  read whole anyway; this needs the account itself among the peers
  kept, `Store::knows_self`, else it still catches up). And what an
  update says can't undo what's newer: an incoming message counts
  unread only if newer than the row's last message and than what's read
  (`counts_unread`), a read only if it reads further (`read_moves_on`),
  and an update that changes a chat's state (archived, read, marked
  unread, muted, pinned) has the chat read again from Telegram a moment
  later, in batches of up to 100 (`confirm`, `getPeerDialogs`), what it
  has now winning.
  **Unknown Senders** (`Chat::unknown`, `model::stranger`): a person who
  isn't a contact (nor verified, nor Telegram's service notifications)
  and whom we've never written to (nothing of ours read there, the
  latest not ours) is in a list of their own, behind its row: no
  notification, no unread count, in no folder, until we write back.
  **Chosen together**: ⌘-click chooses chats one by one (with the one
  open), ⇧-click a run of them, Edit ▸ Select All Chats every one the
  list shows; the Chat menu and a chosen row's menu then act on them
  all (Archive, Unarchive, Mark as Read, Mute, Unmute, Delete…, which
  asks, saying how many; `Cmd::DeleteChat` deletes a person's history
  and leaves a group or channel, as Telegram's apps do).
  **Groups** (`list::Group`: the archive, Unknown Senders, a folder or
  All Chats): a right-click on the archive's row, Unknown Senders', a
  folder's chip or the back row above them (the More chip: each folder
  behind it as a submenu) acts on all its chats, as `list::shown` has
  them for its view: Mark All as Read, Mute All, Unmute All, the
  archive's Unarchive All… (asks, saying how many), Unknown Senders'
  Archive All; Chat ▸ Mark All as Read does it to the group the list
  shows (`mark-all-read`, for agents too), enabled while one of them is
  unread (`list::any_unread`: one pass over the chats, no list made, as
  the menu bar is built at every change). `conv` is the conversation: its header, a forum's
  topics as chips, the messages laid out once per message and width
  (`bubble::Laid`, kept by a digest of what the layout depends on) and
  painted in one canvas inside a `ScrollView`, only those within a
  screen of the view; it stays at the bottom while it was there, keeps
  what's in view where it was when older pages come in above, and
  finds what's under the pointer (`bubble::hit_at`: links, mentions,
  replies, pictures, reactions) from what was last painted, so painting
  needs no pointer. The composer is a multi-line `TextField` (Return
  sends, ⇧Return makes a line) under what's being answered or edited
  and the files going with it; the draft is kept per chat and saved to
  Telegram on leaving it. `bubble` lays out and paints a message:
  replies, forwards, photos and video frames, voice notes' waveforms,
  files, stickers, polls, link previews, reactions, read ticks, and
  the text's entities (code on its ground, spoilers hidden, links),
  colour emoji drawn by the kit's text in line. Both panes scroll, so
  each is a grid of its own for the layout review (`review::own_grid`),
  as are avatars and the time in a balloon's corner. A chat's Info is
  a window over its chat (`WindowOptions::child`; Escape or ⌘W puts it
  away), Forward To a dialog, Contacts a window of its own; deleting
  and signing out ask in an alert (`open_alert`). The chat, topic,
  folder and list width are kept over an upgrade (`View::save_state`).
* **On olo-kit**: `Tg` is the window's view, on its window's looper;
  what the account, the pictures' and stickers' workers, the
  microphone, notifications and another launch say comes through the
  app's proxy and is handed to it whole (`View::Message` is the boxed
  message, `Tg::told`). Info, Forward To and Contacts are windows of
  the main one's on its looper (`open_window_here`), told what they
  show as it changes (`Tg::feed`: the rows, a chat, their pictures)
  and telling it what's picked (`Picked`); a file panel is a window of
  its own that answers by message (`Chosen`). The list, the
  conversation and the composer are drawn by `Tg::body` in the
  window's coordinates, each clipped to its place (`pane`); their
  clicks are the left button's (`LeftClick`: the kit says a click for
  any button, and the right one opens a menu here). A conversation is
  put where it's scrolled to once it's laid out (`reveal_span`: a chat
  just opened is taller than its scroller knew), on a device pixel.
  What it costs (release, 2× headless, the demo account, a chat open):
  idle 0.0% of a core, the caret's 0.9 frames a second at 275 µs; 80
  notches of the wheel 4.2%, 27 frames a second at 978 µs; the pointer
  run down the list 0.6%, 2.2 frames a second at 942 µs; 114 MB.
  Nothing in the layout review at 1×, 1.5× and 2×.
* **What a frame costs**: one `body` says the list, the conversation
  and the composer, and the window draws again what differs. The
  conversation is planned once per
  change to its thread (each entry's top and height), so a frame does
  only what's in view; a newly opened chat is laid out newest first,
  3 ms a frame, the rest guessed until the next; the layouts of the
  last 12 chats left are kept, so going back costs nothing. Measured on
  release builds against the egui app (demo account, 2×): 96 MB
  against 133; 30 pointer moves over the messages 8 frames against
  157; ten chat switches 43 frames and 115–137 ms against 114 and
  175–193 ms; 24 notches of scrolling 204–221 frames, 1.5 ms each
  (egui's 1.2), slowest 3.6 ms; a caret blink 1.2 ms (the window's
  2.6 before the panes).
* **Around it**: new messages notify through Olo's notifications,
  answered from the banner (`Note::reply`, `NoteEvent::Replied`); the
  unread count is Deskbar's badge (`Notifier::badge`); folders, chats
  and messages are commands with keys (`app_keys::TELEGRAM`: ⌘1–8 for
  folders, ⌘9 the archive, View ▸ Unknown Senders, ⌘↑/⌘↓ the previous
  and next chat), and
  every row, bubble and button in view is in the agents' tree (a
  scrolled list's rows painted beyond its edges aren't).
* **Voice messages, recorded** (`apps/telegram/src/voice.rs`): with
  nothing to send, the send button is a microphone. Held down, it
  records: the field gives way to a strip (a red dot, the time, the last
  levels as bars, a level every 100 ms, newest at the right, -50 dB to
  the top) saying what letting go does; let go on the button it's sent,
  away from it (the button pales) thrown away. Let go within `HOLD`
  (300 ms), the press was a click: it goes on recording, the button a
  paper plane (Send Voice Message) and the paperclip a × (Cancel
  Recording), as Escape is; Chat ▸ Record Voice Message does the same
  (and then Send Voice Message, Cancel Recording), for agents. Shorter
  than half a second, it isn't sent (the banner says how; tried with a
  hold timed on app_server's socket: 0.4 s not sent, 1.0 s sent). The default
  microphone (`olo_system::recording::Capture`, mono 48 kHz, opened and
  closed on a thread: each a round trip to the sound server) is coded as
  it comes on the sound client's thread to Ogg Opus in the cache's
  `voice/` (`olo_video::opus`, a page a second; left from before, gone
  after a day), at 24 kb/s; its loudest sample each 100 ms makes the
  waveform (100 bars, 0–31, packed by the backend) and the strip's bars.
  The chat sees "recording a voice message" (every 5 s, `Doing::
  RecordingVoice`; Stopped when it's thrown away); a voice message
  playing stops (the microphone would hear it); switching chats throws
  the recording away; it stops by itself after an hour. Sent, it's
  `Outgoing::voice` (the file, seconds, waveform) and a pending bubble as
  a text is. Measured (release, demo account, `olo-fakesound` with
  `FAKESOUND_MIC` playing olo-voice's test speech, 2×): idle with the
  chat open 0.0% of a core, no wakeups; recording 2.9% (the sound
  thread 2.1%, coding and the fake server's 100 wakeups a second, a real
  one's 40 ms fragments a quarter of that; the window 0.8%: 9.9 frames a
  second of the composer alone, 0.69 ms each). The file, parsed (each
  page's CRC) and decoded again: 11.23 s, 20 kb/s, lined up with the
  speech to the sample at 5.6 dB, what the encoder gives (below).
* **Animated stickers** (`stickers.rs`): a Lottie one's whole file is
  fetched when it's first drawn, read once on a worker, and drawn there
  a frame at a time at the size the bubble shows it (`snap_centred`'s
  device pixels, one to one); each frame is drawn into the conversation
  as it comes, and the next asked for at its time by a timer (nothing
  polled; several playing still draw the conversation once a display
  frame). It plays
  once as it comes into view, again while the pointer is over it, then
  rests on its first frame (drawn at its size, sharper than Telegram's
  thumbnail); out of view it stops and lets its frames go, and frames
  replaced leave the window's atlas when the conversation next paints
  (30 s of one looping: 88.5 → 88.7 MB). The demo account's is in
  Mira's chat. Measured (release, 2×): resting 0.0% of a core; looping
  8.4% (60 frames a second: the conversation drawn 60 times, 0.61 ms
  each, 5.1–5.8%; the worker 2.2% after opaque and empty pixels were
  left out of un-premultiplying, 3.0% before).
  Video stickers (WebM: VP9, 512 pixels, its alpha a second VP9 stream
  in each block's BlockAdditional) are told from Lottie ones by the
  file's first bytes (EBML's magic) and play the same way, decoded on
  the worker at their own size (`olo_images::webm`; the bubble scales
  them, as it does photos and videos, their own shape kept), each in
  view keeping its two decoders there until it leaves. Every sticker's
  picture goes through `bubble::sticker_picture`: a frame drawn for its
  box at the window's scale is drawn exactly its pixels, anything else
  fitted. `OLO_TELEGRAM_DEMO_STICKER=FILE` makes the demo's sticker that
  file (a video sticker to test with: Chromium's `media/test/data/
  bear-vp9a.webm`, 320 × 240, its alpha a flat 68). Measured looping
  that one (release, 2×): 8.1% of a core (the worker 4.9%, both streams
  at 30 frames a second, 1.4 ms a frame; the window 3.1%), 113.2 →
  113.5 MB over 30 s.

**Ogg Opus** (`olo_video::opus::OggOpus`): mono 48 kHz pushed in any
amounts, coded in 20 ms frames by rusty-opus (pure Rust), written a page
(RFC 7845) a second with OpusHead (the pre-skip, `PRE_SKIP`) and
OpusTags first and the last page's position trimming the end to what
was given. Kept to SILK (wideband, VoIP, the voice hint): measured
against the system's libopus 1.6 in a scratch program (decoding
rusty-opus's packets exactly as `opus-decoder` does), SILK matches
libopus's own encoder (5.6 and 8.6 dB on olo-voice's two test voices,
17 on a chirp, at 24, 32 and 64 kb/s), but rusty-opus's CELT and hybrid
modes, which it chose at 64 kb/s or for a tone at 32, came out at −1
to −3 dB where libopus had 6 to 17. Its speech comes 328 samples late,
not libopus's 312, so that's the pre-skip (the test checks the decoded
sound lines up).

## Weather (apps/weather)

Ben, 2026-11-14: a native weather app with every detail, made for
deciding things (a run this afternoon, whether the clouds will be high
enough to skydive or it'll be socked in all day), with an assistant
that's given all the data. On olo-kit; the provider's key in Passwords.

**The window.** Places in a sidebar (each with its sky and temperature
now; Add Place… under them; a place's menu: Show, Remove Place), the
forecast in a well beside them, the assistant at the right (View ▸ Show
Assistant, ⌘J). The forecast: the place, its region, coordinates and
elevation, its own clock ("Sat 14, 20:29 there"); now (the sky's
picture, the temperature, what it is, feels like, the day's high and
low, the sun's times); "Updated … ago · provider" or what's under way
or wrong; six cards (cloud base with ceiling and cover; visibility with
the dew point's spread, "Fog likely" under 2.5 °C; wind with gusts and
where from; precipitation by its kind and this hour's chance; humidity
with dew point and pressure; UV with its level and the day's highest);
the next hour minute by minute (what falls, and "Rain stopping in about
25 minutes"); then three tabs (⌘1–3): Rest of Today (to midnight or
twelve hours, whichever is later), Next 3 Days and Next 7 Days (a row a
day, its sky by day and by night, what it does, low and high on the
week's span, two lines of detail: what falls, how likely and how much,
cloud and its lowest base, visibility when it's poor; wind, UV once
it's moderate, the sun's times, the moon), each over a `Timeline`,
its axis over the panels and kept at the top of the tab once the
chart reaches it (`ScrollView::sticky`; in Next 7 Days only once the
hourly chart comes up, never over the day rows), so what hour is
under the pointer is always in sight
(Temperature with feels like and dew point, freezing marked; Clouds,
each hour shaded from its base up as solid as its cover with the
ceiling darker over it, the clear air under it what's open to fly;
Visibility with the dew point's spread, fog marked; Precipitation
coloured by kind with its chance and thunderstorms'; Wind and gusts,
its arrows; Humidity and pressure; UV coloured by level). Units:
View ▸ Units (metric, imperial, or each measure by itself). The window
opens 1180 × 760 and is never under 1060 × 660 (`view::MIN_WIDTH`,
`MIN_HEIGHT`: each column at its least, the cards three across whole;
the assistant gives up width, 320 to 260, before the forecast does).

**Data.** A `provider::Provider` (`provider::all()`): tomorrow.io
(`tomorrow.rs`: `/v4/weather/forecast` for the minutes, hours and days,
and `/v4/timelines` for the layers that one leaves out, merged by time),
and a made-up one for the demo. `model.rs` has every layer (44: the
temperatures, the clouds' base, ceiling and cover, visibility, every
kind of precipitation and its intensity, amount and chance,
thunderstorms, wind and gusts and direction, pressure, humidity, dew
point, UV, the sun and moon), by the minute (`Step`), hour and day
(`Day`, each layer's min, max, average and sum). The provider's answer
is kept whole (`Forecast::raw`) for the assistant and on disk
(`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/olo/weather/`, by place), so a start shows the last
forecast at once. Fetched on a worker (ureq, rustls, gzip, by network:
`olo_net::PerNetwork`), every 30 minutes (`FRESH`, by a timer set to
when it's due: nothing runs between); a limit hit waits as long as the
provider says (else 15 minutes), unreachable 5. 401, 403 and 429 are
said as what they mean. Every place kept is kept up to date, not only
the one shown (Ben, 2026-11-15: "they should also all refresh without
needing a click on them"; `Weather::refresh`): each read from the cache
as Weather starts, then fetched when its forecast is 30 minutes old, the
one shown first, one fetch at a time (tomorrow.io takes three requests
a second; a fetch is two), a failure waited out by that place alone (a
limit, by them all: it's the key's), and one timer for the next one due:
nothing runs between (0 wakeups a second idle with three places). The
list's skies and temperatures are each place's own. The places are in
the person's order: dragged in the list (the kit's
`Sidebar::on_reorder`), or Move Up and Move Down on a place's menu
(`move_place`; the one shown stays shown, `moved_index`). Places are found by name (Open-Meteo's geocoder:
towns, airfields) and by street address (Photon, komoot's OpenStreetMap
geocoder, made for search as you type; Nominatim's terms forbid that),
both without a key, asked at once on Add Place's worker, the addresses
first when what's typed has a number in it (`places::merge`; Ben,
2026-11-15: "i should be able to put an address into the weather app
and have it autocomplete it and automatically translate to lat/lon for
a hyperlocal forecast"), or are typed as coordinates. A search more
typing overtook isn't sent. A place found by its address is forecast
for that point (tomorrow.io takes four decimals, about 10 m). Each
keeps its own time zone (`chrono-tz`), and every time is shown in the
place's clock: one found without (an address, coordinates) is given
its zone and ground height by Open-Meteo once it's added
(`places::locate`, on a worker; the dialog doesn't wait; again at the
next start if it couldn't be). `OLO_WEATHER_TOMORROW_URL`,
`OLO_WEATHER_GEOCODE_URL`, `OLO_WEATHER_ADDRESS_URL` and
`OLO_WEATHER_ZONE_URL` point them elsewhere (tests).

**The key** (`key.rs`), always in Passwords: typed once in File ▸ Data
Provider… and kept as Weather's own Password item ("Weather: tomorrow.io
API key", `KeepSecret`, read back with `Secrets`), or a secret reference
to one already there (`op://vault/item/[section/]field`, read with
`Reference`, which Passwords answers once the person allows Weather
that secret: "The keychain"). Either waits for Passwords to be
unlocked. The key is held in memory while Weather runs, zeroed when
dropped, and written nowhere else. With no key, the forecast's place
says what's needed and offers Give a Key….

**Deskbar's widgets** (`glance.rs`; Ben, 2026-11-15: "the weather app
should make available a deskbar widget that is customizable and can
show useful stuff like 3/6/12 hour rain/cloud forecast, 7 day high
level forecast"): `olo-weather --glance`, started by Deskbar (see
Deskbar, "An app's widgets"), no window, for the place chosen in
Weather in its units. Now: the sky and temperature, feels like and
the wind, and the next hour short ("Rain stops in 27 min",
`short_sentence`), else the day's high and low. Next Hours (3, 6 or
12; the bars the chance of rain, the cloud cover or nothing): six
times across from now on the place's half hours, hours or two hours
(`next_boundary`, its own clock: a half-hour zone's hours too), each
its sky, temperature and level; over them what the rain does ("Rain
until about 15:00", "Dry for the next 6 hours") or the cover's range.
Next Days (3, 5 or 7): each day's sky and its low to its high. A
timeline each, an entry at each of its times for 24 hours (as far as
the forecast goes), so it moves on with nothing run. Made again as
Weather's settings or cache change (the place, its name, the units, a
fetch by the app), fetched as the app does when the forecast is 30
minutes old (the cache shared: whichever fetched, the other uses it),
5 minutes after an unreachable try and 15 after another failure; with
no place or key, a widget that says so. The demo's forecast with
provider "demo" (tests).

**A place's own name** (Ben, 2026-11-15: "in the weather app i should
be able to set custom names for places i've added"): File ▸ Rename
Place… and a place's right-click Rename… (`dialogs::RenamePlace`: a
name field, the found name its hint, empty to go back to it) keep it
as `Place::label` with the place in `weather.json`. `Place::title` is
what it's called everywhere: the list, the header (with
`found_as`, "Seattle, Washington, United States", beside it), Edit ▸
Copy, and the assistant, told both. Forecasts are kept by the place's
coordinates, so a rename keeps its forecast.

**The assistant** (`assistant.rs`): Preferences ▸ AI ▸ Weather's model
(Astra 6 thinking at Medium by default, through the Token Pool). A
question goes on a worker with the place, its clock now, the person's
units, how to weigh what decides a plan without assuming one (Ben,
2026-11-15: "the prompts shouldn't assume that they should be general
enough to apply to any olo user": being outside, anything in the air,
water and hills, the garden, driving; with none mentioned, an ordinary
day out; rules of thumb only as typical), and the provider's whole
answer as it came (every layer by the minute, hour and day, about
200 KB). The answer is JSON (`schema`): its words, shown as they stream,
and the spans of time it points to (`windows`), marked on the chart in
the tab that shows them all (the narrowest; the tab changes only if the
one showing doesn't) and listed under the answer with their day
("Low overcast · tomorrow 10:00–12:00"), each a link that marks its
answer's spans again. A follow-up carries the conversation; Stop or
Escape lets an answer go (as much as came stays; one stopped before a
word says "Stopped." quietly and isn't carried on); New Conversation
starts again. Ten suggested questions show before the first
(`assistant::suggestions(hour, raining)`; Ben, 2026-11-15: "i want about
10 of them that cover all the common things someone might want to ask
about the weather"): rain (when it stops, while it rains there), what
to wear, how warm (or, late, how cold tonight), wind, storms, the
weekend, the week, the sun (sunscreen, or tomorrow's sunrise), a time
for a run, and the clouds ("How cloudy will it be today?", for anyone:
it was a skydiver's, Ben's words, until he asked for them general);
after five in the evening at the place, the day's become
tomorrow's. Each a link that wraps when the column is too narrow for it
(`LinkButton::wrap_at`, the column's width worked out from the
window's). Tests never call a model
(`OLO_AI_BASE_URL` to a stand-in).

**For agents.** Every command of the menus is on Weather's menus
socket (`{"invoke":…}`), with more: `tab:N`, `place:N` or
`place:NAME` (its own name or the one it was found as),
`move-place:FROM:TO` (by their places in the list, as dragging does),
`rename:NAME` (the chosen place's own name; empty: back to the found
one), `ask:QUESTION`, `units:metric|imperial|c|f|kmh|mph|ms|kt|m|ft|km|mi|mm|in|hpa|inhg`.
The tree has every card (figure and caption), each day's row (its whole
detail), each chart's plots as Figures (each track's first, lowest and
highest values and when), the spans, and the conversation.
`olo-weather --print [PLACE] [--fetch]` prints the forecast as JSON in
the person's units, with the units named, without a window (the cache,
or fetched); Edit ▸ Copy copies it as text. `OLO_WEATHER_DEMO=1` shows a
made-up place and forecast with no key or network (the layout lint's,
`tools/dev/ui-lint`).

**Pictures.** The 18 skies (clear, mostly clear, partly cloudy by day
and night, mostly cloudy, cloudy, fog, drizzle, rain, heavy rain, freezing rain, sleet,
flurries, snow, heavy snow, thunderstorms) are in Olo's Classic look
(`data/icons/weather.txt`, made like the app icons but not in the
manifest: one look for every theme, as a forecast's symbols are a
language of their own); the app's icon is in every theme. tomorrow.io's
codes map to them in `model::icon` (by day and night).

**Cost.** Idle: 0% of a core, no wakeups, no frames (10 s, release).
The pointer over the chart: one frame a position, 0.4–0.9 ms a flush,
only the chart drawn (1 of 102 nodes). Reviewed at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×,
1.75× and 2×, light and dark, every tab scrolled through, the dialogs
too, at its least size and at 1600 × 1000.

## OS Updates (apps/updates, olo_system::dnf, dnf-fake)

Fedora's packages kept up to date, for people who want to see and
choose everything (Ben, 2026-11-14: "a GUI manager for fedora dnf for
upgrading to the latest available fedora packages. design it for power
users where you can drill into all the relevant details and take all
the actions you might want to take either one thing at a time or all
at once. also have it support adding/managing 3rd party repos
everything else that makes sense"). BeOS had no package manager;
Haiku's SoftwareUpdater updates everything or nothing, and HaikuDepot
one thing at a time. OS Updates is Mac OS X's Software Update (a check
box an update, one counted button) with everything dnf knows beside
it, laid out as Activity Monitor is: its sections down the left
(Updates, Repositories, History, Upgrade Fedora), each a
`ColumnListView` with the selected item's details on its right.

**The daemon.** Everything goes through DNF5's own D-Bus daemon
(`dnf5daemon-server`, `org.rpm.dnf.v0` on the system bus), never dnf
run as a program: `olo_system::dnf` (blocking; call it from workers).
A `Session` is a connection of its own (the daemon keeps one session a
client): `updates()` (the upgrades, the installed package each
replaces, the newest of several installed: kernels, and their
advisories by `name.arch`, the most pressing first), `details(nevra)`
(changelog newest first, from Fedora's `other` metadata, asked for at
`Session::open`; dependencies), `repos()`, `history(n)`, `offline()`;
the goal: `upgrade`, `install` (names, NEVRAs or an https .rpm's
address), `remove`, `downgrade`, `reinstall`, `system_upgrade`, then
`resolve` (every item: action, reason, package, sizes; problems), then
`run(offline, comment)`; `hearing(events, f)` hands the session's
signals (each download's progress, a key to trust, RPM's verify and
prepare, each package, scriptlet errors) to `events` while `f` runs,
the call's end said by the thread that hears the signals once it has
passed on every one queued before the reply (`listen`: before, that
thread could still hold the last of them, the transaction's end among
them, when the call returned, and dnf_fake's test lost it one run in
five); `cancel` (only while downloading: the daemon can't stop RPM),
`confirm_key`, `enable`, `cancel_offline`, `offline_then`. The
daemon refuses an attribute it doesn't know (`excluded_pkgs`), so
`REPO_ATTRS` is the list it takes; `mirrors(id)` is asked for alone (a
Fedora repository has a hundred). Read-only against the real daemon,
from the cache (`cargo test -p olo-system --lib dnf::live --
--ignored --nocapture`): 517 updates, 167 advisories, 39 repositories,
7zip resolved in 2 s.

**Never by accident.** Fedora's polkit rule
(`/usr/share/polkit-1/rules.d/org.rpm.dnf.v0.rules`) lets someone in
`wheel`, active at the computer, run a transaction of signed packages
and trust a repository's key **without being asked**. So nothing runs
without the review (below), and `Session::run` refuses unless the
daemon is a test's (`OLO_DNF_BUS`) or this program is in the person's
own session at the computer (`dnf::may_change`, which is
`olo_system::env::at_the_computer`): a test session or an agent's
screen talking to the system's daemon reads, and changes nothing. A
restart is asked of logind only there too.

**Updates.** The search is every Olo list's (`olo_kit::search`):
words find names, summaries, versions, advisory ids and titles and
CVE ids; `kind:` (security, bugfix, enhancement, other), `severity:`,
`repo:` (several), `chosen:yes|no`, each a menu in the filter bar with
its count. The default order is the most pressing first (security by
severity, bug fixes, enhancements, the rest), then by name; a column's
title sorts. Each row's check box is painted in its first column
(`check_box_look`, recorded for agents as a CheckBox named by the
package) and pressed through `on_press`; on a selected row it checks or
unchecks every selected row; a double click does it too. Under the
list, `olo_kit::chosen`: Choose: All · Security Updates · Bug Fixes ·
Enhancements · Other Updates · None, and "Update 12", or "Update 9
Security Updates" (every kind checked to begin with: everything is
what `dnf upgrade` would do); after a change runs, what was chosen goes
back to its kinds. The details: versions (installed, and when; the
update, and when it was built), architecture, repository, download,
disk space, why it's installed, licence, home page; each advisory
(Bodhi's page linked, kind and severity, issued, the CVEs and bugs it
fixes, linked, its text); What Changed: the changelog entries since
the installed version was built (or the last three); what it needs.
A row's menu: Update Only, Reinstall, Choose / Don't Choose (these
rows), Copy Name. Edit ▸ Copy copies the selected updates as "name
old → new".

**The review** (review.rs, its own window and session): a plan (what
to mark) is resolved first and shown. Updates are asked for as dnf
names what's installed (`Update::upgrade_spec`: `name.arch` when the
new build's architecture is the same, else the name alone), and an
update is paired with the installed build of its name in another
architecture when it moves between noarch and one (Ben, 2026-11-15:
"Update 517 packages" said "Nothing to do." and "Packages for argument
'python3-wcwidth.x86_64' available, but installed for a different
architecture": asked by the new build's name.arch, dnf refused it, and
one refused argument empties a whole transaction). Whatever dnf still
refuses (`dnf::refused_arguments`, from its problems) is left out and
it's resolved again without it, a few times at most, saying what was
left out and why ("Left out, as dnf wouldn't take it: …"); refused
all, dnf's problem shows. Then the summary ("This will update 7
packages, install 3 packages and remove 2 packages. It downloads 159.1
MB and takes 63.0 MB more disk space."), every item (action, package,
old → new version, each replaced version paired once with its new one,
the same version first: kernels are installed side by side; from
where, size, why: chosen, needed, recommended, no longer needed), the
problems; then Install Now or Install When Restarting (dnf's offline
transaction: downloaded now, installed as the computer starts). It
runs on a worker: each download, how far in bytes (half the bar, all
of it offline), each package as RPM takes it (the other half), a log
of what went by, Stop while it downloads; a repository's key to trust
shows its user ids, fingerprint, address and age, with Don't Trust and
Trust; at the end what was done ("12 packages changed: 7 updated, 3
installed, 2 removed."), the items still there, and Restart Now when a
kernel, glibc, systemd, dbus, firmware or a kernel module changed (or
the transaction waits for the restart). The main window reads again
when it's done, even if the review was closed (the worker tells it).

**Repositories.** Every repository, on ones first: a check box turns
one on or off (`Repo.enable_with_options`: the daemon writes it, polkit
asks), its name, id, packages, when its metadata was made, its file.
The details: where it's fetched from (base address, metalink, mirror
list), packages and size, made and fetched, how often it's checked,
whether signatures are checked (each package's; its metadata's), its
keys (linked), priority, cost, what happens if it's down, what it
leaves out or keeps to, proxy, its file, and the package it came with
(asked of the daemon by file name). Add Repository… (a dialog): a
.repo file's https address, fetched and read (`parse_repo_file`: every
`[id]` must say where it's from), or a Copr project ("owner/project",
"@group/project": its address for this release and the name dnf's copr
plugin gives its file), shown before it's added, unsigned ones in red;
or RPM Fusion (Free, Nonfree): its release packages installed through
the review, which add its repositories and keys. Remove… takes away a
file in /etc/yum.repos.d (asked first, naming every repository it
holds); one that came with a package is removed with that package, by
the review; Fedora's own (in /usr/share) are turned off, not removed.
The daemon has no call for a .repo file, so `helper.rs` does it as
root: `olo-updates --helper` through pkexec, handed one request on its
input (write NAME TEXT, remove PATH) and answering it, and checking
itself what it's handed: a plain name ending .repo, a .repo file's
text, never over an existing file (written beside it and renamed), a
plain file directly in /etc/yum.repos.d to remove. Only at the
computer; `OLO_UPDATES_HELPER=direct` does it in `OLO_UPDATES_REPOS_DIR`
instead (tests), `=off` never.

**History** lists every transaction (id, when, what it did, who, its
command or comment, the result); the details list each package by what
was done (old → new for an update). Undo… (History ▸ Undo
Transaction…, or a double click) is the opposite as one change to
review: what it installed removed, what it removed installed again at
its version, what it updated downgraded to the version before (if the
repositories still have it), what it downgraded updated back. The
daemon has no undo of its own.

**Upgrade Fedora** says which Fedora this is (`/etc/os-release`), and
whether a newer one is out (fedoraproject.org's releases.json, its
newest version without " Beta"); Prepare the Upgrade to Fedora N… opens
the review of the system upgrade (`releasever` N's session,
`system_upgrade` as distro-sync), which only downloads now and installs
as the computer restarts. What waits for the next start (an upgrade or
updates) shows over Updates and here, with Cancel It and Restart Now.

**For agents.** The menus (`{"invoke":…}`): `check`,
`update-chosen`, `update-selected`, `reinstall-selected`, `choose-all`,
`choose-kind-N`, `choose-none`, `check:NAME` and `uncheck:NAME`,
`section:updates|repos|history|upgrade`, `add-repo`, `repo-on`,
`repo-off`, `remove-repo`, `undo-transaction`, `prepare-upgrade`,
`cancel-waiting`, `restart`. The tree has every row and check box, the
review's items and buttons by their words. `olo-updates --list` prints
the updates as JSON from the cache (name, arch, installed, new,
repository, size, kind, advisories with their references), with no
window.

**Testing.** `dnf-fake [--address A] [--repos DIR]` (`crates/dnf-fake`) plays
the daemon on a private bus: twenty updates of a Fedora 45 computer
with Fedora's kinds of advisory (security with CVEs and severities,
bug fixes, enhancements), changelogs, install-only kernels (the oldest
of three removed), firefox pulling in nss and its langpacks, a Copr
package whose key is asked about, RPM Fusion by its release package's
address, a history to undo (old versions still there), offline
transactions, Fedora 46 (47 isn't out: its metadata is a 404), and a
check that finds one more update; downloads and RPM's steps signalled
as the daemon does, a run cancellable while it downloads. `--repos
DIR` reads the .repo files there as /etc/yum.repos.d. `cargo test -p
olo-system --test dnf_fake` with `OLO_TEST_BUS` set runs the client
against it. In a test session: `dnf-fake --address
unix:path=/var/tmp/olo-dev/NAME/bus --repos DIR`, then `tsession run
NAME OLO_DNF_BUS=unix:path=/var/tmp/olo-dev/NAME/bus
OLO_UPDATES_HELPER=direct OLO_UPDATES_REPOS_DIR=DIR olo-updates` (a
`file://` address is fetched only against a fake). `tools/dev/ui-lint`
runs it against the fake on the session's bus (`@session-bus`).

**Cost.** Idle: 0.0% of a core, no wakeups, no frames (10 s, release,
2×). Moving down the list: two frames a step (the selection, then its
details from a worker), 1.4 ms on average, the slowest 3.7 ms.
Reviewed at 1×, 1.25×, 1.5×, 1.75× and 2×, light and dark.

## Speed Test (apps/speedtest; olo_net::tcp_info)

What the connection carries each way, and everything that can be
measured or read of it as it does (Ben, 2026-11-16: "a new olo native
Network Speed Test app that show not just total up/down but also all the
advaned metrics/data about the connection that we are able to get";
and the same day: "just rename the app to "Speed Test"").
Speed tests elsewhere give two numbers and a ping; this one's point is
the rest: what happens to everything else while the line is busy, and
what TCP did on the way.

**The test** (engine.rs), against Cloudflare's speed test endpoints
(`speed.cloudflare.com`: `GET /__down?bytes=N`, `POST /__up`; the nearest
of its data centres answers, and says which and where it takes this
computer to be), over connections made by hand (http.rs: TCP, TLS with
the system's certificates, the least HTTP/1.1 the requests need), so
each socket is the test's own to ask the kernel about. Never through a
proxy. In order: the name looked up and one connection opened, each
step timed; the round trip with the line idle (20 requests with no
body, each less the time the server says it spent, `Server-Timing`:
Cloudflare's take 20 to 40 ms of their own, and what's left is within a
few milliseconds of TCP's own least round trip, which is shown beside
it); then down and up, four connections each for eight seconds, each
asking for (sending) piece after piece sized to take a few seconds, a
different time each (a piece's end is a round trip with nothing moving:
with four ending together the rate dipped every two seconds), while a
fifth connection goes on measuring the round trip, five times a second.
Ten times a second the bytes moved are counted: down as they're read;
up as the kernel says the server has acknowledged them
(`tcpi_bytes_acked`), since what's written to a socket has only reached
its buffer (counted as written, loopback "uploaded" 242 Gbit/s). The
rate is the mean once going (the first fifth left out), with the best
second.

**What's read of the connection.** This computer's kernel's figures for
each socket (`olo_net::tcp_info`, `TCP_INFO` and `TCP_CC_INFO`, natively,
what `ss -ti` shows): sending, the congestion control and its window,
TCP's round trip, what was sent again and by timeout, how much of the
time the server's window held it, BBR's model of the path where a BBR
sends (the bandwidth it estimates and what it's doing: `bbr3`, "BBRv3
for TCP"); receiving, what arrived out of order. And the server's side
of each connection's TCP, which it says with every answer
(`Server-Timing`'s `cfL4`: its round trip, window and delivery rate,
what it sent again and took for lost): going down the server is the
sender, so those are the download's retransmissions. From both: how
much later a round trip is while the line is busy than idle (what a
queue on the way adds), and round trips a minute under load (as Apple's
networkQuality grades responsiveness). The link is NetworkManager's
(`olo_system::network`: Wi-Fi's name, band, rate and signal, or the
cable's rate; and whether it's metered: then the app asks before moving
gigabytes).

**The window** (view.rs) is the size of what it shows and no other
(`fixed`, `fits_content`), and floats: never a tile or a tab. It was an
ordinary window at first, and tiled or zoomed it was stretched to a size
its four cards didn't fill, its menu bar stopping where they did (Ben,
2026-11-16: "should be floating with max size so it doesn't look
broken"). Its view is as wide as its window all the same, so a width it
is given by anything else has the bar and the cards across all of it.
Start Test and how far it is, then four cards
on the dashboard's gutter (the kit's `dashboard::Card`, as Activity
Monitor's): Download, Upload, Latency, Connection, each a figure, a
graph (but Connection) and its facts. Everything is live as the test
runs (the engine's `Update`s, each a message; a way that's over is shown
whole while the other runs), Stop cuts every connection at once and
keeps what was measured, and the last test is there when the window
opens again (`state_dir()/speedtest.json`; `save_state` across an
upgrade). A card's facts are the same rows whatever is known, each a few
words, so nothing moves or is cut short as they fill in. Copy puts all
of it on the clipboard as text. Agents read every card (a heading with
its figure, each fact a label and value, each graph's latest), and
`start`, `stop` and `copy` are commands. At rest it draws nothing and
wakes for nothing; while testing, 1.1% of a core and 66 wakeups a second
(`tools/dev/cost`, a 680 Mbit/s line).

- `olo-speedtest --print`: a test with no window, its results as JSON
  (every figure, the rate's series, the link), for agents and scripts.
  It moves as much data as the line carries in sixteen seconds.
- `OLO_SPEEDTEST_DEMO=1`: made-up results, nothing connected to (the
  layout lint's, and pictures'). `olo-speedtest --serve PORT
  [BYTES-A-SECOND]` is a speed test server of Olo's own on this
  computer, and `OLO_SPEEDTEST_SERVER=127.0.0.1:PORT` has the test run
  against it: for working on the app without moving gigabytes over the
  person's line.
- Tests: the engine against that server (a whole test's phases, rates
  and figures; stopped part way; what can't be done, said), the
  connections, the words, and the window's lint in every state it shows
  (lint.rs: not tested, each phase part way, finished with every figure
  as long as it gets, failed).

## Kache (apps/kache)

The build cache, watched and run from Olo (Ben, 2026-11-15: "an olo
native kache frontend app that lets me monitor the status of kache, see
stats/metrics/charts etc, configure/tweak settings, manage it like
restart or whatever, and anything else useful to know or do"): our
fork of [kache](https://github.com/kunobi-ninja/kache), `~/src/kache`
branch `olo`. All of it read natively, never kache's CLI.

**What it shows.** Three sections down the left (each row's value: the
service on or off, the day's hit rate):

- *Status*: the service (`kache.service`, the user unit, over systemd's
  D-Bus: `olo_system::systemd::user_unit`), its version, how long it's
  run, its process and memory; Clean Up Now (its band sweeping while
  the daemon cleans up, which takes seconds to minutes: `Button::working`),
  Restart and Stop (or Start). The store (what it holds against its limit, red when over;
  what's on disk once shared files are counted once; what builds'
  target folders still share, which no clean-up can take; the last
  clean-up and what it freed), the last 24 hours (the hit rate of what
  could be cached, hits, misses, what was built incrementally, what
  couldn't be cached, the time hits saved: each hit's original compile
  less what the hit took), Now (the pool's slots held by compiles and by
  tests, of its size, builds waiting, what's compiling) and the day by
  the hour, stacked (hits green, misses orange, built incrementally
  blue, the rest a grey of its own, not the axis's) with its legend, as
  tall as its rows in the width it has (`Element::measured`: two rows
  of two in a third of a screen). **Built incrementally**: what kache
  passes to the compiler on purpose so a crate being worked on builds
  incrementally (its log's `passthrough_reason`: `adaptive seed`,
  `adaptive active`, `automatic worktree seed`; 3,001 of a day's 3,275
  passthroughs here), counted apart from what it couldn't cache
  (`Event::incremental`). Under them, the tests holding slots, each with
  End (`held.rs`: kache's test runner holds a marker a slot under
  `scheduler/tests/`, each locked; the kernel's list of locks names the
  process holding each, so each is its program, its project, its slots
  and since when; End sends it SIGTERM after finding it there again;
  agents' `end-test:PID`).
- *Builds*: the projects built most over the day (builds, hit rate),
  the slowest compiles (misses, by crate), why the misses missed, and
  the latest 300 builds: when, crate, result (a miss with its cause:
  "Miss: its source changed"; a passthrough by why: "Built
  incrementally", "Documentation" for rustdoc, "Not a compile" for a
  compiler asked a question, else "Not cacheable": `Event::said`),
  project, how long, how big; Result takes what a wide list has to
  spare, the figures together at the right. Why (`data::
  causes`): each build records what its cache key was made of (kache's
  `key_fields`: a hash for its compiler, flags, sources, dependencies,
  environment…), so a miss is set against the last build of the same
  crate in the same project with the same flags (a crate built as a
  library and as a test alternates between two keys, each cached): the
  first part that changed, in the order that explains most (a new
  compiler, then the environment, a dependency, its source, other build
  settings); none with its flags but one without, "flags or features";
  none at all, "first build here"; nothing changed, "evicted from the
  store" (it was there; the store is too small); kache's own word where
  it has one ("not supported by kache"). The day's on this laptop
  (2026-11-15): flags or features 10,736 (the per-command features the
  nightly switch ends), a dependency changed 3,669, first build here
  2,749, its source changed 1,028, a new compiler 507, evicted 39.
  Kept small: each key's parts an index and a 64-bit hash.
- *Settings*: the `[cache]` keys worth tuning (`data::SETTINGS`), in two
  groups side by side, the store's (its limit, whether what builds
  share counts toward it, the age limit, idle and orphaned target
  folders) and the pool's (compiles at once, the slots a test takes, how
  long a test waits, letting more in while the machine has room and to
  what), in rows so each pair starts level, each switch in the block of
  the setting it qualifies. Each value a slider over its valid steps
  alone, the one chosen said with its unit (Ben, 2026-11-15: "what is
  store limit supposed to be? mb? percent? make it a slider with only
  valid values possible"; `data::steps`): kache's own first (what kache
  does unset, from its source; the store's as it stands now, "kache's
  own: 102 GB now"), then the store's 10 to 500 GiB, ages of a day to 90
  days, the pool's 1 to twice the processors, a test's wait of 10
  seconds to an hour, room of 50% to 100%; a value the file holds that
  isn't a step (set by hand, "120GiB") one too, in its place, as
  written. Save writes them into `~/.config/kache/config.toml` with
  `toml_edit`, the rest of the file and its comments as they were.
  kache takes them as it starts again: Restart kache is beside Save.

**Where it reads.** The daemon's socket (`~/.cache/kache/daemon.sock`,
a line of JSON each way): `{"stats":{…, "event_hours": 0}}` for the
store and what's in flight (with the day's events the daemon takes
0.17 s an ask; without, 0.035 s), `{"gc_v2":{"mode":"automatic",
"effective_max_age_hours":N}}` to clean up as kache's own CLI asks (N
its settings' `gc_max_age_hours`, 0 none; without it the daemon refuses:
"automatic GC request is missing effective_max_age_hours", 2026-11-15),
its answer said ("309 entries removed, 19.7 GB freed; 4548 kept, still
shared with builds' target folders"). The socket is in kache's runtime
folder: its settings' `runtime_dir`, else the store's folder
(`data::socket_path`). The build log (`events.jsonl`, a line
a compile) read as it grows (`data::Live`: only what was added since
the last look; read again when kache rotates it), and the rotated logs
(`events.jsonl.archive/`, zstd, named by their last and first events'
seconds) that reach into the day, read once and kept. The last clean-up
(`gc_stats.json`; what it held back shown only from a clean-up that
looked at entries: the sweep of locks after a restart looks at none, and
its "0 bytes" isn't what's held). The pool from the kernel's list of locks
(`/proc/locks`): each admitted compile holds a lease file under
`scheduler/permits/` locked, a test its markers under
`scheduler/tests/`; matched by inode (on btrfs the lock's device is the
filesystem's, not the subvolume's `stat` gives), never by taking one.

**When it reads.** On a worker as it opens, after anything done in it,
and when kache's files change (an inotify watch of the build log, the
last clean-up, the daemon's socket, which goes and comes as the daemon
stops and starts, and the settings file): a burst of builds is one look
at most every two seconds. Not the daemon's `daemon.state.json`: that's
a heartbeat, written every five seconds. Nothing runs while nothing
changes; relative times ("46 min ago") follow the clock through
`olo_kit::ago`.

**Deskbar's widget** (`glance.rs`; see Deskbar, "An app's widgets"):
`olo-kache --glance`, started by Deskbar, no window. Build Cache: the
day's hit rate (or "off" with kache stopped), the pool's slots in use,
a note when kache is stopped or the store is over its limit, and the
last 6 or 12 hours across, each its builds and a bar of the share that
were hits; its tip says the store too. Made from `data::read` as
kache's files change, but at most every ten seconds (a burst of builds
writes the log many times a second: nothing is written between), and
as the hour turns. Cost (release, reading this laptop's kache while
agents built, 40 s): 0.1% of a core, 7 wakeups a second (the serve
loop woken by the log and let go, and a look's D-Bus calls every ten
seconds); none with nothing built.

**Doctor** (see Olo Doctor, "The build cache"): kache's daemon not
running, Start It (`olo-kache --start`, `--restart`, `--stop`: the
service with no window, saying how it stands; `--clean-up`, a clean-up,
saying what it did); its store held over its limit by builds' target
folders, Open Kache. `--print` has the day's miss causes and the tests
holding slots too.

**Agents.** Every action is a menu command (`refresh`, `restart`,
`stop`, `start`, `clean-up`, `save-settings`, `revert-settings`,
`open-log`, `show-status`, `show-builds`, `show-settings`); the tree has
each card's facts, the chart's hours as text, the list's rows.
`olo-kache --print` prints it all as JSON (the service, the daemon, the
pool, the last clean-up, the day with its hours, projects and slowest
compiles, the settings), with no window.

**Testing.** `OLO_KACHE_DEMO=1` makes it all up (a day of builds, a
daemon with work in flight, a pool, a clean-up): nothing of the
person's kache is read or touched, and Save, Restart and Clean Up do
nothing. `OLO_KACHE_DIR` and `OLO_KACHE_CONFIG` point it at another
store and settings file. `tools/dev/ui-lint` runs the demo. `cargo test
-p olo-kache`: the daemon's answer, a day of builds by the hour,
projects and slowest, the live log read as it grows (a half-written
line left for next time, a rotation read from the start), the pool's
leases held (taken with `flock` as kache does, and let go), settings
written keeping the file and refused when wrong, switches as kache has
them unset; the widget's words, its hours and its note (stopped, over
the limit).

**Cost.** Idle: 0.0% of a core, no wakeups, no frames (30 s, release,
2×, reading this laptop's kache; a build event in that time: one look,
two frames, 0.7 ms each). Opening: the day read in 0.20 s on a worker
(30,000 events; 0.45 s before the events were read typed and the
daemon asked without its hours). Reviewed at 1×, 1.5× and 2×, light and
dark, each section.

## Rex (apps/rex, crates/rex, crates/rex-vt)

Native Olo desktop client (`olo-rex`, `app_id: "olo.rex"`) for local and
remote Rex workspaces (Rex API rev 19), alongside Terminal.

- **`crates/rex-vt` (`olo-rex-vt`)** wraps the vendored MIT static
  `libghostty-vt.a` (`vendor/ghostty-vt`, rebuilt with
  `tools/build-ghostty-vt.sh`): lossless `GHOSTSNP` snapshot decoding,
  incremental `RenderState` dirty-row extraction, Kitty graphics,
  selection, search, OSC 133/7501, and Ghostty/`.itermcolors` theme
  importers.
- **`crates/rex` (`olo-rex-client` + `olo-rex-glance`)** speaks Rex API
  rev 19 (`rex.control.v1`, `rex.data.terminal.v1`, `rex.data.bytes.v1`,
  `rex.data.tcp.v1`) over local Unix sockets, HTTP/HTTPS/Tailscale, and
  native in-process Rust SSH (`russh` + `ssh2-config` + Olo Passwords
  `SSH_AUTH_SOCK` + native askpass sheets + `direct-streamlocal@openssh.com`
  / `rex __internal dial-stdio` + `-L` port forwarding). `olo-rex-glance`
  is a separate kit-free Deskbar Glance provider binary linking only
  `libc`/`libm`/`libgcc_s`.
- **`apps/rex` (`olo-rex`)** isolates terminal screens in `PanesView`
  so streaming output redraws only the terminal canvas at vsync, while
  serializing keystrokes per host through a strict FIFO writer task.
  Includes adaptive `SidePane` (Sessions & live Activity feed), tabs
  along the top or down the side, recursive splits (auto-stacking
  horizontally on vertical thirds `< 540 pt`), floating/minimized
  layers, Copy Mode, `rex.ui` custom prompts, Path Browser, Quick Look
  with ETag caching, drag-and-drop
  uploads, Remote Access (this computer's server over Tailscale, a
  device paired by a code), the per-host Olo Desktop Bridge (`xdg-open`,
  `op`, `olo-screen` with automatic remote `localhost` `-L` forwarding;
  what a host may use is Preferences ▸ Rex), Tracker `"Open in Rex"`,
  global Command Palette session search, and in-place upgrade state
  restoration.

**Whose settings are whose** (2026-11-21; Ben: "making the ux more olo
native"). Rex has no settings window. It came with one of eight
sections over some sixty settings, two thirds of which nothing read or
which decided chrome that is the desktop's (densities, paddings, fades,
a highlight colour, cursor trails and blinking, a second set of
palettes and an importer of theme files), and with "Auto Approve" and
"Developer Mode", which set a flag nothing acted on. Now:
- *Which hosts there are, what each may do on this computer, which
  changes of an agent become notifications*: the desktop's
  (`settings.rex`, Preferences ▸ Rex), followed live
  (apps/rex/src/shared.rs: `apply` makes the app's copy say what the
  desktop's says and tells what changed; the hub shows a host added
  there, lets go of one removed, renames, reconnects one whose address
  changed). A host added or removed in Rex itself is written there
  too: one list, two places to edit it. Permissions and notices are
  never kept in Rex's own file: with the desktop's settings unread, a
  remote host may do nothing here.
- *What Rex's file held of these before* (rex.json as the merged app
  wrote it) is carried into the desktop's settings once
  (`shared::adopt`): hosts by their ids, each with the permissions it
  had and none it didn't, never over what the desktop already says. It
  is kept aside in the file (`before_preferences`) until that has
  happened, whatever is saved meanwhile; and while the write is on its
  way the desktop's settings aren't followed (`shared::settled`: they
  would say the carried hosts are gone, and Rex would drop connections
  it had just made), five seconds at most.
- *A window's quick choices* are Rex's own file (settings.rs) and its
  menus, as Terminal's: Settings ▸ Text Size, Colors (Match Appearance,
  Always Light, Always Dark; for each mode the look's own colours,
  followed as Preferences ▸ Themes changes, or any of Olo's themes',
  which stays: the same lists as Terminal's menu), Tabs (Along the Top,
  Down the Side); View ▸ Show Sidebar, Show Pane Headers, Sessions or
  Activity, Include Idle Panes in Activity.
- *The cursor is steady*, as Terminal's: where a program asked for a
  blinking one the window drew twice a second for as long as nothing
  happened (measured: 2.0 frames a second at rest, now 0).

**Keys** are Olo's, as Terminal's (2026-11-21). Rex's commands have
their keys from the keyboard profile (`olo_protocol::app_keys`, the
`rex.*` entries: Terminal's keys for what Terminal has too, ⌘W for the
pane the keyboard is in and ⌥⌘W for its tab, ⌘D to split and ⌥⌘D to
split down, ⌘1 to ⌘9 for the tabs, ⌘J for the next agent that waits;
the rest of its menus'
commands are listed with no key, for the person to give one), shown
and changed in Preferences ▸ Keyboard, pressed through the menu bar:
every key has a menu item. Rex is one of Olo's own terminals (above),
so no two of its keys differ by Shift alone. The window's key handler
(`handle_terminal_key`) gives a key, in this order, to: the person's
own Rex configuration, if one of its sequences or modes is under way
and it has the key (a sequence begun more than two seconds ago is let
go of first); the menu bar, if it is the command key's (or one of the
profile's keys for Rex without Control: Shift+F3) and an item that is
on has it; the configuration's bindings (`KeymapEngine`: what the
server answers `client.keymap` with when Rex sends the commands it has
and no keys of its own, so the configuration's alone, with whatever
the old recorder left in rex.json; a `cmd` chord there is the command
key's, Control stays `ctrl` with Windows' keys too); the scrollback,
for Shift with Page Up, Page Down, Home and End; the tabs, for Ctrl+Tab
and Ctrl+Page Up/Down where there is more than one; and the program in
the pane, the command key's as Control's without the Shift it brings.
A key kept down after its command chord was let go is swallowed (its
repeats read as Control with the key: Ctrl+D, after ⌘D). The app came
with 69 keys of its own written for a modifier that doesn't reach an
app in Olo: none could be pressed, each went to the pane as a Control
key, and ⌘D ended the shell where it should have split (checked
headless by pressing them through app_server's real key path,
`tsession key`: AGENT-NOTES, "Keys"). The commands its catalog offered
that nothing carried out are gone from it; what a host's program may
ask of this computer (`bridge_catalog`) is declared to the server and
is in no palette.

**One palette.** Rex's commands and its sessions are found where
every app's are, in Olo's command palette: the commands through its
menu bar (the kit tells the palette a window's menus), the sessions of
every host and the panes of those it shows through the index Rex
keeps in its state folder (`hub::write_palette_index`: written when it
differs from what was last written, never otherwise; apps/palette's
Rex source reads it; a session chosen is shown with `olo-rex
--session`, a pane gone to with `--focus-block`). It came with a
Command Palette and a Go to Anything of its own, drawn over the
workspace, that listed the same two things.

**A tab's name** is one it was given (`hub::tab_label`). The server
names a tab it wasn't told a name for "Window" and the end of its id
("Window 65bb795d"), and the strip, the Tabs menu, Activity and the
palette showed that; they show what the tab's program calls itself, or
its folder's name, or which tab it is, and tabs that would say the
same are told apart (`hub::tab_names`: by their folders where those
differ, "shell · rex", else by their place, "shell 2"). **A pane's
context menu** is the menu bar's commands for that pane, by the names
and with the keys and checks they have there (`menu::resolve` gives
them the profile's keys): the clipboard; its text; the pane; closing
it, alone and last. Keep It Going is there for a pane an agent runs
in.

**Questions an SSH connection asks** (panels.rs `OloAskpass`, the
client's `SshAskpass`) are asked one at a time, each answered for
itself: two hosts connecting at once both ask about their keys, and
with one slot and no turn the answer given to the question shown went
to whichever of the two woke first: "Trust" said of one host's key
could trust the other's, never shown. **A key agent that is slow to
sign** (Passwords locked, or asking the person) is said: after three
seconds the client tells the app (`SshAskpass::waiting_for_agent`; the
connection's deadline waits meanwhile, as it does while a question is
read), and the workspace and the Hosts window say the host waits for
the key agent, where they said "Connecting…" for as long as it took.

**Typing to a far host.** What is typed goes to a host one request at
a time, each answered before the next, so that its order is the order
typed whatever the server does with two at once; and what was typed
while a request was on its way goes together in the next
(`hub::typed_together`: text for the same terminal, as far as the next
key event or change of focus). A request a key was a round trip a key:
to a host 224 ms away, 65 characters typed in 2.8 s took 18.7 s to
arrive; 73 typed in 3.3 s are run there within a second of the last
(measured against a real host over SSH, by the host's own clock).

**The menu bar** is Terminal's model: Rex (the kit's `app_items` with
its two Preferences panels; what is made new; Hosts…, Remote Access…,
Diagnostics…; Close Window, Quit), Edit, View (its last
group the pane's folder: Quick Look, Browse Folders…, Go to Folder…,
and Open in Tracker for a pane of this computer), Tabs (New Tab, Close
Tab, next, previous, and the session's tabs by name), Pane, Agents,
Settings. Every toggle
shows its check (the sidebar, pane headers, the sidebar's list, Zoom
Pane, Type in All Panes, Copy Mode, Keep It Going) and every item is
enabled only when it can act (Copy with a selection:
`GhosttyTerminal::has_selection`, which asks without reading the text
out; the pane items with a pane; Focus with more than one). An item
that went round states one couldn't see is the states by name (the
tabs' place), and one that said "Export" and copied says Copy. Making
the menus is cheap enough to do at every key that may be an item's
(the kit's `MenuBar::of`): the Colors lists were 228 µs of it, every
theme's whole palette copied to read one field, in Terminal too, and
are 5 µs (`olo_theme::looks::terminals` reads the kept palettes).

**Remote Access** (panels.rs `render_access_panel`, `Step`) is one
window for reaching this computer's sessions from elsewhere: the
checkbox that turns the server's Tailscale on, how it stands under it
(or what just went wrong), and one group that keeps its place and size
at every step: nothing to scan yet (a code's three corner marks,
faintly, where it will be); the sign-in (its page opened here, or its
code scanned); the address to pair with, as a code and to copy. The
line under the checkbox answers what the checkbox asks, with a light
of the sidebar's colours before it (grey: only this computer; amber:
waiting for the sign-in; green: the other devices can). It was
a section of the Settings window and a window with a code alone that
said to go and find the other. The code's cells are whole device
pixels at every scale (`qr_code`), so at 1× it may fill less of its
well.

**What the person is told, and where** (2026-11-21, the day the app
was merged; Ben: "it has its own app notifications that show seperate
from olo ones"). Rex draws no notices of its own. Something the person
just did in a window and that failed is said in that window, where they
did it, until they try again (under the control in a panel; the
workspace's status bar); a passing word ("Server configuration
reloaded.") is the status bar's for four seconds (`due::Notice`); and
what happens while they aren't looking at it (an agent in a pane
waiting, done or failed; a host dropped; a remote program's own notice
through the bridge) is an Olo notification through the app's one
`Notifier` (attention.rs): not while that pane is in front, one for a
pane at a time (a newer one replaces it), taken back when the pane is
looked at, its action going to that very pane. The status bar is always
there (the window's host and session at rest): coming and going with
each word it resized the terminals above it twice.

**A pane is never a picture of something else.** The tab strip, the
panes and the keyboard all go by the one selection the sidebar shows
(they were three: a closed terminal left another session's screen
under the wrong name, taking no keys; Ben: "i closed the terminal but
now it is like stuck there"). A session with no terminals, a host with
no sessions, a host or the server gone: each says so where the
terminal would be, by name, with the one thing to do (New Terminal,
New Session, Reconnect).

**What the server really says.** The client's types were written from
documents; `crates/rex/tests/live.rs` and `tests/remote.rs` now hold
every call and event against a scratch server (`tools/dev/rex-check`):
75 methods, the Tailscale ones among them (their answers are wrapped,
`{"tailscale": …}`, which was "json error: missing field `state`" at the
first press of the button), split and resize and ownership as rev 19
has them, byte streams that end early, a reply that can't be read
saying which method and which field. Remote hosts over a scratch sshd
in a private network namespace: every way of signing in, a changed host
key refused (it was accepted on a "yes"), ProxyCommand, a link cut,
frozen or slow, the server killed and started again, forwards and
100 MiB transfers; 28 cases, ten runs each. A link that dies without a
word is found by `ControlClient::probe` when the person types (five
seconds), not by the keepalive minutes on; keys typed into a pane that
is disconnected go nowhere, and nothing unsent is replayed. Not there:
ProxyJump (refused with what to use instead).

**The terminal engine's wrapper** (`crates/rex-vt`) was audited against
the library's headers: its callbacks were registered by the address of
a local variable; a search outlived its terminal; snapshots, pictures,
grids and scrollback had no bounds (`limits.rs` has them now: 256 MiB of
the engine's heap a pane, 128 MiB of snapshot, 64 MiB a picture, 4096
cells an axis).

**Testing.** `OLO_REX_DEMO=1` starts an isolated demo workspace (no real
Rex socket touched; used by `tools/dev/ui-lint --tiles`; with
`OLO_REX_DEMO_TAILSCALE=sign-in` or `on`, its server's Tailscale is to
be signed in to or on, for the Remote Access window's pictures; its
prompts and paths name nobody). Point at a
scratch Rex server (`rex server run --listen unix:///var/tmp/.../rex.sock`)
via `REX_SERVER_SOCKET`. `cargo test -p olo-rex-vt -p olo-rex-client -p olo-rex`
runs VT round-trips, inline APC nonce verification, and live scratch
`rex server run` bootstrap + `GHOSTSNP` -> `RenderState` E2E tests.
`tools/dev/rex-check` runs the client contracts one case per line. The
remote tests give the client, sshd and Rex a private loopback network,
home, credentials and process namespace. Rev-19’s tunnel.dial provider carries
its connections over `rex.data.bytes.v1`. Use `--remote-only --repeat 10`
for repeated SSH, HTTP/TLS, transfer, forwarding and connection-loss checks.
`OLO_REX_TEST_DIR` selects the on-disk scratch parent (default `/var/tmp`).

**Cost.** Measured on release builds in a headless 120 Hz GPU session at
2× against a live Rex rev-19 server:
- Idle (5 s): **0.0% of a core, 0 wakeups/s, 0 frames/s** (`perf stat --no-scale` over 3 s idle: 0 context switches, 0.07 ms task-clock, 3,652 instructions).
  The same with a program in the pane that asks for a blinking cursor
  (`printf '\033[1 q'`): it was 2.0 frames a second, 0.2% of a core,
  for as long as nothing happened; the cursor is steady now.
- Live typing keystroke-to-draw latency (`app_server timings`): **~1.54 ms median** `to_draw_us` (1.28–1.80 ms) end-to-end through the Rex server vs the 8.33 ms 120 Hz budget.
- Sustained colored streaming (100 lines/s over 2 s): **7.5% of a core**, **mean 873 µs** per frame (ui 613 µs, tessellate 0 µs, submit 260 µs; slowest 1.94 ms).
- Resident memory: **62.2 MiB RSS** (`olo-rex`). Reviewed at 1×, 1.5×,
  and 2×, Light and Dark, across all 6 tiling layouts (`ui-lint --tiles`:
  0 errors; `tsession review`: 0 findings across Workspace, Settings,
  Hosts, and Diagnostics).
